body:
Congregations have felt needs — the things they know they want help with. Parenting, marriage, finances, purpose, anxiety. These are real needs, and preaching that consistently ignores them is preaching that has become disconnected from the actual lives of the people in the room. A pastor who is not attentive to the burdens the congregation carries is not serving the congregation, however theologically sophisticated the sermons may be.

But preaching that consistently begins and ends with felt needs produces a congregation that knows how to apply biblical principles to the problems on the surface of their lives while having little formation at depth. The deeper need — for genuine encounter with a holy God, for the transformation of desire itself, for the capacity to suffer faithfully and love without return — is rarely felt acutely until it is urgently needed. And by then, a diet of felt-need preaching has not prepared the congregation for it.

This is the first of five sermon habits that slowly shrink a congregation's faith. It is the most subtle, because it starts with something true — people have real needs — and then goes wrong not by lying but by stopping too soon.

---

## The Felt Need Is Not the Deepest Need

The felt need is not the deepest need. That distinction is the crux.

C.S. Lewis described the human condition as one in which we are too easily pleased — in which we settle for the proximate desire when the deeper longing is what actually drives us. [cite — confirm Lewis, Weight of Glory or Mere Christianity, relevant passage.] The person who comes to church anxious about their marriage has a real problem. But the problem beneath the problem — the formation of character that makes sustained love possible, the theological reordering of expectations, the confrontation with the idol of the marriage as the source of one's identity — is the deeper problem, and it is the one the gospel is actually equipped to address.

The sermon that addresses the anxiety about the marriage without engaging the deeper architecture is helpful as far as it goes. It offers real tools and real encouragement. What it does not do is address the thing underneath the anxiety — the question of what the person is fundamentally oriented toward, what they are trusting in, what would happen to their sense of self if the marriage did not recover. Those are the questions the gospel addresses. Felt-need preaching often cannot reach them because it has defined the problem at the level of the symptom.

---

## When the Surface Holds and the Marriage Fails

The pastoral scene that makes this concrete.

A couple attends a church with a strong reputation for practical, applicable preaching. They have been there for four years. They have heard dozens of sermons on marriage — communication principles, conflict resolution strategies, the importance of date nights, the theology of covenant commitment. The content has been sound and practically useful.

The marriage is quietly failing anyway. Not from lack of trying the principles. From something deeper: a fundamental misalignment of desire, an idolatry of marriage as the source of identity and validation that the marriage itself cannot sustain, a patterns of relating that has theological roots neither of them has been given the vocabulary to address.

> They were not formed in the deeper structure.

The sermons gave them tools for the surface. They were not formed in the deeper structure. They were not confronted with the specific question the gospel raises — not *what techniques will improve your marriage* but *who is the Lord of this marriage, and what does it mean for two people to be known fully and still loved, not by each other but by God, which is the only foundation on which a marriage can bear the weight you are asking it to bear*.

They leave the church when the marriage ends. Not angry at the church — grateful, in fact, for the years of community. But they leave without the resources for what comes next, because those resources were not built in a felt-need preaching diet.

---

## How Jesus and Paul Move Through the Presenting Problem

The New Testament model does not start with felt needs and stay there.

Jesus begins with the felt need constantly — hunger, blindness, grief, desperation. He heals the man at the pool of Bethesda who had been paralyzed for thirty-eight years (John 5:1-9). He feeds the five thousand who are hungry (John 6:1-14). He is not indifferent to the presenting problem. The presenting problem is where the encounter begins.

But he does not leave the person at the presenting problem. After healing the man at Bethesda, he finds him again and says: "See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you" (John 5:14). After feeding the five thousand, he gives the bread-of-life discourse — one of the most demanding theological addresses in the Gospels, which many of the crowd cannot receive and which thins the following substantially (John 6:60-66). The felt need was the entrance. The deeper demand was the destination. Jesus used one to get to the other, and he was not deterred when many preferred the entrance to the destination.

Paul follows the same pattern. His letter to the Philippians addresses real anxiety — the congregation is worried about him, worried about circumstances, worried about internal conflict. His response acknowledges the anxiety and then moves immediately to the theological frame that addresses it: "Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God" (Philippians 4:6). The felt need is named. But the address moves quickly to the deeper structure — the peace that passes understanding, which is not a technique but a theological reality grounded in the character of God and accessible only through relationship with him.

Felt-need preaching that does not make that move — that names the anxiety and offers the steps without pointing through the steps to the God whose character is the ground of peace — has done a smaller work than the text was doing.

---

## The Slow Accumulation of Formation Damage

The formation damage accumulates slowly and invisibly.

A congregation formed primarily on felt-need preaching develops certain characteristics over time. They are consumers of spiritual content — good at receiving, evaluating, and applying what is offered, less formed in the interior capacities that generate faith from the inside rather than receiving it from the outside. They know what Christianity teaches but are not deeply shaped in who Christians are. They can describe the principles of a godly marriage or a generous financial life, but the principles do not go down into the bones in ways that hold under pressure.

When the crisis comes — the diagnosis, the death, the collapse of the thing they had built, the suffering that does not yield to any principle — they find their faith thinner than they expected. Not absent. Real. But not built for this. The sermons formed them for manageable challenges. The crisis is not manageable.

This is not the fault of the person in the pew. The formation they received was the formation the preaching provided. The preaching formed them for the surface of life. Life, at its most determinative, happens at depth — and depth formation requires preaching that goes there regularly, not only in the crisis sermon but in the ordinary course of what a congregation hears.

---

## The Front Door That Becomes the Whole House

The counter-position.

Some will argue that reaching unchurched people requires meeting them where they are — that the church which does not speak to felt needs will not get the opportunity to speak to the deeper needs, because the unchurched person will not return after a sermon that does not seem to address their actual life. The felt-need sermon is the front door; the deeper formation happens as the person becomes more established in the community.

There is something to this. A sermon that ignores all contemporary life in favor of pure theological abstraction is not prophetic — it is disconnected, and disconnection is its own kind of failure. The application to life is not optional; it is where theology becomes practice, which is where it becomes formative.

But the argument breaks down when it becomes the permanent structure rather than the entrance strategy. A person who has attended for two years and is still receiving primarily felt-need preaching is not in the same position as a first-time visitor. They have been formed — by two years of consistently surface-level preaching — in a particular understanding of what Christianity is for. Reversing that formation requires deliberate pastoral investment in deeper material, and the congregation that has been trained on the accessible will resist the difficulty. Which is itself data about what the accessible preaching has produced.

---

## Preaching That Begins at the Surface and Refuses to Stay

The sermon that takes felt needs seriously and then moves through them — that uses the real problem as the entrance to the deeper question the real problem is pointing toward — is harder to preach than either the pure felt-need sermon or the pure theological lecture. It requires the preacher to know the congregation well enough to name the actual presenting concern, to have the theological depth to trace it to its roots, and to make the connection between the two in a way that does not feel like bait-and-switch.

That is pastoral preaching at its most demanding. It is also the preaching that forms people capable of holding their faith in actual life — not because it avoided difficulty but because it trained them to bring the full resources of the gospel to bear on the full texture of their experience.

> The felt need is real. It is the right place to begin. It is never the right place to end.

The felt need is real. It is the right place to begin. It is never the right place to end.

The text almost always has something to say that is larger than the presenting problem, and the congregation is waiting — whether they know it or not — to be led to it. The preacher who stays at the surface has not been kind to them. They have been convenient.

> Convenience is not the pastoral calling. Formation is.

Convenience is not the pastoral calling. Formation is. And formation begins where the felt need is, and goes somewhere the felt need alone could never reach.

Nobody burns out on a Tuesday afternoon and decides they are done. That is not how it works. Burnout in ministry is not a moment — it is a process. A slow, invisible, cumulative erosion that happens beneath the surface of ordinary productivity, often while the pastor is still preaching well, still hitting their meetings, still doing the things that look like a healthy ministry from the outside.

By the time most pastors recognize they are burned out, the process has been underway for months — sometimes years. The slow burn is the most dangerous kind precisely because it allows you to keep functioning past the point of genuine health, building a debt of depletion that eventually comes due all at once.

## The Elijah Problem

The biblical account of Elijah in 1 Kings 19 is the original pastoral burnout text, and it is more honest about the condition than most modern writing on the subject. Elijah has just come off the Mount Carmel confrontation — arguably the most dramatic ministerial success in the Old Testament. Fire from heaven. Four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal defeated in public. The nation's hearts returned to the Lord. By any measurable outcome, it was a triumph.

One threatening letter from Jezebel sent him into the wilderness asking to die.

"It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life" (1 Kings 19:4). Not "I am discouraged." Not "I need a break." He is asking to be done.

The text does not rebuke him. God does not address his theology or his resilience or his perspective. God addresses his body. An angel touches him. "Arise and eat." He eats and drinks. He sleeps again. The angel comes back. "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you." The God of the universe responds to a burned-out prophet with food, water, and permission to sleep.

That sequence is significant. The divine response to Elijah's exhaustion-collapse is entirely physical before it is spiritual. No recalibration of vision. No correction of his self-pity. First: care for the body that has been spent in the work.

Then, forty days later, a question: "What are you doing here, Elijah?" Not accusatory. Genuinely curious about the man's interior state. An invitation to articulate what is actually happening. An invitation to be heard before being redirected.

> The pastor who is experiencing the slow burn most needs what Elijah received: someone who asks the real question and waits for the real answer.

The pastor who is experiencing the slow burn most needs what Elijah received: someone who asks the real question and waits for the real answer.

## What the Slow Burn Actually Looks Like

The early signs are easy to dismiss. You are tired, but you have always been tired — ministry is demanding, and fatigue is part of the calling. You notice that the things that used to energize you are starting to feel like obligations. Sermon prep, which once felt like the best part of your week, is now something you dread starting. Pastoral conversations, which once felt like sacred ground, are starting to feel like transactions you need to get through.

You are more irritable than usual, but you attribute it to a hard season. You find yourself withdrawing from the people who know you best — not dramatically, just a little more inaccessible, a little more guarded. Your prayer life has become mechanical. You are still praying, technically, but the aliveness that used to accompany it has quietly departed.

None of these signs, on their own, would alarm anyone. Taken together, they tell a story of a person whose inner resource is running dangerously low. The problem is that most pastors are so accustomed to running on empty that they have lost the ability to tell the difference between tired and depleted.

## Why Ministry Accelerates the Process

Every profession carries its occupational hazards. Ministry's particular hazard is the near-total absence of internal feedback systems. In most vocations, performance gaps create visible consequences fairly quickly. In ministry, you can be spiritually depleted for an extended period while continuing to produce outcomes that look healthy to everyone around you. The sermons are still coming. The services are still running. The pastoral visits are still happening. The slow burn is masked by the output it is slowly destroying the capacity to sustain.

There is also the theology problem. Many pastors have internalized a framework in which self-sacrifice is the highest virtue, and anything that prioritizes their own wellbeing over the needs of the congregation feels like a betrayal of the calling. This framework is not entirely wrong — ministry does require genuine self-giving. But self-giving is not the same as self-destruction, and a theology that cannot tell the difference between the two will eventually produce pastors who are too depleted to give anything at all.

The distinction that matters here is Pauline: "I can do all things through him who strengthens me" (Philippians 4:13). The strength is *his*, received. The model throughout the New Testament is not exhaustion as virtue — it is the abiding that produces fruit (John 15:4-5). A branch that is not abiding does not produce fruit by trying harder. It produces nothing, because the connection to the source has been severed. The pastor who is running on depletion is not faithfully abiding. They are severed and performing.

## The Warning Signs Worth Taking Seriously

Carey Nieuwhof, who has written candidly about his own burnout experience, describes a progression from cynicism to resentment to emotional numbness that characterizes the slide toward depletion [cite — confirm]. The cynicism comes first — a quiet erosion of the hope that once animated your ministry. You start to notice your inner monologue becoming darker, more skeptical, more prone to assume bad faith in situations that would once have been easier to extend grace.

Then comes resentment — specific, directed, and harder to shake than you expect. The family who takes and takes and never gives thanks. The board member whose criticism is always delivered with a smile. The budget conversation that happens every year and always goes the same way. These resentments are not new information. They are old information that used to be manageable and no longer is.

The numbness is the last stage and in some ways the most alarming, because it feels like relief. The pain of ministry stops hurting, not because things have gotten better, but because something has gone quiet inside that should be alive. If you have arrived at a place where nothing in ministry moves you anymore — not the wins, not the losses, not the people — that is not peace. That is depletion wearing peace's clothing.

## The Counter-Position and Its Real Danger

Some traditions in pastoral formation argue that the language of burnout is therapeutic culturalization of what is actually a spiritual problem — that the pastor who is depleted needs not self-care but the deeper surrender of self, the kind of crucifixion that Galatians 2:20 describes. The argument is that the solution to depletion is not rest but death — a more complete dying to self that enables the life of Christ to flow through without resistance.

This position can be preached in a way that sounds very spiritual and produces very damaged people. There is a kind of spiritualized self-neglect that the language of the cross can cover. It is not faithfulness. It is a failure to take seriously that the body is a temple (1 Corinthians 6:19), that pastoral gifts are stewarded resources (1 Peter 4:10), and that a pastor who destroys their health in the name of serving the church has not served the church — they have deprived it of decades of fruitful ministry that discipline and rest would have preserved.

The "die to self" framework, applied correctly, is about pride and ego and the will to control outcomes. It is not about the physical and emotional capacity of a human being who has been entrusted with a difficult calling. Distinguishing between the two is one of the most important things a pastoral formation program can teach — and most of them do not.

## Catching It Early

The single most effective intervention for the slow burn is the kind of ongoing, honest relationship that most pastors do not have. Not a formal accountability structure where you report metrics, but a genuine friendship with someone who has permission to ask the hard questions and who knows you well enough to notice when your answers are off.

Regular, honest check-ins with a pastoral peer — not just professional colleagues, but someone who is invested in your actual condition — can catch the slow burn long before it becomes a crisis. Communities like the Pastors Connection Network exist precisely to provide this kind of relational infrastructure. Not a program that monitors you, but a people who know you.

The slow burn does not have to become a full collapse. But stopping it requires honesty before you feel ready to be honest — which means building the relationships now, in the ordinary seasons, that will give you somewhere to turn when the heat begins to rise.

The angel touches the sleeping prophet and says: arise and eat. The journey is too great for you.

> It is too great for you to make alone, on empty, in silence.

It is too great for you to make alone, on empty, in silence. That is not weakness. That is the condition God acknowledged before redirecting Elijah to the next assignment.

You are allowed the same.

New pastors often arrive with a clear vision of what the church should become. The problem is that vision, however accurate, must be built on relationships — and relationships take time. When a new pastor begins dismantling systems, restructuring programs, or challenging long-held traditions before they have earned deep trust, they create resistance that can define and derail their entire tenure.

This is the first and most common mistake pastors make in new ministry contexts. It is also the one that is hardest to recognize from inside it, because the vision is usually real and the problems being addressed are usually genuine. The new pastor is not wrong about what needs to change. They are wrong about the sequence — about what has to come first.

---

## The Shepherd Is Not a Consultant

The pastoral relationship is not a management relationship. It is a covenantal one.

A consultant hired to restructure an organization has the authority of the engagement and the expertise as credentials. They can assess quickly, recommend confidently, and implement based on the client's authorization. The congregation did not hire a consultant. They called a shepherd — a word that implies presence over time, proximity to the flock, the kind of knowledge that comes from being with people in the actual conditions of their lives. Shepherds do not arrive with a restructuring plan. They arrive and learn where the sheep are.

Moses did not begin his leadership of Israel with a vision for the tabernacle. He began it by standing on holy ground and encountering the God who would lead — and then by forty years of learning what it meant to lead the specific people he was given (Exodus 3, Numbers 14). The tabernacle came later. The Promised Land came later. Most of the significant moves of his leadership came after he had established — through presence, through proximity, through the slow accumulation of shared experience — the kind of trust that could carry a community through the wilderness.

> The new pastor who skips that process is not a failure of vision. They are a failure of sequence.

The new pastor who skips that process is not a failure of vision. They are a failure of sequence.

---

## The History the New Pastor Cannot Yet See

Consider the specific thing that happens when change is attempted too soon.

The congregation that has been in place for twenty or forty years has history the new pastor cannot yet see. The worship service that looks inefficient to the outside observer was designed, fifteen years ago, by a volunteer who gave two years of their life to it and whose daughter still attends. The program that appears redundant was started in response to a specific crisis the congregation survived together, and its continuation is a form of communal memory. The tradition that seems merely habitual was once the practice that kept the church together during a division that almost ended it.

None of this will be in the materials the new pastor reviewed during the candidating process. It lives in the tissue of relationships, in the stories people have not yet told because there has not been enough time for them to know whether this pastor is safe. When the new pastor arrives and begins changing the things that hold that history, they are not, from the congregation's perspective, removing an inefficiency. They are dismissing the history — telling the people who built those things, by action if not by word, that what they built does not matter.

The resistance that follows is not simply status quo protectionism. It is the response of people who have invested themselves and are watching that investment be discarded by someone who does not yet know what it cost.

---

## Eleven Weeks Is Not Enough to Know What a Service Carries

A concrete pastoral scene.

A new pastor arrives at a congregation that has a Sunday evening service with about thirty regulars. He has assessed the situation: Sunday evenings are not culturally normative in his region, the service is not drawing new people, the resources devoted to it could fund two additional missional programs. His analysis is correct. The evening service is probably not the best use of congregational energy.

He proposes the change at his third board meeting. He has been there eleven weeks.

Three of the board members push back with a force that surprises him. He presents the data again. They push back harder. The meeting ends badly, and something has shifted in the room.

What the pastor does not know, because he has been there eleven weeks, is that the Sunday evening service is where two of those board members' parents met. That it was the service during which the congregation came together after the split of 1987 that almost closed the church. That one of the regulars, a woman in her eighties, walked to that service through two Michigan winters after her husband died because it was the only place she felt him still present.

The service can probably still be changed. The analysis is probably still right. But not now, and not like this. Not before the pastor knows what he does not yet know.

---

## Earning the Right to Lead Where They Have Not Been

> you earn the right to lead people where they haven't been by first proving you understand where they've been.

The rule most experienced pastors eventually learn, usually the hard way, is this: you earn the right to lead people where they haven't been by first proving you understand where they've been.

That proof is not a rhetorical claim. It is not a sermon illustration about honoring the past or a stated commitment to listening. It is earned in the actual hours — the hospital visits at 2 a.m., the counseling sessions where the real story comes out, the dinner tables where the family history appears that has never been shared with anyone outside the family, the deacon's meeting where the old argument surfaces and the new pastor sits quietly and learns its shape.

Eugene Peterson described the pastoral calling as attending to people — a specific quality of attention that is not primarily active or problem-solving but present, receptive, genuinely interested in what is actually happening in a person rather than what the pastor needs them to do. [cite — confirm Peterson, relevant work, if a specific passage is cited.] That quality of attention is what makes change possible, because it is what makes trust possible — and trust is the only medium in which genuine pastoral leadership can travel.

The congregation that does not trust the pastor will not follow them. They will comply, perhaps, if the formal authority is used. They will appear to change. But the change will not go deep, and it will not last, and the relationship will be marked by the experience of being managed rather than led — which is not the pastoral relationship, and cannot produce what the pastoral relationship is supposed to produce.

---

## When the Building Is Actually on Fire

The steel-manned counter-position.

Some situations genuinely require rapid intervention. A church in genuine crisis — financial collapse, moral failure, abusive systems, theological drift that is actively misleading people — may not afford the new pastor the luxury of an extended season of listening before action. Bonhoeffer did not have the luxury of relationship-building before confronting the Deutsche Christen. [cite — confirm Bonhoeffer's early confrontations with the German Christian movement.] There are situations where the building is actually on fire and the responsible leader does not organize a listening circle before calling for exit.

Those situations exist. They are not the common situation of the new pastor arriving at a functional if imperfect congregation. The discernment required is the ability to distinguish between genuine emergency and the impatience of a leader who has a vision and wants to implement it.

Most of the time, what the new pastor experiences as urgent is not an emergency. It is the normal friction between an inherited situation and a new vision — friction that is real but that does not require immediate resolution. The urgency the new pastor feels is often their own discomfort with the distance between where the congregation is and where they believe it should be. That discomfort is valuable. It will sustain the vision through the longer work of building the trust that makes it achievable. But it is not a reliable guide to action in the first year.

---

## Imposition Versus Invitation

Listen before you lead. Learn before you change.

A year of genuine relationship-building will accomplish more than five years of vision-casting to a congregation that doesn't trust you yet. Not because the vision is less important than the relationships, but because the vision cannot travel without the relationships. The preacher can say the right things from the pulpit every Sunday and produce no change in the congregation if the congregation has not decided — through the slow accumulation of trust-building experiences — that this is a person worth following.

The pastoral relationship is irreducibly personal. The congregation is not following the vision. They are following the person. And the person is only known over time, through the kind of presence that cannot be hurried or manufactured, that builds in the specific hours of being present for specific people in specific need.

The new pastor who understands this is not abandoning their vision. They are protecting it — building the relational foundation that will carry it when the time comes for it to be offered. The vision that is offered too soon, to people who do not yet know the person offering it, will be received as imposition. The same vision, offered after a year of earned trust, will be received as invitation.

That difference — imposition versus invitation — is the difference between the pastor who changes everything in the first year and creates resistance that never fully resolves, and the pastor who changes everything in the third or fifth year and carries the congregation with them.

Both have the same vision. One of them has built the road. That road is trust, and it is built the old way — in hours, in presence, in the quiet accumulation of arriving, one person at a time, until the congregation knows that the person they called knows them.

> That knowledge changes everything. It just takes longer than the new pastor wants it to.

That knowledge changes everything. It just takes longer than the new pastor wants it to.

Of all the things that are slowly changing in pastoral culture, the stigma around professional counseling may be the most stubbornly persistent. Despite growing awareness of mental health issues in ministry, despite Barna data showing that 18 percent of pastors have thought about self-harm or suicide in the past year [cite — confirm], and despite the visible collapse of pastor after pastor who carried burdens they could not carry alone, many pastors still resist the idea of seeing a therapist with a tenacity they would never apply to, say, seeing a cardiologist for chest pain.

The resistance is not random. It is rooted in specific beliefs and cultural norms that are worth examining directly, because until those roots are addressed, the argument for counseling will continue to feel like an argument against something the pastor holds dear.

## The Reasons Pastors Give

The most common reason pastors cite for not seeking counseling is theological: they believe that the Scriptures, prayer, and the Holy Spirit should be sufficient for any struggle they face, and that turning to a secular professional implies a deficiency of faith. This is a real conviction sincerely held, and it deserves a real response rather than dismissal.

The response is this: God works through means. He heals bodies through doctors, teaches through educators, and adjudicates through lawyers. The consistent pattern of Scripture is not that God works exclusively through direct, unmediated action of the Spirit, but that He works through created agents and institutions as instruments of His grace. The Hebrew prophets understood this — Isaiah's own emotional and spiritual depletion under the juniper tree in 1 Kings 19 was addressed by God through the mundane means of food and sleep before the word of the Lord came again. Elijah did not need more prayer in that moment. He needed bread, and God sent an angel with it. A skilled counselor who understands the human mind and has been trained in evidence-based approaches to emotional and psychological health is not an alternative to God's provision. They are one of its forms.

The Reformation itself reasserted this logic against a form of spirituality that sought to bypass the ordinary means of grace. Luther's insistence on the Word, Calvin's doctrine of common grace — both represent a theological commitment to the idea that God's goodness reaches human beings through creaturely channels, not only through direct spiritual intervention. To refuse professional counseling on the grounds that the Spirit is sufficient is to apply a standard to psychological health that we would apply to no other area of human need.

## The Historical Moment We Are In

The pastoral mental health crisis is not a recent phenomenon. It has structural roots that run deep into the nature of the pastoral vocation. The nineteenth-century pastor worked in a community where ministry was one of the most socially respected professions, where the pastor's authority was largely unquestioned, and where the expectations placed on the pastor — though significant — were bounded by the social and geographic limits of a defined community. That world is gone.

The twenty-first-century pastor works in a context of institutional distrust, constant availability through technology, the expectation of professional-level competence across an impossible range of disciplines, and the performative demands of a culture in which pastoral identity is constructed and broadcast in public. The pastor must be an executive leader, a skilled therapist, a compelling public speaker, a social media presence, a fundraiser, a crisis counselor, a theologian, and a visible model of spiritual health — all simultaneously, often without the formation or support that any of these roles would require on its own. The structural weight of this is not a character failure. It is an institutional reality that produces suffering in largely predictable ways, and the refusal to seek help for that suffering is not courage. It is something closer to pride.

## A Steel-Manned Counter-Position

I want to take the theological resistance seriously on its strongest terms, not its weakest. The most sophisticated version of the argument goes like this: the categories that secular therapeutic culture uses to describe human suffering — disorders, trauma, attachment styles, dysregulation — are not neutral. They carry embedded anthropologies that often conflict with a Christian understanding of sin, grace, and human nature. The pastor who enters therapeutic culture uncritically may absorb a framework that explains all suffering as psychological and all solutions as psychological, and this may actually impoverish their pastoral ministry by replacing theological categories with therapeutic ones.

This is not a frivolous concern. James K.A. Smith has argued [cite — confirm] that our formative practices shape our imagination more deeply than our explicit beliefs, and a pastor who spends years in an unreflective therapeutic framework may find that they have slowly replaced the language of sin and repentance with the language of trauma and healing in ways they never consciously chose. The concern is real.

The answer to this concern is not to avoid counseling. It is to bring the same theological discernment to counseling that the pastor brings to any other practice. A pastor who engages therapy thoughtfully — who is willing to examine the anthropological assumptions behind a therapeutic framework and hold them against a biblical one, who brings their own theological convictions into the room rather than leaving them at the door — will likely find that the two disciplines, while genuinely different, are not as antagonistic as the caricature suggests. The best therapeutic practitioners are not ideologues. They are skilled students of human suffering who have developed genuine expertise in helping people through it. That expertise is worth engaging, critically and carefully.

## The Practical Concerns

Beyond theology, pastors also resist counseling for practical reasons: cost, time, confidentiality concerns, and the fear that being seen entering a counselor's office might generate questions they do not want to answer. These concerns are real, and they deserve practical responses.

On cost: many counselors offer sliding scale fees, and some denominations and pastoral care organizations provide counseling benefits specifically for pastors and ministry families. On confidentiality: licensed professional counselors are bound by strict confidentiality rules that protect your information with very limited exceptions. On being seen: telehealth has made it possible to receive high-quality counseling from the privacy of your own home or office without anyone needing to know you are doing it.

> It is the fear that honesty is too expensive. And it is precisely backward.

There is also a deeper practical concern that pastors rarely name but often feel: the fear that a counselor will find something that invalidates the calling. The fear that if someone actually looked closely at the interior life, they would discover that the pastor is not as spiritually healthy as the role requires — and that this discovery would unravel something they have spent their life building. I recognize this fear because I have felt it. It is the fear that honesty is too expensive. And it is precisely backward. The unexamined interior does not stay stable. It leaks. It shapes the preaching and the pastoral care and the marriage and the parenting in ways that careful, honest self-knowledge would at least allow to be chosen rather than merely suffered.

## A Concrete Scene

I think of a pastor I know — fifteen years in ministry, three churches, a reputation for pastoral wisdom among his peers. He came to counseling in his early forties not because he was in crisis but because a trusted friend looked at him across a table and said: "You are not as okay as you present." He was not. The first six months of counseling surfaced grief he had not allowed himself to name: the death of a vision he had carried for a decade, the slow erosion of a friendship with a former associate who had left under painful circumstances, the unresolved anger at his own father that was surfacing — he could see it clearly only in retrospect — in how he related to criticism from the church's elders. None of this was visible from the outside. All of it was shaping everything.

He is still in ministry. His preaching has more weight than it did before, which is not a coincidence. The weight came from the willingness to carry what was actually there rather than managing it out of awareness.

## What Counseling Actually Offers

What a good counselor offers is not what the pastor's accountability partner offers, and not what their mentor offers, and not what their spouse offers — though all of those relationships have genuine and irreplaceable value. A counselor offers a trained, structured, confidential space for examining the patterns, histories, and internal dynamics that most directly affect the pastor's wellbeing and leadership.

Many pastors who begin counseling discover that the presenting issue — burnout, anxiety, a difficult relationship — is connected to much older patterns they have been managing unconsciously for decades. Families of origin, early formative experiences, deeply embedded beliefs about their own worth and performance — these are not things that prayer and accountability naturally surface, not because those tools are insufficient, but because they are not designed for this particular kind of excavation. Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 4:7 that we carry this treasure in jars of clay, and the jars are real. They crack under pressure in ways that have identifiable patterns, and those patterns can be known, addressed, and changed.

Bonhoeffer wrote in *Life Together* that the person who cannot bear to be alone will damage community [cite — confirm]. The inverse is equally true: the person who refuses to be genuinely known — whose interiority is managed rather than inhabited — will eventually find that their external ministry is sustained by a kind of hollow performance. The counselor's room is not where holiness is produced. But it is often where the obstacles to it become visible.

## A Word to Church Boards and Congregations

If you are a church leader reading this and thinking about your pastor: one of the most significant investments you can make in the long-term health of your church is to provide your pastor with a counseling benefit and the explicit permission — from the pulpit, in the elder board, in the culture of the church — to use it without shame. The pastor who has access to ongoing professional support is a safer pastor, a more stable leader, and a more sustainable presence in the church than one who is carrying everything alone.

The congregation that expects its pastor to model perfect composure and spiritual steadiness in all circumstances — that treats pastoral vulnerability as a liability rather than an asset — is asking for a performance. Performances are not the same as pastoral care. The pastor who has done the interior work is the pastor who can sit with someone in a hospital room at midnight and actually be present rather than managing the moment. That presence is not accidental. It is formed. And counseling is one of the primary means of its formation.

The stigma will not disappear overnight. But it will begin to dissolve when the leaders of the church are willing to be honest about their own needs, and when the structures around them make that honesty possible without cost.

> We tell the people we serve that they do not have to carry it alone. We should stop exempting ourselves.

We tell the people we serve that they do not have to carry it alone. We should stop exempting ourselves.

Depression does not care about your theology. It does not make exceptions for people who have been called to preach the hope of the resurrection. It does not lift because you have memorized the right Scriptures or counseled enough other people through dark seasons. Depression is a clinical condition with biological, psychological, and circumstantial dimensions — and it affects pastors at rates that are significantly higher than the general population.

The Barna Group's ongoing research on pastoral wellbeing consistently reveals that depression is among the most common and least addressed challenges facing ministry leaders. Yet many pastors — and many congregations — continue to approach it through a framework that treats it primarily as a spiritual problem, which means that people who need clinical help are instead receiving spiritual interventions that may help at the margins but cannot address the underlying condition.

## What Depression Actually Is

Clinical depression is not the same as sadness, and it is not the same as the ordinary grief and discouragement that are part of any honest life of faith. Major depressive disorder is characterized by persistent changes in mood, energy, sleep, appetite, concentration, and the capacity to experience pleasure — changes that are significant, sustained, and not explained by the ordinary circumstances of the person's life.

Depression in pastors often presents somewhat differently than in the general population. The public performance demands of the role can mask depressive symptoms for extended periods, allowing pastors to appear functional and even vibrant from the pulpit while experiencing profound internal darkness. The pastor who seems engaged and effective on Sunday may be barely making it through the week — and may not recognize their own condition because they are still producing.

There is a particular irony in this. The same capacity that makes a pastor capable — the ability to summon pastoral presence on demand, to move fluidly between their internal state and the demands of the public role — is what allows depression to remain hidden until it is severe. The performance continues long past the point where the cost has become unsustainable.

## The Faith Problem Framing and Why It Fails

The most damaging thing that happens to pastors with depression is when the condition is interpreted by themselves or others as evidence of inadequate faith. This framing is not only clinically inaccurate — it is theologically inaccurate. The biblical record is full of people who experienced profound darkness: Elijah under the juniper tree, asking God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4). David in the depths of the lament psalms, crying out from places where no light seemed to reach: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Psalm 22:1). Jeremiah cursing the day of his birth (Jeremiah 20:14). Job, who had done nothing wrong, losing everything and sitting in ash.

These are not presented in Scripture as failures of faith. They are presented as honest human experiences that God met with presence, provision, and patience — not immediate relief, but genuine accompaniment. When Elijah collapsed in exhaustion and despair and asked to die, God did not rebuke him for his inadequate trust. God sent an angel with food and water. "Arise and eat," the text says, "for the journey is too great for you" (1 Kings 19:7). The divine response to Elijah's breakdown was not a sermon about faith. It was bread and sleep and presence.

> Shame is not a therapeutic agent. It is an amplifier.

The pastor who treats their own depression as a spiritual failure not only carries the depression but carries it alone and in shame, which makes it significantly worse. Shame is not a therapeutic agent. It is an amplifier.

## The Counter-Position Worth Taking Seriously

There is a position held by some within the pastoral community — and it deserves to be engaged honestly rather than dismissed — that all suffering is ultimately spiritual in nature, that the category of mental illness is a medicalization of what is in fact a crisis of the soul, and that the church's response to depression should be distinctly different from the culture's response: more prayer, more Scripture, more repentance, more community. This view is not always as crude as its critics make it, and it arises from a genuine commitment to the sufficiency of Scripture and a warranted suspicion of a culture that pathologizes ordinary human experience.

The concern is real. We do over-diagnose. We do sometimes reach for medication before we have asked honest questions about sin, soul-neglect, and the absence of genuine Christian community. These are legitimate observations.

But the position fails where it matters most. It fails the pastor who has prayed faithfully and consistently and found that the darkness does not lift — not because their faith is insufficient, but because the condition they are experiencing has biological substrates that prayer does not directly address, any more than prayer directly heals a broken femur. It fails the person who is told to "fight with faith" against a condition that has, among its primary symptoms, the inability to access the very emotional and cognitive resources that faith-fighting requires. And it fails theologically: the incarnation itself is a statement that bodies matter, that the material and the spiritual are not hermetically sealed from each other, that God meets human beings in their embodied reality — including the embodied reality of a brain chemistry that has gone wrong.

The biblical categories of lament, of groaning, of a creation that is not yet healed, of a body that suffers in ways not caused by personal sin — all of these make room for clinical depression in a way that the "it's a faith problem" framework simply does not.

## What Actually Helps

Clinical depression in its moderate to severe forms typically requires clinical intervention. This may include therapy — specifically modalities like cognitive behavioral therapy or interpersonal therapy that have strong evidence bases for depression treatment [cite — confirm]. It may include medication, which for many people is neither a permanent solution nor a sign of weakness, but a genuine tool that makes the other work possible. It almost always includes the kind of community and connection that reduces the isolation that feeds depression.

Spiritual practices — prayer, Scripture reading, worship, honest lament, community — are genuinely supportive and should not be abandoned. But they work alongside clinical care, not instead of it. The pastor who is receiving appropriate treatment for depression is not choosing medicine over faith. They are choosing stewardship of the body and mind that God gave them, using the means He has provided.

This is not a theological capitulation. Thomas Aquinas, writing in the thirteenth century, made the elementary distinction between natural and supernatural causes and effects. The fever has a natural cause; treating it with medicine is not a failure to trust in divine healing. The same basic framework applies here. God heals. God also gave the brain its chemistry, and when that chemistry is disordered, the means of addressing it are part of God's provision, not a replacement for it.

## The Unique Burden of Pastoral Depression

There is something specific to the pastoral experience of depression that deserves naming. Most people who struggle with depression struggle privately. The pastor struggles publicly, or performs publicly while struggling privately, which is its own kind of hell.

The pastor is expected to be the hope-bearer. The one who has something to say about suffering. The person who visits the dying, sits with the grieving, preaches the resurrection with conviction on Sunday morning. All of that is required while they are, themselves, unable to access hope. The cognitive dissonance of this — preaching what you cannot feel, proclaiming what you cannot receive — compounds the depression and adds a layer of spiritual disorientation that is not present in the same way for people outside the pastoral role.

> preaching what you cannot feel, proclaiming what you cannot receive

I have sat with pastors who described standing at the pulpit and telling the congregation that God is near the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18) while experiencing God as completely absent. They did not feel like hypocrites. They felt like people holding a lifeline they could not quite reach. That is not hypocrisy. That is something closer to faithfulness under conditions that faith was never supposed to face alone. But it is also unsustainable, and it is a sign that help is needed before the distance between what is proclaimed and what is experienced becomes permanent.

## For the Congregation

If you are a congregation member and you suspect your pastor is struggling with depression — or if they have told you they are — the most helpful thing you can offer is not a Scripture verse and not a challenge to pray more. It is the same thing you would offer to anyone you loved who was dealing with a serious medical condition: compassion, practical support, patience with a timeline that is not yours to set, and the explicit reassurance that their worth in your eyes is not conditional on their performance.

The pastor who feels safe enough to be depressed in front of their congregation, and to receive care without losing their position or their people's confidence, is in a far better place to recover than the one who must maintain the performance of health while falling apart. That safety is a gift the congregation can give — if they choose to.

Practically: ask your pastor, with genuine curiosity and without the undertone of evaluation, how they are doing. Ask more than once. Create the conditions in which an honest answer is possible. Protect their time off. Fund their counseling. Let them take a leave of absence when they need one, with the full assurance that the position will be waiting when they return.

## What the Church Gets Right in Its Better Moments

The church has resources for this that the clinical world does not. Genuine community — the kind described in Acts 2 and lived out imperfectly across the centuries — provides something that no therapy can replicate: the experience of being known and loved across time, in one's particular history and struggle, by people who are not being paid to care. The lament tradition of the Psalms gives language for suffering that the diagnostic manuals do not. The theology of the resurrection — the insistence that the darkness does not have the final word — is not a platitude when it is held alongside the reality of the darkness rather than in place of it.

Eugene Peterson spent decades writing about what he called "the contemplative pastor" — the leader formed not by management technique but by long immersion in Scripture and prayer and honest attention to the soul [cite — confirm]. That formation is itself a kind of preventive medicine for depression, or at least for the kind of depression that is produced by the drivenness and performance anxiety that characterize so much of contemporary pastoral culture.

The church at its best has always known that the shepherd needs shepherding. The question is whether the particular congregations and denominations and pastoral cultures we have built are capable of providing it.

## The Pastoral Community's Responsibility

No pastor should be navigating depression alone. The isolation that makes depression worse is partly circumstantial — the pastoral role is structurally isolating in ways that other professions are not — and partly chosen, because admitting the struggle feels like a threat to the position and to the congregation's confidence.

The Pastors Connection Network exists partly to address this. A community of pastors who know each other at depth, who have permission to ask hard questions and offer honest presence, who can sit with a colleague in the darkness without demanding that it resolve quickly — this is not a luxury. For many pastors in the grip of depression, it is the difference between a crisis that is survived and a career that ends in collapse.

The God who sent bread and water to Elijah in the wilderness is the same God who works through the hands and voices of people willing to say: I see you. I am staying. The journey is too great to take alone. Let us not pretend otherwise.

They look like virtues from the outside. The pastor who prepares for Sunday with extraordinary care. The leader who cannot let a decision go until every angle has been considered. The shepherd who lies awake thinking about the person in their congregation who is struggling and wondering what more could be done. These qualities look like dedication, conscientiousness, love — and to some extent, they are.

They are also, in many pastors, expressions of anxiety and perfectionism that have been dressed up in the language of calling. The difference between genuine pastoral care and anxiety-driven pastoral performance is one of the most important and least-discussed distinctions in ministry formation. Getting it wrong costs the pastor their health. And it costs the congregation a pastor who is serving them out of genuine freedom rather than driven compulsion.

## The Perfectionism Trap

Perfectionism in pastoral ministry is particularly insidious because it is so thoroughly rewarded in the early stages of a career. The young pastor who works eighty hours a week, who never delivers a Sunday without extraordinary preparation, who responds to every email within hours and never misses a hospital visit — that pastor gets affirmed. They get called faithful. They get offered larger churches. The perfectionism looks like the thing producing the success, and it is, for a while.

What the affirmation does not account for is the trajectory. Perfectionism is not a sustainable operating system. It is a high-performance engine running without the maintenance it requires, producing impressive results until the day it simply stops. The perfectionist pastor either learns to identify and address the pattern early — before the body or the marriage or the ministry forces the reckoning — or the reckoning arrives on its own schedule.

The reckoning usually arrives in one of three forms: physical collapse, relational collapse, or the quiet hollowing of the inner life that precedes both. The body gives out. The marriage reaches a breaking point that could not arrive suddenly because it had been building for a decade. Or the person who stands in the pulpit on Sunday morning realizes they have nothing left, that the well they have been drawing from to fill everyone else's cup has been empty for longer than they have admitted.

## The Historical and Theological Roots

Perfectionism is not a contemporary phenomenon, and its presence in the church is older than the word itself. The Pharisaic tradition in first-century Judaism — the tradition from which Paul himself came and against which Jesus' teaching cut most sharply — was in part a perfectionism of the religious life. The scrupulous observance of every commandment, the multiplication of hedges around the law, the construction of a system in which adequate performance could be tracked and measured — this was, among other things, an anxiety-management system. If I can do it correctly enough, I will be safe.

Jesus' confrontation with this system in Matthew 23 is not primarily about hypocrisy, though hypocrisy is part of it. It is about the fundamental misdirection of the perfectionist religious impulse: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness" (Matthew 23:23). The problem is not that they were careful about the details. The problem is that the carefulness about details had become the substance of the faith, displacing the deeper things that no detail-perfecting can achieve.

The perfectionist pastor is not usually a Pharisee in the pejorative sense. They are not performing for external approval in a cynical way — most of them genuinely care. But the structure is the same: the belief that adequate performance produces safety, that thoroughness is a shield against criticism, that the way to avoid being found insufficient is never to be anything less than exceptional.

## Anxiety as the Engine Underneath

Perfectionism is usually driven by anxiety — specifically, the anxiety of inadequacy. The deep, often unconscious conviction that the pastor is not quite enough, that their best is not quite sufficient, that one mistake or one mediocre Sunday will reveal what they have been secretly afraid is true about them. This anxiety is so common in high-performing pastoral leaders that it is almost a defining characteristic of the type.

It is also frequently rooted in family of origin dynamics — early experiences that taught the person that love and approval were conditional on performance, that failure was not safe, that excellence was the price of belonging. Ministry, with its constant performance demands and high-stakes consequences, can become the perfect arena in which to continue enacting the patterns learned in childhood — patterns that feel like faithfulness but function like compulsion.

I am not describing people I have observed from a clinical distance. I am describing the pattern I have recognized in myself and in the pastors I know well. The drivenness that looks like calling is sometimes calling. Sometimes it is the childhood wound finding a new arena. Often it is both, and the two are difficult to disentangle.

## The Counter-Position Worth Taking Seriously

The counter-position that deserves honest engagement is the one that insists high standards in ministry are not anxiety — they are faithfulness. That the pastor who refuses to deliver a mediocre sermon is not driven by perfectionism but by reverence for the word of God. That the leader who agonizes over decisions is not anxious — they are appropriately weighty in their stewardship. That the call to excellence is embedded in Paul's own language: "present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth" (2 Timothy 2:15).

This position is not wrong. Standards matter. The sermon that was not prepared is not just a pastoral failure — it is a failure of stewardship of the most important hour of many people's week. The decision that was not thought through can harm real people. The care that was not given cannot be retrospectively provided.

But the position fails when it cannot distinguish between standards and anxiety, between genuine care and compulsion, between the pastor who prepares thoroughly because they love the congregation and the pastor who prepares obsessively because they are terrified of being exposed. The external behaviors can be identical. The interior drivers are not. And the interior driver determines the trajectory — whether the high standards are sustainable over a career, or whether they are the engine of a machine that is running itself into the ground.

> The test is not the quality of the output. It is whether the person can stop.

The test is not the quality of the output. It is whether the person can stop. The genuinely excellent pastor can have a bad Sunday and survive it — not without disappointment, but without existential crisis. The perfectionist cannot. The quality of the output is the same. The brittleness is not.

## Breaking the Cycle

The cycle of anxiety and perfectionism does not break through willpower or self-discipline. It breaks through insight and, usually, through sustained professional support. A counselor who understands the psychology of perfectionism can help a pastor trace the pattern back to its roots and begin to build a different relationship with their own imperfection — one that allows for genuine rest, for genuine delegation, for genuine freedom from the tyranny of the standard that can never quite be met.

Practically, the cycle also breaks through the development of concrete tolerances for imperfection — deliberate choices to do things at eighty percent and experience that the sky does not fall, to delegate things and discover that others can do them adequately, to let a conversation go unresolved until tomorrow without the anxiety making it impossible to sleep. These practices feel dangerous to the perfectionist. That is how you know they are working.

The Sabbath, again, is the theological institution that addresses this directly. The fourth commandment is not only about rest. It is about the regular, structured practice of stopping — of releasing the conviction that the world cannot function without continuous personal effort. "Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God" (Exodus 20:9-10). On the seventh day, the perfectionist is commanded to stop being productive and to trust that what does not get done on that day will be held by a God who does not sleep.

For many perfectionist pastors, genuine Sabbath observance — not a half-day when the sermon is mostly ready, but a full, protected day of genuine rest and worship — is one of the most spiritually demanding practices they can undertake. It requires the daily death of the conviction that adequate performance is what sustains the world.

## The Gift of Imperfect Ministry

There is a deeper theological truth underneath the practical case for addressing perfectionism: the congregation does not need a perfect pastor. They need a human one. A pastor who has come to terms with their own limitations, who extends grace to themselves with something approaching the generosity they extend to others, who preaches the gospel of unearned love from a place of having actually received it — that pastor is more effective, not less, than one whose performance anxiety drives them to maintain an impossible standard.

2 Corinthians 12:9-10 is not merely a devotional comfort. It is a homiletical and pastoral statement: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me." The pastor who can say this in the first person — who can stand before the congregation not as someone who has arrived but as someone who is being sustained by the same grace they are proclaiming — preaches with an authority that no perfectionist performance can match.

> The most compelling testimony to grace is a life that has learned to live in it.

The most compelling testimony to grace is a life that has learned to live in it. Your congregation is watching to see whether what you preach is something you actually believe about yourself. The sermons that move people are rarely the ones that were most perfectly prepared. They are the ones where the preacher was most honestly present — most visibly a person who needs what they are offering.

Let them see that you do. The imperfection is not a failure of the ministry. It is, when received with honesty and offered back to the congregation, the most credible evidence that the gospel they are hearing is true.

Somewhere along the way, the attendance count became the pastoral report card. Not officially, perhaps — most churches do not formally evaluate their pastor based on Sunday numbers. But informally, in the conversations that happen after services and in elder meetings and at denominational gatherings, the question underneath most conversations about how a pastor is doing is: how is the church doing? And "how is the church doing" almost always means: are more people coming, or fewer?

This conflation — between the church's numerical trajectory and the pastor's worth — is one of the most damaging dynamics in contemporary ministry. It produces pastors who make decisions based on what will sustain or grow attendance rather than what genuine faithfulness requires. It produces leaders who hide seasons of numerical decline rather than leading through them honestly. And it produces a generation of pastoral anxiety that is directly correlated to a metric over which pastors have far less control than the culture assumes.

## What Numbers Can and Cannot Tell You

Attendance is not meaningless. The size and trajectory of a congregation tells you something — though considerably less than most people think, and considerably less than the pastoral culture treats it as communicating. A church that is genuinely reaching its community and genuinely making disciples will tend, over time, to grow. And a church that is losing people without gaining others is likely experiencing some combination of leadership, cultural, or contextual challenges that deserve honest examination.

But the relationship between attendance and pastoral faithfulness is far less direct than the common assumptions suggest. Geography matters enormously. A church in a growing suburb has structural advantages that a church in a dying rural community simply does not have, regardless of the quality of leadership. Demographics matter. A church with a rapidly aging congregation faces numerical headwinds that the most gifted pastor in the country cannot reverse through skill alone. And the health of a congregation — the genuine depth of discipleship, the quality of community, the faithfulness of mission engagement — is almost entirely invisible in the attendance count.

A congregation of two hundred people who are being genuinely formed by the gospel, who are making real disciples, who are caring for their neighbors, who are honest about their failures and persistent in their faithfulness — that congregation cannot be distinguished from a congregation of two hundred people who attend regularly, give enough to keep the lights on, and are largely unchanged by the encounter with Scripture, on the basis of the number alone.

## The Historical and Theological Background

The identification of numerical growth with divine favor has ancient roots and, in the American context, a specific modern genealogy. The revivalist tradition of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries — from Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield through Charles Finney and Dwight Moody — was partly responsible for introducing a culture of measurable outcomes into Protestant church life [cite — confirm]. The revival's success was documented in conversion numbers. The evangelist's effectiveness was measured in the size of the crowd.

This created a framework that was then absorbed into the church growth movement of the twentieth century, which developed increasingly sophisticated methods for analyzing and pursuing numerical growth. The contributions of this movement — the attention to cultural accessibility, the focus on removing unnecessary barriers to the gospel — were genuine. The residue it left behind was the deep embedding of numerical growth as the primary marker of ministry success, a framing that the movement's own best voices did not fully intend and have since partially retracted.

The prophetic tradition in the Hebrew scriptures consistently complicates this framework. Isaiah preached for decades to a people who did not respond — and God told him at the outset that this would be the case (Isaiah 6:9-10). Jeremiah's entire ministry was, by the numbers, a failure. He was imprisoned, thrown in a cistern, mocked, and ultimately watched the very disaster he had been predicting unfold, unable to prevent it, unheard even as the evidence accumulated. The New Testament itself closes with a letter to seven churches in Asia Minor — most of whom have significant problems, several of whom are in serious danger, only one of whom receives the unqualified commendation of the risen Christ (Revelation 2-3). By any attendance metric, these were not thriving congregations.

Faithfulness and fruitfulness are not the same thing, and confusing them does profound damage to the people who are called to be faithful in contexts where the numbers are not cooperating.

## The Idol of Growth

The church growth movement, for all its genuine contributions to pastoral thinking, left behind a particular residue: the deep embedding of numerical growth as the primary marker of ministry success. This residue is in the culture, in the conferences, in the way pastors talk to each other and evaluate each other, and — most damagingly — in the way pastors talk to themselves.

The pastor who has internalized attendance numbers as their primary identity marker is practicing a form of idolatry that the tradition has language for: the works-righteousness of the performance-based life. Not justified by faith in what Christ has done, but justified by numbers — by the measurable evidence that the ministry is producing something the culture recognizes as success.

This is not merely a psychological problem. It is a theological one. The congregation does not belong to the pastor. It belongs to the God who called it into being and who holds it in his hands. The pastor is a steward, not an owner. And the steward's faithfulness will be evaluated by different criteria than the owner's profit margin.

## The Counter-Position Worth Taking Seriously

The counter-position deserves honest engagement. It goes something like this: numerical decline is often a symptom of real problems — poor preaching, failure to evangelize, a congregation turning inward — and the pastor who shrugs at the numbers by appealing to the faithfulness of Jeremiah is not being prophetically patient; they are avoiding accountability for genuine failure. Numbers are not the only metric, but they are a metric. The church that never challenges itself to reach beyond its existing membership has allowed mission to become optional.

This is true. The appeal to prophetic faithfulness can become a self-protective narrative that insulates a pastor from honest examination of whether their ministry is actually reaching people. Jeremiah is not a template for every pastoral situation. Not every declining church is a faithful remnant. Some declining churches are declining because the leadership is poor, the mission is absent, and the congregation has been allowed to calcify.

> attendance is one data point among many

But the position fails when it reduces the entire evaluation of a ministry to a number that is influenced by dozens of factors the pastor cannot control. The honest position is that attendance is one data point among many, that it deserves to be taken seriously without being treated as the definitive measure, and that the pastor who uses prophetic faithfulness to avoid honest self-examination is as mistaken as the one who uses numerical decline as the only evidence that something has gone wrong.

## A Different Metric

What if the primary question you asked about your ministry was not "how many" but "how deep"? What if the report card had categories like: Are people genuinely encountering God here? Is genuine community forming that can sustain people through difficulty? Are disciples being made who are making disciples? Is the mission of the gospel being carried beyond the walls of the building? Are the poor and marginalized finding welcome?

These questions are harder to answer with a single number. But they are closer to the questions that Scripture seems most interested in. The sheep that the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to find is not a growth strategy — it is a statement about the nature of God's attention, which is not primarily aggregate (how many are in the fold?) but particular (where is the one who is lost?).

And they produce a different kind of pastoral leadership — one that is less anxious about the count and more focused on the quality of the community that is gathering around the table. One that can honestly say in a season of numerical decline: we are genuinely forming disciples, we are genuinely caring for the poor, we are genuinely reaching the people in this specific community who are reachable, and we will do this faithfully whether the numbers move or not.

## The Pastor and Their Own Identity

The deeper issue underneath the attendance anxiety is identity. The pastor who experiences a decline in attendance as a personal threat — who feels the number as a verdict about their adequacy — has allowed the metric to colonize territory it was never meant to occupy. Their worth as a pastor, as a person, as a child of God, is not determined by whether more people are coming this year than last year.

Galatians 1:10 — "For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ" — is a text about the fundamental orientation of the pastor's work. The approval that matters is not the approval of the attendance counter or the denominational assessment or the elder board's satisfaction with the trajectory of Sunday morning. The approval that matters is the verdict of the one who called.

That verdict will not come in the form of a Sunday attendance report. It will come in the form of the words that Matthew 25:21 describes: "Well done, good and faithful servant." Not "well done, large and growing servant." Not "well done, trending in the right direction servant." Faithful.

> You are not your attendance number.

You are not your attendance number. Your worth as a pastor is not determined by whether more people are coming this year than last year. It is determined by whether you are faithful to the God who called you and genuinely present to the people He has given you. That is the record that matters. Let it be the one you build toward.

The number on the attendance sheet will be forgotten. The person you invested in on a Tuesday afternoon, who is now walking with God because someone was faithful enough to sit with them — that is a number that gets counted differently. Build toward that.

Walk into almost any established congregation in America and look at the range of people sitting in the pews. There is the retired teacher who has been attending for forty years and whose faith is formed by a lifetime of Scripture and tradition. There is the millennial couple who came for the first time six weeks ago, who have no church background and came because their neighbor invited them during a hard season in their marriage. There is the college student home for the summer who is somewhere between faith and genuine doubt and has not decided yet whether this Sunday will be their last. There is the single mother who is exhausted and needs something more than information. There is the businessman who came to evaluate whether the pastor is worth his time.

The preacher stands before all of them with one message to give. The gospel is singular. The audience is not. And the tension between those two realities is the central homiletical challenge of every Sunday.

## Why This Is Harder Than It Used to Be

Preaching to diverse congregations has always been demanding, but the complexity has increased significantly in recent decades. The cultural range in a typical congregation has widened. The gap between churched and unchurched backgrounds is larger than it has ever been. The attention span and the information environment in which congregants live have changed the way people receive and process communication. And the political and cultural divisions that have fractured public life have not stopped at the church door.

A sermon that lands powerfully for a fifty-five-year-old elder who grew up in the tradition may be functionally inaccessible to the thirty-year-old who came for the first time. A preaching style that resonates with people who value intellectual engagement may leave the grieving mother cold. The preacher who optimizes for one part of the congregation consistently tends to lose the others — not all at once, but gradually, as they sense that the sermon is not for them.

> The gospel does not change. The angle of approach does.

This is not a new problem. It is Paul's problem in 1 Corinthians 9: "I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some" (1 Corinthians 9:22). Paul is not describing shapeshifting or the abandonment of the gospel's content. He is describing a homiletical posture — the willingness to consider the particular hearer and to let that consideration shape the form, though never the substance, of the message. The gospel does not change. The angle of approach does.

## The Historical Arc of the Problem

The early church faced a version of this challenge that makes our contemporary diversity look manageable. The Jewish Christian communities of Jerusalem, the Gentile communities of Antioch and Corinth and Ephesus, the Greek philosophical milieu of Athens — each required a different entry point into the same news about Jesus of Nazareth. Paul's sermon on Mars Hill in Acts 17 begins with the altar to an unknown God. His letter to the Romans begins with natural revelation. His sermon in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia in Acts 13 begins with the Exodus. Three different openings. One proclamation.

What Paul understood, and what the homiletical tradition has periodically recovered and periodically lost, is that the point of contact is not the same as the point of arrival. The point of contact must be where the hearer actually is.
