The point of arrival is always the same: the crucified and risen Christ, the forgiveness of sins, the possibility of genuine reconciliation with God and each other.

Tim Keller spent three decades at Redeemer Presbyterian Church in New York building a congregation of people who were explicitly drawn from the skeptical, educated, urban professional class — people who had left the tradition or never been in it — without abandoning the theological substance of Reformed Christianity [cite — confirm]. His model was not to simplify the gospel for the secular audience but to do the patient cultural translation work that made the gospel's claims legible to people who thought they had already heard and dismissed it. That is the homiletical challenge in its most demanding form.

## Preaching to the Text, Not the Type

One of the most reliable approaches to diverse-congregation preaching is a thorough, text-centered method that allows the Scripture itself to make its claims before the preacher shapes those claims for the audience. When the sermon begins with honest, careful attention to what the text is actually saying — in its original context, with its original force — it has a chance to do what sermons optimized for specific audiences often cannot: surprise everyone.

The person who came expecting to be confirmed in what they already believed gets disrupted by what the text actually says. The person who came expecting to be dismissed by religious language encounters something that speaks to their actual condition. The text, taken seriously on its own terms, has a range that no preacher's audience analysis can fully anticipate. Trust it.

This is not a license for historical or linguistic obscurity. The congregation does not need to know the Hebrew lexeme to encounter its force. But the preacher who has genuinely sat with the text — who has been surprised by it, troubled by it, met by it — preaches with a quality of attention that communicates itself across enormous differences in theological background and life circumstance. The congregation can feel the difference between a preacher who has done the exegetical work and one who is using the text as a launching pad for what they already wanted to say.

## The Art of the Layered Sermon

Skilled preachers who serve diverse congregations often learn to build layered sermons — messages that work at multiple levels of familiarity and engagement simultaneously. The surface is accessible: clear, concrete, illustrative, connected to ordinary human experience. Beneath the surface are implications that deepen for those who are prepared to go deeper. The theological substance is present and real, but it does not require prior theological formation to access the primary impact of the message.

This is not dumbing down. It is the recognition that every person in the room is a full human being who deserves the full truth of the gospel communicated in a way that genuinely reaches them. The preacher who uses inaccessible vocabulary is not being more faithful — they are being less attentive.

The layered sermon requires what Eugene Peterson called "the contemplative pastor" — the leader who has spent enough time in Scripture and prayer and honest attention to human beings that they can speak at the surface and the depth simultaneously without splitting the sermon into two different messages [cite — confirm]. The surface and the depth have to be the same thing, expressed differently. This is the work.

## The Counter-Position Worth Considering

There is a preaching philosophy — associated with certain strands of Reformed and confessional tradition — that holds that the congregation's diversity is not a homiletical problem to be solved but a reality to be accepted: the preacher's job is to preach the text faithfully, without audience optimization, and trust the Holy Spirit to do the particular work of application in each hearer. On this view, the attempt to tailor the message for diverse audiences is itself a form of unbelief — a failure to trust that the word of God is "living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword" (Hebrews 4:12) and therefore does not require the preacher's help to reach the skeptic or the grieving mother or the college student on the edge of leaving.

This position has genuine theological weight. The word does work that the preacher cannot. The sovereignty of the Holy Spirit in application is real. And there are preachers who have preached for decades in a single register, ignoring the diversity of their congregations, and have nonetheless seen genuine and lasting transformation.

But the position fails as a homiletical method when it is used to justify pastoral inattentiveness — when the refusal to consider the hearer is dressed as theological conviction rather than acknowledged as preference or limitation. The incarnation itself is a statement about context: the eternal Word became flesh in a particular time, a particular culture, a particular language. Not because flesh is superior to spirit, but because the hearer is embodied and the Word's reaching them required that attention to particularity. The preacher who ignores particularity is not being more faithful to the incarnation. They are being less.

## The Non-Negotiable of Genuine Humanity

Perhaps the single most universally connecting element in any sermon, regardless of the theological formation or cultural background of the congregation, is the preacher's genuine humanity. The sermon that begins or ends with a moment of honest vulnerability — not manufactured emotion, but real acknowledgment that the preacher is wrestling with the same human realities as the congregation — tends to build the kind of trust that makes the rest of the message receivable.

People from wildly different backgrounds and stages of faith share one thing: they are human beings who are struggling, hoping, wondering, and trying to make sense of their lives. Preach to that. Let the gospel address that. The gospel, after all, is not ultimately for any particular demographic. It is for people. And every room you preach in is full of them.

Self-implication is the technical name for what this requires of the preacher. Not confession as spectacle. Not vulnerability performed for effect. But the honest presence of a person who is inside the same struggle they are describing, who is not pointing at the congregation from a position of arrival but speaking from within the ongoing reality of trying to believe what the text claims. The retired teacher and the college student on the edge of leaving and the grieving mother and the skeptical businessman — none of them needs a preacher who has it figured out. They need a preacher who is still working it out, with enough honesty that they can see the work actually happening.

The Sermon on the Mount — the most universal and most demanding homiletical unit in the New Testament — begins not with doctrine but with condition: "Blessed are the poor in spirit" (Matthew 5:3). The entry point is human poverty. The room full of people who are nothing alike are united at the level of their poverty. Begin there. Trust the text to do the rest.

> The gospel does not need a narrower audience. It needs a more honest preacher.

The gospel does not need a narrower audience. It needs a more honest preacher. Those two things — the breadth of the audience and the honesty of the preacher — are not in tension. They are the same solution.

Admitting your preaching has gone stale carries a shame all its own. You are a minister of the Word — your whole vocation is organized around the conviction that these ancient texts have living power, that the God who speaks through Scripture is still speaking, that the gospel is inexhaustible. And yet you are sitting in your study on a Tuesday afternoon and you cannot make yourself care about the passage you are supposed to preach on Sunday. You have said this before. You know what you think it means. You are going through the motions of a process that used to feel alive.

This is a more common experience than most pastors will admit publicly, and it is not a sign that the calling has ended or that the faith is gone. It is a sign that something in the preaching ecology has stopped being fed, and that a change — not a dramatic one, necessarily, but a real one — is needed.

## The History of This Particular Struggle

The staleness of preaching is not a modern problem. George Herbert, the seventeenth-century Anglican priest and poet whose collection *The Temple* contains some of the most theologically precise devotional poetry in the English language, wrote extensively about the condition he called "dryness" — the experience of coming to the altar or the pulpit in a state of spiritual flatness that felt like a betrayal of the office [cite — confirm]. His response to it is instructive: he did not conclude that the dryness invalidated the ministry or the faith. He concluded that it was a condition to be inhabited honestly, brought before God in its full weight, and allowed to speak in the sermons themselves.

Charles Spurgeon, who preached to thousands at the Metropolitan Tabernacle and was perhaps the most celebrated preacher of the nineteenth century, suffered periods of depression so severe that he would lie in his study unable to prepare, unable to rise, convinced that the words had stopped coming [cite — confirm]. He named this from the pulpit when it was over. He wrote about the "Minister's Fainting Fits" in his pastoral lectures — not as a shameful aberration but as a structural feature of the preaching life that required pastoral honesty rather than concealment.

The pattern runs through the history of preaching: the moments of staleness and dryness are not interruptions to the ministry. They are part of it. The preacher who expects to sustain thirty or forty years of weekly proclamation without seasons of flatness has misunderstood the nature of the vocation.

## Why Preaching Goes Stale

The most common cause of homiletical staleness is the collapse of genuine personal engagement with Scripture outside the preaching task. When a pastor's primary relationship with the Bible is as sermon raw material — texts to be mined for Sunday content — the hunger that makes preaching alive tends to diminish. The text becomes a task rather than an encounter, and the congregation senses it even when they cannot name what is different.

Walter Brueggemann has argued, in a different context, that the prophetic imagination requires what he calls "counter-cultural" practices — disciplines that create a kind of interiority that the dominant culture cannot produce and does not value [cite — confirm]. The preacher who has allowed the efficiency demands of ministry to crowd out genuine contemplative engagement with the text has, functionally, conformed to the dominant culture's logic rather than resisting it. The result is a preacher who processes texts rather than inhabits them.

> The preacher who expects to sustain thirty or forty years of weekly proclamation without seasons of flatness has misunderstood the nature of the vocation.

A second common cause is the absence of genuine curiosity about the congregation's life. Preaching is always a dialogue, even if only one person is speaking. The preacher who is genuinely curious about what the people in front of them are actually experiencing — what they are afraid of, what they are hoping for, what they are carrying into the room — tends to preach sermons that engage those realities. The preacher who has stopped being curious about their congregation tends to preach at them rather than to them.

A third cause — less often named but very real — is the absence of genuine intellectual stimulation. The preacher who has stopped reading broadly, who has narrowed their intellectual diet to sermon preparation materials and ministry resources, will eventually run out of the material that preaching draws on: the understanding of the human condition, the historical imagination, the awareness of what is happening in the culture and why. The sermon becomes a closed loop — Scripture interpreted by Scripture, theological concepts arranged and rearranged without the friction of contact with the world outside the church.

## A Steel-Manned Counter-Position

The strongest version of the case against the diagnosis I have just offered goes like this: the preacher who is always looking for intellectual stimulation, who insists on fresh experience and new curiosity as preconditions for vital preaching, has made their own psychological state the center of the preaching enterprise. But the text does not change. The gospel does not change. The work of the Holy Spirit through the proclaimed Word does not depend on the preacher's subjective experience of freshness. The congregations who most need the Word preached are often in contexts where the preacher is exhausted, depressed, and experiencing no particular freshness whatsoever — and the Word preached under those conditions is not therefore less the Word. The preacher who waits to feel alive before they can preach has made their own interiority the gatekeeper of what the congregation receives.

This is a real concern. The theology of the Word's power is not dependent on the preacher's psychological state, and the pastor who has confused their own staleness with the gospel's inadequacy has made a category error.

But the argument proves too much. The same logic would exempt the preacher from any investment in their own formation, since the Word is powerful regardless of the instrument. We do not actually believe this. We invest in preaching training, homiletics, biblical scholarship, and pastoral formation because we believe that the instrument matters — not that it determines the outcome, but that it shapes the quality and depth of what the congregation receives. The preacher who is alive to the text, to the congregation, and to the world is not producing the power of the Spirit. They are removing impediments to it.

## Feeding the Preacher

> The soil was amended, and the roots went deeper.

The most direct remedy for homiletical staleness is an investment in the preacher's own spiritual and intellectual life that is entirely disconnected from sermon production. This means reading broadly — not just theological and pastoral works, but history, literature, biography, science, poetry, whatever expands the preacher's imagination and their understanding of the human condition. It means personal prayer and Scripture engagement that has no sermonic agenda. It means experiences that bring the preacher into genuine contact with realities outside their usual orbit.

Karl Barth is reported to have said that the preacher should preach with the Bible in one hand and the newspaper in the other [cite — confirm]. Whatever the accuracy of that specific attribution, the instinct is right: the preacher who is cut off from genuine contact with the world the congregation inhabits will eventually have nothing to say to that world. The sermon must come from somewhere — from genuine encounter with the text, genuine attention to the congregation, and genuine engagement with the culture in which both preacher and congregation are trying to live as followers of Jesus.

Genuine encounter is not produced by technique. It is produced by exposure. The preacher who takes a week to read a novel they have been meaning to read for three years, or who spends a day in a part of their city they have never spent time in before, or who has a long conversation with someone whose life experience is significantly different from their own — that preacher may find, weeks later, that something in the preaching has changed. Not because of the technique. Because of the exposure. The soil was amended, and the roots went deeper.

## A Concrete Scene

I know a pastor in his early fifties who had been preaching in the same congregation for fourteen years when he realized, sitting in his study one Wednesday morning with the passage for Sunday in front of him, that he had nothing to say. Not that he had run out of words — he had plenty of words. He could have assembled a technically competent sermon in two hours. What he did not have was anything he actually wanted to say, anything he genuinely believed the congregation needed to hear, anything that felt like it had come from somewhere real.

He did something he had not done in years: he closed his notes, got in his car, and drove to the neighborhood around the church. He walked for two hours. He talked to two business owners and a man sitting on the steps of a vacant building who turned out to have more theological insight than most of the seminarians the pastor had trained with. He came back and preached on Sunday with something he had not had on Wednesday: a reason.

Not a new topic. Not a new technique. A reason. He had been reminded of the actual people the sermon was for.

> The staleness is a signal. Not a sentence.

## Practical Experiments Worth Trying

If the preaching has gone stale, consider changing something about the process — not the commitment to biblical faithfulness, but the mechanics that surround it. Preach through a book of the Bible you have never preached before, one that genuinely challenges you. Invite a small group of laypeople to engage the text with you before you preach it and bring their questions and observations into the sermon. Change where you do your study. Change when you do your primary exegesis. Take a Sunday to preach something personal and difficult — not for the sake of drama, but because there is something you have been carrying that the congregation needs to hear.

Sometimes the staleness is not about the preaching at all — it is about the pastor's overall condition, and no homiletical adjustment will address what a genuine season of renewal needs to. If the staleness is accompanied by the other markers of depletion — disconnection, numbness, loss of joy — the sermon is not the problem to solve. The pastor is the condition to address, with the gentleness and seriousness that requires.

## The Weight of the Work

The congregation is not waiting for a polished performance. They are waiting, in the words they would never use, for someone who has been with God and can tell them what it was like. That is still the work. It was always the work.

The staleness is a signal. Not a sentence. The preacher who is honest about it, who takes the signal seriously and responds to it with the investment it requires, will find — most of the time, not always — that the dryness is not permanent. That the Word still has something to say through a person who has stopped pretending they already know what it is.

Go find out. Preach what you find.

Preaching that genuinely forms disciples — that actually changes how people think, pray, love, and engage the world — is one of the hardest things in ministry to do and one of the easiest to only appear to do. The sermon that sounds good, that generates positive feedback, that leaves the congregation feeling inspired and affirmed, is not necessarily the sermon that is doing the deep work of spiritual formation. And the habits that produce inspiring-but-shallow sermons are often deeply embedded in the preacher's practice long before anyone notices the formation gap.

This article names five of those habits directly — not to condemn but to surface, because the first step toward better preaching is honest recognition of what the current preaching is actually doing.

---

**Habit 1: Preaching to the Felt Need Without the Deeper Need**

Congregations have felt needs — the things they know they want help with. Parenting, marriage, finances, purpose, anxiety. These are real. Preaching that addresses them has genuine pastoral value, and a preacher who is tone-deaf to the actual burdens people carry is not serving the congregation, however theologically sophisticated the sermons may be.

## When the Inspiring Sermon Does the Shallow Work

But preaching that consistently *begins and ends* with felt needs tends to produce a congregation that knows how to apply biblical principles to the problems on the surface of their lives while having little formation at depth. The deeper need — for genuine encounter with a holy God, for the transformation of desire itself, for the capacity to suffer faithfully and love generously in the absence of visible reward — is rarely felt acutely until it is urgently needed. And by then, a diet of felt-need preaching has not prepared the congregation for it.

The person who has spent years receiving practical-application sermons about felt needs comes to the crisis of their life — the diagnosis, the grief, the slow collapse of the thing they had built — and finds that their faith, while real, is thin at the places where weight is now being applied. They were formed to handle the problems they expected. They were not formed to handle the problems that come without warning and do not yield to the principles.

The text often begins with felt needs and moves through them to something else — something that reorders the felt need by placing it inside a larger reality. Jesus does not simply address the anxiety of the crowd about food. He uses it to reveal who he is (John 6). Paul does not simply address the Corinthians' conflicts. He moves through them to the mystery of the cross as the subversion of every human hierarchy of wisdom and power (1 Corinthians 1-2). The felt need is the entrance. The preacher's job is to take the congregation where the text actually goes.

---

**Habit 2: Always Resolving the Tension**

> Great preaching creates tension before it resolves it.

Great preaching creates tension before it resolves it. The text creates a problem — about God, about human nature, about the gap between what is and what should be — and the sermon holds that tension long enough for it to do real work before offering resolution.

Many preachers rush to resolution because sitting in homiletical tension is uncomfortable and generates less positive feedback than comfort does. The sermon that leaves the congregation unsettled, that names the problem without offering an easy way through, will receive more ambivalent responses than the sermon that moves efficiently from problem to solution. The preacher who is managing their feedback will develop a systematic bias toward early resolution.

But the sermons that stay with people — that genuinely reshape them — are often the ones that held them in discomfort long enough for something to shift. The lament psalms do not resolve quickly. Psalm 88 does not resolve at all. Job holds the tension for forty-one chapters before God speaks, and when God speaks he does not explain the suffering — he describes himself in terms that make explanation beside the point (Job 38-41). The resolution comes, but it comes after the full weight of the problem has been named and carried, and it is a different kind of resolution than the one Job was asking for.

The congregation that has been trained, week after week, to expect early resolution loses the capacity to hold tension. They become consumers of spiritual comfort rather than people capable of sustained theological engagement. Monday comes, and the comfort of Sunday dissipates, and the discomfort of the actual life reasserts itself, and there is no interior formation to meet it — because the preaching never trained them to sit in it long enough for it to become ground.

---

## The Formation Gap Beneath the Applause

**Habit 3: Illustrating Everything With Success Stories**

The consistent use of success stories as sermon illustrations — here is someone who applied the principle and it worked out beautifully — creates a systematic distortion in the congregation's theological imagination. It implies that faithful application of biblical truth reliably produces good outcomes in visible, timely ways.

This is not the testimony of Scripture. Abel offered an acceptable sacrifice and was murdered (Genesis 4:8). Jeremiah preached faithfully for decades and watched his nation be destroyed. Stephen preached with full theological authority and was stoned immediately afterward (Acts 7:60). Paul applied the principles of the gospel with extraordinary faithfulness and ended in prison, in chains, and ultimately in execution.

The person in the pew who is applying the principles faithfully and not seeing the promised results begins to wonder what is wrong with them — rather than questioning the implied framework the preaching has built. That is the formation damage. Not doubt in God but doubt in themselves, created by a preaching habit that built an implied prosperity framework one success story at a time.

> They were formed to handle the problems they expected. They were not formed to handle the problems that come without warning and do not yield to the principles.

Include the laments. Include the failures. Include the stories where the faithful thing was done and the outcome was not what was hoped for. That is where most of the congregation actually lives, and they need to know that the gospel has something to say to them there — not as a consolation prize but as the deep thing itself.

---

**Habit 4: Never Preaching Anything That Costs You Something**

The safest sermon to preach is the one everyone agrees with in advance. The most dangerous is the one that names what the congregation would prefer not to name, confronts what they would prefer to leave unconfronted, and calls them to something that genuinely costs.

## Why the Costly Sermon Builds Trust

Most preachers have a mental list of the topics they systematically avoid — the things that would generate pushback, that would make certain powerful members uncomfortable, that would require the harder conversation on Monday. Those avoidances are costing the congregation more than the feedback they spare the preacher.

Ezekiel was told: "Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me. If I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you give him no warning… his blood I will require at your hand" (Ezekiel 3:17-18). The watchman's job is not to say what the city wants to hear. It is to say what the city needs to hear, at the cost of the watchman's comfort. That is the office. The preacher who systematically avoids the costly sermon is not being pastoral. They are being negligent — and they have confused the negative feedback they are avoiding with the thing it would have served.

The congregation, whatever they say on Sunday mornings, knows when the pastor is flinching. They can feel the avoidances as surely as they can feel the text being engaged honestly. The flinching builds, over time, a gap between the pulpit and the pew — a sense that the preacher is managing the congregation rather than serving them. The costly sermon, preached from genuine conviction, does more for pastoral trust in one Sunday than a year of comfortable sermons can undo.

---

**Habit 5: Ending Every Sermon With the Same Application Structure**

> The watchman's job is not to say what the city wants to hear.

If your sermons consistently end with three practical steps, or a salvation invitation, or a call to join a small group — regardless of which text was preached — you are training your congregation to anticipate the landing rather than be genuinely surprised by where the text takes them.

The text does not always end in three steps. The Psalms end in lament and doxology and raw, unresolved anguish. The prophets end in judgment and hope and the kind of ambiguity that requires the reader to keep living inside it. Lamentations ends with a question God does not answer (Lamentations 5:22). A preacher who imposes the same application structure on every text has decided, in advance, what shape the sermon should have — and that decision is made before the text is consulted.

The congregation that is trained on consistent structure loses the capacity to receive the sermon that does not fit it. They need to know what to do next. But the formation that actually sustains a life of faith is not the knowledge of what to do next. It is the deep interior capacity — the resilience, the capacity for lament, the ability to sit in unresolved tension and remain faithful — that comes from years of genuine encounter with the full texture of Scripture.

Great preaching is formally responsive to the specific passage. It ends where the text ends. It applies what the text applies. It demands what the text demands. And it trusts the congregation to carry what cannot be neatly resolved — which is most of what the life of faith actually requires.

---

## Letting the Text Decide the Shape

These five habits are not exotic. They are present in most preaching at some level, including mine. The formation gap they create is not dramatic or visible from one Sunday to the next. It accumulates quietly, over years, in the gap between what the congregation knows theologically and what they have been formed to hold in the actual conditions of their lives.

The Pastors Connection Network exists, in part, for exactly this kind of honest conversation — not critique from above but the collegial honesty that good preaching requires and pastoral isolation prevents. These habits are surfaceable. They are changeable. But only after they are seen.

That is what this naming is for. Not condemnation. Recognition. The work that follows it is the preacher's own.

Carey Nieuwhof's 2025 church trend research surfaced a statistic that should stop every pastor cold: only one percent of pastors rate their church as very effective at reaching people who have no church background. One percent. After decades of outreach programming, evangelism training, church growth methodology, and cultural relevance conversations, the overwhelming majority of churches in America have a Sunday morning that is almost entirely inaccessible to the people who most need what happens there.

Part of this is structural — the church has always struggled to reach those who do not come. But part of it is homiletical. The way most preachers are trained to preach assumes a level of biblical literacy and theological familiarity that a growing percentage of the culture simply does not have. The room that is there — the one full of people who already know the language and the stories and the assumptions — gets fed. The room that is not there yet — the one full of people who would be confused, alienated, or talked past by the average Sunday message — never gets invited back.

## The Historical Roots of the Problem

The homiletical tradition most American pastors inherited was shaped primarily for Christian audiences. The great preachers of the church's history — Augustine, Chrysostom, Luther, Wesley, Spurgeon, Jonathan Edwards — were, by and large, preaching to communities in which the Christian frame was culturally assumed. Even the revivalists of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries preached to audiences with significant prior exposure to Scripture and church culture. The unchurched person at a Whitefield meeting had still grown up in a Protestant England where the King James Bible was the national book.

The cultural context has shifted dramatically and relatively quickly. Robert Bellah's analysis of American individualism in *Habits of the Heart* [cite — confirm] identified the declining force of biblical religion as a public moral language as early as 1985. Charles Taylor's *A Secular Age* describes the movement from a society in which belief in God was the default, the unchallenged background, to one in which belief is one option among many [cite — confirm]. The person walking into your church for the first time in 2025 does not share the background assumptions that were still common in the person walking into a church for the first time in 1975.

And yet the preaching has not changed proportionally. The sermon that assumes biblical literacy, that uses insider language without explanation, that makes its arguments from scriptural authority without establishing why scriptural authority should be accepted — that sermon is operating in 1975 while standing in a room full of people from 2025.

## Understanding Who Isn't in the Room

The unchurched person who might one day find their way into your church does not share your background assumptions about the authority of Scripture, the basic contours of the gospel, or the meaning of common religious language. They may have a vague spirituality that bears little resemblance to Christian theology. They may have been hurt by a church or a religious family member and carry that wound into the room. They may simply be curious — responding to an invitation from a friend, open to something but not knowing what — and completely without the cultural competence to decode what is happening around them.

They are not stupid. They are not hostile. They are not a problem to be solved. They are people made in the image of God, for whom Christ died, who are sitting in your church because something brought them there, and who will decide within the first few minutes of your sermon whether to come back based on whether what you are saying seems to have anything to do with their actual life.

> They are not stupid. They are not hostile. They are not a problem to be solved.

The preacher who has never consciously imagined this person is preaching to a room that will never include them. The preacher who has genuinely imagined them — who has sat with their questions, who has felt the weight of their skepticism, who has asked what a person with no Christian background would hear in this sentence, this illustration, this appeal — is doing something that requires both homiletical skill and genuine pastoral empathy.

Tim Keller modeled this consistently in his years at Redeemer Presbyterian Church in Manhattan, where the congregation included a significant proportion of unchurched professionals who were intellectually serious and spiritually skeptical. His approach was not to simplify the gospel but to surface and answer the objections that his unchurched listeners would raise rather than assuming away the need for an apologetic [cite — confirm]. He took the questions of the room that was not yet there seriously enough to make them the starting point of his preaching.

## Preaching That Includes Without Compromising

Preaching to the unchurched does not mean abandoning theological substance or diluting the gospel to the point of inoffensiveness. The goal is not a message that does not challenge anyone. It is a message whose challenge is accessible, whose terms are defined, and whose assumptions are made explicit rather than assumed.

In practice, this means defining terms that feel obvious to the regular attender but are not. What is grace, exactly — not the theological definition that the congregation could recite, but the thing it actually refers to in human experience, the thing that makes it distinct from what the world offers in its place? What does "the cross" mean, and why does it matter — not to someone who grew up in Sunday school, but to someone who has spent their adult life constructing a moral framework that does not include it? What is the church, and what is it for — and how is the answer different from what the person sitting in that seat has assumed based on every interaction they have had with Christianity so far?

It means connecting the text to universal human experiences — longing, failure, grief, hope, the search for meaning — before connecting it to specific theological categories. The person who has no framework for "justification by faith" has a framework for the experience of being found acceptable, of being forgiven for something that felt unforgivable, of receiving something they did not earn. Start there. The theological category will follow if the human experience is genuinely entered first.

And it means adopting a posture in the pulpit that is genuinely curious and genuinely inviting rather than one that speaks from assumed authority to assumed agreement. The unchurched person is listening for contempt — for the preacher's implicit communication that people who do not already believe are less intelligent, less moral, or less worthy of being taken seriously. They have experienced enough of it to have an excellent detector for it. Remove it entirely from your preaching.

## The Pastoral Scene

> Start there. The theological category will follow if the human experience is genuinely entered first.

A young woman named Sarah attended a church for the first time on Easter Sunday, brought by a friend who had been asking her to come for two years. She had no church background, had read exactly none of the Bible, and arrived with the specific expectation that the service would be irrelevant to her actual life and that she would be making a quiet exit as soon as it was socially acceptable.

The pastor's sermon that Sunday was on John 20 — Mary Magdalene at the empty tomb, the disciples running, the conversation between Mary and the risen Jesus. The pastor began not with the resurrection's theological significance but with what Mary was actually doing there: she had come to care for a body. She expected death. She was bringing what you bring when someone you love is irreversibly gone. The pastor spent four minutes describing what that felt like — the specific kind of grief that is the grief of the day after, when the shock has worn off and the finality is settling in.

Sarah told me later that those four minutes were why she came back the following Sunday. Not the theology. The recognition. The preacher had accurately described something she had felt at her mother's graveside three years earlier, and that accurate description created enough trust for her to stay for the rest.

The resurrection arrived in the sermon after the grief had been genuinely entered. She could receive it because she had been met first.

## What Happens to Your Regular Attenders

Here is what many pastors fear but should not: that preaching in a way that is accessible to the unchurched will bore or diminish the experience for the theologically formed regular attender. The opposite tends to be true.

Sermons that begin with genuine human reality, that take the time to surface and answer objections rather than assuming agreement, and that connect the gospel to the actual texture of ordinary life tend to be more engaging for everyone — including the person who has been in the church for decades. Depth and accessibility are not opposites. The best preaching achieves both, and does so not by splitting the difference between them but by refusing to accept the premise that they are in competition.

> Depth and accessibility are not opposites.

The regular attender who has heard the resurrection story fifty times has not heard the version of it that genuinely answers a thoughtful skeptic's best objection. Watching their pastor answer that objection with genuine intellectual honesty is often one of the most formation-producing experiences they have in the pew.

## The Verdict

One percent. That is the number to sit with. One pastor in a hundred rates his congregation as genuinely effective at reaching the people the church claims to be trying to reach.

The gap between what the church says it is for and what its Sunday morning actually produces is enormous, and the sermon is one of the primary places where that gap either narrows or widens.

The room that is not there yet is full of people who deserve a preacher who has imagined them before he arrived at the pulpit — who has asked what they would hear, what they would need, what would have to be true of the next sixty minutes for them to consider that coming here was worth their Sunday morning.

Ask that question before you preach. Let it shape the opening. Let it shape the terms you define and the objections you answer and the human reality you enter before the theological category you name.

The room that is not there yet will fill, or it will not. But the first step is preaching as if it could.

The statistic from Tony Morgan and The Unstuck Group has become one of the most-cited in pastoral leadership conversations, and it has become that because it refuses to let the church pretend the situation is better than it is: eighty to eighty-five percent of churches in America are either plateaued or declining [cite — confirm]. Not growing — maintaining at best, losing ground at worst. And the pastors leading these churches often know something is wrong but cannot quite name what it is.

The first and hardest step toward addressing a plateau is the honest acknowledgment that it exists. This sounds obvious, but it is not easy in practice. The language of faith — of seasons, of God's timing, of faithfulness over fruitfulness — can become a sophisticated way of avoiding the honest assessment of whether the church is genuinely stuck and why. Seasons can be real. They can also be convenient. The pastor who cannot tell the difference between patient faithfulness and comfortable avoidance is at risk of leading a church that stays stuck.

## The Longer History of This Problem

The plateau problem is not new, though the scale of it is newly visible. The mainline Protestant denominations began their sustained numerical decline in the late 1960s, and sociologists at the time identified it as a structural shift rather than a temporary dip — a consequence of the loosening of the social pressures that had maintained religious affiliation across several generations [cite — confirm]. The evangelical church, which had largely grown through those same decades and interpreted its growth as the fruit of theological fidelity, began to face its own plateau in the early years of this century, and the metrics that emerged were sobering.

The church growth movement of the 1970s and 1980s — built on the insights of Donald McGavran and church growth researchers at Fuller Theological Seminary — had promised that the application of social science to ecclesiology would produce measurable growth [cite — confirm]. The experiments that followed produced some genuine fruit and also produced a generation of churches that were better at marketing than at discipleship, better at attraction than at formation. By the 1990s, Willow Creek Community Church itself had commissioned research suggesting that its seeker-sensitive model was producing large audiences without producing formed disciples, a conclusion that its own leadership publicly acknowledged with remarkable honesty [cite — confirm].

The plateau crisis is, in part, the harvest of several decades of church strategy that prioritized attendance over formation. A church that optimized for gathering people was not, necessarily, optimizing for the thing that produces growth in the New Testament sense: genuine disciples who make genuine disciples, who carry the gospel into their networks and communities in ways that generate genuine new life.

## What a Plateau Actually Looks Like

> Seasons can be real. They can also be convenient.

A plateau is not always a period of flat attendance. A plateau is the condition of a church that is not fulfilling its potential for the mission it has been given in the community it inhabits. A church can be numerically stable and deeply plateaued — maintaining its numbers through transfer growth while having no genuine impact on the unchurched people in its community. A church can even be growing numerically and still be plateaued in its actual discipleship impact, adding attendees without producing disciples.

The more honest diagnostic questions are not about attendance trajectory but about mission effectiveness. Is the church reaching people who were not previously connected to any church? Is there evidence of genuine life transformation in the congregation? Are people being sent from the church into the community and the world with the gospel, or is the church primarily organized around gathering and consuming? Is the leadership of the church deepening and multiplying, or is it dependent on the same small group of people doing the same things they have always done?

These are harder questions to answer than attendance questions, and they require a kind of honest self-examination that is uncomfortable for leaders who have invested their professional identity in the health of the institution they lead. I have sat in rooms with pastors who could describe every metric of their church's activity in precise detail and who had no idea whether any of it was producing genuine disciples. The metrics they tracked were not the metrics that mattered. That is a form of blindness that is very common and very hard to see from the inside.

## A Steel-Manned Counter-Position

The most serious pushback on plateau-focused pastoral leadership comes from a direction that deserves to be heard: the argument that the numerical growth framework itself is the problem, not the solution. This argument says that the preoccupation with growth metrics — attendance, giving, baptisms, small group enrollment — has distorted the church's understanding of its own mission. Faithfulness is not the same as fruitfulness. The prophets preached in declining Israel. Jeremiah's ministry produced no visible success by any metric and enormous personal suffering. Jesus himself watched his crowd thin dramatically in John 6 after the feeding of the five thousand and appeared to accept the departure as a consequence of faithfulness rather than a failure of strategy. Perhaps the plateaued church is not failing. Perhaps it is being faithful.

This is not a frivolous argument. It names something real: the church is not a business, growth is not the only measure of faithfulness, and the preoccupation with scale has produced genuine distortions in pastoral ministry. A pastor who leads a congregation of forty people faithfully for thirty years, knowing them deeply, loving them genuinely, and forming them slowly in the way of Jesus, has done something that cannot be dismissed because it does not show up well on a church growth chart.

> Culture eats strategy for breakfast — and it also eats church growth methodology.

But the argument overreaches in one specific direction. The same Jesus who watched the crowd thin in John 6 gave the Great Commission in Matthew 28. The same Paul who wrote about suffering and weakness as the condition of apostolic ministry also described his ambition to preach the gospel where it had not yet been heard. The church that uses the theology of faithfulness to exempt itself from the question of whether it is actually reaching its community has made faithfulness a justification for disengagement. That is not faithfulness. It is contentment with smallness dressed in theological language.

## Common Causes of Plateaus

Tony Morgan and the Unstuck Group have identified several patterns that appear consistently in plateaued churches [cite — confirm]. One is leadership that has not kept pace with the church's development — a pastor who led the church effectively at two hundred people but has not developed the skills and structures needed to lead at five hundred. Another is internal focus — a church whose energy and resources are predominantly directed inward, toward serving its own members, rather than outward, toward the community it was placed to reach. A third is structural rigidity — systems and processes that were designed for an earlier season and have become barriers to effectiveness in the current one.

A fourth, often overlooked, is cultural health. A church that has allowed toxic relational dynamics, unresolved conflict, or a culture of criticism to take root will struggle to grow regardless of the quality of its programs or preaching. Culture eats strategy for breakfast — and it also eats church growth methodology.

## A Concrete Scene

I know a pastor who led a congregation for eleven years while it plateaued quietly around two hundred and twenty people. He was not a bad pastor. He preached well, cared genuinely, and managed the church's internal life with competence. What he had never done was ask the question that most needed asking: Who is this church for? The congregation had a clear implicit answer to that question — it existed for the people who already attended — and everything it did reflected that answer. The pastoral care was for members. The programming was for families already connected. The Sunday experience was designed to serve the people already in the room.

> The plateau is not a verdict. It is a condition.

He brought an outside consultant who spent two days asking the congregation that question in different forms. What emerged was not a program change. It was a reorientation of the church's self-understanding — from a community that served its members to a community sent to its neighborhood. The growth that followed was slow and not dramatic. But it was genuine: people who had no prior church connection, who had been in the neighborhood for years while the church focused elsewhere, who began to find a reason to walk through the door.

## Starting the Honest Conversation

If you suspect your church is plateaued, the most useful thing you can do is bring an outside perspective into the diagnosis. Not because you cannot see the situation accurately, but because the pastor is so embedded in the church's culture that certain things become invisible through familiarity. An outside coach, a trusted peer network, or a structured assessment process can surface what proximity conceals.

The Pastors Connection Network exists partly to give pastors access to this kind of perspective — not as a consulting firm, but as a community of peers who have navigated similar terrain and can offer the honest, experienced, relationally-grounded perspective that coaches are paid for but friends give freely. If your church is stuck, you do not need to figure it out alone.

The plateau is not a verdict. It is a condition. Conditions can change. But they do not change without honesty about what they are.

The contemporary church conversation is dominated by large churches. The conferences feature their pastors. The podcasts interview their leaders. The methodology books emerge from their experiments. The implicit message — rarely stated directly but consistently communicated — is that the large church is the model toward which all faithful churches should aspire, and that smaller churches are simply earlier stages in a developmental arc that points toward scale.

This framing is not only condescending to the majority of pastors and congregations in America — the vast majority of churches in the US have fewer than one hundred attendees [cite — confirm] — it is also wrong. Small churches do not simply do what large churches do, but less of it. They do some things differently, and in doing them differently, they often do them better. Those differences deserve to be named, celebrated, and learned from.

## The Historical Record

The small congregation has been the normative form of Christian community for most of the church's history. The house churches of the first century that Paul addresses in his letters — the congregation meeting in Priscilla and Aquila's home (Romans 16:5), the gathering in Nympha's house (Colossians 4:15), the community at Philemon's table — were small by any contemporary definition. Not small as a developmental stage waiting to graduate to something more significant. Small as the basic form through which the gospel moved through the Roman world with a speed and penetration that the imperial government found threatening enough to persecute.

The Reformation's parish structure, whatever its failures, was organized around the assumption that a pastor should know the actual people in their care — that the relationship between shepherd and sheep required a scale at which genuine knowledge was possible. The nineteenth-century circuit rider, the twentieth-century neighborhood church, the rural congregation that has served the same families for four generations — these are not relics. They are expressions of something the Christian tradition has consistently understood to matter: that genuine community requires a scale at which genuine community is possible.

The megachurch is the historical anomaly. Not a failure — genuine megachurches have produced genuine disciples and genuine kingdom impact — but a departure from the norm, and departures from the norm carry costs that are worth examining honestly.

## Genuine Community Is Harder to Fake

In a congregation of forty or sixty or eighty people, there is nowhere to hide. Everyone knows everyone. People know when someone is missing from Sunday and they call to find out why. People know who is sick, whose marriage is struggling, whose kids are going through something hard. The pastoral care is embedded in the fabric of the community itself, not delivered by a staff person whose job title is Care Pastor.

This is one of the most significant gifts of small church life and one of the hardest things to reproduce at scale. Large churches work hard and spend significant resources attempting to create the conditions of genuine community — small groups, neighborhood groups, affinity-based gatherings — that the small church has naturally, by virtue of its size. The small church does not need to manufacture belonging. It simply is a place where you belong.

> The megachurch is the historical anomaly.

Robert Bellah's work in *Habits of the Heart* [cite — confirm] identified the erosion of genuine community as one of the defining losses of American modernity — the replacement of thick, accountable, face-to-face community with thin, voluntary, easily exited associations. The small church is one of the few remaining institutions in American life that provides what Bellah was describing: a community where people are genuinely known, genuinely accountable, and genuinely needed. That is not a small thing. In the context of an epidemic of loneliness and disconnection, it may be one of the most countercultural gifts the church can offer.

## A Steel-Manned Counter-Position

The strongest version of the case for large church ministry needs to be heard before it is answered. The argument is this: small churches often produce small vision. They are frequently inward-focused, conflict-ridden, and resistant to change precisely because everyone knows everyone — the same relational intimacy that produces community also produces the dynamics of a family system, with all the dysfunction that implies. Large churches can mobilize resources, develop specialized ministries, and reach populations that small churches simply cannot access. The growth is not vanity. It is capacity.

This is a real argument and it is sometimes correct. The small church that has become a chaplaincy for its existing members — organized entirely around serving the people already inside rather than reaching the community outside — is not doing what the New Testament envisions. And the conflict that can metastasize in small churches, where a single controlling family or a long-standing grievance can hold an entire congregation hostage, is a genuine pathology that scale can sometimes dilute.

But the answer to small church dysfunction is not to abandon the small church as a form. It is to address the dysfunction. A healthy small church is not a scaled-down version of a healthy large church. It is something genuinely different, with its own strengths and its own temptations, and the work of pastoral leadership in a small congregation is not the work of preparing it to become large. It is the work of helping it become faithfully itself.

## The Bivocational and Volunteer Reality

Many small churches are led by bivocational pastors and sustained by volunteer leaders who give their time and gifts because they genuinely love the congregation and the mission — not because they are professional religious workers. This produces a different kind of ministry ownership than staff-driven churches tend to generate.

When a church member teaches the children's class because there is no one else to do it and because they love those kids, something different happens in that classroom than when a hired director runs a curriculum-based program. The love is not borrowed from an organizational chart. It is personal. It is specific. It is the love of someone who has known these particular children in this particular neighborhood for years and who is not going to take another position when a better opportunity presents itself.

> The small church does not need to manufacture belonging. It simply is a place where you belong.

The small church tends to produce high levels of lay ownership of the ministry. People who would be consumers in a large church with excellent programming become contributors in a small church where contribution is simply what you do. That ownership produces a depth of investment in the congregation's life and mission that large churches often try hard to generate through volunteer recruitment systems. In the small church, it is not recruited. It is structural.

Eugene Peterson spent most of his pastoral ministry in a single congregation — Christ Our King Presbyterian Church in Bel Air, Maryland — precisely because he believed that genuine pastoral work required the long attentiveness that only a stable, particular, small-enough community could make possible [cite — confirm]. His vision of the pastor as a spiritual director rather than an organizational CEO was not abstract. It emerged from the specific conditions of a congregation small enough to know by name.

## Adaptability and Proximity to the Community

A small church in a specific neighborhood tends to know that neighborhood with an intimacy that a regional large church, drawing from a wide geographic area, cannot match. The small church pastor knows the local school principal, knows the families in the surrounding streets, knows the specific struggles of the particular community they inhabit. This proximity is a missional asset.

I think of a congregation I know in a mid-sized industrial city — sixty-five people, meeting in a building they have worshipped in for forty years. When the largest employer in their neighborhood closed and the unemployment in their ZIP code doubled in eighteen months, they did not need a staff meeting to figure out what to do. They already knew who needed help. They already had the relationships. They were already in the room. Their response was immediate and specific because their knowledge was immediate and specific.

A large church bringing resources to that same neighborhood would have done genuine good. But it would have arrived as an institution serving a community. The small church did not arrive. It was already there.

Small churches can also change direction more quickly than large institutions. A large church that decides to shift its community engagement strategy has to move through staff structures, budget processes, and communication campaigns. A small church can decide on Sunday and start on Wednesday. This adaptability makes small churches genuinely effective in specific community ministry contexts that require responsiveness and relationship.

## What the Numbers Actually Mean

The pastoral scorecard of the contemporary church has been almost entirely quantitative: attendance, giving, baptisms, small group enrollment. These numbers matter. But they do not tell the full story, and in some cases they actively obscure what the story actually is.

> The small church did not arrive. It was already there.

A small church can measure: the percentage of its congregation that is actively serving in the community rather than only attending services. The number of people who have been genuinely known by name for more than a decade. The pastoral care hours that were provided by members of the congregation to other members, not by paid staff. The families that were held together in crisis by the community surrounding them. These are not soft metrics. They are measures of what the church is actually for.

The congregation that is small and genuinely alive — genuinely caring for one another, genuinely engaging the community, genuinely making disciples who make disciples — is not a failure waiting to be fixed. It is the church doing what the church is for. We would do well to notice that, and to say it aloud.

## What Large Churches Should Learn

The conversation does not need to be adversarial. Large churches have gifts and capacities that small churches lack, and genuine collaboration across size is one of the things the Pastors Connection Network is designed to facilitate. But the learning needs to go in both directions. Large churches should be asking: What have we lost at scale that was genuinely valuable? How do we recover the conditions of genuine community? How do we produce the lay ownership and neighborhood intimacy that small churches have as their natural inheritance?

The answers to those questions may be the most important leadership work in the American church for the next generation. Not because every large church should become small, but because the things small churches do naturally — know people, hold people, be present in places — are the things the gospel requires, and they require intention and sacrifice at scale that small churches provide simply by being what they are.

Most pastors leading small churches will never speak at a conference. Their names will not appear on the podcasts. Their methodology will never be packaged and sold. And their congregations — forty, sixty, eighty people gathered in worship in a particular neighborhood — are doing some of the most faithful work in the American church.

It is time we said so.

Great preaching creates tension before it resolves it. The text creates a problem — about God, about human nature, about the gap between what is and what should be — and the sermon holds that tension long enough for it to do real work in the congregation before offering resolution.

Many preachers rush to resolution because sitting in homiletical tension is uncomfortable and generates less positive feedback than comfort does. The sermon that leaves the congregation unsettled — that names the problem without immediately offering the way through it, that holds the hard question open long enough for it to become genuinely difficult — will receive more ambivalent responses than the sermon that moves efficiently from problem to solution. Preachers who manage their feedback develop, over time, a systematic bias toward early resolution.

But the sermons that stay with people — that genuinely change them — are often the ones that held them in discomfort long enough for something to shift. Not discomfort for its own sake. Discomfort in service of the text's actual work.

---

The texts that form people most deeply do not resolve quickly. That is not accidental.

## What the Unresolved Texts Are Doing in the Canon

Psalm 88 is the only lament psalm in the Psalter that does not end in praise. It moves through fourteen verses of sustained darkness — "my soul is full of troubles," "I am shut in so that I cannot escape," "your wrath has swept over me" — and it ends in darkness: "darkness is my closest friend." [cite — confirm Psalm 88:18, exact translation.] No resolution. No turn. The psalm is in the canon because it is a true account of a real human experience that the people of God need to be able to pray — the experience of being genuinely lost inside suffering, without the immediate comfort of a turn toward light.

The preacher who cannot preach Psalm 88 without inserting a resolution that is not in the text has told the congregation, by the insertion, that that experience — darkness without immediate resolution — is not a legitimate resting place for faith. The person in the pew who is living in exactly that experience learns two things: first, that the Bible does not speak directly to their condition; second, that the church cannot hold what they are carrying. Both are false, but the premature resolution made them feel true.

Job holds the tension for forty-one chapters. The speeches of Job's friends are exactly the kind of efficient resolution the pastor who rushes to comfort would provide — they name the problem (suffering), offer the explanation (sin), and propose the solution (repent). They are theologically tidy and pastorally catastrophic, and God tells them at the end that they have not spoken rightly (Job 42:7). The resolution, when it comes, is not an explanation. It is an encounter — God speaking from the whirlwind, describing the creation in terms that make human questions about suffering seem differently sized, not answered but reframed by being placed inside a reality larger than Job had apprehended (Job 38-41).

That is the resolution Scripture offers for the deepest suffering: not explanation but encounter, not answers but a God large enough that the questions become differently weighted. The preacher who rushes to the efficient explanation has offered Job's friends' sermon when the text is asking them to take the congregation to the whirlwind.

---

> Great preaching creates tension before it resolves it.

The formation that happens in the tension is not available without the tension.

When a congregation is held inside a real problem — when the preacher has named something honestly and has not immediately rescued them from the naming — a specific kind of interior work becomes possible. The problem lands. It connects with the actual experience people carry into the room. It stops being an abstract theological issue and becomes a live thing, something with weight, something that generates a genuine need for what the gospel is going to say.

The resolution that follows is received differently. It is received as rescue, as word that arrives after real need has been established, as the thing the congregation actually requires rather than the thing they expected. The emotional and spiritual register is different from the resolution that arrives before the tension has had time to do its work — different the way food tastes different when you are genuinely hungry rather than eating by schedule.

This is not a technique. It is a natural consequence of taking the text seriously. The texts that form people were not designed with efficient resolution in mind. They were written by people who had been in the tension themselves — who had cried from the depths (Psalm 130:1), who had wrestled through the night (Genesis 32:24), who had sat by the rivers of Babylon without a song to sing (Psalm 137:1) — and who knew that the word from God that mattered was the word received after the full weight of the problem had been carried.

## The Formation That Happens Only Inside the Tension

---

A concrete pastoral scene.

A woman in the congregation is in the second year of an illness that has not improved. She has prayed. She has been prayed for. She is not losing her faith but she is losing her certainty that God operates the way the sermons have implied — that faithfulness is followed, in timeframes that make practical sense, by the visible love of God in changed circumstances.

She comes to church on a Sunday when the text is Romans 8:28: "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good." The preacher resolves the tension in the verse within four minutes. God is in control. The trials will have purpose. The outcome will be positive. Here are three things to remember when you are in the valley.

She leaves knowing the verse better. She leaves unchanged, and more alone, because the resolution arrived before the tension was allowed to be what it actually is — before the sermon was willing to hold the question that the verse raises: what do you do in the period between the affliction and the good that is supposed to come from it, which may be very long, which may outlast the life, which may be visible only from a vantage point you will not occupy on this side of the resurrection?

> That is the resolution Scripture offers for the deepest suffering: not explanation but encounter, not answers but a God large enough that the questions become differently weighted.

That question is in the passage, in the context of Romans 8. The chapter includes "the sufferings of this present time" (Romans 8:18), and the groan of creation and the groan of the Spirit (Romans 8:22-26), and the intercession of the Spirit for those who do not know how to pray because the pain has taken the words (Romans 8:26). The passage holds the tension for the full chapter before the declaration of Romans 8:38-39. The preacher who resolves it in four minutes has not preached Romans 8. They have extracted a verse from it and offered it as a comfort that the chapter was building to, not starting with.

---

The counter-position has pastoral weight.

Some congregants come to church in genuine crisis, and the last thing they need is a sermon that adds to their burden. The person who has been in the darkness all week does not need the church to increase the darkness on Sunday morning. They need the light — and the preacher who withholds it out of a commitment to holding tension longer is prioritizing craft over compassion.

## When Comfort Is the Faithful Word

That argument has real force in specific situations. There are pastoral moments — the Sunday after a community tragedy, the sermon during a specific congregational crisis — where the primary need is the word of comfort, and the preacher who insists on full homiletical tension before the comfort arrives has misread the room.

But the argument breaks down as a general principle. The person in crisis needs the comfort that is adequate to the crisis — which means the comfort that has been through the same territory, not around it. The most powerful pastoral word is not the word that never entered the darkness. It is the word that went all the way in and came out the other side carrying something. "For our light and momentary troubles are achieving for us an eternal glory that far outweighs them all" (2 Corinthians 4:17) — Paul writes this from inside the afflictions he described three verses earlier: hard pressed, perplexed, persecuted, struck down (2 Corinthians 4:8-9). The comfort has authority because it was earned in the darkness, not spoken from outside it.

The preacher who has been in the tension personally, and who preaches the comfort from inside the full weight of what it is answering, offers something entirely different from the preacher who moves efficiently to the resolution before the tension has been felt. The congregation can tell the difference. They may not be able to articulate it, but they feel it.

---

> The preacher who rushes past it is not being kind.

Learning to sit in the tension — as a preacher, not as a technique but as a practice — requires the preacher to develop tolerance for the discomfort of not resolving things. Many preachers are people who are constitutionally motivated to fix things, to find the answer, to move through difficulty toward clarity. That is a good impulse in many pastoral contexts. In the pulpit, it sometimes works against the text.

The disciplines that build this tolerance are mostly outside the pulpit. Sitting with Lamentations and not moving on too quickly. Sitting with the patients who are not getting better and not offering the platitude that insults the severity of what they are carrying. Sitting with the family after the funeral when there is nothing to say and not filling the silence with things designed to make the silence more bearable.

Those disciplines form a preacher who knows, in their body and not just in their theology, that there is something on the other side of the darkness. And that knowledge — not as information but as formation — is what produces preaching that can hold the tension long enough for it to do its work without drowning in it.

---

The sermon that genuinely changes people holds them in the gap long enough for the gap to feel real. The gap between who they are and who they are called to be. The gap between what they experience and what they have been promised. The gap between the God they were taught and the God they have encountered in the hours when the teaching did not hold.

## Forming the Preacher Who Can Hold the Gap

That gap is not the enemy of faith. It is the place where faith develops — where the easy confidence that does not know what it costs gives way to the harder trust that has been tested and held.

The preacher who rushes past it is not being kind. They are denying the congregation the sermon they came for — the one that names the thing they have been carrying alone and holds it long enough that they know: this is the territory the gospel is built for.

End there sometimes. Not as a structural move, but because that is where the text ends, and the text knows what it is doing.

New pastors often feel that being available to everyone at all times is the highest expression of pastoral love. In reality, it is a path to burnout that serves no one well. A pastor who has no margin has no depth — and depth is exactly what people need in a crisis.

That equation sounds simple. It is not. The pull toward total availability is not laziness or boundary confusion — it is something that feels, in the moment, like love. The phone rings at 10 p.m. and someone is struggling, and saying yes to the call feels like giving yourself away for the flock. It feels like the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one (Luke 15:4). And it is not wrong to feel that pull. What is wrong is mistaking the feeling for a theology of ministry.

The shepherd in that parable comes back. He finds the lost sheep and he carries it home, and then there is a feast. The parable is not about a shepherd who spent every hour searching every hillside for every sheep simultaneously. It is about focused attention at a moment of acute need, followed by restoration, followed by community. There is a shape to it. The shape matters.

## The Structural Trap

The mistake most new pastors make is not moral. It is architectural. They build a ministry structure that has no design for rest, for preparation, for the pastor's own spiritual formation — and then they are surprised when the building collapses under its own weight. Eugene Peterson called this "the busy pastor" in his writing on pastoral ministry, and he was not gentle about it [cite — confirm]. He argued that busyness in a pastor is not a sign of dedication. It is a sign of disorder. The busy pastor has confused activity with faithfulness, and the confusion costs everyone, most of all the people who need genuine spiritual care.

What does total availability actually produce? Consider what it does to the sermon. A pastor who has given his full attention to the urgencies of the week arrives at Sunday morning depleted, with whatever he could scrape together in the hours that remained. The congregation receives something that was assembled under pressure. They do not know this. They receive it as care, because they trust the pastor. But what they are actually receiving is the residue of a man who has given everything to the immediate and had nothing left for the considered.

The congregation deserves the prepared pastor. Preparation requires time that is protected from interruption. That time is not selfishness. It is part of the pastor's job — arguably the most important part, the part that allows everything else to be done well.

> The mistake most new pastors make is not moral. It is architectural.

## What Genuine Care Requires

Genuine pastoral care requires a pastor who has been nourished themselves. Setting boundaries on your availability is not selfishness — it is stewardship of the resource your congregation most needs: you, at your best.

The word stewardship applies here precisely because the pastor does not belong to himself. He belongs to the congregation and to God. And the congregation's long-term interest is not a pastor who is present at every moment but gradually hollowing out. Their long-term interest is a pastor who is present at the moments that matter most with something real to give.

I have made the other mistake. I have prided myself on being the pastor who always picks up the phone, who never says no to a hospital visit, who returns every message the same day. And I have stood in the pulpit on Sunday having given away everything that week and preached something that I am not proud of — not because I do not care about the text, but because I arrived at the text with nothing left. The congregation that week did not receive care. They received performance. The distinction matters and I did not always have the courage to admit it.

The counter-position deserves an honest hearing: is there not a risk that a pastor who schedules and protects his time will become inaccessible, distant, the kind of leader who cares more about his study than his sheep? Yes. That risk is real. It is the failure mode in the opposite direction. The pastor who has so fortified his calendar that crises feel like intrusions has mistaken order for ministry. He has confused a healthy structure with a spiritual discipline, and the people in his care will feel the coldness of it.

The answer is not to swing between the two errors. It is to develop the discernment that the structures are meant to serve. Protected time is not a rule to follow; it is a value to practice — the value of arriving at the work with depth enough to actually do it. When genuine urgency arises, the prepared pastor can give himself away freely because he is not already empty. The margin makes the interruption possible without becoming the pattern.

> He has constructed a pastoral identity that is functionally self-sufficient, and self-sufficiency is not a Christian virtue. It is the fall's signature.

## The Theological Ground

There is a theological claim underneath all of this that is worth making explicit. The pastor who cannot receive care — who cannot name his own need, protect his own soul, or acknowledge that he too is a creature with limits — has subtly placed himself outside the Gospel he preaches. He has constructed a pastoral identity that is functionally self-sufficient, and self-sufficiency is not a Christian virtue. It is the fall's signature.

Jesus withdrew. Not once, as an exception, but repeatedly, as a pattern. He withdrew to pray (Luke 5:16). He withdrew after the feeding of the five thousand (Matthew 14:23). He withdrew before the crucifixion to Gethsemane, and the withdrawal was not escape — it was preparation, the night before the hardest hour. If the Son of God built withdrawal into his own ministry rhythm, the pastor who believes he cannot afford to is not being more faithful than Jesus. He is being less honest about his own nature.

Paul makes the same point structurally. He asks the Thessalonians to pray for him (1 Thessalonians 5:25). He asks the Romans to strive together with him in prayer (Romans 15:30). The apostle to the Gentiles, the man who planted churches across the Mediterranean world, publicly acknowledged his need for the prayers of the people he served. He did not perform self-sufficiency. He named a real dependence. The pastor who refuses to do the same has not surpassed Paul. He has simply closed himself off from something Paul was wise enough to receive.

## What to Build Instead
