Karl Barth's Theological Declaration of Barmen in 1934 was written against German Christians who had accommodated the Nazi state, and its central claim — that Jesus Christ alone is the Lord of the church — was a directly political claim made against the political theology of the moment [cite — confirm].

> Silence in the face of injustice is a posture.

These precedents are not exact analogies to the present situation, and the pastoral instinct to draw too-clean historical parallels should be resisted. But they establish something important: the question of how the church relates to political power is not a new one, and the temptations that pastors face in politically charged environments are not new either. The temptation to alignment and the temptation to silence have both appeared before. Both have led churches away from their calling. Both are available again today.

## The Temptations on Each Side

The temptation on one side is to align the church with a political identity — to become, in effect, a religious expression of a particular political tribe. This is the path of least resistance for pastors in politically homogeneous congregations, and it produces short-term unity at the cost of the church's prophetic independence and its capacity to speak to anyone outside the tribe. When the church becomes politically captured, it loses the very thing that makes it valuable to the people inside and outside its walls: the capacity to speak from a perspective that is genuinely other than the culture's prevailing options.

The sociologist Robert Bellah noted in his later work that the great danger for American religion was its tendency to become the religious ratification of American culture rather than its prophetic critic [cite — confirm]. That tendency — which Bellah traced across the full sweep of American religious history — reaches an extreme form when the church becomes the religious expression of a political party. The god of that church is no longer the God of the Scriptures. It is the political tribe's idealized self-image dressed in theological language.

The temptation on the other side is to retreat into a false neutrality — to refuse any engagement with political realities in the name of keeping the peace. This is sometimes called "not being political," but it is itself a political act. Silence in the face of injustice is a posture. Refusal to speak to the moral dimensions of political questions is a choice, and it is a choice that has consequences for the church's integrity and its relationship to the communities it serves.

Lesslie Newbigin argued that there is no such thing as a gospel that has no public implications [cite — confirm]. The claim that Jesus is Lord is a claim about the ordering of all things — about power, about the treatment of the poor, about justice and mercy and the dignity of human beings made in the image of God. A church that preaches this gospel without ever applying it to the publicly contested questions of its day has not achieved neutrality. It has achieved irrelevance, which is a different failure but a failure nonetheless.

## A Steel-Manned Counter-Position

The strongest version of the case for pastoral restraint in political matters is not cowardice but a genuine concern for pastoral authority. The argument goes: a pastor who is perceived as politically partisan loses credibility with the members of the congregation who belong to the other political tribe, and in losing that credibility, loses the capacity to pastor them. The preacher who has become a political commentator has destroyed the one thing that makes the pastoral office distinctive — the authority that comes from being seen as a person who serves God rather than a party.

There is wisdom in this. The pastor who cannot be trusted to hold the congregation's political diversity with genuine care — who regularly signals their own political loyalties from the pulpit in ways that make members of the other party feel judged rather than pastored — has damaged their effectiveness in ways that are not easily repaired. Pastoral authority is relational. It is built over years and can be eroded in a single sermon.

But the answer to this concern is not to say nothing. It is to say the right things in the right way. The pastor who engages the moral dimensions of political questions while refusing the partisan framing of those questions has not surrendered pastoral authority. They have exercised it in its truest form: by calling the congregation to a standard that transcends the options the political culture provides.

## What the Pulpit Actually Owes the Congregation

What the congregation deserves from the pulpit is not political analysis, not partisan commentary, and not the pastor's personal political preferences dressed up in theological language. What they deserve is the consistent, faithful application of the Scriptures' witness to the questions of justice, power, the common good, and the dignity of every human being — applied with enough specificity to be genuinely relevant and enough care for the full range of the congregation to be genuinely pastoral.

Amos spoke against the economic exploitation of the poor with a specificity that made the comfortable deeply uncomfortable: "They sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals — they trample the heads of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the afflicted" (Amos 2:6-7). That is not a partisan statement. It is a prophetic one. It does not endorse a candidate or a party. It applies the justice of God to the conditions of a specific society with enough precision to be genuinely challenging.

This means naming moral realities without endorsing candidates. It means addressing systemic injustice without adopting any particular political party's framing of the problem or the solution. It means holding the congregation's political diversity with enough pastoral care that people across the spectrum feel genuinely cared for, while being clear that the gospel makes demands that no political identity can fully satisfy.

## A Concrete Scene

> He lost three families that month.

I know a pastor who leads a congregation in a politically divided suburban church — roughly split between families whose political identities are deeply held on both sides. In the summer of 2020, he preached through Romans 13 and Romans 12 together: the passage about submitting to governing authorities alongside the passage about being transformed by the renewing of the mind, not conformed to the pattern of this world. He did not tell his congregation how to vote. He did tell them that Christians were called to love neighbors who did not share their political assumptions, that the church's primary loyalty was not to either of the options the culture was offering, and that the peace of the congregation was not more important than the truth of the gospel.

He lost three families that month. He has not recovered them. He told me he does not expect to. He also told me that the remaining congregation is more deeply bonded than it was before — that something about having been willing to name the hard thing together, without taking political sides, had produced a trust that sermons designed to avoid offense had never produced.

## Practical Approaches That Help

Several practical approaches have proven helpful for pastors navigating this terrain. First: establish the authority of Scripture clearly and consistently, so that when you engage difficult topics, the congregation understands that you are trying to be faithful to a text, not to a party. Second: engage specific passages that speak to justice, power, and the common good rather than offering general political commentary — let the Scripture lead. Third: model genuine humility about the policy applications of biblical principles, acknowledging that faithful people can and do disagree about specific policy questions while sharing the same underlying moral commitments.

And fourth: pastor the congregation across the political divide with genuine care for the actual people in the room. The person who feels that their political community is the one the pastor is critiquing needs to feel, nonetheless, that the pastor loves them and respects their genuine attempts at faithfulness. That pastoral care is what creates the safety for the prophetic word to be received rather than rejected.

## What the Church Owes the Culture

The congregation that emerges from this kind of preaching — genuinely committed to the justice of the Scriptures, genuinely free from partisan capture, genuinely holding its political diversity with care — is a witness in itself. It is a community that the culture around it cannot easily categorize, and the difficulty of categorization is itself a form of testimony.

The church is not useful to the world as a religious expression of either party. It is useful to the world as a community organized around a different set of loyalties — as a foretaste of the peaceable kingdom, where the old divisions do not have the last word.

That is a hard thing to sustain from the pulpit. The forces pushing toward capture — from both directions — are relentless. But the pastor who keeps the church free is doing some of the most important work in the American church right now.

> It is useful to the world as a community organized around a different set of loyalties — as a foretaste of the peaceable kingdom, where the old divisions do not have the last word.

The political parties will survive without the church's endorsement. The gospel will not survive being confused with either of them.

Church splits are among the most painful experiences in ministry, and they are more common than the pastoral culture likes to acknowledge. The mythology of church unity — the conviction that genuine faith communities should be immune to the kind of fracturing that plagues other institutions — makes the experience of a split particularly devastating, because it carries not just the ordinary pain of broken community but also the weight of spiritual failure.

If you have been through a church split, you know this. If you are in the middle of one, you are in one of the hardest seasons of your pastoral life. This article will not promise that the split is God's will, because that is not always true. It will not promise a clean resolution, because those are rare. It will try to offer something more honest: a framework for surviving, learning, and eventually moving forward.

## The Church Has Always Split

> It is evidence that you are in the same story as everyone else who has ever tried to build the community of God among flawed and disagreeable human beings.

The first thing to say is that church splits are not a modern invention or a distinctly American failure. They are as old as the church itself.

The conflict between Paul and Barnabas over John Mark in Acts 15:36-41 ended in their separation — not a church split in the formal sense, but a fracture between the church's two most significant missionary leaders that sent them in different directions. The church at Corinth was riven with factions — "I follow Paul," "I follow Apollos," "I follow Cephas" (1 Corinthians 1:12) — and Paul's letters to that church are, among other things, pastoral triage for a community that had experienced the functional equivalent of a split along party lines.

The Reformation of the sixteenth century was, from one perspective, the most consequential church split in history — the fracturing of Western Christianity into a multiplicity of confessional traditions that has never been fully reassembled. The divisions within Protestantism itself — the splits between Lutheran and Reformed, between Anglican and Nonconformist, between frontier revivalists and established denominations — produced the sprawling denominational map of American Christianity, which is the product of centuries of churches dividing over doctrine, worship, governance, ethnicity, and class.

None of this makes your church split less painful. But it does mean that the experience of fracture is not evidence of unique spiritual failure. It is evidence that you are in the same story as everyone else who has ever tried to build the community of God among flawed and disagreeable human beings.

## What a Split Actually Is

Not every significant departure from a church is a split. A split — in the specific sense that makes it categorically different from ordinary attrition — is the organized departure of a significant portion of the congregation, usually under the leadership of someone from within the church's community, often accompanied by the founding of a new congregation from the departing group. It typically involves a decisive rupture in relational trust that has been building over time and that gets resolved through separation rather than reconciliation.

> The people who left will not be won back by the right argument. The people who stayed need the right presence.

Splits almost never happen without a history. By the time a significant portion of a congregation decides to leave together, something has been building — a conflict that was not addressed early enough, a leadership disagreement that calcified over time, a difference of vision that was not honestly surfaced, or a pattern of hurt or exclusion that accumulated until the departure felt necessary.

This is not to assign blame to any particular party. Sometimes the conflict was genuinely irresolvable. Sometimes the leadership failure was on the departing side, sometimes on the remaining side, sometimes on both. But understanding that history honestly — without the distortions of grief and anger that make clear thinking so difficult in the immediate aftermath — is part of what makes healing possible.

## Surviving the Immediate Aftermath

The immediate aftermath of a church split is characterized by grief, anger, confusion, and the practical challenges of leading a congregation that is smaller and more shaken than it was before. The pastor is usually doing pastoral triage — caring for the people who remained, addressing the narrative that is circulating in the community, and trying to maintain their own stability in the midst of genuine personal loss.

Some of what circulates in those early weeks is true, some is distorted, and some is fabricated. The pastor's temptation is to counter every narrative, to correct every mischaracterization, to defend the church's side of the story in every conversation it enters. This temptation should usually be resisted. The congregation needs its pastor to be stable and present, not to be reactive. The people who left will not be won back by the right argument. The people who stayed need the right presence.

The most important things in this period are: clarity about the facts that can be shared, pastoral presence for the people who are grieving, and the pastor's own care. This is not the time to analyze or theologize the split. It is the time to be genuinely present with the community, to acknowledge the pain honestly without stoking it, and to take care of yourself with at least as much urgency as you take care of everyone else.

Psalm 46 was written for exactly this kind of moment: "God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear, though the earth give way and the mountains fall into the heart of the sea." The split is not the mountains falling into the sea. But it can feel that way, and the psalm does not require you to pretend it feels otherwise.

## A Concrete Scene

I know a pastor — I will call him David — who experienced a split that took nearly a third of his congregation. The proximate cause was a worship style conflict, but the conflict was itself a symptom of something deeper: a set of relationships in the congregation's founding family that had accrued enormous informal power over fifteen years, and a moment when that power was challenged by the direction David was trying to lead the church.

The first three months after the split, David told me, he could not read his Bible in his study without crying. The loss was personal — people he had married, buried, celebrated with, built with — and the sense that he had somehow failed them was almost constant.

What kept him was a spiritual director he had been seeing for two years before the split, a woman who had no stake in the church's politics and whose primary contribution was the consistent reminder that his identity was not his church's health, that God's faithfulness was not contingent on his competence, and that the grief he was carrying was real and deserved to be carried rather than managed.

The spiritual direction was not a luxury. It was what made the pastoral presence possible. He could not have given his congregation what it needed if he had not had somewhere to go with what he was carrying.

## Learning Honestly

After the immediate crisis has passed — and this may take months — the work of honest examination becomes essential. Not in the spirit of self-flagellation. Not in the spirit of grievance. But in the spirit of genuine growth.

What was the conflict at the root of the split, and how was it handled? Were there early signals that were not addressed? What would the pastor do differently with the benefit of hindsight?

I have been in rooms where this question is asked too early, before the grief has settled enough to allow honest thinking, and the examination produces only defensiveness and blame. I have also been in rooms where it is asked too late, after the defensive narratives have hardened into settled history, and the examination produces only confirmation of what the pastor already believed about what happened.

The window for genuine learning is specific and finite. It requires that enough time has passed for the acute pain to have subsided. It requires that not so much time has passed that the specific details have faded and the narrative has solidified. It requires someone from outside — a trusted mentor, a peer with no stake in the outcome, or a professional counselor with experience in organizational conflict — to provide the perspective that the pastor cannot provide for himself.

I did not handle this well in the one significant departure I experienced in my years in ministry. I examined too quickly, while I was still too hurt to be accurate, and the conclusions I reached were shaped more by self-protection than by genuine honesty. The examination I needed came later, with help, and produced things I had not been willing to see on my own.

## Moving Forward

> Lead from it.

Moving forward does not mean forgetting what happened or pretending it did not. It means building a church that is shaped by what was learned rather than permanently defined by what was lost.

The congregation that has survived a split carries something the never-split congregation does not carry: the knowledge that community is fragile, that unity is maintained rather than assumed, that the work of honest relationship is not a program but a permanent practice. That knowledge, rightly received, can produce a culture of greater honesty, earlier conflict address, and more genuine pastoral attentiveness than existed before.

Some of the best congregations I know have a split in their history. Not because the split was God's will in some providential determinism that removes the pain and the failure from the equation, but because the community that survived it learned something about itself that it needed to learn, and was changed by it.

The church you lead now is the church on the other side of what happened. You cannot undo it. You can lead well from here.

What you carry out of the experience — the grief, the learning, the humility about your own limitations, the deepened dependence on the God whose faithfulness is not contingent on the tidiness of the story — is not baggage. It is formation.

Lead from it. The congregation still in front of you deserves the pastor that the split made you.

I want to be honest about how skeptical I was going in. Reformed theology and charismatic practice have been on opposite ends of a particular theological divide for most of their modern histories, and the conversations between representatives of the two traditions have often generated more heat than light. The cessationist and the continuationist have met at many tables over the years, and the encounters have rarely ended in genuine breakthrough.

What I did not expect was what actually happened when the Pastors Connection Network brought a group of us together — Reformed Baptist pastors, Word of Faith-adjacent charismatics, classical Pentecostals, and a few people who described their theology as "post-charismatic but not cessationist, which I realize doesn't make sense" — to simply spend time together and talk honestly.

## The Long History of a Particular Divide

The charismatic-cessationist divide is not as old as it feels. Classical Pentecostalism emerged in the early twentieth century — most historians trace its institutional birth to the Azusa Street Revival of 1906 in Los Angeles, which produced a form of worship and a set of convictions about the ongoing gifts of the Spirit that spread rapidly across racial and economic lines in a way that surprised everyone, including those at its center [cite — confirm]. The Reformed tradition, by contrast, had been working out its cessationist convictions since at least Benjamin Warfield's systematic arguments in the late nineteenth century, and the encounter between these two streams produced genuine suspicion on both sides.

The charismatic renewal of the 1960s and 1970s moved the gifts of the Spirit into mainline Protestant and Catholic communities, which raised the stakes further. By the time the "Third Wave" of the Spirit associated with John Wimber and the Vineyard movement emerged in the 1980s, the conversation had been going on for nearly a century and had accumulated layers of caricature on both sides — the Reformed tradition seen by charismatics as dry, intellectualist, and practically cessationist out of fear rather than conviction; the charismatic tradition seen by Reformed pastors as emotionally manipulative, theologically shallow, and prone to the kind of subjectivism that makes genuine accountability impossible.

> The relationship is not a substitute for the theological work. It is the precondition for it.

These caricatures, like most caricatures, contained enough truth to be plausible and enough distortion to be unjust.

## The First Obstacle: We Expected to Debate

Almost everyone in the room arrived expecting a theological negotiation — the careful positioning of positions, the finding of areas of agreement while clearly marking the disagreements. This is the default mode for ecumenical conversations between traditions that have real differences, and it produces a kind of theological diplomacy that is usually polite and rarely productive.

What disrupted the expected format was the decision to begin not with theology but with story. We went around the table and each person shared, for five minutes, how they had come to faith and what had shaped their understanding of the Holy Spirit. These were not position papers. They were human beings talking about encounters with God that had been definitive for them.

Something shifted. The cessationist heard the Pentecostal describe an experience of healing that bore no resemblance to the televangelism he had associated with the tradition. The charismatic heard the Reformed pastor describe a life of extraordinary fruitfulness built on careful, disciplined engagement with Scripture that did not fit the stereotype of dead orthodoxy. Before the theological questions were even on the table, the categories had already begun to break down.

## A Steel-Manned Counter-Position

The strongest version of the case against this kind of cross-tradition gathering needs to be heard. It goes like this: the differences between cessationist and continuationist theology are not peripheral. They shape ecclesiology, they shape how the congregation is formed, they shape the criteria for evaluating spiritual experience, and they shape how the church reads the New Testament. Gathering for meals and sharing personal stories creates warmth without clarity, and warmth without clarity is not the same as unity. The unity the New Testament envisions is unity in truth, not merely in affection. A Reformed pastor and a Word of Faith pastor may enjoy each other's company. That enjoyment does not resolve the question of whether the prosperity gospel is a distortion of the gospel. Pretending it does is not ecumenism. It is avoidance dressed as friendship.

This is a real concern and it deserves a real answer. The answer is not that the theological differences do not matter. They do. They shape real pastoral practices and real congregational lives, and treating them as though they can be dissolved by personal warmth is intellectually dishonest.

The answer is that genuine theological engagement requires the kind of trust and goodwill that does not exist between parties who only know each other as theological positions. The relationship is not a substitute for the theological work. It is the precondition for it. The cessationist who has never met a Pentecostal who is theologically serious, personally disciplined, and genuinely humble before the Scripture is arguing against a caricature. The relationship breaks the caricature. What happens after that — the theological wrestling — can be genuine rather than performative precisely because the people in the room have stopped performing for each other.

## What the Disagreements Actually Were

> There is something almost sacramental about that — the meal that precedes the mission, the shared table that makes the shared work possible.

The disagreements were real. We did not pretend otherwise. On the question of tongues, healing, prophecy, and the ongoing presence of the apostolic gifts, people in the room held genuinely different convictions rooted in genuinely different interpretations of Scripture and experience. These were not peripheral matters for any of us — they had shaped our ecclesiology, our discipleship practices, and our pastoral approaches in significant ways.

The most substantive exchange came on the question of how to evaluate claimed experiences of the Spirit — what the criteria are for distinguishing genuine from counterfeit, and who bears the authority to make that judgment in a community. The Reformed pastor argued from 1 John 4:1 — "test the spirits to see whether they are from God" — that the testing function belongs to the community's theological discernment and requires objective criteria that transcend individual experience. The Pentecostal pastor argued that the same text assumes the ongoing activity of the Spirit that the cessationist has already ruled out, and that the criteria for testing cannot preclude the kind of encounter the text envisions.

We did not resolve this. But in the context of the relationships forming across the table, the disagreement became something different: not walls, but honest differences between people who were genuinely trying to be faithful to the same God and the same Scriptures.

## What We Discovered We Had in Common

The list of shared convictions was longer than anyone expected: the authority of Scripture, the necessity of genuine repentance and faith for salvation, the centrality of prayer, the importance of genuine discipleship over mere attendance, the desperate need for genuine revival in the American church, and a deep weariness with the tribalism that had kept our traditions at arms' length from each other at precisely the moment when the mission most needed them to collaborate.

We also discovered shared struggles: the isolation of pastoral leadership, the challenge of reaching a post-Christian culture, the difficulty of sustaining a genuine prayer life in the midst of the demands of ministry. These were not theological conversations. They were human ones. And in the humanity, the barriers that the theology had built began to look more surmountable than they had before.

What Lesslie Newbigin observed about the ecumenical movement applies here: the unity of the church is not primarily achieved through theological agreement but through shared witness to the world [cite — confirm]. The mission creates the conditions for unity that the theological debates alone cannot. When Reformed and charismatic pastors discover that they are serving in the same city, working with the same underserved populations, and needing each other's resources and relationships to accomplish the work effectively, the theological differences become something to manage together rather than something to separate over.

## What Happened After the Table

The table did not resolve the theological differences. What it did was create the conditions for genuine friendship across those differences, and genuine friendship is the foundation on which real collaboration becomes possible. We have since partnered on community outreach in a shared city. A Reformed congregation and a Pentecostal congregation now share resources in a food ministry that neither could sustain alone. That would not have happened if we had not first sat down to eat.

There is something almost sacramental about that — the meal that precedes the mission, the shared table that makes the shared work possible. The table of Jesus in Luke 15 is open to the tax collector and the Pharisee, not because their differences do not matter but because they both needed what only the table could give. The mission begins there, at a table where the people who should not be together have chosen to be present to one another.

## What the PCN Has Learned

The Pastors Connection Network was not designed to produce theological consensus. It was designed to create the conditions for genuine pastoral community across the divisions that have kept pastors isolated from one another. The Reformed-charismatic gathering was one expression of that — an experiment in finding out whether genuine relationship was possible across a divide that both sides had assumed was too wide for anything but careful, guarded diplomacy.

> The table is worth setting.

It was possible. It is possible. Not because the theological differences are trivial, but because the mission is larger than the differences, and the isolation of pastoral life is lonelier than the disagreements are important.

The table is worth setting. Even when — especially when — the people around it are not supposed to get along.

There is a moment that most pastors who have experienced a genuine city-wide worship gathering can describe with unusual precision. The moment when the room is full of people from churches that would never normally be in the same building — different ethnicities, different traditions, different musical idioms, different theological emphases — and the worship somehow holds all of it, and something that feels genuinely like the body of Christ becomes visible in a way that no single congregation can make visible on its own.

These moments are not automatic. They require significant coordination, genuine humility from the pastors and leaders involved, and a willingness to set aside the particular cultural preferences of any single congregation in the interest of something larger. They are not easy to produce. But they are worth producing, and the case for making them a regular, intentional practice is stronger than most pastoral communities have yet been willing to act on.

## What the Theological Tradition Demands

The case for city-wide gathering is not primarily pragmatic. It is theological, and the theology is demanding.

The New Testament's vision of the church is not a network of discrete congregations each pursuing its own mission in its own community. It is a singular body — the body of Christ — that takes plural and locally differentiated forms without losing its fundamental unity. When Paul writes "there is one body and one Spirit" in Ephesians 4:4, he is not describing an aspiration. He is describing a reality that the church's visible behavior is meant to express. When he describes the church at Corinth as "the body of Christ" (1 Corinthians 12:27), he does not mean the individual congregation — he means the community of all who call on the name of Christ in that city.

The early church's practice in the city of Rome, where multiple house churches functioned in relationship with one another without a single unified building, was not experienced as fragmentation. It was experienced as the one church of Rome expressed in multiple gathering points, with genuine relationship between them and genuine accountability to a common identity. The fragmentation that characterizes the modern city — where the church exists as hundreds of independent organizations with no meaningful relationship to one another — is not a continuation of this pattern. It is a departure from it.

Lesslie Newbigin argued in *The Gospel in a Pluralist Society* that the credibility of the gospel in a pluralistic culture depends significantly on the visible quality of the community that the gospel produces [cite — confirm]. A city full of churches that never gather together does not provide the watching city with evidence that those churches believe something that actually overcomes the divisions of the world. They provide evidence that the church has organized itself according to the same divisions that organize everything else.

The city-wide gathering is one of the primary practices by which the church's theological claim — that it is one body despite its diversity — is made visible and therefore believable.

> The city-wide gathering is one of the primary practices by which the church's theological claim — that it is one body despite its diversity — is made visible and therefore believable.

## What City-Wide Gatherings Actually Do

The most important thing a city-wide gathering does is make the invisible visible. The body of Christ in any given city is real — it includes people from every tradition, every ethnicity, every economic background who share a common allegiance to the same Lord. But in ordinary practice, that reality is completely invisible. Each congregation experiences itself as a discrete unit. The larger body is a theological conviction, not a lived experience.

When the pastors of a city decide to gather their congregations together for worship, mission, or prayer, they make the theological conviction experientially real. People encounter the breadth of the church in a way that permanently expands their sense of what it is and what it can be. The Baptist who has spent twenty years convinced that contemporary worship is theologically shallow encounters the Pentecostal congregation whose worship is both contemporary and deeply formed. The evangelical who has privately assumed that mainline Christians are not really serious encounters the Methodist pastor whose biblical depth and pastoral seriousness dismantles that assumption.

These are not incidental outcomes. They are the kinds of formation that cannot happen within a single congregation's walls, no matter how excellent that congregation's programming is. The exposure to the breadth of the church is itself a form of theological education.

And the witness to the city of a unified church is dramatically more compelling than the witness of a thousand separate congregations each doing their own thing. When multiple congregations mobilize together for a prayer service before city elections, or join forces for a shared service initiative in the city's lowest-income neighborhood, or simply fill an arena for an evening of worship that is visibly diverse and visibly unified — the watching city sees something it does not expect and cannot explain from within its ordinary categories.

## The Pastoral Work That Makes It Possible

City-wide gatherings do not emerge from organizational momentum. They emerge from pastoral relationships. The pastors who have met regularly, who know each other's names and stories, who have developed enough trust to work through the inevitable decisions about who leads, who speaks, whose music is used, and whose tradition sets the liturgical tone — those pastors are the ones who can make a genuine city-wide gathering happen.

The decisions are genuinely difficult. Which pastor will preach? Whose worship team will lead? Will there be communion, and if so, whose liturgical tradition will govern it? Will the gathering represent only the evangelical stream or will it include the full breadth of the city's Christians? Every one of these decisions carries weight, and every one of them requires the pastors involved to subordinate their own preferences and their congregations' expectations to the larger purpose.

This requires the kind of maturity that comes only from genuine relationship. The pastor who does not know the pastor across town well enough to have an honest disagreement with him cannot make a city-wide gathering with him. The relationship is the prerequisite, and the relationship takes time.

This is part of why organizations like the Pastors Connection Network matter beyond their explicit programming — the ongoing relationships they build between pastors are the infrastructure that makes genuine collaboration possible when the moment calls for it. The gathering does not create the relationship. The relationship makes the gathering possible.

> The gathering does not create the relationship. The relationship makes the gathering possible.

## The Steel-Manned Objection

The strongest objection to city-wide gathering emphasis is ecclesiological: if the gathered congregation is the primary expression of the church in the New Testament — and it is — then the gathered congregation should be the primary focus of pastoral investment, and the energy that goes into city-wide coordination is energy drawn away from the community that is the pastor's primary pastoral responsibility.

This objection is not wrong about the priority of the gathered congregation. It is wrong to construct a competition between that priority and the larger commitment to the church's unity. The pastor who invests in city-wide relationships is not neglecting his congregation. He is modeling for his congregation what it means to understand their church as part of something larger than itself — which is formation that the congregation genuinely needs.

Moreover, the city-wide gathering consistently produces energy that flows back into the local congregation rather than away from it. Every pastor I know who has participated in a genuine cross-church collaboration reports that their congregation came away from it with renewed sense of the church's mission, renewed generosity, and renewed engagement. The gathering does not drain the congregation. It expands it.

## Starting Smaller Than You Think You Need To

The city-wide gathering does not need to be a stadium event on its first attempt. It can begin with three churches sharing a prayer service in the lead-up to Easter. It can begin with a joint outreach project in a neighborhood that no single church has the capacity to address alone. It can begin with a Thanksgiving service that rotates between congregations, gradually expanding as trust develops and logistics become familiar.

I have participated in gatherings of fifteen hundred and gatherings of sixty. The gathering of sixty — three congregations in a neighborhood church on a Wednesday evening before Good Friday, led by a worship team assembled from all three churches, with a message shared by a pastor none of the three congregations had previously heard — produced something in those sixty people that I have not forgotten.

The visibility of the body of Christ does not require scale. It requires the genuine presence of people who would not normally be in the same room, gathered around the one thing that makes them one.

> The visibility of the body of Christ does not require scale.

Start where you are, with who is willing. The pastors in your city who would say yes to an invitation are probably closer than you think. The first gathering will be imperfect. It will also produce something none of the individual congregations could have produced alone.

That something is the point. Let that be reason enough to make the call.

Every pastor makes referrals — to counselors, to other ministries, to specialists in areas outside their competence. The reality of pastoral ministry is that the needs people bring to their pastor span an enormous range of domains, and no single pastor can adequately address all of them personally: addiction recovery, financial crisis, legal trouble, mental health conditions, domestic violence, grief, medical crises, and a hundred other specific situations that require specific expertise.

The quality of those referrals matters enormously. A pastor who refers people to resources that are genuinely helpful — that meet the person where they are and provide competent, caring support — becomes a meaningful point of connection to the broader ecosystem of care in their community. A pastor who refers people to resources without knowing whether those resources are actually effective, or who gives generic suggestions without genuine relationships with the people or organizations being recommended, is not serving the person well.

## Why Most Pastors' Referral Networks Are Inadequate

Most pastors' referral networks are built accidentally rather than intentionally. They know the counselor who goes to their church, the ministry that spoke at a conference they attended, the organization whose brochure is in the church lobby. These resources may or may not be well-suited to the people being referred to them. They may or may not have capacity. They may or may not share enough theological and relational framework with the pastor to provide continuity of care.

Building a genuinely effective referral network requires intentional investment — getting to know the specific resources in your community, understanding their approaches and their limitations, developing the relationship between pastor and referral partner that allows for genuine coordination of care, and maintaining awareness of what is available and what is not so that referrals are genuinely useful rather than perfunctory.

The inadequacy of most referral networks is not a reflection of pastoral negligence. It reflects the structural isolation in which most pastors operate. The pastor who works in a large church with a pastoral care team and established community partnerships has far better referral infrastructure than the solo pastor of a congregation of eighty. And the congregation of eighty is, statistically, the normative American church context — which means the problem of inadequate referral networks is widespread and mostly invisible.

## The Theology Beneath the Practice

There is a theological claim beneath the referral network question that is worth naming explicitly. The good Samaritan in Luke 10 does not simply leave the wounded man on the road with a prayer and a word of encouragement. He binds the wounds, transports the man, installs him in a place of care, and provides for his ongoing needs with his own resources (Luke 10:34-35). The parable's claim about what love of neighbor looks like is not abstract. It is specific, resourced, and followed through.

The pastor who gives a referral and considers the pastoral care completed has not quite reached the standard of the parable. The pastoral relationship does not end at the referral. It includes the ongoing relationship with the person being referred, the follow-up to know whether the referral landed well, and the willingness to remain present with the person through the process of getting help that the pastor cannot personally provide.

> The pastoral relationship does not end at the referral.

That is more demanding than most pastoral care training describes. It is also what the people who come to the pastor's office in crisis most need — not just a name and a phone number, but the confidence that their pastor is still with them, that the referral does not mean abandonment.

## The Core Relationships Worth Building

Every pastor should have developed genuine relationships with at least one competent Christian counselor or therapist — ideally several, with different specializations, since the needs that come to the pastor's office are varied. These relationships should be built on actual knowledge: the pastor should know the counselor's approach to their work, their faith, their specific areas of competence, their availability, their fee structure, and whether they have capacity to receive referrals.

Beyond counseling, the effective referral network includes: legal aid resources for people facing legal crises without financial resources, financial counselors who can provide competent guidance on debt and financial recovery, domestic violence and family crisis resources, addiction recovery communities (both faith-based and secular, since different people will be best served by different approaches), and medical social workers who can help people move through healthcare systems when illness or disability creates crisis.

Each of these relationships is built the same way: through deliberate, repeated personal contact. The pastor who has met the executive director of the local domestic violence shelter, who has toured the addiction recovery program, who has had coffee with three different counselors and knows their names and their specific gifts — that pastor is in a position to make referrals that actually help people. The pastor who has a brochure in a drawer is not.

## The Steel-Man Against Building This Network

A serious counterargument: the pastor who spends significant time building external referral relationships is investing time that could be spent in prayer, Scripture study, sermon preparation, and direct pastoral care. The pastor's primary gifts and calling are theological and spiritual. Becoming a social services navigator is not what the office requires. Let the deacons and the congregational care team manage these relationships; the pastor's time is better spent in the work that only the pastor can do.

This is a real argument. There is genuine wisdom in it — particularly for pastors who have a tendency toward activity over depth, who find the networking and relational building of community partnerships more energizing than the harder interior work of spiritual formation. The referral network should not displace prayer. It should be built by someone in the congregation, with the pastor providing oversight and theological direction rather than doing all of it personally.

But the counterargument proves too much if it concludes that the pastor can be completely ignorant of the referral options available and delegate it entirely without losing something pastoral. The pastor who has never met the counselor to whom they refer people, who does not know whether that counselor is actually competent or genuinely caring, who has no basis for confidence in the referral beyond institutional reputation — that pastor is providing a kind of pastoral care that stops at the door of the real need. The people who come in crisis deserve better than a referral to an unknown resource. They deserve a pastor who knows what they are sending them toward.

> The people who come in crisis deserve better than a referral to an unknown resource. They deserve a pastor who knows what they are sending them toward.

## How Other Pastors Fit In

One of the most underutilized referral resources for any pastor is other pastors. The pastor whose congregation does not have the particular community of faith that a specific person needs — the person of a different cultural background, the person working through a very specific identity question, the person who has been hurt by a congregation similar to yours — deserves to be connected to a pastor and community that can genuinely serve them.

This kind of referral requires enough genuine relationship with other pastors to know what their congregations are actually like — whether they are genuinely welcoming, what their culture is, whether the person being referred will be well-received. The relational investment in other pastors is not just for the pastor's own benefit. It is for the benefit of every person they will ever need to refer.

A pastor referral network is, in this sense, a form of care for people the pastor has not yet met — the person in crisis who will arrive two years from now in a situation that requires a congregation the pastor does not lead. The relationships built now make that future care possible.

## Building the Network Practically

The practical steps are less complicated than the conceptual framework. Begin with the five or six referral categories where you most regularly feel inadequate: counseling, addiction, financial crisis, legal, domestic crisis, and cross-cultural or cross-congregational referrals. In each category, identify who is genuinely excellent in your community. Schedule meetings. Get to know them as people. Understand how they work and who they serve best. Tell them what your congregation looks like and what kinds of referrals you make. Build the relationship before you need it.

This takes time. Set aside one meeting per month for referral network development, and within a year you will have a functioning network that most pastors have spent decades without. The investment is not large. The return — in the quality of care your congregation receives when they are in crisis — is significant.

And then tell your congregation that it exists. The people who need it most are often the ones who will never ask for it directly — who will suffer in silence because they do not know that the pastor has actual relationships with actual people who can help. Making the network visible is part of making the care available.

## What the Network Is For

A concrete pastoral scene: a couple came to me in financial crisis — not a management problem but a genuine collapse, the kind that involved multiple creditors, a house they were about to lose, and a shame so thick it had taken them eight months to ask for help. I could pray with them. I could listen. I could provide a theology of grace that was genuinely needed. What I could not do was help them make a plan.

Because I had spent time building relationships with a financial counselor at a local nonprofit who shared enough theological framework to hold the spiritual dimension of the conversation, I was able to make a referral that was specific, warm, and followed through. I called the counselor myself that afternoon. I told him the couple was coming. I stayed in touch with the couple through the process.

That is what a healthy referral network looks like in practice. Not a list of resources. A set of relationships built in advance of the need, activated on behalf of a specific person in a specific crisis, with the pastor still present throughout.

> Not a list of resources. A set of relationships built in advance of the need, activated on behalf of a specific person in a specific crisis, with the pastor still present throughout.

The couple kept their house. More importantly: they came back. They are still in our congregation. The referral was not a hand-off. It was a form of pastoral presence extended beyond what the pastor alone could provide.

That is the whole point.

The conversation started at a pastors' lunch — three pastors from three different small churches in the same mid-sized city, meeting monthly as part of a loose network of local pastors who had been trying, with mixed success, to build genuine relationships across their denominational differences. The conversation that started the whole thing was not particularly visionary. It was actually a complaint.

One of the pastors — I will call him Marcus — was describing a neighborhood about four miles from his church building: a rapidly growing area of new apartment developments, young families moving in, almost no established churches in the immediate vicinity. "Every time I drive through there, I feel the pull," he said. "We should have a church there. But we're already maxed out. I can't do it."

The second pastor said, "We've been thinking the same thing about the same neighborhood." The third said nothing for a moment, and then: "What if we did it together?"

## Why Small Churches Have Been Told They Cannot Plant

The dominant model of church planting in American evangelical culture for the last several decades has been the large-church send model: a congregation of significant size and resources identifies and resources a church planter, sends a launch team, and provides financial support for the first three to five years of the new congregation's existence. This model has produced many successful plants. It has also created, implicitly, a belief that church planting is something large churches do and small churches watch.

This belief is not supported by the New Testament. The church in Antioch, which sent out Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary journey (Acts 13:1-3), was not the largest or most resourced congregation in the early church. It was a young, multiethnic congregation in a Gentile city, formed only a few years earlier, and it acted on the Spirit's prompting without waiting to achieve a scale that would make the mission comfortable.

The model that most constrained small churches was also the model that concentrated the energy and resources of the church's planting efforts in communities that could support large-church launches — which tended to be growing suburban contexts rather than the urban neighborhoods, rural communities, and lower-income areas where the church's presence was most needed and where the large-church send model was least financially viable.

The small-church collaborative model does not replace the large-church send model. It fills the geography that the large-church send model cannot reach.

> The small-church collaborative model does not replace the large-church send model. It fills the geography that the large-church send model cannot reach.

## Working Through the Obvious Obstacles

The obstacles were real and the three pastors named them honestly. Different theological traditions — one Baptist, one non-denominational, one Anglican-influenced. Different views on church governance, worship style, and several secondary theological matters. Different financial situations, with none of the three having significant reserves. And the practical challenge of how to lead a church plant that was genuinely shared rather than dominated by whoever contributed the most.

These are not trivial obstacles. The history of ecumenical cooperation in American Christianity is littered with initiatives that began with genuine enthusiasm and ended in either compromise that satisfied no one or conflict that damaged the relationships it had tried to build. The three pastors in this story were not naive about the risks.

They spent three months meeting regularly before committing to anything. During those months, they mapped their areas of genuine theological agreement — which turned out to be more extensive than any of them had initially assumed — and their areas of difference. They agreed on the essentials of the faith as the foundation. They agreed to hold the secondary matters with openness and ongoing conversation rather than requiring prior agreement. They agreed that the primary mission of the plant — reaching people who currently have no church connection — would function as the organizing principle that subordinated their differences without erasing them.

The willingness to sit with genuine theological difference rather than resolving it artificially or papering over it was the relational achievement that made everything else possible. They did not agree on everything. They agreed on enough, and they trusted each other enough to work together despite the rest.

> They did not agree on everything. They agreed on enough, and they trusted each other enough to work together despite the rest.

## How the Structure Worked

Each of the three churches committed a portion of its annual budget — not a large portion, but a meaningful one — to a shared plant fund. Each church identified one or two families who felt genuine call to be part of a church planting team and were willing to relocate to the target neighborhood. The three pastors together identified and called a lead planter — a young pastor who had expressed interest in church planting and who was theologically comfortable enough with all three traditions to be genuinely supported by each.

The governance was explicitly collaborative: the lead planter was accountable to a joint oversight team that included representatives from each of the three churches. This created real accountability without a single church having controlling authority — and it required the kind of trust that only the prior months of relationship-building made possible.

The financial arrangement addressed the power dynamics directly. Each church's contribution was proportional to its size, not equal, which prevented the largest of the three from having disproportionate influence through the weight of its contribution. The joint oversight team made decisions by consensus rather than majority vote, which required the three churches to work toward genuine agreement rather than allowing any two to outvote the third.

This was slower. There were conversations that took three meetings to resolve because the consensus requirement meant that no one could be simply outvoted. The slowness was, in retrospect, the point — it built the relational trust that allowed the partnership to endure.

## The Theological Case for Collaboration

The model deserves its theological scaffolding, not just its organizational description.

John 17 records Jesus praying for the unity of his disciples — not a procedural unity, not a doctrinal uniformity, but a unity that would be visible to the watching world and would function as the primary evidence of the gospel's truth. "May they be brought to complete unity to let the world know that you sent me" (John 17:23). The visibility of unity is, in Jesus' own framing, an evangelistic act. The church that is divided — not on essential doctrine but on tradition and preference and institutional territory — is withholding from its community a form of gospel witness that it could be providing.

The three churches in this story were not merely being organizationally efficient when they planted together. They were being evangelistically obedient. The church in the new neighborhood that emerged from three different traditions working together was itself a form of witness that no single-tradition plant could have provided.

Lesslie Newbigin argued in *The Gospel in a Pluralist Society* [cite — confirm] that the primary apologetic for the gospel in a skeptical culture is the quality of the community that the gospel produces — specifically, its capacity to hold together people who would otherwise be separated by the forces that divide the world. The co-planted church was a proof of concept for exactly this claim.

> They were being evangelistically obedient.

## What Happened

The church launched eighteen months after that original lunch conversation. In its first two years, it baptized thirty-one people, the majority of whom had no prior church background. All three of the sending churches reported that the act of sending had energized their own congregations — that the experience of being part of a mission larger than their individual church had produced new generosity, new engagement, and a renewed sense of what the church was actually for.

This is a documented phenomenon in church planting research, though it runs counter to the intuition that sending will deplete a congregation. Churches that send tend to grow, not because sending guarantees numerical growth, but because the experience of genuine mission redirects the congregation's energy from self-maintenance to outward purpose, and that redirection tends to produce both spiritual vitality and, over time, numerical health [cite — confirm].

The three sending churches did not lose the families they sent to the plant. They gained a purpose that their internal programs had not been generating.

## The Pastoral Ending

The three pastors still meet for lunch — still meeting monthly, still building the relationship that started this whole story. Marcus said something to me that stayed: "The plant is great. But honestly, the best thing that came out of it is that we are genuinely friends now. I don't know what I would do without these two."

The organizational achievement — a new congregation, thirty-one baptisms, a neighborhood now served by a church community it previously lacked — is real and significant. But the friendship is not incidental to the story. It is the condition that made everything else possible, and it is the fruit of the story that the organizational metrics do not capture.

The three small churches that could not plant alone planted together, not because they had solved all their differences, but because they had built enough trust across them to act on a shared conviction.

Your church probably cannot do this alone. There is likely another pastor within driving distance who is looking at the same neighborhood you are looking at, feeling the same pull, and also concluding that he cannot do it alone.

Make the call. Go to the lunch. Let the complaint become the question: what if we did this together?

You cannot do what they did. You can start where they started.

Few things energize a pastor like the vision for a new ministry. The need is clear, the gifting is present, the timing feels right, and the energy in the room when the idea is presented confirms that something real is being tapped. The next steps are obvious: form a team, develop a plan, build a budget, launch.

Before those next steps happen, there is a question worth asking that pastoral culture almost never asks: Is someone else already doing this? Not as a reason to abandon the idea — the need may be genuinely larger than any one church can meet — but as a starting point that might lead somewhere much more effective than a separate launch.

## Why Churches Do Not Ask

The failure to ask this question is not laziness. It is structural, and the structure runs deep.

American evangelicalism has been shaped by a broadly competitive ecclesiology — a view of church life in which each congregation is primarily accountable to its own vision and its own growth, in which the church across town is, at best, a sister institution and, at worst, a competitor for the same population of potential attenders. The language of "our mission" and "our calling" reinforces this frame. The instinct to launch rather than to collaborate is the natural product of a culture in which the success of the individual congregation is the primary unit of measurement.

This competitive ecclesiology is not theologically neutral. It assumes that the church in a given city is best understood as a collection of discrete organizations rather than as a single body of Christ that has taken multiple institutional forms. The Pauline vision in 1 Corinthians 12 — where the body's diversity of gifts is precisely the evidence of its unity, where each member's function serves the whole rather than competing with it — does not fit easily into an ecclesiology where each congregation's ministry is defined primarily by its own vision rather than by its relationship to the larger mission.

The pastor who launches a food pantry without asking whether the church six blocks away already operates one has not sinned. But he has operated from an assumption about the church's structure that is worth examining.

## Why Duplicate Ministry Exists

Duplicate ministry exists primarily because churches do not know what each other is doing. The food pantry that three different churches operate independently in the same neighborhood — none of them large enough to have real impact, each of them proudly featured in its own church's announcements — are a collective resource that, if pooled, would produce a genuinely effective community resource. The afterschool tutoring program at your church and the identical program at the church six blocks away are each running at partial capacity while the need in the neighborhood remains unmet. The duplication is not malicious. It is the product of churches operating in silos, each pursuing its own vision without reference to what the broader church community is already doing.

The waste is real. A 2020 survey of urban ministry organizations found that duplication of services was consistently identified by community organizations as one of the primary inefficiencies in faith-based community engagement [cite — confirm]. The financial resources, the volunteer hours, the organizational energy that go into maintaining duplicate programs could instead be directed toward meeting needs that are currently going unmet.

> The waste is real.

And beyond the efficiency argument, there is the witness argument. The watching city sees not a unified community of people who love it, but a collection of churches each promoting its own programs in competition with each other. That is not the witness the gospel intends the church to provide.

## The Pastoral Scene

A pastor named Kevin told me the story of how he spent fourteen months developing a recovery ministry for people coming out of addiction — building the curriculum, recruiting the volunteers, designing the space, building the budget. Three weeks before the launch, he received a call from a pastor across town who had heard about the program and called to ask whether they might want to partner.

That pastor had been running an identical program for four years. Kevin had not known it existed.

The conversation that followed was, by Kevin's account, one of the most uncomfortable and most important conversations of his ministry. The other pastor was gracious. The redundancy was clear. The question of what to do with it was genuinely difficult — Kevin had invested enormous energy and his congregation had significant ownership of the program they had helped develop.

They merged them. It took six months of negotiation and produced a program that serves three times the number of participants that either of the original programs could have served alone. Kevin told me that the merger produced something unexpected: his own congregation's sense of mission expanded. They were no longer doing their program — they were part of something larger than themselves.

## The Practical Case for Asking First

Asking the question — "Is anyone else already doing this?" — requires a level of pastoral relationship with other churches in the community that many pastors simply do not have. You cannot ask the question if you do not know the people to ask. This is one of the most practical and concrete arguments for investing in pastoral relationships across congregational lines: they make you more effective at your own church's mission by connecting you to the broader ecosystem of ministry in your community.

The conversation that begins with "we're thinking about launching X — are you doing something similar?" can lead in several directions, all of them more productive than the default silo launch. It might reveal that the other church is indeed doing the same thing and would welcome partnership or expanded capacity. It might reveal that they tried and found it did not work, which saves you from a predictable failure. It might reveal that you are filling a gap they have identified but not been able to address, opening the door to genuine collaboration from the beginning rather than after the fact.

The Pastors Connection Network exists, in part, to create the relational infrastructure that makes this kind of asking possible. Pastors who know each other can ask each other questions that strangers cannot ask. The relationship is the prerequisite.

## When to Launch Anyway

After doing the survey, there will sometimes be a clear answer that no, nobody else is doing this, and the launch is warranted. Sometimes the existing ministry is genuinely insufficient — it does not have the capacity to meet the need, or it serves a different population, or it approaches the work in a way that is genuinely inadequate to what the situation requires. In these cases, launching is the right call.

The steel-manned objection to the general approach here is worth stating directly: the command to pursue the mission does not include a prior obligation to check whether someone else is already pursuing it. The Spirit moves through multiple channels simultaneously. The fact that someone else is already running a food pantry does not mean your congregation is not also called to feed people, and forcing collaboration on congregations with different theological frameworks, different leadership cultures, and different relationships with the community may actually produce less effective ministry than two separate programs with genuine ownership from two separate communities.

This objection has real merit. Forced collaboration is worse than no collaboration. The goal is not a unified ministry bureaucracy in which every church must check with every other church before it can act. The goal is a pastoral culture in which the default question before launch is whether the mission is already being served and whether a relationship exists that could produce something better than separate action.

> Forced collaboration is worse than no collaboration.

Ask first. Then decide. The church that has developed the habit of asking — of situating its own ministry vision within the broader context of what the church in its city is already doing — tends to produce ministry that is more effective, better resourced, and more genuinely collaborative than the church that operates as though its own ideas are always the beginning of the story.

The city is the mission. Every church in it is a partner in that mission, whether the partnership is acknowledged or not. Acknowledging it changes what is possible.

> The city is the mission. Every church in it is a partner in that mission, whether the partnership is acknowledged or not.

Make the call before you build the budget. What already exists out there might be exactly what you were going to build, and the pastor who built it has been waiting for someone like you to ask.

There is a deeper issue here that the efficiency argument does not fully capture. The church that perpetually reinvents what already exists has, in some fundamental sense, decided that its own vision is more important than the mission's outcomes. That is a form of institutional pride dressed as pastoral initiative. The question "is someone already doing this?" is not a bureaucratic checkpoint. It is an act of humility — the acknowledgment that the Spirit may have been at work in this city before your congregation arrived at the idea, through people you have not yet met, in a ministry that is already serving the people you want to serve. Finding it is not a defeat. It is an invitation. Take it.

Conversations about racial diversity in predominantly white churches have been happening with increasing frequency for a decade or more, and the quality of those conversations varies enormously — from genuine engagement with Scripture and history and relationship that actually changes communities, to well-intentioned but ultimately shallow performances of commitment that change very little and leave the people they claim to be reaching for unconvinced and sometimes wounded.

This article is not an attack on the impulse. The impulse toward multiethnic, multicultural community in the church is a genuinely biblical one — the vision of Revelation 7, the breaking down of ethnic and social walls in Ephesians 2, the surprising inclusivity of Jesus throughout the Gospels, the radical social implications of the church in Acts where Jew and Gentile ate at the same table. The desire to embody that vision is right.

The mistakes that derail it, however, are common enough and specific enough to be worth naming directly.

## The Historical Weight of the Separation

American Christianity did not arrive at its racial homogeneity accidentally. The segregation of American churches is one of the most thoroughly documented features of American religious history, and its roots are not aesthetic or organic — they are structural and theological, the product of deliberate choices by the white church that bear examination before any conversation about diversity can be honest.

The denominational splits of the 1840s over slavery — which produced separate Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian denominations along sectional and racial lines — established institutional structures for racial separation that outlasted slavery by a century [cite — confirm]. The theological defense of segregation offered by Southern white churches from Reconstruction through the Civil Rights era was not a fringe position. It was a mainstream position, articulated by theologians and pastors who cited Scripture in its support. The white churches that were silent during the Civil Rights era were not passive observers — their silence was a form of complicity that allowed the system to function without the moral opposition that the church, of all institutions, was positioned to provide.

Martin Luther King Jr.'s "Letter from Birmingham Jail," written in April 1963 [cite — confirm], was addressed not to avowed segregationists but to moderate white clergy who counseled patience. Their moderation was, in his analysis, a greater obstacle to justice than the opposition of declared opponents. The church that is now, sixty years later, having earnest conversations about diversity is having them in the shadow of that history, whether it acknowledges it or not.

Acknowledging it is the beginning of having the conversation honestly. The predominantly white church that begins its diversity conversation without this historical context is trying to build on a foundation it has not yet examined.

> Acknowledging it is the beginning of having the conversation honestly.

## Mistake 1: Treating Diversity as a Goal Rather Than a Fruit

Diversity in a congregation is not something you produce through programming and intentional recruitment. It is something that grows from genuine relationships of mutual respect and care across racial and cultural lines. The predominantly white church that sets a demographic target — "we want to be X percent non-white by Y year" — has mistaken the fruit for the goal and is likely to pursue it in ways that feel extractive to the people they are recruiting.

The question is not "how do we get more diverse people in our church?" The question is "are we genuinely committed to the wellbeing and belonging of every person who walks through our door, and to the relationships that would produce a community where different kinds of people would genuinely want to stay?" The second question is harder, slower, and more likely to produce the fruit the first question is chasing.

The distinction matters because the predominantly white church that pursues demographic diversity as a goal tends to interpret the presence of people of color as evidence that the goal is being achieved, regardless of whether those people are genuinely belonging, genuinely influencing, and genuinely at home. A Black family sitting in your congregation on a Sunday morning is not evidence of a healthy multiethnic community if that family is invisible to the culture of the church, if their presence is noted and celebrated but their perspective is never consulted, if they experience the church as a place where they are welcome to attend but not to fully belong.

## Mistake 2: Making People of Color the Teachers Without Making Them the Leaders

A common pattern in predominantly white churches that are genuinely trying to grow in racial awareness is to invite people of color to speak, to share their experience, to educate the congregation about the realities of racism — while the actual leadership of the church remains predominantly white. This is not integration. It is the use of people of color as educational resources for the benefit of white congregants, without the commensurate power-sharing that genuine partnership requires.

> This is not integration.

Jemar Tisby, in *The Color of Compromise*, argues that this dynamic is itself a form of racial accommodation — the white church finding a way to benefit from the presence and perspective of Black believers without being fundamentally changed by it [cite — confirm]. The church that hosts a racial reconciliation Sunday and invites a Black pastor to preach has not changed its culture. It has added an event.

If the church's commitment to diversity is genuine, it will show up in leadership — in who is on the elder board, in who occupies staff positions, in whose voice shapes the culture of the community. The church that hires a "diversity pastor" while the senior leadership team remains unchanged has added a role without changing the culture. It has found a way to address the appearance of the problem while leaving its structure intact.

This is not an accusation. It is a description of a pattern that I have observed in churches where the desire for change is genuine but the willingness to share power has not yet caught up with the desire. Shared leadership is not just an organizational adjustment — it is a theological statement about whose wisdom the church trusts.

## Mistake 3: Asking People of Color to Come to You Rather Than Going to Them

The final and perhaps most fundamental mistake is the assumption that a diverse church is built by convincing people of color to attend a white church. This assumption contains, often unexamined, a hierarchy: the white church is the center, and the people being invited are being asked to accommodate its culture, its worship idiom, its relational patterns, its unspoken norms.

The more genuinely biblical vision is for predominantly white churches to pursue genuine relationship with predominantly minority churches — to be genuinely in each other's spaces, to collaborate on shared mission, to let the relationship reshape both communities rather than asking one community to accommodate the culture of the other.

This requires white pastors to be genuinely willing to receive from, be shaped by, and follow the leadership of their brothers and sisters of color. It requires sitting in their churches and noticing that the worship is different and that different is not deficient. It requires the humility to acknowledge that the white church's cultural practices are not the universal standard against which other Christian traditions are measured.

Ephesians 2:14-16 describes Christ as having "made the two groups one and has destroyed the barrier, the dividing wall of hostility." That wall was a specific, structural, theological barrier — not a feeling, not a preference, but a dividing structure that organized the community of God's people by separating them. The churches in your city that are predominantly white and predominantly non-white are separated by something structural, not something natural. The work of breaking down that structure cannot be done by asking one side to move toward the other. It requires both communities moving together.
