## The Counter-Position Answered

The strongest objection to emphasizing racial diversity in the church is that it imports the categories of secular identity politics into the community of God's people, where the only relevant category is "neither Jew nor Gentile, slave nor free" (Galatians 3:28), and that the church's excessive attention to racial identity reflects a capitulation to cultural pressure rather than fidelity to the gospel.

This objection has genuine theological content that deserves a real answer rather than a dismissal.

The answer is this: Galatians 3:28 is not a statement that racial and ethnic difference ceases to exist in Christ. It is a statement that racial and ethnic difference ceases to determine access, status, or belonging in Christ. The Jewish identity of the apostles did not disappear at Pentecost — it was sanctified and brought into the service of a mission that transcended it. The argument that the church should be racially and ethnically indifferent does not reflect the vision of Revelation 7, where the nations are gathered in their particularity before the throne — not erased into uniformity, but united in the worship of the one who made them all.

The church that is not attending to the racial dynamics of its community is not being racially neutral. It is allowing the default patterns of racial separation in American life to organize the body of Christ without examination. That is not faithfulness. It is passivity dressed as theology.

> It is allowing the default patterns of racial separation in American life to organize the body of Christ without examination. That is not faithfulness. It is passivity dressed as theology.

## What Honest Progress Looks Like

A pastor I respect leads a predominantly white church in a mid-sized Midwestern city. Three years ago, he began a formal partnership with a predominantly Black church eight blocks away — not a diversity program, but a genuine pastoral friendship between the two senior pastors that expanded into shared worship, shared mission in their common neighborhood, and eventually shared governance of several joint initiatives.

He told me that the hardest part was not the logistics. It was the moment he realized that the partnership was changing him — that the worship idiom of his partner church was awakening something in his own congregation's worship that a decade of inside-the-tradition renewal had not produced. He was not absorbing the Black church's culture. He was encountering it, and the encounter was doing something in him that no program had managed.

That is what the fruit of genuine partnership looks like. Not a demographic target met. Not a hiring milestone achieved. A community that looks more like what God intended it to be, because the people in it allowed themselves to be genuinely shaped by people unlike them.

It is slower. It requires more of everyone. It produces something more real than a diversity initiative has ever produced.

The wall does not come down by talking about it. It comes down when the people on both sides of it decide that what is on the other side is worth the cost of the crossing.

I grew up in a church that was racially and culturally homogeneous — not by design, or at least not by conscious design, but by the accumulated effect of a thousand small choices about location, culture, language, and which community the church positioned itself to serve. It was a good church, and I am grateful for what I received there. But it was a church that never required me to be genuinely formed by anyone who was significantly different from me.

Pastoring a multiethnic congregation for the first time — which happened not because I sought it out but because the neighborhood around our church changed significantly while I was there — taught me more about the gospel than a decade of seminary had prepared me for. This article is an attempt to pass on some of what I learned, imperfectly and still in process.

## The Bible Reads Differently in a Diverse Room

The first and most jarring discovery was what happened to the Scriptures when they were read and discussed and preached across cultural lines. Passages I had read hundreds of times suddenly opened in ways I had never seen. The parable of the Good Samaritan, discussed with a congregation that included people who had personal experience of being the Samaritan — the one whose help was unexpected, whose community was the source of theological suspicion — broke open something I had missed for decades.

The Psalms of lament, which I had always engaged primarily as individual spiritual exercises, became communal in the mouth of a congregation where some members carried the specific, historical weight of generational injustice. The resurrection narratives, filtered through the stories of people who had come to faith in contexts where the gospel arrived with liberation rather than with cultural imperialism, had a different texture than the resurrection narratives I had been preaching to people whose theological heritage was primarily the tradition of the colonizers.

This was not relativism. The text does not mean different things to different cultures. But the text has depths that any single cultural reading will miss, because no single culture has the full range of human experience that the Scripture addresses. The congregation that is genuinely diverse is not a harder congregation to preach to — it is a richer one, because it surfaces the layers of the text that cultural homogeneity keeps buried.

Walter Brueggemann has argued for years that the prophetic imagination requires the church to hear the voices of those at the margins, because the margins are where the distortions of the center become visible [cite — confirm]. Pastoring a multiethnic congregation put that claim in my body in a way that reading Brueggemann alone could not. The voices I had not heard were the voices that knew something about the text that I did not.

> The voices I had not heard were the voices that knew something about the text that I did not.

## Conflict Had to Be Named Differently

The second discovery was that the conflict management skills I had developed in homogeneous ministry were inadequate for multicultural ministry. The assumptions I brought about how conflict should be expressed, what a productive conflict conversation looked like, how quickly resolution should be sought, and what a successful outcome felt like — all of these were culturally shaped in ways I had never examined, because I had never been in a context where they were challenged.

Learning to move through conflict across cultural lines required me to be genuinely curious about how my own cultural assumptions were shaping my approach, to listen more and conclude less quickly, and to create space for forms of conflict engagement that looked different from what I had been taught but were not for that reason less legitimate. The humility required to do this well was a different kind of humility than the pastoral humility I thought I already had.

I thought I was humble. I had been told I was humble. The first time a member of my congregation with a different cultural background told me, with specific gentleness, that my approach to a conflict felt like an extension of the dynamics she had experienced as a person of color in white-led institutions — that my confidence in my own conflict-resolution process was itself a form of cultural power — I did not receive it well. Not at first. The initial response was defensive. It took days to hear what she was actually saying: not that I was a bad person, but that my cultural location had given me tools that worked primarily for people like me, and the congregation I was now leading was not primarily composed of people like me.

That conversation was more formative than most of my seminary training. I am still being formed by it.

> That conversation was more formative than most of my seminary training. I am still being formed by it.

## The Steel-Man

The serious counterargument to the emphasis on multicultural ministry sounds like this: cultural homogeneity is not a failure — it is often the result of effective contextualization. The principle that people come to faith most readily through people who share their cultural background has substantial missiological support. Donald McGavran's church growth research argued extensively that homogeneous unit churches grow faster and reach their cultural communities more effectively than diverse ones [cite — confirm]. The emphasis on multicultural congregations as a theological ideal may be importing a social-justice framework into ecclesiology that is not native to it.

This deserves an honest answer. McGavran is not wrong that homogeneous communities often evangelize their own cultural group more effectively. But the New Testament does not present the homogeneous congregation as the ideal destination. It presents the multiethnic community as the eschatological reality that the church is called to embody now. Revelation 7:9 does not show every tribe in its own section of heaven. It shows every tribe, language, people, and nation standing together before the throne. Paul's insistence in Galatians 3:28 — "neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" — is not merely a future hope. It is a present claim about the community that has been formed by the cross.

Homogeneous churches may be more effective at certain kinds of evangelistic growth. They are less capable of demonstrating the specific thing that the New Testament says the church exists to demonstrate: that the divisions of the old humanity have been overcome in Christ.

## What Unity Actually Feels Like

The unity that a genuinely multicultural congregation produces is not the comfortable unity of a homogeneous community where everyone already agrees on the significant things. It is a harder-won, more surprising, and more genuinely beautiful unity — the unity that emerges from people who are genuinely different choosing to be bound together by something they share that is deeper than the things that divide them.

I have seen that unity in the grief that crosses cultural lines when someone in the congregation suffers. I have seen it in the shared prayer that is awkwardly multilingual and more moving for it. I have seen it in the table fellowship that includes foods and customs and languages from half a dozen backgrounds and that images, however imperfectly, the feast that Revelation promises.

There was a memorial service for a member of our congregation — a woman in her eighties who had grown up in Central America and spent the last thirty years of her life in our pew. The service included hymns in Spanish, prayers offered in English by people she had served with for decades, and a long, public silence that her family had asked for and that the rest of us did not know how to fill and then, slowly, found we could sit in together. That silence, shared across every cultural boundary represented in that room, was more theologically weighted than most sermons I have preached.

> That silence, shared across every cultural boundary represented in that room, was more theologically weighted than most sermons I have preached.

## The Formation It Requires

Pastoring across cultural lines requires the pastor to be a genuinely humble learner in a setting where the pastor is supposed to be the teacher — and to model that learning publicly, without pretending it is easy or that they have already mastered what they are trying to practice. The congregation that watches their pastor get it wrong, receive the correction, and grow from it is receiving a form of discipleship that the polished sermon cannot provide.

I have not mastered this. Fifteen years into pastoral ministry I am still discovering the cultural assumptions I carry that I have not yet examined — still finding the places where my approach to Scripture, to community, to conflict, and to God has been more shaped by my location in American culture than by the text I claim as my authority. The multicultural congregation is, among other things, the gift that keeps revealing that.

The unity it produces is not comfortable. But it is the kind the New Testament points toward. And I would not trade what I learned from pastoring across those lines for the comfort of a church that never required it of me.

That remains true even on the weeks when the requirement felt like more than I could carry.

Which is most weeks. And which may be the point.

The statistic is stark enough that it bears repeating slowly: in the United States, churches are closing at three times the rate at which new churches are being planted. For every congregation that opens its doors for the first time, three are closing theirs for the last time. This is not the trajectory of a movement in expansion. It is the trajectory of a movement in significant contraction — and the implications for the gospel's reach into American communities, and for the global mission that depends on a healthy sending church, are profound.

Carey Nieuwhof identified this as one of the most significant trends in the recent American church, and it has continued into the mid-2020s [cite — confirm]. The reasons are multiple and reinforcing: an aging pastoral workforce, declining attendance that makes financial sustainability increasingly difficult for smaller congregations, the cultural headwinds against institutional religion, and the challenge of reaching successive generations who are increasingly distant from the church's cultural milieu.

## What This Means for Communities

When a church closes, it does not simply disappear from a building — it disappears from a community. The food pantry that was serving thirty families a week closes. The presence that kept the building lit on Thursday evenings for the AA meeting is gone. The pastoral care for the elderly members who had nowhere else to turn is no longer available. The gathering point for community in a neighborhood that is already struggling with isolation and fragmentation ceases to exist.

This is not sentimentality about institutional religion. It is a recognition that healthy local churches provide genuine, irreplaceable services to their communities — services that are not simply replicated when the church closes and the people disperse to other congregations. The church that closes in a rural community or an urban neighborhood that is already underserved leaves a gap that the market will not fill and the remaining churches, already stretched, usually cannot fully address.

Robert Putnam's research on social capital documented what most pastors already knew intuitively: that religious congregations are among the most important generators of what he calls "bridging social capital" — the connections between different kinds of people that make communities resilient [cite — confirm]. When those congregations close, the social capital they generated does not simply transfer elsewhere. It dissipates. The community becomes less connected, less able to respond collectively to crisis, less able to provide the informal support networks that protect vulnerable members from the worst consequences of hardship.

## The Historical Weight

The history of the church in Europe is an instructive if cautionary parallel. The de-Christianization of Western Europe did not happen through persecution or dramatic confrontation. It happened through gradual institutional decline — through the slow erosion of church attendance, the aging of congregations, the closure of parish churches that had served communities for centuries, and the eventual disappearance of the intergenerational, community-embedded institutional presence that the church once represented. By the early twenty-first century, the majority of European nations had become post-Christian in any meaningful demographic sense, and the question of how to re-evangelize cultures that had already rejected one version of Christianity had become one of the most urgent missiological challenges in the world [cite — confirm].

The American church is not Europe in 1950. But the trajectories are similar enough to warrant serious attention. The church that assumes institutional decline is someone else's problem — that the closure of congregations in rural communities or aging suburbs does not affect the urban megachurches that are growing — is misreading the interconnectedness of the church's presence in a community and the nation. When the ecosystem thins, everything in it is affected.

> When the ecosystem thins, everything in it is affected.

## The Counter-Position

The counterargument from some church growth researchers is that church closures, properly understood, represent healthy consolidation rather than alarming decline. Congregations that are no longer viable — that have lost the critical mass to sustain genuine community, that no longer have enough financial resources or pastoral leadership to function effectively — should close. Their members should join stronger, healthier congregations. The result is a church that is smaller in number of institutions but healthier in quality of community, more concentrated, more effective, less spread across buildings that have outlasted their missional usefulness.

There is something to this. Not every church closure is a tragedy. Some churches have been dying for decades in ways that have not served their communities or their members well, and the closure that allows their people to find genuine community elsewhere is a mercy to those people. The number of congregations is not itself a sacred metric.

> The number of congregations is not itself a sacred metric.

But the counterargument proves too much if it suggests that the geography of church closures is neutral. The congregations that are closing are not closing uniformly across the country. They are closing disproportionately in rural communities, in aging urban neighborhoods, in economically declining regions — precisely the communities where the remaining institutional presence is thinnest, where the alternatives for people displaced by church closure are fewest, and where the need for genuine community and pastoral care is, if anything, higher than the national average. The consolidation model works for people who have multiple options. It does not work for people who are already living with fewer.

## The Church Planting Response

The most direct response to closing churches is new church plants — and the church planting movement has produced genuine fruit over the past several decades. Churches planted in the last twenty years tend to be more diverse, more missionally focused, and more culturally engaged with their communities than the churches they are replacing. The problem is the math: planting at one-third the rate of closure means the total number of congregations is declining, the geographic coverage of the church is shrinking, and the communities that are hardest to reach are increasingly the ones with the least church presence.

This means the church planting rate needs to significantly accelerate. And it means that the churches that are closing need to be helped to close well — to transition their resources, their people, and their legacy into new expressions of ministry rather than simply folding with nothing to show for what they built. The congregation that closes its doors and deeds its building to a new church plant, that commissions its remaining members as the founding core of a fresh work in the same community, has not failed. It has completed its mission and passed the baton.

## The Multiplication Imperative

The New Testament's vision for the expansion of the church is not primarily the growth of existing congregations — it is the multiplication of new ones. Paul's missionary strategy, described through Acts and implied in the letter to the Romans, was not to build one large congregation that would serve a region but to plant communities across multiple cities and then move on, trusting the Spirit and the local leadership to sustain and extend what had been begun [cite — confirm]. The measure of success in that strategy was not any single congregation's health but the total presence of the gospel community across every geographic and cultural territory Paul had reached.

That multiplication vision requires a different organizational logic than the one most American churches operate on. It requires treating congregation multiplication as a primary measure of health, not a secondary program. It requires seeing the deployment of gifted leaders into church planting as the highest use of those leaders — not a loss to the deploying church, but its most significant investment in the mission. It requires a willingness to send rather than keep.

> It requires a willingness to send rather than keep.

## What Every Healthy Church Can Do

Every healthy church has a role in reversing this trend, and it begins with a simple question: are we investing in church planting? Not merely giving to a denominational church planting fund, but actively participating in the mission — identifying and sending planters from within the congregation, partnering with church plants in underserved communities, and treating the planting of new congregations as a primary expression of the church's mission rather than an optional add-on.

The collaborative model — churches partnering together for church planting in communities where no single congregation has the capacity to plant alone — addresses both the resource problem and the isolation problem that makes so many potential church plants fail. The church planting movement's most effective recent work has tended to be collaborative: networks of congregations that pool resources, share leadership development, and hold one another accountable for the planting mission.

## The Weight of What Remains

Three to one. Three closures for every plant. The math is not moving in the right direction, and the communities feeling the absence are not the ones that need more Instagram content about the church's irrelevance. They are the communities that needed the food pantry to stay open, the elderly woman who needed the pastoral visit that no one from the megachurch forty miles away will make, the man in the addiction recovery meeting who needed the church to keep the lights on on Thursday nights.

The mission is too urgent and the resources too limited for churches to address it in isolation. The math only works if we work together. And the churches that are healthy enough to plant, to send, to partner, to close well — those churches are making a decision about whether the gospel's presence in American communities will contract further or whether someone is willing to pay the cost to expand it.

That decision is not abstract. It is made or unmade in every annual budget meeting, every leadership pipeline conversation, every moment when a congregation turns inward to serve itself rather than outward to plant something new.

The three to one ratio is the verdict on years of those decisions made the wrong way.

The verdict on the next decade is still being written.

Every church has conflict. Pastors who pretend otherwise are either new or dishonest. The mistake most new pastors make is trying to handle it in isolation — without a mentor, a peer who can offer outside perspective, or a coach who has been through similar terrain.

Conflict handled in isolation tends to escalate or calcify. Bring it to someone you trust outside your congregation. Their perspective will almost always reveal angles you cannot see from inside the situation.

That piece of advice is correct and almost never followed. The reasons why it is not followed are worth examining, because they are not trivial. They have to do with shame, with the pastoral role's peculiar loneliness, and with a misunderstanding of what it means to lead well.

## Why Pastors Go It Alone

The loneliness of pastoral leadership is structurally produced. The congregation needs the pastor to be the strong one, the settled presence in the storm. That role creates a relentless pull toward the management of appearances — toward performing stability even when the interior is not stable, toward projecting competence even when the situation is beyond what any one person can manage alone. And conflict, more than almost anything else in ministry, exposes the gap between the managed appearance and the actual reality.

When a deacon challenges the pastor's direction in a board meeting. When a long-tenured family begins moving people to their side. When the associate pastor you hired and mentored begins conducting his own shadow conversations. These situations produce a kind of interior weather that the pastoral role was never designed to house alone — anxiety, anger, second-guessing, the specific grief of being opposed by people you love and have served at cost. The pastor who tries to carry that weather without outside help is not being strong. He is being isolated, and isolation does not produce good decisions.

> The pastor who tries to carry that weather without outside help is not being strong. He is being isolated, and isolation does not produce good decisions.

I have tried to handle it alone. I have sat with a conflict situation for weeks, turning it over in my mind, running the same mental loops, arriving at the same confused conclusions, without once calling someone outside the congregation to say: *I am in a difficult situation and I do not know what to do.* What I told myself was that I was being discreet, protecting people's privacy, keeping the conflict from spreading. What I was actually doing was protecting myself from the humility required to admit I was stuck.

## What Isolation Does to a Conflict

Conflict handled in isolation does one of two things. It escalates — because the pastor, without any external check on his own anxiety or his own reactive instincts, handles the situation from a place of internal pressure that the situation does not deserve. Or it calcifies — because the pastor, afraid of making the wrong move, makes no move at all, and the unaddressed conflict hardens into permanent relational damage.

Neither outcome is what the congregation needs. And neither outcome is the mark of a leader. Real leadership in conflict requires something that solo processing cannot provide: the perspective of someone who is not inside the emotional field of the situation.

When you are inside a church conflict, everything is too close. The anxious elder seems like a threat to the entire ministry. The dissenting voice in the board meeting sounds like the voice of a faction trying to undermine everything. The family that is unhappy seems like the leading edge of a exodus. The proximity distorts. It makes small things large and large things larger. You need someone outside who can say: this is a difficult situation, and it is also manageable, and here is what people in your position have done that worked.

That external voice is not a luxury. It is a leadership requirement.

> That external voice is not a luxury. It is a leadership requirement.

## The Biblical Shape of Counsel

The Book of Proverbs is direct about this: "Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety" (Proverbs 11:14). The word translated "guidance" in that text is from a Hebrew root meaning the art of steering a ship [cite — confirm]. The image is navigation — not in the abstract, but in the practical sense of getting a vessel through difficult water without wreck. The proverb is saying that the person who tries to steer through dangerous conditions without counsel is not brave. He is reckless.

Jethro gives Moses the same advice in Exodus 18. Moses is trying to adjudicate every dispute in Israel by himself, and his father-in-law watches and says, plainly: "What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone" (Exodus 18:17-18). Jethro is not criticizing Moses's capability. He is naming a structural impossibility. The load is not designed to be carried by one person, and the one person who keeps trying to carry it will break before the load does.

The advice Moses receives is about distributing judicial responsibility, but the principle reaches further. The pastor in conflict is in the same position — carrying something that is structurally too heavy for one person to carry well — and the Jethro principle applies. Get help. Not because you cannot lead, but because leadership requires it.

## What Outside Perspective Actually Provides

The mentor, peer, or coach you bring in outside your congregation provides several things that you cannot provide for yourself.

First, they provide emotional regulation. The person outside your congregation is not afraid of your conflict the way you are. It is not their ministry, their livelihood, their identity. That distance allows them to look at the situation without the distortion that proximity creates, and their relative calm can be transferred to you through the conversation. You arrive at the call tightly wound, and you leave it with a more accurate read of the actual scale of the problem.

Second, they provide pattern recognition. Someone who has been in ministry for twenty years has seen this particular conflict in its various forms before. The deacon who challenges the pastor's direction. The dissatisfied family. The associate who is growing his own following. These are not unique situations. They are patterns, and the person who has walked through the pattern before knows what the end of the road looks like — knows which moves tend to help and which tend to harm, which confrontations are necessary and which create more problems than they solve.

Third, they provide accountability. The pastor who processes a conflict alone processes it with his own instincts, his own reactivity, his own fear or anger driving the conclusions. The pastor who processes it with a trusted outside voice has to articulate the situation to someone else, and articulation requires clarity that internal rumination does not. You cannot give someone a muddled account without noticing that it is muddled. The discipline of explaining the situation is already a step toward understanding it.

## The Counter-Argument

The counter-position is real and worth taking seriously: there are situations where involving outside people in a church conflict makes things worse. Conflict spreads. Involving a coach or mentor sometimes means the situation becomes more people's knowledge than it needs to be. Some conflicts are genuinely private, and privacy protects the people in them.

All of that is true, and none of it is an argument for navigating conflict alone. It is an argument for choosing the outside voice carefully. The mentor in another city who has no connection to your congregation is not a vector for the conflict to spread — he is a sealed container in which you can process the weight without it leaking. The peer supervisor whose confidentiality you trust is not adding to the conflict. He is helping you survive it.

The pastor who uses the risk of spreading conflict as a reason to avoid all outside counsel is not being careful. He is being afraid. Fear dressed as wisdom is still fear.

> Fear dressed as wisdom is still fear.

## Building the Structure Before You Need It

The best time to identify the outside voice you will call in conflict is before the conflict arrives. Not when the elder is already hostile. Not when the faction has already formed. Before.

This means building peer relationships with pastors in other churches, at least one of whom is senior enough in ministry to have seen what you haven't. It means having a mentor relationship that is genuine — not the kind where you present the polished version of your ministry, but the kind where the other person actually knows you. It means being in a context — a cohort, a denomination's peer group, a coaching relationship — where you are known well enough that calling them in a crisis does not require starting from scratch.

The pastor who builds those relationships in the ordinary seasons of ministry will find, when the conflict comes, that he has something to call on. The pastor who only reaches out when things are already bad will find that a cold call to someone who barely knows him produces a generic and limited response.

This is not complicated. But it requires acknowledging, before the conflict, that the conflict will come. Every church has it. Pastors who pretend otherwise are either new or dishonest.

You are not the exception. You will need someone outside your congregation to help you see clearly. Build the relationship now. The conflict is already on its way, and you will be grateful you did.

The safest sermon to preach is the one everyone agrees with in advance. The most dangerous is the one that names what the congregation would prefer not to name, confronts what they would prefer to leave unconfronted, and calls them to something that genuinely costs.

Most preachers have a sense of which topics they systematically avoid — the things that would generate pushback, that would make certain powerful members uncomfortable, that would require the preacher to have the harder conversation on Monday. Those avoidances are costing the congregation more than the feedback they spare the preacher. And they are costing the preacher something more fundamental than the feedback — they are costing the integrity of the call.

This is not a theoretical problem. It is the most common form of pastoral failure, and it is almost never recognized as failure because the sermon that avoids the costly thing still sounds good, still receives positive responses, still fulfills the formal requirements of a Sunday sermon. The congregation leaves satisfied. No one files a complaint. The pastoral evaluation comes back strong. And the deep work that the congregation needed — the word that would have unsettled something that needed to be unsettled — never arrived.

---

## The Watchman and the Blood on His Hands

The biblical office of the watchman is the relevant theological framework.

Ezekiel was told: "Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me. If I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, in order to save his life, that wicked person shall die for his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand" (Ezekiel 3:17-18).

The watchman's job is not to deliver the word the city wants to hear. It is to deliver the word the city needs to hear, at the cost of the watchman's own comfort and at risk to the watchman's own standing. The accountability is explicit: if the watchman fails to give the warning, the blood of the one who was not warned is on the watchman's hands. The silence is not neutral. It is a choice with consequences — consequences that are not primarily experienced by the preacher in the short term but by the congregation over time.

> The silence is not neutral.

That framework puts the calculation in its proper terms. The preacher who avoids the costly sermon is not being cautious. They are being negligent — trading the congregation's formation for the preacher's comfort, offering the appearance of the office without the substance of its obligation.

---

## When Avoidance Becomes a Pattern

The avoidance is systematic, which is what makes it so damaging.

One avoided sermon on one Sunday is a pastoral judgment call. The preacher who looks at the text and the room on a specific Sunday and decides that a different angle serves better — that is not cowardice; it is discernment. The problem is the pattern: the topics that are never addressed, the applications that are always softened, the congregational assumptions that are consistently affirmed rather than examined, the powerful members whose positions are never challenged.

The congregation learns this pattern faster than the preacher realizes. They learn it not by analyzing the sermons but by sensing the avoidances — the slightly different energy when the text is going somewhere uncomfortable, the pivot away from the implication, the application that could have gone further but did not. They notice. They may not be able to articulate what they are noticing, but it registers as a gap between the pulpit and the real, between what the preacher is willing to say and what the situation actually requires.

Over time, this gap produces a specific kind of pastoral authority deficit. The congregation begins, often unconsciously, to discount the preacher's voice — not the content, which may be excellent, but the weight. A preacher who has never said anything that cost them something is a preacher the congregation has not fully trusted, because they have not been shown what the preacher is willing to lose for the sake of the truth. The prophetic credibility is the credibility of the person who told the hard thing when there was a price for telling it.

> A preacher who has never said anything that cost them something is a preacher the congregation has not fully trusted, because they have not been shown what the preacher is willing to lose for the sake of the truth.

---

## The Territories Pastors Learn to Skirt

Consider the specific categories where the avoidance most commonly lives.

Wealth and generosity. The congregation's economic behavior — the gap between average income and average giving, the financial decisions that reflect values other than the ones professed on Sunday, the way money is discussed in homes that attend services on the importance of generosity — is among the most sensitive territories in pastoral ministry. The preacher who addresses it specifically, who moves from the general principle to the actual implications for the people in the room, will receive the most direct pushback of any sermon topic. Jesus addressed it more than almost any other subject. Most pastors address it least.

Power and accountability. Congregations have power dynamics, and those dynamics often include people whose giving, tenure, or social influence has allowed them to establish a kind of informal veto over pastoral direction. Preaching that names the misuse of power, that addresses the dynamics of control and manipulation, that calls the congregation's most influential members to the same accountability as its most vulnerable — this preaching will create the most direct and personally targeted conflict the preacher experiences. Most avoid it entirely.

Sexuality. Not the easy version — the sermons that address sexual ethics in ways the congregation already agrees with — but the hard version. The sermon that addresses the congregation's actual sexual culture, including the behaviors that are widespread and quietly normalized, including the ways the church's public positions and its private realities diverge, including the genuine pastoral complexity that rigid positions often cannot hold. That sermon requires the preacher to risk accusation from multiple directions simultaneously, which is why it is almost never preached.

Racial and social justice. In the current moment, this territory has become a proxy war, and many preachers have responded to the proxy war by going silent. The silence is not neutrality. It is a position — a position that tells the congregation that this question, which the prophets addressed with relentless clarity, is not sufficiently important for the preacher to risk the conflict it would produce.

---

## Courage Without Wisdom Is Not Prophetic

The steel-manned objection.

Some will argue that the pastoral relationship requires a specific kind of political intelligence — that the preacher who consistently chooses confrontation over diplomacy will eventually lose the platform that makes preaching possible, and a preacher without a platform can preach nothing to no one. The preacher who drives out the wealthy donors with sermons about wealth, who inflames the politically engaged members with sermons about power, who fractures the congregation with sermons on contested social issues — that preacher has not served the congregation. They have indulged themselves at the congregation's expense.

The argument has genuine weight. Courage without wisdom is not prophetic; it is self-destructive, and the self-destruction does not benefit the congregation. The pastor who consistently chooses the most inflammatory possible angle on every difficult topic, who mistakes unnecessary offense for prophetic boldness, who has not learned to speak the hard thing with the pastoral care that makes it hearable — that pastor is not a model.

But the argument proves too much if it becomes the permanent justification for systematic avoidance. The distinction that matters is between unnecessary confrontation and necessary confrontation — between the sermon that inflames for its own sake and the sermon that says the thing the text requires, with whatever pastoral care the relationship allows, and then accepts the consequence.

Bonhoeffer was not needlessly inflammatory. He was theologically precise, pastorally engaged, relational in his leadership. And he still said the things that cost him the approval of the majority of the German church, and ultimately cost him his life. [cite — confirm Bonhoeffer's final years and execution, 1945.] The question is not whether to be diplomatic. The question is whether the diplomacy is in service of the message or whether it has replaced the message.

---

## The Pull in My Own Preaching

I have felt this pull in my own preaching.

I have known what the text was going toward on a Thursday afternoon and spent the rest of my sermon preparation time finding the angle that said less of it. I have arrived at Sunday having softened the application in ways that were about my own comfort and called the softening pastoral sensitivity. I have let the powerful person's potential reaction be in the room with me while I was in the room with the text, and I have let that presence shape what I said.

It costs the congregation more than it costs me. That is the thing I have to keep telling myself.

> It costs the congregation more than it costs me.

---

A pastor in my acquaintance preaches to a congregation where the majority of the adult members are in financial positions that the New Testament's teaching on wealth directly addresses. He knows the text. He believes the text. He preaches around it with enough frequency that it has become a pattern, and the congregation has come to expect the pattern, and the giving has remained steady and the powerful members have remained satisfied and the pastoral relationship has remained comfortable.

And the congregation has been formed, year after year, in the confidence that their financial lives are substantially untouched by the gospel — that Christianity is a matter of inner transformation and Sunday practice and private morality, but that the economic life belongs to a different jurisdiction.

The text does not support that formation. Jesus was explicit about where the heart follows the treasure (Matthew 6:21). The early church sold possessions and distributed to any who had need (Acts 2:45). The epistle of James is the most economically direct document in the New Testament, and it is in the canon. The pastor who has not preached James in its full weight to a congregation of relative wealth has not done the job.

---

## Naming the Accountability and Preaching Accordingly

The congregation does not need a pastor who makes them comfortable. They need a pastor who tells them the truth — with love, with pastoral care, with the relational investment that makes the hard word hearable. But the truth, finally and fully, even when it costs.

The watchman who sees the danger and says nothing because the city might not want to hear it has not been kind to the city. They have been complicit in whatever follows.

That is the accountability. Name it honestly. Then preach accordingly.

Every pastor reaches moments when they wonder if they should quit. This is not a sign of weak faith or insufficient calling. It is a sign of the genuine difficulty of the work. The question is not whether you will have those moments — you will. The question is how to tell, when they come, whether they are telling you something true.

There is a real and important difference between being tired and being done. Tiredness is a condition. Doneness — genuine, deep, holy doneness — is a conclusion. And conflating the two is one of the most consequential mistakes a pastor can make. The pastor who quits in a moment of exhaustion that was actually recoverable loses something they may spend years grieving. The pastor who stays in a role they have genuinely completed, out of obligation or fear or the inability to tell the difference, does damage to themselves and to the congregation they are no longer able to genuinely serve.

> Tiredness is a condition.

## The Texture of Tiredness

Tiredness in ministry has a particular texture. It feels heavy and relentless, but beneath the heaviness, something still cares. The tired pastor still loves their congregation, even when they cannot feel it acutely. They still believe in the mission, even when they cannot access the energy to pursue it with their usual intensity. They still have something to say on Sunday mornings, even if finding it requires more effort than it used to. The caring is still there — it is just buried under a layer of depletion that needs to be named and addressed.

Tiredness is also contextual and responsive to change. When the tired pastor gets a real vacation, or takes a genuine sabbatical, or steps back from a specific responsibility that had been draining them, something shifts. Not everything — tiredness that has accumulated over years does not resolve in a week. But the response to genuine rest is a sign. If something in you breathes when you are given space, you are tired. If the rest arrives and the deadness remains, you may be looking at something more significant.

> If something in you breathes when you are given space, you are tired.

The biblical record has language for this kind of tiredness. Elijah, fresh from the heights of Carmel, ran from Jezebel's threat and collapsed in the wilderness, asking God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4). This was not a man who had lost his calling. This was a man whose body and soul had hit the floor after years of warfare. God's response was not to challenge his readiness or question his fitness for the role. It was bread, water, and sleep — twice — and then a word: "The journey is too great for you." Not a verdict about his future. A diagnosis of his present.

The tired pastor needs to hear the same thing Elijah heard: your condition has a name, it has a cause, and there are means of addressing it. That is not a pastoral failure. It is the honesty that makes recovery possible.

## The Biblical Arc of Exhaustion

The Psalms are the most sustained record we have of a person's emotional and spiritual interior, and they do not flinch from exhaustion. Psalm 88 is the darkest psalm — it ends without resolution, without the customary turn toward praise, in complete darkness: "darkness is my closest friend" (Psalm 88:18). The psalmist is not abandoned by God. They are simply in a place from which they cannot see the way out. And the text treats this as legitimate. As something worth saying out loud to God rather than managing privately.

What this suggests is that the tradition has always made room for the pastor who is exhausted, overwhelmed, and unable to access the hope they are supposed to be proclaiming. The question is not whether that experience is legitimate. It is what the experience is telling you.

## The Texture of Done

Being genuinely done looks different. Not every pastor who finishes a particular ministry is burned out — sometimes the season truly is complete, the work truly is finished, and staying past the completion would be its own kind of unfaithfulness. This is the productive kind of done, and it deserves to be honored.

But there is also the done that arrives through depletion, through accumulated harm, through a fundamental mismatch between the pastor and the congregation that has been ignored too long, or through a call that has genuinely shifted. This done is harder to name because it carries more weight — the sense that not just this role but this whole vocation may need to be reconsidered.

The markers of genuine done include: a sustained absence of love for the people you serve, not just an absence of feeling but a resistance to caring that prayer and rest do not address; a loss of belief in the possibility of the congregation's flourishing; a fundamental misalignment between your convictions and the direction the church is moving that cannot be resolved with time; or a clear, confirmed sense of call to a different kind of work that is not rooted in escape but in genuine vocation.

Paul's language in Philippians 4:11 — "I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content" — is often read as a text about attitude adjustment. It is more than that. It is a description of a man who has arrived at a place of genuine settledness about his role and his calling that did not come from circumstances going well. It came from clarity about who he was and what he was for. That clarity is what genuine done sometimes requires: not the absence of difficulty, but the settled sense that this particular difficulty is no longer mine to carry.

## The Counter-Position Worth Engaging

There is a strain of pastoral theology — and it is not without merit — that treats the desire to leave ministry as essentially a failure of nerve, a moment of weakness to be overcome through prayer, recommitment, and the recovery of vision. The argument is that calling is not contingent on comfort, that the prophets all wanted to quit and were called back, that the very desire to stop is often the sign of spiritual attack rather than spiritual truth.

This position deserves serious engagement, not dismissal. It contains a real corrective to a pastoral culture that is too quick to frame burnout as a vocation problem when it is actually a sustainability problem. The prophet Jeremiah declared, "I will not mention his word or speak anymore in his name," and then immediately said, "but his word is in my heart like a fire, a fire shut up in my bones. I am weary of holding it in; indeed, I cannot" (Jeremiah 20:9). That is tiredness. Not doneness. The fire was still there.

But the position fails when it is used as a battering ram against the pastor who genuinely needs to stop — who is not resisting the call but responding faithfully to a body and soul that have reached their limit, or who is in a context that is genuinely toxic and cannot be changed from the inside. Calling is not the same as endurance at all costs. Moses led for forty years and did not reach the Promised Land. The completion of a calling can look like handing it off as much as seeing it through to a human definition of success.

## Why This Distinction Matters So Much

The confusion between tired and done produces pastoral casualties in both directions. Pastors who are tired and conclude they are done leave callings they were meant to continue, and often carry a grief and sense of failure that follows them for years. Pastors who are done but tell themselves they are merely tired stay past their time, growing increasingly hollow in a role that is no longer theirs to fill, doing quiet damage to both themselves and the congregation that needed them to move on.

I have seen both. I have sat with men who left in exhaustion and spent the next decade wondering what might have been. I have sat with men who stayed in a role that had become a slow suffocation, who believed the staying was faithfulness and did not recognize until much later that it was something else — a kind of stubbornness dressed in the language of calling. Neither outcome is good. Both were avoidable.

The damage is not only to the pastor. Congregations that lose a pastor to avoidable burnout suffer in ways that are real and lasting: disrupted community, broken trust, a season of uncertainty during which people slip away and mission slows. Congregations that keep a pastor who has genuinely completed their tenure suffer differently: a slow decline in energy and vision, a leader who is going through the motions, a kind of low-grade institutional depression that nobody can quite name because the pastor is still technically present.

## How to Tell the Difference

You cannot tell the difference alone. This is perhaps the most important thing to say. The question of tired versus done requires witnesses — people who know your history, who have observed your pattern over time, who have the standing to offer honest perspective rather than simply validate what you are already feeling.

> You cannot tell the difference alone.

The tools of self-examination are necessary but insufficient. You are too close to your own story. You have too much at stake in the answer. The pastor who retreats to their study and does intensive journaling about whether they should quit is not doing worthless work — but they are doing incomplete work. The interior examination has to be paired with exterior witness.

A trusted pastoral peer, a mentor who has walked longer roads than yours, a counselor who can help you sift through the layers of history and emotion and discernment — these are the people who can help you answer this question honestly. A spiritual director who has learned to distinguish between the voice of God and the voice of exhaustion, between the nudge toward something new and the flight from something hard, is one of the most valuable figures a pastor can have in this season.

The Pastors Connection Network exists partly for this: to give pastors a community capable of walking alongside them in the moments when the most consequential questions are on the table. Not to tell you the answer. Not to pressure you in either direction. But to know you well enough that when you ask the question, the people around you can say with some authority: that sounds like exhaustion. Or: that sounds like completion. Or: I am not sure, but let us sit with it together before you decide.

Do not answer this question alone. You deserve better than that. And so does the congregation that is depending on the answer being right.

The question itself — am I tired or am I done? — is not a sign that something has gone wrong with you. It is a sign that you are taking both your calling and your limits seriously enough to ask. That is not weakness. It is the beginning of wisdom. Answer it with witnesses, with patience, and with the kind of honesty that has never been safe to perform but has always been the only path to what comes next.

Most congregations have heard more missionary presentations than they can count, and the impact of those presentations, on average, is disappointingly modest. The missionary couple stands at the front with a slideshow of photographs and statistics and a map with pins in it. The need is described. The cost is named. An invitation to give is extended. A small percentage of the congregation responds generously. The majority files out and returns to ordinary life largely unchanged.

This is not because the need is not real, or the missionaries are not compelling, or the congregation does not care. It is because the presentation format — however much care goes into it — is not designed to produce the kind of genuine engagement with a distant reality that moves people from sympathy to genuine investment. Moving the congregation on global mission requires a different approach.

## The Problem Is Theological Before It Is Communicational

The presentation problem is a symptom. The underlying issue is that most congregations have not been formed to understand global mission as anything other than a program the church supports — a department of Christian activity that is funded through a portion of the budget and staffed by unusually courageous people who are not like the rest of us.

The biblical vision is different. In Genesis 12:1-3, God's call to Abram is not a special program for specially called individuals. It is the structure of the covenant: I will bless you so that you will be a blessing. The blessing runs outward by definition. The community formed by God's covenant exists not for its own sake but for the world. This is not a missions program. It is the shape of what it means to be the people of God.

Lesslie Newbigin, who spent decades in India as a missionary before returning to England to address the Western church, argued that the Western church had lost this missionary self-understanding — had come to see itself as a gathered community that occasionally sends representatives out rather than as a missionary community that gathers in order to be sent [cite — confirm]. The solution to the missions presentation problem is not better presentations. It is the slow, patient work of forming a congregation whose entire self-understanding is missionary — whose imagination is shaped by the God who sends, whose prayers are structured around specific people in specific places, whose giving reflects a genuine stake in the advance of the gospel beyond their own community.

Without that theological foundation, better presentation techniques are cosmetic. With it, even the slide show has a different weight.

## The Problem With Statistics

Statistics create scale but not connection. "There are 7,000 unreached people groups in the world" is a fact. It is an important fact. But it is too large and too abstract to generate the emotional engagement that produces sustained giving, genuine prayer, and real mission participation. The human brain is not wired to feel compassion at scale — it is wired to feel compassion for specific people in specific situations.

> The human brain is not wired to feel compassion at scale — it is wired to feel compassion for specific people in specific situations.

This is not a weakness to be overcome through better statistics. It is how God made us — beings of particular love, embedded in specific communities, capable of genuine commitment to actual people in ways that our capacity for abstract caring about statistical populations is not. The same structure that makes us capable of loving our children deeply also limits our ability to feel the weight of millions of strangers equally. The missions communicator who tries to move the congregation through sheer scale of need is working against the grain of human love.

The congregation that knows the name of the national pastor their church partners with, that has heard his voice on a video call, that has prayed for him by name in Sunday services, is far more invested in his ministry than the congregation that has received a quarterly report about "our ministry partners in Region X."

## Making the Distant Near

One of the most effective tools for closing the geographical and cultural distance between a congregation and its global mission partners is live connection. A five-minute video call with a national pastor, broadcast on a Sunday morning before or after the sermon, does more for congregational investment in global mission than an hour of presentations. Hearing an actual human voice from an actual specific place, seeing an actual face, hearing about an actual situation — this makes the mission real in a way that photographs and statistics cannot.

Coordinate these connections regularly. Pray specifically, by name, for people the congregation has seen and heard. Share the stories of what God is doing through those specific people and specific partnerships in ways that honor the dignity and agency of the people the church is partnering with, rather than presenting them as passive recipients of Western generosity.

The dignity question is not incidental. The missions communication that presents global partners as helpless, suffering people who need Western resources to save them — the communication that centers the generosity of the sending church rather than the faith and agency of those working in the field — is both theologically inaccurate and practically counterproductive. It trains the congregation to see themselves as the active subjects of the mission story and the global partner as the object of their benevolence. That training produces a paternalistic relationship with global mission that eventually becomes more about the congregation's sense of its own goodness than about genuine partnership in the gospel.

The story told well puts the national pastor at the center — their faith, their discernment, their courage, their specific knowledge of the community and culture that the Western church cannot replicate. The congregation is not the hero of this story. It is the partner. That reframing changes the emotional texture of missions communication from charity to solidarity.

> The congregation is not the hero of this story.

## The Counterargument From the Pew

The serious objection from a congregation's perspective is this: we are asked to care deeply about people we have never met, in places we cannot imagine, through situations we cannot verify, on the basis of institutional trust in organizations whose actual effectiveness is difficult for us to evaluate. The missions conference asks us to feel what the statistics cannot make us feel, and the honest response from the pew is that we try and mostly fail, and then feel guilty about failing.

This is an honest admission and it deserves an honest response. The response is not to generate better guilt or more emotionally compelling presentations. The response is to create the conditions under which genuine relationship, however limited, becomes possible — through the video call, through the specific name prayed weekly, through the furloughing missionary who eats dinner in congregational homes rather than standing at the podium for one presentation before disappearing again.

The relationship does not need to be deep to be real. A congregation that has prayed for the same Kenyan pastor by name for three years, that knows his wife had surgery last spring and his daughter started university in the fall, has something real — a genuine stake in a genuine person in a genuine place. That is not a manufactured feeling. It is what genuine relationship produces, even across an enormous cultural and geographic distance.

## Integrating Mission Into the Whole Life of the Church

The congregation that engages most deeply with global mission is not the one that has the biggest missions budget — it is the one where global mission is woven into the ordinary life of the community rather than isolated in an annual missions conference. This means: praying for specific global partners in every Sunday service. Teaching the children about the countries and people groups the church is connected to. Studying the global church in small groups. Celebrating the arrivals of missionaries on furlough with the same energy the church brings to any other significant communal event.

It means integrating global mission into the preaching calendar not as a special missions Sunday insert but as the natural expression of what the Scripture texts are actually about — because Scripture is, from Genesis to Revelation, a story about God's purposes for all nations, and a preaching program that never surfaces that dimension is reading a different book.

## A Concrete Scene

A small congregation in a Midwest community had supported the same missionary family for over a decade — dutifully, generously, without much real connection. The quarterly newsletter came, a check was written, and the missionary family remained, in the congregation's imagination, a pleasant abstraction.

At the suggestion of a pastor who had been reading differently about missions engagement, the congregation began scheduling monthly video calls — five minutes on a Sunday morning, projected onto the screen where the sermon slides usually appeared. Within six months the dynamic was unrecognizable. People in the congregation knew the missionaries' children by name. They prayed for the specific challenges that had been named in the last call. When the missionary family came home on furlough, they were received not with the polite interest one shows to a church guest but with the warmth reserved for family that has been away too long.

The missions budget did not change significantly. The congregational investment changed completely. The mission had become real — not through statistics or presentations but through the specific, repeated, named encounter with specific people in specific places doing specific things.

That is how the distant becomes near. Not through better information. Through genuine relationship.

## Mission Is Not a Program

Mission is not a program. It is a posture — the conviction that the local church exists not for itself but for the world. And when that posture is genuinely embedded in the church's culture, talking about global missions stops being an obligatory insertion into the church calendar and becomes the natural expression of who the community understands itself to be.

> Mission is not a program.

The church that has been formed this way does not need to be convinced to care about global mission. It already cares, specifically and personally, because it already knows the people involved, already prays for the places by name, already feels the stakes of the work it is genuinely partnered in.

The missionary presentation that moves the congregation does not move it from indifference to sympathy. It moves it from care to deeper care — because the relationship in which that care was built has been cultivated patiently, specifically, and honestly for years before the presentation is ever made.

That cultivation is the pastor's work. It is slow, unremarkable, and invisible in the quarterly report. It is also the thing on which everything else depends.

The congregation that has been formed to care will care. The congregation that has only been informed has heard a lot of presentations.

The short-term mission trip is one of the most common and most debated practices in contemporary evangelical church life. Millions of Americans participate in short-term missions annually, spending billions of dollars to travel to developing nations for periods ranging from one week to several months. The intentions behind these trips are almost universally good. The outcomes are considerably more mixed.

> The intentions behind these trips are almost universally good.

This is not an argument that short-term missions are inherently problematic or that churches should stop doing them. It is an argument that the question of whether a specific trip will genuinely help or inadvertently harm the people it intends to serve is worth asking honestly, before the commitment is made, with reference to research and the perspectives of people in the receiving communities.

## The Historical Problem Behind the Practice

Short-term missions as a mass practice emerged largely in the second half of the twentieth century, shaped by a confluence of factors: the rise of commercial air travel that made international movement affordable for ordinary Americans, the growth of evangelical para-church organizations that could coordinate large groups, and a genuine missionary energy that the church was right to cultivate.

But it also emerged from a theological assumption that was rarely examined: that the presence of American Christians in a foreign context was itself a form of blessing, that the desire to serve was sufficient qualification for service, and that the good news of the gospel could be adequately translated across cultural, linguistic, and relational distances in seven to ten days.

The missiological tradition should have complicated this assumption earlier than it did. Roland Allen's 1912 work *Missionary Methods: St. Paul's or Ours?* [cite — confirm] was already arguing that the Western missionary enterprise had systematically failed to plant indigenous, self-sustaining churches because it had never genuinely trusted indigenous leaders. Andrew Walls' scholarship on the historical transmission of Christianity from the West to the Global South documented how the gospel took root not when it was delivered by outsiders but when it was received and reinterpreted by indigenous believers [cite — confirm]. The short-term mission movement inherited the structural assumptions that Allen and Walls had already identified as problematic, and scaled them up with jet engines.

## When They Help

Short-term mission trips tend to generate genuine benefit in specific conditions. When they are part of a long-term partnership — when the short-term team is building on an ongoing relationship between sending and receiving churches, contributing to work that the receiving community has identified as a genuine priority, and operating under the leadership of national believers rather than assuming their own leadership — the experience tends to produce genuine value for both participants and community.

Short-term trips also tend to be genuinely beneficial when the skills being brought are genuinely scarce in the receiving context. A team of medical professionals providing care that is genuinely unavailable locally, a construction team building what the community cannot build with available local skills and resources, an English-language training team meeting a specific educational need — these are contributions that the community actually benefits from, rather than contributions that displace local workers or communicate that outsiders can do what locals cannot.

The third condition under which short-term trips help is when they are primarily designed to form the participants rather than to benefit the host community — and when that design is honest about it. The college student who spends two weeks serving alongside national believers in Guatemala, not because her skills are uniquely needed there but because the exposure to the global church and the poverty it works within will permanently reshape her understanding of the gospel — that trip can be genuinely valuable, if the host community is compensated for its time and not burdened by the participants' inexperience.

## When They Hurt

The research on the harm caused by short-term mission trips is substantial and sobering. Steve Corbett and Brian Fikkert in *When Helping Hurts* [cite — confirm] and Robert Lupton in *Toxic Charity* [cite — confirm] have documented the specific ways in which well-intentioned short-term trips can produce dependency, damage local economies, undermine national leadership, and communicate — despite the best intentions of the participants — that the Western team knows better than the local community what the local community needs.

The mission trip that sends unskilled volunteers to build structures that local workers could build more efficiently and economically is not providing help. It is providing a cross-cultural experience at the expense of the local economy. The wages that would have gone to local construction workers — men with families, men with needs — go instead toward the airfare and logistics of Americans whose primary qualification is their willingness to serve.

The team that arrives with a predetermined program and implements it without reference to what the community has asked for is not serving the community. It is serving its own vision of what service looks like.

And the trip that produces a flood of social media posts and speaking engagements and emotional testimonies when the participants return home — while the community that hosted them returns to the structural poverty that a week of American enthusiasm has not altered — has produced a spiritual commodity for the Western church at the cost of the dignity of the people who were treated as its raw material.

I have been on some version of these trips. I have returned with the photographs and the stories and the enlarged sense of my own generosity. I did not ask, while I was there, whether my presence was the best use of the money it cost to send me. I should have asked.

> I have been on some version of these trips.

## The Steel-Manned Defense

The strongest defense of the short-term mission trip is not about the material outcomes. It is about formation.

The argument goes like this: American Christians are, on the whole, profoundly insulated from the global suffering of the majority of the world's population, from the vitality of the church in the Global South, and from the cultural parochialism of their own faith. The short-term trip ruptures that insulation. It produces an embodied encounter with global Christianity and global poverty that reading books about it simply does not produce. The student who returns from two weeks in Rwanda is not the same person who left. That formation is worth taking seriously.

This argument has genuine merit. Paul's vision in Philippians 4:11 of contentment that is learned rather than assumed — "I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content" — was itself formed through the embodied experience of deprivation and abundance. Formation through encounter is a real thing. The church's investment in the global encounter of its members, particularly its young people, is not nothing.

But the defense still does not answer the question of whether the communities receiving these short-term teams are bearing the cost of American formation. That is the question the defense must answer, and it usually changes the subject instead.

## Questions Worth Asking Before the Next Trip

Before organizing or committing to a short-term mission trip, honest reflection on several questions is warranted.

What has the receiving community asked for? Not what does the sending team feel called to provide — what has the receiving community, in its own voice, identified as a genuine need and a genuine welcome?

What would it cost to hire local people to do what the team plans to do, and is that a better investment of the funds that will be spent on airfare and logistics? If the answer is yes, have the honest conversation about who the trip is actually for.

What is the long-term relationship between the sending and receiving communities, and does this trip strengthen or complicate it? A trip that is a single transaction — with no ongoing relationship before or after — is almost certainly benefiting the participants more than the hosts.

How will the trip be evaluated — by the experience of the participants, or by the genuine and measurable benefit to the receiving community? If the evaluation criteria are primarily about transformation in the participants, name that honestly, and make sure the host community is being served rather than used in the process.

## The Pastoral Scene

I sat with a pastor a few years ago who led a mid-sized suburban church with an active short-term missions program. He had taken groups to the same community in Central America for twelve consecutive years. He knew the national pastor by name, knew his wife's name, knew their children's names. He had stayed in their home. He had watched the local congregation grow from forty members to over two hundred.

He told me that the first four or five years, his teams had come with plans and left with photographs and had produced, in his honest assessment, very little that the community could not have done better and cheaper without them. What changed it was a conversation in year six when the national pastor told him, with the particular combination of grace and directness that genuine friendship permits: "What we need from you is not your volunteers. We need your pastors' network. We need you to help us get our young leaders into theological training that we cannot access from here."

The program changed. The trips became smaller, focused on connecting rather than building. The money that had gone to logistics began funding scholarships for local seminary students. The church in Michigan became a genuine partner rather than a periodic benefactor. That is what mission looks like when the receiving community is finally allowed to define it.

> That is what mission looks like when the receiving community is finally allowed to define it.

The communities on the receiving end of American mission trips deserve that level of care. The gospel deserves to be pursued with enough wisdom to genuinely serve the people it claims to love. The question of whether the next trip will help or hurt is worth sitting with long enough to answer honestly — even if the honest answer is inconvenient.

Start with what they asked for. End with whether they were better served than you were formed. Let the gap between those two questions be the work of this year's trip planning.

When the church talks about unreached people groups, the conversation almost always faces outward and away — toward the ethnic and linguistic communities in the Global South and East who have not yet heard the gospel, toward the distant places where Christian witness has not yet taken root, toward the mission frontiers that require the crossing of significant geographic and cultural distance.

This outward orientation is right and necessary. There are billions of people in the world who have not heard the gospel in any meaningful way, and the church's responsibility to them is real and urgent. But there is a blind spot in the conversation that is worth naming: the unreached and underreached communities that exist not on the other side of the world but in the communities where most American churches are already located.

## The Geography of Avoidance

The history of American Christianity and its relationship to its near neighbors is not a simple story of neglect. It is a more complicated story of selective engagement — of the church's consistent ability to be globally passionate while remaining locally comfortable, to send missionaries abroad while walking past mission fields on the way to the airport.

This pattern has deep roots. In the nineteenth century, American Protestant missionary societies channeled enormous energy toward foreign missions — the China Inland Mission, the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions, the Student Volunteer Movement that recruited thousands of college students to overseas service. These were genuine expressions of gospel passion. They were also, in ways that were not always examined, more comfortable than the missions to indigenous peoples on American soil, to recently emancipated Black Americans in the post-Reconstruction South, to the immigrant communities crowding into Northern industrial cities whose foreignness was threatening rather than romantic.

The pattern persists. The church that fundraises for a medical clinic in Uganda and has never visited the refugee resettlement office four miles away is not being asked to choose between those two forms of faithfulness. It is being asked to see both clearly.

## The Refugee Community Two Miles From Your Church
