In almost every mid-sized American city, there are refugee and immigrant communities that represent some of the world's most significant unreached people groups — people who have been relocated by war, political instability, or economic necessity and who are now living within driving distance of churches that have never intentionally engaged them. Somali Muslims in Minneapolis. Karen refugees from Myanmar in the suburbs of Indianapolis. Haitian communities in South Florida. Iraqi families in Detroit.

These communities often have minimal access to gospel witness, not because they are geographically unreachable but because they are culturally beyond the reach of the churches nearest to them. They speak different languages. They come from different religious backgrounds. They inhabit different social networks. The church that is committed to reaching the unreached in distant countries but has never walked across town to meet its Somali neighbors has a mission scope worth examining.

The practical barriers are real: language difference, cultural unfamiliarity, the awkward reality that most American churches have almost no experience engaging people from majority-Muslim backgrounds or from the specific cultural worlds represented by Karen Christians or Congolese Pentecostals. But they are not insurmountable barriers, and they are certainly no greater than the barriers faced by foreign missionaries who cross oceans and language families to pursue the same work.

Acts 17 describes Paul in Athens — not Jerusalem, not Antioch, but a foreign cultural center whose intellectual and religious complexity could have been a reason for withdrawal. He engaged it instead, finding in its altars and its poetry the points of genuine contact through which the gospel could speak. The church's responsibility to its nearest unreached neighbors requires the same posture: genuine curiosity about their world, genuine study of what they actually believe, genuine relationship built over time rather than a program designed to convert them quickly.

## The Incarcerated Population

America incarcerates more people per capita than any other nation on earth, and the prison population represents one of the most significant and systematically underserved mission fields in the country. Chaplaincy programs in correctional facilities do important work, but the local church's engagement with the incarcerated — and with people returning from incarceration — tends to be minimal compared to the scale of the need.

The statistics are staggering. As of recent years, more than two million people are held in American correctional facilities at any given time [cite — confirm]. The majority have no meaningful ongoing connection to a church or Christian community. The recidivism rate for people who return from incarceration without strong community support is significantly higher than for those who do [cite — confirm]. The church's capacity to provide exactly the kind of community that reduces recidivism — belonging, accountability, forgiveness, a narrative of identity that is not defined by the worst thing a person has done — is precisely what makes this a mission field that should be close to the center of every congregation's attention.

Every church that is serious about the mission of the gospel has a question to answer about the men and women in the correctional facilities in its geographic area. What is our responsibility to these people? What would genuine engagement look like? Not just prison visitation as a program, but the genuine welcome of returning citizens into the community of the church — the hardest kind of welcome, the one that makes people uncomfortable, and often the one that matters most to the person being welcomed.

The language of Isaiah 61 — the proclamation of liberty to captives, the opening of the prison to those who are bound — is not only a metaphor. Jesus quotes it in Luke 4:18 as his inaugural statement of mission. The church that reads that text on Sunday and ignores the county jail on Monday has not yet understood what its Lord was claiming.

## The Spiritual-But-Not-Religious Population

Research on people who claim no religious affiliation — the so-called "nones" — has identified four distinct categories within this growing population, and the largest of these is not atheists or agnostics but people who retain a genuine spiritual openness while remaining skeptical of institutional religion [cite — confirm]. This population is enormous, it is growing, and it is largely unreached by the methods the church has historically used for evangelism.

These are not hostile people. They are people who have been failed by the church — by its hypocrisy, its abuse of power, its answers that did not match their questions — and who left without losing the spiritual instinct that brought them there. They are people for whom the word "church" carries a complex freight of experience and disappointment, but for whom the questions of meaning, death, forgiveness, and love remain stubbornly alive.

Reaching them requires new relationships, new points of contact, and new modes of witness that begin where they are rather than where the church expects them to be. It requires pastors who can speak to doubt without dismissing it, who can acknowledge the church's failures without making those failures the whole story, who have enough intellectual credibility to be taken seriously when they make claims about God.

This is not a distant population. It is the person in the next cubicle, the neighbor whose child plays with your child, the sibling who stopped attending church ten years ago and has not come back. The mission to the spiritual-but-not-religious is not a foreign mission. It is the mission that begins in every relationship the church's members already have.

## The Steel-Manned Challenge

The strongest objection to this local-mission emphasis is that it risks becoming a retreat from the genuinely unreached peoples of the world in favor of the more comfortable and familiar mission to Western post-Christians. The global church's under-resourced frontier missions — in the 10/40 Window, among the hundreds of people groups who have no access to the gospel in their heart language — are the church's most urgent responsibility, and any frame that redirects attention toward domestic mission risks becoming a reason to stay home.

This objection is right about the global urgency. It is wrong to construct a zero-sum competition between global and local mission. Jesus does not, in Acts 1:8, instruct his disciples to choose between Jerusalem and the ends of the earth. He describes a mission that moves simultaneously and expansively in every direction. The church that says it cannot pursue both has made an organizational decision and dressed it as a theological one.

The pastor who builds genuine relationships with the Somali community in his city is not abandoning global mission. He may be pursuing it from within it — because the Somali diaspora in Minneapolis has family networks that reach back to Somalia, and the relationships built here can carry the gospel there in ways that no Western missionary's visa application will ever accomplish.

## The Pastoral Scene

A friend of mine pastors a church in a mid-sized Michigan city. Three years ago, he noticed that within six blocks of his church building, there were approximately forty Congolese families who had been resettled by the local refugee agency. He had driven past them for two years without considering that they were, by every missiological definition, an unreached people group within his parish.

He started by making a phone call to the resettlement agency. He learned that what these families needed most was not a Sunday service in English — it was English conversation practice, help navigating the school system, and the basic dignity of being known by name. He recruited six families from his congregation to build those relationships, deliberately, over twelve months, with no programming agenda and no evangelism quota.

At the end of twelve months, two of the Congolese families had started attending the church. Not because they were recruited. Because they had been genuinely known.

> Not because they were recruited. Because they had been genuinely known.

The mission field closest to your church is probably visible from your parking lot. The question is not whether the need is there. The question is whether you are willing to see it.

> The mission field closest to your church is probably visible from your parking lot.

The ends of the earth begin at your address.

> The ends of the earth begin at your address.

The word "missionary" has carried, for most of Western church history, a fairly consistent set of images: the Western European or North American believer who leaves the comfort of their home culture to take the gospel to peoples and places that have not yet received it. This image is not entirely wrong — it reflects a real history and a genuine expression of Christian mission that has borne significant fruit. But it is increasingly incomplete, and the incompleteness is reshaping the global mission enterprise in ways that have profound implications for every church that takes the Great Commission seriously.

The redefining is being done primarily by the national pastors themselves — the indigenous believers, trained leaders, and church planters in the Global South and East who are reaching their own nations and neighboring peoples with a depth of cultural competence, relational trust, and contextual wisdom that no outside missionary can replicate.

## How We Got to This Moment

The Western missionary enterprise that produced the modern mission movement had genuine theological integrity at its best. William Carey's 1792 pamphlet arguing for the church's obligation to the unevangelized world [cite — confirm] — "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God" — was not colonial triumphalism dressed as theology. It was a genuine conviction that the gospel was for all peoples, and a challenge to a church that had domesticated that conviction into near-irrelevance.

What followed, over the next two centuries, was remarkable in its reach and genuinely complex in its outcomes. Western missionaries did plant churches. They did translate Scriptures into hundreds of languages. They did establish schools and hospitals and institutions that transformed communities. The debt of the global church to the Western missionary movement is real, and the critics who acknowledge only its failures have made an argument that is more ideologically convenient than historically honest.

But the movement also carried, with varying degrees of consciousness, a theological assumption that was rarely examined: that the Western believer bringing the gospel to a non-Western people was not merely carrying a message across a cultural boundary but was, in some sense, bringing civilization along with it. That the missionary was not simply a servant of the gospel but a representative of a cultural order that was itself part of what was being offered. That the indigenous church that emerged from the mission should look, worship, and organize itself according to Western models, because those models were assumed to be most aligned with the gospel itself.

Roland Allen identified this assumption as the primary failure of the missionary enterprise as early as 1912, arguing in *Missionary Methods: St. Paul's or Ours?* that Paul planted churches and immediately trusted them to the Spirit's guidance and indigenous leadership, while the Western mission had produced dependent churches that could not function without Western organizational support [cite — confirm]. Andrew Walls, writing decades later, documented how the center of global Christianity had shifted dramatically from the Western North to the Global South — not as the failure of the Western mission, but as its unexpected and ironic fulfillment [cite — confirm].

## The Numbers Tell the Story

The global church has grown from approximately 600 million Christians in 1900 to over 2.5 billion today, and the most significant portion of that growth has happened in Africa, Asia, and Latin America — driven not primarily by Western mission agencies but by indigenous believers sharing the gospel with their own communities.

In China, where Western missionaries were expelled following the Communist revolution in 1949, the church has grown from approximately one million believers to an estimated sixty to one hundred million today [cite — confirm]. In sub-Saharan Africa, the church has grown from approximately nine million Christians in 1900 to over six hundred million today [cite — confirm]. In Latin America, the Pentecostal movement has grown from a few thousand at the beginning of the twentieth century to hundreds of millions — the vast majority of that growth driven by indigenous leadership rather than Western mission [cite — confirm].

These are not the outcomes of Western mission strategy. They are the outcomes of the Spirit of God working through the indigenous church. The implication is not that Western missions have been ineffective — the early planting of the church in many of these regions by Western missionaries was genuinely important. The implication is that the model that produced those early plants is no longer the primary engine of global church growth, and that the Western church's continued insistence on its centrality in global mission reflects a theological assumption about the superiority of the Western missionary that the evidence does not support.

> These are not the outcomes of Western mission strategy.

## What National Pastors Are Actually Doing

The national pastors who are reaching their own nations and neighboring peoples are not working with the resources of Western mission agencies. They are working with the resources of their own communities, supplemented by relationships with global partners who understand their role as support rather than direction.

In Ethiopia, indigenous church planting movements have established thousands of congregations in the last two decades, many of them in regions where no Western missionary has ever worked — reaching their own ethnic neighbors with the gospel through relationships and trust that no outsider could establish in a comparable timeframe [cite — confirm]. In India, Dalit Christian leaders are reaching other Dalit communities with a gospel that speaks directly to their experience of exclusion and dignifies them as bearers of the image of God — a message with profound contextual power that a Western missionary's cultural framework would have difficulty accessing [cite — confirm].

In the Middle East, where Western mission access is either legally restricted or culturally counterproductive, national believers are reaching Muslim-background people through networks of relationship that function entirely outside the structures and visibility of Western mission agencies. The gospel is advancing. It is advancing without Western leadership, and in many cases, the absence of Western visibility is a strategic asset rather than a deficit.

> The gospel is advancing.

## What National Pastors Actually Need

If the national pastor is increasingly the primary agent of gospel advance in the hardest-to-reach regions, the question for the Western church is not "how do we go there?" but "how do we genuinely support them?" And the answer to that question requires genuine listening — to the national pastors themselves — about what they actually need, rather than the assumption that what they need is what Western churches would need in their situation.

Consistent themes emerge when national pastors in underresourced regions are asked about their needs. Theological training that is contextually appropriate rather than a transplant of Western seminary curricula — training that engages the specific biblical and theological questions that arise from their cultural context, their religious neighbors, and their political circumstances. Peer community with other national pastors who understand the specific challenges of their context — the kind of pastoral companionship and professional development that the Western pastor takes for granted and the national pastor often lacks entirely. Financial support that is structured to build sustainability rather than dependence — the kind that funds infrastructure and training rather than salaries that will disappear when the Western relationship ends.

And the dignity of being treated as genuine partners in the mission rather than beneficiaries of Western generosity. This is not a sentimental point. It is a theological and missiological one. The national pastor who is treated as a project — as the recipient of Western expertise and Western resources, as a junior partner in an enterprise whose strategic direction is set somewhere else — is being positioned in a way that undermines both his effectiveness and the indigenous health of the church he leads.

## The Implication for How Western Churches Think About Mission

The theological reconstruction this requires is significant. The Western church must be willing to move from the posture of sender to the posture of partner — from the assumption that its primary role in global mission is to produce and deploy missionaries to the recognition that its primary role may be to resource and accompany the national pastors who are already deployed in the places it wants to reach.

This is not a retreat from global mission. It is a more accurate reading of what global mission actually looks like in the twenty-first century. The Great Commission in Matthew 28:18-20 does not specify that the disciples who make disciples of all nations must be Western. It specifies that the mission includes all nations, proceeds under the authority of Christ, and continues until the end of the age. The Spirit is fulfilling that commission through the indigenous church with a scope and a depth that the Western church is only beginning to understand.

The international partnership model that the Pastors Connection Network is building — not sending Western missionaries, but coming alongside national pastors with theological training, peer community, and dignifying partnership — is one form of that reorientation. It begins not with the assumption that the Western church has something the national church needs, but with the question the national pastor was never asked: what do you actually need, and how can we genuinely provide it?

That question changes the relationship. The relationship changes the mission.

The center of gravity of global Christianity has moved. The missionary image that has dominated the Western church's imagination for two centuries is being replaced by something more accurate and more demanding: a vision of partners scattered across the Global South and East who are reaching their own peoples with a depth the Western church cannot replicate, and who need us not to lead them but to genuinely serve them.

> The center of gravity of global Christianity has moved.

That is what the national pastor is redefining. The only question is whether the Western church has the humility to follow.

The American church has developed a sophisticated relationship with comfort. Its buildings are climate controlled. Its services are crafted for maximum accessibility and engagement. Its theology has been shaped, over generations, by a cultural environment in which Christianity was the dominant social framework — where being a Christian was the normal thing to be, the socially advantageous thing, the thing that came with cultural benefits rather than cultural costs. This environment has produced a particular kind of Christianity: genuine in many of its expressions, but often inadequately formed for the experience of genuine suffering.

The global church — specifically, the churches in the Global South and East that have grown so dramatically over the past century — has developed in a profoundly different environment. In China, Nigeria, Iran, India, and scores of other nations, becoming a Christian can cost a person their family, their social standing, their livelihood, their freedom, and sometimes their life. The theology that has emerged from these contexts is not a different gospel. It is the same gospel, forged in conditions that have produced a depth of faith and a theology of suffering that the comfortable Western church desperately needs to receive.

> It is the same gospel, forged in conditions that have produced a depth of faith and a theology of suffering that the comfortable Western church desperately needs to receive.

## The Historical Arc

The shift of Christianity's center of gravity from the Global North to the Global South is one of the most significant demographic and theological developments of the past century. Philip Jenkins documented this transformation in his landmark work, noting that by the early twenty-first century, the majority of the world's Christians lived in Africa, Asia, and Latin America — not in Europe and North America, where Christianity had been institutionally dominant for over a millennium [cite — confirm].

This is not merely a statistical fact. It represents a fundamental shift in where the theological center of Christianity is being generated. The church that has suffered — the church that has watched its members imprisoned, that has held worship services underground, that has baptized people who knew the baptism might cost them their family — is producing theology from the bottom of the experience of faith rather than the top of cultural privilege. That theology deserves to be received as the serious, tested thing it is.

The Western church's theological tradition was largely formed in conditions of cultural power. The councils that shaped Christian doctrine met under imperial patronage or, in later centuries, under the protection of established churches with state backing. The tradition is not invalid because of this — the Spirit works through history's specific conditions. But it means that certain aspects of biblical teaching about suffering have been systematically underemphasized in the Western tradition, because the conditions in which that tradition was formed did not require them.

## Their Theology of Suffering Is Different

The Western church's primary framework for suffering has tended toward two poles: the prosperity gospel, which treats suffering as a sign of insufficient faith that will be removed by adequate belief; and a more mainline therapeutic framework, which treats suffering as a problem to be managed and reduced through the resources of psychology and community support. Both of these frameworks are oriented toward the elimination of suffering. Neither of them is adequate for the believer who faces suffering that cannot be eliminated.

The theology of suffering that has emerged from persecuted churches tells a different story. Not that suffering is good or desired, but that it can be the site of genuine encounter with a God who is present in it — that the cross is not merely a theological mechanism for salvation but a model for the shape of genuine discipleship, that following Jesus has always meant the willingness to carry cost. This is not masochism. It is the realistic faith of people who have had to find God in the darkness because there was no other place to look.

> It is the realistic faith of people who have had to find God in the darkness because there was no other place to look.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a context of genuine political cost for his faith, understood something that the comfortable church has always found difficult: that "the cross is laid on every Christian" — that suffering is not an interruption of the Christian life but a constitutive feature of it [cite — confirm]. The persecuted church in China, Nigeria, or Iran does not need to read Bonhoeffer to arrive at this conclusion. They have lived it.

## The Counter-Position

The counterargument from a comfortable Western church context is worth naming honestly: the theology of the persecuted church risks romanticizing suffering, making an idol of hardship, and implicitly shaming believers who live in comfort through no fault of their own. The person who lives in a safe, free country, who has never faced persecution for their faith, did not choose their circumstances any more than the persecuted believer chose theirs. To suggest that real faith requires suffering, or that the theology of the suffering church is more genuine than the theology of the comfortable church, is to create a hierarchy of authenticity that Scripture does not support.

This is a real concern. The response is not to claim that suffering is superior to safety, or that the persecuted church's theological insight is inaccessible to the comfortable church. The response is to say that the persecuted church's theological tradition has emphasized aspects of Scripture — Philippians 1:29, 1 Peter 4:12-13, 2 Corinthians 1:3-7, the entire letter of Revelation — that the comfortable church has systematically underemphasized because its conditions did not require them. The comfortable Western believer can receive this tradition as a gift: not as a condemnation of their circumstances but as an expansion of their theological vision. The suffering the Western Christian has not faced externally, they will face in other forms — illness, loss, grief, the suffering of those they love. The theology of the persecuted church prepares the believer for that, in ways that the therapeutic framework does not.

## Their Prayer Life Is Different

The prayer life of the persecuted church tends to be characterized by a desperation and a specificity that is difficult to manufacture in comfortable circumstances. When the prayer for safety is genuinely urgent — when the believer asking for protection is facing actual threat — the prayer has a different texture than the same words spoken from a position of security. The Western Christian who has encountered the prayer life of believers in genuinely dangerous contexts often reports the experience as profoundly humbling and deeply instructive.

The church in China, which spent decades of severe persecution praying for the growth of the church, and then watched the church grow beyond anything the persecutors intended to suppress, has a testimony about the power of prayer in adversity that reshapes the Western church's understanding of what prayer is and what it is for. The estimate that the Chinese church grew from approximately 750,000 Christians in 1950 to somewhere between 60 and 100 million by the early twenty-first century — during a period of sustained state opposition — is not a statistical anomaly [cite — confirm]. It is a theological testimony.

The God who presided over that growth was not granting prosperity or comfort. He was doing something in the middle of suffering that the prosperity framework cannot explain and the therapeutic framework cannot contain. The prayer life that sustained that growth was shaped by the conviction that God was present in the suffering and active through it — not despite it.

## Receiving Rather Than Sending

The church in the Global South has gifts to give the Western church — theological, spiritual, missional — that the Western church has rarely been positioned to receive because it has been so accustomed to seeing itself as the giver. The missions history of the past two centuries has largely been the story of Western Christians sending resources, personnel, and theological frameworks to the Global South. That story contains genuine acts of faithfulness. It also contains deep failures — the conflation of the gospel with Western culture, the paternalism that assumed the Western church had what the rest of the world needed and that the traffic ran only in one direction.

The partnership model — the conviction that the mission works in both directions, that the Western church has as much to receive as to give, and that the genuine humility required to receive well is itself a form of formation that the Western church needs — represents a more theologically coherent posture. The Western pastor who sits with a Nigerian bishop or a Chinese house church leader as a student rather than a teacher is not simply being polite. They are practicing the theological receptivity that Paul commends in Romans 12:10 — "give preference to one another in honor" — in its most demanding cross-cultural form.

## A Concrete Scene

A pastor I know returned from a partnership visit to a church community in a region where Christians face genuine legal risk. He had gone to provide: training, resources, encouragement from the West. What he received was a theology of presence — a conviction, embodied in every conversation and every prayer meeting he attended, that God was specifically, personally, irreplaceably present in the gathering of his people, even when the gathering had to be clandestine, even when the cost was high, even when everything the Western church would identify as "resources" was absent.

He came back and sat in his well-funded, climate-controlled office and felt, for the first time in years, that he had been in the presence of something he could not produce with his budget. The church he had visited was not better than his church in every way. But it had been formed by conditions that had burned away the assumption that the presence of God and the presence of comfort are the same thing.

He is still being changed by that distinction.

## What the American Church Needs to Receive

The suffering church's testimony is not a critique of the comfortable church's faithfulness in its own context. It is an invitation to a larger theological vision — a vision that takes seriously the biblical insistence that the cross is the shape of genuine discipleship, that the road to resurrection runs through suffering rather than around it, and that the God who is present in the darkness is not waiting for the lights to come on before he does his deepest work.

The American church that is willing to receive this — to sit with the theology of the persecuted, to learn from the prayer life of the desperate, to accept partnership with the church of the Global South as a genuinely two-directional relationship — is a church that is being formed for what the twenty-first century will actually require of it.

The comfort will not last forever. It never does. The question is whether the theology will be strong enough to hold the weight of what comes next.

> The comfort will not last forever.

The persecuted church already knows how to carry that weight. The American church has the opportunity to learn from them before the necessity arrives.

This is not the time to be a slow student.

The first time a church sends someone from its own congregation into cross-cultural mission — not just giving money to a distant agency, but releasing one of its own people from the community they have built together, commissioning them, blessing them, and committing to support them over the long haul — something changes in the church permanently. The mission stops being abstract. It becomes personal. The congregation has skin in the game now, in the most literal sense, and the skin belongs to someone they love.

> The mission stops being abstract.

The churches that are most missionally vital tend to be sending churches — churches that have made the deliberate commitment to identify, develop, and release people from within their own congregation into the broader work of the gospel. But most churches have never done this, and the path from never having sent anyone to having a genuine sending culture is not obvious. This article is an attempt to map it.

## The Sending Culture Does Not Start With Sending

The first step toward becoming a sending church is not identifying someone to send. It is cultivating a congregation whose imagination is shaped by the global mission — a community that reads Scripture through the lens of the God who sends, that prays regularly and specifically for the unreached, and that understands the local church not as a destination but as a deployment center.

This formation happens in worship, in preaching, in how the church uses its giving, and in the stories it tells about itself. A church that celebrates the person who leaves for the mission field with the same energy it would celebrate the person who joins the staff — that treats sending out as a sign of health rather than a loss — is building the cultural infrastructure that makes genuine sending possible.

The biblical case for this is not obscure. From Genesis 12, where God tells Abram "I will bless you so that you will be a blessing," the direction of God's purposes has always been outward. The covenant community exists not for itself but for the world. Jesus' commission in Matthew 28 is not a program the church adds to its existing agenda — it is the shape of the church's existence. And the church in Antioch, described in Acts 13, models what the Spirit-led sending community looks like: the congregation is worshipping and fasting when the Spirit says, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them" (Acts 13:2). They do not merely release these two. They fast, they pray, they lay hands on them, and they send them off.

The Antioch church did not get there overnight. Acts 11 describes its formation through the ministry of Barnabas and Saul, through the prophetic ministry of people who had come from Jerusalem and Cyprus and Cyrene, through the multiethnic community that was built before the sending ever happened. Sending culture was the fruit of prior formation. It still is.

> Sending culture was the fruit of prior formation.

## The Theological Problem Underneath

Most churches that have never sent anyone are not opposed to mission. They give to mission agencies. They have a missions line in the budget. They host the occasional missionary who comes home on furlough and shows slides. The problem is not indifference. It is a theological misunderstanding about what the local church is.

Lesslie Newbigin spent his ministry — first as a missionary to India, then as a theologian addressing the Western church — arguing that the church is not primarily a gathered community that occasionally sends out individuals. The church is, by its nature, a missionary community [cite — confirm]. The gathering is in service of the sending. The worship equips the witness. The community is formed so that it can be dispersed. When the local church treats mission as a department — something the missions committee handles, funded by a percentage of the budget — it has accepted a structural lie about what the church is and what it is for.

Getting to a genuine sending culture requires correcting this theological error at the level of ecclesiology, not just programming. It requires the pastor to preach, with clarity and regularity, that the church exists for the world and not for its own comfort — that the highest expression of a congregation's health is not a beautiful campus or a flourishing program but the willingness to release its best people into the service of the unreached.

I have preached this and felt the discomfort it produces. The family whose children grew up in this church does not want to watch them go to Southeast Asia. The elders who invested years in developing a gifted young leader do not want to send him to a place where he cannot be replaced. These are real losses, and the pastor who minimizes them is not being more missional — they are being less honest. The call to send costs something. Churches that have never sent anyone have often, at some level, been protecting themselves from that cost.

## The Counter-Position, Answered

The counterargument from a cautious elder board sounds like this: our church has real needs right here. Our neighborhood is underserved. Our congregation has people in genuine crisis. The idea that we should invest in sending someone overseas when there are unreached people at our own doorstep is a failure of stewardship and a misreading of mission priority.

This is a serious argument. It deserves a serious answer. The answer is that it presents a false binary. The New Testament does not pit Jerusalem against the ends of the earth — it puts them in sequence and holds them together simultaneously (Acts 1:8). The church in Antioch that sent Paul and Barnabas to Asia Minor and Greece was also, simultaneously, the church that collected funds for the poor in Jerusalem (Acts 11:27-30). Sending into global mission and serving the local community are not competing goods. They are expressions of the same missionary orientation.

Moreover, the experience of the churches that have sent is consistent: sending does not drain a congregation. It expands it. The church that has skin in the game — that is praying weekly for specific people in specific places, that is receiving reports and seeing God at work in ways they participated in — tends to become more generous, more praying, more engaged with mission at every level. The sending creates the culture that makes the local work more vital, not less.

## Identifying Potential Missionaries

Potential missionaries — people who may be called to cross-cultural ministry — are almost always already in the congregation, often unaware that the church would recognize and affirm that calling if they named it. The job of a sending church is to create the context in which that calling can be identified, named, tested, and developed.

This means preaching about vocation and calling in ways that include the possibility of missionary service as a genuine option for ordinary church members. It means asking questions — in pastoral conversations, in small group settings, in annual conversations about how members understand their calling — that surface the people who are already feeling the pull. And it means responding to those people with genuine investment: not just a referral to a mission agency, but the commitment of the church community to walk with them through discernment, training, and preparation.

## The Commitment of the Sending Church

Sending someone is not primarily a financial transaction. It is a relational commitment. The sending church that commissions a missionary and then relates to them primarily through a quarterly newsletter has not sent them — it has offloaded them. The sending church that maintains genuine, ongoing, personal relationship with the people it has sent — praying for them specifically, communicating regularly, receiving them well when they come home on furlough, advocating for them in the congregation as real people with real struggles — has sent them in the biblical sense.

This level of commitment is demanding. It requires someone in the church to take responsibility for the ongoing relationship, to maintain the connection between the congregation and the missionary, and to be the advocate for the missionary's wellbeing and needs within the church community. That role — the mission advocate or church missions liaison — is one of the most important lay leadership roles a church can cultivate. When it is filled by someone with genuine passion and relational capacity, the connection between church and missionary tends to thrive and deepen in ways that benefit both.

## A Concrete Scene

A family in our congregation spent three years preparing before they were sent. During that time the church walked with them through fundraising, language study, and the emotional arc of leaving — the selling of a house, the farewell to parents, the last Sunday, the commissioning service that felt both like a celebration and a grief. The congregation prayed them out the door.

Eighteen months later, at a Sunday service, we played a short video they had recorded from their apartment in the city where they served. They named the colleagues they had been praying with. They described a family in their building who had begun asking questions about Jesus. They asked the congregation to pray for a specific conversation coming the following Thursday.

The room was different after that video. Not dramatically, loudly different. Quietly different. The mission was no longer a line in the budget or a map on the wall. It was their people, in a specific apartment, praying for a specific family, going into a specific Thursday. We had sent them and they had taken us with them. That is what a sending culture does: it binds the whole congregation to the frontier, whether they cross the ocean or not.

## The First Step

The church that has never sent anyone begins not by identifying who to send but by confessing, honestly, why it has not sent anyone. The reasons are almost always the same: the cost felt too high, the need felt too abstract, the internal needs felt more urgent, or no one asked the question seriously enough to force a decision. Naming that, from the pulpit, with genuine repentance and genuine vision for what is possible — that is the first act of a sending church.

The God who said "as the Father has sent me, I am sending you" (John 20:21) was not offering an optional program. He was describing the shape of the church's existence. The congregation that receives that commission as its own — that allows it to reorganize not just its missions budget but its whole imagination of what the church is for — will find that the act of sending is not a sacrifice it makes for the mission. It is the thing that makes the church most fully itself.

The church exists to be sent. The sending culture is not an advanced feature for mature congregations. It is the baseline expression of what the church is.

> The church exists to be sent.

That is the weight the pastor carries into the first conversation about becoming a sending church. And it is heavy enough to be worth carrying.

There was a time — not that long ago in historical terms — when the average congregation was not a cross-section of the political spectrum in quite the way that most congregations are today. Political diversity within a congregation existed, but political identity was not the kind of defining framework that it has become — was not the thing that people felt most keenly when they sat next to someone who voted differently, attended the same church as someone who held views they found incomprehensible, and tried to take communion alongside someone who they suspected did not share their sense of what was at stake in the world.

Today it is. The pastor who pretends otherwise — who acts as though the political diversity in the pew is not there, or not charged, or manageable through carefully crafted neutrality — is pastoring an imaginary congregation rather than the actual one in front of them.

## What Is Actually at Stake

> The challenge of pastoring across political division is not primarily a political challenge. It is a theological one.

The challenge of pastoring across political division is not primarily a political challenge. It is a theological one. The question is not how to manage different political opinions in the same room — that is a management challenge. The question is whether the gospel is genuinely bigger than the political identities that have come to define so much of American life, and whether the church is capable of being that embodied demonstration.

Paul's argument in Ephesians 2 is that the cross does not just reconcile humans to God — it reconciles humans to each other, creating a new community from people who were genuinely, historically divided. The Jew and the Gentile. The citizen and the foreigner. The free person and the slave. These were not minor differences in perspective. They were the defining fault lines of the ancient world, the divisions that organized social reality and determined status, safety, and belonging. And Paul's claim is that the church — specifically the church — is the community in which those divisions are being overcome.

The political divisions of twenty-first-century America are serious. They are not, by any historical measure, as serious as the Jew-Gentile divide that Paul is addressing. That was a chasm forged over centuries of mutual hostility, religious boundary-keeping, and social apartheid. And Paul's word to the Ephesians is that the cross has made "one new humanity in place of the two" (Ephesians 2:15). If the cross could accomplish that, the premise that it cannot hold a congregation divided over tax policy or immigration enforcement is a failure of theological nerve.

## The Historical Weight of This Moment

The current political polarization in American life is not simply a disagreement about policy. Sociologist Robert Bellah identified decades ago that America has always carried within it the tension between its civil religion — its sense of special national destiny — and the prophetic tradition that calls all national stories to account before the God of Scripture [cite — confirm]. What has happened in the twenty-first century is that the civil religion has fractured into competing tribal versions, each claiming the authority of ultimate conviction, each demanding the kind of loyalty that properly belongs to God alone.

James K.A. Smith's analysis of how our loves are formed by cultural liturgies — the rituals and practices and narratives that shape what we desire before we reason about it — helps explain why this is so intractable [cite — confirm]. People do not simply hold political opinions the way they hold opinions about restaurants. Their political identity has been formed through a long process of liturgical formation: the news they consume daily, the community that affirms their view of reality, the enemy-narrative that gives shape and meaning to their sense of the world. Changing that formation requires the same kind of patient, long-term, countercultural liturgical work that genuine discipleship has always required.

> I did not have a clever word to resolve it. I still do not.

The pastor who faces a politically divided congregation is not simply managing a disagreement. They are standing at the intersection of two competing liturgical formations, each of which believes it is not merely political but moral — perhaps even sacred. The pastoral work required is not conflict management. It is counter-formation.

## What the Pastor Can and Cannot Do

The pastor can model. The pastor can preach a gospel that is genuinely larger than any political framework and embody, in their own relationships across political lines, what reconciliation looks like. The pastor can refuse to allow the church's gatherings to become partisan rallies in either direction. The pastor can speak the prophetic word that no political identity fully accommodates — challenging both sides with what the gospel actually demands.

What the pastor cannot do is eliminate the tension. The tension is real. The differences are real. The pastor's job is not to pretend they do not exist but to insist, from the authority of the gospel, that they are not ultimate — that the thing that unites the congregation in Christ is more fundamental than the things that divide them in the public square. Making that case compellingly, consistently, and with enough pastoral care for the real people on each side to feel genuinely received — that is the work.

## The Counter-Position, Honestly Held

There is a serious counterargument that must be named and answered. It goes like this: the church's claim to transcend politics is itself a political act — an exercise of power that privileges those who can afford to depoliticize their faith, who have never needed the church to be a site of resistance to injustice, who find the status quo comfortable enough that "rising above politics" means leaving it unchallenged. The person who has been harmed by specific policies, who has watched specific political decisions affect specific people they love, cannot simply set that down at the door and call it discipleship.

This is not a cynical argument. It is a serious one. And the response cannot be to dismiss it. The response is this: the prophetic tradition within Scripture — Amos, Micah, Isaiah, Jesus himself — was deeply political in its content while refusing to be domesticated by any political party. The prophets were not neutral. They named injustice with precision. But they named it from within the covenant framework, from within the claims of God on the whole life of the community, in ways that condemned both the false comfort of the powerful and the false despair of the oppressed. The church that refuses to name injustice in the name of political neutrality has abdicated the prophetic function. The church that names it only through the frame of one political party has surrendered it. The pastor's work is to recover the prophetic imagination that is genuinely independent — beholden not to a platform but to the kingdom.

> It is the only thing we have. It turns out to be enough.

## A Pastoral Scene

I have sat across from two members of my own congregation — people I love, who love Jesus, who would both die for the other if the need arose — and watched them look at each other with the specific pain of people who suspect they are enemies. One had attended a school board meeting and come away shaking with anger about what was being taught to children. The other had watched the same footage and come away shaking with anger about who was being targeted. They were responding to the same event with the same emotional intensity and the same conviction that something sacred was at stake.

I did not have a clever word to resolve it. I still do not. What I had was the Communion table, and the stubborn conviction that both of them belonged at it. What I had was the reminder that the same Paul who wrote Ephesians 2 wrote Romans 14 — that the community of faith has always contained people whose disagreements ran deep, and that the call is not to agree but to receive one another as Christ received us (Romans 15:7). That is not neutrality. It is a harder and higher demand than agreement.

## Practical Pastoral Strategies

Several specific practices help. First: preach through passages that address political realities — justice, power, care for the vulnerable, the sovereignty of God over human governments — and engage them honestly, without partisan framing, letting Scripture make its own claims. Romans 13, Revelation 13, Micah 6:8, Luke 4:18 — these texts have political freight. Preach them straight. Trust the congregation to receive them.

Second: create intentional space for cross-partisan relationship within the congregation — small groups that are not organized by affinity, service opportunities that bring different kinds of people together around shared mission, social gatherings that cross the informal social boundaries that parallel political ones.

Third: be willing to name the idolatry in both directions. The person who has made their political identity the organizing center of their life — who cannot imagine being genuinely committed to someone who votes differently — has placed something in the seat that belongs to Christ. Augustine's definition of idolatry as disordered love — loving something that is good with the kind of love that belongs only to God — applies here with precision [cite — confirm]. Politics is not nothing. But it is not ultimate. The pastor who cannot name that, from the pulpit, with equal charity toward both sides, has abdicated the prophetic function of the office.

Fourth: model cross-partisan friendship publicly. The pastor whose personal relationships with leaders in the community visibly cross political lines demonstrates, in action, what they are asking the congregation to practice. Hypocrisy in either direction — the pastor who preaches unity but privately dismisses one side — will be noticed by the people who trust that pastor most.

## The Steel Test

The congregation that has been genuinely formed by the gospel should be unable to be fully claimed by any political party. Both parties, in any healthy pluralist democracy, contain positions that a serious reading of Scripture affirms and positions that it challenges. The congregation that is a reliable voting bloc for one party — regardless of which party — has already been shaped by something other than the gospel as its primary loyalty.

I have said this from my own pulpit. I have watched the discomfort it produces on both sides of the aisle. That discomfort is not a pastoral failure. It is, I think, the gospel doing its work — unsettling the idolatries that political tribes require, insisting on an allegiance that precedes and exceeds every human political project.

Not every political opinion is equally valid. Prophetic preaching names injustice by name. But the community that can only hear the indictment of the other side's sins has ceased to be a congregation and become a caucus.

## The Weight at the End

The Communion table is the answer the church has been given, and it is an inadequate answer in the sense that it does not resolve the disagreements, and it is the only answer in the sense that nothing else can hold the room. This is the body of Christ given for you. Not for your tribe. For you. And for the person beside you who voted the way you did not, and whose fear for the country is as real as yours, and who belongs here as fully as you do.

The pastor's job is not to fix the polarization of American political life. It is to maintain, Sunday after Sunday, the stubbornly inconvenient claim that there is a unity deeper than politics and a loyalty that precedes every party platform. Most weeks, that claim will feel inadequate to the moment.

It is the only thing we have. It turns out to be enough.

The "nones" — people who claim no religious affiliation when surveyed — are the fastest-growing religious demographic in the United States. They now represent a quarter to a third of the American adult population, depending on the survey, and their numbers have been rising consistently for decades [cite — confirm]. The church that is serious about reaching its community cannot afford to treat this population as a monolith, as unreachable, or as simply the product of cultural decline. They are the neighbors, coworkers, family members, and strangers whose lives intersect with the church's community every day.

Thom Rainer's research on the religiously unaffiliated has identified something important that changes the pastoral calculus: the "nones" are not a single group [cite — confirm]. They are several distinct populations with significantly different profiles, needs, and receptivity to the gospel. Treating them as a single category produces evangelism and outreach strategies that are poorly calibrated for any of them.

## The Historical Context

The rise of the "nones" is not simply a story of religious decline. It is a story about the collapse of a particular form of cultural Christianity that had been maintained in America not primarily by genuine belief but by social expectation, family tradition, and the civic function religion performed in neighborhoods and communities. That form of religious affiliation — what sociologists called "nominal Christianity" — was real even if its roots were shallow. It provided a baseline of religious literacy, a network of community connections, and a social identity that made the church recognizable and the gospel at least minimally legible to most Americans.

> The rise of the "nones" is not simply a story of religious decline.

Charles Taylor's account of the "secular age" describes this shift as a move from a world in which religious belief was the default — in which unbelief required explanation and justification — to a world in which belief is one option among many, and the burden of explanation has been reversed [cite — confirm]. In Taylor's framing, the "nones" are not primarily defectors from genuine faith. They are people who have simply stopped maintaining an affiliation that was already largely formal, in a cultural environment that no longer pressures them to maintain it.

This matters for pastoral strategy because it means that the "nones" are not, in most cases, people who encountered Christianity at its best and found it wanting. Many of them encountered Christianity at its most nominal — tepid, culturally accommodated, failing to make a case for itself — and found it insufficient. That is a different problem. And it is, in some ways, more amenable to a solution than the problem of people who have heard the genuine gospel and rejected it.

## The Four Types

Rainer's research identifies four primary categories within the "nones." The first is the "loose connection" group — people who have some residual connection to religious belief and practice, who may pray occasionally, who consider themselves "spiritual but not religious," and who retain genuine openness to the possibility of faith. This is the largest category and the most receptive to thoughtful, relational engagement. They are not hostile to faith — they are disillusioned with institutional religion, which is a different thing.

The second is the "drifted away" group — people who were once connected to a religious community and have gradually disengaged without dramatic break or decisive rejection. They may still have positive associations with the church, residual faith convictions, and relationships with people in religious communities. The barrier to re-engagement is often inertia and the sense that returning would be awkward, not deep conviction against it.

> That is a different problem.

The third is the "convinced secular" group — people who have made a more deliberate and considered move away from religious belief, who identify as agnostic or atheist, and who are significantly less receptive to conventional approaches to faith sharing. This group is smaller than the cultural conversation about secularism suggests but represents a genuine and growing portion of the population in certain demographics and geographic areas.

The fourth — and often overlooked — is the "burned and gone" group: people who had genuine religious experience but were hurt by a specific community, a specific leader, or a specific set of institutional failures, and who left with a combination of grief and anger that has not resolved. For this group, the barrier to engagement is not intellectual or motivational. It is relational and specifically located in a wound that the church inflicted.

## A Steel-Manned Counter-Position

The most serious theological challenge to research-driven outreach strategies targeting the "nones" comes from a direction most pastors have not fully considered. It goes: the church that designs its outreach around the preferences and receptivity profiles of the unchurched has already conceded the fundamental question of who sets the terms for the encounter. The gospel is not a product to be calibrated for different market segments. It is a word addressed to human beings in their need — a need they may not recognize, and which the church is not called to make palatable before addressing. The prophets did not research their audiences. The apostles did not adapt the kerygma to the felt needs of different demographic clusters.

This is a genuine theological concern and it cuts against a certain form of market-driven church growth methodology that has done real damage to pastoral integrity. The gospel is not infinitely flexible. It has a content that cannot be eliminated in order to make it more accessible without ceasing to be the gospel.

But the concern, properly understood, is not an argument against knowing your context. It is an argument against compromising your content. Paul in Acts 17, addressing the Areopagus, begins with a careful observation of Athenian religious culture — "I see that in every way you are very religious" — before moving to the proclamation of the God they do not know. He met his audience where they were. He did not leave them there. The knowledge of the audience was in service of the proclamation, not a substitute for it. That is the right relationship between research and proclamation, and it is one the church has largely maintained when it has been functioning well.

## What Actually Reaches Each Group

The "loose connection" nones tend to be most effectively reached through genuine friendship and invitation rather than programmatic evangelism. They are curious but cautious, open but wary of pressure or manipulation. The most effective point of contact is relationship with a genuine Christian who is not primarily trying to convert them — who is interested in them as a person and who shares their faith naturally as part of that relationship rather than as a sales pitch.

This has always been the case. The sociologist Rodney Stark has argued that the explosive growth of early Christianity was primarily a function of social networks — Christians sharing their faith with people they were in genuine relationship with, and those relationships providing the social plausibility structure that made the message credible [cite — confirm]. What is different about the present moment is not the basic dynamic of relational evangelism but the cultural suspicion that any relationship with a Christian might be instrumental — that the friendship is really a recruitment strategy. That suspicion is often warranted, given the church's history with it. Overcoming it requires the genuine article: friendship that is not conditional on a conversion outcome, and faith sharing that is an overflow of relationship rather than its purpose.

The "drifted away" nones tend to respond most to genuine welcome and the removal of the awkwardness of return. A personal invitation from someone they know. Explicit verbal permission — from the pulpit, in the culture of the church — for people who have been away to come back without judgment or explanation. The recognition that the barrier to re-engagement is often relational rather than theological.

The "burned and gone" require something different still: the willingness to acknowledge the wound directly, to hear the story without deflecting it, and to refuse the pastoral temptation to explain away the harm in service of the institution. The church that cannot say — genuinely and specifically — "what happened to you should not have happened, and I am sorry" will not reach the people it has hurt. This requires a pastoral humility that is rarer than it should be.

> The "nones" are not the enemy. They are the mission field.

## A Concrete Scene

I know a pastor who leads a congregation in a mid-sized Midwestern city with a significant population of former evangelicals — people who grew up in church, were hurt by a specific community or leader, and spent years constructing an identity organized around their departure. He began hosting what he called "honest conversations" — monthly evenings with no agenda except to let people who had been hurt by the church say what they experienced, with someone from the church present who was willing to listen without defending. He lost members who felt the church was being unfairly criticized. He gained twenty families in two years who had never imagined returning to a church. The door for most of them was not a compelling sermon. It was the experience of being heard by someone who represented the institution that had hurt them.

## The Larger Shift Required

Reaching the "nones" effectively requires a shift in the church's self-understanding — from a community that gathers the already-convinced to a community that genuinely welcomes the questioning, the doubting, the disillusioned, and the curious. This is a different culture from the one most churches have been formed to be, and it requires genuine change rather than programmatic addition.

It also requires patience. The path from "none" to genuine faith community member is rarely short, and the church that expects quick results from relational engagement with the religiously unaffiliated will be disappointed and may give up before the relationship has had a chance to bear fruit. The long game — genuine friendship, genuine community, genuine witness sustained over years — is the game worth playing.

The "nones" are not the enemy. They are the mission field. And many of them are closer to the kingdom than they know, waiting for someone to show them what the gospel actually looks like when it is lived without pretense.

The church exists to be that someone. That is still the work.

The conversation about artificial intelligence and the church has moved remarkably quickly from "this is interesting to consider" to "this is something every pastor needs to actually grapple with." AI tools are already being used by pastors for sermon research, administrative writing, communication tasks, and in some cases for aspects of sermon drafting. The congregation that knew nothing about AI two years ago now has members who use it daily at work and who will notice, or at least sense, when the content they are receiving on Sunday morning was generated rather than genuinely wrestled with.

The question for pastoral ministry is not whether AI will be used — it is being used — but how it should be used, and what limits are appropriate, and what the rise of AI means for the specifically human and specifically pastoral dimensions of ministry that cannot be replaced or replicated by any machine learning system currently available.

## The Historical Comparison

Every generation of preachers has faced a version of this question — what does a new technology mean for the ministry of the Word? When Gutenberg's press made the Bible available in vernacular languages in the mid-fifteenth century, it transformed preaching irrevocably: the preacher could no longer assume that only they had access to the text. When radio and then television enabled preaching to reach audiences of millions, it created new possibilities and new distortions — the celebrity pastor, the disembodied voice, the audience that received the Word without any accompanying community. When the internet made sermons universally available and searchable, it produced both remarkable accessibility and new temptations toward plagiarism and imitation.

> The press did not preach. The radio did not preach. The sermon database did not preach. Neither does the AI.

AI is a more disruptive development than any of these, but it is in the same category of tools that promise efficiency and require wisdom. The press did not preach. The radio did not preach. The sermon database did not preach. Neither does the AI. The technology changes the conditions of preaching without changing what preaching fundamentally is: a human being, formed by genuine encounter with the living God and with a specific community, standing before that community to speak what the Spirit has given them from the text.

That definition is not romanticized. It is load-bearing. It is what distinguishes preaching from religious content delivery.

## What AI Can and Cannot Do

AI language models can process and synthesize large amounts of information with remarkable speed. They can produce fluent, well-organized prose on almost any topic. They can identify relevant Scripture passages, summarize commentaries, suggest sermon illustrations, draft administrative correspondence, and perform many of the tasks that have historically consumed significant amounts of pastoral time. These capabilities are real and the productivity gains they make possible are significant.

> Not wrong. Hollow.

What AI cannot do is preach from genuine encounter with the living God. It cannot bring the weight of a person who has wrestled with a text through the specific circumstances of their own life and community. It cannot carry the pastoral presence of someone who was in the hospital at 2 AM with a dying parishioner last Thursday and who brings that experience into the pulpit on Sunday. It cannot be known and trusted by a congregation in the way that a human pastor is known and trusted. It cannot suffer, or grieve, or hope, or believe — which means it cannot genuinely communicate what it means to do any of those things in the light of the gospel.

The Psalms do not come from a system trained on human expressions of emotion. They come from a man who was hunted, betrayed, elated, terrified, and convinced that the God of Israel was present in all of it. Psalm 88 ends without resolution — "darkness is my closest friend" — not because the author ran out of content to generate but because that is where the prayer actually was. That darkness has weight precisely because it was real. The congregation that receives a sermon drawn from genuine pastoral suffering hears something the congregation that receives polished content cannot hear. They hear testimony. That difference is not an aesthetic preference. It is the difference between the Word made flesh and the Word made text.

## A Steel-Manned Counter-Position

The strongest argument for more aggressive AI use in pastoral ministry is a practical and pastoral one, and it deserves a direct hearing. The bivocational pastor who works forty hours at their day job and spends whatever energy remains trying to prepare a substantive Sunday message does not have the same options as the full-time pastor with a well-staffed church and protected study time. If AI can give that bivocational pastor access to research that would otherwise require hours they do not have, enabling them to preach with greater depth and less exhaustion, then the pastoral outcome may be better than a sermon prepared without AI but also without adequate time.

There is something to this. The church does not exist to protect the pastoral preparation process as a form in itself. It exists to make disciples. If a tool enables better disciple-making, the burden of proof is on the argument against the tool, not on the argument for it.

The answer to this is not to condemn the tool but to clarify what is actually at stake. The research the AI provides is not the sermon. The sermon is the encounter between a specific person, a specific text, and a specific community. The AI can shorten the research phase without touching the encounter phase — provided the pastor does not confuse the two. The risk is not that AI will produce bad sermons. The risk is that AI will produce fluent, competent, technically sound content that the pastor adopts without genuine encounter, and that the congregation will receive theological information rather than pastoral testimony. The former is not nothing. But it is not what the people in those pews actually need.

## The Authenticity Crisis

Carey Nieuwhof has noted that in an age of AI-generated content — when the digital environment is increasingly saturated with fluent, polished, technically competent communication that was produced without genuine human experience — the capacity to perceive authenticity becomes a genuine cultural asset [cite — confirm]. People are increasingly able to sense the difference between communication that emerged from real human experience and communication that was assembled from pattern-matching on existing content.

> No tool produces it. The tools can protect time for it. They cannot substitute for it.

The pastoral moment is, in some ways, perfectly positioned relative to this shift. The thing the congregation most needs from their pastor — the genuinely human presence of a person who has actually lived the faith they preach, who has actually prayed the prayers they lead, who has actually struggled with the doubts they name from the pulpit — is precisely the thing that AI cannot provide. The pastor who leans into this — who is willing to be genuinely present, genuinely human, genuinely formed by genuine encounter with God — offers something that no AI tool can replicate.

Eugene Peterson spent decades insisting that pastoral work is essentially local and particular — that the pastor's calling is to this congregation, in this neighborhood, in this moment of their specific communal life [cite — confirm]. That particularity is not a limitation to be overcome by technology. It is the source of pastoral authority. The sermon that lands in a specific life on a specific Sunday is not the one that was most efficiently produced. It is the one that was most faithfully inhabited.

## A Concrete Scene

A pastor in his mid-forties told me about the Sunday he preached a sermon he had largely assembled using AI tools. He was behind, he was exhausted, a family crisis had consumed the middle of the week, and the AI gave him something that was theologically coherent, structurally sound, and — he could tell, even as he was preaching it — hollow. Not wrong. Hollow. He could hear the difference in his own voice. He could feel the absence of the place in the text where his own life had broken open.

Three members of his congregation mentioned, separately, that the sermon had felt different from his usual preaching. None of them could articulate what the difference was. He knew what it was. He had given them content without cost. The cost is not incidental to the content. It is part of the content. The sermon that costs the preacher something carries that cost into the room, and the congregation receives it — not as information, but as witness.

## Appropriate Use and Appropriate Limits

Using AI to research background information for a sermon, to help with administrative writing, to brainstorm approaches to a topic, or to check grammar and clarity in communication — these uses do not compromise pastoral substance because they are tools in service of the pastor's own genuine engagement with the text and the congregation. Using AI to generate the substantial theological argument, the illustrative material, the personal application of a sermon — and then delivering that content as though it emerged from personal engagement — is a different matter: one that involves a form of misrepresentation to the congregation about what they are receiving.

The line is real, though where exactly it falls is a question pastoral communities need to develop the wisdom to answer together. This is not a question that can be resolved by denominational policy or ethical frameworks drafted in the abstract. It requires the kind of discernment that develops in genuine pastoral community — among peers who are all navigating the same terrain and who can hold each other accountable for the choices they make about what they bring to the pulpit.

## What Remains

The AI will produce more content, not less. The cultural environment will become noisier, not quieter. The congregation will receive more polished, more fluent, more algorithmically optimized communication from more sources than any previous generation. In that environment, the thing the pastor offers that cannot be replicated is not expertise. It is presence. Formed, costly, specific, genuinely inhabited presence.

That presence takes time to develop. It requires solitude, prayer, genuine encounter with the text, genuine attention to the community, and the willingness to bring what is actually happening in the pastor's own interior life into the service of the Word. No tool produces it. The tools can protect time for it. They cannot substitute for it.

The congregation is not waiting for the most efficiently produced sermon. They are waiting for someone who has genuinely been with God and who can tell them what that was like. That is still the work. It will remain the work after every technology the next generation produces.

It happens gradually, and then suddenly. The church that began with a genuine theological identity — a specific understanding of the gospel, a commitment to Scripture, a particular tradition of worship and community — finds itself, over the course of several years, more recognizable by its political tribe than by its theological one. The culture of the congregation has shifted. The sermon illustrations draw more from current events than from Scripture. The pastoral vision is increasingly framed in terms of cultural battle rather than the advance of the kingdom. And the people who are most engaged — who give the most, who volunteer the most, who show up to every event — are the ones whose primary motivation is political and cultural rather than deeply theological.

This is one of the most significant and least-discussed dangers facing American churches in the current moment, and it cuts across the political spectrum. The church that has been captured by the political right and the church that has been captured by the political left are both exhibiting the same underlying pathology, even when they would each define the other as the problem.

## How It Happens

> Political capture of a church rarely happens through deliberate decision.

Political capture of a church rarely happens through deliberate decision. It happens through a thousand small accommodations, each of which seems reasonable in the moment. The pastor makes a comment from the pulpit that resonates with one political tribe and generates enthusiastic response — and learns that this kind of response is easier to produce than the response to careful expository preaching. The church takes a public position on a social issue and discovers that the position, rather than the gospel, becomes the thing it is known for in the community. The congregation's leadership structure gradually populates with people who are primarily motivated by the cultural-political project rather than the theological one.

By the time the drift is visible, the congregation's culture has already shifted. The people who were there for the gospel have quietly departed. The people who remain are increasingly there for the political identity. And the pastor — who usually did not intend this outcome — is now leading a congregation that would be significantly disrupted by a return to genuine theological focus.

## The Historical Precedent

This is not a new danger. The church has always faced the temptation to collapse its theological identity into the political and cultural frameworks of the surrounding world.

In Germany in the 1930s, the German Christian movement — the Deutsche Christen — attempted to synthesize Protestant Christianity with National Socialist ideology. Pastors preached sermons that aligned the church with the aims of the regime. The swastika and the cross appeared together in sanctuaries. By the time the Confessing Church, led by figures like Dietrich Bonhoeffer and Karl Barth, declared through the Barmen Declaration in 1934 that the church's Lord was Jesus Christ and not any other authority, the institutional church in Germany had largely already made its accommodation [cite — confirm].

The Barmen Declaration's first thesis is a direct repudiation of political capture: "Jesus Christ, as he is attested for us in Holy Scripture, is the one Word of God which we have to hear and which we have to trust and obey in life and in death... We reject the false doctrine that the church could and should recognize as a source of its proclamation, beyond and besides this one Word of God, yet other events, powers, historical figures, and truths as God's revelation [cite — confirm]."

> Bonhoeffer paid for his theological independence with his life.

The political circumstances of twenty-first-century America are not Germany in 1934. The comparison should not be made glibly.
