I have had the resources to give them those things. I have had a partner. I have had stable housing and adequate income and the social capital that comes with being a pastor in a community that regards me with some measure of trust.

The children born two miles from where I live — same city, different zip code — are growing up in very different conditions. Mothers stretched to a breaking point by two jobs and no partner and no savings and housing that is structurally unsafe. Schools that are underfunded relative to the schools in the wealthier neighborhoods because school funding is tied to local property values [cite — confirm]. Neighborhoods with higher rates of environmental toxins because industrial facilities are consistently located in poor communities rather than wealthy ones [cite — confirm].

Those children bear the same *imago Dei* as mine do. The conditions they are growing up in are not accidents. They are the product of choices — policy choices, investment choices, zoning choices, budget choices — made by people with the power to make different ones. The theology of the image of God requires that I take that seriously. If every child bears God's image, then the conditions in which that image is being formed are a direct theological concern.

## What Jesus Said That Should Keep Us Up

Matthew 18 is the passage that should trouble every Christian leader. Jesus calls a child, stands the child in the center of the disciples, and says: "Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him to have a great millstone fastened around his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea" (Matthew 18:6). The violence of the image is intentional. Causing children to stumble — exposing them to conditions that damage and diminish them, that make the life Jesus describes as flourishing less accessible — is among the most serious things in the catalog of what Jesus says he cares about.

The word translated "cause to sin" is *skandalizo* — to place a stumbling block, to create the conditions under which someone falls. A child growing up in a food-insecure household, attending a chronically underfunded school, breathing air that is measurably more toxic than the air in the neighborhood three miles away, who has never had a stable adult male presence — that child has had stumbling blocks placed before her. Not by a single malicious individual. By a system that the church largely inhabits without challenging.

The millstone language is extreme because the offense is extreme. Jesus is not using proportionate language. He is using disproportionate language to indicate that the casual indifference of the comfortable to the conditions of the most vulnerable is not, in his economy, casual.

## The Counter-Argument

The steel-man here is about complexity: the causes of child poverty are multiple, the solutions genuinely contested, and the appropriate role of government versus church versus family is a real debate. Some of what creates child poverty — family breakdown, addiction, the collapse of working-class employment — involves conditions that are not straightforwardly addressed by policy change. The argument that child poverty is primarily a justice problem that requires systemic solutions can obscure the ways in which community-level and family-level responses are also essential and are sometimes more effective in specific cases.

I take this seriously. The complexity is real. Policy debates about the mechanisms of anti-poverty work are legitimate debates, and the church that reduces every question about child poverty to a partisan policy prescription has done its prophetic work badly.

But the theological claim is not complex. A society that has resources sufficient to prevent children from going hungry and chooses not to deploy them for that purpose has made a statement about whose children matter. The church that sits inside that society and directs its moral energy primarily toward private behavior and personal virtue while remaining largely quiet about the conditions of the poorest children has made a complementary statement. Both statements are theologically wrong. Scripture does not offer significant ambiguity on this point, even if the policy solutions are genuinely contested.

The prophets did not first resolve the policy debate before speaking. They named the condition and named the community's responsibility for it. The specific mechanisms were secondary to the indictment.

## The Community the Church Is Called to Be

Deuteronomy's gleaning laws, Ruth's gleaning laws, the Year of Jubilee — the entire economic structure of the law is designed to prevent the permanent immiseration of the vulnerable. It is not designed to provide charity after the fact. It is designed to structure economic life so that the conditions that crush children cannot fully establish themselves in the first place. The church that treats child poverty as a charitable cause to address rather than a structural condition to prevent has misread the economic theology of the law.

The early church's response to poverty was structural: "All the believers were together and had everything in common. They sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need" (Acts 2:44-45). This was not a program. It was a reorganization of economic relationships in response to the claim that every person in the community bore equal dignity and equal claim on the community's care. That claim had implications for children — for whose children were fed, educated, protected, and given access to the conditions of flourishing.

The church today is not the early community in Jerusalem. Direct application of Acts 2 to twenty-first century church life is not straightforward. But the principle — that the children among us are not an afterthought, that the conditions in which they are growing up are a theological concern that the community is responsible to address — is not contextually limited.

## What Remains

The kingdom belongs to children. That sentence, coming from Jesus's mouth in the presence of the disciples who were pushing the children away, is a verdict on every community that decides, functionally, that the children at its margins are someone else's responsibility.

The church that reads Matthew 18 and 19 and Isaiah 1 and Deuteronomy 24 and does not ask hard questions about what its budget, its advocacy, its silence, its political alliances, and its neighborhood relationships say about whose children matter — that church has not yet allowed the texts to function as texts.

The children who are the measure of our faithfulness are not primarily in our pews. They are outside them. In the neighborhoods the church's members may have left when the schools got worse or the demographics changed. In the schools that are underfunded because the church's members live where the property values are higher. In the food systems that leave some children chronically hungry in a city where the church has significant real estate.

The statistics about children in poverty are a prophetic indictment. Not of poor parents. Of us. Of the church. Of the systems we sustain through our silence and our votes and our choices about where our money goes and where we will not go ourselves.

The kingdom belongs to such as these.

That sentence still reads as a verdict.

There is a story American Christianity tells about itself regarding public life — that the church retreated from politics to protect the gospel, that the separation of church and state is a theological commitment as much as a constitutional one, that keeping faith private preserves its integrity. It is a coherent story. It is also, historically, mostly false. And understanding why the church abandoned the public square requires understanding that the retreat was not a principled stand. It was a defeat that was later reframed as virtue.

## The Church as Architect of the Public Square

The church was not always absent from the public square. It was, for centuries, the primary architect of it.

In the medieval synthesis — the world that Dante describes, that Aquinas systematized — the categories of the sacred and the secular had not yet been pried apart in the modern sense. The church managed hospitals, educated children, structured the calendar of civic life, and adjudicated disputes that we would now call civil matters. This was not an arrangement without serious problems. Power concentrated in institutions that claimed divine mandate produced the abuses the Reformers rightly named. But the pre-modern church did not suffer from the particular pathology that afflicts its modern descendant: the belief that faith is essentially a private affair between an individual and God, with no particular claim on the arrangements of public life.

The Reformers themselves did not embrace that privatization. Luther's controversy with Rome was about the terms of salvation, not a declaration that salvation had no public implications. Calvin's Geneva was an attempt — however coercive and problematic — to order a city around theological convictions. The English Puritans crossed the Atlantic not simply to practice faith in private but to construct a "city on a hill" — Winthrop's phrase from Matthew 5:14 — that would be a public demonstration of what covenant life looked like. This was not the church abandoning the public square. It was the church staking an enormous claim in it.

## The Rupture Came in Waves

The rupture came later. And it came in waves.

The first wave was the Enlightenment, which constructed a new account of public reason — a way of arguing about common life that proceeded from natural reason rather than revealed religion. Locke's political philosophy, Kant's moral philosophy, and eventually Jefferson's constitutional settlement proposed that the public square could be governed by principles accessible to everyone, regardless of their religious commitments. This was not, in its original intention, an attack on religion. It was an attempt to create a shared civic space in which people of different faith commitments could nonetheless reason together. But it had a long-term consequence that its architects did not fully anticipate: it gradually established the norms of public discourse in terms that systematically disadvantaged arguments grounded in Scripture or tradition.

The second wave was the Scopes Trial of 1925. The historiography of that moment has been thoroughly revised since H.L. Mencken wrote his contemptuous dispatches from Dayton, Tennessee [cite — confirm], but the cultural damage was real. Whatever the merits of the legal and scientific arguments, the trial became, in the popular imagination, a symbol of religion as backward, anti-intellectual, and unsuited for serious public engagement. The fundamentalist response was, in large part, a strategic withdrawal — a decision to build parallel institutions (schools, seminaries, radio networks) rather than to contest the mainstream public square. That withdrawal felt like faithfulness. It had the effect of ceding the terms of public discourse to those who had defined religion out of it.

The third wave was the post-World War II suburbanization of American Christianity. The church that moved to the suburbs moved with a particular class and a particular set of interests. The prophetic tradition — the tradition of Amos and Micah and Jeremiah, the tradition of speaking uncomfortable truth to power, the tradition that got prophets expelled from the sanctuary and executed outside the city gates — that tradition was not compatible with the suburban church's primary social function, which was to bless the aspirations of its members and provide a morally serious backdrop for a comfortable life. Walter Brueggemann has spent a career documenting what the church lost when it accepted this settlement [cite — confirm]. What it lost was the capacity to stand outside the dominant culture and name what the dominant culture refused to name.

This is the thing that needs to be said directly: the church did not abandon the public square because it had a theology that demanded privatized faith. The church that gave us Wilberforce and the abolitionist movement did not believe that. The church that gave us Bonhoeffer did not believe that. The church that animated the Civil Rights movement — which was a profoundly theological movement before it was a political one — did not believe that. The church that abandoned the public square did so because engagement was costly and withdrawal was comfortable, and it constructed a theology to justify the withdrawal after the fact.

## The Price of the Withdrawal

> The church that abandoned the public square did so because engagement was costly and withdrawal was comfortable, and it constructed a theology to justify the withdrawal after the fact.

The price of that construction has been high. When the church has no voice in the public square — when it has defined itself as an institution that addresses private faith and not common life — it has no standing to speak about the systems that impoverish the people it claims to serve. It can feed the hungry at the food pantry on Thursday morning, but it cannot address the wage structures and agricultural policies and housing policies that produce the hunger. It has voluntarily amputated the prophetic arm of its witness and then wondered why its service is so inadequate to the scale of the suffering it encounters.

I want to be precise about what I am not arguing. I am not arguing that the church should become a partisan political actor, that pastors should endorse candidates, or that the church's task is the capture of political power. The Constantinian settlement — the church aligning itself with the empire — produced its own devastating distortions of the gospel that took centuries to name clearly. Reinhold Niebuhr was right that Christians who enter politics must account for the particular temptations of power, including the temptation to baptize their own preferences with divine authority [cite — confirm].

But that is a counsel of caution about how the church engages the public square, not a counsel to avoid it. And the church has used legitimate cautions about political entanglement as cover for a wholesale retreat from prophetic engagement — from speaking publicly about the conditions that produce poverty, the systems that perpetuate injustice, the specific arrangements of power that determine whose children have full stomachs and whose do not.

## Prophetic Witness Is Not Partisan Power

The prophetic tradition of Israel was not primarily about elections. It was about the conduct of kings, the treatment of the poor, the fairness of the courts, the honesty of the markets. The prophets named specific practices — the taking of bribes in the gate (Amos 5:12), the joining of house to house and field to field until there is no room for anyone else (Isaiah 5:8), the grinding of the faces of the poor (Isaiah 3:15). They were not interested in the separation of religion from public life. That separation had not yet been invented. They were interested in whether the arrangements of public life honored the God who made all people in his image.

The church that has accepted the modern settlement — faith in the pew, silence in the square — has accepted a settlement that none of the prophets would have recognized as faithfulness. It has confused political non-partisanship with prophetic witness, when they are two entirely different things. The church can decline to endorse a candidate and still name what is unjust. It can refuse to be captured by any political party and still speak clearly about the conditions under which the image of God is honored or dishonored in a society.

## Returning Without Repeating the Pathology

What would it mean for the church to return to the public square without repeating the pathologies that made the withdrawal seem like a reasonable response?

It would mean recovering the distinction between prophetic witness and partisan power. The prophets had no interest in running the empire. They were interested in speaking truth to the empire about the terms of covenant faithfulness. The church can learn this distinction. It is not easy — the temptation to translate prophetic conviction into political power is strong, and the machinery of partisan politics is designed to absorb and instrumentalize religious energy. But the distinction is real, and it is the beginning of a public witness that does not become what it opposes.

It would mean recovering the full arc of what Scripture requires of public life. This is not a selection of proof texts about marriage and sexuality, though those texts exist and have standing. It is the full weight of what the canon demands: care for the widow, the orphan, and the stranger (Deuteronomy 10:18); honest weights and measures (Leviticus 19:35-36); the cancellation of debt in the year of jubilee (Leviticus 25); justice in the courts for the poor (Leviticus 19:15); the principle that the worker deserves his wages (Deuteronomy 24:15). A church that engages public life on the full terms of what Scripture demands will be comfortable in no political camp, which is exactly where it belongs.

It would mean the church being willing to speak when speaking is costly. The church that only speaks when its speech is welcome is not a prophetic voice. It is a chaplain. Chaplains are necessary. They are not prophets. The test of whether the church has actually returned to the public square is whether it is willing to speak the truth that costs it something — relationships, donors, influence, political access — because the truth is what the moment requires.

The church abandoned the public square. The abandonment was not a theological achievement. It was a failure of nerve dressed as a principle.

The question now is whether the nerve can be recovered.

Not to win. Not to rule. To witness. To speak. To stand where the prophets stood — at the gate of the city, where commerce and justice were administered, where the poor and the powerful moved through the same space — and say what God requires of the arrangements by which people live together.

That is the church's calling in the public square. It has always been.

> The abandonment was not a theological achievement.

> Not to win. Not to rule. To witness.

The data on American church decline is not new. Researchers have been tracking it for decades — the drop in weekly attendance, the rise of the religiously unaffiliated, the acceleration of closures among small and mid-sized congregations that were already operating on margins too thin to survive the disruptions of the early 2020s [cite — confirm]. What is new is the scale and the pace. The closure rate now significantly outpaces the planting rate. The American church is contracting [cite — confirm].

That fact invites two responses, and most of the church has chosen the wrong one.

The wrong response is panic dressed as strategy. It looks like church leaders spending extraordinary energy on programs designed to attract people back to a model that was already in trouble before they left — better production values, more relevant sermon series, more sophisticated platforms, the latest conference circuit's prescription for congregational renewal. These are not bad things. They are answers to the wrong question.

---

## What the Numbers Reveal

The right response begins with a harder question: not "How do we reverse the numbers?" but "What do the numbers reveal?" Because the closure of a congregation is not first a marketing failure. It is a diagnostic. It tells us something about the health of what was there, about the formation that did or did not happen, about whether the people who sat in those pews were equipped to be the church outside those pews when the building was no longer available as the organizing center of their faith.

This is not a kind question. But it is the necessary one.

> The most important number in this conversation is not the closure rate.

The most important number in this conversation is not the closure rate. It is the post-closure discipleship rate — the percentage of people who were members of a church that closed who remained active in another congregation within two years [cite — confirm]. If that number is low, and there is reason to believe it is, then what we are witnessing is not the rearrangement of Christians between institutions but the loss of people from the practicing community of faith altogether. That is a different crisis than the institutional one.

And it points to a different failure.

---

## Consumers, Not Disciples

The church that produces disciples who are dependent on the institution for their practice of faith — who require a building, a program, a professional pastor, a Sunday morning structure to sustain their connection to God and the community of faith — has not, in fact, made disciples. It has made consumers. And consumers stop consuming when the product changes or becomes unavailable.

This is the formational crisis underneath the institutional one. It has been accumulating for generations, in the decades when American Christianity's metrics of success were primarily institutional — attendance, giving, programs, staff headcount, campuses. These metrics are not worthless. They track real things. But they do not track formation. They do not measure whether the person in the seat on Sunday has been shaped by their participation in the community in ways that will survive the community's absence.

The German-American theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote, from inside a church that was watching the institutional Christianity of the Reich capitulate to political pressure, about the difference between cheap grace and costly grace [cite — confirm]. Cheap grace, he argued, is the grace that is dispensed without discipleship — the forgiveness that asks nothing, the community that requires nothing, the church that offers comfort without calling anyone to the cross. Cheap grace produces a kind of Christianity that is exactly as deep as the cultural support for it, and no deeper. Remove the cultural support — remove the building, the program, the Sunday morning social structure — and there is nothing beneath it.

Costly grace produces something different. It produces the person who has actually taken on the yoke of Jesus (Matthew 11:29), who has actually counted the cost (Luke 14:28), who has actually been changed in ways that persist when the institutional scaffolding comes down. That person is not dependent on the institution's continued existence for their practice of faith, because their practice of faith is not primarily institutional. It is relational, disciplined, rooted in the text, habituated by prayer and mutual accountability.

---

## A Faith That Does Not Close

The disciple that Paul describes in his letters does not require institutional infrastructure to function. He meets in homes (Romans 16:5), he sustains the community through mutual burden-bearing (Galatians 6:2), he is accountable to brothers and sisters whose names he knows rather than to an anonymous congregation whose members nod at him in the lobby. The earliest Christian communities met in the spaces available to them — workshops, private homes, occasionally rented halls — without the institutional apparatus that most contemporary American pastors treat as the baseline for viable ministry. That kind of faith is portable. It does not close when the church building locks its doors for the last time.

This does not mean institutions are the problem. The church has always needed institutional forms — gathering places, sustained communities, shared resources, trained leaders, doctrinal accountability. The history of church institutions is not simply a history of co-optation and decline. Institutions are how movements survive across generations. They are how the tradition is maintained, how the community is formed, how the mission is coordinated.

The problem is not institution. The problem is institution that does not produce the formation it exists to produce — institution that has become an end rather than a means, whose continuation has become the goal rather than the mission it was created to serve. That kind of institution will close, and the people it contained will scatter, and no one will be equipped to gather them again because the institution never taught them how to gather themselves.

---

## The Argument From Pruning

There is a counter-position worth engaging honestly. It says: the closure of small, theologically marginal, or culturally isolated congregations is not a crisis. It is a natural pruning. The denominations and church forms that are declining are often declining because they failed to maintain theological integrity or cultural relevance. Their closure makes room for new forms that are better suited to the current moment. The Spirit is always doing something new, and the anxiety about institutional decline is often the anxiety of people who have confused the form of the church with the church itself.

This has some truth to it. Not every closure is a tragedy. Some churches should close because they have become obstacles to the mission rather than servants of it — because the cultural form they embody is a barrier to the Gospel reaching the people in their immediate vicinity, or because the internal dynamics have become so corrupted that the community is producing damage rather than formation.

But the argument from pruning can become a way of avoiding the harder question. If the closures are primarily producing pruning — removing forms that have outlived their usefulness — then the communities that survive should be demonstrating stronger formation, deeper discipleship, more missionally capable congregants. The evidence for that is not strong. What the numbers suggest is not a healthy pruning but a broad institutional contraction in which the people exiting are not relocating to better-formed communities. They are simply exiting.

---

## The Response Is Formational, Not Structural

This means the pastoral response to the closure crisis is not primarily structural. It is formational. The pastor who wants to matter to the mission of the church in America in the next generation will not be measured by his attendance numbers. He will be measured by whether the people he shaped can still pray when there is no one to lead them, still gather when there is no building to gather in, still preach the Gospel when there is no pulpit to stand behind.

That formation is slow. It resists the metrics we use. It does not show up in the church growth report. The pastor who shifts his attention from institutional metrics to formational ones will spend years doing work that he cannot easily defend to a board looking at attendance trends.

But it is the only work that actually addresses the crisis rather than managing its surface.

I am not certain I have done this. I am not certain the people in my congregation could sustain their faith and their community without the infrastructure I provide. That uncertainty matters. It is the question that should be driving my pastoral decisions this year, not the question of how to grow the attendance numbers.

The church that is serious about the mission must become serious about the question: What are we actually forming?

Are we forming consumers who need our product, or disciples who carry the Gospel?

The answer to that question will determine whether the institution closes and the mission dies with it, or whether the institution closes — as institutions eventually do — and the mission continues because it was never actually located in the institution.

---

## The Small Gathering as the Unit of Formation

There is a pastoral practice that grows out of this reckoning, and it is deceptively simple: start treating the small gathering as the unit of formation rather than the large gathering. The Sunday morning service is visible and measurable and satisfying to institutional metrics. The small gathering — the dinner table, the accountability group, the two or three gathered in Jesus's name (Matthew 18:20) — is not. It does not appear in the annual report. It does not justify the building's square footage. It does not impress the denomination's regional leadership.

But it is where people are actually formed. It is where the text meets the specific life of a specific person, where accountability has a face and a name, where the mutual burden-bearing that Paul describes in Galatians 6:2 can actually happen between people who know each other's actual burdens. The large gathering is the occasion; the small gathering is the formation. The church that invests its pastoral energy in the large gathering and treats the small gathering as an optional supplement is investing backward.

The pastor who wants to matter when the institutions are contracting must spend his energy building the thing that survives the contraction. That thing is not the program. It is not the building. It is the community of people who are accountable to each other in Christ — who know how to pray together without him, who know how to read the text together without a professional's guidance, who know how to carry grief together and hope together and sustain each other's faith when the institutional scaffolding comes down.

This is the form of Christian community that has survived every persecution, every institutional collapse, every cultural shift that made public Christianity costly or unavailable. It is the form that met in the catacombs, in the fields, in the house churches of the first century and the house churches of the persecuted church today. It does not close. It cannot be closed. It is the thing that cannot be taken by the mechanisms that take buildings.

I am not certain I have built it. I am certain I need to.

The church that is serious about the mission must become serious about the question: What are we actually forming?

Are we forming consumers who need our product, or disciples who carry the Gospel?

The answer to that question will determine whether the institution closes and the mission dies with it, or whether the institution closes — as institutions eventually do — and the mission continues because it was never actually located in the institution.

Everything else is maintenance.

And maintenance ends.

> I am not certain I have built it. I am certain I need to.

> Everything else is maintenance.

The American church has made peace with a level of economic inequality that the prophets would have named without hesitation. We have not named it. We have organized our congregations around it, built our worship experiences for the people who benefit from it, and developed a theology that, if not actively defending it, at least refuses to disturb it.

This requires explanation, because the Scriptures do not cooperate.

---

## Amos Was Not a Radical

Amos was not a radical. He was a farmer from Tekoa, a southern shepherd with no particular interest in politics. God sent him north to Israel during the reign of Jeroboam II in the eighth century BC [cite — confirm] — a period of relative prosperity in which, as Amos describes it, the wealthy were selling the poor for a pair of sandals and trampling the heads of the poor into the dust of the earth (Amos 2:6-7). The surface of Israelite society in this period was impressive: military expansion, economic growth, religious observance, functioning institutions. Beneath the surface, the poor were being consumed by those who ran the system.

Amos did not argue that poverty was regrettable or that the wealthy should be more generous with their surplus. He argued that God would not forget what was being done. That the worship of a people who oppressed the poor was an offense to God — that the incense and the music and the offerings were not only worthless but actively disgusting to the God who had heard the cries of the poor. "I hate, I despise your feasts, and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies. Even though you offer me your burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them; and the peace offerings of your fattened animals, I will not look upon them. Take away from me the noise of your songs; to the melody of your harps I will not listen. But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream" (Amos 5:21-24).

The question is why the contemporary church reads Amos and concludes that his indictment was for a different era, a different people, a different arrangement.

---

## The Confession of a Comfortable Preacher

I have been comfortable with inequality. I have preached in buildings that cost more than the median household income in my county, to congregations whose combined assets were significant, about a God whose concern for the poor I named without implicating myself or the community I was leading in the structures that perpetuate poverty. I have preached sermons about generosity that were, functionally, invitations to give a little more from the surplus while the arrangements producing the surplus went unexamined. This is a kind of homiletical cowardice I have practiced long enough that I mistook it for pastoral wisdom.

The early church was not comfortable with inequality. Acts 2 and Acts 4 describe a community where "no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common" (Acts 4:32), where "distribution was made to each as any had need" (Acts 2:45). The interpreters who spend most of their energy arguing that this was not communism and was not prescriptive for all time are, in one sense, correct — and in another sense, missing the point. The early community's economic practice was not a political program. It was the community's natural response to the resurrection — the recognition that if death has been defeated, then the anxious accumulation of security against death has also been defeated, and something different is possible. The economic life of the community followed from the theology of the community.

> The economic life of the community followed from the theology of the community.

The point is not that every church must hold all property in common. The point is that the early community's ease with radical redistribution across class lines was not felt as an exceptional demand. It was felt as the obvious implication of the gospel they had received. They had not yet developed the theological apparatus required to make it optional.

---

## What Changed Was the Sociology, Not the Theology

By the fourth century, when Constantine had made Christianity safe and then powerful, the church's relationship to wealth had changed substantially. John Chrysostom, Bishop of Constantinople in the late fourth century, preached against the wealth of the church with a ferocity that embarrasses most contemporary preachers [cite — confirm]. He called the person who has more than they need and does not give it away not a person who falls short of the ideal — a thief. The comparison was not rhetorical excess. It was a careful theological argument: if the goods of the earth belong to God and are given for the use of all human beings, then keeping what you do not need while others starve is a form of taking what does not belong to you.

Chrysostom was not considered a radical voice from outside the tradition. He was considered orthodox, standing squarely in the trajectory of the prophets and the apostles. The tradition that now treats prophetic challenge to wealth as politically motivated overreach has simply forgotten where it came from.

What changed was not the theology but the sociology. A church that is powerful, that owns property, that has wealthy benefactors whose giving sustains its institutional life, has structural incentives to develop a theology that protects those relationships. The prophetic edge gets dulled not through a single decision to compromise but through a thousand small decisions not to go quite that far this week — not to challenge this arrangement, not to name this exploitation, not to ask the question that would make the important donor uncomfortable.

---

## The Justifications and Their Answers

What is the theological justification for the church's comfort with inequality? Several have been proposed, and they deserve honest engagement rather than dismissal.

The prosperity tradition argues that wealth is evidence of divine blessing — that God rewards faithfulness with material prosperity and that the wealthy have, in some sense, earned their position through virtue or effort. This theology has deep roots in American Protestantism, particularly in its Calvinist strains, where the doctrine of election was gradually connected to the sociological observation that the elect seemed disproportionately to flourish economically. The prosperity gospel of the twenty-first century is not an aberration of this tradition. It is its logical conclusion.

The biblical response to this argument is not gentle. Amos preached to a prosperous society. He did not take its prosperity as evidence of divine approval. Jesus warned that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God (Matthew 19:24) — a warning addressed to disciples who had just watched a wealthy man walk away from discipleship rather than relinquish his wealth. The disciples' response was astonishment: "Who then can be saved?" Their astonishment reveals that they shared the prosperity assumption that wealth was a sign of divine favor. Jesus challenged the assumption directly.

A second justification appeals to Matthew 26:11: "You will always have the poor among you." This verse is used with some frequency to suggest that poverty is a permanent and therefore acceptable feature of human society — that Jesus himself acknowledged that poverty cannot be eliminated and therefore should not be treated as a justice crisis requiring structural response. This reading requires ignoring the fact that Jesus is quoting Deuteronomy 15:11 — a passage that, in its original context, commands generous provision for the poor precisely because the poor will always be present. "For there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, 'You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land.'" The text Jesus cites is a mandate for ongoing obligation, not a license for indifference.

---

## The Institutional Pressure Behind the Silence

The more honest account of the American church's comfort with inequality is not theological but institutional and sociological. The church's financial survival depends on the generosity of its wealthiest members. The twenty percent of givers who provide the largest proportion of any congregation's budget tend to be people for whom the full prophetic tradition on wealth is most costly. A pastor who preaches Amos 5 and Micah 3 and James 5 with genuine force is preaching to the people whose giving determines whether the staff are paid next month.

This is not a reason to avoid the preaching. It is a reason to understand why the avoidance is so persistent and so rationalized. The preacher is not primarily a coward. He is a person embedded in institutional structures with real survival pressures, making the small accommodations that those pressures demand, and calling the accumulation of those accommodations prudence.

> I have called it prudence. I am less convinced than I used to be.

I have called it prudence. I am less convinced than I used to be.

The God announced by the prophets is not prudent in this sense. He does not adjust his requirements to the financial health of the institutions that bear his name. He does not evaluate the charge against Israel on the basis of whether naming it will disrupt the temple's revenue. He says to Amos — a farmer, with no institutional platform and nothing to protect — go to the capital and say the thing. And Amos goes.

---

## The Feast That Ends the Arrangement

The feast Isaiah describes in chapter 25 — the feast on this mountain for all peoples, rich food and well-aged wine, the best things, the things that the wealthy monopolize in every current arrangement — is not reserved for those who have succeeded under existing economic conditions. It is the feast that puts an end to existing conditions. "He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord God will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth" (Isaiah 25:8). The reproach of his people. The shame that comes from powerlessness, from being sorted into the category of those who do not count, from having the world's arrangements consistently demonstrate that you are expendable.

That shame is swallowed. That death is ended. That arrangement is over.

The church that has made peace with inequality has not yet made peace with the God who announced this feast. It has substituted a more manageable deity — one who blesses prosperity and asks for gratitude, rather than one who asks what you are doing with what he gave you and why the people at the bottom of your economy are still there. The comfortable church has a comfortable God, and the comfortable God is not the one the prophets announced.

The God of Amos and Isaiah and the early church is still pressing the charge. The mountains are still the witnesses. The arrangement being judged is still the arrangement in which we are deeply, institutionally, complicitly comfortable.

The church's comfort with inequality does not require explanation in the sense that it is hard to understand how it happened. The explanation is obvious. What it requires is the kind of explanation that is also a confession — the acknowledgment that we have organized our institutional life around the very arrangements that the God we claim to follow has consistently, unambiguously named as incompatible with his character.

The Scriptures are more uncomfortable than we have allowed them to be. We have allowed them to be less uncomfortable because the alternative is costly. The prophets did not find a way around that cost. Neither did the God who sent them.

> The prophets did not find a way around that cost.

The church has not been silenced. Let that be established first. It has platforms, enormous media presence, and political influence that would have astonished the martyrs who built its first communities while hiding from Roman authorities who executed members for sport. The church in America can speak. What it has lost is not the capacity to speak. What it has lost is the credibility to be heard.

## Lost Credibility Is Harder Than Suppression

That is a harder problem than suppression. Suppression can be weathered. A community that has been silenced by force can keep the faith in private until the force relents — as the underground church in China demonstrated, as the church under Soviet communism demonstrated, as the Confessing Church in Germany demonstrated when it maintained the faith against a state that wanted to absorb it entirely. Communities whose silence is imposed from outside carry the authority of the persecuted, and that authority endures and often grows. But a community that has lost credibility among the people it claims to serve has lost something more difficult to recover — the right to be heard, which is not given by power and cannot be reclaimed by power. It is earned by costly faithfulness, and it is lost by its absence.

The loss has been accumulating for decades. Not in a single dramatic moment but through an accumulation of episodes, each one individually explicable, that together constitute a pattern that the people watching have had no trouble seeing.

## The Pattern the Watching World Has Seen

The abuse scandals — Catholic first, then evangelical, then Southern Baptist and the broader evangelical world as the Guidepost Solutions investigation of 2022 documented — [cite — confirm the Guidepost Solutions SBC investigation] revealed not isolated failures of individual ministers but institutional patterns: the protection of accused abusers, the silencing of victims, the deployment of theological authority against the people who brought complaints rather than against the people who harmed them. Survivors of clergy abuse who went to the church for justice were told, in various ways, that the institution's reputation mattered more than their pain. That calculation was made not once but repeatedly, across institutions, across decades, across denominations. The pattern is not anecdotal. It is documented.

The political alignment of large sectors of American Christianity with specific partisan agendas produced a church whose prophetic witness became indistinguishable from its political preferences. When the church's positions on policy questions align with perfect reliability to one party's platform, the watching world is not persuaded that the church is applying eternal theological principles. It concludes that the church is supplying theological cover for political commitments that arrived first. The credibility of a witness depends in part on the witness being willing to condemn what its allies do as readily as what its opponents do. That kind of evenhandedness has been rare.

The prosperity theology that promised material blessing in exchange for faithful giving left congregations with nothing to say to suffering that did not fit the formula — and suffering that does not fit the formula has a way of finding the formula's victims in the pew and making them feel not only afflicted but responsible for their affliction. A gospel that cannot speak honestly to failure is not the gospel. It is a transaction, and transactions fail their beneficiaries at the moments when beneficiaries need help most.

Then there are the ordinary, undramatic failures that do not produce investigations or headlines but accumulate in the consciousness of the people who experience them: the church that claimed to love its neighborhood but appeared in it only to recruit; the pastor whose private life contradicted every public word, not spectacularly but in the small, steady, unmistakable ways that the people near him had to see; the congregation that maintained strong opinions about other people's moral failures and very little willingness to examine its own.

These are not isolated incidents that hostile observers have aggregated to build a case. They are a pattern. And the people who walked away because of them are not unreasonable for having done so. They are doing what honest people do when the evidence they have accumulated reaches the threshold where it requires a conclusion.

## The Defense and Why It Does Not Resolve the Problem

The strongest version of the defense deserves full engagement. Institutions always have failures at the margins. The overall witness of Christians across history includes hospitals, universities, the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade through the sustained campaign that Wilberforce and the Clapham Sect led in Britain [cite — confirm], the civil rights movement that was organized in large measure through Black churches, the care of the dying, the feeding of the hungry in every generation. That witness is real and it matters. Any accounting of Christianity's historical role that omits it is as dishonest as an accounting that omits the Crusades or the church's use of Scripture to defend chattel slavery.

The defense is accurate. It does not resolve the credibility problem.

Because credibility is not assessed across centuries. It is assessed in the present moment, by specific people who needed the church to speak and found it silent, or needed the church to protect them and found it protecting itself instead. Those people are not wrong about their own experience. And their experience has become the experience of enough people to constitute something that cannot be addressed by historical reference to Wilberforce.

> The defense is accurate. It does not resolve the credibility problem.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer's credibility rests not on his theology — which was shared by others who stayed in their study chairs when the cost became clear — but on the fact that he went back to Germany in 1939 when he could have remained safe in America, knowing what going back would eventually require of him. [cite — confirm Bonhoeffer's 1939 return] He died in April 1945 at Flossenbürg, a few weeks before the war ended. His theology was not unique. His willingness to pay the cost his theology required was what gave the theology its weight. The Barmen Declaration of 1934 [cite — confirm] mattered because the people who signed it lost things for signing it — positions, security, freedom. Witness at no cost is not witness. It is brand management.

## The Slow, Costly Labor of Becoming Trustworthy

The path back toward credibility is not a communication strategy. It is not better messaging or a more accessible tone or a rebranding effort or a statement of renewed commitment. Those things are available to any institution that wants to appear to have changed. They are not available as substitutes for the actual thing. The actual thing is the slow, costly labor of becoming trustworthy again in specific communities, among specific people, through specific acts of fidelity that absorb risk on behalf of those who have no one else to absorb it for them.

This means naming what the church has done wrong without defensive qualification. Not "mistakes were made" but "we did this, and here is what we are going to do about it." It means standing with people whose standing is costly to share — the abuse survivor pressing charges, the immigrant facing deportation, the family in foreclosure, the prisoner seeking reentry. It means preaching texts that indict the powerful when the powerful are in the room — which requires the pastoral courage to let the text say what it says without redirecting its force toward safer targets. It means the congregation being present in the neighborhood — physically, materially, consistently — long before it asks the neighborhood to be present in the sanctuary.

It means the kind of witness that cannot be faked, because it takes too long to produce and costs too much to maintain. It takes a generation. Not a branding cycle. A generation.

The institution does not recover credibility by explaining why it did not deserve to lose it. It does not recover credibility by a communication strategy that presents its better self more effectively than it has before. It recovers credibility by doing what it said it was going to do, in the presence of people who are watching to see if it means it.

## Presence at Cost

There is a pastoral dimension to this that goes beyond the institutional. The individual pastor who has inherited a credibility problem he did not personally create carries a specific weight. He did not cause the abuse scandals. He did not author the political alignments. He may have spent his entire ministry trying to be exactly what the gospel requires. But he speaks from within an institution that the people in his city have reasons to distrust, and his own credibility will be built or destroyed by the specific daily decisions of his specific ministry — whether he appears in the neighborhood before he asks the neighborhood to appear in his sanctuary, whether he preaches texts that cost him something with people who are in the room, whether the institution he leads is demonstrably present at the points where his community most needs presence.

That presence is what has always distinguished the witness that lasts from the witness that only appears to last. In the second century, when the Roman Empire was being devastated by waves of plague, it was the Christian communities that stayed in the cities and cared for the sick — including Romans who had no claim on their charity — while others fled. [cite — confirm this account, associated with Rodney Stark's *The Rise of Christianity*] That witness was not a communications strategy. It was people dying of plague in order to care for other people dying of plague. The credibility that the early church built in that century was not built by message discipline. It was built by presence at cost.

The modern church has the resources and the people to produce that kind of presence. What it often lacks is the institutional willingness to make the decisions that presence requires — to allocate resources toward the unglamorous, to speak when speaking costs relationships, to protect the vulnerable even when the vulnerable are not the church's preferred demographic, to be, in the most basic sense, present rather than represented.

The witness that survives is the witness willing to speak when speaking costs something. Everything else is brand management.

That is still possible. It begins not with a strategy but with a decision to be the thing the strategy has been pretending to be. The decision is harder than the strategy. The decision is, as it has always been, a matter of faithfulness to the gospel rather than to the institution.

Begin there. The credibility follows — slowly, if it follows at all, but it does not come any other way.

> His willingness to pay the cost his theology required was what gave the theology its weight.

> Witness at no cost is not witness.

A woman in a crisis pregnancy is not a political cause. She is a person in the middle of the hardest decision she may ever face, usually alone, often afraid, and listening — whether she says so or not — to see if anyone in the room actually cares about her.

The church has often failed this moment. Not by having a wrong position, but by having a position without a presence. By being louder in the public square than in the hospital waiting room. By caring more about what she decides than about what happens to her after she decides it.

> By being louder in the public square than in the hospital waiting room.

This is not a minor discrepancy. It is the difference between having a theology of life and performing one.

> It is the difference between having a theology of life and performing one.

## Ruth and the Shape of Covenantal Love

Ruth's story is, among other things, a study in what unconditional loyalty actually looks like when someone has nothing to offer in return. Naomi had lost her husband and both sons. She was returning to Bethlehem in poverty, without prospects, and without the capacity to provide Ruth with anything resembling a future. She told her daughters-in-law to return to their own families and gods. The reasonable thing for Ruth to do was to take that permission and use it.

Ruth refused. "Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God" (Ruth 1:16). The word behind this refusal — hesed, covenantal loyalty — appears throughout the book and describes not only Ruth's commitment to Naomi but God's commitment to both of them. Hesed does not calculate whether the other person deserves the commitment. It extends the commitment precisely when the other person cannot reciprocate.

The church's response to the woman in crisis pregnancy needs to take that shape. Not a conditional welcome contingent on the right outcome. Not support that evaporates when the decision has been made. Not presence that extends only as far as the delivery room. A loyalty that persists through the outcome into whatever comes after it — including the outcomes that are complicated, the outcomes that do not match what the church hoped for, the outcomes that are expensive and long and require more than a one-time donation to a crisis pregnancy center.

## What a Specific Woman Actually Needs

The mistake the church most frequently makes is moving from principle to program without passing through the person. The principle is clear: human life is sacred, the unborn child deserves protection, women deserve support. The program gets launched: a pregnancy resource center, a baby shower fund, a partnership with an adoption agency. The program is real and it is good and it still misses the thing the woman in the room most immediately requires.

What she needs first is someone who will sit with her before someone who will advise her. The difference is not small. The advisor has something to offer — information, options, theological perspective, practical resources. The person who sits with her first is offering something the advisor cannot: evidence that she is known before she is assisted, that her experience matters before her decision does, that the church's first move is presence and not management.

She needs material support — not a pamphlet with a list of resources, but actual housing, actual food, actual childcare, actual prenatal care, offered by people who will be available after the referral has been made. The woman who is afraid to continue a pregnancy because she cannot afford to house a child and keep her job and manage without any family network nearby is not facing a crisis of conviction. She is facing a crisis of infrastructure. The church that gives her a pro-life sermon when she needs a co-signer on an apartment has missed the assignment.

She needs the community to still be present six months after the decision, when the attention has moved on. The pastoral bandwidth that flows toward a woman in crisis pregnancy tends to peak around the decision and drop sharply once the immediate drama has resolved. But the woman who chose life and is now alone with a three-month-old and no sleep and a job she can barely hold and no one returning her texts — she is in a different kind of crisis, one that the church's programmatic response was not designed to address. She needs the community to still be there.

She needs to know that her shame, whatever it is and wherever it comes from, is not the last word the church will speak over her.

## "Carry Each Other's Burdens"

Paul's instruction in Galatians 6:2 — "Carry each other's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ" — is not metaphorical. He is not describing emotional support. The Greek word for burden, baros, refers to a weight so heavy that bearing it alone is not possible. It is the weight you carry when someone helps, not the inconvenience you manage on your own.

The law of Christ that Paul says this burden-carrying fulfills is not the promotion of a particular legislative outcome. It is the carrying of actual weight alongside actual people. The fulfillment of that law is not achieved by voting correctly or by funding a crisis pregnancy center's annual gala. It is achieved by specific people taking on specific weight for specific women over extended and inconvenient periods of time.

I do not think most congregations have a fully honest picture of how much that costs. A crisis pregnancy is not a discrete event that ends at birth. It is the beginning of a life that will require support for years. The woman who chose life with the church's encouragement and then found herself abandoned by the church's follow-through has been given something and then had it taken away, and that is worse than not having been given it at all.

## The Counter-Argument About Institutional Limits

The honest counter-argument is that the church is not a social services agency and cannot be expected to function as one. Congregations have finite budgets, finite volunteer bandwidth, and a primary calling to worship and proclamation that must not be colonized by ancillary social programs. The attempt to turn every church into a comprehensive support system for every crisis it encounters produces congregational burnout and institutional diffusion that ultimately serves no one well.

This argument has real force. The church is not the government. It cannot be expected to solve systemic problems with volunteer programs. There is a real danger in the expectation that congregational care can substitute for the structural supports — healthcare, childcare policy, housing assistance, parental leave — that would actually change the conditions in which crisis pregnancies occur.

But the counter-argument proves less than it claims. It establishes that the church cannot do everything; it does not establish that the church should do nothing beyond its political position. The gap between "we cannot solve the problem systematically" and "we can care for this specific person in our congregation who is in front of us" is large, and most congregations have not come close to exhausting the second before claiming the impossibility of the first.

The church does not need to be a social services agency to show up for the woman in its own building. It does not need a comprehensive program to offer a meal, a ride, a co-signed lease, a friend who will return texts at midnight. These things require willingness more than infrastructure.

## What the Political Position Without Presence Actually Communicates

When the church is loudest about abortion in the abstract and quietest about the specific woman in the third row who is considering one, it is communicating something. Not what it intends to communicate — not that it has a high view of human life. What it is actually communicating is that the theological position is more important than the person the position is about.

That is a communicative failure with consequences. It tells the woman in crisis that the church's concern is the outcome, not her. It tells the woman who has already made the choice that there is no room for her here. It tells the watching world that the church's pro-life commitment is primarily a political identity rather than a pastoral practice.

The church that is pro-life in its politics but not in its practice has chosen the cheaper version of the conviction. The more demanding version requires presence — not once, but all the way through. Through the decision and past it. Through the pregnancy and past it. Through the delivery and past it. Through the first year and the second and the third, until the woman who received the church's commitment is actually standing on her own feet and can say, with something more than charity, that the church's presence made the choice possible.

That version of the commitment is harder than a vote. It is also the version that takes the conviction seriously enough to pay for it with something other than other people's money and other people's time.

She is still in the room. She is still listening. What the church does next is the sermon she will actually hear.

The United States executes people in the name of the state. It does so with the broad support of white evangelical Christianity, which for decades has been among the strongest institutional voices for capital punishment in American public life. A 2021 Pew Research survey found that white evangelical Protestants favor the death penalty at higher rates than any other religious group in the country [cite — confirm]. The same community that preaches the infinite worth of every human soul, the redemptive power of the gospel, and the possibility of genuine transformation votes, and prays, and advocates for the killing of people by the government.

This is not a minor inconsistency. It is a theological fracture that runs through the center of evangelical witness in America, and the church has largely chosen not to name it.

> This is not a minor inconsistency.

The argument for capital punishment from within the Christian tradition is not trivial. It deserves honest engagement. Genesis 9:6 — *whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed, for in the image of God has God made mankind* — is the foundational text, and it carries real weight. The argument runs that the taking of human life is so grave an act, so fundamental a violation of the imago Dei, that it demands a commensurate response. Romans 13:4 describes the governing authority as the servant of God, *an agent of wrath to bring punishment on the wrongdoer* — which has been read by serious theologians, from Augustine to Luther to Calvin [cite — confirm], as providing a biblical basis for the state's power over life and death. This is not a fringe position. It is the majority position of Christian theology for most of the tradition's history.

## The Biblical Case Worth Taking Seriously

I have held versions of this position. I understand the internal logic. I am not dismissing it.

But the logic breaks under the weight of what capital punishment actually is and actually does in the United States of America in 2026.

The imago Dei argument for execution rests on the premise that execution honors the sacred worth of human life by taking seriously the gravity of its violation. The problem is that the system as actually practiced does not honor the sacred worth of all human life. It honors it selectively, in a pattern that follows the same lines of race and class that run through every other form of injustice in this country. Since 1976, when executions resumed after the Supreme Court reinstated capital punishment, Black defendants have been executed at rates disproportionate to their representation in the general population [cite — confirm]. The race of the victim matters even more: defendants convicted of killing white victims are significantly more likely to receive death sentences than defendants convicted of killing Black victims [cite — confirm]. The Innocence Project has documented more than 185 death row exonerations since 1989 [cite — confirm] — meaning that the system has sentenced to death, at minimum, scores of people who did not commit the crimes for which they were to be executed.

## What the System Actually Does

An execution that kills an innocent person is not a defense of the imago Dei. It is a violation of it. There is no theological framework in which the killing of an innocent person by the state honors the sanctity of human life. And a system that has produced this outcome at this rate is not a system that can be redeemed by appealing to the principle that undergirds it.

The deterrence argument fares no better under scrutiny. States with the death penalty do not have meaningfully lower murder rates than states without it [cite — confirm]. The certainty of punishment, not its severity, is what the criminological evidence suggests affects criminal behavior. The death penalty, as practiced, is not a deterrent. It is a ritual of vengeance that satisfies something in the public — a sense that justice demands an ultimate response to the ultimate violation — while doing none of the things that justice actually requires: accountability, repair, the protection of future victims.

> An execution that kills an innocent person is not a defense of the imago Dei. It is a violation of it.

Vengeance is mine, says the Lord (Romans 12:19). Paul quotes Deuteronomy in the context of a command to do the opposite — to feed the enemy, to refuse personal retribution, to overcome evil with good. The text is not a charter for state execution. It is a claim that vengeance belongs to God, which is a reason not to claim it for the state, not a reason to outsource it to the state.

## Vengeance That Belongs to God

The tradition of restorative justice — a framework rooted in part in biblical shalom, the Hebrew vision of right relationships restored — represents a serious alternative that the church has been slow to embrace [cite — confirm]. Restorative justice does not deny the reality of harm or minimize the suffering of victims. It asks a different set of questions: what has been broken, and what would it take to repair it? Who has been harmed, and what do they need? What responsibility does the offender bear, and how can that responsibility be taken seriously in a way that does not destroy the possibility of redemption?

The gospel's account of redemption is directly relevant here. The argument that some people are beyond redemption — that some crimes disqualify a person from the possibility of transformation — is not a Christian argument. It is a claim that the grace of God has limits, that there are people the cross cannot reach. That argument cannot be made on Christian grounds without fundamentally altering what the cross means.

## The Limits of Redemption Examined

Paul was a murderer before his conversion. He stood at the execution of Stephen, approving and holding the coats (Acts 7:58). By the logic that some crimes place a person beyond the reach of redemption, Paul's story should have ended at Damascus. It did not. The same Paul who approved Stephen's death wrote a substantial portion of the New Testament. I am not arguing that this means murderers should not face accountability. I am arguing that a theology that makes death the required response to death has not fully reckoned with the implications of the resurrection.

The specific gravity of the death penalty debate in the United States is inseparable from the history of American racial violence. Lynching — the extrajudicial killing of Black Americans by white mobs, predominantly in the South from Reconstruction through the mid-twentieth century — was not simply mob violence. It was a system of terror with explicit theological sanction from many white Southern churches [cite — confirm]. The continuity between lynching and capital punishment is not a rhetorical move. It is a factual claim about the demographics of who the system kills and what purposes it serves in maintaining racial hierarchy. Bryan Stevenson's work at the Equal Justice Initiative has documented this continuity at length [cite — confirm]. The church that has not reckoned with this history cannot offer a theologically serious account of capital punishment.

What I am not saying is that the victims of violent crime deserve less than full acknowledgment. The loss of a child to murder. The violation of the body. The grief that does not resolve. These deserve naming, fully. The impulse toward accountability — toward ensuring that serious harm is met with serious consequence — is not simply vengeance. It is a real dimension of the human need for justice. The pastoral failure would be to treat that impulse as only base and never legitimate.

## The Shadow of Lynching

But there is a difference between accountability and execution. A sentence of life without parole is serious consequence. It takes seriously the gravity of the harm. It protects future victims. It does so without the irreversibility of death — an irreversibility that becomes a catastrophe when the system makes errors, which it does. The imago Dei argument, pressed to its actual conclusion, demands that we take the image of God seriously in every person involved in the criminal system: the victim, the offender, the innocent person wrongly convicted, the executioner.

The church that supports capital punishment without engaging the racial disparities, without engaging the wrongful conviction data, without engaging the deterrence evidence, has not thought theologically about the matter. It has absorbed a cultural position, wrapped it in a proof-text, and called it Christian.

I have done this. I have preached positions I absorbed from the culture and held with the grip of conviction without having examined them carefully. The death penalty was one of them. The examination changed me. It will not change everyone. But the church cannot afford to exempt its most consequential positions from theological examination.

The question the gospel presses is not whether violent crime deserves serious response. It does. The question is whether the state's taking of human life is the response that honors the image of God in every person the system touches. Given the evidence of what capital punishment in America actually is and actually does — who it kills, how often it kills wrongly, what it costs, what it does not deter — the answer that emerges from honest theological engagement is no.

## The Cost of Saying No

That answer will cost something to say. The evangelical culture that has treated capital punishment as a Christian position will receive this as a betrayal. But the church that refuses to examine its political positions against the full weight of what it claims to believe has not protected the gospel. It has protected its comfort.

> The stakes are literal. People are being executed.

The stakes are literal. People are being executed. Some of them did not commit the crimes for which they were condemned. All of them bear the image of God. The church has something to say about that, and the time to say it is not after the execution.

She has been sitting in your pews for years. She tithes. She serves in the children's ministry. Her husband is a deacon, or a worship leader, or a reliable presence in the men's small group who is known as the one who always seems to have a word of encouragement. She is suffering in private. She may never tell you. And if she does tell you, everything about the theological training you received, the pastoral culture you absorbed, and the institutional pressures of your role has prepared you, however unintentionally, to make it worse.

This is not a marginal scenario. Domestic violence affects approximately one in four women in the United States. [cite — confirm] The research on whether religious involvement reduces that rate is at best mixed. Some studies suggest that religious couples who practice their faith together have lower rates of intimate partner violence. Other studies suggest that women in conservative religious contexts report higher rates of staying in abusive relationships due to religious pressure. [cite — confirm] What the data does not suggest is that the church is consistently a safe place for women disclosing abuse. The data suggests the opposite: that women in many church contexts face significant barriers to disclosure, face theological frameworks that can be weaponized to keep them in danger, and face pastoral responses that prioritize marital preservation over survivor safety.

> The church has much to answer for here. It is time to name what we have enabled.

The church has much to answer for here. It is time to name what we have enabled.

**The Theology That Does the Harm**

No serious theological tradition teaches that husbands have the right to physically or psychologically abuse their wives. The harm is not located in an explicit endorsement of violence. It is located in a set of theological structures, selectively applied and frequently distorted, that create conditions in which abuse is sustained and victims are silenced.

## The Submission Texts Severed From Their Context

The first structure is a distorted theology of submission. Ephesians 5:22 — "Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands as you do to the Lord" — has been taught in countless evangelical contexts as a unilateral obligation of the wife that exists regardless of the husband's behavior, character, or treatment of her. This teaching severs the verse from its context. The sentence before it, Ephesians 5:21, is "Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ." The mutuality of submission is the opening premise of the entire section. The husband's love for his wife is immediately modeled on the self-giving love of Christ for the church — a love that gave itself up, that nourished and cherished, that sought the flourishing of the beloved (Ephesians 5:25-29). The passage is not a power structure. It is a description of mutual self-giving between two people who image the relationship between Christ and the church.

When submission is taught without mutuality, when the wife's obligation is foregrounded and the husband's costly love is treated as aspirational rather than binding, when the authority structure is emphasized while the servant-leadership expectation is softened — the theological result is a framework that can be used by an abusive husband to require compliance and by pastoral counsel to enforce it. That result is not accidental. It is the predictable outcome of a selective reading that serves the interests of those with power and disciplines those without it.

## Covenant Permanence Turned Into a Cage

The second structure is a theology of covenant permanence that has been applied in ways that treat the wife's suffering as the acceptable price of marital integrity. Divorce is sin. Marriage is forever. The covenant must be preserved at whatever cost. These convictions, held in their proper scope, have real theological substance. Covenant matters. Permanence in marriage witnesses to the faithfulness of God. But the theology of covenant was never designed to serve as a theological cage for a woman being beaten in her own home. When covenant language is invoked to persuade an abused wife to return to the man who has harmed her, it has been separated from the God whose covenant with Israel was always, simultaneously, a covenant with the vulnerable and a judgment on those who harmed them.

The third structure is the church's institutional interest in protecting its own — in avoiding the scandal of a leader's abuse becoming public, in managing the reputational cost of a visible divorce in a prominent family, in maintaining the appearance of a congregation populated by intact marriages. This interest is not theological. It is self-protective. But it has been dressed in theological language often enough to have done sustained damage to the women who trusted the church enough to speak.

**What Actually Happens When She Tells**

## What Happens When She Tells the Church

The research on pastoral responses to domestic violence disclosure is sobering. Women who disclose to pastors often report being counseled toward reconciliation before their safety has been assessed, being encouraged to examine their own contribution to the marital conflict, being advised to pray more or submit more or trust God to change their husband, being warned about the spiritual consequences of divorce, and being encouraged to keep the matter private within the church leadership rather than involving external authorities. [cite — confirm]

Some of these responses come from pastoral ignorance rather than malice — from men who received no training in recognizing or responding to abuse, who have no framework for the dynamics of coercive control, who genuinely believe that the right application of biblical counsel will resolve a situation they do not fully understand. The ignorance is real. It does not reduce the harm.

Domestic violence is not a marital conflict that requires better communication skills. Coercive control — the pattern of behavior in which an abuser uses fear, isolation, financial control, and psychological manipulation to maintain dominance over a partner — does not respond to marital counseling. Joint counseling with an abusive partner is, in fact, contraindicated by most experts in intimate partner violence, because it provides the abuser with information about the survivor's inner life that can be used against her. [cite — confirm] The pastor who refers an abused woman and her husband to marital counseling is not being pastoral. He is unwittingly providing the abuser with a new venue for control.

**What the Bible Actually Demands**

## What the Protection of the Vulnerable Demands

The biblical witness on the protection of the vulnerable is not ambiguous. The repeated insistence in the Torah, the prophets, and the New Testament that the widow, the orphan, and the stranger — the people without social protection — are the specific objects of God's care and the test of the community's faithfulness is not incidental decoration.
