It is the spine of the biblical account of justice. The woman being harmed in her own home is precisely the vulnerable person the biblical tradition exists to protect.

> The woman being harmed in her own home is precisely the vulnerable person the biblical tradition exists to protect.

Proverbs 31:8-9 commands: "Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights of all who are destitute. Speak up and judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy." The woman who cannot speak for herself because the theology she has been taught requires her silence, because the institutional culture of the church has trained her to absorb harm rather than disclose it, is the person this text was written for.

The church that claims to honor Scripture while being passive toward the abuse of women within its own walls has not been faithful to Scripture. It has been selective in a way that protects the perpetrator and burdens the victim.

**What the Church Must Do**

The first obligation is to be a safe place for disclosure — which requires explicit, regular, unapologetic communication that the church takes abuse seriously, that no theological conviction about marriage will be used to pressure a victim to remain in danger, and that the pastor is a mandatory reporter of child abuse and has an obligation to help survivors connect to safety resources. This communication must happen from the pulpit, not just in a policy document filed with the church secretary.

The second obligation is training. Pastors need to understand the dynamics of coercive control, the cycle of abuse, the reasons survivors often return to abusive relationships, and why that return is not evidence that the situation is not serious. This is not specialized knowledge reserved for counselors. It is the minimum competence required to pastor any congregation of significant size without causing harm.

The third obligation is referral — not as a way of removing responsibility, but as the application of the biblical wisdom that recognizes different forms of expertise. The pastor who insists on handling every situation himself because he is the spiritual authority is often the most dangerous responder in the room. Domestic violence advocates, counselors trained in trauma and coercive control, legal resources for protection orders — these are the resources a pastor must be prepared to offer quickly, clearly, and without theological conditions.

## Naming the Disqualification of Abusive Leaders

The fourth obligation is the hardest. It is the willingness to name abusive men in the church's leadership as disqualified from their roles. Not to excommunicate them before a process of accountability, but to recognize that the man who is controlling and harming his wife in private is not fit to lead the public community, and that the church's silence about his role sends a message to every survivor in the building about whether this is a safe place.

The man in the worship team who beats his wife at home is not leading the congregation in worship. He is managing his public reputation while she carries the cost of his private behavior. The church's continued platformizing of him is not grace. It is the ongoing sacrifice of the vulnerable to the comfort of the institution.

**The Weight of the Verdict**

I have sat with women who stayed in abusive marriages for years longer than they should have because the men they told at church told them to stay. I cannot undo what I have not done rightly. I can name it for what it is and commit to doing differently.

The church is not the only institution that has failed in this. But it carries a specific responsibility because it claims to speak for the God who defends the vulnerable. Every time it does the opposite — every time it deploys theological language to keep a woman in danger, every time it protects the reputation of a leader at the cost of his victim's safety, every time it treats marital preservation as the higher value than human dignity — it is not being faithful to that God.

It is betraying him.

> It is betraying him.

The church fathers — the theologians and bishops who shaped Christian doctrine in the first four centuries of the faith — are among the most vigorously misrepresented figures in the tradition. They were not writing systematic theology textbooks. They were fighting for the survival of a faith under enormous intellectual and political pressure.

We have made them boring. That is an achievement, because they were not boring. They were ferocious.

> We have made them boring. That is an achievement, because they were not boring. They were ferocious.

## Athanasius and the Iota That Was Everything

Athanasius of Alexandria spent more than seventeen years of his episcopal career in exile — driven out of his see five separate times by emperors who found his theology politically inconvenient [cite — confirm number and details of exiles]. The controversy he was fighting was not an abstract academic dispute about the metaphysics of divine essence. It was a fight about whether Jesus was actually God or merely the most exalted of creatures, and the answer to that question changed everything about whether the cross accomplished anything at all.

The Arian position, advanced by the Alexandrian presbyter Arius in the early fourth century, was deceptively simple: the Son was the first and greatest of all created beings, not co-eternal with the Father, not God in the full sense, but exalted above all others [cite — confirm; Arius active c. 318-336]. The political appeal of this position was real — it allowed the emperor to fit Christ into the existing framework of divine hierarchy without requiring the philosophically awkward claim that God had died on a Roman cross. The theological consequence was catastrophic. If the Son is a creature, then the incarnation is not God entering human existence. If the incarnation is not God entering human existence, then the cross is the death of a very holy man, and the resurrection is impressive but not decisive. If the cross is not the death of God in human flesh, then sin has not been addressed at the level where sin actually lives — not at the level of behavioral failure, but at the level of the broken relationship between humanity and God that no creature, however exalted, can repair.

The formula Athanasius spent his career defending — that the Son is *homoousios*, of the same substance as the Father — was ratified at the Council of Nicaea in 325 [cite — confirm]. It was not a comfortable committee process. It was a conclusion reached under imperial pressure, by men who understood that getting it wrong would produce a church that could offer an inspiring example but not a Savior.

The instinct of our era is to find the doctrinal debates of the early church fussy and sectarian. Homoousios versus homoiousios — of the same substance versus of similar substance. One iota of difference, we say, as though the smallness of the Greek letter proves the smallness of the distinction.

It does not. The iota was everything.

> It does not. The iota was everything.

If the Son is of similar substance but not the same substance as the Father, then God did not enter human existence at the incarnation. If God did not enter human existence, then the cross is not God bearing the full weight of human sin and death from the inside. If the cross is not that, then the resurrection is not God's vindication of his own life given for ours. The iota was not a doctrinal technicality. The iota was the hinge on which salvation turned, and Athanasius knew it, and he was willing to be exiled five times rather than surrender it.

## Augustine and What He Was Actually Arguing

Augustine of Hippo — North African bishop, rhetor trained in Carthage, former Manichean, former skeptic, convert after a long and painful interior struggle that the *Confessions* documents with a candor unusual in any era — wrote more theology than almost any other single human being, and most Western Christians know almost none of it beyond the *Confessions*. The *Confessions* is a masterpiece. It is also only the beginning [cite — confirm dates of Augustine's major works].

The Pelagian controversy, which occupied Augustine from approximately 411 onward, was not a dispute about whether human beings are capable of decent behavior. Pelagius was not arguing for moral laxity. He was arguing for moral seriousness — insisting that God's commands were genuine commands that human beings were genuinely capable of obeying, and that the claim of human incapacity was a convenient excuse for sloth. His position had pastoral appeal and intellectual coherence.

Augustine's response was not that people are incapable of good behavior in general. It was that the human will, in its fallen condition, is not merely weak but bound — oriented away from God, capable of choosing among lesser goods but not capable, in itself, of turning toward God, because the very will that would need to turn is the will that has turned away. Grace does not assist an intact will. Grace must first repair a broken one.

The question was not academic. It determined what a preacher should say to a person who wants to change but cannot. It determined whether the Gospel announcement was primarily motivational — here is an example to follow, here is a standard to aspire to — or salvific — here is a rescue that makes a new kind of life possible that was not possible before. Augustine's primary text was Paul in Romans 7: "For I do not do the good I want to do, but the evil I do not want to do — this I keep on doing. Now if I do what I do not want to do, it is no longer I who do it, but it is sin living in me that does it" (Romans 7:19-20). That is not the testimony of a will that needs encouragement. That is the testimony of a will that needs rescue.

The church sided with Augustine at the Council of Ephesus in 431, which condemned Pelagianism [cite — confirm council and date]. But Pelagianism has never stayed condemned for long. It re-emerges in every generation in whatever vocabulary the cultural moment provides, because the claim that human effort is sufficient is always more comfortable than the claim that it is not. The preacher who tells a struggling congregation to try harder is always easier to hear than the preacher who insists that the trying cannot precede the rescue.

## Why the Questions Have Not Aged

The church fathers matter because the questions they were answering are still our questions. Every one of them.

Who is Jesus, exactly? The church has never stopped answering this, and the Arian temptation — to make Jesus a supreme example rather than God incarnate — has never stopped recurring. It recurs in every theology that reduces Jesus to a moral teacher, in every church that preaches his life without his resurrection, in every framework that makes the cross primarily a demonstration of love rather than an event with ontological consequence.

What did the cross actually accomplish? The fathers' multiple answers to that question — victory over the powers, satisfaction of the divine honor, rescue of captive humanity — were not resolved by later tradition. They were refined, and the refinement left all of them standing, because no single account could carry the weight of what the New Testament says happened.

What is wrong with human beings at the deepest level? Augustine's answer — that the will is bound and requires more than encouragement — is the answer Paul gives in Romans 1-3 and 7, and it is the answer that every honest account of human behavior keeps running back into. The therapeutic alternatives are not wrong in their details. They are wrong in their confidence that the problem is primarily one of dysfunction rather than rebellion, wound rather than will.

## What We Lose Without Them

Reading the church fathers is not an exercise in antiquarianism. It is an exercise in reality-checking. The fathers wrote under pressure, with stakes high enough that bad theology had immediate consequences — exile, execution, the loss of entire congregations to positions that the more careful thinkers believed were catastrophically wrong. That pressure tended to produce clarity. The luxury of our era, in which almost no theological position carries immediate cost, tends to produce confusion — the comfortable blurring of distinctions that the fathers would have recognized as the prelude to catastrophe.

They were not writing for tenure or for reputation management. They were writing because they believed that getting the doctrine right was a matter of whether the church could offer a Savior or only an example, a rescue or only an inspiration. That conviction — that the precision of the doctrine is a pastoral concern, not an academic one — is the lesson they teach that we are most likely to ignore.

We have made them boring by reducing their arguments to footnotes in systematic theology textbooks, by treating the councils as historical curiosities rather than the record of live fights over questions that are still live. They deserve better. So does the theology we are trying to practice in a moment that is not less confused than theirs.

> That love is still required. Those questions are still ours.

Athanasius stood alone against the world's most powerful empire for a single Greek word. He was not wrong about its importance. The church that produced him understood that precision in these matters was not pedantry. It was love — the love that refuses to give a congregation a smaller Christ than the one the New Testament describes.

That love is still required. Those questions are still ours.

The prayer most Christians have memorized word for word contains an economic demand most have never followed.

"Give us this day our daily bread" is not a metaphor. The disciples who first said it were first-century Jews living in an occupied territory under Roman taxation, dependent on subsistence agriculture, close enough to the edge of hunger that the request was not aspirational but urgent. When Jesus taught them to ask for bread, he was teaching them to ask for what people actually need to stay alive — not abundance, not prosperity, but the daily minimum. And he was teaching them to ask for it *together*: not give me my bread, but give us ours. The plural is doing theological work that American Christianity has nearly destroyed.

Food insecurity in the United States affects roughly 44 million people in any given year [cite — confirm]. This in the wealthiest economy in human history. The number includes one in five children at some point in their lives. It is not confined to the imagined geography of concentrated urban poverty. It lives in rural counties, in suburbs, in neighborhoods where the lawns are mowed and the cars are late-model and the food pantry line forms on the far side of the building where passersby cannot easily see it. Hunger in America is often invisible, which is part of how the church has been permitted to treat it as an occasional mercy project rather than the ongoing moral emergency that it is.

The biblical record does not permit the church that luxury.

## The Wilderness Economics of Enough

God's provision of manna in Exodus 16 is structured by a theology of enough that the church has almost entirely forgotten. God provides daily. Not a week's supply, not a month's reserves. Each family gathers what they need for a day. When some gathered more than they needed, trying to hoard against uncertainty, what they kept overnight bred worms and became putrid (Exodus 16:20). The provision was designed structurally to prevent accumulation and to sustain equality. "The one who gathered much did not have too much, and the one who gathered little did not have too little" (Exodus 16:18). Paul quotes this verse in 2 Corinthians 8:15 when making his argument for the collection for the church at Jerusalem — explicitly connecting God's wilderness economics to the obligations of wealthier churches toward poorer ones.

This is not accidental. The manna narrative is the model. What God built into the architecture of provision was a structural guarantee against the combination of surplus and deficit that the market economy produces naturally and the prophetic tradition condemns consistently.

> The biblical record does not permit the church that luxury.

The gleaning laws developed from the same theological premise. Leviticus 19 commanded farmers not to harvest their fields to the edges, not to pick up what had fallen, not to strip their vineyards bare. The margins of the harvest belonged by legal right to the poor and the stranger. The book of Ruth shows this system working as designed — not as charity, but as structured access. Ruth does not beg Boaz. She exercises a covenant right. She labors; the field's edges were built to meet her. When Boaz exceeds the legal requirement through extraordinary generosity, the story notes it as extraordinary. The law created a floor. His compassion exceeded it. Both the floor and the compassion appear in the narrative as necessary.

We have dismantled the floor and congratulated ourselves on the charity.

## Amos and the Streams of Justice

The prophet Amos preached in the eighth century BCE against a prosperity that looked, from the outside, like national success. The economy of the northern kingdom under Jeroboam II was growing [cite — confirm]. The wealthy were building summer houses and winter houses and lying on beds inlaid with ivory. The worship calendar was full. The sacrifices were elaborate. And the poor were being sold "for a pair of sandals" (Amos 2:6), trampled into the dust, denied access to the grain they needed to survive. Amos did not separate the economic diagnosis from the theological one. The religious performance was worthless precisely because the social arrangement it served had abandoned justice: "I hate, I despise your religious festivals; your assemblies are a stench to me" (Amos 5:21). What God wanted instead was for justice to "roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream" (Amos 5:24).

> We have dismantled the floor and congratulated ourselves on the charity.

The church today has religious festivals in abundance. The question Amos puts to those festivals is whether the streams of justice are running alongside them — whether the worship is connected to the world outside the building, where the people who cannot afford enough food are not, for the most part, present.

There are theological problems in how many American churches engage food insecurity when they engage it at all.

## How the Charity Framework Fails to See

The first is the charity framework. Charity treats food insecurity as a surplus problem: the church has extra, the hungry have need, the church gives some of its extra to the hungry, the need is partially met, the church feels good, and nothing structural has changed. This is not nothing. In an acute crisis, emergency provision saves lives, and the church that runs a food pantry is doing something genuinely good. But the charity framework cannot see what produces food insecurity, because seeing that would require asking questions about economic arrangement, land use, wage levels, and political structures that the church finds uncomfortable to address. It is far more comfortable to give away canned goods than to ask why, in the wealthiest economy in history, forty-four million people need them.

The second is the spiritualization tendency. Many churches have historically treated hunger primarily as an opening for evangelism — we will feed you, and then we will tell you about Jesus. The body is the means; the soul is the end. This is both pragmatically sensible and theologically deficient. It is sensible because it is true that the greatest need of any human being is reconciliation with God. It is deficient because it implicitly suggests that the body's needs are secondary, instrumental, not ultimately important — which is not what Jesus suggests when he says "I was hungry and you gave me food" (Matthew 25:35) without any recorded conversion requirement. The people in Matthew 25 who are commended did not feed Jesus in order to win his soul. They fed him because he was hungry. The act itself was the obedience.

The third is the structural separation of the church from the communities where food insecurity is most concentrated. Churches that relocated to suburbs in the second half of the twentieth century, following the wealth migration that was often also a racial migration, are now geographically distant from the populations most affected by food insecurity. This is not a moral indictment of every suburban congregation. It is a description of how physical distance produces social and perceptual distance — the church does not see what it does not live near.

---

## The Steel-Man for Staying Silent

The steel-man for the church's limited engagement with food insecurity goes something like this: the church is not a social service agency. Its primary calling is the proclamation of the gospel and the formation of disciples. When the church becomes primarily a food distribution network, it has lost its theological center and become indistinguishable from a nonprofit. Better to preach the kingdom that addresses the root condition of all human suffering — sin — than to address only the symptoms of that brokenness through social programs.

There is truth in this. The church that reduces itself to social service has lost something irreplaceable. The proclamation of the resurrection, the formation of human beings in the image of Christ, the life of prayer and Scripture and sacrament — these cannot be traded for a pantry without catastrophic loss.

But the argument proves too much when it becomes a reason for silence. The same logic that says the church should not become a food distribution network would have prohibited the early Jerusalem community from selling its property to give to anyone who had need (Acts 2:44-45), prohibited the Macedonian churches from their extraordinary generosity toward the Jerusalem poor (2 Corinthians 8), prohibited the specific commands in James that rebuke the congregation that says "go in peace, be warmed and filled" while failing to give what the body needs (James 2:16). The New Testament does not resolve the tension by choosing one priority over the other. It insists on both.

The church is not a food bank. But the church that prays for daily bread while being systematically indifferent to who has daily bread has separated its liturgy from its life in a way that the people who wrote the liturgy would not recognize.

## The Children Fainting in the Streets

Lamentations 2 contains a verse that has stayed with me since I first read it carefully: "The children and infants faint in the streets of the city. They say to their mothers, 'Where is bread and wine?' as they faint like the wounded in the streets of the city, as their lives ebb away in their mothers' arms" (Lamentations 2:11-12).

The poet is not writing from a safe distance. He is watching it happen. The grief in his voice is not general concern. It is the specific, particular, bodily grief of someone who has seen children dying of hunger in the streets, who has watched mothers hold dying infants, who cannot write about it in the measured theological language of systematic theology because the reality of it has broken through all his frameworks.

I read this in a sanctuary with a coffee shop in the lobby. I read it in a country with enough food to feed every person inside its borders and enough infrastructure to deliver it. The children in Lamentations 2 were dying in a besieged city where delivery was structurally impossible. The children in our food deserts are not dying in a siege. They are going hungry in the presence of abundance, in a system that distributes its excess according to purchasing power rather than human need, and the church that meets two blocks away from the school where they are going hungry has choices to make.

Every prayer for daily bread is a prayer that implicates us. The question is whether we mean it.

The table is full. The margins of the field are empty. The gleaning laws are still law. The manna economics are still the model.

God heard their groaning. He still hears it.

> God heard their groaning. He still hears it.

The church has a remarkably consistent posture toward gun violence in America: wait, grieve, post, move on.

We wait for the news cycle to do its work. We grieve with appropriate pastoral warmth. We post something about prayer — the genuine kind, not the performative kind, we are careful to say. And then we move on, because what else is there to do? The question is political. Ministry is not political. Our job is to love people through grief, not to wade into policy arguments that divide the congregation.

I understand that logic. I have used it. And I have come to believe that it is, in most of its applications, a failure of prophetic nerve dressed in the clothes of pastoral wisdom.

---

## The Scale of Preventable Death

Begin at the level of scale. The United States experiences gun deaths at a rate that has no comparable peer among wealthy nations. [cite — confirm] This is not a disputed fact. It is a matter of international public health data. The causes are genuinely complex — firearm availability, mental health systems, urban poverty, cultural mythology about self-reliance and armed resistance. The policy solutions are contested, some more effectively than others, and the church does not have clean expertise in every dimension.

But the church has Scripture. And Scripture has something very specific to say about the deaths of the poor, the deaths of children, the deaths that result from the failure of communities to protect the most vulnerable.

> The knowing is the accountability.

Proverbs 24:11-12 is direct: "Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter. If you say, 'Behold, we did not know this,' does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who keeps watch over your soul know it, and will he not repay man according to his work?" The knowing is the accountability. Once you know that people are dying preventably, the profession of helplessness becomes a moral position. It is the position of the man who drove past Lazarus at the gate every day. He knew. He chose not to interrupt his life with the knowledge.

---

The history of the church's relationship to violence in America is not simple, and it deserves honest examination.

## Whose Deaths Register as Emergency

The Black church in America has been confronting gun violence in its communities for generations — not as an abstract policy debate but as the specific question of which funerals they were conducting and why. The prophetic tradition that produced civil rights preaching was formed in communities where violence was not a statistical abstraction but a Tuesday. The white evangelical church's arrival at the "gun violence conversation" in the early twenty-first century, largely prompted by mass shootings that affected predominantly white spaces, came with an unfamiliarity that the Black church could not share. The pastors of Watts and the South Side of Chicago had been preaching funerals for decades while suburban churches waited for the issue to become "really serious."

That asymmetry is itself a theological datum. It tells us something about who we have trained ourselves to see, whose deaths register as an emergency, whose suffering triggers the prophetic response. When Walter Brueggemann describes the prophetic imagination as the capacity to "speak against the numbness" of dominant culture, he is describing exactly this: the numbing that allows some deaths to recede into acceptable background noise while others mobilize the national conversation. [cite — confirm] The church that responds loudly to the mass shooting in a school and silently to the chronic violence in its neighboring city has not made a neutral judgment. It has made a theological one.

---

The counterargument comes in two forms, both worth taking seriously.

## The Two Objections Worth Taking Seriously

The first says: gun policy is genuinely contested, and reasonable people can disagree about what policies would most reduce gun deaths. Therefore the church should not speak specifically on policy. There is something true in this. The church is not a policy research institution, and its authority in the area of policy specifics is limited. The church does not have clean answers about which combination of background check requirements, red flag laws, waiting periods, and other interventions would produce what effects. The policy space is genuinely complex.

But this concession applies narrowly. It applies to the specific policy debate. It does not apply to the moral claim that gun violence is a justice issue — that the disproportionate deaths of poor people, of people of color, of children in particular circumstances are an indictment of a society's failure to protect the most vulnerable. On that the church has spoken for three thousand years. You do not need a policy position to state the moral claim. The prophets made moral claims without policy platforms. They named the injustice, named its human cost, named the moral failure of the community that permitted it, and left the specific institutional response to those whose institutional role it was to produce.

The second counterargument says: the church's role is the gospel, and the gospel is about spiritual transformation, not political advocacy. This is the more theologically serious objection, because it raises the question of what the gospel actually is and what its scope includes.

> The silence is not neutrality. It is a choice.

The answer the Gospels give is the answer Jesus gives to John the Baptist in Matthew 11:4-5: "Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them." The good news is not separable from its material consequences. The kingdom that Jesus announces is the kingdom in which human bodies are healed and human lives are restored. A church that limits its gospel to "spiritual" outcomes while treating the deaths of the poor as outside its remit has not found a biblical theology of the gospel. It has found a gnostic one.

---

## What the Church Can Say Without a Policy

There are specific things the church can actually say and do that do not require a particular legislative position.

The church can name the deaths. Not in the abstract — "gun violence claims tens of thousands of lives" — but specifically, with the pastoral specificity it uses for every other death. The family in your congregation who lost their child. The neighborhood adjacent to your building where the statistics are personal. The names.

The church can speak theologically about the culture of violence — the narrative of the armed individual as the basic unit of self-defense, the mythology that safety is primarily a matter of personal armament. This is not a partisan claim. It is a theological claim about where human security comes from, about the limits of individual self-sufficiency as a moral framework, about the communal structures that God intends as protection for the vulnerable. The theology of shalom is explicitly communal. The Lord's Prayer asks for protection for "us," not "me."

The church can refuse to allow its sanctuaries to be co-opted by any political movement's claim to own the question. The peculiar American situation in which gun rights have been treated as a quasi-theological position by portions of the evangelical community — in which the right to bear arms has been discussed in some contexts as a God-given right with religious overtones — is not a position the church as such has a stake in defending. It is a political position, and a relatively recent one, and the church's prophetic independence requires it to hold that distinction.

---

The pastoral reality is this: in most congregations, there are people who have lost someone to gun violence and people who are deeply committed to the constitutional framework around firearms. Both are in the room. The pastor who says nothing on this topic because it might divide them has not achieved peace. He has achieved a church that does not speak to reality, which is not peace. It is managed silence.

## The Watchman and the Trumpet

The prophetic tradition does not counsel silence in the face of preventable death. Ezekiel's image of the watchman is about exactly this: "If the watchman sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, so that the people are not warned, and the sword comes and takes any one of them, that person is taken away in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at the watchman's hand" (Ezekiel 33:6).

The watchman is not responsible for manufacturing his own security force. He is responsible for naming what he sees. The naming is not optional. The pretense of not having seen anything is not available to the one who has.

The church has seen this. It has seen it for decades. The silence is not neutrality. It is a choice. And every choice in the face of preventable suffering has a name.

The family that buried a child in a city your church borders has not been served by your silence. The congregation that needed a pastor willing to stand in the difficulty of this question has not been served by a man who decided the difficulty was too great. The prophetic calling does not offer a provision for topics too culturally complicated to address.

We have seen the sword coming. The trumpet is our responsibility.

> We have seen the sword coming. The trumpet is our responsibility.

The United States incarcerates more people per capita than any nation on earth. [cite — confirm current figures] The people held in its prisons and jails are disproportionately poor, disproportionately Black and Brown, and disproportionately drawn from communities the church claims to care about. Many of them are fathers. Many of them are sons. Some of them are members of congregations that have not spoken their names from the pulpit since they were arrested.

The church has been mostly quiet about this. That silence is not neutrality. It is a statement about whose suffering qualifies for prophetic attention.

> The church has been mostly quiet about this. That silence is not neutrality.

## What the Texts Say

Jesus, in Matthew 25, names the incarcerated explicitly among those with whom he identifies: "I was in prison and you came to me." Not you visited the prison as a ministry. Not you donated to the prison chaplaincy budget. You came to me. The incarcerated person is, in Jesus's own account, the site of his presence. To visit is to encounter Christ. To ignore is to pass him.

This is not an incidental detail. Matthew 25:31-46 is one of the most structurally significant passages in the Gospels — the judgment scene where the nations are divided, where the basis of the division is not doctrinal fidelity or ritual observance but care for "the least of these." Hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick, imprisoned — these six categories constitute Jesus's description of his own location among the vulnerable. He does not say he is spiritually present with the respectable. He says he is concretely present with the abandoned. The church that has ignored this passage's specific instruction about prisoners has not read it carefully.

The early church took this seriously. Prison epistles — Paul writing from Roman custody to the Philippians, to Philemon, to Timothy — form a significant portion of the New Testament. The early Christian community maintained contact with imprisoned members at considerable personal risk. [cite — confirm on personal risk of visiting prisoners in Rome] By the third century, care for the imprisoned was considered a standard obligation of the Christian community, not a specialized ministry for the particularly zealous. John Chrysostom in the fourth century preached repeatedly about the obligation to visit the imprisoned and named the failure to do so as a failure of love toward Christ himself. [cite — confirm Chrysostom reference]

The medieval church had prison ministry. The Reformers wrote from prison — Luther at the Wartburg, though under protective custody, not criminal confinement; Tyndale in a Vilvoorde cell before his execution; Bunyan in a Bedford jail where he wrote Pilgrim's Progress. The Quakers, in the eighteenth century, pioneered prison reform as a theological conviction — John Howard's work on prison conditions in England in the 1770s grew directly from Quaker commitments about human dignity. [cite — confirm Howard] Elizabeth Fry, a Quaker minister, organized systematic ministry to women in Newgate Prison in the early nineteenth century and became one of the most significant prison reformers in British history. [cite — confirm Fry details]

This history is not incidental. It is the record of what the church believed it was obligated to do, and it ran continuously until something changed.

## What Changed

The carceral expansion in the United States began in earnest in the 1970s and accelerated through the 1980s and 1990s. Policies that produced mandatory minimum sentences, three-strikes provisions, and the militarized prosecution of drug offenses produced an incarcerated population that grew from roughly 300,000 in 1975 to over two million by the early 2000s. [cite — confirm these figures] These were policy choices, not the inevitable response to rising crime. In many cases, crime fell while incarceration rose. The expansion was political.

The church was not absent from the politics of this era. White evangelical Christianity was, in many places, an enthusiastic constituency for the policies that produced the expansion. The language of law and order, the equation of toughness on crime with moral seriousness, the cultural positioning of the incarcerated as the deserving victims of their own choices — these were not theologically neutral positions. They were positions the church, in many cases, baptized.

This is not a comfortable sentence to write. I hold conservative convictions on many things. I believe in personal responsibility. I believe sin is real and that actions have consequences and that consequences are not always unjust. But the prophetic tradition does not permit selective application of those convictions. The same evangelical churches that affirmed the dignity of the unborn were, in many cases, simultaneously affirming policies that stripped dignity from people once they were born and convicted. The consistency the gospel requires was not consistently applied.

And the racial dimension cannot be separated from the theological analysis. Michelle Alexander's argument in *The New Jim Crow* — that mass incarceration functions as a system of racialized social control — is contested in its specifics but the underlying pattern is observable without any particular theoretical framework: Black Americans are incarcerated at approximately five times the rate of white Americans [cite — confirm], despite roughly comparable rates of drug use across racial groups. [cite — confirm] The system does not operate neutrally. The church that affirms the equal dignity of every human being while accepting a system that operates with such a dramatic racial disparity has affirmed a doctrine it is not actually applying.

## The Specific Forms of the Silence

The silence takes several shapes. There is the silence of the congregation that has no prison ministry, no reentry support, no relationship with the county jail, no advocacy for the people cycling through the system in its neighborhood — and has never named this as a gap. There is the silence of the preacher who addresses addiction, sexual sin, anger, and pride from the pulpit, and has never once named the racial disparities in drug prosecution that land a young Black man in a federal cell for a crime that earns a young white man a treatment referral. There is the silence of the denomination that has position papers on marriage and sexuality and medical ethics and has nothing systematic to say about an incarceration system that costs families generations.

These silences are choices. They are shaped by who is in the pews and who is not. The families of the incarcerated, the people who carry the stigma, the ones who can't get housing or employment because of a conviction from twenty years ago — they are less likely to be in the room when the elders decide what the church cares about. Absence from the room produces absence from the agenda. What the congregation cannot see, the church does not name. And what the church does not name, the congregation does not reckon with.

The incarcerated man who gave his life to Christ in a prison ministry service, who has been mentored and changed, who is released and wants a church home — this man faces a reception in most evangelical congregations that is considerably more complicated than the gospel he received promises it should be. The stigma travels. The background check travels. The restricted housing options travel. The employment barriers travel. The church that led him to faith is not typically the church that walks with him through the obstacles the state has erected around his reentry. That gap is a form of silence too.

## The Counter-Position

The serious objection: the church has limited resources and many legitimate needs, and prison ministry is genuinely difficult and genuinely specialized. Reentry support requires institutional relationships, legal knowledge, and persistent commitment that smaller congregations cannot easily develop. The silence may be less about indifference than about capacity.

There is something real in this. Ministry to the incarcerated and to people in reentry is hard, and the church should not be guilt-tripped into programs it cannot sustain. Better to do nothing than to start a prison ministry for the sermon series and then abandon it when the difficulty becomes apparent.

But the argument proves too much. The silence of most evangelical churches about mass incarceration is not primarily about program capacity. It is about whether the issue is on the moral map at all. Churches that have no prison ministry often also have no position, no preaching, no congregational awareness, no theological framework for thinking about the two million people in American cages and the seven million more under some form of correctional supervision. [cite — confirm figures] The absence is not logistical. It is categorial. The issue simply does not register as the kind of thing the church needs to reckon with.

That is the silence that requires naming.

## What Faithfulness Looks Like

Not silence. Not the silence of confusion or the silence of overextension or the silence of "we don't want to be political." The silence of the prophets was not a posture they adopted when the situation was complex. Jeremiah did not stay quiet about the conditions under which people were held captive and exploited. Isaiah 61:1, which Jesus stands and reads in the Nazareth synagogue when he announces his own ministry, is explicit: he has been anointed to "proclaim liberty to the captives and the opening of the prison to those who are bound." This is not metaphorical in its first-century context. Jesus was reading that text in a world where the Roman carceral system was real and present. He named liberation from imprisonment as part of the agenda of the kingdom of God.

Matthew 25 does not ask the church to have a carefully calibrated position on sentencing reform. It asks whether we visited. Whether we came. Whether the man in the cell knew that there were people outside it who had not forgotten him.

That is where it starts. The policy work is downstream from the visiting. The advocacy is downstream from the relationship. The reformation of an unjust system is downstream from the church deciding that the people inside it are not invisible.

They were never invisible to Jesus. We chose not to see them.

The silence was a choice. It can be unmade. The question is whether the cost of ending the silence — the discomfort of the sermon, the disruption of the congregation's self-understanding, the inconvenience of the visit — is something we are willing to bear in behalf of the people whose invisibility we have been sustaining with our quiet.

The man in the cell is not waiting for us to resolve the policy question. He is waiting for someone to come.

> They were never invisible to Jesus. We chose not to see them.

> The man in the cell is not waiting for us to resolve the policy question. He is waiting for someone to come.

Jesus sat down opposite the treasury and watched.

That detail in Mark 12 is worth pausing on. The temple treasury was located in the Court of Women — the area of the temple to which all Jews had access, not just the priests. There were thirteen trumpet-shaped receptacles for offerings, each designated for a specific purpose: wood for the altar, incense, gold for the sanctuary furnishings [cite — confirm]. Jesus sat and watched the crowd putting money in. He watched the wealthy put in large amounts. He watched a widow put in two small copper coins — the Greek is *lepta*, the smallest currency unit in circulation — worth together less than a fraction of a day's wage.

And he called his disciples to come and see, and said: "Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more into the treasury than all the others. They all gave out of their wealth; but she, out of her poverty, put in everything — all she had to live on" (Mark 12:43-44).

The standard reading of this passage in American evangelical culture treats it as an encouragement to sacrificial giving and leaves it there. That reading is not wrong. It is radically incomplete. The context in which this scene occurs should keep every pastor with a building fund up at night.

## The Scene Before the Scene

The story immediately preceding the widow's offering is Jesus's denunciation of the scribes: "Beware of the teachers of the law. They like to walk around in flowing robes and be greeted with respect in the marketplaces, and have the most important seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets. They devour widows' houses and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will be punished most severely" (Mark 12:38-40).

They devour widows' houses.

The juxtaposition is not accidental. The widow at the treasury appears immediately after Jesus denounces the scribes who exploit widows. She is the face of those widows. She is putting into the treasury of the institution that the scribes represent — and Jesus watches her do it, and he says she has given everything she had to live on.

Ched Myers and other liberation theologians have argued [cite — confirm] that this passage is not primarily a commendation of the widow's generosity. It is a lament. Jesus is watching a vulnerable person, with nothing to spare, give her last coins to an institution that will use them to pay the scribes who are devouring her house. The institution will commend her. It will point to her as an example. And it will not change the conditions of her poverty. That reading is contested, but the discomfort it produces is precisely the discomfort the text has always been capable of producing if we allow it to function as a critique rather than only as an encouragement.

Whatever position one takes on that interpretive debate, the structural problem remains: Jesus is watching an institution receive the gifts of the poor while the wealthy give proportionally little, and his commentary on the scene is explicitly about proportionality. Not about total amount. About proportion. About cost.

## What Our Spending Reveals

The American church in the aggregate has built its institutions on a spending pattern that looks, on examination, far more like the behavior of the wealthy in the temple than like the widow's offering. Estimates of total American church expenditure on buildings and facilities run into tens of billions of dollars annually [cite — confirm]. The percentage of that expenditure directed toward the poor and toward missions has historically been a small fraction of total budgets — figures vary by denomination and congregation, but across most American evangelical and mainline churches, the percentage of budget directed toward outreach and mercy is significantly smaller than the percentage directed toward salaries, facilities, and programs for existing members [cite — confirm].

This is not a condemnation of every church building project. Buildings serve real purposes: they create gathering space, they house ministries, they provide infrastructure for the work. The question is not whether churches should have facilities. The question is what the proportion of the spending reveals about what the church values.

Jesus did not commend the widow's offering because the amount was large. He commended it because it was total — because it represented everything she had. The benchmark is not the sum. It is the sacrifice. What does this congregation's budget reveal about what we are actually willing to sacrifice for the kingdom?

## The Prophetic Tradition on Institutional Wealth

The prophets are clear-eyed about what happens when religious institutions acquire wealth and lose their connection to the vulnerable. Amos 5:21-24 is God's denunciation of Israel's religious festivals delivered alongside denunciations of their economic exploitation of the poor: "Away with the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps. But let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream!" The worship and the justice are not separable in God's assessment. The quality of the singing is irrelevant if the singers are exploiting the poor.

Micah 3 denounces religious leaders who "build Zion with bloodshed and Jerusalem with wickedness" and then say, "Is not the Lord among us? No disaster will come upon us" (Micah 3:10-11). The building project — the physical construction of the city — is explicitly linked to the violence done to the poor. The leaders are building with the proceeds of injustice and assuming God's continued favor. Micah says: no.

Isaiah 1 opens with a denunciation of Israel's worship that is among the most uncomfortable passages in Scripture: "Your appointed festivals my soul hates... When you spread out your hands in prayer, I hide my eyes from you; even when you offer many prayers, I am not listening. Your hands are full of blood" (Isaiah 1:14-15). The hands that spread in prayer are the same hands used in the economic exploitation that God catalogs in the surrounding verses. The institutions of worship have become complicit with the systems of injustice. God is not impressed by the building.

## The Counter-Argument, Honestly Held

The strongest response to this line of argument is that buildings are not inherently antithetical to ministry, and that attacking church construction projects is a rhetorical device that rarely produces the transformation it claims to seek. A large congregation with a significant facility can serve thousands of people — running food pantries, hosting recovery programs, providing daycare, offering counseling. The facility is infrastructure for the ministry. The comparison to the widow's mite, on this reading, is sentimentalist moralizing that ignores the actual good that well-funded churches do.

This is not a foolish argument. It is true that large facilities can serve significant populations, and it is true that the binary between building projects and care for the poor is often false. A church can do both.

But the proportionality question does not disappear. The congregation that allocates 70 percent of its budget to staff and facilities and 5 percent to the poor has made a theological statement about priorities whether or not it intended to. The $50 million sanctuary built in a city where thousands sleep outside has made a theological statement whether or not the congregation said what they meant. The statement is the spending. The spending is the text. The text can be read.

## What Sacrifice Actually Costs

When Jesus praised the widow, he was not praising poverty. He was naming a principle: genuine giving is measured by cost, not by total. The wealthy who gave large amounts gave "out of their wealth" — it did not cost them anything material. The widow gave out of her poverty — it cost her everything.

The church that has never asked what its spending is costing — specifically what it is not doing with the resources it is committing to facilities and programs for existing members — has not yet had the conversation that Jesus's observation in the temple demands.

What would it cost this congregation to redirect 10 percent of its building fund toward the families living in poverty in its zip code? What would it cost to make the food pantry as well-funded as the worship arts program? What would it cost to hire a full-time staff person whose only job is the homeless population rather than upgrading the sanctuary?

The cost would be real. Some things would not be built. Some preferences would not be met. Someone in the room would be disappointed. That is the point. Cost is the point. The widow's offering was noticed because it cost something. The church's spending is noticed by the same standard.

## The Verdict

Jesus sat opposite the treasury and watched. He is still watching. The question is not whether our spending is legal or even whether it is technically within the norms of religious institutional behavior. The question is what it costs, and whose cost it is, and whose condition it ignores.

The widow gave everything she had. The institution received it and went on being what it was.

The story ends there. Jesus does not say what should have been done differently. He names what happened, clearly, and leaves the weight of it with the reader.

The weight has not lifted.

> They devour widows' houses.

> The statement is the spending. The spending is the text. The text can be read.

> The weight has not lifted.

The temple treasury was elaborate.

Herod's temple complex, constructed over decades and still under construction when Jesus walked through it, was among the architectural achievements of the ancient world. [cite — confirm the specific timeline of Herod's temple construction] Enormous courts, massive stones, the porticoes where teachers held discourse and merchants exchanged currency — a building project that employed thousands and that was, by any standard of its time, an overwhelming statement about what Israel's God deserved and what Israel's leaders could produce. Josephus, writing after its destruction in 70 AD, described it as one of the most magnificent structures in the known world. [cite — confirm Josephus's description]

Into this magnificent structure, in the final days of his ministry, Jesus sat down across from the treasury and watched.

## The Ledger That Is Not the Treasurer's

> He is watching. He is calculating. And his ledger is not the same as the treasurer's.

The rich gave large sums. The donations were public, audible — coins dropping into metal receptacles in a way that made the gift visible and the giver identifiable. Into this display, a widow put in two lepta, the smallest coins in circulation, worth a fraction of a day's laborer's wage. And Jesus called his disciples together and made a statement that should permanently unsettle every church budget conversation that has occurred since: "Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the treasury. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on" (Mark 12:43–44).

He is watching. He is calculating. And his ledger is not the same as the treasurer's.

What Jesus is measuring is not gross contribution. He is measuring the ratio of sacrifice to capacity — what was given as a proportion of what was held. The wealthy donor's large gift, given from a surplus that did not change the shape of his life, registers in Jesus's accounting as less than the widow's two coins, because she gave from need, not from abundance. The scale is not amounts. The scale is cost.

## The Avoidance Built Into the Campaign

I want to sit with that for a moment before making any application, because this is not a simple argument.

The church that spends heavily on a facility expansion is not automatically wrong to do so. Buildings serve purposes. Gathered worship requires space. Christian community requires infrastructure. The great cathedrals of medieval Europe — whatever we might say about the economic arrangements that produced them — were genuine acts of communal devotion, expressions of theological conviction in stone, and have shaped the spiritual imagination of people across centuries. Augustine Dupré, writing about sacred architecture, argued that a community's willingness to build for God reflects a theology of presence — that God is worth the expenditure, that this place matters, that something real happens here. [cite — confirm] That argument has weight. I am not dismissing it.

But the question Jesus raises at the treasury is not whether the building is beautiful or even whether the building is useful. The question is what the building costs the people building it, and what the cost reveals about what they actually value. That is a harder question, and it is one that most church budget conversations are structured to avoid.

## The Argument That Justifies the Next Building

Here is the shape of the avoidance: a congregation launches a capital campaign. The vision is compelling, the need is real, and the excitement is genuine. The large gifts arrive from the households that have the capacity to give large gifts. The campaign reaches its goal. The building rises. And because the campaign succeeded financially, the success is interpreted as confirmation — the congregation was obedient, God blessed it, the building stands as a sign of faithful investment.

What that narrative often conceals is that the campaign cost the giving households very little. A family earning $300,000 annually that gives $50,000 to a capital campaign has made a substantial gift by any conventional measure and has meaningfully altered neither its lifestyle nor its security. The widow's ledger looks at that gift and sees something smaller than the widow's two coins. Not because the dollar amount is wrong, but because the sacrifice as a ratio of total capacity is low.

Meanwhile, the congregation's benevolence budget — the line that funds direct care for the poor, for the hungry, for people in crisis — often sits at a fraction of the building budget. I have seen churches allocate $40 million to a facilities expansion and $180,000 to benevolence. I have approved budgets that communicated, without ever intending to say it plainly, that the congregation valued comfort and impressiveness over the direct alleviation of the poverty that exists within walking distance of its sanctuary. I was not malicious. I was not even fully aware of what I was approving. I was operating inside an unexamined momentum — the church builds because churches build, the measure of a serious congregation is its facility, and no one pauses to ask whether Jesus would recognize the arithmetic.

## The Extraction Beneath the Magnificence

He would not. He sat across from the treasury in the most magnificent building his tradition had ever produced, watched the largest gifts in the room drop in, and said none of them counted as much as two coins given from nothing.

The counter-position deserves honest engagement. The argument is that facility investment and benevolence are not in competition — that a better building draws more people, who give more, who enable more ministry, who reach more of the poor that the unimpressive building would have missed. The prosperity of the institution serves the mission of the institution, and building up the congregation's material capacity is how you build up its kingdom capacity. Bill Hybels used a version of this argument to defend the massive building programs at Willow Creek in the 1980s and 1990s, and he was not entirely wrong. [cite — confirm] Crowds require space, and the infrastructure of a large congregation is not morally simple.

The argument has partial merit. It also has a way of becoming self-justifying, which is the danger of any argument that happens to align perfectly with institutional comfort. The building argument will always be available to justify the next building, and the one after that, and it never quite produces the moment where the congregation says: we have built enough, and the next dollar should go to the widow rather than to the lobby.

What Jesus's observation at the treasury demands is not the elimination of all building expenditure. It demands a different calculus. It demands that the first question in every budget conversation be not "how much do we need for this facility?" but "what does this expenditure cost us, and what does that cost reveal about what we value?" It demands comparison — not the comparison of our budget to other churches' budgets, but the comparison of our spending to the ratio that impressed the one who said that what you do to the least of these you do to me (Matthew 25:40).

## The Widow Still in the Room

The temple economy of Jesus's time was not incidental to his observation at the treasury. The temple system required every observant Jew to convert Roman currency into temple currency before purchasing animals for sacrifice — a mandatory exchange that carried a surcharge, controlled by the money changers whose tables Jesus would overturn in John 2. [cite — confirm the temple money-changing economics] The system was not evil in its original design; it maintained the purity of offerings. But it had become, by Jesus's time, a mechanism of extraction: a mandatory cost imposed on every worshiper, falling most heavily on the poor who had the fewest coins to spare and the least power to object to the exchange rate. The widow who gave two lepta had likely paid her share of that extraction before she gave what remained.

The system that claimed to serve God was extracting from the people who could least afford it, and the magnificence of the building it sustained was, in this light, not simply an expression of devotion but the physical product of a thousand transactions like the widow's — compulsory contributions from people at the bottom of the economic order. The building stood partly on her coins, and the coins she gave voluntarily at the treasury were, in a sense, what was left after the institution had already taken its share.

That context sharpens what Jesus says. He is not observing an isolated act of generosity in an otherwise fair system. He is watching the final contribution of a person who has already been extracted from, and he is naming it as the measure by which all the larger gifts should be assessed. The richest gift in the room came from the person the system had most diminished.

Titus Flavius Josephus described the temple as a wonder. Jesus described the same building complex as a place where the scribes devour widows' houses (Mark 12:40). The contrast is not accidental. The building that is the glory of the tradition can simultaneously be the engine of the tradition's moral failure. It is a building, not a guarantor of faithfulness. What goes on inside the building — who is served, who is protected, who is seen — is the actual measure.

She is still in the room. The widow. She is the one who cannot cover the medical bill, whose rent exceeds her income, who gives to the church because she believes it is doing something worth giving to. What she sees her gifts building, what her sacrifice is funding, is a statement about what the community believes matters most. She is reading the building. She is reading the benevolence line. She knows something about the institution's actual priorities that the capital campaign brochure will not tell her.

Jesus is still sitting across from the treasury. He is still watching. He is still counting by a different ledger.

That ledger is the one that will matter when every building we have ever built has returned to dust, which all of them will, and the only question before us is what we did for the least of these. The magnificent temples do not survive. The woman who gave from her poverty is still being talked about two thousand years later, in every language the church has ever spoken.

That is not an accident. That is the lesson. Whether we are willing to let it be the lesson is a different question, and the answer is visible in the budget.

> The system that claimed to serve God was extracting from the people who could least afford it

> That is not an accident. That is the lesson.

She has been sitting in your congregation for years. She sings on the worship team, or she volunteers in the nursery, or she teaches your daughter's Sunday school class. And she has never told anyone — cannot tell anyone — because the culture of the church has made it clear what the response would be.

The silence is not indifference. It is the most rational response to an environment that has taught her what the cost of honesty would be. She has watched what happens when people in her church are vulnerable about the wrong things. She has calibrated accordingly.

And so she carries it. Every pro-life Sunday, every political sermon, every casual conversation where someone says something breezy and devastating about women who have made the choice she made — she carries it alone, in the building that is supposed to be the place where no one has to carry anything alone.

> The silence is not indifference.

## The Scene in John 8

The Gospel of John, chapter 8, records a scene that has never stopped being relevant. A woman caught in an act the law condemned is brought into the center of the room. The people around her are not conflicted. They have their stones ready. They have a clear position and they are prepared to act on it.

And Jesus bends down and writes in the dirt — a gesture whose content we are not told and whose significance we cannot reduce. Then he stands and offers something no one in the crowd was offering: the possibility that there is more to say about her than what she did.

"Neither do I condemn you," he says. And then: "Go and sin no more." Both sentences matter. In that order. The absence of condemnation comes before the call to change. The welcome precedes the instruction. The space to be human is opened before the moral direction is given.

This is not sentimentality. Jesus does not pretend that what she has done is nothing. The "go and sin no more" is as real as the "neither do I condemn you." But the sequence matters enormously, and the church has often reversed it — leading with the moral verdict and wondering why the people who most need the welcome never arrive.

## What the Culture of a Church Actually Communicates

Church culture is not what appears in the mission statement. It is what people learn by observation — what they hear casually said about others, what they notice when someone is vulnerable in the wrong way, what happens to people who confess the things the congregation is not prepared to receive.

A church culture that speaks casually and confidently about abortion — in sermons, in hallway conversation, in the tone of the bulletin inserts around election season — is communicating something to every woman in the room who is carrying this. It is telling her that her secret is not safe here. It is telling her that the thing she most needs to bring into the light is the thing most likely to get her expelled from the community. It is making the silence obligatory.

I have led church services where the political language was clear and the pastoral consequences were invisible to me. I did not see the women in the room for whom that language was not abstract. That is my failure to name, not someone else's.

> She does not need another sermon about abortion.

The pastoral question is not whether the church has a conviction about abortion. The pastoral question is whether the church's expression of that conviction has made space for the people whose lives are the subject of the conviction — or whether it has made that space impossible.

## What Silence Does Over Time

The silence required by this kind of church culture does not stay contained. It spreads. When a person learns that one category of her life must be hidden from her community, she learns that the community is not actually safe. She brings less of herself over time. She maintains the surface performance of belonging — attendance, service, generosity — while the real person recedes behind the performance. Eventually the distance between the person and the performance becomes unsustainable. She leaves, and the congregation notices the departure without understanding the cause.

Or she stays, and the weight of the accumulated silence becomes the architecture of her spiritual life. Not a relationship with God conducted in honesty and freedom, but a relationship shaped by what she cannot say. The Gospel that was supposed to set her free has become, in practice, another form of management.

Neither of these is what the church is for.

## The Counter-Argument and Its Limits

> They deserve better than that distance.

There is an honest pastoral concern on the other side: that creating a culture of openness about abortion risks communicating that the church has no convictions about it. That if women can speak freely about their abortions in the congregation, the implicit message is that abortion is not a serious moral matter. That pastoral welcome and theological conviction cannot both be maximized, and that a church with strong pro-life convictions will inevitably create environments where women who have had abortions feel some tension.

This concern is not entirely without merit. Pastoral welcome cannot dissolve theological conviction without destroying the thing it is trying to protect. A church that communicates "your choices have no moral weight" has not offered grace; it has offered something smaller than the Gospel.

But the concern overreaches when it assumes that the only alternative to shame is approval. Jesus did not approve of the woman's conduct. He also did not stone her. The space between approval and condemnation is large, and it is in that space that genuine pastoral ministry lives. A church can hold a clear pro-life conviction and still be a place where the woman who has not lived up to that conviction can be honestly present, honestly grieved, honestly received.

What is required is not the abandonment of convictions. It is the abandonment of the casual cruelty — the offhand political comment, the breezy certainty, the congregation-wide declaration that this particular category of person is not safe to be honest here.

## What She Actually Needs

She does not need another sermon about abortion. She has heard them. They are part of what she carries.

She needs what every person in the room with a serious, shameful secret needs: evidence that the community can hold what she is holding. That the God who is described in Psalm 34:18 as "near to the brokenhearted" is actually accessible in this building, not only in the privacy of her car on the way home. That there is a pastor or a trusted person in the congregation who will not be destroyed by the information, who will not immediately become her confessor's liability, who knows the difference between receiving a person's story and administering a verdict on it.

This requires actual pastoral infrastructure — not a program, but a culture. A culture where hard confessions are received well. Where vulnerability is protected. Where the conversation that begins with "I need to tell you something" does not end with that person on the front of a prayer chain.

Creating that culture requires the pastor to be honest about his own limits. I am not always capable of being the person whose response does not wound. I have said things in response to confession that made the confession a mistake. That is the starting point for pastoral self-knowledge, not a disqualification from trying.

## The Gospel Has a Different Shape

A church culture where someone can confess the thing that is eating her alive — not to receive a lecture, not to receive a theology lesson, but to receive the thing the Gospel actually offers — is not a church that has abandoned its convictions. It is a church that has understood them well enough to practice them.

The thing the Gospel offers is not tolerance. It is the possibility of being fully known and not finally condemned. It is the removal of the necessity of the performance. It is the reality that God's knowledge of you precedes his judgment of you, and that what he does with that knowledge is something other than what the people with stones ready would do.

"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus," Paul writes to the Romans (Romans 8:1). That sentence does not apply to everyone in the abstract. It applies to specific people in specific rooms carrying specific things. It applies to her, sitting in the third row, singing the words she means and carrying the thing she cannot say.

The question is whether the church she is sitting in has created the conditions under which she can discover that.

The question is not whether abortion is wrong. The question is whether the women who have had one are allowed to be human inside your building. If the answer is no, you have built a church for people who do not need one. The people who need it are the ones outside the gate, standing at a distance they did not choose, having learned that the cost of coming closer is too high.

They deserve better than that distance. So does the Gospel.

That weight does not resolve. It asks something.

Elijah collapsed under a broom tree and asked God to let him die (1 Kings 19:4).

This was not a crisis of faith in the abstract. It followed the most dramatic spiritual victory of his ministry — the confrontation on Mount Carmel, fire from heaven, the killing of the false prophets, the end of three years of drought. A moment of unambiguous, visible, public divine action. And then Jezebel threatened his life, and he ran. Not for a few days. He ran a day's journey into the wilderness, sat under a tree, and said: It is enough. Take away my life. I am no better than my fathers.

What God sends in response is not a theological argument. Not a vision. Not a word of rebuke for his lack of faith. God sends an angel who touches him and says: Arise and eat. There is food and water. God treats the collapse not as a spiritual deficiency to be corrected but as a human being who has reached the end of what a human being can sustain, and who therefore needs, before anything else, physical care: food, water, rest. The angel comes twice. Twice the provision. Then the word: "The journey is too great for you" (1 Kings 19:7). God names the exhaustion honestly. God does not minimize it. God provides for it.

## Treating Collapse as Spiritual Failure

I begin there because the church's historic relationship with mental illness has often been the inverse of what God did with Elijah. We have treated depression, anxiety, and psychological crisis as primarily spiritual failures requiring primarily spiritual solutions — more prayer, more faith, more trust, more Scripture, more commitment. We have sometimes added the cruelest word the tradition offers: more repentance, as though the suffering itself were evidence of unconfessed sin. We have sent people back to their wilderness carrying the additional weight of shame, as if their exhaustion were something they had done rather than something that had happened to them.

That is not biblical. It is a category error, and it has cost lives.

## Mental Illness as a Justice Problem

> It is a justice problem, concentrated in the communities bearing the greatest social weight.

Mental health conditions are not failures of spiritual discipline. They are disorders that affect the brain and the body, shaped by genetics, early childhood experience, chronic stress, social isolation, poverty, and a range of environmental factors that are themselves distributed along the lines of social inequality. The research on this is not ambiguous: rates of serious mental illness — depression, anxiety, PTSD, psychosis — are significantly higher among people experiencing poverty, food insecurity, housing instability, and social marginalization. [cite — confirm the specific statistics] This is not because poor people are weaker than other people. It is because the conditions of persistent material stress produce neurological and psychological effects that express themselves as illness. The stress is not metaphorical. Its effects are not metaphorical.

This means mental illness is not merely a clinical problem distributed randomly across the population. It is a justice problem, concentrated in the communities bearing the greatest social weight. The question "why are so many people in this neighborhood struggling with depression?" is not just a clinical question. It has an answer that includes the loss of stable employment, the foreclosure crisis, the school system that cannot give children what they need, the absence of green space and adequate nutrition and social connection, and the chronic experience of powerlessness in the face of systems that seem indifferent to survival. Those are not merely contributing factors. They are, in many cases, the primary cause.

A church that treats mental illness as a private spiritual struggle while ignoring the social conditions that produce disproportionate rates of it in poor communities has failed to connect the pastoral and the prophetic. Both are required.

## The Pastoral and the Prophetic Together

The pastoral response is care: reducing the stigma that prevents people from seeking help, making clear from the pulpit that mental illness is a medical condition and not a spiritual verdict, connecting people to clinical resources, building communities of genuine support, following up with people in crisis rather than praying for them at church and leaving them alone at home. This is necessary work and most churches can do more of it than they currently do.

But the prophetic response asks the harder question: why do our most vulnerable neighbors have the least access to mental health care? [cite — confirm statistics on mental health access by income level] A middle-class congregation in a suburban zip code often has therapists available within a reasonable drive and with manageable waiting times. The low-income neighborhoods across town, where the concentration of stress and trauma and mental illness is highest, often have nothing between the emergency room and an eight-month waiting list for a community mental health clinic that has been cut to half its previous capacity by state budget reductions. The people who need mental health care most are the ones least likely to be able to access it, and the gap is not an accident. It is a policy choice, made over and over again, and the church that does not name it is not being appropriately humble about the limits of its social commentary. It is being strategically silent about something that has political costs to name.
