> God kept the prayer of the person who could not manage a hopeful ending.

I am not writing from a neutral position here. I know people in my congregation who were suffering from what I can now recognize as clinical depression, and I gave them spiritual counsel without ever asking whether they were seeing a therapist or whether they could afford one or whether they had any idea that what they were experiencing had a name and a treatment protocol. I told myself I was being a pastor. In some sense I was — I was present, I prayed, I cared. But I was also operating from a framework that divided the soul from the body and the spiritual from the material in a way that left people carrying more weight alone than they needed to carry.

The Psalms are the biblical tradition's clearest evidence that God does not require mental and emotional wellness as a precondition for honest prayer. Psalm 88 has no resolution. It begins in darkness and ends in darkness: "darkness is my closest friend" (Psalm 88:18). There is no turn toward hope. There is no recovery of faith. There is only the unfinished cry of a person at the edge of what can be borne, offered to God in its unresolved state. It is in the canon. God did not edit it out. God kept the prayer of the person who could not manage a hopeful ending.

## What Advocacy Requires Beyond Prayer

That is not a theology of despair. It is a theology of honesty — the insistence that God can receive the full weight of human suffering without requiring us to process it into something more manageable before bringing it to him. The church that teaches people to suppress the Psalm 88 moments, to project hope they do not feel, to perform spiritual health in the presence of genuine crisis, is not serving those people. It is teaching them to suffer alone in a community that should be capable of accompanying them.

Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 1:4 that God comforts us in all our troubles so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received. The comfort flows from honest experience of suffering, not around it. The church's capacity to minister to people in mental health crisis depends in part on its willingness to be honest about the crisis within its own membership — to name depression from the pulpit, to share stories of recovery that include clinical treatment, to remove the unspoken hierarchy in which the person with cancer deserves a casserole and the person with severe anxiety is expected to pray harder.

What justice requires beyond the pastoral is advocacy: for mental health parity in insurance coverage, for adequately funded community mental health infrastructure, for the reduction of the economic stress that is itself a major driver of mental illness, for the school-based and community-based interventions that reach people before crisis arrives. These are not peripheral concerns. They are the conditions under which people can actually access the care they need. The church that prays for the depressed without advocating for the systems that give them access to treatment has separated what God joined — the pastoral and the prophetic, the care for persons and the care for the conditions in which persons actually live.

## The Question God Asks at the Cave

Elijah received food, water, rest, and honest acknowledgment that the journey was too great for him. Then, eventually, he received a question: "What are you doing here, Elijah?" (1 Kings 19:9). Not a rebuke. A question that required him to name his actual condition. And then, after he named it, God did not argue with him. God gave him what the next part of the journey required.

That is the model. Not the systematic dismissal of human limitation as spiritual failure. Not the insistence that faith is sufficient to the biological realities of a suffering brain. But the provision of what the person actually needs — physical and emotional and social and clinical, in whatever combination the situation requires — and then the gentle question that invites them to name where they actually are.

> The journey is too great for you.

The tree Elijah collapsed under is not a private location. It is everywhere the weight of a human life has become unbearable — which is in every congregation, in every zip code, more concentrated in some than others, and present in all of them.

God is still sending provision. The question is whether the church is willing to be part of what gets sent — not just the prayer, but the referral, the advocacy, the reduction of stigma, the naming from the pulpit that this is a condition and not a judgment.

The journey is too great for you. That is not a verdict of failure. That is a statement of fact, and God said it first. The church that is willing to say it too will reach people who have been waiting years to hear someone say it without shame.

In most American cities right now, the cost of housing is consuming a proportion of working-class income that previous generations would have considered a crisis. It is a crisis. The median rent in most major metropolitan areas has outpaced wage growth for two decades. [cite — confirm] Teachers, nurses, sanitation workers, the people the city requires to function, cannot afford to live in the city they sustain. They commute long distances. They share cramped apartments. They are one unexpected expense from losing the roof they have.

The church has largely treated this as someone else's problem.

When a family in your congregation cannot afford to live within thirty miles of your building, that is not a real estate problem. It is a justice problem, and justice problems have always been the church's business.

## Shalom Has a Spatial Dimension

> The church has largely treated this as someone else's problem.

---

The Hebrew concept of shalom — the comprehensive flourishing that God intends for human life — has a spatial dimension that the church has been slow to emphasize. To dwell, in the Hebrew imagination, is to be placed. Stability of place is part of what it means to be a creature in a world God made for habitation. The promise to Abraham is a land. The promise to Israel in Deuteronomy is a land where each family will sit under its own vine and fig tree (Micah 4:4). The return from exile in Ezekiel is described as a resettlement, a rehousing, a restoration of each person to their place. The eschatological vision of Revelation is the New Jerusalem — the city, the dwelling of God with his people (Revelation 21:3). Homelessness in the Scripture is not merely physical deprivation. It is a condition that violates the deep structure of what it means to be a creature made to inhabit a world God called good.

## The Crisis as Policy, Not Personal Failure

The book of Nehemiah begins with a man weeping over broken walls. Walls and gates — the structures that make a city habitable, that provide protection and community — are the substance of his grief. When the walls are rebuilt, when the city is reorganized and the people are settled, the text treats this as an act of faithfulness to the covenant. The work is practical and theological at once. The physical and the spiritual are not separate categories in the biblical imagination, and a theology that treats them as separate will always end up deciding that the spiritual is what really matters while the physical is someone else's concern.

---

The modern housing crisis is not primarily a failure of individual ambition or personal responsibility. It is the downstream consequence of deliberate policy choices made over decades.

## The Faces Behind the Housing Numbers

> The mechanism changes. The concern does not.

Single-family zoning, established in American cities largely during the mid-twentieth century, restricted the density of housing in desirable areas, limiting supply and driving prices up. In many cities these policies were explicitly designed to limit which populations had access to which neighborhoods — the connection between exclusionary zoning and racial segregation is well documented. [cite — confirm] The language of those policies has changed. The effect on who can afford to live where has proven durable.

At the same time, federal disinvestment in public housing and affordable housing subsidies beginning in the 1970s and accelerating through the 1980s left cities without the mechanisms that had previously housed working-class families. [cite — confirm] The mortgage interest deduction — the single largest federal housing subsidy — has overwhelmingly benefited homeowners rather than renters, wealthy households rather than poor ones. The system was not neutral. It was designed, through accumulated policy choices, to make housing an asset-building mechanism for those who already had assets, and a source of extraction for those who did not.

I am aware that this sounds like policy analysis, and the objection arrives quickly: the church should not be in the business of zoning advocacy or housing policy. But the prophets of Israel did not refrain from addressing the economic and legal structures that produced poverty among God's people. Micah condemned those who "covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away; they oppress a man and his house, a man and his inheritance" (Micah 2:2). The specific legal and economic mechanism by which the powerful appropriated housing from the vulnerable was precisely the prophetic concern. Not a side issue. The center.

## What a Home Is in the Biblical Imagination

The mechanism changes. The concern does not.

---

There are people in most congregations who know the housing crisis from the inside. Not as a policy debate but as a life.

## The Assets the Church Already Holds

The single mother who is working two jobs and still cannot make rent. The young couple who grew up in the neighborhood and cannot afford to stay in it. The senior member who bought a home in 1978 on a single income and watches her children unable to replicate what she had. The recently arrived family navigating the rental market without the credit history most landlords require. The family sleeping in a car. These are not statistical abstractions. They are in your pews, or they were before the commute made Sunday attendance impossible.

Their housing precarity shapes everything else. Mental health. Marital stress. Children's school stability and academic performance. Capacity to participate in the life of the congregation. When the church refuses to name the system that produced their precarity, it is asking them to bring their suffering into a space that has quietly agreed not to discuss its cause. That is a form of pastoral failure. It is also a failure of prophetic nerve.

> The two are the same crisis.

The prophet Amos did not merely express sympathy for the people the merchants were cheating at the gates. He named the transaction. He named the price. He made explicit the connection between the economic behavior of the prosperous and the suffering of the poor. "Because you impose heavy rent on the poor and exact a tribute of grain from them, though you have built houses of well-hewn stone, you will not live in them; you have planted pleasant vineyards, but you will not drink their wine" (Amos 5:11). The welfare of the poor and the economic practices of the comfortable were not separate subjects. They were the same subject.

---

The theological question underneath all of this is: what is a home?

It is not, in the biblical imagination, primarily an investment vehicle. It is not a commodity to be held for appreciation or extracted for profit. It is a place — a specific location in the world where a person can be rooted, can be known, can participate in the life of a community over time. The theological vision of Leviticus and Deuteronomy treats the land not as private property in the modern sense but as a trust — something God owns and humans inhabit, always with accountability to the covenant community and to the God whose terms the community lives under.

The Jubilee laws of Leviticus 25 make this concrete: every fifty years, land reverts to its original allotment. The point is not communism. The point is that accumulated dispossession — the slow concentration of land and housing in the hands of the few through the ordinary mechanisms of debt and misfortune — was periodically interrupted by a divine requirement that the basic capacity for self-sufficient dwelling be restored to every family. The system had a structural correction built in. It acknowledged that markets, left to themselves, tend to produce dispossession. And it said that this outcome was theologically unacceptable.

We do not live under Jubilee law. But the theology behind it — that God's economic intent for human communities includes the basic ability to dwell, and that this intent creates obligations on the prosperous and on the community as a whole — does not require Jubilee law to remain active.

---

What can the church actually do?

Speaking is not sufficient, but speaking is where faithfulness begins — naming the crisis as a theological issue, not just a policy debate, making visible the faces of the people whose housing precarity is not an accident but a consequence.

The church has assets: land, buildings, institutional relationships, organized volunteer capacity, and presence in neighborhoods that makes it one of the few actors positioned to respond to the housing crisis at a local level with both prophetic voice and practical action. Congregations have built affordable housing on surplus land. [cite — confirm] Church coalitions have engaged city councils on zoning reform. Congregations have organized to prevent the displacement of long-term residents from gentrifying neighborhoods.

This work is not the whole gospel. But the gospel that does not touch the housing status of the family sleeping in their car in the parking lot is not the whole gospel either.

Isaiah 58:7 asks: "Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house?" The house in that verse is not a metaphor. It is a dwelling. A roof. A place where a person is safe enough to sleep and known enough to be called by their name.

The church knows how to talk about homelessness as a spiritual crisis. It has been slower to talk about housing as a justice crisis rooted in policies we have the power to examine and the prophetic obligation to name. The two are the same crisis. We do not get to address the spiritual emergency while ignoring the physical one.

That kind of selective theology has a name. The prophets used it.

The word is not polite, and it is not quiet. But it is accurate.

A pastor who gives without receiving will eventually have nothing left to give. Every pastor agrees with that sentence. Almost none of us build a life around it.

We have made a quiet trade in American ministry. We took the word *faithful* and tied it to *tired*. The faithful pastor is the busy one. The serious pastor is the depleted one. The man who guards a day of rest is suspected, gently, of guarding himself. The man who sees a counselor is managing a deficiency. The man who takes his vacation without his laptop is being irresponsible. These are not the official positions of our churches. They are the unspoken premises that run below our official positions, and they are destroying pastors at a rate we have mostly chosen not to measure.

I have not always pastored from a full place. I have worn my exhaustion like a credential. I have let a full calendar stand in for a full soul, and I have called the substitution *commitment*. So this is not a warning issued from a rested distance. It is a confession from a man who learned the hard way that a tank can run dry while the gauge still reads faithful.

## The Quiet Trade Between Faithful and Tired

---

> We are not indispensable.

Begin with the theological claim, because this is not primarily a wellness argument. It is a theological one.

The Sabbath is not a reward for productive weeks. It is a command. Exodus 20:8–11 does not say "rest when you have earned it." It says "remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy." The ground given is not human need — though human need is served — but divine pattern. God rested on the seventh day. We are made in the image of a God who rested. The refusal to rest is therefore not merely foolish. It is a form of idolatry — a quiet insistence that the world will not hold together without our effort, that the church is kept alive by our availability, that we are, functionally, indispensable.

## Sabbath as Command, Not Reward

We are not indispensable. That is the freeing and humbling truth. The church belongs to Christ, was bought by Christ, and is kept by Christ. Your congregation will survive your day off. It will survive your vacation. It will, one day, survive you entirely — as it survived the pastor before you and will survive the one who comes after.

The pastor who cannot believe this has a theological problem. He has placed himself, functionally, at the center of what only God can occupy. And the irony is that his unavailability — the depletion that comes from a closed system that only pours out and takes nothing in — will produce in his congregation exactly the outcome he feared his absence would produce: a pastor with nothing left to offer.

---

## The Withdrawal That Made Everything Possible

Jesus withdrew. Mark says it plainly and more than once. The crowds were still coming. The need was still there. The paralyzed were still waiting at the edges. And he left. "Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up, left the house and went off to a solitary place, where he prayed" (Mark 1:35). His disciples found him and told him what he already knew — "Everyone is looking for you!" He redirected them toward the next towns. He did not stay because the need demanded it.

This is the model the church has largely failed to adopt. Jesus did not empty himself for us by running himself ragged. He emptied himself on a cross, once, having spent thirty years and three years of ministry refusing to be hurried by anyone's emergency but the Father's. The discipline of withdrawal was not a luxury he allowed himself. It was the structural practice that made everything else possible.

## What the Busyness Hides

Eugene Peterson spent decades arguing that the pastoral office, as it tends to be constructed in American churches, is a systematic arrangement for keeping the pastor away from God [cite — confirm specific work]. The pastor is so busy providing spiritual services that he has no time for spiritual formation. He is so busy feeding others that he does not eat. The congregation gets exactly what it appears to want — a pastor who is always available — and gets, at the same time, a pastor whose spiritual depth is thinning like topsoil in a dry summer.

---

> The curiosity went first.

Here is what the busyness hides. A pastor who never receives slowly forgets how. He becomes a closed system — pouring out, taking in nothing, and mistaking the dryness for depth. The sermons get thinner even as the hours get longer. The pastoral conversations become technique — the right phrases deployed in the right order — rather than genuine presence. The prayers become administrative. The love becomes competence.

None of it shows up in the metrics the church watches, which is exactly why the church keeps rewarding the man right up until the morning he cannot get out of the car. By the time burnout is visible, it has been invisible for years. The gradual erosion — of joy, of curiosity, of genuine feeling, of the ability to be moved by what should move you — happens beneath the surface of ordinary productivity. The conference talks. The sermons go out. The meetings happen. But the man inside the machinery has been leaving slowly for a long time.

Elijah, in 1 Kings 19, is a man who has just done the most significant single act of his prophetic career — the confrontation with the prophets of Baal at Mount Carmel, the demonstration that Yahweh is God and Baal is nothing — and then immediately collapses under a broom tree and asks to die (1 Kings 19:4). Elijah is not weak. He is empty. The triumph was followed by a death threat, the crowd turned, the moment passed, and there was nothing left to sustain him. God's response is not a pep talk. God does not rebuke him for his collapse or commission him immediately back to his assignment. God feeds him twice, lets him sleep, and then speaks to him gently at the entrance of a cave, not in wind or earthquake or fire but in a still small voice (1 Kings 19:12).

## The Lie That Things Will Settle Down

The ministry of God to his depleted prophet is: rest, food, presence, and a new direction. Not productivity. Not a return to schedule. Reception, first.

---

The specific failure mode I have seen most often — and lived myself — is the pastor who tells himself he will rest once things settle down. Once the capital campaign is finished. Once the staff situation is resolved. Once the series is done and the special event is behind him. Once things slow down.

Things do not slow down. This is the structure of the work: it always has more in it than you can give. Every pastor who has been in ministry for more than five years knows this, and yet the logic of "once things settle" keeps its grip because it lets you defer the harder work indefinitely. You are not avoiding rest because of the demands of ministry. You are using the demands of ministry to avoid the discomfort of stopping.

## What It Looks Like to Receive

The discomfort of stopping is real. When you stop, you feel it. The anxiety you were outrunning catches up. The questions you were too busy to sit with arrive. The emptiness beneath the activity becomes visible. This is not a reason to keep running. It is a reason to stop sooner, in a context where you have support, rather than running until the stop is involuntary.

A pastor friend once told me — and I have thought about this for years — that he recognized his burnout only after he realized he had stopped being curious. He had been a voracious reader. He had been genuinely interested in his congregation's lives. He had found theology delightful. All of that had quietly switched off, replaced by a functional competence that looked like pastoral care and was not. He was doing all the pastoral things from a place where nothing was generating them anymore.

The curiosity went first. Then the joy. Then, slowly, the love — not the commitment to act lovingly, which held, but the genuine feeling of love that had once made the acting easy.

---

The practical question, then: what does it look like to receive? Not as a technique for extending ministry longevity — though you will last longer — but as a genuine practice of the pastoral life.

It looks like a Sabbath you keep, not because you can justify it but because the God you serve kept one and you are made in his image. A day structurally different from the other six. A day when the phone is not the first thing you reach for and the last. A day when you are a human being before you are a pastor.

> Your busyness was never the gift. You were.

It looks like relationships in which you are not the provider. Every pastor needs at least one person — ideally more — to whom he can say the true, unflattering sentence about how he is doing and receive a response that does not manage him. The pastoral isolation of too many pastors — the loneliness that comes from being always the one who gives — is not a sign of strength. It is a sign of a closed system.

It looks like the willingness to see a counselor, a spiritual director, a therapist — not as a sign of deficit but as a sign of the same wisdom that leads you to recommend those things to your congregation. The pastor who recommends professional mental health care and never receives it has separated what he preaches from how he lives. That separation has a cost.

And it looks like letting the gospel reach you — not just your congregation. The pastor who teaches justification by grace through faith and lives by a performance-based approval from his church has not been formed by the thing he teaches. The gospel says you are not your output. The church does not need your busyness. God is not measuring your available hours.

---

There is a word of grace at the end of the Elijah passage. After the rest and the food and the still small voice, God gives Elijah a successor and a companion — Elisha, who will carry the prophetic work forward (1 Kings 19:16, 19–21). Elijah is not abandoned in his depletion. He is not required to produce his way back to legitimacy. He is given rest, presence, and a friend.

The church does not need more tired pastors. It has plenty. It needs a few who are still alive in the soul by the time they reach sixty — who have something left to give because they spent thirty years letting themselves be filled.

Your busyness was never the gift. You were.

The church does not need you to be everywhere. It needs you to be somewhere — present, grounded, honest, alive. That presence requires more of you than your schedule. It requires your soul. And the soul does not fill by running faster.

Be one of those pastors. Not the busiest one. The living one.

There is a moment in the drift — and every pastor who has watched it happen knows it — when the church stops being recognizable by its confession and starts being recognizable by its political identity. The drift is rarely dramatic. It happens in sermon illustrations that only land for one kind of voter. It happens in the unspoken assumptions about which cultural enemies are being addressed from the pulpit. It happens in the candidates who get applause at church events and the ones who do not. And then one day someone from outside the congregation visits on a Sunday morning and walks away knowing exactly which party the church voted for, but uncertain whether they heard the Gospel.

That is the moment the church has become a political brand. And by the time most pastors recognize it, the congregation has organized a significant portion of its identity around the association.

---

## When a Church Becomes a Political Brand

This is not a new problem. It has an old name and a long history.

The term for it, in the history of political theology, is Constantinianism — the arrangement, first formalized in the fourth century under the Roman Emperor Constantine, in which the church's institutional interests and the empire's political interests become so entangled that each begins to function as a legitimating structure for the other [cite — confirm]. The church gives the empire theological sanction. The empire gives the church institutional protection and social prestige. The arrangement is mutually beneficial for both institutions and catastrophic for the church's prophetic integrity.

## The Old Name for an Old Problem

> This is not a new problem. It has an old name and a long history.

John Howard Yoder spent much of his career arguing that the Constantinian settlement was the most consequential and most underexamined event in the history of Western Christianity [cite — confirm]. His argument was not primarily that political engagement is wrong. It was that the specific exchange of prophetic independence for institutional favor produces a church that is no longer capable of speaking against power, because it has become dependent on power for its own survival and status.

Yoder's concern materializes in specific, visible ways in American Christianity. The pastor whose church is closely identified with a political party cannot effectively challenge that party's failures. The congregation whose identity is partly organized around political loyalty will hear a prophetic word against that loyalty as an attack on the community's identity rather than as a call to deeper faithfulness. The church that needs the political arrangement in place to sustain its cultural influence has made a trade it did not fully examine at the time, and it is now living in the downstream consequences.

---

I have seen this from inside. I have felt the pull of it myself — the way a congregation's agreement can be generated more reliably by touching political anxieties than by opening the Scripture, the way certain phrases create immediate warmth in a room that the Gospel alone does not always produce. That pull is a form of temptation, and like most temptations, it offers something real: unity, energy, clarity about who is inside and who is outside. What it does not offer is the thing it costs.

## The Pull of Political Agreement

What it costs is the church's ability to speak to anyone outside its political tribe. The prophetic voice is always addressed to the whole people, and it is always capable of reaching across political lines — because the prophets were not targeting one party's sins. Amos condemned the wealthy in Israel without regard for their political affiliation. Isaiah indicted the religious establishment regardless of which faction it belonged to. Jesus managed to offend the Pharisees and the Sadducees in the same week. That breadth is the mark of a genuinely prophetic ministry. The church that can only speak to its own political friends has lost the range.

The letters to the seven churches in Revelation 2–3 were written to communities experiencing a very specific form of this temptation. The Roman imperial cult was not simply a political preference. It was an identity claim, a loyalty demand, a social pressure that organized economic and civic life around demonstrated allegiance to Caesar as Lord. The churches at Pergamum and Thyatira were accommodating to this demand — allowing the language and rituals of imperial loyalty to coexist with the confession of Christ's lordship (Revelation 2:14-15, 2:20). The risen Christ's word to them is direct and unsparing: you have compromised the confession. The two lordships cannot coexist.

The American church's temptation is structurally similar. Not identical — the coercion is not the same, and the cost of resistance is not the same. But the mechanism is the same: a worldly authority making a loyalty demand that the church, in exchange for cultural favor and institutional protection, is being gradually absorbed into.

## The Way Back Is Not Neutrality

---

> The way back is not neutrality.

The way back is not neutrality. Neutrality is its own form of failure — the decision to say nothing consequential about anything that matters. The way back is theological clarity about what the Gospel actually claims and the willingness to let those claims land with equal force across the political spectrum.

This requires something specific from the preacher. It requires preaching texts that discomfort the right and texts that discomfort the left, in the same calendar year, without softening either. It requires naming justice concerns that the progressive wing cares about and moral concerns the conservative wing cares about — not to achieve balance for its own sake, but because the canon of Scripture contains both, and selective preaching produces a selective congregation. It requires being willing to lose the applause of people who came to have their political instincts baptized rather than their lives transformed.

This is more costly than it sounds. The congregation that has organized part of its identity around political loyalty does not receive prophetic challenge to that loyalty as spiritual growth. It receives it as betrayal. The pastor who preaches it will face the same response that Amaziah gave Amos: "Go, prophecy somewhere else." Some people will leave. Some people will campaign against the pastor to people who stayed. Some people will make the pastor feel, for a season, as though the ministry is unraveling.

That is the cost. It is not optional. There is no path back from political brand status that does not pass through the willingness to be misread, mischaracterized, and temporarily depleted.

## The Disorientation That Begins Recovery

---

Practically, the path back from a political brand identity begins with a season of deliberate theological grounding. Not a sermon series called "Let's Talk About Politics" — that is guaranteed to generate more heat than light. A sustained engagement with texts that accomplish the reorientation of primary loyalty. The Sermon on the Mount. The prophetic literature. The early chapters of Revelation, which were written to a church being pressured to conflate faithfulness with imperial loyalty. These texts were written to situations not unlike ours, and they produce the same disorientation: you thought your political category was substituting for your theological category, and you were wrong.

This disorientation is the beginning of recovery. The congregation that encounters the Beatitudes seriously — "Blessed are the peacemakers," "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness" (Matthew 5:9, 6) — is being asked to organize its imagination around categories that do not map cleanly onto any partisan platform. The congregation that sits with Isaiah 58 and hears the specific list of things that constitute genuine fasting — loosing the bonds of wickedness, letting the oppressed go free, sharing bread with the hungry — is being asked to locate its justice commitments in the text rather than in the party platform.

## An Alternative the World Most Needs

That reorientation does not produce political unanimity. It should not. The congregation that comes through this disorientation will not agree on every policy question. But it will share something more durable than political agreement: the conviction that its primary citizenship is elsewhere (Philippians 3:20), and that what it owes the world is the Gospel — not the Gospel as one party's mascot, but the Gospel as an announcement that destabilizes all earthly powers equally.

---

There is a long tradition within Christianity of maintaining precisely this prophetic distance. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from within a regime that was explicitly demanding the church's political loyalty, drew the distinction between the church's two roles: counseling the state on justice, and sometimes being obligated to jam the wheel that is crushing the innocent — but always from a position that did not confuse the church's mission with the state's agenda [cite — confirm]. The church has a word for every political power. It does not have a loyalty to any of them.

> Not a party. An alternative.

That tradition is worth recovering not because it produces a politically disengaged church — it does not; Bonhoeffer's own life makes clear that the tradition produces extraordinary engagement — but because it produces a church whose engagement is governed by the Gospel rather than by the political alliance.

The congregation that is known in its city primarily as a political bloc has lost its distinctiveness in the wrong direction. The congregation that is known as a community of people whose common life demonstrates something that neither party can produce — genuine forgiveness, genuine solidarity across class and race, genuine care for the weak and the strange — that congregation is the political witness the world most needs. Not a party. An alternative.

That alternative is worth recovering. It always has been.

The question is whether the pastor is willing to pay the price of the recovery.

That is not a rhetorical question. It is a pastoral one.

I am asking myself.

Before the policy arguments and the border statistics and the think-tank reports, there is a child. Eight years old, or eleven, or four. Sleeping in a camp or a detention facility or a church basement three thousand miles from the city where she learned to walk. She did not choose the war that emptied her neighborhood. She did not choose the drought that made the crops fail or the gang that made the streets impassable after dark. She is here because staying was not survivable, and she is here because the alternatives were all terrible and this one was the least terrible. She is a refugee. And whether the church sees her as a theological problem or a theological test will say more about the church's actual convictions than fifty years of doctrinal statements.

The refugee is not a modern category. The Bible begins with displacement.

## The Bible Begins With Displacement

> The refugee is not a modern category. The Bible begins with displacement.

Adam and Eve are expelled from the garden. Cain becomes a fugitive and wanderer. Abraham is commanded to leave everything he knows for a land he has never seen. Jacob flees his brother's rage. Joseph is sold and transported as a slave. The people of Israel spend four hundred years as strangers in a land that is not theirs, in conditions that begin as hospitality and end as bondage. Ruth is a foreigner in a field that does not belong to her. Naomi is a woman with no land rights, surviving on the mercy of a system designed for people exactly like her. The Psalms are full of the language of exile: *By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept* (Psalm 137:1). *How can we sing the songs of the Lord while in a foreign land?* (Psalm 137:4).

This is not background color to the biblical story. It is the story. The God of Israel is the God who knows what it means to be displaced, because the people who carried his story knew it in their bones. The law they were given at Sinai was shaped by that knowledge: *Do not oppress a foreigner; you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners, because you were foreigners in Egypt* (Exodus 23:9). The repeated command is rooted not in abstract ethics but in remembered experience. You know this. You have been this. You will not do to others what was done to you.

The word translated "foreigner" or "stranger" in most English versions is the Hebrew *ger* — the resident alien, the one without full legal standing in the community, dependent on the community's willingness to extend the protections that citizens carry automatically [cite — confirm]. The Torah provisions for the *ger* are extensive: gleaning rights (Leviticus 19:9-10), legal protection (Deuteronomy 24:17), inclusion in the Sabbath rest (Exodus 20:10), participation in the covenant festivals (Deuteronomy 16:11). These are not charitable extras. They are built into the legal structure of the community. The *ger* is not an object of pity. The *ger* is a participant, protected by law, included in the life of the people.

## The Ger as Protected Participant

When Jesus stands in the synagogue at Nazareth and reads from Isaiah 61 — *the Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor* — the list that follows is not random (Luke 4:18-19). The poor, the captive, the blind, the oppressed, the one in the year of the Lord's favor. These are the categories the prophetic tradition had always attached to God's deepest concern. When he tells the parable of the sheep and goats in Matthew 25, the test is not theological correctness. The test is whether the people fed the hungry, gave drink to the thirsty, welcomed the stranger (*xenos* — the foreign one, the one who does not belong), clothed the naked, cared for the sick, visited the imprisoned. *I was a stranger and you welcomed me* (Matthew 25:35). The incarnation runs precisely here: God is found in the face of the displaced person. Not symbolically. Literally.

## The Prior Question Is Theological, Not Political

The counter-argument is political and it deserves honest engagement. The state has legitimate interests in controlling borders. The church is not the state. Questions of immigration policy are genuinely complex, involving security concerns, economic effects, rule of law, and the management of finite resources. Christians can hold different views on specific policy questions and be faithful. The church should not pretend these complexities do not exist or that there is a single policy position that the Gospel mandates.

> But there is a prior question, and that question is not political.

But there is a prior question, and that question is not political. It is theological. Do you believe that the person seeking refuge bears the image of God? Do you believe that God's stated concern for the displaced is normative for the people who bear God's name? Do you believe that Matthew 25 was written about real people in real conditions and that its claims have real consequences for how you behave? If you answer yes to those questions, the policy arguments begin from a different place. The question is no longer whether the church should respond but how — not whether the displaced person's humanity commands a response but what form that response should take given the complexities of the context.

## What the Early Church Recovered

The church in the first three centuries did not have the luxury of deciding this question abstractly. It was the church — not the empire, not the temples of the old gods — that built the first systematic infrastructure for caring for strangers in late antiquity [cite — confirm]. Julian the Apostate, the Roman emperor who tried to revive classical paganism in the fourth century, complained bitterly that the Christians were out-caring his priests: they supported not only their own poor but other people's poor as well. The reputation of the early church was not built on its theological precision, however real that was. It was built on the fact that when plague swept through a city, the Christians stayed and the others fled. When abandoned infants were left on the rubbish heaps of Rome — a common practice in the ancient world — the Christians picked them up. When the displaced arrived at the city's edge, the Christians had structures in place to receive them.

That reputation is worth recovering. Not as a strategic move for institutional credibility — though it would produce that. But because it is what bearing the name of Jesus requires.

What does it look like concretely?

## What Costly Welcome Looks Like

It looks like the congregation that learns the difference between a refugee, an asylum seeker, and an undocumented immigrant — not because the legal category determines the worth of the person but because knowing the actual situation is the beginning of actually helping rather than performing concern. It looks like the pastor who has a relationship with the resettlement agency in his city and knows which families arrived last month and what they specifically need. It looks like the church that does not just donate to the food pantry that serves refugee families but sends its members to sit at the table, to learn names, to witness the specific shape of the specific loss.

It looks like the congregation that speaks, when speaking is costly. The political environment around immigration has become so charged that many churches have made a studied decision to say nothing, to avoid the controversy, to keep everyone in the room. The silence feels like wisdom. It is capitulation. When a community of people bearing the image of God is being dehumanized in public discourse, the church's silence is not neutrality. It is consent. The prophets did not choose silence because the political climate was unfavorable.

It looks like the pastor who has read Leviticus 19 carefully and knows that the command to love the stranger as yourself — *love him as yourself, for you were strangers in Egypt* (Leviticus 19:34) — is not a minor provision in an obscure law code. It is the same chapter that contains the command Jesus called the second greatest: love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18). The stranger is the neighbor. The refugee is the neighbor. This is not a liberal political position. It is the text.

## A Crisis of Imagination

> The stranger is the neighbor. The refugee is the neighbor.

The global refugee crisis is not primarily a crisis of borders or policy. It is a crisis of imagination — a failure of the human imagination to hold the humanity of people who are far away, who speak differently, whose children do not look like our children. The church's peculiar resource in this moment is not political influence or institutional prestige. It is the Gospel's capacity to expand the imagination. To make real what policy has made abstract. To put a name on what statistics have made numerical. To say, with the specificity that only direct contact produces: this is Maria. This is her son. This is what they left and what it cost them to leave it. This is what they need from us.

The watching world is not persuaded by the church's doctrinal statements. It is persuaded by what the church does with its body and its resources when the cost of doing it is real.

Before the policy arguments, there is a child. The church's answer to that child will be the church's answer to the question Matthew 25 has already asked.

The food pantry is a good thing. The coat drive is a good thing. The Christmas toy distribution, the back-to-school supply event, the Thanksgiving turkey giveaway — these are good things, and the congregations that sustain them year after year are doing real work in real neighborhoods.

But charity and justice are not the same thing, and confusing them has cost the poor in ways we have not been willing to count.

Charity responds to the wound. Justice asks about the weapon. Both are necessary. Only one of them threatens the arrangements that produce the wound in the first place. And we have historically chosen the one that does not.

> Charity responds to the wound.

## The Ancient Pattern

This is not a new failure. The prophet Amos, preaching to eighth-century Israel, did not condemn the wealthy for failing to give alms. He condemned them for participating in the systems — the rigged scales, the short measures, the grain sold at extortion prices during famine (Amos 8:4–6) — that made the poor poor. The problem was not an absence of benevolence. The problem was active extraction. The prophets understood something that institutional Christianity has spent two thousand years forgetting: charity can coexist with injustice. It can even function as its alibi.

The early church was known for material care of the poor, including those outside the community. Tertullian noted that pagans remarked on it: "See how they love one another" [cite — confirm]. By the fourth century, Constantine's church had inherited the empire's social welfare apparatus and turned it into a Christian institution. Basil of Caesarea built a complex in the fourth century that housed the sick, the poor, and travelers — what some historians have called the first hospital in the ancient world [cite — confirm]. The hospital was a Christian invention. The orphanage was a Christian institution. These are real achievements. I do not dismiss them.

But the institutionalization of charity made the church the primary social service provider for the empire — and that role shaped what the church was willing to say about the empire's economic arrangements. You do not bite the hand that funds the hospital. You do not name as unjust the system that makes your charity necessary if that system is also what your most powerful members administrate.

## What the Church Has Been Afraid to Say

Charity is politically safe. It asks nothing of the donor except resources and time. It leaves the donor's position in the system untouched. The businessman who gives generously to the food pantry and whose business practices contribute to the poverty that makes the food pantry necessary has made a very comfortable arrangement with his conscience. The church that accepts this arrangement and calls it faithfulness has done the businessman a disservice. It has also done the poor a disservice. It has allowed the cycle to continue by making the cycle's symptoms manageable enough that no one is forced to ask about the cause.

Justice is not safe. Justice examines the system. It asks who benefits from poverty's persistence. It names the structures — zoning laws that concentrate poverty, lending practices that extract wealth from the poor, wage structures that guarantee income insufficient for basic needs — and demands something of those who participate in them. Not just generosity. Accountability.

The prophetic tradition has always made this distinction. Micah does not ask for more generous Israelites. He asks for mishpat — right order in the social arrangement — and tsedaqah — restored relationships between those the system has severed. Neither of these is satisfied by a check to the food bank.

## A Brief History of How We Got Here

> Charity is politically safe.

The Reformation, for all its theological recovery, had an economic dimension that was not universally beneficial to the poor. The dissolution of the monasteries in England under Henry VIII in the 1530s [cite — confirm] eliminated the primary medieval social welfare infrastructure — the monasteries had operated the hospitals, the almshouses, the systems of outdoor relief for the poor. What replaced them was less comprehensive and less reliable. The Protestant theological emphasis on individual conversion and personal moral responsibility, combined with the Calvinist reading of prosperity as a possible sign of election, created conditions in which poverty was more easily read as a spiritual failure than as a structural condition.

Max Weber traced the connection between the Protestant work ethic and the spirit of capitalism [cite — confirm] — the way that the theological valorization of disciplined labor and the moral suspicion of idleness shaped the emergence of a capitalist economic order. Whatever the precise causal chain, the result was a religious culture that found it easier to help the individual poor person than to examine the systems that produced poverty.

The twentieth-century American evangelical world made this arrangement explicit. The social gospel movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries — Walter Rauschenbusch's insistence that the kingdom of God required the transformation of social structures as well as individual souls [cite — confirm] — was largely rejected by the fundamentalist movement as a dilution of the gospel. The personal gospel and the social gospel were framed as competitors. You chose one. Most chose the personal. The poor could be evangelized. The economic systems that produced their poverty were left to others.

## The Specific Comfort We Have Chosen

I have been a pastor long enough to know why we choose charity. The donor base of most American congregations lives significantly above the median income of the surrounding neighborhood. They are not the poor. They are the giving class. And the giving class, however sincere its concern for the poor, has a structural interest in explanations of poverty that do not implicate its own economic position.

If poverty is primarily the result of individual failure — poor decisions, inadequate discipline, lack of education — then charity is the correct response. You help the individual. You address the failure. The system that produces the failure is not under indictment, because the system is not the problem.

If poverty is partly the result of systemic conditions — policy choices, accumulated disadvantage, capital concentration — then justice is required alongside charity, and justice will eventually ask something of the people in the pews who benefit from those conditions. That question is expensive to ask, and most of us have not asked it.

I have not always asked it. I have stood in front of congregations and celebrated the generosity of the coat drive while knowing, from the income data of my own city, that the people receiving the coats lived in neighborhoods where the educational investment per pupil was a fraction of what it was in the neighborhoods where the donors lived. I preached about generosity and said nothing about the structures. I let charity be the whole story.

> Justice aims for its own obsolescence.

## The Cost of the Choice

The poor are not a ministry category. They are, in the prophetic tradition, the measure by which God evaluates the faithfulness of the community. "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free?" (Isaiah 58:6). The fast that God refuses is the fast that does not produce justice. The worship that God rejects is the worship that coexists with the trampling of the poor (Amos 5:21–24).

Charity does not satisfy this standard. Neither does preaching about charity without naming what charity cannot reach.

The steel-man version of the charity-first position deserves honest engagement: structural advocacy is slow, contentious, and often ineffective, while direct service to the poor is immediate and tangible. The person who is hungry today cannot eat while you argue about minimum wage policy. The church that provides food while working for systemic change is doing more than the church that refuses charity while waiting for policy to shift. True. The argument against prioritizing charity is not an argument against charity. It is an argument against charity as the ceiling of the church's response.

The problem with charity as the ceiling is that it requires the perpetual reproduction of the conditions that make charity necessary. The food pantry that opens every Thursday needs poverty to persist in order to continue performing its function. Not consciously, not cynically, but structurally. An institution organized to respond to need has an institutional interest in the continuation of need, even if every person within it is genuinely motivated by compassion. The institution cannot want its own extinction. The charity model, at scale, has baked into it a quiet accommodation to the permanence of poverty.

Justice aims for its own obsolescence. The system that produces the wound being addressed is the thing justice intends to change. When the change is accomplished, the justice work is done. Charity, organized and permanent, is often the signal that the justice work has never begun.

## What the Church Has to Do

The church that chooses charity has not chosen badly. It has chosen partially. And partial faithfulness, sustained long enough, begins to look like unfaithfulness to those on the wrong side of the system it has declined to name.

The food pantry opens again on Thursday. Someone will be there because they have nowhere else to go. They will receive something real. They will leave still poor, and the week after that they will come back. The question is not whether to feed them. The question is whether feeding them is all we have been called to do.

It is not. The God who commanded the Jubilee, who spoke through Amos about the scales, who promised through Isaiah the loosing of unjust bonds — that God has always asked for more than the coat drive. The coat drive is a beginning. The prophetic tradition has always asked where it ends.

The answer is: when the systems that make coat drives necessary have been changed. That goal is distant and difficult and requires more than a church can accomplish alone. It requires exactly the kind of long, patient, structural engagement that makes good institutions uncomfortable.

That discomfort is precisely where the prophetic tradition points. Not past the coat drive, not instead of it. Beyond it. The charity is the floor. Justice is the ceiling. And the ceiling is what the prophets were always building toward.

H. Richard Niebuhr spent a book cataloguing the ways the church has answered the culture question — Christ against culture, Christ of culture, Christ above culture, Christ and culture in paradox, Christ transforming culture. [cite — confirm] The catalogue itself is instructive not because it provides the answer but because it reveals that the question has been live in every generation, and that every generation has reached for a different settlement.

We are living through a moment when the settlement our parents inherited is dissolving, and we do not yet know what will replace it.

## The Dissolving Settlement

> We are post-Christian in the sense that Christianity is no longer the default.

The Constantinian arrangement — the broad alignment between Christian faith and Western cultural assumption that began in the fourth century and shaped Western civilization for more than a millennium — is not quite over, but its legitimacy is. The culture no longer defers to Christian claims. The institutions that once carried Christian assumption into public life without argument — schools, courts, civic ritual, the default moral vocabulary of the neighborhood — have either abandoned those assumptions or are actively contested about them. We are not post-Christian in the sense that Christianity is gone. We are post-Christian in the sense that Christianity is no longer the default.

---

For many Christians, this is primarily experienced as loss. The cultural conditions that made the faith easy have been removed, and the faith now requires more active choice, more deliberate formation, more willingness to be countercultural in ways that are actually costly rather than merely nominal.

## The Church Most Prophetic Under Pressure

This is disorienting. And the instinct it produces is understandable: fight to restore the conditions. Recover the cultural establishment. Legislate the norms. Force the culture back into a shape where the faith is at home.

I have felt this instinct. I understand it. And I think it misreads both the moment and the tradition.

## Distinguishing the Gospel From Its Cultural Form

> The gospel is not Western. It is not American.

The church was not at its most prophetic when it was culturally established. The church at its most prophetic was the church under pressure — the early communities that held a different account of reality while the imperial account surrounded them, who were outlawed and intermittently persecuted but who maintained the practices and the witness with a clarity that shaped the ancient world more permanently than any of the powers that tried to destroy them. It was the Confessing Church in Germany in the 1930s and 1940s, which maintained the integrity of the gospel while the German church capitulated to nationalist ideology. It was the Black church in America during the century of Jim Crow, which kept alive a theology of human dignity and divine justice in the very society organized to deny both. It was the underground church in contexts where Christianity carries genuine legal risk.

What those communities share is not cultural comfort but theological clarity. They knew what they believed, because they had to. The pressure removed the option of comfortable ambiguity.

---

## The Two Temptations of Culture War and Relevance

The pressure that post-Christendom creates is not without grace. It is clarifying. It forces a congregation to ask what it actually believes, as opposed to what it has inherited and never examined. It forces a distinction between the gospel and the cultural form the gospel wore in a particular time and place.

This distinction matters enormously and has been lost in the political alignment of American Christianity in recent decades. The gospel is not Western. It is not American. It is not a product of any civilization, though every civilization has both received it and distorted it. The church that conflates the gospel with a particular political arrangement or cultural moment will discover — is already discovering — that the arrangement's decline feels like the gospel's decline, and that recovery of the arrangement becomes confused with faithfulness to the gospel.

These are not the same thing. They have never been the same thing. And the confusion between them has cost the church something very difficult to recover: the capacity to speak to the culture from outside the culture's own assumptions.

## Faithfulness Stripped of Cultural Scaffolding

Lesslie Newbigin returned to England after decades as a bishop in India and wrote about what he saw: a culture that had been shaped by the gospel but had forgotten the gospel, and a church that had become so accommodated to that culture that it no longer knew how to speak with a distinct voice. [cite — confirm] He argued that the church's challenge in the West was missionary in the fullest sense — not bringing the gospel to people who had never heard it, but bringing it afresh to people who thought they already knew it and had decided it was not relevant. That missionary challenge requires that the church know the difference between what it believes and what the culture around it assumes.

---

The contemporary temptation runs in two directions, not one.

## The Practices That Form People Into Christ

The first temptation is toward culture war — the recovery of cultural establishment through political force. This strategy misunderstands both what was lost and what the church's purpose is. What was lost was not the kingdom. What was lost was a particular cultural arrangement that, at its best, provided favorable conditions for Christian practice and, at its worst, allowed the church to mistake cultural dominance for gospel faithfulness. The culture war response doubles down on the mistake. It treats the restoration of cultural dominance as the goal of Christian witness, which converts the church into a political faction and the gospel into a platform.

The second temptation is toward relevance — the church that reshapes its message and practice to remain acceptable to a post-Christian culture. This strategy also misunderstands the moment. A church that has nothing to say except what the culture is already prepared to hear is not a church. It is an echo. The post-Christian person who encounters an echo of their own values in religious language is not encountering the gospel. They are encountering themselves.

Both strategies fail because they are responses to the same anxiety: the fear of being culturally irrelevant. The church that is desperate to remain culturally relevant will do almost anything to stay in the room. The church that is confident in its calling can afford to be strange — to practice the hospitality, the forgiveness, the economic solidarity that the surrounding culture finds implausible — and trust that the strangeness is its own kind of argument.

> The culture has never been the ultimate audience.

---

Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in 1943 from his prison cell about what he called "religionless Christianity" — the possibility of a faith that did not depend on the cultural scaffolding of Western religion for its vitality. [cite — confirm] He was writing in a context where that scaffolding had collapsed catastrophically, where the church that had depended on it had largely capitulated to the power that destroyed it. He was asking what the gospel looked like when stripped of every cultural advantage — when being a Christian cost something real, when the institutional supports were gone, when the faith had to live on its own resources.

That question is not yet as urgent in contemporary America as it was in Bonhoeffer's Germany. But the direction of travel is clarifying. The cultural conditions that once made Christian faith easy are changing. The question of what remains when the easy conditions are gone is becoming less hypothetical.

---

What the church is called to in this moment is not primarily a cultural strategy. It is faithfulness to a set of practices that form people into the image of Christ — practices that were always countercultural to some degree and are now more visibly so.

Gathering. Not for a performance to attract the spiritually curious but for the formation of people who know how to be in covenant with one another across disagreement and difference. Prayer. Not the public display of spiritual confidence but the honest bringing of the actual condition of one's soul before the God who does not need the performance. Scripture. Not as a cultural artifact or a sourcebook for values but as the living word of the God who is working toward a kingdom that no cultural arrangement can capture or contain. Table. The Eucharist's insistence that the body broken and given is the center of reality, not any political or cultural project. Hospitality. The practice that enacts the theological claim that every person who arrives is made in the image of God and therefore belongs at the table. Reconciliation. The refusal to accept the culture's account of who is irredeemably other.

These practices are not dependent on cultural establishment for their efficacy. They worked in the Roman Empire before Constantine. They work in the underground church today. They will work in post-Christendom America if we are willing to pursue them with the seriousness the moment requires rather than mourning the cultural conditions that once made them easier.

---

Not every generation gets to be culturally at home. The tradition is older than any single culture. It has survived arrangements far more hostile than the one we currently inhabit.

The early church did not have Christian assumptions in the broader culture. It did not have favorable legal status. It did not have cultural prestige or political access. It had the practices and the witness and the Spirit, and it changed the world.

The question is not whether the culture will accommodate us. The culture has never been the ultimate audience.

The question is whether we are willing to be the church anyway — whether we will practice the faith with the seriousness that the moment requires, whether we will hold the costly things at cost, whether we will be strange enough to be worth explaining and honest enough to be believed when we do.

That is not a cultural strategy. It is a decision about what we love and whether we love it enough to carry it through conditions that do not favor it.

The tradition has been carried through worse. The question is whether we are willing to carry it now.

The Bible contains roughly 2,350 verses addressing money, wealth, poverty, and economic justice [cite — confirm]. One scholar I read years ago put the number at over 2,000 for economic themes alone — making it the subject addressed more frequently than any other in the canon, including prayer, faith, and eternal life. Against that canon, the church's teaching on economic ethics has been, in most of the congregations I have served and most of the conferences I have attended, remarkably thin.

On sexual ethics, the church has not been thin. On sexuality, the church has maintained a clear, consistent, publicly stated position and defended it against considerable cultural pressure. Sermons are preached. Books are written. Denominational battles are fought to their bitter conclusions. The clarity is real and the courage sometimes genuine.

The disproportion requires explanation.

---

## Why the Disproportion Demands an Answer

I am not arguing that the church's sexual ethics are wrong to hold or wrong to teach. The biblical witness on sexuality is coherent and worthy of careful proclamation. But it is worth asking why the subjects on which the Scriptures are most extensive have received the least consistent pastoral attention, while the subjects on which the Scriptures are less extensive have received the most.

The answer is not primarily theological. It is sociological.

> The disproportion requires explanation.

Sexual ethics make demands on the behavior of individuals. They govern what happens between consenting people in private. They address choices that do not depend on economic position or social power — choices that are equally available to the poor and to the wealthy, to the powerful and to the powerless. When the church proclaims a sexual ethic, it challenges the choices of individual members without necessarily challenging the structures from which those members benefit. The rich man and the poor man are equally subject to the sexual ethic. Their bank accounts are not touched by the sermon.

Economic ethics are different. Economic ethics make demands on systems. They challenge the structures that produce inequality, concentrate wealth, and convert human beings into instruments of production. When the church proclaims a full economic ethic — the kind the prophets proclaimed — it challenges not just the choices of individual members but the arrangements from which the wealthiest members benefit most. The sermon about money does not just address what people do in private. It addresses what they do with everything they have and how those decisions connect to the conditions of people they will never meet. And it implies a verdict about the structures that produce those conditions.

This is a much more uncomfortable sermon to give. It is also a much more uncomfortable sermon to receive, if you are receiving it in the congregation of a suburban American church while sitting next to people whose combined financial assets would address significant human need.

I have been more comfortable talking about sex. I have preached careful sermons about sexuality with more confidence and less anxiety than I have preached about wealth and poverty and economic obligation. This is a failure I can identify, and naming it is the first step toward doing differently.

---

## The Prophets Made No Such Separation

The prophets did not make this separation. The eighth century BC prophets — Amos, Hosea, Micah, Isaiah — were not primarily concerned with the sexual behavior of Israel. They were concerned with economic exploitation, with the crushing of the poor, with the corruption of the legal system by those with money to buy verdicts, with the accumulation of land by those who had the power to take it from those who did not. Amos describes a society where "they sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals — those who trample the head of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the afflicted" (Amos 2:6-7). This is the grievance. This is what God is bringing to judgment.

Micah pronounces woe on "those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds. When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand. They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away; they oppress a man and his house, a man and his inheritance" (Micah 2:1-2). The sin Micah names is economic predation — the systematic use of legal and economic power to take from those who cannot protect what they have. It is not adultery. It is not false worship, though false worship follows from it. It is the organization of economic life around the accumulation of the powerful at the expense of the vulnerable.

Isaiah 5:8 pronounces the same woe in language that has not aged: "Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land." The accumulation of real estate. The elimination of neighbors through displacement. The production of a world where the wealthy hold everything and everyone else has been crowded out. If this does not sound recognizable in twenty-first-century America, you are not paying attention to the housing market.

---

## What Jesus Taught About the Rival Master

Jesus talked about money more than he talked about almost anything else except the kingdom of God — and the connection between those two subjects was, in his teaching, very close. The parable of the rich fool in Luke 12. The parable of the rich man and Lazarus in Luke 16. The story of Zacchaeus. The encounter with the rich young ruler. The cleansing of the Temple. The widow's offering. The Sermon on the Mount, where the accumulation of treasure on earth is named as an act of divided loyalty: "No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money" (Matthew 6:24).

That last verse is used in stewardship campaigns. It is very rarely preached to its full conclusion. If money is a rival master — a claim on loyalty that competes with God's claim — then the church's silence about economic structures is not a neutral position. It is a form of service to the rival master. Every time the church proclaims a clear sexual ethic and a vague economic ethic, it is, functionally, telling its wealthiest members that their money is not subject to the same scrutiny as their bodies. That the kingdom of God makes robust claims on their sexuality and attenuated claims on their bank accounts. That God is interested in what happens in their bedrooms and largely uninterested in what happens in their portfolios.

Jesus did not teach this. The prophets did not teach this. James did not teach this — and James 5 is about as explicit an economic indictment as the canon contains: "Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up treasure in the last days. Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts" (James 5:1-4).

The wages kept back by fraud. Crying out. The ears of the Lord of hosts. This is not a suggestion about generous giving. It is an indictment.

---

## The Institutional Survival of the Church

> Every prophetic word loses someone.

The honest account of why the American church is more comfortable with sexual ethics than economic ethics is this: the sexual ethic, however challenging to individuals, does not threaten the institutional survival of the church. The economic ethic, preached consistently and to its full implications, very well might.

Churches are funded by the generosity of their wealthiest members. The twenty percent of givers who produce eighty percent of the budget [cite — confirm] tend to be people for whom the economic ethic is most costly. A pastor who preaches the full prophetic tradition on wealth and poverty and economic justice is preaching to the people whose giving keeps his church operational. That is a conflict of interest that is structural, not personal, and it shapes what gets preached without anyone consciously deciding to compromise. The avoidance is often not cowardice. It is the accumulated effect of a thousand small decisions not to go quite that far this week.

I have made those decisions. I recognize the calculation. I have told myself that the congregation is not ready, that the political implications are too easily misread, that the prophetic word needs to be earned through relationship before it can be received. Some of that is true. None of it is entirely honest.

---

The way forward is not to stop teaching sexual ethics. It is to start teaching economic ethics with the same clarity and courage. To preach James 5 with the same willingness we bring to 1 Corinthians 6. To name wage theft as the Scriptures name it. To say clearly that the organization of an economy around the systematic extraction of wealth from those who cannot protect themselves is not a matter of political opinion — it is a matter of prophetic judgment, and the prophetic tradition is not ambiguous about it.

This will lose some people. Every prophetic word loses someone. The rich young ruler walked away. Jesus watched him go. He did not revise his statement about what the man needed to do.

## The Whole Gospel or a Partial One

> The Bible has a lot to say about money. It is time the church started saying it.

The church that only challenges the sexual choices of its members while leaving their economic arrangements unexamined has not yet proclaimed the whole gospel. It has proclaimed a partial gospel — a gospel comfortable enough to be received without cost by those whose social position is determined by the very arrangements the full gospel would challenge.

The prophets spoke to the whole life. Jesus taught about the whole life. The church that speaks about only part of the life is not being prophetic. It is being selective, which is another name for cowardice dressed in theological clothing.

The Bible has a lot to say about money. It is time the church started saying it.

Nobody tells you, in seminary, what it feels like to watch the congregation break in two. The curriculum covers church history, Koine Greek, hermeneutics, the minor prophets. It does not cover the Sunday morning when half the room is missing and the other half is watching your face to see if you will hold.

I have been in that room. It is one of the loneliest places in ministry.

Church splits are not unusual. They are, in the long arc of Christian history, extraordinarily common — from the Corinthian factions Paul addressed in the first century to the denominational fractures of the nineteenth century to the congregational ruptures that happen every year in ordinary churches across this country. They are common, and they are still devastating. Something about knowing that others have walked this does not actually make it lighter when you are carrying it.

---

## The History the Church Keeps Repeating

The history is instructive, and not in the way we usually use it.

The first significant theological split in the Christian movement — the Jerusalem Council controversy of roughly 49 CE [cite — confirm], in which the question of Gentile inclusion nearly fractured the young movement — was resolved by a gathering in which all parties had to speak and be heard, not by the winning side simply overrunning the losing side. Acts 15 is careful to record the testimony of Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:12), the intervention of James (Acts 15:13-21), and the letter produced by the community together (Acts 15:22-29). The resolution came through a process that gave everyone standing — not just the powerful.

The Donatist controversy of the fourth century did not resolve that way. Augustine argued against the Donatists with force and rigor, and the imperial church used its alliance with Constantine's successors to suppress them [cite — confirm]. The Donatists had real concerns about the integrity of the clergy and the validity of sacraments performed by those who had compromised under persecution. Those concerns were not entirely without merit. What happened instead was a political settlement rather than a theological resolution, and the questions the Donatists were asking did not disappear — they simply went underground, resurfacing in every subsequent reform movement that asked whether the institutional church's corruption invalidated its ministry.

The history of church splits is the history of communities failing to do what Acts 15 models: create a process in which the real question gets heard, in which the parties with genuine standing have a real role, in which the resolution produces a document that names what was actually at stake.

Most church splits do not get that process. They get the conversation that should have happened two years earlier happening now, too late, when the factions have already formed and the outcome is already partially determined by who has controlled the narrative.

---

## The Honest Question the Pastor Must Ask

> Unaddressed conflict does not heal.

What the pastor in the middle of a split needs first is not strategy. It is honesty. The honest question — the one that requires real courage — is this: What role did I play in this?

Not the whole role.
