Sometimes splits are driven entirely by power struggles, unresolved theological disagreements, or the arrival of a charismatic disruptor who never had any intention of submitting to the community's discernment. Those things happen. The pastor is not always responsible for the origin of the conflict. But the pastor is always responsible for how the conflict was handled, what was tolerated, what was avoided, how long the dysfunction was allowed to metastasize before anyone named it.

The cracks in a congregation rarely appear suddenly. They widen over months, sometimes years, while the pastor tells himself the situation will stabilize. It usually does not. Unaddressed conflict does not heal. It goes underground, and what goes underground grows in the dark. The subterranean conflict builds a pressure that eventually has to surface somewhere — in a board meeting, in a parking lot conversation, in the anonymous letter that arrives on a Tuesday, in the sudden and unexplained departure of people the pastor thought were stable.

The temptation, once a split has happened, is to write a narrative in which you are primarily the victim. The other side left. They took people with them. They sent the critical letter. They organized the parking-lot meetings. All of that may be true, and it still does not answer the harder question of what formed in the soil of your leadership that allowed that particular seed to take root.

This is not self-flagellation. It is stewardship. The pastor who cannot examine his own failures honestly will repeat them in the next church, and the one after that.

---

## The Cross as the Argument Against Division

Paul's letter to the Corinthians is a manual for leading through division — not because it resolves all conflicts neatly, but because it refuses to resolve them cheaply. "Is Christ divided?" (1 Corinthians 1:13) is not a rhetorical flourish. It is the theological ground from which all conflict in the church must be assessed. The unity of the body is not sentimental. It is purchased. And splitting the church is not a minor administrative event. It is a wound in the body of Christ.

Paul is aggressive about this. He names the factionalism explicitly — "I am of Paul," "I am of Apollos," "I am of Cephas" (1 Corinthians 1:12) — and he does not manage the factions. He confronts them. He names them as incompatible with the cross — with the logic of the one who did not divide the community but gave himself for it. The cross is Paul's argument against the split. Not a program. Not a process. The theological weight of the cross.

This is the resource the pastor in a splitting church has that no management consultant can provide: the theological claim that unity costs something and is worth that cost, that the body's division is not merely a loss of institutional effectiveness but a rupture of something that belongs to Christ. That claim, preached honestly and lived at cost, is the only pastoral response that actually addresses the wound rather than managing its consequences.

---

## When a Split Is Surgery Rather Than Failure

That said: some splits are necessary. A church that splits because the pastor finally confronted a pattern of spiritual abuse, or because the gospel was being distorted to protect an unhealthy power structure, or because a teaching that was genuinely incompatible with Christian faith was being permitted to spread unchallenged — that church may be healthier after the division than before it. Not all fractures are failures. Some are surgery.

The difficulty is knowing which is which when you are inside it. The person who left is convinced they were following their conscience on a matter of principle. The person who stayed is convinced the departure was driven by pride, by a refusal of accountability, by loyalty to a charismatic leader rather than to the truth. Both sides have evidence for their reading. Both sides have genuine grievances. Both sides have probably also done some things they would do differently now.

The pastoral task in the aftermath is not to win the narrative contest. It is to lead the community that remains through grief and toward clarity — toward an honest account of what happened that does not whitewash the pastor's own failures, that grieves genuinely for the relationships and the shared history that were lost, and that names what the community learned about itself that it did not know before.

---

## Grief and Examination as the Way Forward

> Sit in the grief.

Moving forward requires two things that do not come naturally to most pastors: grief and examination.

Grief, because what was lost deserves to be mourned — the relationships, the shared history, the vision that never got to fully form. You cannot bypass this. The pastor who moves immediately to "what's next" without sitting in the weight of what was broken will eventually find that the grief surfaces sideways: in bitterness toward the people who left, in a defensive posture with newcomers who feel too similar to the ones who caused damage, in a low-grade pastoral numbness that the congregation will read as detachment.

Sit in the grief. Name it from the pulpit if appropriate. Psalms of lament were written for communities in exactly this situation — communities that had lost something, that could not understand how God was present in the loss, that needed language for the grief before they needed a path forward. The congregation that is permitted to grieve together will be capable of moving together in ways that the congregation that was rushed past the grief is not.

Examination, because the congregation that remains is watching to see whether their pastor has learned anything — whether this cost him something that will make him wiser, more careful, more genuinely humble about the limits of his own perception and authority.

The church that survives a split and asks the right questions afterward may become the strongest version of itself. The wound, examined honestly, sometimes reveals a clarity about identity and mission that the earlier, comfortable version of the church never had access to.

What were we really about? What did we compromise that we should not have? What did we defend that was worth defending? Who were we protecting when we should have been challenging, and who were we challenging when we should have been protecting?

Those questions, answered honestly in the aftermath of real damage, produce a community that knows itself more deeply than it did before. Not happier. Deeper. More sure of what it is, more clear about what it is not, more willing to pay the cost of what it is because it has already paid a cost and survived it.

It is not restoration to what was. It is something harder and more honest.

That is worth something. Sometimes it is worth everything that was lost to arrive at it.

> That is not optimism. That is resurrection faith.

Ministry continues after the worst things happen.

That is not optimism. That is resurrection faith.

The law is direct. Leviticus 19:13: *Do not defraud or rob your neighbor. Do not hold back the wages of a hired worker overnight.* Deuteronomy 24:14–15: *Do not take advantage of a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether that worker is a fellow Israelite or a foreigner residing in one of your towns. Pay them their wages each day before sunset, because they are poor and are counting on it. Otherwise they may cry to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin.* The malakh — the hired worker — is named, protected, and the specific mechanism of exploitation is described in detail: holding wages. The law does not address an abstraction. It addresses a specific practice by which employers extract additional value from workers by delaying or withholding what is owed.

Three thousand years of canonical clarity on this point, and the American church has nearly nothing to say about wage theft.

## Three Thousand Years of Canonical Clarity

Wage theft — the failure to pay workers what they have legally and contractually earned — is not a minor problem at the margins of the economy. By the most comprehensive analysis conducted, wage theft costs American workers more annually than all property crimes combined [cite — confirm]. The Economic Policy Institute estimates that minimum wage violations alone — employers paying workers less than the legal minimum — affect approximately 2.4 million workers and cost them roughly $8 billion per year [cite — confirm]. This is theft. The label is not rhetorical: it describes the taking of what belongs to another person. The employer who does not pay the agreed wage has taken something. The law says so. The Scriptures say so at greater length than they address most things the church treats as urgent.

> Wage theft is theft.

Wage theft takes several forms, each worth naming concretely. Minimum wage violations are the most straightforward: paying less than the legal minimum, either by keeping wages formally below the threshold or by stealing hours through mandatory off-clock work. Overtime violations are among the most common: requiring workers to work more than forty hours without paying the mandated overtime rate, often by misclassifying employees as managers exempt from overtime requirements. Tip theft occurs when employers skim gratuities workers earned from customers. Illegal deductions reduce a paycheck below what is owed. Off-the-clock work requirements — arriving early, staying late, working through unpaid breaks — extract labor for which the worker receives nothing.

These are not primarily the practices of small fly-by-night operations. They occur systematically in major industries: food service, retail, domestic work, agriculture, construction [cite — confirm]. The workers most affected are, with remarkable consistency, the ones who least have the power to challenge the arrangement: workers without documentation, workers who fear job loss, workers who do not know their legal rights, workers in industries where retaliation is common and reporting mechanisms are inaccessible. The geography of wage theft maps onto the geography of poverty and marginalization. It is not random. It is structural — the exploitation of vulnerability by those who have arranged the power relationship to their advantage.

## The Specific Mechanisms of Exploitation

Deuteronomy's specific instruction is illuminating. *Because they are poor and are counting on it.* The command to pay the worker before sunset is not about the ledger. It is about the person behind the labor — a person who is counting on the wage to buy food that night, who has structured their life around the expectation that what was promised would arrive, who lacks the financial cushion that makes delayed payment merely inconvenient rather than catastrophic. The law encodes a specific attentiveness to vulnerability — a recognition that the power differential between employer and worker requires protective constraint, not because employers are necessarily malicious but because the logic of accumulation, left unrestrained, tends toward the extraction of everything it can take from the people who have the least power to resist.

James 5:1–6 is one of the most severe passages in the New Testament, and it is addressed to the wealthy who have withheld the wages of their field workers: *Look! The wages you failed to pay the workers who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty.* The image is striking — the unpaid wages themselves are crying out, as if the abstracted economic harm has become a living complaint before God. James does not soften this. He is describing a specific structural sin — not personal moral failure, not sexual ethics, not any of the categories the American church has organized its moral concern around. Economic exploitation of workers. The wages held back. The luxury of the employer purchased at the cost of the worker's survival.

## Why the Pulpit Stays Silent

> I have been that pastor.

The church's near-total silence on this is not an oversight. It reflects the social composition of many congregations — specifically, the presence of business owners and managers in leadership roles, people whose institutional interests are not served by prophetic attention to wage theft. This is worth naming honestly. The congregation in which a significant portion of the giving comes from business owners is a congregation in which the pastor faces institutional pressure when addressing economic justice. The pressure is rarely explicit. It operates structurally, through the sense of what is preachable, what will be received as pastoral and what will be received as political. Most pastors absorb that pressure and preach accordingly, without ever consciously deciding to do so.

I have been that pastor. I have looked at texts like James 5 and found ways to preach about financial anxiety in general rather than wage theft in particular. I have treated the prophetic indictment as a metaphor for spiritual displacement from God rather than a concrete condemnation of a concrete practice. The shift was not dishonest — the spiritual dimension is real. But it evacuated the text of its most immediate and disturbing specificity. The workers whose wages are crying out are not metaphors. They are the two and a half million Americans who will work this week and receive less than what they are owed.

The steel-man for restraint is worth taking seriously. The argument runs that the church is not a labor regulatory agency, that wage and hour law is complex, that pastors lack the technical expertise to adjudicate specific employment claims, and that churches that wade into these waters risk politicization and congregational division. These are not frivolous concerns. The church that turns every Sunday into a policy seminar is not a church — it is a progressive advocacy organization with liturgy attached, and that is a failure mode as real as any other.

## Preaching Scripture Without Preaching Policy

But there is a distance between preaching policy and preaching Scripture. James 5 does not require the pastor to propose regulatory reform. It requires him to read the text, explain the practice it condemns, and let the congregation sit with the implication that God hears the wages being withheld from workers and will not remain silent about it indefinitely. That is preaching Scripture. The congregation can do its own discernment about what it means for how they run their businesses, how they vote, and what they support. The pastor's job is to refuse to protect them from the texts that address those questions.

The Deuteronomic vision of the economy is not market neutrality. It is a system of obligations, protections, and limits designed to prevent the concentration of power at the top from destroying the conditions of life at the bottom. The Jubilee, the sabbath year debt release, the gleaning laws, the prohibition on wage withholding — these are not a comprehensive economic plan. They are a set of structural commitments to the proposition that the poor worker is not simply a production input whose compensation should be minimized by every available means. He is a person. He is counting on it.

The wages crying out have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty. That is not a small statement. It is a claim about what God hears when the church is silent. It is a claim that the silence of the pulpit on a practice the law specifically condemns is not neutrality but complicity.

Jeremiah wrote to Israel that the way to know God is to do justice — to judge the cause of the poor and needy (Jeremiah 22:16). *Is that not what it means to know me?* The church that knows God but does not judge the cause of the worker whose wages are being stolen has not yet fully known the God it claims to serve.

Wage theft is theft. The Scriptures say so. The question for the church is whether it will say so too, or whether it will continue to let the management of institutional relationships determine which thefts are worth naming.

There is a practical dimension to this that the church has largely left unexplored. Congregations contain workers who have experienced wage theft and employers who may have practiced it. They sit in the same pews, often at some distance from one another in terms of wealth and power. The sermon that names James 5 without flinching, that reads Deuteronomy 24 as applying to the employment decisions of the people in the room — that sermon creates an uncomfortable but genuinely necessary confrontation between what people confess and how they operate during the other 167 hours of the week.

## The Confrontation the Sermon Creates

> The workers are counting on it.

The congregation that navigates that confrontation honestly — where the business owner hears the text and asks hard questions about his own practices, and where the worker who has been shorted hears the text and understands that God has heard his cry — is being formed into something resembling the community the prophets envisioned. Not comfortable. Not tidy. But alive to the same God who spoke through Amos and James and who has not changed his mind about what the wages withheld from workers represent.

The last word belongs to the text. Deuteronomy 24:15 closes with an observation that functions as a warning: *Otherwise they may cry to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin.* The cry has already gone up. The question is whether the church will speak before the verdict arrives — or whether it will wait, as it has waited on so many other prophetic questions, until the cost of silence has already been paid by the people who could least afford it.

The workers are counting on it. They were counting on it in the wilderness, at the edge of Canaan, in the first-century Jewish diaspora, and in the restaurants and fields and warehouses of America in 2026. The God who hears their cry is not waiting for the church's permission to respond. The church's choice is whether to join its voice to what God has already said, or to protect the arrangement by preaching around it.

American Christianity owns a great deal of property.

Sanctuaries with professional lighting rigs. Multi-campus facilities with commercial kitchens and gymnasium floors. Endowments, investment portfolios, media budgets. The precise aggregate is debated, but no one disputes the basic fact: the institutional church in America controls resources on a scale that would have been incomprehensible to the communities in which the New Testament was written. Those early communities shared possessions, sold property, and distributed to anyone in need (Acts 2:44–45). They were also, in most cases, economically marginal — a gathering of artisans, freedpersons, and the occasional household of modest means, meeting in borrowed rooms.

> The contrast is not a reason for guilt. It is a reason for examination.

The contrast is not a reason for guilt. It is a reason for examination.

I have sat in budget meetings where we spent more time discussing the replacement of aging pew cushions than we spent on benevolence allocations. I have done that. I have approved facilities expenditures while hearing, in the very next agenda item, about the family in the congregation facing eviction. I am not pointing from a distance. I know what it costs to maintain a building and to keep a staff and to run the programs that form the visible life of a congregation. I know those costs are real and those programs are not meaningless. I am saying they are not the whole conversation. And we have made them the whole conversation.

## What the New Testament Actually Says

The question the New Testament will not let us avoid is not "can a wealthy church be faithful?" but "what does faithfulness require of a wealthy church?" The answer the early church gave was concrete. When the Jerusalem community faced famine, the Gentile churches took up a collection — Paul describes it in 2 Corinthians 8–9 with language about equality and surplus meeting need. "Your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need" (2 Corinthians 8:14). This is not an abstract principle. It is a description of how wealth was expected to move: from where there was more, toward where there was less.

Paul sets up the collection by pointing to a theological foundation that modern stewardship campaigns typically omit. He does not say: the Jerusalem church needs your help, so give. He says: "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). The incarnation is the prototype for this movement. God's abundance moved toward human poverty. That movement is not a strategy to be imitated selectively. It is the shape of the gospel, and the church's economic life is supposed to reflect it.

John says it plainly in his first letter. "If anyone has the world's goods and sees a brother or sister in need, yet closes his heart against them, how does God's love abide in him?" (1 John 3:17). The Greek word is bios — the material conditions of living. To have bios and withhold it from someone who lacks bios is not merely stinginess. It is evidence that God's love does not actually abide in us. John intends this strongly. He is not warning about the spiritual danger of indifference. He is saying that indifference is evidence of a love that was never there.

James is the harshest voice in the New Testament canon on this question, and he is writing to people who are gathered in Jesus's name. "Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire" (James 5:2–3). He is not writing to pagan merchants who have never heard the gospel. He is writing to the assembly. The wealth he indicts is Christian wealth held while brothers and sisters lacked. The corrosion is not metaphorical. It is the physical decay of resources left in storage while people starved.

## The Historical Arc

The early church's relationship to wealth was shaped by the specific social composition of the movement. Rodney Stark has argued [cite — confirm] that early Christianity spread in part through its practice of caring for the sick, the poor, and the dying at a time when other social institutions offered nothing. During epidemics in second and third century Alexandria and Carthage [cite — confirm], Christians stayed to care for the dying when others fled. They buried the dead at personal risk. They provided material relief to people the broader Roman social network had abandoned. This was not a program. It was the logical outworking of a theology that said every person bears the image of God, and that bearing that image means you are never expendable.

By the fourth century, the settlement with Constantine changed the church's position dramatically. Imperial patronage brought resources; it also brought the temptation to use those resources to build institutions rather than to redistribute wealth toward those who lacked it. The construction of the great basilicas — monuments to the Christian empire's power and prestige — was not entirely divorced from the tradition. But it began a centuries-long negotiation between the church's prophetic instinct toward redistribution and its institutional interest in accumulation. That negotiation has never been resolved cleanly.

The Reformation addressed many things. It did not substantially address the church's relationship to accumulated wealth. Luther's theology of the two kingdoms [cite — confirm] tended to locate economic questions in the secular sphere, leaving the institutional church relatively undisturbed in its management of property. The Social Gospel movement of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries tried to reconnect the church's economic life to its prophetic tradition, but it was largely reduced to charity rather than transformed into justice. Walter Rauschenbusch, whose *A Theology for the Social Gospel* appeared in 1917 [cite — confirm], understood that personal conversion without structural change left the structures intact to produce the same misery generation after generation. The American church absorbed his concern for the poor while resisting his analysis of the systems that produced them.

## The Steel-Man Position

The honest defense of institutional church wealth deserves engagement. Institutional resources exist for institutional purposes, and a church must maintain itself to serve at all. Programs require staff. Staff require salaries. Buildings require maintenance. A congregation that gives away its operational budget has no operational capacity. The megachurch with its enormous facilities is, in many cases, genuinely serving thousands of people — running addiction recovery programs, operating food banks, providing counseling, supporting mission organizations around the world. The resources do not simply accumulate. They circulate.

This is true. And the question is not whether to have buildings or budgets. The question is proportion, and who decides what proportion is faithful. What percentage of collective resources reaches people outside the walls? What percentage is consumed by the maintenance of the institution that is supposed to serve them? When those numbers are examined honestly — and many churches resist examining them — the results often call for theological reckoning rather than institutional satisfaction.

> Budgets are confessions.

The deeper question is not operational. It is theological: what does the way we spend our money say about what we actually believe? Budgets are confessions. The line items in a church's operating budget reveal its priorities more accurately than its mission statement. When a congregation spends four times as much on facilities maintenance as on benevolence, it has made a statement. The statement may not be intentional. It may be the accumulated result of decisions made over decades, each of which seemed prudent in isolation. But the total is a testimony, and it is not the testimony of 2 Corinthians 8.

## The World's Poverty Is Not an Abstraction

Over 700 million people globally live on less than $2.15 per day [cite — confirm]. Not as a conceptual statistic but as specific people in specific places — the woman in the Nairobi slum, the child in the Central American village, the elderly man in rural India — who lack what the average American church building cost to construct. The gap between the church's accumulated resources and the world's documented need is not a natural fact. It is the result of choices about who gets access to what.

I am not arguing for a simple redistribution prescription. The relationship between institutional church resources and global poverty is complex, and naive divestment would destroy the very institutional capacity that makes sustainable engagement possible. I am arguing that the gap must be held before us, not as a cause for despair but as a spur to the kind of uncomfortable self-examination that might produce something more than it has.

Zacchaeus, when he encountered Jesus, did not wait for a systematic theology of wealth redistribution. He stood and made a declaration: half of what he owns he will give to the poor, and anyone he has defrauded he will repay fourfold (Luke 19:8). Jesus says, in response, that salvation came to this house. Not that Zacchaeus had intellectual assent to correct doctrine. That salvation came. The evidence of salvation in the house of Zacchaeus was a changed ledger.

> The audit of our own ledgers is not comfortable.

The audit of our own ledgers is not comfortable. I have not conducted it with the honesty it deserves. I have presided over institutions that accumulated while the world's poor remained poor, and I have found ways to describe that accumulation as stewardship.

That is also a theological statement. It is not the one I want to be making. But the only way to make a different one is to stop pretending the question does not exist, and to sit in the discomfort of what Paul's language about equality actually requires — not a vague aspiration toward generosity, but the concrete movement of surplus toward need, because that is the shape the gospel takes when it is not merely preached but practiced.

We cannot claim to follow Jesus through a building he wouldn't recognize while the people he specifically named as the measure of our faithfulness sleep outside.

The gap between the church's wealth and the world's poverty is not an indictment we can preach past. It is the condition in which we preach, and it will shape the credibility of everything else we say.

There is a city that the prophet Jeremiah addressed in a letter to the exiles, and the instruction he gave them was this: "Seek the shalom of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its shalom you will find your shalom" (Jeremiah 29:7). He did not say: seek the shalom of your particular congregation. He said the city. The whole city.

Most of us preach that text and then go back to competing with the church three blocks over for the same pool of transfer Christians.

---

## The Fragmentation Was Not Inevitable

The fragmentation of the church was not inevitable. The church described in the opening chapters of Acts was a single community that met across multiple households, held goods in common, and was understood by its own members and by outside observers as a coherent body rather than a collection of competing congregations (Acts 2:42-47). The development of distinct local congregations, each with its own leadership structure and gathering, emerged gradually as the movement grew and spread — and Paul's letters are largely an extended argument against the tendency of those congregations to regard their particular expression as primary and the larger body as secondary.

The Corinthian church had already begun fragmenting in Paul's lifetime: "I follow Paul," "I follow Apollos," "I follow Cephas" (1 Corinthians 1:12). His response was not to adjudicate which teacher was better but to insist that the division itself was the problem. "Is Christ divided?" (1 Corinthians 1:13). The question was rhetorical. The answer was supposed to be obvious. That the answer has become increasingly less obvious in the fifteen centuries of Western Christian history since the Constantinian settlement is one of the most significant failures of the movement.

We have, in many American cities, a situation that would have been unrecognizable to the Corinthian community: dozens or hundreds of congregations within a few square miles, most of them unknown to each other, almost none of them sharing resources, many of them quietly regarding each other as rivals. The language we use to describe this — the "local church model," the "autonomy of the congregation," the "sovereignty of the individual expression" — has a theological vocabulary that obscures what it often actually is: institutional tribalism.

---

## The Competition No One Acknowledges

> I have done this.

I have done this. The competition is real, and it is almost never acknowledged honestly. Pastors will talk about the kingdom while keeping meticulous track of who left their church to attend the newer one with the better sound system. We dress it in the language of stewardship — we are responsible for our own flock — and there is truth in that. But the stewardship argument has a way of becoming cover for the thing it is covering: the provincialism of the local church at the expense of the body of Christ in a given place.

The congregation does not belong to the pastor. The city does not belong to any congregation. The church in a given place is one thing — one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one baptism, one God and Father of all (Ephesians 4:4-6) — expressed in multiple locations, multiple traditions, multiple worship styles, multiple languages and ethnicities. Until pastors believe that at the level of their calendars, it remains a pious idea.

---

At minimum, genuine city-wide ecclesiology looks like the pastors of that city knowing each other. Not performing unity at a ministerial breakfast while quietly regarding each other as competitors. Actually knowing each other — the struggles, the failures, the things that keep them awake at three in the morning. The referral network, the resource-sharing, the collaborative response to the neighborhood's needs — all of that depends on relationships that go deeper than the professional courtesy we typically extend to each other at association meetings.

But this is not primarily strategic. It is theological. The pastor who regards himself as a co-laborer in a single city-wide mission will make different decisions than the pastor who regards himself as the CEO of a rival enterprise. The former will celebrate when the church down the street baptizes thirty people. The latter will wonder what that does to the attendance projections for September.

At least once a year, the theological conviction should be made visible to the congregation.

## Making the One Body Visible

A city-wide gathering — churches from different traditions, different demographics, different theological emphases, meeting in a park or an arena or the largest sanctuary that will hold them — does something that no individual congregation can do alone. It makes visible what is otherwise invisible: that the church in this city is one thing, larger than any of its expressions, more durable than any single pastor's tenure, accountable to a story that began before any of us arrived and will continue after all of us have gone.

The formation that happens in that gathering is not easily replicated by preaching. When the people in your congregation see their pastor standing alongside the pastor of the historically Black church across town and the pastor of the Latino congregation meeting in the strip mall and the pastor of the Korean congregation in the office park, and they worship together to music that is not what any of them expected, something shifts in how they understand the body of Christ. They see that the Spirit is not confined to their worship style. That the kingdom extends beyond the zip code they drive to on Sunday morning. That the church they belong to is considerably larger than the building they attend.

---

## Answering the Practical Objections

The practical objections are real. Theology divides — Reformed and Pentecostal, Baptist and Methodist, churches that practice closed communion and churches with open tables. Logistics are difficult. Egos are involved. Somebody will not want to share a stage with somebody else, and the reasons will be dressed in doctrinal language while being mostly personal.

The theological objection deserves a direct response: genuine unity does not require doctrinal uniformity. It requires the acknowledgment of a common Lord. Paul's argument in Ephesians 4 is precisely that the gifts of the Spirit are distributed across the body, which means that no single congregation possesses all of them, and a church that operates as though it does is impoverishing itself. The Reformed congregation has things to learn from the Pentecostal congregation, and vice versa. The historically Black church has been formed by centuries of suffering and survival that the white suburban church has not experienced, and that formation produces a depth of faith that the comfortable church desperately needs. The gathering is not an exercise in theological compromise. It is an exercise in recognizing what the body of Christ actually looks like when it is not divided by institutional convenience.

The logistical objection is real, and the answer is: do it anyway. The difficulty of the logistics is not an argument against the gathering; it is part of the work. Every good thing requires effort, and the congregation that sees its pastor do hard work for the sake of the city rather than the sake of the brand learns something about ministry that sermons cannot teach.

I understand all the objections. I have been the pastor who found reasons not to show up. I have protected the Sunday morning program at the expense of the city-wide relationship. I have told myself it was stewardship and known, somewhere below the rationalizations, that it was something smaller.

---

The Reformation, for all its genuine theological recovery, fractured the Western church into pieces that have been multiplying ever since. There are an estimated 45,000 Protestant denominations worldwide [cite — confirm]. In any given mid-sized American city, you can find congregations that share the same confession of faith and have not shared a pulpit in decades because of a church split in 1987 over carpet color or staff compensation or a particular interpretation of a secondary doctrine. The divisions that divide the church in a given city are almost never about the things that matter most. They are about the things that matter least, and they have calcified into institutional identities that we now treat as load-bearing walls.

They are not load-bearing walls. They are partitions.

## Partitions, Not Load-Bearing Walls

> They are not load-bearing walls. They are partitions.

Jeremiah sent his letter to people who wanted to go home — who regarded exile as an interruption of their real life in their real city. He told them instead to plant gardens, build houses, raise families, and pray for the city they were in (Jeremiah 29:5-7). The instruction presupposes that they would be there long enough for the planting to matter.

We have been planted in this city. The question is whether we are praying for it together, or whether we are each praying for our own corner of it and calling that faithfulness.

---

> That is witness. Not the programmatic kind. The kind that requires something to actually be true.

What does a city-wide gathering produce in the long run? Not unity as the absence of disagreement — that is not a New Testament vision of anything. What it produces is visibility. The watching city sees a church that is larger and more diverse than any single congregation. The watching city sees people who cross ethnic, economic, and denominational lines because they believe they serve a Lord whose body does not observe those lines. The watching city — which has been, in many cases, watching the church argue about itself for a generation — sees something that it cannot fully account for.

That is witness. Not the programmatic kind. The kind that requires something to actually be true.

The early church was known for it. Tertullian's observation — "see how they love one another" [cite — confirm] — was not a compliment about their worship programming. It was an observation about a community that defied the social logic of the ancient world, a community in which slave and free, Jew and Greek, male and female sat at the same table and called each other family.

That is the church the city needs. It is assembled not building by building but together, at least once a year, long enough for the people in the seats to see what they belong to.

Long enough to remember that it is bigger than what they can see from where they usually sit.

The number is contested but the direction is not. Conservative projections estimate that by mid-century, climate displacement — people forced from their homes by rising seas, desertification, catastrophic flooding, and the collapse of agricultural systems — will reach into the hundreds of millions. [cite — confirm] The more severe scenarios project figures that exceed any refugee crisis in recorded human history. These are not primarily projections about the distant future. They are projections about people who are children now, who will be adults when the displacement arrives, and who will be looking for somewhere to go.

The church in the Global North will be asked a question it has not prepared for. How that question is answered will say something definitive about what the church actually believes about the image of God in the bodies of people it has never met.

## The Geography of Culpability

Begin with the geography of culpability. The nations most responsible for the accumulated carbon emissions that are driving the climatic disruptions — primarily the industrial economies of North America, Western Europe, and historically the United Kingdom — are not the nations that will absorb the primary consequences. The nations most exposed to sea-level rise, desertification, and agricultural collapse are predominantly in South Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific Islands. Bangladesh, home to approximately 170 million people, stands to lose a significant percentage of its land area to flooding within decades. [cite — confirm] The Pacific Island nations — Kiribati, Tuvalu, the Marshall Islands — are not facing the risk of inconvenience. They are facing the termination of national existence. Their people, bearing the image of God, are being displaced by a crisis they did not cause, originating in economic patterns primarily developed and maintained by people in countries that will largely be insulated from the worst effects.

This is not a natural disaster in the morally simple sense. Natural disasters — earthquakes, volcanic eruptions — fall outside human causation. Climate displacement is a different category. It is the accumulation of consequences from choices made by identifiable actors over identifiable periods of time, choices that benefited some populations enormously while imposing costs primarily on others. The theological term for the transfer of costs from those who benefit to those who do not is injustice. It is the same category the prophets used when they condemned the wealthy in Amos's Israel for "selling the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals" (Amos 2:6). The mechanism is different. The structure is the same.

## The Law of the Stranger

> The mechanism is different. The structure is the same.

The Mosaic law is explicit about the stranger. "You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt" (Leviticus 19:34). The command is grounded in historical experience — Israel knew displacement, knew the vulnerability of living in someone else's land, and was therefore required to carry that knowledge into its treatment of those who arrived in their territory. The stranger was not a threat to be managed. He was a neighbor to be welcomed, a person with legal standing in the covenant community, someone whose vulnerability created a corresponding obligation in those with the stability and resources to help.

Deuteronomy returns to this command repeatedly. "He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing. Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 10:18–19). The love of the sojourner is not a secondary ethic derived from a more primary principle. It is placed alongside the justice of God for the fatherless and the widow as a core expression of covenantal faithfulness.

In the New Testament, Jesus's parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31–46) names the welcome of the stranger as one of the criteria of final judgment. "I was a stranger and you welcomed me" (Matthew 25:35). The Greek word for stranger — *xenos* — is the root of xenophobia, the fear of the stranger. Jesus is not addressing a secondary pastoral concern here. He is placing the welcome of the stranger at the center of the eschatological reckoning.

## The Climate Refugee as the Sojourner of Our Century

The climate refugee is the sojourner of the twenty-first century. He arrives not because of war, though climate displacement frequently produces conflict as it goes. He arrives because the conditions that made his land habitable have been altered by forces outside his control. He brings children. He carries documents that may or may not be recognized. He speaks a language that is not the language of the border he crosses. He is, in many cases, a Christian — the church in Bangladesh, in the Philippines, in sub-Saharan Africa is alive, vibrant, and significantly larger per capita than many of the churches in the wealthy nations that will be asked to receive the displaced. The climate refugee is not an abstraction. He is a brother in many cases, a neighbor in all cases, and a person carrying the image of God in all cases.

## The Argument for Borders and Its Limits

The counter-argument that the church most frequently hears from its political culture goes like this: nations have the right to control their borders, and unlimited migration is not a sustainable response to climate displacement. There are questions of national sovereignty, cultural capacity, economic integration, and security that cannot simply be dissolved by theological appeal. This is not an argument without content. Nations do have legitimate interests in how they manage migration. The practical questions of absorbing displaced populations are real. The argument deserves a hearing rather than dismissal.

But the argument is regularly deployed to justify not a measured response but no response — to treat the scale of the problem as an excuse for avoiding the obligation entirely. The Christian tradition does not permit this move. The obligation to the sojourner is not contingent on whether the sojourner's arrival is convenient. It is not suspended when the numbers are large. The law that required Israel to welcome the stranger did not contain an exception clause for high-volume displacement. The sheep and the goats parable does not offer a threshold above which the welcome of the stranger becomes optional.

## What the Church Can Actually Do

> The climate refugee is the sojourner of the twenty-first century.

What the church can do is not nothing. In the immediate term, the congregation that takes this seriously will support the organizations that are already working with climate-displaced communities — the advocacy organizations pushing for legal frameworks that recognize climate displacement as a category deserving protection under international law, the direct service organizations providing material support to communities currently in transition, the churches in affected regions that need material solidarity from the global communion. [cite — confirm]

In the medium term, the congregation has a formational responsibility: to produce members whose understanding of the climate crisis includes its justice dimensions, who know the geography of culpability and do not pretend it is morally neutral, who can hold the conversation about borders and belonging without reducing the image of God in the displaced person to a political inconvenience. Preaching that handles Leviticus 19 and Deuteronomy 10 and Matthew 25 as live texts — not as historical artifacts but as claims on the present — forms that congregation.

In the longer term, the question of how wealthy-nation churches engage their own political processes on behalf of climate action and climate refugees is unavoidable. It is, again, not a question about partisan alignment. It is a question about whether the people in the pews understand that their comfort is not theologically neutral, that the carbon economy that has funded their prosperity has a balance sheet that runs in the direction of Bangladesh and the Pacific, and that the people on the debit side of that balance sheet are children of God.

There will be, in the coming decades, more people displaced by climate than by any other cause in human history. The church will be present in both the countries of origin and the countries of destination. Whether the global body of Christ is a community of genuine solidarity across those borders, or a set of nationally bounded institutions that protect their own and manage the arrival of everyone else, will be one of the defining testimonies of twenty-first century Christianity.

The early church was itself a community of displaced people. The letter of 1 Peter opens by addressing the recipients as "elect exiles of the Dispersion" (1 Peter 1:1) — people scattered across provinces far from home, holding their identity and their hope in a kingdom that had not yet fully arrived. The posture of the church toward the displaced is therefore not charity from the settled toward the uprooted. It is recognition: we are, in the deepest sense, the same kind of people. The difference is degree, not kind. The Christian who has spent thirty years in the same house on the same street and the climate refugee who has lost both hold the same ultimate address — a city "whose designer and builder is God" (Hebrews 11:10). That shared eschatological citizenship is the deepest basis for the welcome the stranger requires.

> Do you know his name? Do you have room?

The stranger at the gate is coming. He is already here in some communities and arriving in others. The question that the text has always asked has not changed.

Do you know his name? Do you have room?

In 1934, Karl Barth gathered with other German pastors at Barmen and produced the Barmen Declaration — a theological document that crossed Lutheran and Reformed lines to say a single clear thing: Jesus Christ alone is Lord, and the German church would not confess the Nazi state as a second source of revelation alongside Scripture.

The Confessing Church that emerged from Barmen was not uniform. The men who signed that declaration disagreed with each other on baptism, on church governance, on eucharistic theology. They had been separated by four centuries of institutional division rooted in the bitterest conflicts the Reformation produced. What they discovered at Barmen was that when the essential thing is under attack, the things that divide become secondary not by being dismissed but by being properly ordered. The confession that Jesus is Lord is prior to the disagreement about how baptism should be administered. Crisis clarified the hierarchy.

> I want that clarity without requiring crisis to produce it.

I want that clarity without requiring crisis to produce it.

## The History We Are Inside

Denominationalism as we know it in America has a specific history, and that history is worth knowing because it explains what we are actually navigating. The great denominational divisions of Western Christianity — Catholic and Protestant at the Reformation, Lutheran and Reformed within Protestantism, Anglican and Nonconformist in England, the Baptist and Presbyterian splits in America, the Methodist movement under Wesley — were not primarily about personal preference or institutional competition. They were about genuine theological disagreements that people were willing to die over.

The question of how a sinner is justified before God — by faith alone, through the imputed righteousness of Christ, or by grace working through the sacramental system of the church — was not a minor adjustment. People were burned at Smithfield over it. The question of whether infants could receive the covenant sign of baptism, or whether baptism belonged only to those who confessed faith, divided communities that shared Scripture, shared prayer, and shared the Lord's table. John Calvin and Ulrich Zwingli disagreed so sharply about the nature of the Eucharist at the Marburg Colloquy of 1529 [cite — confirm] that they could not reach agreement, and their traditions have not shared the table since.

I do not say this to minimize the differences. I say it because the differences are real and the history is real and the communities that formed around those differences built rich theological traditions that have formed generations of Christians into genuine faith. The Baptist insistence on believer's baptism is not stubbornness. It is a theology of the gathered community, a conviction about conversion and covenant, that has produced some of the most vigorous missionary movements in Christian history. The Reformed tradition's insistence on God's sovereignty in salvation is not fatalism. It is a posture of radical humility before a God who is not domesticated by human decision. These are not trivial.

## What the Moment Requires

We are in a post-Christendom moment in the West. The social conditions that made denominational distinctiveness feel like the primary issue have shifted significantly. When Christianity was the default cultural religion — what Robert Bellah called the civil religion of American public life [cite — confirm] — the differences between denominations functioned like the differences between competing restaurants on the same block: you chose based on preference, and the competition was the relevant category. When Christianity becomes a minority position in a secular culture, the picture changes.

The relevant category is no longer the differences between Christian communities. It is the shared claim that the risen Christ is Lord of creation — a claim that the culture around us finds increasingly implausible. The New Atheism of the early twenty-first century, the decline of institutional religion documented by every major sociological survey since 2008 [cite — confirm], the formation of the largest religious demographic in American history — the Nones, who are not atheists but are not Christians either — these are not peripheral data points. They describe the cultural air the church now breathes.

> I have done this, in fits and starts, in the communities where I have served.

Against that backdrop, the energy Christians spend fighting each other over secondary questions looks, from the outside, like a family arguing about the paint color while the house burns. I understand why the paint color matters. I am not dismissing the real theological differences between traditions. I am questioning whether the posture of competition and suspicion between Christian communities is the appropriate posture for this moment.

## What Paul Actually Said

Paul's letter to the Ephesians insists that the church's unity is not merely organizational aspiration. It is theological reality: "one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to one hope when you were called — one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all" (Ephesians 4:4–6). The unity exists. The question is whether we are willing to practice it visibly rather than confining it to the level of doctrine while the actual communities remain in separate corners.

The high priestly prayer of John 17 makes the stakes explicit: "that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me" (v. 21). The visible unity of the church is, on this account, not primarily an intra-church concern. It is a missional one. It is the ground of the world's belief. When the church is visibly fractured, the message that the risen Christ has reconciled all things to God is undermined at the level of its primary evidence. We are claiming a reconciliation we have not demonstrated.

That is a serious problem.

## What Collaboration Actually Looks Like

The practical form of collaboration does not require doctrinal capitulation. I do not need to pretend the differences between baptistic and paedobaptist traditions do not exist. I do not need to behave as if ecclesiology is irrelevant. What I can do is show up in the city where I serve alongside other pastors who hold Christ as Lord, work together on the needs of the community neither of us can address alone, and model to the watching city that the confession we share is more determinative than the practices that divide us.

I have done this, in fits and starts, in the communities where I have served. What I have found is that the collaboration does not flatten distinctiveness. It clarifies it. When I am working alongside a pastor whose tradition handles things differently than mine, I understand my own tradition more precisely — what I actually believe about it, what I hold firmly and what I hold loosely, and where the genuine disagreements lie. The encounter with difference is instructive rather than threatening, provided I am secure enough in my own convictions not to feel them challenged by contact with someone else's.

The Pastors Connection Network I lead is built on precisely this premise: that pastors from genuinely different theological traditions can share the burdens of ministry, support each other in the loneliness of leadership, and become more effective in their specific contexts by learning from people whose contexts are different. The network is not a doctrinal homogenization project. It is a community of practice built on the confession that precedes the differences — that Jesus is Lord, that the church exists for mission, that pastoral ministry is both a calling and a weight that no one carries well alone.

## The Steel-Man Objection

The objection worth taking seriously is this: genuine theological disagreements are not trivial, and collaboration across genuine disagreement can blur the distinctions in ways that eventually harm the communities involved. If I am collaborating with a pastor whose soteriology I believe is defective, am I not implicitly validating a distortion of the gospel? Is the unity I am performing misleading people about what actually divides these traditions?

This is a serious concern. It is not, however, an argument against collaboration. It is an argument for honesty within collaboration — for being clear about what you share, what you do not share, and why the distinction matters in each context. The Barmen Declaration did not pretend that Lutherans and Reformed had resolved their differences. It stated, clearly and publicly, the ground on which they could stand together, and distinguished that ground from the ground that remained contested. That is the model. Not pretended agreement. Honest identification of what is prior.

The church that is too afraid of other traditions to work alongside them has confused the tradition for the Lord of the tradition. It has made the container the content. And that confusion is its own kind of theological error — arguably a more dangerous one than the doctrinal differences it is trying to protect against, because it has placed institutional self-preservation above the mission for which the institution exists.

## What the City Is Watching

There is a city outside our buildings full of people who find the claim of the gospel implausible. They find it implausible for many reasons — intellectual, moral, experiential. But one of the reasons, less often acknowledged, is the visible contradiction between the message of reconciliation and the reality of a church that cannot appear in the same room as its nearest theological neighbors.

A unified witness — different expressions of the same fundamental confession, working together on the actual needs of the actual city — is at least a more interesting argument. It demonstrates something. It says: whatever we disagree about, we agree that the kingdom of God matters more than institutional protection, and we are willing to spend ourselves together in its service.

Barth and his colleagues understood this. Crisis taught them. The crisis concentrated their attention on what was actually primary and forced the secondary into its proper place.

> We can decide, before the house is burning, that the Lord of the house is worth more than the paint color.

We do not have to wait for crisis to learn what they learned. We can do the harder work of making that judgment in ordinary time, out of theological conviction rather than emergency. We can decide, before the house is burning, that the Lord of the house is worth more than the paint color.

That decision produces a different kind of church. A different kind of city. A witness that at least has the possibility of being heard.

I am still learning to make it consistently. The denominational instincts are deep. But I have seen enough of what the alternative produces — a church too busy protecting its distinctives to serve its neighbors — to know that the learning is worth it.

The color-blindness argument has a sound theological instinct at its center: that every human being bears the image of God and that racial categories are not ultimate. In the Kingdom of God, Paul announces, there is neither Jew nor Greek (Galatians 3:28). The eschatological vision of Revelation 7 shows the redeemed gathered from every tribe and language and people and nation. The church that knows this theology should not treat people differently on the basis of race.

This is true. It does not mean color-blindness is a virtue.

## The Eschatological Reality and the Present One

The error is confusing the eschatological reality with the present one. Galatians 3:28 is a declaration about what is true in Christ — about the identity that baptism confers and the standing that grace creates. It is not a sociological description of the present world. In the present world, racial categories are real because their effects are real. A theology that claims not to see race does not thereby undo the effects of seeing it for four centuries.

Consider what color-blindness actually accomplishes in practice. It enables the person who claims it to skip the question of what historical racial harm has produced in the present. If I do not see race, I do not see the gap in wealth, the gap in health outcomes, the gap in educational opportunity, the gap in incarceration rates that runs along racial lines in every major American city [cite — confirm]. I do not see these things not because they are invisible but because I have adopted an ideology that tells me not to look.

## The History Color-Blindness Refuses to See

> This is true. It does not mean color-blindness is a virtue.

To understand what this costs, you need the history. The legal apparatus of American racial hierarchy — chattel slavery, the Dred Scott decision, the Black Codes, Jim Crow, redlining — did not end in a moment. Redlining, the federal practice of denying mortgage loans and insurance to residents of predominantly Black neighborhoods, was codified by the Home Owners' Loan Corporation beginning in the 1930s and enforced by policy and practice for decades [cite — confirm]. The effect was to systematically exclude Black families from the primary wealth-building mechanism available to postwar American households: homeownership. That wealth gap has compounded across generations. The color-blind ideology that says "I don't see race" does not undo a single generation of compounded exclusion. It merely refuses to see the evidence.

The prophets did not avert their eyes from the specific. Amos named the specific transaction in which the poor were sold: a pair of sandals (Amos 2:6). Isaiah named the specific people being crushed: the widows, the orphans, the ones without advocates in the gate (Isaiah 1:17). Jeremiah named the specific institution that was failing: the temple establishment that cried "peace, peace, when there is no peace" (Jeremiah 6:14). Prophetic vision is always particular. It sees the thing that is happening, names it, and refuses the comfortable abstraction that makes it invisible.

Color-blindness is a comfortable abstraction. It offers the emotional benefit of being a person who transcends racial division without requiring any engagement with the actual conditions that racial division has created. It is the theological equivalent of saying "I don't see poverty" as a way of not seeing the poor.

## Prophetic Vision Is Always Particular

I grew up in contexts where color-blindness was considered the Christian position — where saying "I judge people by the content of their character, not the color of their skin" (invoking King's phrase, always out of context) was treated as the fullness of racial ethics. Martin Luther King Jr. was speaking in that sentence about a future hope, not a present description. He was naming a destination, not claiming to have arrived. To invoke that phrase as a reason not to examine the present is to conscript King into the defense of an arrangement he spent his life opposing. I held that misreading long past the point where I should have known better. It was easier. It did not require me to look at specific things. It gave me a clear conscience without giving me an examined one.

The counter-position deserves to be stated honestly: those who embrace color-blindness often argue that *naming* race perpetuates racial thinking — that the solution to a history of racial categorization is to stop categorizing racially, and that those who insist on naming race are themselves prolonging the problem. There is something in this. A politics of identity can, in certain forms, deepen division by making every interaction a performance of group allegiance. The concern is not invented.

But the response is not to move from racial obsession to racial blindness. Both positions have in common the refusal to look clearly. Racial obsession sees only race; racial blindness sees nothing but pretends that is virtue. What the prophetic tradition asks for is something different: the willingness to see what is actually there, with precision, without the distortion of either extreme. To see that a person is a full human being made in the image of God — and also to see that this particular person has been marked by a specific history, has inherited specific conditions, has experienced specific treatment because of a characteristic that society has invested with enormous and often destructive power. Both truths at once. Neither canceling the other.

## Seeing Both Truths at Once

The Revelation 7 vision of every tribe and nation and tongue worshiping together is not a vision of a world where difference has been erased. It is a vision of a world where difference has been honored within unity — where the specific history and culture and language of each people is present and celebrated in the worship of a God who made all of them and redeemed all of them. The nations do not disappear. They are brought in, each bearing their distinctiveness into the presence of God. John Stott observed that the preserved diversity of the nations in Revelation is not an accident of the text but a theological statement: the redeemed community is not homogeneous [cite — confirm]. God does not eliminate what he has made. He redeems it.

Taking the Revelation vision seriously means caring about the specific history that has shaped each particular people — including the history of how some peoples have treated others, and the damage that history has left. You cannot celebrate the healing without naming the wound. You cannot celebrate the gathering of the nations without accounting for how some nations have been treated by others.

The practical consequence for the local church is this: a congregation that claims color-blindness but whose leadership, programming, liturgy, and institutional culture reflect only one racial heritage is not actually blind. It is ignoring what everyone can see. And the people whose heritage is not represented — whose hymnody is absent, whose theological tradition is not engaged, whose particular history of suffering is not acknowledged — are not deceived by the language. They know what they are not seeing. The color-blind declaration lands among them as a request to be invisible.

## How Liturgy Forms a Congregation's Sight

> Color-blindness is a comfortable abstraction.

James K.A. Smith argues, following Augustine, that the practices of a community shape what its members love before they know they love it — that liturgy and habit form the affections long before the intellect catches up [cite — confirm]. The implication for racial formation in the church is uncomfortable: a congregation that has never sung a song from the Black church tradition, that has never heard the theological account that emerged from under the weight of the Middle Passage, that has never sat under the pastoral witness of someone who carries that inheritance — that congregation has been formed in a particular direction whether it acknowledges it or not. Its color-blindness is not neutral. It has a shape.

The church that claims to see no color is not practicing the eschatological vision. It is practicing avoidance. The eschatological vision requires seeing clearly enough to name the gap between where we are and where God is taking us — and then doing the actual work of closing that gap, which requires seeing exactly what color-blindness refuses to see.

Here is what seeing requires in practical terms. It requires learning the history you were not taught — not as guilt-acquisition but as the same kind of intellectual honesty you would bring to any other subject where your initial formation was incomplete. The history of the Black church in America, for instance, is one of the most theologically rich traditions in the Christian story: a community that read the Exodus with their own bodies, that sang of freedom in coded language under a system that forbade literacy, that produced theologians and preachers of extraordinary depth precisely because their faith had to bear weight that the comfortable church never encountered. Howard Thurman's *Jesus and the Disinherited* (1949) was written for people who lived "with their backs against the wall" — people for whom the gospel had to mean something practical or it meant nothing [cite — confirm]. The white church that has never engaged that tradition has a gap in its theological education, not just its social awareness.

It also requires a different kind of listening than most predominantly white congregations have practiced. Not the listening that receives another community's experience as evidence to be weighed before reaching your own conclusions, but the listening that holds the speaker's testimony as primary data — that says: you have access to your experience in a way that I do not, and I need to hear it before I can respond faithfully. Miroslav Volf's work on embrace and exclusion argues that genuine reconciliation requires "the will to give space in oneself to the other" — to allow the other's reality to enter and reshape your perception before moving to response [cite — confirm]. This is not comfortable. It was not designed to be comfortable.

To see clearly is not the same as to treat people unjustly on the basis of race. Seeing clearly is the precondition of justice, not its enemy.

> The first act of repair is always the same.

The first act of repair is always the same. You stop pretending you cannot see. You look at what is actually there. You let what you see make its demands on you.

That sequence is not the full work. But nothing else begins without it.

The comfortable Christian position in a culture with genuine injustice is neither endorsement nor active resistance. It is something more subtle and more convenient: the claim of non-involvement, the insistence that the church is above the political fray, the cultivation of a carefully maintained neutrality that allows the institution to maintain its relationships with all sides while making no enemies and taking no risks.

We have a word for what we think that is. We call it innocence. Scripture calls it something else.

It calls it complicity. And complicity is not innocence.

## The Text That Takes Away the Exit

We badly want there to be a safe third option between doing wrong and paying the cost of doing right — a place where we can keep our hands clean by keeping them in our pockets. The Bible keeps refusing to grant it. Proverbs 24:10-12 is direct: "If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small. Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those stumbling to the slaughter. If you say, 'Behold, we did not know this' — does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who keeps watch over your soul know it, and will he not repay man according to his work?"

Notice what the text anticipates. It does not assume that the bystander is malicious. It assumes that the bystander will have an excuse — we did not know, we were not informed, the situation was unclear, we stayed out of it to keep the peace. The text dismisses the excuse before it is offered. The God who weighs hearts is not fooled by a silence we have arranged in order to remain comfortable.

> There is no clean way to walk past the man in the ditch.

This is the priest and the Levite on the Jericho road (Luke 10:30-37). They did not beat the man. They did not rob him. They did nothing at all — they saw him in the ditch and passed by on the other side — and Jesus tells the story precisely so that their nothing becomes the sin. The Samaritan is the neighbor not because he avoided causing harm but because he absorbed cost. He stopped. He bound the wounds. He brought the man to the inn. He paid out of his own resources and promised to pay more. The parable was constructed to remove the comfortable middle position. There is no clean way to walk past the man in the ditch.

## The Historical Arc

This is not a new theological problem. The prophets of Israel were addressing it in the eighth century before Christ. Amos, writing during the reign of Jeroboam II in a period of Israeli prosperity, was not primarily angry at the oppressors. He was angry at the religious community that maintained its worship life while the economic arrangements of the society were grinding the poor into the ground, and said nothing, and thought that its continued temple attendance was innocence. "I hate, I despise your feasts, and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies" (Amos 5:21). The God who says that is not drawing a distinction between the evil and the neutral. He is collapsing the distinction. The worship that continues while injustice continues is not neutral. It is, in God's accounting, hateful.

The same logic appears in Isaiah 1, where the opening chapter of the whole book consists of God rejecting the religious performance of a community that has neglected the widow, the orphan, and the oppressed: "Your hands are full of blood" (Isaiah 1:15). The hands were full of blood not because the worshippers had been violent. They had been merely absent. They had performed the right rituals while the society they inhabited crushed the people God had commanded them to protect. The prophet calls it blood.

Ezekiel 33 uses the image of the watchman who sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet. The watchman does not invite the sword. He does not sharpen it. He merely fails to warn, and the text holds him responsible for the deaths that follow. Silence in the face of a known danger is not neutrality. It is complicity. The text says so.

## The Mechanism Worth Understanding

Here is how good people end up complicit without ever deciding to be. Injustice does not generally require the cooperation of the cruel. It requires only the silence of the decent. The systems that have sustained the greatest human suffering throughout history were not primarily built on the energy of the malicious. They were sustained by the routine non-participation of people who privately found the situation troubling but publicly kept their discomfort to themselves.

In the antebellum American South, the slave economy did not need every white Southerner to be a slaveholder. It needed a sufficient number of non-slaveholding whites to find the arrangement acceptable enough that they would not disrupt it. It needed the churches to stay focused on personal piety and eternity. It needed the reasonable people to believe that the question was too complicated for a simple answer, that speaking up would only make things worse, that they were protecting their family by keeping their heads down. That reasoning was offered in real time, by real people, many of whom were churchgoing Christians with sincere faith [cite — confirm general pattern; specific examples need verification]. And the silence was as much a structural support for the institution as the chains were.

> Injustice does not generally require the cooperation of the cruel. It requires only the silence of the decent.

I have done this. I have looked at situations where the suffering of a specific category of people was visible and the cost of saying something was real, and I have calculated that cost and decided I could not afford it. I have dressed the calculation in theological language — I don't want to be reactionary, I want to think carefully before I speak, the church should be careful about political entanglements — and the language was not entirely wrong, but it was not entirely honest either. The honest name for most of my carefully maintained neutrality was not prudence. It was self-protection.

This is a confession before it is a critique.

## The Counter-Position Answered

The danger on the other side is real and requires honest engagement. A church that makes itself the vehicle for every political grievance — that treats every issue as the hill on which the witness must be planted, that conflates the Gospel with a particular political coalition, that burns its credibility on fights that have little to do with the cross — will eventually lose the ability to speak at all, because the credibility that makes speech heard will be gone.

That danger is real. But the solution to that danger is not silence on everything. It is discernment about what the Gospel actually requires speech about. And there is a category of human suffering — particularly the suffering of those the Scripture specifically identifies as the objects of God's special concern, the poor, the orphan, the widow, the stranger, the imprisoned — where the church's silence is not careful neutrality. It is the failure of the witness.

The distinction is worth preserving: not every political question is a Gospel question, but some political questions are Gospel questions, and the ones that involve the dignity and survival of the vulnerable almost always are. The church that cannot tell the difference between the two, that lumps all public questions into "political" and therefore out-of-bounds, has made a theological decision while pretending to make no decision at all. The decision it has made is to let the present arrangements stand by declining to challenge them.

## What the Witness Costs

The world is not primarily persuaded or repelled by the church's words. It watches what the church will risk. A church that always finds a reason to stay out of it — that is reliably absent from the ditch, that never says anything that might cost it a relationship or a budget line or an uncomfortable conversation — teaches the watching world that the Gospel is a private comfort with no claim on public suffering. The world is right to find that unconvincing.

The witness of the early church was not primarily its correct theology, though the theology was correct. It was the visible practice of a community that absorbed cost for others. They took in the abandoned infants left to die on the hillsides outside Roman cities. They buried the dead during the plague when no one else would. They shared resources across the lines that the surrounding culture considered fixed. The watching world did not say: what an interesting set of doctrines. It said: look how they love — and the love was visible precisely because it cost something.

> It watches what the church will risk.
