The requirement is not institutional complexity. It is personal honesty in one or two relationships. That honesty is harder than it sounds, because the pastoral vocation provides almost unlimited cover for avoidance. You can be busy. You can be necessary. You can be always about to have time for the conversation that would actually matter. The busyness is real. It does not justify the avoidance.

What makes accountability work is not the structure. It is the willingness to be known. And that willingness is exactly what isolation trains out of you over time. The longer you protect the assembled version, the more the protection itself becomes your identity, and the less capable you are of offering the real version to anyone who might hold it well.

## The Witness Requires Proximity

Paul's description of his own ministry in 2 Corinthians is striking for how personal it is — how much of his own weakness, fear, and failure he is willing to name and attribute to the shaping work of God. "We are hard pressed on every side, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair" (2 Corinthians 4:8). The perplexity is admitted. The despair is resisted. Both are on the table. This is not performed vulnerability in the service of relatability. It is genuine disclosure in the service of theological argument: that the treasure in the clay jar is God's power, not ours, and the only way to make that clear is to be honest about the jar.

The pastor who presents only strength has obscured the very thing his ministry is supposed to demonstrate: that God's sufficiency works through human insufficiency, that grace operates where need is admitted, that the power is not ours to perform but ours to receive.

The way back from isolation is almost always through the thing you least want to say out loud. That sentence you have been practicing in your head but have not said to anyone. That failure you have been explaining away to yourself. That fear beneath the confidence.

Say it to someone. The right someone.

Everything else — the drift, the distortion, the danger — begins to lose its hold at the moment of honest speech.

That is not therapeutic technique. That is confession. The tradition has always known it was the beginning of healing.

## The Beginning of Healing

The fourth-century desert fathers developed a practice they called *exagoreusis* — the disclosure of thoughts to a trusted elder, not as formal sacramental confession but as the regular practice of bringing what was hidden into the light [cite — confirm]. The purpose was not absolution but clarity: the thought that is spoken loses much of its power. The sin that is named can be addressed. The temptation that remains secret grows in the darkness. What the monks discovered in the Egyptian wilderness — that isolation was spiritually lethal, that the soul required a witness — has been confirmed in every pastoral era since, and in the accumulating evidence of ministerial collapse in our own.

The pastor who has built a life without genuine accountability has not achieved freedom. He has achieved danger. The pastoral platform that insulates him from honest feedback has not given him authority. It has removed the safeguard that honest feedback provides against the self-deceptions that accumulate in isolated powerful men.

> It is that they share nothing in private.

The size of the platform matters here, and not in the way success culture suggests. The larger the congregation, the more the pastor's words are received without challenge, the more his interpretations go unchecked, the more his behavior is explained away by people whose institutional survival depends on his success. The small-church pastor who is known by everyone in the building has accidental accountability that the megachurch pastor must deliberately construct. The small church's limits are also, in this respect, its protection.

Find the someone who tells you the truth. Not the someone who manages you. Not the someone who needs you to succeed. The someone who loves you enough to say the thing that might cost them access to you.

That person is the grace that pastoral isolation refuses. Receive it while you can.

Somewhere in the formation of American pastoral identity, we absorbed a theology of the indispensable pastor. The man who is first to arrive and last to leave. The man who handles the hospital calls and the sermon prep and the board meeting and the counseling caseload and the building project, because no one else can do it the way it needs to be done. We have baptized exhaustion and called it calling.

> We have baptized exhaustion and called it calling.

I have been that man. I know exactly what it tells itself at night — that the congregation needs this, that delegation means settling for less than the best, that the pastor's job is to give everything. The self-story sounds like sacrifice. It is mostly control. And the difference between those two things is exactly the kind of difference that is very hard to see from the inside.

---

## The Theology of the Indispensable Pastor

What the book of Exodus shows us, in a passage that does not get preached nearly enough, is a man in exactly this position and a mentor unafraid to name it. Moses was settling disputes from morning until evening. The whole nation was lined up in front of him. His father-in-law Jethro sat watching for a full day and then delivered a judgment that would have been painful to hear from anyone else: "What you are doing is not good. You will surely wear out, both yourself and these people who are with you, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone" (Exodus 18:17-18).

Read that carefully. Jethro was not questioning Moses's devotion. He was not suggesting that Moses was doing the work badly. He was questioning the theology that made Moses assume the work was his to do alone — the operating assumption that bearing the whole weight was a sign of faithfulness rather than a failure of leadership.

The phrase that lands hardest is "you are not able to do it alone." This is a statement about human finitude, not about Moses's particular limitations. No person is built to hold everything. The pastoral calling does not exempt you from the limits that God built into human beings at creation. The six days and the seventh are not a suggestion about productivity. They are a revelation about what kind of creature you are and what you require to function over the long arc.

Jethro's solution was not to make Moses lazy. It was to build a structure: capable men over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. Moses would handle the difficult cases that genuinely required his wisdom and authority. The rest would be distributed to people trained and trusted to carry them. The work did not diminish. Moses did not become irrelevant. The mission became sustainable — which is to say, it became capable of continuing beyond any single person's capacity to carry it alone.

---

## Jethro at the Judgment Seat

Paul understood the same logic from his own experience. He did not plant churches and then manage them alone from a distance. His letters are full of names — Titus, Timothy, Epaphras, Priscilla and Aquila, Phoebe, Lydia — people he entrusted with specific work in specific places, people he regarded as partners and co-laborers rather than subordinates executing his vision. "I thank my God in all my remembrance of you... because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now" (Philippians 1:3,5). Partnership, not dependence. Shared carrying, not sole carrying.

> Partnership, not dependence. Shared carrying, not sole carrying.

The First Corinthians 12 argument about the body is precisely an argument against the indispensable pastor model, even though it is rarely preached that way. "The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you,' nor again the head to the feet, 'I have no need of you.' On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable" (1 Corinthians 12:21-22). The pastor who decides he has no need of the people around him — that he is the eye and therefore the hands are decorative — has misread the text that gives his office its meaning. He has made himself the body and everyone else the accessories, which is a Christological error dressed as pastoral dedication.

The Spirit distributes gifts to the whole body, not primarily to its visible leaders. Every congregation contains people whose gifts are being suppressed by a leadership structure that does not create room for them. The pastor who holds everything is not protecting those gifts — he is burying them.

---

## When Resistance Is Control in Pastoral Clothing

Here is what delegation actually requires, and why it is harder than it sounds: it requires you to believe that other people can be trusted with things that matter.

That belief is threatened in specific ways. I have heard pastors say they tried delegating and it did not work. What they often mean is that someone else did the thing differently than they would have — not worse, differently — and they could not live with the difference. That is not a delegation problem. That is a control problem wearing pastoral clothing.

There is a legitimate version of this concern. Not all delegation is wise. Not every person in the congregation is ready for every responsibility. The pastor who delegates carelessly — who hands significant responsibilities to people who lack the character or capacity for them — creates damage that sometimes takes years to repair. Wise delegation requires discernment: you are looking for what 1 Timothy 3 describes, not brilliance or charisma or eagerness to be entrusted, but proven trustworthiness, self-control, the ability to teach and be taught, a household that reveals the character of the person rather than just his public performance. These qualities take time to observe.

But the answer to careless delegation is wise delegation, not no delegation. The answer to trusting the wrong person is learning to identify the right person, not concluding that the work is best held by you alone.

The test of whether your resistance to delegation is discernment or control is this: when someone does the task competently but differently than you would have, can you live with it? When a capable person in your congregation carries a responsibility and does not do it the way you would have done it, are you grateful for the work done or frustrated by the difference? The answer tells you something true about yourself.

---

## A Single Point of Failure

The ministry that depends entirely on you is not a strong ministry. It is a single point of failure. When you are sick, it struggles. When you travel, it drifts. When you take a day off — which the God who rested on the seventh day intended you to take — the work suffers. When you eventually cannot sustain the pace, and you will not be able to sustain the pace because no one can, the whole structure comes down because it was built around one person rather than around a mission that outlasts any individual.

This is not an argument for the pastor's dispensability. The pastor's role is irreplaceable in ways that matter — the consistent proclamation of the word, the pastoral care that requires the authority of the office, the prophetic voice that comes from sustained theological formation and genuine relationship with the congregation. These things cannot simply be distributed. But they are not the only things required. And the pastor who tries to do everything forfeits the ability to do the things that only he can do, because he is exhausted by the things that others could have carried.

I have watched gifted men leave ministry in their fifties not because of moral failure but because they had built structures that required everything from them and gave nothing back — structures where the whole weight passed through a single person, where no one else had been developed to share it, where the success of the work became identical with the individual's capacity to sustain the pace. When the capacity faltered, the work faltered with it. And in every case, the pastor had been warned years earlier, by his own exhaustion if nothing else, and had interpreted the warning as a call to more effort rather than a call to different structure.

---

## Trust as an Act of Faith

The theological issue beneath the management issue is trust. Not trust in people — though that too — but trust in the God who placed those people in the congregation. Every congregation contains people whose gifts are exactly what the mission needs. Finding them requires paying attention rather than assuming. Developing them requires investment over time rather than immediate deployment. Releasing them into genuine responsibility requires the willingness to step back from the center in ways that feel, at first, uncomfortably like relinquishing control.

That discomfort is not a sign that something is going wrong. It is a sign that something is going right. The moment the ministry begins to function in ways that do not require you at the center of every decision is the moment it has started to become what the New Testament describes: a body, not a platform; a community, not a personality cult in pastoral vestments.

Leadership is not the accumulation of responsibilities. Leadership is the development of people who can carry responsibility. Moses had to become a leader of leaders. The whole point of Jethro's intervention was not to lighten Moses's load — it was to multiply his impact by multiplying the number of people capable of carrying the work. The man who distributed leadership across a structure that could function without him was more effective, not less, than the man who was the only point through which everything passed.

> Delegation is, underneath the management language, an act of faith.

The man who will not give anything away has not learned to trust — not people, and not the God who placed those people in the congregation for reasons that include their usefulness to the mission. Delegation is, underneath the management language, an act of faith. It says: God has provided enough people, and enough grace in those people, that this does not all have to run through me.

You are not the church. You are a servant of it. Serve it by building it to work without you at the center.

That is the hardest thing I have had to learn. I have to keep learning it every time the temptation returns to hold what should be released. The path toward sustainable ministry runs directly through the willingness to trust other people with things you love. There is no other way.

There is a difference between being tired and being done, and a pastor who cannot tell them apart will make one of two mistakes. He will quit a calling he was only tired in — walk away from the field during a hard season that rest would have healed. Or he will white-knuckle through a depletion that is telling him something true, mistaking *done* for mere tiredness, and grind himself into wreckage. Both errors come from the same failure: not knowing which one he is in.

The stakes of the confusion are high. One direction leads to abandoned congregations and unfinished callings. The other leads to collapsed marriages, broken health, and the kind of ministry that poisons the well it is supposed to fill. Pastors have gone both ways, and the tragedy is not distributed evenly between the two. In my experience, the more common catastrophe is the second one — the man who stays because staying feels like faithfulness, and who does not discover until very late that he has confused endurance with obedience.

---

## What Tired Costs and What Rest Heals

Tired is normal. Tired is the honest cost of real work, and it is not a crisis. Ministry is demanding; love is depleting; a faithful pastor will be tired often, the way a farmer is tired at harvest or a parent is tired at 3 a.m. The mark of tired is that it responds to rest. Take the day, take the week, take the sleep and the Sabbath and the genuine time away — not the performance of rest while still answering emails, but the actual relinquishment of the work — and tired lifts. You come back wanting the work again. The fatigue was real and it was answerable, and the answer was rest.

> The mark of tired is that it responds to rest.

The Sabbath command in Deuteronomy 5 is precisely about this. God did not rest on the seventh day of creation because he was depleted — the Creator of the cosmos does not experience exhaustion in the way creatures do. He rested as a pattern, a gift, a structure for the creatures made in his image who do get depleted. *Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God. On it you shall not do any work* (Deuteronomy 5:13-14). The command is not a suggestion about work-life balance. It is an anthropological claim: you are a creature, not a machine, and creatures require the rhythm of work and rest or they break. Tired that receives the rest the Sabbath was designed to provide will heal.

## When Rest Does Not Touch It

Done is different, and rest does not touch it. Done is not in the body; it is deeper down. It is the quiet, settled sense that something has shifted at the level of calling or capacity — that the well is not low but dry, that you return from the sabbatical no more able to face Monday than when you left. Done does not lift with a vacation. That is precisely how you tell it from tired: you rested, genuinely, and nothing came back.

## Elijah and the Still Small Voice

The prophet Elijah in 1 Kings 19 is the canonical study. He has just called fire from heaven. He has executed the prophets of Baal at the Wadi Kishon (1 Kings 18:40). He has prayed the drought to an end. By any metric of ministry productivity, he is at the apex of his effectiveness. And then Jezebel threatens him, and something inside him gives way. He flees into the wilderness and asks to die: *It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers* (1 Kings 19:4). The depletion in that prayer is not merely physical. It is existential — a man who has given everything he has and discovered that the giving has not produced the outcome he sacrificed himself for, and who now questions whether the calling itself was sound.

What is fascinating about the divine response is what it does not do. God does not give Elijah a new vision. He does not explain the plan or defend the calling. He lets him sleep, touches him, and says: *Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you* (1 Kings 19:7). Bread. Water. Sleep. The next forty days of walking. Then a cave, a wind, an earthquake, a fire — and then a still small voice (1 Kings 19:12) that asks the same question twice: *What are you doing here, Elijah?* The question is not rhetorical. It is diagnostic. God is asking Elijah to name where he is, which is the beginning of knowing what comes next.

Even here, what follows is not retirement. It is realignment. A new assignment. A different companion in Elisha. The story of Elijah's depletion is not a story of a man who quit — it is a story of a man who was honest about his location, received genuine care rather than performance, and was given a path forward that accounted for his actual condition rather than the condition he was supposed to be in.

---

## The Opposite Responses

The two require opposite responses, which is why the diagnosis matters so much. Tired calls for rest and re-engagement — and to quit while merely tired is to abandon a calling over a passing weather front. Done calls for discernment, counsel, and sometimes change — a different role, a different field, occasionally a release from the work entirely. To push through done as though it were tired is not faithfulness. It is a slow self-destruction that takes the pastor's health, his family, and often his congregation down with it.

I have been in both, and I learned the hard way that I could not read myself accurately from inside. When I was merely tired, I sometimes felt the dramatic certainty that I was done — the lie that grows in exhaustion, that this time the dryness is permanent. And in at least one season when I was genuinely closer to done than I knew, I told myself I was just tired, and kept going long past the point where honesty would have stopped me. The view from inside the fatigue is not reliable. That is the first thing to admit.

The steel-man argument on the other side is that many pastors use "done" as cover for discouragement, that the history of the church is full of men who wanted to quit at the hardest moment and are grateful they stayed, and that the language of burnout and pastoral exhaustion can become a rationalization for avoiding the ordinary suffering that faithful ministry has always required. This is not wrong. Jeremiah wanted to quit. Jonah wanted to die. The Psalms are full of desperate men who cried to God in exhaustion and were not released from the work but carried through it. There is a place for the kind of stubborn perseverance that stays at the post when every nerve says go. The church needs pastors who know that staying is sometimes the act of faith.

But the argument fails when it ignores the body's language. The depletion that manifests as chronic insomnia, as emotional numbness, as the inability to feel anything in worship, as the dread that arrives on Sunday morning where the longing used to be — these are not spiritual failures to be overcome by willpower. They are diagnostic signals. A doctor who ignored these symptoms in a patient and told him to push through would be committing malpractice. A pastor who ignores them in himself and tells himself it is just tired is doing something similar to his own soul.

> They are diagnostic signals.

---

## A Diagnosis You Cannot Make Alone

Which is why this is not finally a diagnosis you can make alone. The line between tired and done is exactly the kind of thing a depleted man cannot see clearly about himself, and exactly what the people who know him can. A spouse, a mentor, a counselor, a few who have permission to tell you the truth — they can often see which one you are in long before you can, because they are not looking through the fog you are standing inside.

The pastor without those people will guess, and he will tend to guess in whatever direction his fear or his pride is pushing. Fear will say he is done when he is only tired, because quitting is available and staying is costly. Pride will say he is only tired when he is genuinely done, because admitting done means admitting limits, and a pastor who has built his identity on his capacity for ministry does not admit limits gracefully.

This is not a theoretical observation. I have watched both errors destroy men I respect. The one who left too early still wonders, two decades later, what would have happened if he had stayed through that particular season. The one who stayed too long through the wrong kind of depletion — who mistook grinding through done for sanctified perseverance — lost his marriage and his faith in the same year, and neither has fully recovered.

Honest people who know you can prevent both outcomes. They can say, in the first case, *you are not done, you are empty — rest and come back.* And in the second case, *something is wrong at a level that vacation will not fix, and you need to stop and figure out what it is.* That intervention requires relationship deep enough to have standing, and honesty enough to actually say it rather than murmur something vague about self-care.

Build that community before you need it. The diagnosis that is clearest to everyone around you is the one you are most likely to miss in yourself, precisely because it matters most.

> Tired is a season. Done is a turning.

Tired is a season. Done is a turning. Confuse them and you either leave a calling you were meant to keep or destroy yourself keeping one you were meant to lay down.

The still small voice asks the question Elijah needed, and that every exhausted pastor eventually needs: *What are you doing here?* Not as accusation. As invitation to be honest about your actual location, so that what comes next can actually help you.

Answer honestly. The journey is too great to travel by the maps you made when you were not this tired.

There is a pattern in how injustice works that the church should recognize by now, because the prophetic tradition has been naming it for three thousand years. The resources that enable human flourishing — land, water, shelter, education — are not distributed randomly. They concentrate. They follow the lines of existing wealth and power. And the communities with the least access to those resources are systematically the communities that already had the least.

The digital divide is that pattern applied to the infrastructure of the twenty-first century.

> It is disconnected from the systems through which society now distributes its resources and opportunities.

Access to reliable high-speed internet and the devices that use it is no longer a luxury for the technologically enthusiastic. It is the basic requirement for education, employment, healthcare access, civic participation, and increasingly the ability to manage the administrative demands of everyday life. The family without it is not disconnected from convenience. It is disconnected from the systems through which society now distributes its resources and opportunities.

---

## The Geography of Access

The geography of internet access in the United States follows the geography of poverty and race with a fidelity that should stop us.

Rural communities — disproportionately poor, disproportionately communities of color — have the lowest rates of broadband access. Urban low-income neighborhoods have access to the infrastructure but often cannot afford the monthly cost, which for the family already under financial pressure is not a trivial calculation. The Federal Communications Commission has documented the access gap; independent researchers have consistently found the gap is larger than official data captures. [cite — confirm] During the period when schools moved to remote learning in 2020-2021, the disparity became unmistakable: the children who already had the least advantage were conducting school from parking lots trying to access a library's wireless signal, while children from more advantaged households attended class from dedicated home offices.

That is not an accident. That is a system producing exactly the outcome it was built to produce — not through malice in most cases, but through the accumulated effect of infrastructure investment decisions that have consistently favored markets with existing capacity to pay. Private broadband providers build where the return on investment is clearest. That means wealthy suburbs get fiber and exurban rural counties get nothing. The theological category for this is not a complicated one. It is the opposite of the gleaning laws. Instead of ensuring that the margin of the harvest reaches the poor, it ensures that the margin of the infrastructure reaches the wealthy.

---

## The Vineyard Has Changed Form

The argument against treating this as a theological issue rather than a technical one goes like this: internet access is a product of private markets, not a fundamental human right or a matter of biblical concern. The prophets did not say anything about broadband, and importing policy preferences into the pulpit under prophetic cover is a category error.

There is something to this. The specific policy levers — municipal broadband, universal service requirements, subsidized device programs, public-private partnerships — are genuinely contested, and the church does not have technical expertise in the comparative effectiveness of these approaches. The church should be cautious about treating any particular policy solution as the biblical answer.

But the objection does not touch the underlying moral claim. The prophetic tradition has consistently named access to the basic resources required for human flourishing as a justice issue — not because these resources were mentioned by name in Leviticus, but because the principle is stated repeatedly in terms that translate across changing material conditions. "You shall not strip your vineyard bare, neither shall you gather the fallen grapes of your vineyard. You shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner" (Leviticus 19:10). The gleaning laws did not catalog every possible form of resource; they established the principle that the productive capacity of the community carried an obligation to those who had been excluded from its full benefits.

The vineyard has changed form. The obligation has not.

> The vineyard has changed form. The obligation has not.

---

## The Weight That Falls on Children

The practical consequences of the divide land most heavily on children.

Education in America has been restructured around the assumption of digital access. Research projects, homework assignments, college application processes, standardized testing registration, financial aid applications — these are not optional components of the educational system. They are the system. The child who does not have reliable home internet access and a functioning device is not working at a disadvantage in some competitions; she is excluded from the basic infrastructure through which educational opportunity is currently distributed.

The long-term consequences compound. The young adult who entered the digital economy without adequate preparation — who did not have the access that made skill development possible, who could not participate in the learning and credential-building that now largely happens online — faces an economic environment that has pre-selected against her. The gap that began with a missed homework assignment becomes a gap in employability, a gap in earning potential, a gap in the ability to build the stability that makes every other dimension of flourishing more possible.

James 2:14-17 asks a question that applies directly: "What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him? If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, 'Go in peace, be warmed and filled,' without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that?" James is not describing an exceptional case. He is describing the gap between what is spoken and what is done — the gap between acknowledging a need and addressing it.

The church that acknowledges the digital divide as a real problem and does nothing about it has produced exactly this: words without works. Faith without the things needed for the body.

> Faith without the things needed for the body.

---

## The Shame the Divide Produces

The pastoral dimension is particular to this issue in a way that requires naming.

The digital divide is experienced as shame. The child who cannot submit the assignment. The adult who cannot complete the application. The senior who cannot access the telehealth appointment. Each of these moments carries the weight of technological inadequacy — the sense of being left behind by a system that the rest of the world is navigating smoothly. The shame is not warranted. The failure is systemic, not personal. But shame does not care about the origin of the failure. It attaches to the person who experiences it.

The church that sees this shame, names its systemic origin, and works to address it is doing pastoral work and prophetic work simultaneously. It is saying: your inability to get online is not evidence of your inadequacy. It is evidence of a system that has failed to extend its benefits equitably. And we are going to say so publicly and work on it practically.

Congregations in many cities have done exactly this: providing devices, partnering with programs that offer subsidized internet, advocating for municipal broadband, creating digital literacy training for seniors who were never integrated into the technological transition the rest of society went through. [cite — confirm] These are not grand gestures. They are the gleaning law applied to the harvest of the twenty-first century.

---

## The Gleaning Question of Our Moment

The question is not whether the church has the technical expertise to build the infrastructure. It does not.

The question is whether the church has the prophetic clarity to name whose children are being left behind and why, the pastoral presence to sit with the shame that the divide produces, and the practical commitment to use its organizational capacity to narrow a gap that is not accidental.

We have known for most of human history that access to resources concentrates. We have known what happens to the communities that end up on the wrong side of that concentration. The prophets knew. The law knew. Jesus knew, in the most specific terms, who the vulnerable were in his world and what the failure to reach them indicated about the heart of the community that called itself faithful.

The mechanisms change. The pattern does not. The obligation does not.

We know who is on the other side of this particular gap. The question is what we intend to do with that knowledge.

The prophetic tradition in Israel was not abstract about these things. It named the mechanisms — the specific ways that power and resources and access concentrated in the hands of those who already had them, at the direct cost of those who did not. It named the people who benefited from those arrangements and the people who were harmed by them. And it called the community that claimed to follow the God of the Exodus to the same standard God applied to Egypt: the measure of a community's faithfulness is not how well it treats those who have everything, but how it treats those who have nothing.

Access to education, to economic opportunity, to the systems through which contemporary society distributes its goods — this is the gleaning question of our moment. The vineyard has changed. The people left at the margins have not changed. The God who required the margin to be left for them has not changed.

The church that sees the gap and names it, that refuses to accept its children's exclusion from the infrastructure of opportunity as someone else's concern, is not engaging in politics. It is doing what faithfulness has always required: standing where the vulnerable stand, refusing to look away, and putting the weight of its organizational presence on the side of access rather than the side of comfortable silence.

There is a man in my congregation who has worshiped God in a wheelchair for twenty years. He comes early, parks in the accessible spot, enters through the side door that the rest of the congregation does not use, and sits in the space we have designated near the back. He does not complain. He is generous with his presence and quieter than most about what his Sunday morning costs him.

I have never preached a sermon on disability justice. That is a confession, not a preamble.

The image of God — the *imago Dei* of Genesis 1:26-27 — is the most foundational claim Christian theology makes about human beings. Every person, without exception, bears this image. The text does not say: every person who can hear the sermon, every person who can climb the steps, every person whose body works in the way the architecture assumes. It says every person. The theological weight of that word has implications the church has largely refused to follow to their conclusions.

## The Image of God in Every Body

The history of Christian theology on this point is not uniformly inspiring. Augustine's reading of the *imago Dei* located it primarily in the rational soul, which led to implicit hierarchies of image-bearing based on intellectual capacity [cite — confirm]. Aquinas followed a similar line, associating the image with the intellect and will in their capacity to know and love God [cite — confirm]. These were not neutral academic positions. They had pastoral and ethical consequences: the more the image was located in cognitive capacity, the easier it became to suggest that those with severe cognitive disabilities bore it less fully — or, in the darkest versions of this reasoning, barely at all.

The text does not support this move. Genesis 1:26-27 uses the image language with striking breadth: *Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness, so that they may rule over the fish in the sea.* The *imago Dei* is not primarily an intellectual faculty. Scholars today tend to understand it in the ancient Near Eastern context as a royal designation — the one who bears the image represents the king's authority in a territory, and the king's honor is implicated in how the image-bearer is treated [cite — confirm]. Applied to humanity, the claim is that every person — regardless of capacity, regardless of function, regardless of what the body can or cannot do — represents God in the creation and carries a dignity that is therefore not negotiable.

> What the body can do is not the measure of the dignity it bears.

What the body can do is not the measure of the dignity it bears. This is not a difficult theological conclusion. It is simply the *imago Dei* followed to where it leads.

## Pastoral Accommodation and the Question of Justice

We have, as institutions, treated disability as a pastoral problem rather than a justice problem. This distinction matters. A pastoral problem calls for compassion and accommodation. A justice problem calls for examination of the systems that produce exclusion and structural change to those systems. The wheelchair ramp added to the side door is pastoral accommodation. Asking why the front entrance was built without one — and who decided it wasn't necessary — is the beginning of justice.

The Americans with Disabilities Act was signed into law in 1990 [cite — confirm]. It required physical accessibility in public accommodations and prohibited discrimination based on disability. It was a legal codification of what Christian theology had always implied but rarely enforced at the institutional level. The fact that the civil law got there before most churches is worth sitting with. The church that should have been the leading advocate for the full inclusion of people with disabilities was, in most cases, not leading. It was accommodating, imperfectly and under legal pressure.

## The One Who Reinstates

The Gospels are striking in how consistently Jesus is surrounded by people whose bodies do not meet the expectations of the religious establishment. The blind, the deaf, the lame, the hemorrhaging woman who could not enter the temple courts. In each case, Jesus does not simply heal and move on. He reinstates. He restores the person to full participation in community life, because the exclusion they have suffered is not merely physical. It is social, religious, economic. The healing is not only of the body. It is of a system that has used the body as a reason for exclusion.

The man born blind in John 9 is the clearest case. Before Jesus touches him, the disciples ask: "Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?" (John 9:2). The question assumes that disability is punishment — that the condition of the body is a theological verdict, a sign of divine disfavor. Jesus refuses the premise: "Neither this man nor his parents sinned." The blindness is not moral judgment. It is the location where God's work will be made visible. The rebuke of the disciples' question is a rebuke of the entire framework that treats disability as stigma.

> The exclusion of people with disabilities is not a minor oversight in church programming. It is a distortion of the body.

The early church seems to have grasped this with more clarity than its descendants. Paul's description of the body of Christ in 1 Corinthians 12 is deliberate: the members that seem weaker are indispensable, the parts we think less honorable we treat with special honor (1 Corinthians 12:22-23). This is not sentimentality. It is ecclesiology — a claim about what the church is. The body of Christ cannot be fully itself if it is composed only of the conventionally able. The exclusion of people with disabilities is not a minor oversight in church programming. It is a distortion of the body.

The counter-position that requires honest engagement is this: the church's primary task is spiritual, and physical accessibility concerns, while important, are not theological matters in the strict sense. The church can love people with disabilities spiritually even in buildings that are not fully accessible; the accessibility is a practical, not a theological, question.

This argument underestimates what architecture communicates. The philosopher Charles Taylor has argued that our moral frameworks are "embedded in practices, institutions, and ways of relating" [cite — confirm] — that what we believe is expressed and reinforced by what we build and how we organize. The church building that is inaccessible to wheelchair users does not merely inconvenience them. It communicates a message, however unintentionally, about who the gathering is designed for and who is an afterthought. The message is received. People with disabilities have been receiving it for a long time.

I have visited churches with no sign-language interpretation where Deaf people sat through services designed entirely for the hearing. I have been in buildings where a person using a mobility device could not reach the communion table. I have watched programs for children with cognitive disabilities treated as a ministry for the few — a niche, a specialty — rather than a standard expectation of what the church is for. Each of these is an architectural and programmatic choice. Every architectural and programmatic choice is a theological statement.

## Architecture as Theological Statement

What would it mean for the church to take *imago Dei* seriously enough to make disability justice a design requirement rather than an afterthought? It would mean consultation with disabled people in the planning stages, not after the building is built. It would mean hiring people with disabilities into positions of actual authority, not only into the programs designed for them. It would mean sermons that name the theological stakes — that say plainly: the exclusion of a person who bears the image of God is not a facilities problem. It is a sin against the one whose image that person carries.

I am learning this later than I should have. The man in the wheelchair near the back of my sanctuary has been a patient teacher. His patience is greater than I deserve. He enters through the side door because I built — or inherited, and did not change — a building that required it.

The kingdom of God, in the vision of Isaiah and the announcement of Jesus, includes the blind seeing and the lame walking — not as the elimination of disability, but as the restoration of full participation in the life of God's people (Isaiah 35:5-6; Luke 7:22). That vision begins here. It begins with who we build for. It begins with who we design our gatherings around. It begins with whose presence we treat as indispensable rather than accommodated.

> The image of God arrives in every body.

The image of God arrives in every body. The question is whether the church is ready to receive it — through the front door.

## A Site Where Theology Is Reconsidered

Amos Yong, a Pentecostal theologian who grew up with a brother with Down syndrome, argues that disability theology is not a subspecialty of theology but a site where the whole of theology must be reconsidered [cite — confirm]. The church's systematic theology was developed, largely, by men whose bodies were not the subject of the conversation — who could assume their own capacity as the norm and everyone else's difference as the variation. When you center the person with a disability in the theological conversation, the conversation changes. The question of what it means to be made in God's image cannot be answered abstractly. It must be answered in the presence of specific bodies, specific stories, specific exclusions.

Nancy Eiesland's *The Disabled God* (1994) proposed a theology of disability rooted in the resurrection appearance of Jesus — who appears to Thomas not with a glorified body that has transcended injury, but with wounds still visible, still available to touch (John 20:27) [cite — confirm]. The risen Christ is not a Christ whose scars have been erased. He is a Christ who carries them into the new creation. This has implications for how we understand disability in relation to the eschaton: not the elimination of all difference, but the presence of difference in a community where it is no longer the basis of exclusion.

The person with a disability in your congregation is not waiting to be healed before she can participate fully in the life of God's people. She is already bearing the image of God. The question is whether the church's architecture and practice are adequate to receive what she brings.

Most of the time, they are not. The answer is not despair. The answer is the same answer it always is when the church has failed to follow its own theology to its conclusions: repentance, which is the turning around that makes movement toward faithfulness possible.

The building can be modified. The liturgy can be made accessible. The programs can be redesigned. These are not primarily architectural or logistical questions. They are theological ones, and the answer to them begins with the confession that we have excluded people God told us were indispensable.

That confession is overdue. It is also the beginning of something better.

Micah 6:8 is eight words in English. It takes longer to say than to dismiss. It has been dismissed.

The dismissal takes several forms. There is the spiritualized reading: justice, mercy, and humility are interior virtues, matters of the heart, and the text is about personal piety rather than social action. There is the privatized reading: these are the requirements for the individual's relationship with God, and they say nothing about what the political community owes the poor. There is the selectively applied reading: justice means God's punishment of sin, mercy means personal kindness, and humility means not bragging — a version of the verse that makes no demands on the structures of power and costs nothing.

The prophet Micah wrote none of those versions.

---

## Micah and the Economy of Dispossession

Micah spoke in the eighth century BCE, roughly contemporary with Isaiah, in a moment of extraordinary economic violence. The northern kingdom of Israel was nearing its end. In the south, Judah was nominally stable — but the stability was purchased at the price of the poor. Micah 2:1-2 is precise about the mechanics: "Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they carry it out because it is in the power of their hand. They covet fields and seize them, and houses and take them away; they oppress a man and his house, a man and his inheritance." This was not a spiritual problem in the first instance. It was a problem of legal mechanisms for dispossession — of powerful men using courts and contracts and the cover of legality to take from the poor what the poor had.

Micah 3:1-3 extends the indictment to the rulers themselves: "Is it not for you to know justice? — you who hate the good and love the evil, who tear the skin from off my people and their flesh from off their bones, who eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them, and break their bones in pieces and chop them up like meat in a pot, like flesh in a cauldron." This is not the language of general moral failure. This is the language of specific, systematic violence against the bodies of the poor, carried out by the people whose job was to protect them.

Into that context comes Micah 6:8. God has brought his lawsuit against Israel. The people ask what they can offer — burnt offerings, calves, oil, rivers of oil, their firstborn children. God's answer is the refusal of all of it. What God has already told them, what God has always required: *do justice, love mercy, walk humbly with your God.*

---

## Three Angles on a Single Posture

The three requirements are not three separate items. They are a single posture described from three angles.

*Mishpat* — justice — is not primarily a feeling or an aspiration. It is an action. The verb is *asah*: to do, to make, to accomplish. Mishpat is the active establishment of right order in human community — the righting of wrongs, the protection of the vulnerable, the fair administration of courts, the structural conditions under which the poor can live with dignity. In the Psalms, mishpat is repeatedly attributed to God himself: "The LORD works righteousness and justice for all who are oppressed" (Psalm 103:6). The God who does mishpat is the model for the community that is called to do it. To do justice is to participate in what God is already doing in the world.

*Hesed* — mercy, steadfast love, covenant faithfulness — is the relational depth out of which mishpat flows. It is the quality of God's relationship with Israel that does not give up even when Israel deserves to be given up. It is loyalty that costs something. In Ruth, Boaz's treatment of the Moabite widow is called hesed (Ruth 3:10) — a practical act of social protection for a vulnerable woman, rooted in the covenant character that shapes how Boaz sees her. Hesed is not sentiment. It is the quality of love that shows up in the specific situation of the specific person who is vulnerable in front of you, and acts.

*Walking humbly with your God* is the posture that prevents mishpat and hesed from becoming pride and performance. The prophet who does justice and forgets that the justice he does is God's will, that the wisdom he applies is borrowed from a source larger than himself, becomes the kind of prophet that Isaiah and Jeremiah warned against — the one who speaks his own mind and calls it the word of the LORD. Humility before God is not a private spiritual practice disconnected from public action. It is the ground under justice and mercy that keeps them from collapsing into ideology.

Together they form a single description of what the covenant life looks like when it is actually operating. Not doing justice as a political program while neglecting the interior life. Not cultivating the interior life while remaining indifferent to the poor. Not the prophetic without the pastoral, not the pastoral without the prophetic. Both, simultaneously, rooted in the particular kind of humility that knows all of it is a response to what God has already done.

---

## The Verse Divided Against Itself

The American church has divided Micah 6:8 against itself. The conservative tradition claimed the personal piety — the interior life, the doctrinal precision, the individual moral formation — while treating the justice demand as optional or as an incursion of political ideology into the pure gospel. The progressive tradition claimed the justice demand — the structural analysis, the advocacy for the poor, the prophetic critique of power — while sometimes losing the theological grounding that gives justice its force and the humility that prevents it from becoming self-righteousness.

> Both traditions took a piece of the verse and treated it as the whole thing. Neither tradition had Micah.

Both traditions took a piece of the verse and treated it as the whole thing. Neither tradition had Micah.

Micah was not primarily concerned with the soul of the individual wealthy Israelite, though he was surely concerned with that too. He was concerned with the system — the legal and economic system that was devouring the poor — and with the behavior of the covenant community that was supposed to represent God's character in the world. The covenant people's failure to do mishpat was not a secondary failure. It was the primary evidence that they did not actually know the God they claimed to worship. "He has told you, O man, what is good" — the *you* in that verse is second person singular, addressed to the individual. But the *mishpat* it requires is the just ordering of human community. The individual and the structural are inseparable in the prophetic imagination.

## I Have Preached It Without Doing It

I have preached Micah 6:8 without doing it.

I have stood behind a pulpit and called my congregation to justice while running an institutional church that required the majority of its resources to sustain itself. I have described the hesed of God while maintaining a distance from the people who most needed to experience it through the church's actual presence. I have talked about walking humbly with God while being considerably less humble in the room where the church's budget was set.

The self-implication is not theater. It is the only honest ground from which to preach the text. The prophet who stands outside the indictment and points at the congregation is not prophesying. He is performing prophecy, which is one of the most effective ways of avoiding the actual cost of it.

> The word becomes the prophet's food before it becomes the community's confrontation.

Amos understood this. Micah understood this. The prophets who spoke the word of the LORD knew that the word landed on them before it landed on anyone else. Jeremiah ate the scroll before he spoke it (cf. Ezekiel 3:1-3 for the image). The word becomes the prophet's food before it becomes the community's confrontation.

## What This Manifesto Is Manifesting

This is a manifesto. Here is what it is manifesting:

The church that has stopped doing justice in order to protect its donor base has traded the gospel for institutional survival. It has committed the same transaction Micah names in chapter three: using the position of religious authority for personal comfort while the poor suffer.

The church that has stopped loving with hesed — with the covenant loyalty that costs something — and replaced it with programs that serve the poor at a safe organizational distance, has not kept the command. Hesed requires presence. It requires vulnerability. It requires the willingness to be changed by the encounter with the person you are serving, which means the encounter must be real enough to change you.

The church that has stopped walking humbly — that has become confident in its justice analysis, certain in its prophetic positions, comfortable with the sound of its own prophetic voice — has lost the ground under its feet. The church that knows what justice requires without the daily discipline of asking God whether it is seeing clearly is not doing mishpat. It is doing ideology with a Bible verse attached.

All three are required. All three, simultaneously, in the specific neighborhood where the specific church stands, among the specific people the church has been given to serve.

---

The verse is eight words in English. Here they are again, without the buffer of theological commentary:

Do justice.

Love mercy.

Walk humbly with your God.

This is the call to the church. It has been the call since Micah stood in Judah and said it to people who were worshipping God with expensive offerings while their neighbors were being dispossessed. The form of the worship changes. The expensive offerings change. The mechanism of dispossession changes. The call does not change.

We have been told what is good. The question is what we are going to do with the knowledge.

> We have been told what is good.

That question is not behind us. It is standing in front of us right now, wearing the face of whoever in your city is most vulnerable and most thoroughly abandoned by the systems and structures that were supposed to protect them.

What are you going to do?

In 1493, Pope Alexander VI issued a papal bull called *Inter caetera* declaring that any land not inhabited by Christians was available to be "discovered," claimed, and brought under the dominion of the Catholic monarchies of Spain and Portugal. The logic was simple: the earth belongs to those who confess Christ, and those who do not confess Christ have no standing to prevent Christian nations from claiming what they have left unclaimed — which is to say, anything they happen to occupy.

This is the Doctrine of Discovery. It is not ancient history. It is the legal and theological foundation on which the Supreme Court of the United States still decides cases involving Native American land rights [cite — confirm]. It was cited as recently as 2005 in *City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation*, when the Court used the doctrine to prevent the Oneida from reasserting sovereignty over land their ancestors held before it was taken. A legal framework derived from a fifteenth-century papal document about the right of Christian nations to dispossess non-Christians remains embedded in American property law.

The American church has not reckoned with this. It is past time to say so plainly.

## Theology, Not Secular Policy

The Doctrine of Discovery was not secular policy dressed in religious language. It was theology. It was an argument about what the God of Scripture requires of Christian nations — namely, that they extend Christ's dominion by claiming the earth for the church. The missionaries who accompanied the conquistadors, who stood on the shore and read the *Requerimiento* to people who did not understand Spanish — a legal notice informing them that they were now subject to the Spanish Crown and the Church, and that if they resisted they would be enslaved — those missionaries believed they were doing God's work. That is not incidental to the doctrine. It is the doctrine.

American Protestantism inherited and adapted this framework. The Puritan settlers of New England understood their mission in explicitly covenantal terms that did not differ substantially from the Catholic logic of *Inter caetera*. They were God's people, entering a land promised to them, displacing a pagan population that had no standing before the God who was giving them the land. John Winthrop's famous "city on a hill" sermon drew on the language of Deuteronomy — the covenant people, the promised land, the blessing and curse — without questioning whether the inhabitants of the continent they were entering might also be people with standing before God and claims upon the earth they occupied.

> That is not the God of the Hebrew prophets. It is not the God of Jesus.

The theological problem is not subtle. The Doctrine of Discovery requires that the imago Dei — the image of God borne by every human person — be selectively applied. It requires that the God who declares in Genesis 1 that every human being is made in the divine image, and who declares in Deuteronomy 27:19 that cursed is anyone who withholds justice from the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, be understood to have authorized the dispossession of millions of people bearing that same image. The doctrine requires a God who is the God of Christian nations first and the God of humanity second. That is not the God of the Hebrew prophets. It is not the God of Jesus.

## The Objection That Deserves an Answer

The response I most commonly hear from theologically serious Christians is that the Doctrine of Discovery represents a historical abuse that does not implicate the contemporary church. The errors were real but they are past. What has that to do with us?

I want to answer this honestly, because it deserves a real answer.

The errors are not past. The legal structures built on those errors continue to operate. The land was taken under a doctrine the church produced, the dispossession was total and is unreversed, and the communities that bear the consequences — Native communities with some of the highest rates of poverty, suicide, and preventable death in the United States [cite — confirm] — are not historical abstractions. They are people living with the present-tense results of five centuries of Christian-justified theft. When the church says that is not our problem because we did not personally do it, the church is claiming a kind of individual innocence that its own theology does not permit. The prophets did not repent only for their own individual sins. They repented for the sins of the nation, including the sins committed before they were born. Daniel prayed: "We have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled, turning aside from your commandments and rules" (Daniel 9:5). The *we* is not an individual confession. It is a communal one.

There is also the question of ongoing benefit. The land on which American churches stand was, in many cases, taken under policies that derived their legitimacy from the Doctrine of Discovery. The theological argument that authorized the taking was produced by the institution that now occupies the land. The church that prays on land taken in the name of Christ and then says the taking has nothing to do with it is claiming a disconnection between its theology and its history that it would not accept in any other context.

## What Reckoning Requires

What does reckoning look like? I do not pretend this is simple, and I am not interested in answers that cost nothing. The beginning is knowledge. Most American Christians do not know what the Doctrine of Discovery is. Most American Christians do not know that Supreme Court land decisions affecting Native communities are still being decided on its basis. Most American Christians have never heard of the *Requerimiento*, have never read the text of *Inter caetera*, have never learned the specific theology that was used to justify the dispossession of the people who lived on this continent before European Christianity arrived.

Ignorance is not neutral. It is a choice, repeated across generations, to not know things that are difficult to know. The church that does not know its own history cannot confess it. The church that does not confess it cannot be released from it.

> Ignorance is not neutral.

In Numbers 35, God establishes cities of refuge — places where the person who has caused death unintentionally can flee and find protection from the avenger of blood. The mechanism acknowledges that some forms of harm require institutional response, not merely individual guilt. The harm caused by the Doctrine of Discovery is not accidental — it was deliberately constructed theology — but the principle matters: some harms require communities to take protective, restorative action rather than simply declaring their personal innocence.

## The Tradition That Will Not Permit Neutrality

The prophetic tradition, from Amos to Isaiah to Micah, never permits the faithful community to declare neutrality on behalf of the exploited. "Seek justice, rebuke the oppressor, defend the fatherless, plead for the widow" (Isaiah 1:17). The tradition does not say: seek justice unless the injustice happened before you were born, or unless the systems of oppression are legally complex, or unless reckoning would be uncomfortable. The tradition simply says: seek justice.

James 2:14–17 makes the connection between confession and action in terms that the American church should find inescapable: "If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, 'Go in peace, be warmed and filled,' without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that?" Saying the right things about historical injustice without acting toward present-tense repair is the precise dynamic James is describing. The faith that does not work is dead. The repentance that does not produce fruit is not repentance.

I am not standing outside this indictment. I have stood in church buildings on land with a complicated history and led worship without asking what that history was. I have preached on the justice of God in the abstract while not knowing who stood on the ground I was standing on before there was a church building there. That ignorance was not innocent. It was comfortable.

The Doctrine of Discovery requires the American church to do something it has been reluctant to do in any sustained way: reckon with the specific theological arguments it produced that caused specific, documented harm to specific people who continue to bear those consequences. Not as an exercise in guilt management. Not as a progressive political gesture. As theological work — the hard, necessary work of a community that takes seriously the claim that God is just and that injustice done in God's name matters to God.

The church that produced the Doctrine of Discovery is also the church that produced the prophetic tradition of confessional repentance. Both are part of the inheritance. The question is which one we live from.

> The faith that does not work is dead. The repentance that does not produce fruit is not repentance.

That question has not yet been answered.

## The Silence That Is Itself a Statement

The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted in 2007 with the United States initially voting against it [cite — confirm], affirms that indigenous peoples have the right to the lands, territories, and resources they have traditionally owned, occupied, or used. The American church — which claims to care about human rights as a theological category, which invokes the imago Dei in abortion debates and poverty debates and immigration debates — has been largely silent about a declaration that directly addresses the ongoing consequences of the theology it produced.

The silence is itself a theological statement. What the church will not speak is also a position.

Nehemiah 9 is the great confessional prayer of the returned exiles — a sustained recounting of the sins of the people across generations, naming specific failures, owning specific histories, asking for mercy not as individuals but as a people with a people's history. "We are in great distress," the prayer concludes (Nehemiah 9:37). Not: *they* are in great distress because of what *our ancestors* did. We. The communal confession does not create temporal distance from the harm. It closes it.

The church that produced the Doctrine of Discovery can also produce that prayer. Not as a performance. As the beginning of repair.

The text is not ambiguous. Acts 2:44-45: "All the believers were together and had everything in common. They sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need." Acts 4:32-34: "All the believers were one in heart and mind. No one claimed that any of their possessions was their own, but they shared everything they had... God's grace was so powerfully at work in them all that there were no needy persons among them. For from time to time those who owned land or houses sold them, brought the money from the sales and put it at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to anyone who had need."

No needy persons among them.

> No needy persons among them.

That is a remarkable claim. It is also a description of a practice — not a theology, not an aspiration, not a metaphor. A practice. The early church, in Jerusalem, in the first years after Pentecost, had organized its common life so that there were no needy persons among them. They sold assets. They distributed to anyone who had need. The sharing was not voluntary in the sense that contemporary evangelicals mean when they use that word — meaning, you can do it if you want to but the expectation is that you will keep what is yours. The sharing was constitutive. It was what the community was.

## A Practice, Not a Metaphor

This text has been handled in several ways by American Christianity, most of them designed to neutralize it.

## The Historical-Theological Evasion

The most common move is the historical-theological one: this was an early, unique expression of the Jerusalem church, shaped by the specific expectation that Christ would return imminently, and it did not work even for them — see Acts 6 and the dispute over the distribution to Hellenistic widows. The practice was unsustainable and was not repeated in the Pauline churches. The collections Paul organizes in 1 Corinthians 16 and 2 Corinthians 8-9 are voluntary and proportional, not total.

This argument is partially right. The Jerusalem community faced specific conditions — the concentration of believers in a single city, the hostility of the surrounding religious establishment, the early theological expectation of an imminent end — that made a particular form of economic sharing natural. The precise form of Acts 2 was not replicated wholesale across the Pauline mission churches.

But the argument is also evasive. Because Paul's collections for the Jerusalem church in 2 Corinthians 8 do not describe a different theology of economic sharing — they describe the same theology in a different form. "For if the willingness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. Our desire is not that others might be relieved while you are hard pressed, but that there might be equality. At the present time your plenty will supply what they need, so that in turn their need will supply what you need" (2 Corinthians 8:12-14). The goal Paul names is *equality* — the Greek word is *isotes*, meaning equalization. The goal is not charity. The goal is the elimination of the disparity. That is continuous with Acts 2, not a departure from it.

## The Individualist Evasion

The second move is the individualist one: this was a voluntary act of individual generosity, not a community practice, and it teaches us about the spirit of generosity rather than any specific economic arrangement. Barnabas was admired for selling his field and bringing the money to the apostles (Acts 4:36-37). Ananias and Sapphira were judged not for withholding money — Peter says explicitly, "Wasn't the land yours before you sold it? And after it was sold, wasn't the money at your disposal?" (Acts 5:4) — but for lying about the amount. Therefore this is about individual integrity and generous hearts, not about any particular economic practice.

This argument also fails, for the same reason: it addresses the mechanism while ignoring the aim. The community aim, stated plainly, was that there would be no needy persons among them. However that aim was achieved — through voluntary sales, through communal distribution, through proportional giving — the aim itself was the standard. The question the text puts to the contemporary church is not "did they have a mandatory sharing policy?" but "do you have any needy persons among you?" And if you do — and you do — what does that say about the adequacy of your current practice?

## The Honest and Uncomfortable Reading

The third move is the most honest and the most uncomfortable: yes, this is what the early church practiced, and no, the American church is not practicing it, and the gap between those two realities is one of the most significant ways that the American church has accommodated itself to the values of its surrounding culture rather than the values of its Lord.

> These are not compatible claims.

The surrounding culture teaches that what you earn is yours and what you do with it is your private business. The New Testament teaches that everything belongs to God and that the community of Jesus is accountable for the condition of its most vulnerable members. These are not compatible claims. The American evangelical church, for the most part, has resolved the tension in favor of the surrounding culture and called it a theological position. It is not a theological position. It is a capitulation.

Deuteronomy 15:7-11 sets the expectation in terms that leave little interpretive room: "If anyone is poor among your fellow Israelites in any of the towns of the land the LORD your God is giving you, do not be hardhearted or tightfisted toward them. Rather, be openhanded and freely lend them whatever they need." The text then addresses the natural objection — what if a sabbath year is coming and I will lose the debt? — and answers it with a command: "Do not be hardhearted or tightfisted toward them." The economic system of Israel included mechanisms — gleaning laws, sabbath years, Jubilee — specifically designed to prevent the permanent accumulation of wealth by some and the permanent destitution of others. These were not voluntary. They were covenantal obligations.

The early church understood itself as the fulfillment of this covenantal tradition, reinterpreted through the resurrection and the arrival of the Spirit. The community that had the Spirit of God was the community in which the vision of Deuteronomy — no needy persons among you — was actually realized. The fact that they failed to sustain it perfectly, that Acts 6 describes a distribution dispute, that Paul has to correct the Corinthians' behavior at the Lord's Table (1 Corinthians 11:17-34) because the wealthy are not waiting for the poor — none of that changes the standard. It confirms that the standard was real and that failing to meet it was treated as a failure, not a theological alternative.

The contemporary church that has replaced this vision with individual tithing to a budget that the congregation does not control and does not understand has not recovered the theology of Acts 2. It has institutionalized a different thing and called it the same. And I am not standing outside that observation. I have led a church with a budget, received tithes, and distributed money through programs without asking whether the people in my pews who were struggling had what they needed. The institutional structure I was working within was not designed to know. It was designed to fund.

The question the text puts to us is not "are we doing the Acts 2 experiment again?" The early Jerusalem church's specific form was time-bound and historically particular. The question is: do the people in your congregation who have need know that the community will meet it? Do they feel the freedom to say they have need? Is the economic life of your community organized in any way around the principle that no one among you should go without what they need while others have abundance?

If the answer is no — and for most American congregations, the answer is no — then the question is not whether Acts 2 is binding. The question is what we are actually practicing, and what that practice reveals about what we actually believe.

> The early church practiced something the contemporary American church mostly will not.

The early church practiced something the contemporary American church mostly will not. The gap is not a minor liturgical preference. It is a theological statement about whether the resurrection changed anything real about how we hold our stuff.

That statement is still being made. We are making it right now, with our budgets and our boundaries and our carefully maintained financial privacy in the company of the people we call brothers and sisters.

No needy persons among them.

We should not read past that phrase as quickly as we have been reading past it.

## Naming the Failure and Returning to the Standard

The early church did not hold this standard perfectly. Acts 6 shows the community in dispute over fairness in the daily distribution. The Corinthians were shamed for their behavior at the Lord's Table, where the wealthy ate their fill while the poor went hungry at the very meal meant to declare their equality (1 Corinthians 11:20-22). The letters of James and John address wealthy members who were treating the poor badly. The record is not a record of communities that had arrived at shalom. It is a record of communities that held the standard, failed to meet it, were corrected, and were expected to try again.

That is the tradition we are called to inhabit. Not the tradition that achieved Acts 2:44 and moved on. The tradition that named the failure, returned to the standard, and kept going.

The contemporary church has largely stopped naming the failure. It has replaced the standard with a more comfortable metric and called it a theology of grace. That is not grace. Grace is what we need when we fail to meet a real standard. Replacing the standard is something else entirely.

Psalm 24 opens with a statement so simple it can be missed: "The earth is the LORD's, and everything in it, the world, and all who live in it." This is not poetry about sunsets. It is a claim about property rights.

The earth belongs to God. We are tenants.

> The earth belongs to God. We are tenants.

This is where the conversation about creation care should begin — not with climate data, not with policy debates, not with the question of what evangelicals think about environmentalism, but with who owns what. If the earth belongs to God, then the way we treat it is an act of stewardship, and stewardship is accountable. You do not get to trash what belongs to someone else and call it freedom. You are responsible for what you were given to tend.

## The Priestly Vocation of the Garden

The account in Genesis 2 uses a specific word for the human relationship to the garden: *abad* — to work, to serve. The same root is used for priestly service at the temple. The connection is not accidental. Adam's vocation in the garden is priestly in structure: he tends the place where God is present, exercises a representative function between Creator and creation, maintains the ordered beauty of what has been made. When the church reads the dominion mandate of Genesis 1:28 as permission for extraction and consumption, it has badly misread what dominion means in its own cultural context.

Ancient Near Eastern kingship was characterized by the king's responsibility to protect and sustain the land and its people. The king who dominated through exploitation was the bad king — the tyrant, the one who devoured what was entrusted to him. The king who fulfilled dominion was the one who cultivated, protected, extended the flourishing of what was under his care. Dominion in Genesis 1 carries this same expectation. It was stewardship. It was never license.

The fall in Genesis 3 disrupts this priestly vocation with consequences that are ecological as well as relational. "Cursed is the ground because of you; through painful toil you will eat food from it" (Genesis 3:17). The broken relationship between humanity and God produces a broken relationship between humanity and the soil. The corruption of the image affects the whole creation it was commissioned to tend. Paul makes this explicit in Romans 8:19–22 — the creation "has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth right up to the present time," subjected to frustration, waiting for the liberation that comes with the restoration of the children of God. Creation's suffering is not incidental to the human story. It is part of the same story.

## A Cultural Anxiety Mistaken for Biblical Conviction

---

> But they do not constitute a biblical position.

I grew up in a tradition that treated creation care as a liberal distraction. Environmental concern was soft. It was political. The real issues were souls, not soil. I preached from that tradition without examining it, which means I preached a truncated gospel — one that cared for human beings while dismissing the world God made, the world God called good, the world God inhabits.

## The End of the Story Is Earth Restored

The tradition I was formed in was not stupid. It had reasons for its suspicion of environmentalism. Some of those reasons had to do with the theological error of treating creation as an end in itself rather than a gift from and to God.
