Some had to do with legitimate concerns about certain strands of environmental politics that displaced human dignity in favor of nature. These are real concerns.

But they do not constitute a biblical position. They constitute a cultural anxiety that was used to suppress a biblical concern. The church's abandonment of creation care was not the result of careful exegetical work. It was the result of culture war politics that sorted environmental concern into the wrong coalition and then declared the concern itself suspect.

The psalmist, the prophets, and the apostle Paul did not make that error.

## When Creation Care Becomes Creation Justice

---

The vision of the renewed creation at the end of the biblical story is not escape from the earth. It is the earth restored.

John's Revelation does not describe the saints escaping to heaven and leaving the world behind. It describes the New Jerusalem coming down to a renewed earth (Revelation 21:1–2). The trajectory of redemption is not away from matter. It is toward matter made whole. The New Jerusalem is a city — a social, material, architectural reality — not a cloud. The river of the water of life, the tree of life whose leaves are "for the healing of the nations" (Revelation 22:2) — these are not metaphors for spiritual states. They are the restored creation, finally fulfilling the vocation it was given in Genesis 2.

## Faithfulness Without a Political Coalition

If that is where the story ends, it has implications for how we live in the middle of it. The church that treats the physical world as a waiting room to be abandoned at the end has not read the last two chapters of the Bible carefully. The eschatology of Scripture is creational, not escapist. The end is not the annihilation of matter but its redemption.

This has immediate consequences for how we think about the creation we are currently tenanting. We are not occupying a world about to be discarded. We are occupying the world God is in the process of renewing. What we do to it matters in that framework — not only as a moral question, but as a theological one.

---

> The earth is the Lord's.

Climate change is a justice issue as well as a creation issue, and these are not separable.

The populations most affected by rising seas, extreme weather events, crop failures, and water scarcity are disproportionately the world's poor — those with the fewest resources to adapt and the least political power to demand protection. [cite — confirm] The small island nations that will be uninhabitable within decades are not large emitters. They are the recipients of consequences produced overwhelmingly by wealthy industrialized economies. The subsistence farmers in sub-Saharan Africa whose crops are failing because of rainfall pattern disruptions did not produce the carbon that disrupted the patterns. They are absorbing the cost of someone else's consumption.

The church that cares about the widow, the orphan, and the stranger — the church that takes seriously the biblical insistence that God stands with the vulnerable — cannot be indifferent to a crisis that falls hardest on those same populations. To ignore creation justice is to ignore justice. The categories do not divide cleanly. They are the same category, seen from different angles.

Wendell Berry has written for decades about the connection between how we treat the land and how we treat each other — that the logic of extraction and exploitation applied to the earth is the same logic applied to the poor. [cite — confirm] The community that treats the soil as a resource to be used up rather than a gift to be tended has already made a decision about its relationship to the creation's other inhabitants. The farm that depletes its soil for short-term yield and the economic system that depletes its workers for short-term profit are operating from the same theological error: the assumption that the world and its contents exist to be consumed, not stewarded.

---

The early monastic communities understood something about creation that the contemporary church has mostly lost. The Benedictine rule of *ora et labora* — pray and work — included working the land with care, treating the material world as a site of encounter with God rather than a resource to be extracted. [cite — confirm] The monks who cleared forests and drained swamps in medieval Europe to create productive land were doing theology as well as agriculture. They were enacting the priestly vocation of Genesis 2 — tending the place where God is present, serving the creation as an expression of service to its owner.

That instinct was not environmentalism in the contemporary sense. It was older than that, and more basic. It was the recognition that the ground under your feet is holy because its owner is holy — that the care of the material world is a form of worship rather than a distraction from it.

---

What does faithfulness look like here? Not primarily a policy program, though policy matters. It looks like the church refusing to treat creation care as a partisan position — which means refusing the cultural alignment that made environmental concern a left-wing issue and indifference to it a right-wing virtue. The earth does not belong to any political coalition. It belongs to God. The question of how we treat it is a theological question before it is a political one.

It looks like congregations examining their own energy consumption, their own land use, their own patterns of waste and production and consumption, with the same seriousness they bring to examining their budget or their membership rolls. It looks like preachers willing to say from the pulpit what Psalm 24 says: this is not our world to consume. It belongs to God. We are accountable for what we have done to it.

It looks like Christian communities taking seriously the theological claim that creation itself has been included in the scope of God's redemptive work — that our bodies and the earth we inhabit are not incidental to the gospel but part of what the gospel is about.

---

The earth belongs to God. We have treated it as if it belonged to us, and more specifically as if it belonged to the present generation, free to consume in proportion to our capacity and to hand the consequences to people who had no voice in the decisions.

That is not stewardship. That is the old sin, dressed in modern machinery: the refusal to live within limits, the insistence that we are accountable to no one, the ancient hunger to be as God rather than to serve the God who made all of this and called it good.

The Psalmist does not ask whose it is. He states it. The claiming is already settled. The earth is the Lord's.

What remains is whether we will live accordingly — whether the people who claim to worship the earth's owner will treat it with the accountability that ownership implies, or whether we will continue to perform worship of God while treating God's world as our own to use up.

Those two things cannot both be true.

One of them has to give.

There is a version of the American story that goes like this: anyone who works hard enough can get an education, and education is the ladder out of poverty, and the ladder is available to everyone. We have told this story for so long and so loudly that many of us have stopped noticing what it requires us not to see.

What it requires us not to see is the funding structure. In most of the United States, public school funding is tied substantially to local property tax revenue. This means that a child who lives in a wealthy suburb attends a school with more resources per pupil than a child who lives in a low-income neighborhood. The structural outcome is that the children who most need educational investment receive the least of it, and the children who would succeed in almost any environment receive the most. The ladder is real. The rungs are not evenly spaced.

This is not a new observation. Jonathan Kozol documented it with shattering specificity in *Savage Inequalities*, published in 1991 [cite — confirm year], comparing per-pupil spending in wealthy and poor school districts in cities like Chicago, Camden, and East St. Louis. What he found was not merely difference but a difference that tracked almost perfectly with race and class — affluent white districts spending two to three times as much per student as poor Black and Latino districts in the same metropolitan area. The numbers have shifted over the decades, but the basic structure has not.

The church has, by and large, filed this under "policy question" and moved on. That is an error.

## The Theological Frame of Shalom

---

> The ladder is real. The rungs are not evenly spaced.

Begin with the biblical frame, because this is not primarily a policy question. It is a theological one.

## The Racial History of the Funding Structure

Proverbs 22:6 is often quoted in parenting discussions: "Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it." But the broader context of Proverbs is a vision of wisdom as the foundation of human flourishing — and wisdom, in the Hebrew tradition, is not purely spiritual. It is practical, material, cultivated through instruction and formation across years. The investment in children's learning is an investment in their capacity for tsedaqah — right-relatedness to God, neighbor, and community. To systematically under-invest in the formation of some children while over-investing in others is not just bad policy. It is a violation of the vision of shalom — the comprehensive flourishing of the whole community — that runs through the Hebrew prophets.

Isaiah 58:6–7 names what the fast God actually requires: "to loose the chains of injustice and untie the cords of the yoke, to set the oppressed free and break every yoke... to share your food with the hungry and to provide the poor wanderer with shelter." The "cords of the yoke" in the context of education inequality are the structural mechanisms that keep poor children tied to poor outcomes — not by accident, not by individual failure, but by system. The gleaning laws in Leviticus 19 built structural provision for the vulnerable into the economic order. The question is what the equivalent structural provision looks like in an educational economy.

## Formation Beyond the Test Score

The prophet Micah's indictment in Micah 2:1–2 is precise: "Woe to those who plan iniquity, to those who plot evil on their beds! At morning's light they carry it out because it is in their power to do it. They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them. They defraud people of their homes, they rob them of their inheritance." The inheritance seized is not always land. Sometimes it is the education that would have opened every subsequent door.

---

## When Complexity Forestalls Prophetic Clarity

> The naming is the prophetic work.

The property-tax funding structure has a history that cannot be separated from the history of race in America. The residential segregation of American cities — enforced through redlining, racially restrictive covenants, and discriminatory mortgage lending practices that persisted through the mid-twentieth century [cite — confirm timeline] — deliberately concentrated Black and Latino families in lower-value property. Since school funding followed property value, segregated housing produced segregated educational resources. The mechanism was not legally identified as racial discrimination. But the outcome was.

The Supreme Court took this question up in *San Antonio Independent School District v. Rodriguez* in 1973 [cite — confirm year], in which a group of Mexican American families in a poor Texas school district challenged the property-tax funding system as a violation of equal protection. The Court ruled 5-4 that education was not a fundamental right under the federal Constitution and that wealth-based disparities in school funding did not constitute unconstitutional discrimination [cite — confirm]. The decision effectively left the funding structure intact and left the challenge to individual states.

Some states have done significant work on equalization since then. Many have not. The basic pattern — that where you are born substantially determines the quality of education you receive — has remained remarkably persistent.

## Faith That Produces What It Claims to Care About

---

What does this mean for children concretely? It means some children arrive at kindergarten already behind, attend schools with larger class sizes, less experienced teachers, fewer counselors, deteriorating facilities, and outdated materials — and then are told that their lower test scores reflect their effort and ability rather than their circumstances. The meritocracy narrative requires the pretense that the starting conditions are comparable. They are not.

> Children in underfunded schools are not failing. They are being failed.

James K.A. Smith has argued, following Bourdieu, that formation is always embodied and environmental — that we become what we habitually practice, and that the habits we are able to practice depend significantly on the environments in which we develop [cite — confirm specific work]. A child in a well-resourced school environment is being formed — in habits of inquiry, in confidence, in relational skills, in the experience of institutional care — differently than a child in an under-resourced one. This is not primarily about test scores. It is about who you become over twelve years of daily formation in an institution.

The church talks about discipleship as formation. It does not always apply the same logic to the question of what schools form in children, and in whose children, and at whose expense.

---

The steel-man position here is worth engaging honestly. It goes like this: the evidence on what produces educational outcomes is genuinely complicated. Per-pupil spending correlates with outcomes in some studies and less strongly in others [cite — confirm state of research]. Teacher quality matters enormously, and throwing money at under-resourced schools without addressing the conditions that make good teachers leave those schools is insufficient. The problem of education inequality is real, but the solution is not simply equalized funding — it requires more comprehensive thinking about poverty, family structure, community stability, and the conditions that support learning.

This is a serious argument. Funding alone is not the answer. Teacher retention, school leadership, curricular quality, family stability, community investment — all of these matter, and some of them are not solved by funding formulas. The complexity here is genuine.

But notice the move again: the genuine complexity of solutions is used to forestall prophetic clarity about the injustice itself. The fact that solutions are complicated does not mean the pattern is not unjust. The fact that equalized funding is insufficient does not mean current funding inequity is acceptable. The complexity of the answer does not dissolve the clarity of the problem.

Amos was not offering a twelve-point economic reform plan. He was naming what was wrong. "They trample on the heads of the poor as on the dust of the ground and deny justice to the oppressed" (Amos 2:7). The naming is the prophetic work. The policy development follows the naming. The church that waits for a perfectly worked-out policy answer before naming the injustice will wait forever and call the waiting careful stewardship.

---

There is a dimension of this that the church encounters directly in its own communities: the way educational inequality shapes who shows up in its pews and who does not, what assumptions its teaching makes about literacy and access and cultural competence, and what it communicates to families whose children are in failing schools about whether the church sees them and their circumstances.

The congregation that has no idea what the school funding situation is in its own neighborhood has not been paying attention to the people it claims to love. The pastor who knows the name of every member's adult child's career but does not know whether the neighborhood elementary school has current textbooks has his attention organized around the wrong center.

Paying attention to the conditions of children's lives in the community is not an optional add-on to pastoral care. It is part of what it means to love your neighbors concretely rather than abstractly.

---

The New Testament is insistent that faith without works is dead (James 2:17). The works James is describing in that letter are not generalized spiritual activities — they are the specific, material responses to specific, material needs. He has just given the example of a person who is cold and hungry and is told, warmly, to be warm and fed without receiving warm clothes or food. The theological point is not subtle. The difference between a living faith and a dead one is whether it produces the thing it claims to care about.

If the church claims to care about children — and it does, loudly, in many contexts — then it has to ask what it means to care about children whose educational circumstances are structured against them. Not just their children. All children. Including the ones in the ZIP codes that do not share a property tax base with the church's neighborhood.

The vision of the kingdom that Jesus announced in Luke 4:18–19 — good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, recovery of sight to the blind — is a vision that reaches into every system that binds people. Educational systems that concentrate disadvantage in poor communities of color bind people. The vision of liberty the church proclaims is not just spiritual. It has always had material dimensions. The prophets knew this. The church's amnesia about it is a recent development.

Children in underfunded schools are not failing. They are being failed. There is a difference, and every institution that has the standing to name it and does not has made a choice.

The ladder is real. The church's job is to say plainly that some of its rungs are missing — and to ask, with prophetic seriousness, who took them.

The statistics are not new. Somewhere between 80 and 85 percent of American churches are not growing — they are holding, or they are shrinking, or they are in that particular purgatory where the numbers are stable but the median age keeps climbing and the children's wing gets quieter every year [cite — confirm]. Most pastors know this in the abstract. Fewer know it about themselves, because the knowledge that something is wrong is far easier to manage from a distance.

I have been the pastor of a plateaued church. I know what it feels like to look at the same forty-seven faces on a Sunday morning and tell yourself the story of faithfulness — that numbers are not the measure, that quality matters more than quantity, that God is at work even when you cannot see it. Most of that story is true. But some of it is a way of avoiding a harder question.

## Plateau Is a Diagnosis, Not a Verdict

---

Plateau is a diagnosis, not a verdict. It tells you something is not working — but it does not tell you what. And the failure mode most plateaued pastors fall into is to stop asking the diagnostic question, because the possible answers are unsettling.

> Plateau is a diagnosis, not a verdict.

The possible answers include: the community has genuinely changed, and the church has not changed with it. The preaching is solid, but the pathways for a newcomer to belong are broken. The culture of the church is warm to insiders and invisible to outsiders. The pastor is exhausted and the congregation has absorbed that exhaustion. The church's vision is compelling to the people who were already there in 2009 and entirely opaque to anyone who arrived after. None of these are failures of faith. All of them are failures of attention.

## The Invisible Costs of Good Decisions

There is a theology that needs to accompany this conversation, and it goes back further than any church growth literature. The letters to the seven churches in Revelation 2–3 are addressed to specific communities with specific pathologies. Ephesus has orthodoxy without love (Revelation 2:4). Sardis has a reputation for being alive and is dead (Revelation 3:1). Laodicea is neither hot nor cold, and that temperature is the problem — not the absence of belief, but the comfort that has made belief inconsequential. What is striking is that the risen Christ does not simply console these churches. He names the condition and calls for repentance.

This is the word the plateaued church most needs and most resists. Not "try harder." Not "add a program." Repentance — which in the Greek is metanoia, a turning, a reorientation of the whole person and the whole community toward the direction that had been abandoned or neglected. The word carries in it the assumption that there was a departure, and that recovery requires acknowledging the departure and returning. That acknowledgment is what most plateaued churches are not willing to do, because the acknowledgment requires naming something that will be uncomfortable for someone — usually the pastor, sometimes the long-tenured members, sometimes the entire culture the congregation has settled into.

## A Common Life Indistinguishable From the Culture

---

> It is being comfortable.

The plateau often has a history that begins before the numbers flatten. It begins with a set of decisions — not bad decisions, sometimes very good ones — that had invisible costs. The pastor who built a strong community of insiders and never developed the competency of welcome. The congregation that found its identity in a particular theological or stylistic niche and became, over time, a culture legible only to people who already fit the niche. The church that planted its flag during a season of cultural alignment that has now shifted — the neighborhood changed, the demographics changed, the questions the culture is asking changed, and the church kept preaching answers to questions its neighbors stopped asking.

## The Remnant and the Difference From Inertia

These are not moral failures. They are adaptive failures. And they are common precisely because the things that produced the plateau are often the things the church is most proud of. The theological depth that appeals deeply to seminary graduates and almost no one else. The liturgical seriousness that sustains the faith of people formed in high-church traditions and bewilders everyone outside that formation. The relational density of a community that has been together for twenty years and is genuinely, warmly, completely closed to any new person trying to break in.

The plateaued church often believes it is being faithful. It is being comfortable. And comfort and faithfulness are not the same thing.

---

> The question is whether the pastor is willing to hear it.

Acts 2 is the text that haunts this conversation. The early Jerusalem community after Pentecost added three thousand in a day (Acts 2:41) and continued adding to their number daily (Acts 2:47). That number gets cited in church growth conversations as aspiration. What rarely gets cited is the specific description of what that community was actually doing: devoted to the apostles' teaching and fellowship, to breaking bread and prayer, selling their possessions and giving to anyone who had need, holding everything in common (Acts 2:42-45). The growth was not the product of better marketing. It was the product of a community whose common life was so unusual, so genuinely different from anything the surrounding culture offered, that people were drawn to it as to something they had not seen before.

## The Audit the Congregation Resists

The plateaued church is often a church whose common life has become indistinguishable from the surrounding culture — except that it adds a Sunday morning meeting. The belonging is no deeper than what a good service organization offers. The mutual commitment is no more demanding than what a gym membership requires. The shared conviction is no more costly than a bumper sticker. When the community's life has nothing distinctive to offer, the plateau is not a mystery. It is a natural consequence.

---

The steel-man for staying the course exists and deserves respect: faithfulness in a declining context is a genuine calling, and not every church is supposed to grow numerically. The church that buries the dead, that sustains the elderly, that holds a small community together for another generation — that is real ministry, and it should not be despised. The prophetic tradition itself includes the remnant theology — the idea that faithfulness is sometimes expressed not in expansion but in endurance, in the refusal to compromise in the face of cultural pressure, in being the seven thousand who have not bowed the knee to Baal (1 Kings 19:18) even when the numbers are not impressive.

That tradition is real and it matters.

But faithfulness is not the same as inertia. The seven thousand who had not bowed the knee were not passive. They were actively faithful in a hostile environment. Their smallness was the result of their commitment, not the evidence of it. The church that is small because it refuses to compromise the Gospel is a different community than the church that is small because it has stopped asking whether it is actually engaging anyone.

The plateaued church needs to be honest about which of these it is. And the only way to be honest about it is to ask, with genuine openness to the answer, whether the plateau is the result of faithful distinctiveness or comfortable stagnation.

Most plateaued churches, if they are genuinely honest, will find elements of both. The faithfulness is real. The comfort is also real. And they have been using the faithfulness narrative to avoid examining the comfort.

---

The pastor who leads this examination has to begin with himself. Not with the congregation's failures, not with the community's changes, not with the cultural headwinds that every church in America is facing. With himself. What has he stopped seeing? What has he stopped asking? Where has he settled into the rhythm of the work without asking whether the work is actually producing the thing it is designed to produce?

The plateaued pastor is often exhausted. The plateau itself is demoralizing — the sense of working hard, of genuinely loving the people, of preaching as well as he knows how, and seeing nothing change. That exhaustion makes the diagnostic question harder to hold because he does not have the energy to sit with an answer that requires more from him than he currently has.

This is where the community of pastors matters — the friend or colleague or network that can hold the diagnostic question with him without flinching, that has seen enough plateaued churches to know the patterns, that can offer the specific and honest observation that the pastor cannot generate about himself. The pastor who is trying to diagnose his own plateau in isolation will almost always arrive at the most comfortable diagnosis available.

Plateau is a message. It is not comfortable. It is not delivered with cruelty, but it is delivered with weight. Something is not working, and the something may be something the congregation has been defending for years.

The question is whether the pastor is willing to hear it.

---

There is a specific move that the diagnostic process requires, and most plateaued pastors skip it because it is the most personally costly step: the community audit. Not a survey. Not a focus group. A genuine attempt to understand, from the perspective of people who visited and did not return, what they encountered. Why they left. What they found that they were not looking for, and what they were looking for that they did not find.

Most pastors do not do this because the honest answers are painful. The visitor who attended once and never came back is not invested in protecting the pastor's feelings. They will say directly what the loyal congregation member will never say — that the community felt closed, that the service felt performative, that the connection between what was preached and the actual lives of the people preaching it was not visible, that the community's real priorities were legible in its use of time and money even when the stated priorities were different.

Those answers are a gift. They are delivered without cruelty because they are delivered by people who are no longer invested enough in the community to be cruel. They are simply reporting what they observed before they left.

The pastor who receives those reports honestly — who does not deflect them into the narrative of "people want something easier" or "the culture is moving away from the church" — has access to diagnostic information that no internal process can produce. He can begin to see the gap between what the congregation believes it is and what the person in the parking lot on their way out actually encountered.

That gap is where the plateau lives.

Closing it requires the pastor to lead the congregation into a form of institutional self-examination that feels, to many long-tenured members, like criticism of something they love. It is criticism of something they love. Delivered carefully, with genuine affection and genuine hope, it is also the most loving thing the pastor can do for the community — to name what is true about what they have become, and to call them toward what they were created to be.

The willingness is the beginning of everything that follows.

The law comes to Moses in the wilderness, and among its provisions is a command that recurs with enough insistence to suggest it is load-bearing for the whole structure: *Stand up in the presence of the aged, show respect for the elderly and revere your God* (Leviticus 19:32). The instruction appears in the same chapter as the commands to leave grain at the field's edge for the poor and the foreigner, to not defraud or rob your neighbor, to not oppress the hired worker. The honor of the elderly is not a category of sentimental social custom. It is law, in the same legal register as the prohibitions on theft and oppression.

The church has preached this in the general. It has largely missed it in the specific. The specific is this: elder abuse — the physical, emotional, financial, and sexual abuse of older adults — is one of the most widespread and underreported forms of violence in America, and the church has treated it as though it is not there.

Approximately one in ten Americans over the age of sixty experiences some form of elder abuse each year [cite — confirm]. That figure is almost certainly an undercount. Elder abuse is notoriously underreported because its victims are often dependent on their abusers, isolated from community, cognitively impaired, or living with the particular shame of being abused by the people they trusted most. The perpetrators are frequently family members — adult children, spouses, paid caregivers — which means the victim faces a choice between naming the abuse and losing the relationship or remaining silent and enduring the harm. Most remain silent.

## What the Church Is Positioned to See

The church is in a position to see what the general society misses. The older adults who attend services, who receive pastoral visits, who are known to the congregation by name — these are exactly the people whose isolation and dependence can be interrupted by genuine community. A pastor who visits, an elder who checks in, a deacon who notices that the woman who used to be in every Sunday is missing — these are not extraordinary acts. They are the ordinary functions of a community that takes its theology of the elderly seriously.

> But this requires the church to first take the problem seriously.

But this requires the church to first take the problem seriously.

## The Missing Theology of Aging

The invisibility of elder abuse in the church's prophetic discourse is partly a function of the invisibility of the elderly in the broader culture. The United States does not have a strong theology of aging. The culture of youth, productivity, and independence treats the old as people who have finished doing the things that matter and are now waiting for what comes next. The congregation reflects this: the programs, the growth strategies, the outreach efforts are overwhelmingly oriented toward young adults, young families, the demographic groups the church considers its future. The elderly are present, often generously present in their giving and service, but they are rarely the focus of deliberate pastoral attention.

This is a theological failure before it is a programmatic one. The biblical tradition does not treat the elderly as people who have finished being useful. Psalm 92:12–14 describes the righteous who still bear fruit in old age, full of sap and green — an image of continued vitality and contribution that contradicts the culture's account of aging as primarily loss. The wisdom tradition in Proverbs and Job treats the accumulated experience of the elderly as a genuine form of knowledge that the young cannot access through their own effort. Leviticus 19:32 makes the honor of the aged a direct expression of reverence for God — *revere your God*, the command concludes, which means that dismissal of the elderly is not simply a social failure. It is a theological one.

## Naming the Specific Forms of Abuse

The specific forms of elder abuse deserve concrete naming, because the church tends to engage more readily with what it can see and name.

Financial exploitation is the most common form, and it frequently goes undetected in congregational settings. An older congregant gradually transfers control of finances to an adult child who begins to use those resources for personal benefit. A cognitively declining member signs documents she does not understand. A paid caregiver with power of attorney begins to access accounts. The external presentation at church can remain entirely normal — the person arrives on Sunday, appears to be cared for, seems comfortable — while the exploitation proceeds invisibly at home. The pastoral relationship that includes genuine, regular conversation about how the person is actually living is the thing that can interrupt this pattern.

Physical and emotional abuse are less common but more severe. The older adult who arrives at church with unexplained injuries, who flinches at certain interactions, who seems afraid to speak honestly in the presence of a particular family member — these are signs the congregation is equipped to see if it has been taught to see them. Most have not.

Sexual abuse of the elderly is the form most difficult to discuss, and therefore most completely absent from the church's attention. It happens, disproportionately in institutional settings and at the hands of trusted caregivers [cite — confirm]. The silence around it in the church is not different from the silence around every other form of sexual abuse the church has been slow to name. The same dynamics — shame, disbelief, the instinct to protect institutions and relationships — operate here. The corrective is the same: naming it, creating safe channels for disclosure, believing the person who reports it.

Isolation is both a form of abuse and the condition that makes other forms possible. The abuser who separates an older adult from the community that would notice — from the congregation, from the adult children who don't live nearby, from the neighbors — has created the conditions in which everything else becomes possible. The congregation that maintains regular contact with its older members is not only providing fellowship. It is providing protection.

## Beyond the Pastoral Constraint

> The response to complexity is not silence.

Proverbs 31:8–9 issues a direct command: *Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights of all who are destitute. Speak up and judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy.* The older adult whose cognitive impairment or social isolation has made self-advocacy impossible is exactly the person this command is addressing. The church that regards the command as applying in principle but lacks the structures to implement it in practice has not yet obeyed the command.

The steel-man for the pastoral constraint is real: the church is not a social services agency. Pastors are not trained as elder abuse investigators or geriatric care specialists. The complexity of family systems, the legal dimensions of intervention, the risk of false accusation — these are genuine considerations that should not be dismissed. A congregation that begins accusing families on the basis of incomplete information can do serious harm.

## The Test the Prophets Keep Returning To

This is true. And it does not resolve the obligation. The response to complexity is not silence. It is preparation: training congregational care teams in the signs of elder abuse, building relationships with social service agencies and adult protective services, creating clear channels through which members can raise concerns, and cultivating the kind of pastoral relationship with older congregants that makes honest disclosure possible. None of this requires the pastor to be a forensic investigator. It requires the congregation to take seriously that the people it has been entrusted with include some of the most vulnerable people in its community.

The theological test the prophets return to, again and again, is the treatment of those who cannot protect themselves. The widow, the orphan, the stranger — the triad that appears across Exodus, Deuteronomy, the Psalms, and the prophets as the measure of the community's faithfulness. The list is not exhaustive. It is a principle: God's interest is particularly with the ones who are vulnerable to exploitation because they lack the power to prevent it. The elderly person who is cognitively declining, financially dependent on an adult child, isolated from community, and afraid to speak — that person is exactly the human being the prophetic tradition most demands the community protect.

> Naming it does not absolve me.

The congregation that walks past this vulnerability — that attends to the programs and the preferences of the visible and the vocal while the elderly sit quietly and endure what they are enduring — has not failed a program objective. It has failed the theological test.

I have been in rooms with elderly congregants and known something was not right and said nothing because I did not know what to say, because I did not want to create conflict, because I was not sure. I have prioritized my comfort over their safety in moments when the pastoral call was to speak. That is my part in the failure I am describing. Naming it does not absolve me. It identifies what the correction requires.

Honor the face of the old man (Leviticus 19:32, ESV). Not as sentiment. Not as courtesy. As law, grounded in reverence for the God who made him — and who will hold accountable the community that looked away.

Emotional labor is not a clinical term. It is a sociological one, introduced by Arlie Hochschild to describe the invisible management work involved in anticipating needs, maintaining the emotional temperature of a relationship, and ensuring that the people around you feel cared for [cite — confirm]. In a marriage, it includes things like remembering the anniversary, initiating the difficult conversation, tracking the family's emotional calendar, and being the one who notices when something is wrong before it becomes a crisis.

One spouse usually does most of it. In most marriages, that spouse is the wife. In some marriages, it is the husband. In nearly all marriages, the spouse doing it is exhausted, and the spouse not doing it has no idea the work exists.

That last part is the important part. The unawareness is not a moral failure. It is a blindspot — shaped by formation, by default, by the simple fact that invisible work does not announce itself. But unawareness, once named, becomes a choice. And the choice to remain unaware after it has been named is something different.

> One spouse usually does most of it.

## The Theological Frame

Philippians 2:4 says "let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others." Paul is writing to a community, but the verb — *skopeō*, to observe closely, to fix one's eye on — implies active attention. Not the passive assumption that what you are not noticing does not exist. Looking.

The verse is embedded in one of the most demanding passages in the New Testament. Verses 3-4 call for humility that considers the other person "more significant than yourselves" — which in Greco-Roman culture was not a virtue at all. It was the disposition of a slave. Paul is inverting the honor economy of his world and asking believers to enact that inversion in the most immediate relationships of their lives.

Applied to the emotional labor question: the spouse who has defaulted into not noticing is not enacting the Philippians 2 posture. They are doing the opposite — seeing their own interest, their own comfort, their own freedom from the work, as the natural default. The work gets done because someone else does it. That is an arrangement, not a partnership.

The failure in most marriages with an emotional labor imbalance is not malice. It is the failure to look. The exhausted spouse has been managing the invisible work so competently that their competence has made the work invisible. They handle it so nothing falls. Nothing falling registers as nothing happening. And the managing spouse concludes, in their loneliest moments, that the only way to stop being alone in this is to stop doing it — which terrifies them, because they know what falls when they stop.

**The person who manages everything so nothing falls is invisible until they stop. That is a terrible way to be seen.**

## The Historical and Cultural Roots of the Imbalance

The emotional labor imbalance in marriage does not come from nowhere. It comes from a long history of gendered division of what counted as work. The Industrial Revolution produced a sharp separation between the workplace — where productive labor happened and was economically valued — and the household — where reproductive and relational labor happened and was considered natural rather than work [cite — confirm]. Women's labor inside the home was not called work. It was called being a wife, being a mother, being good at those things.

> The work gets done because someone else does it. That is an arrangement, not a partnership.

The mid-twentieth century expansion of women into the workforce did not automatically redistribute the household and relational labor. It added a second set of demands to an existing set that had never been valued or measured. The result — documented extensively in sociology since the 1980s — is what scholars call the "double burden" or "second shift": women working full-time outside the home while still carrying the majority of domestic and emotional management inside it [cite — confirm].

The church has not always helped here. The theological language of "servant leadership" applied asymmetrically — wives called to serve, husbands called to lead — has in many contexts functioned to spiritualize the imbalance rather than address it. The Proverbs 31 woman is held up as the model of competent domestic management without sufficient attention to what the text is actually doing: it is praise poetry written about a woman by a mother to her son, describing the extraordinary scope of what a woman can be, not prescribing a template of domestic burden for every wife.

## A Concrete Pastoral Scene

A woman I know — a professional, a mother of three, a person with an actual theology of service — told me she had been the emotional manager of her household for so long that she could not remember what it felt like to not be on call. Her husband was not unkind. He was oblivious. And she had never named it, because naming it felt like either complaint or accusation, and she did not want to be the kind of wife who complained.

What she eventually named — in a session, in tears, with her husband sitting across from her — was not the specific tasks. It was the weight of being the only person in the marriage who was paying attention to the marriage. That is a different and heavier thing.

Her husband's response, to his credit, was not defensive. He was genuinely shocked. The work had been so thoroughly managed that he had simply never seen it. What he said, after a long silence, was something like: "I thought everything was fine because nothing was going wrong. I didn't realize that was because you were holding everything up."

That recognition was the beginning of something. Not the resolution — the beginning. Real change in how a marriage distributes invisible work requires ongoing attention, specific redistribution, and the willingness of the previously unaware spouse to develop a new set of habits. None of that happens in one conversation. But the conversation is where it starts.

## The Counter-Position Honestly Stated

Some would argue that the framing of emotional labor as an imbalance to be corrected imports a transactional logic into what should be a self-offering relationship. In a marriage ordered by genuine love, each partner gives freely rather than keeping score. The wife who has carried the emotional management has been practicing exactly the self-giving that the gospel calls for. The demand for equitable distribution is the language of contract rather than covenant.

This objection has a kind of theological attractiveness that obscures its practical effect. In practice, "she gives freely so don't keep score" produces the same result as "she gives freely so don't share the burden" — which is a permanent structural imbalance that exhausts one person while insulating the other from the cost of partnership. Covenant love is not the evasion of shared responsibility. It is its deepest ground.

The scriptural instruction is mutual: "Husbands, love your wives" (Ephesians 5:25). "Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another" (Ephesians 4:32). "Bear one another's burdens" (Galatians 6:2). None of these are instructions for one partner to bear more. They are descriptions of mutual practice. The partner who is not paying attention to the emotional life of the marriage is not practicing covenant love. They are benefiting from it without contributing to it.

## What Has to Change

For the spouse carrying the imbalance: the work has to be named, not just felt. "I do this and this and this, and it does not get done unless I do it" is a different conversation than "you never help me." Specificity creates the possibility of change. Generalized grievance creates defensiveness.

For the spouse who has been unaware: the question to ask is not "what should I do" — that question, ironically, shifts the management back to the exhausted person. The question is "what am I not noticing?" Noticing is the job. What doesn't get noticed doesn't get managed. Learning to notice is the first act of genuine shared partnership.

And for both: the expectation that this work should be invisible is worth examining. We do not admire professionals for making difficult work look effortless and then conclude the work was not hard. We should apply the same logic at home.

## Three Questions for This Week

If you are carrying the imbalance: what is the single most exhausting invisible task you manage? Have you named it specifically to your spouse — not complained about it, but described what it actually requires of you?

If you may be the unaware spouse: spend one day actively noticing what gets managed in your household that you have not managed. Make a list. The length of the list is information.

For both: what would a genuinely equal partnership look like in your specific household? Not equal in the abstract — equal in the specific distribution of the specific tasks that actually exist.

**This week:** the aware spouse names one thing. The unaware spouse takes ownership of one thing — fully, without requiring management — and does it without being asked.

Marriages in which the emotional labor is shared do not happen by accident. They happen because two people decided to pay attention to what the other person is carrying and to refuse to let invisible work remain invisible.

Seeing your spouse clearly is one of the primary acts of love available to you.

Start by looking.

> Seeing your spouse clearly is one of the primary acts of love available to you.

They are not atheists, most of them. That is the first thing the data tells us, and it is the thing most churches have gotten most wrong about the religiously unaffiliated — the category researchers call the "Nones," the people who mark "no religion" on surveys. The surveys consistently show that a substantial majority of American Nones believe in some form of God or higher power, pray occasionally, and retain spiritual impulses they do not know what to do with [cite — confirm].

They left — or never arrived — not because they resolved the God question in the negative. They left because the institutional church failed to meet them where the real questions live.

That is a more demanding diagnosis than hostility would be. Hostility has a clear response: make a better argument, find common ground, extend an invitation. But institutional failure that has become personal — the Catholic who left after the abuse revelations, the evangelical who watched her church consume itself over politics, the young man who asked genuine questions about suffering and received platitudes — that is not fixed by a sharper apologetic or a more engaging worship service. It requires something closer to repentance.

## A Diagnosis More Demanding Than Hostility

---

> It is trust.

The growth of the religiously unaffiliated in the United States is one of the most significant cultural shifts of the last half-century. In 1972, roughly 5 percent of Americans identified as having no religious affiliation [cite — confirm]. By the early 2020s, that number had grown to somewhere between 26 and 30 percent, depending on the survey [cite — confirm]. That is not a rounding error or a sampling anomaly. It is a generational shift that has continued through economic booms and recessions, through periods of cultural conservatism and cultural liberalism, through everything the church has tried to reverse it.

The church's primary response to this shift has been programmatic: better music, better communication, more culturally relevant services, targeted outreach to specific demographics. The programs have not reversed the trend. They have, in some cases, slowed the decline in specific congregations for specific periods. But the overall direction has been consistent, which is itself a diagnostic: if the problem were primarily one of presentation, better presentation would have solved it by now.

## The Problem Is Not Presentation. It Is Trust

The problem is not primarily presentation. It is trust.

---

The research on why people leave, and why they stay away, points consistently toward three things [cite — confirm]. First: hypocrisy perceived between the church's stated values and its institutional behavior. Second: the sense that the church was not a safe place for honest doubt. Third: the absence of intellectually serious engagement with the questions they were actually carrying.

## Honesty as the Posture of Credibility

> This is not a posture of weakness. It is a posture of credibility.

These are not primarily communication problems. They are formation problems, and they took decades to produce.

The hypocrisy problem is specific and documented, not a vague feeling. The sexual abuse scandals in the Catholic Church, extending across multiple continents and implicating the institutional hierarchy in systematic cover-up rather than protection of victims — these are not stories about a few bad actors. They are stories about institutional culture, about the prioritization of institutional reputation over the welfare of the most vulnerable. The evangelical institutions that have faced similar revelations in the past two decades have added their own chapters to the same story. People who left citing institutional hypocrisy are not offering a subjective feeling. They are naming something real. The church that is serious about reaching them will not paper over that reality with better messaging.

The doubt problem runs deeper in the tradition than most pastors realize. The Psalms contain prayers of lament and accusation and abandonment that the church rarely reads in worship. Job's friends are consistently wrong in the text, and Job — the man who argues with God, who refuses the comfortable answers, who demands to be heard — is the one God ultimately vindicates. Thomas, who demanded to see the wounds and touch them, is given that encounter by the risen Christ without rebuke; John 20:27 does not record Jesus scolding him for his refusal to believe the other disciples' report. The canonical testimony is that God is not threatened by doubt and does not require its suppression as a condition for relationship. The church that treats doubt as a spiritual failure has not learned from Job or Thomas. And the people who felt unwelcome with their questions — who were told to have more faith when what they needed was someone to sit with the hard thing — remember that exactly as it was.

## Making Room for the Psalm 22 Question

---

What does this mean for the pastor who wants to reach his own community's Nones?

It means starting with honesty about what the church has been. Not self-flagellation — that can be its own form of performance, the institution that catastrophizes its failures to demonstrate that it takes them seriously, which is still performance. But the genuine acknowledgment that the institution has, in specific and documented ways, failed the people it claimed to serve. This is not a posture of weakness. It is a posture of credibility. The church that cannot name its own failures has given people every reason to trust it with nothing.

## The Resurrection Witness as Non-Negotiable

Lesslie Newbigin, writing in the late twentieth century about the challenge of Christian witness in the post-Enlightenment West, argued that the church's primary apologetic task was not intellectual argument but embodied demonstration — that the congregation itself was the hermeneutic of the gospel, that the most compelling evidence for the truth of Christian claims was a community that actually lived by them [cite — confirm]. That argument reads differently now than it did when Newbigin wrote it. Because the question the Nones are asking is not "can you make a compelling argument?" It is "is there a community that actually lives what it claims?" And the honest answer, in too many cases, is no — or not consistently enough to be credible.

The communities that have had success reaching the unaffiliated are not primarily the communities with the best apologetics program or the most culturally current worship. They are communities where the gap between stated values and actual practice has been narrowed by sustained, costly commitment. Where the response to abuse allegations was protection of victims rather than protection of reputation. Where the doubter was welcomed rather than managed. Where the poor were actually served, not used as sermon illustrations.

> They are mostly waiting.

---

It means creating space for actual questions. Not questions that end in predetermined answers — which is what most seeker-sensitive ministry has meant in practice — but questions that are allowed to remain unresolved while the community continues to gather around them.

The Psalms are full of unanswered questions. Psalm 22 opens with "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — not a rhetorical question, not a question the psalmist is about to answer, but a genuine cry from abandonment. Jesus quotes it from the cross. The canon of Scripture contains more lament and confusion than most church services do. The person who left because their doubts were unwelcome will not return for a church that only tolerates doubt as a stage on the way to certainty. She will return for a church that has room for the Psalm 22 question without immediately rushing to Easter Sunday.

It means being present in the community before you ask anyone to show up on Sunday. The Nones are your neighbors, your coworkers, the parents sitting across from you at the school board meeting. They are not a target demographic. They are people. Meeting them as people — with genuine interest in their lives, not as a strategy for eventual conversion — is both the ethically right thing and, over time, the only thing that actually works.

The instrumental relationship — I am interested in you because you are a potential convert — is one of the things the Nones are most practiced at identifying. They have been on the receiving end of enough transactional connection, in enough contexts, to know when someone is interested in them rather than in a version of them they need. The pastor who shows up in the neighborhood because he lives there and loves it, who coaches the soccer team because the kids on it need coaching, who attends the city council meeting because the city he serves is the city that meeting governs — that pastor has something to offer the Nones that the targeted outreach program does not.

---

I have seen this done well. I have seen it done poorly. The difference is not theological sophistication or program quality. The difference is whether the congregation genuinely loves the people it is trying to reach — whether the Nones in the neighborhood are seen as objects of mission or as people to whom the church owes a debt of honesty about its own failures and a genuine witness to the resurrection.

The resurrection witness is the non-negotiable. The church that has become so sensitive to the Nones' institutional wariness that it no longer makes the specific, costly, intellectually demanding claim that Jesus rose from the dead has nothing to offer that a good therapist or community organization cannot provide. The pastoral move is not to suppress the claim but to earn the credibility to make it — to be a community whose life is evidence that the thing it proclaims has actually changed it.

That witness is costly. It requires the church to be what it says it is before it invites anyone in. That is not a communications strategy. It is discipleship. And it is the only thing the Nones, many of them already suspicious of the gap between word and deed, will ultimately trust.

The thirty percent who have left are not mostly gone. They are mostly waiting. Waiting to see if there is a community that means what it says.

Whether they find one depends on what the church decides to do with that diagnosis.

There is a map you can pull up. It overlays two datasets — the location of toxic waste sites, industrial polluters, highways built through residential neighborhoods, lead pipe water systems — and the racial composition of those neighborhoods. You do not need a statistics degree to read it. The overlap is not subtle. It is not coincidental. It is the story of a country that decided, across a century of policy, whose air would be clean.

That is the blunt claim, and it deserves to be made bluntly before we dress it in any theological language. Environmental racism is not a conspiracy theory. It is a documented pattern of environmental burdens falling with consistent, measurable disproportionality on communities of color. It is in the siting decisions of the 1930s through the 1970s that placed freeways through Black and Latino neighborhoods. It is in the industrial zoning choices that put refineries and chemical plants adjacent to low-income communities of color. It is in Flint, Michigan — not far from this desk — where a decision made in 2014 by unelected emergency managers exposed a predominantly Black city to lead-contaminated water for eighteen months while state officials disputed the evidence their own scientists were producing.

The church that cannot name this is not preaching a full gospel. Not even close.

## The Vocation Beneath the Stewardship

> The church that cannot name this is not preaching a full gospel. Not even close.

---

Begin earlier. The biblical theology of creation does not begin with stewardship as an afterthought. It begins with vocation. Genesis 1–2 places the human creature inside a created order that is declared good before human beings arrive in it. The land, the water, the air — they carry intrinsic value in the economy of creation before they carry instrumental value to us. To be placed in the garden was not to be given a resource extraction operation. It was to be given a home to tend and a world to protect.

The Hebrew word is *shamar* — to keep, to guard, to watch over (Genesis 2:15). It is the same word used later in the Aaronic blessing: the Lord *keep* you (Numbers 6:24). The earth is not ours to exhaust. It is a trust. And a trust can be violated.

## The Documented History and Its Shape

When Ezekiel 34 accuses the shepherds of Israel of ruining the pastures and fouling the water with their feet so the sheep must drink what the shepherds have muddied (Ezekiel 34:18), it is speaking of leaders, not of factory owners. But the logic maps precisely. Power fouling what others must drink. That is the structure of environmental racism — not in every case the product of deliberate malice, but the predictable output of systems in which the powerful do not have to live downstream of the decisions they make.

The poor communities, the communities of color, the communities without political weight — they live downstream. They always have.

---

## Flint, Slowly Considered

The documented history is long, but some moments carry specific weight. Robert Bullard, a sociologist at Texas Southern University, published *Dumping in Dixie* in 1990 [cite — confirm year], one of the first systematic studies to document the correlation between race, income, and proximity to hazardous waste facilities in the American South. What he found was not random distribution. It was pattern — a consistent finding that Black communities hosted a disproportionate share of landfills, incinerators, and industrial facilities. The book catalyzed an environmental justice movement that evangelical Christianity largely watched from the outside.

In 1987, the United Church of Christ's Commission for Racial Justice released a report titled *Toxic Wastes and Race in the United States* [cite — confirm year and organization], which found that race was the most significant predictor of proximity to hazardous waste facilities — more significant than poverty, more significant than home values. This report generated significant public attention and essentially no evangelical response of record.

> Charity distributes bottled water. Justice asks why the lead is in the pipes.

Meanwhile, the largely white evangelical environmental movement — when it finally emerged — organized itself primarily around climate change as an issue of stewardship and creation care, which is a legitimate frame. But it largely left the environmental justice dimension — who bears the worst costs of environmental degradation — underaddressed and often unspoken.

## When Complexity Arrives at Silence

That silence has a shape. The shape is race.

---

Consider the particulars of Flint, and consider them slowly, because they are not ancient history. They are 2014 through 2016. They are children drinking lead-contaminated water. Lead is neurotoxic at any level of exposure. There is no safe dose for a developing brain. The children who drank that water will carry the neurological effects of that exposure into adulthood — cognitive effects, behavioral effects, health effects that follow them through life. The state of Michigan's own scientists raised alarms [cite — confirm]. Those alarms were dismissed. The community continued to drink the water. When a pediatrician named Mona Hanna-Attisha published blood-lead data demonstrating the contamination's effects on children [cite — confirm name and timeline], she was publicly challenged by state officials before being vindicated.

## The Image of God and Who Deserves Clean Water

Flint is seventy percent Black. That fact does not explain every decision made in that crisis. But it is naive — or dishonest — to pretend it explains none of them. The structure of American governance has not, historically, applied the same standards of urgency to the health crises of Black communities that it applies to others. That is not a political accusation. It is a historical finding.

> We are not separate.

The church in Flint showed up. Local churches opened their doors as water distribution points, organized volunteers, took in donations. The generosity was real. But the church that only does charity when the crisis is acute — and does not ask how the crisis was allowed to develop, and does not name what the pattern suggests — has done something less than prophetic.

Charity distributes bottled water. Justice asks why the lead is in the pipes.

---

The steel-man case against calling this a justice issue worth prophetic attention goes roughly like this: these are complex policy questions involving competing economic interests, regulatory tradeoffs, and technical expertise. The church should not oversimplify them. The pattern, while real, does not always reflect explicit racial intent — often it reflects poverty, since poor communities of any race have less political power. The church risks politicization when it takes up these issues under a justice frame.

There is something to this. Policy is complex. Correlation does not always indicate explicit discriminatory intent. The church should speak with humility about mechanisms it does not fully understand.

But notice what this argument does. It begins with complexity and arrives at silence. It uses the genuine difficulty of policy questions to justify disengagement from the human consequences. The children in Flint did not need the church to have a sophisticated position on water infrastructure finance. They needed the church to see them, name what was happening to them, and refuse to be quiet about it.

And the prophetic tradition — the tradition of Amos, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Micah — did not wait for policy clarity before naming what the powerful were doing to the vulnerable. It named it. The prophets spoke about economic systems that ground the poor into the dust (Amos 8:4–6), about scales falsified in the markets, about land seizure and legal systems turned against the defenseless. They did not hedge those indictments with careful notes about systemic complexity. The complexity was real. The injustice was also real. The prophets named the injustice.

The church today is not asked to choose between complexity and clarity. It is asked to hold both — to understand the systems and still name the harm.

---

The theology underneath this is *imago Dei* — the image of God. Genesis 1:26–27 locates the image of God in every human being regardless of race, class, or any other marker. This is not a spiritual abstraction. It is a claim about who deserves clean water. It is a claim about which children deserve air that does not make them sick. It is a claim about which communities deserve to have their health crises treated with the same urgency as anyone else's.

If the image of God is borne equally by the child in a wealthy suburb and the child in a neighborhood adjacent to a refinery, then the different quality of air those children breathe is not just a policy problem. It is a theological problem. It is a violation of something fundamental about the created order.

The apostle Paul, writing to the Galatians, is unambiguous: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). This does not erase the categories. Paul knows perfectly well those categories continue to exist and to carry social weight. What he is saying is that in the economy of the kingdom, they cannot be permitted to determine who is valued and who is expendable.

They cannot. But they do. And the church is called to name the distance between what the kingdom says and what the present order produces.

---

Some churches in communities of color have been doing this work for decades without significant support from white evangelical institutions. The environmental justice work of faith-based organizations in places like Houston's Fifth Ward and along Louisiana's Cancer Alley [cite — confirm] has been persistent and largely invisible to the broader evangelical world. These communities have lived the intersection of race, poverty, and environmental harm. They have organized against it. They have prayed over it. They have buried their dead from it.

That witness deserves more than discovery. It deserves solidarity — the theological commitment, rooted in membership in one body, to treat what happens to those communities as something that has happened to us.

We are not separate. The body does not function when it decides that some of its members do not matter.

---

What does this require in practice? It requires the church to know where it lives. To understand the environmental conditions of the community it claims to serve. To ask, specifically, whether the people in its neighborhood have clean water and breathable air. To ask whose children are bearing the worst of whatever pollution exists nearby. To speak — not vaguely, not only about creation care in the abstract, but about the concrete distribution of environmental harm and the communities that bear it.

It requires the willingness to name race. The church that discusses environmental stewardship without discussing environmental racism has named the right problem and described only part of it.

And it requires the long commitment that prophetic witness always requires. The families living near petrochemical facilities in Louisiana have been fighting those facilities for generations. Their fight is not over. The church's solidarity with them cannot be a news-cycle response. It has to be the kind of presence that shows up before the cameras and stays after they leave.

The map is legible. The pattern is documented. The children are still breathing the air.

The question the church has to answer is not whether environmental racism exists. That question has been answered. The question is whether we will name it or manage it — whether we will stand inside the evidence and speak from it, or manage the discomfort of it from a careful distance.

Managing discomfort is not prophetic. It is its opposite.

The earth is the Lord's, and everything in it (Psalm 24:1). Including the lungs of the children who live downstream.

The word eschatology comes from the Greek eschaton — the last thing, the final moment, the end toward which everything is moving. It is the branch of theology that deals with what happens at the end of history: the return of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, the judgment, the new creation. In most American evangelical churches, it produces either charts or embarrassment. The charts belong to the prophecy conference circuit — elaborate dispensational timelines with color-coded dispensations and rapture sequences and tribulation chronologies. The embarrassment belongs to everyone else who has watched the charts be wrong again and again while the chart-makers adjust their timelines and proceed as though nothing has happened.

Both responses miss the point. The eschatology that actually matters is not a predictive timeline. It is a fundamental orientation toward reality — a set of convictions about the ultimate destiny of history that determines how the community of faith lives in the present.

## Where This Conversation Has to Start

> Both responses miss the point.

Dispensational premillennialism entered mainstream American evangelicalism largely through the influence of John Nelson Darby's teachings in the nineteenth century, popularized in the Scofield Reference Bible published in 1909 [cite — confirm]. The system divided history into discrete epochs of God's activity and located the church in a parenthetical age between the postponement of the kingdom and its future establishment. The practical consequence was a sharp dualism between the present age and the coming age — and a corresponding devaluation of work done in the present order. If the rapture is imminent and the world will be burned up and replaced, then investment in the political and social structures of the present age is not only unnecessary but theologically confused.

This is not marginal theology. It has shaped the instincts of tens of millions of American Christians across the twentieth century. It is the background assumption against which any engagement with questions of justice, environmental care, and political responsibility has had to argue. When someone says "why rearrange the deck chairs on the Titanic," they are expressing an eschatology. They may not know it. They are.

## The Eschatological Community of the New Testament

The New Testament church was an eschatological community. This is not an observation about their theology. It is an observation about the lived structure of their common life. They believed that Jesus had been raised from the dead — not symbolically, not spiritually, not metaphorically, but bodily. They believed that his resurrection was the firstfruits of a general resurrection that was coming (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). They believed that history was moving toward a definitive moment in which God would complete what the resurrection had begun — the renewal of all things, the defeat of death, the restoration of the creation that had been subjected to futility.

That belief shaped what they did with their lives. If death is defeated, then no threat of death can ultimately control the community's behavior. If the resurrection is coming, then investment in the poor and the sick and the imprisoned is not lost labor — it is seed sown into a harvest that God will bring in. If God is working toward the renewal of all things, then the material world — bodies, meals, the care of the earth, the structures of human community — has ultimate weight rather than being a temporary stage that will soon be discarded.

This is why Paul, in 1 Corinthians 15, after his long argument for the resurrection, ends with a completely unexpected practical instruction: "Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain" (v. 58). The resurrection is not a comfort for the afterlife. It is the ground for present-tense action. The work you do now matters because it is being gathered into an ultimate story in which it will be honored.

N.T. Wright has argued at length [cite — confirm] that the resurrection of Jesus is not the beginning of a purely spiritual existence for the departed but the beginning of the new creation — the first act of God's renewal of the physical world that will be completed at the consummation. To believe in the resurrection, on this reading, is not to believe in escape from the material world. It is to believe that the material world has a future, and that work done in and for the material world participates in that future.

## The Gnostic Alternative We Have Absorbed

The alternative to eschatological hope — the practical eschatology that operates below the surface in a lot of American Christianity — is something closer to ancient Gnosticism than to biblical Christianity. The Gnostics believed that the material world was not the good creation of the good God but the flawed product of a lesser deity, and that salvation consisted in the escape of the spiritual soul from its material prison. The material world was ultimately worthless. What mattered was the spiritual reality above it.

> This is not the eschatology of the New Testament.

American Christianity has not embraced Gnosticism explicitly. It has absorbed a functional version of it. The body does not ultimately matter — what matters is the soul's eternal destiny. The earth does not ultimately matter — it will be burned up anyway. History does not ultimately matter — it is all moving toward the rapture, after which God starts fresh. The political and social structures of the present age do not ultimately matter — they are temporary arrangements of a fallen world that will soon be replaced.

This is not the eschatology of the New Testament. Revelation 21–22 does not describe the creation being destroyed and replaced by something entirely different. It describes the New Jerusalem coming down from heaven to earth — the heavenly reality descending into the material world, renewing and completing it. "Behold, I am making all things new" (Revelation 21:5) — not replacing all things with different things. The distinction is enormous. If creation is renewed rather than replaced, then the work done in creation — the justice sought, the relationships repaired, the earth tended — is not discarded. It is taken up and completed.

The word translated "new" in Revelation 21:5 is kainos — new in quality, renewed, rather than neos — new in the sense of having not existed before. The Greek is doing work there that the English flattens. God is making the old creation new, not making an entirely different thing and discarding what existed. The new creation is the resurrection of this creation.

## What Two Eschatologies Produce

A community that believes history will be burned up and replaced will have little motivation to work on its political and social structures. Why rearrange the deck chairs? The present order is not worth investing in because it has no ultimate future.

A community that believes God is working toward the renewal of all things will invest in the structures of the present order — not because the present order is not broken, but because the broken present is the raw material of the renewed future. The work of justice done now is seed sown into the ground of what God is bringing. It is not wasted. It will be gathered.

These are not identical communities. They will make different choices about where to spend their energy and their resources. They will answer differently the question of whether to build affordable housing or simply preach about the poor. They will answer differently the question of whether to advocate for just criminal sentencing or simply minister to people in prison. They will answer differently the question of whether the church has any stake in the political structures of the society it lives inside.

The steel-man version of the dispensational position is worth hearing: perhaps the very urgency of eschatological expectation produces its own kind of engagement — if people are dying and eternity is real, then nothing is more important than the proclamation of the gospel, and everything else takes second place. Paul himself seemed to operate this way in some of his letters. The urgency of the coming end concentrated attention.

The problem is that this logic, followed consistently, produces a community that withdraws from the structural work of the world and confines itself to a version of the gospel that addresses souls but not the systems in which souls live. And the New Testament does not actually support this reading.
