The same Paul who expected the Lord's return also organized collections for the poor churches of Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8–9), argued for the dignity of every human person as image-bearer (Galatians 3:28), and wrote that creation itself groans in expectation of the revelation of the children of God who will participate in its liberation (Romans 8:19–22). Paul's eschatology was not a reason to disengage from the material order. It was a reason to pour everything into it.

## The Pastoral Consequence

I have believed the wrong things about the end, and acted accordingly, for parts of my ministry. The consequences of getting this wrong are not merely theological. They are pastoral. They shape who we help, what we say, and what we are willing to leave behind.

If I believe the creation is destined for the trash heap, I will not preach about the care of it. I will not ask my congregation to think hard about consumption and ecological responsibility and what we owe the children who will inherit the earth we are currently managing. I will consign those questions to a category I call "political" and step back.

If I believe the poor are souls to be saved rather than bodies to be sustained in a renewed creation where their humanity is fully honored, I will build a church that prioritizes evangelism over justice — and I will call that a theological commitment rather than a failure of theological imagination.

The eschatology of renewal says that nothing done in the Lord is in vain. The healing of the sick, the feeding of the hungry, the advocacy for the imprisoned, the planting of a tree — these are not footnotes to the real work. They are the real work. They are seeds sown into the soil of what God is bringing into full flower.

The end shapes the now. It always has. The question is which end you believe in — the bonfire that consumes what we have built, or the renewal that takes what we have offered and makes it whole.

I have been changed by sitting with that question. The community I lead has changed with me.

That is what eschatology produces when it is taken seriously. Not charts. Not dates. A different life, lived in a different direction, toward an end that gives the present its weight.

> The end shapes the now. It always has.

The Exodus is not one story among many in Israel's memory. It is the story that all the other stories refer back to. When the prophets need to say something about who God is, they return to the Exodus. When the psalmists need to argue for God's faithfulness, they return to the Exodus. When Paul needs to describe the nature of salvation in Romans, he uses the Exodus pattern. When John needs to describe the end of history in Revelation, he saturates the vision with Exodus imagery. The story of God freeing slaves from Egypt is the paradigm that Israel and the early church used to understand everything else that God was doing.

This means the church cannot relegate the Exodus to the category of interesting ancient history. It is load-bearing.

---

## God Hears Before God Acts

The Exodus begins with God hearing. "God heard their groaning and he remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac and with Jacob. So God looked on the Israelites and was concerned about them" (Exodus 2:24-25). Before any act of liberation, there is attention. God notices. God hears. The cry of the oppressed reaches him, and he is not indifferent to it. This is a theological claim about God's character that the church affirms in its creed and largely ignores in its practice.

> The question is whether the church has constructed a sanctuary quiet enough that the cry does not reach it.

If God hears the cry of the oppressed, then the church that does not hear it is the church that has structured its life around not hearing it. The Israelites were heard because their suffering was real and their cry was genuine. The suffering of the poor in our cities is real. Their cry is present. The question is whether the church has constructed a sanctuary quiet enough that the cry does not reach it.

Consider what the Israelites were enduring: "They made their lives bitter with harsh labor in brick and mortar and with all kinds of work in the fields; in all their harsh labor the Egyptians worked them ruthlessly" (Exodus 1:14). They were building treasure cities for Pharaoh — Pithom and Rameses (Exodus 1:11) — without wages, without legal recourse, without standing in the social order that extracted their labor. This was not occasional hardship. It was systemic. It was the economy of Egypt organized around their subjugation. And when Pharaoh feared they were becoming too numerous, he extended the system to include population control: kill the male children at birth. The violence escalated because the system depended on maintaining the subjugation, and the threat to the system produced deeper violence in its defense.

The church that reads this and sees only a spiritual metaphor for individual salvation has missed something important. The metaphor is real. Paul develops it deliberately and powerfully. But the typological meaning does not erase the original. God's concern in Exodus 2 is for people in physical bondage, economic exploitation, and the daily brutality of a system that treated them as instruments of production rather than bearers of divine image.

---

## Liberation Through Human Weakness

What God does next is equally instructive. He does not send an army. He does not strike Pharaoh immediately. He calls a shepherd from the back of beyond — a man who is hiding from his past, who cannot speak well, who offers five separate objections to the assignment — and he sends him back to Egypt with a staff and a message. The liberation God enacts is not purely miraculous. It moves through human agency, human weakness, human fear overcome by a word God keeps repeating: "I will be with you" (Exodus 3:12).

This is a theological claim about how liberation works. It is not delivered wholesale from the sky. It is worked out through the bodies and choices and courage of people who have heard something that others have not heard — that the God of the oppressed has seen, has heard, has remembered, and is moving.

Walter Brueggemann [cite — confirm] argues that the Exodus creates what he calls an "alternative consciousness" — a community formed by a different story than the dominant story, capable of imagining a world organized on different principles than the empire's principles. The people of God are, in Brueggemann's reading, always a counter-cultural community, shaped by the memory of liberation rather than the logic of power. When the church forgets that memory, it loses its capacity to see what the empire cannot see.

The church has forgotten that memory in direct proportion to the degree it has become comfortable within the empire. The church that has political access, cultural prestige, and economic security does not easily identify with the slave. The slave's story is not its story. It has, in the language of the Exodus, moved into the house of Pharaoh.

---

## The Wilderness and the Slow Work of Formation

The Exodus is not finished with liberation. What follows is harder.

The wilderness period — forty years of wandering, complaint, rebellion, golden calves, murmuring against Moses — is the story of a liberated people who do not know how to be free. They had been formed in the logic of Egypt. They had internalized the values of Pharaoh's world. Freedom disoriented them because they had no internal framework for organizing themselves that was not built around subjugation and scarcity. They wanted to go back to Egypt (Numbers 14:3-4). Better slavery with predictable food than freedom with an uncertain supply of manna that bred worms when you tried to hoard it.

This part of the Exodus is rarely preached in its full weight. The liberation does not produce, automatically, a liberated people. Formation takes longer than deliverance. The generation that crossed the sea would not enter the land. Their children, formed in the wilderness on the covenant rather than in Egypt on imperial logic, would be the ones ready.

> Formation takes longer than deliverance.

The church that thinks proclamation of liberation produces liberated people without the slow work of formation has misread the wilderness. Liberation theology that skips the formative arc — the patient, unglamorous, community-building work of shaping people into a new imagination — ends in impatience, in the idol-making that always follows when the hard work of waiting for God feels less urgent than the immediate satisfaction of a visible alternative.

---

## The Prophets Read Exodus as Mandate

The prophets read the Exodus as both memory and mandate. Hosea writes of God's relationship to Israel: "When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son" (Hosea 11:1). The Exodus is the foundational act of love, the defining moment of the relationship, the event that makes everything else in the covenant's history legible. When Israel goes after other gods, Hosea's indictment is precisely that the people have forgotten the Exodus — forgotten who brought them out, forgotten what that liberation cost, forgotten that the God who freed them from Egypt has particular and ongoing concern for the oppressed.

Micah 6:4 invokes the Exodus as the covenant's ground: "I brought you up out of Egypt and redeemed you from the land of slavery." The redemption is the context for the requirement that follows: act justly, love mercy, walk humbly. The justice requirement is not abstract. It is anchored in a particular historical act of liberation that defines what God is like and therefore what God's people are called to be like.

Isaiah 43 uses the language of the Exodus to describe a coming new act of liberation: "Forget the former things; do not dwell on the past. See, I am doing a new thing!" (Isaiah 43:18-19). But the new thing is an extension of the pattern, not a departure from it. The same God who freed slaves is about to free exiles. The pattern repeats. God is always on the side of the people who cry out from bondage. The prophet knows this because the Exodus is the data on God's character that the whole tradition builds on.

---

## The Particularity Objection

The counter-position worth sitting with: Does invoking the Exodus in contemporary justice conversations strip it of its theological particularity? The Exodus was a specific act of God in a specific covenant history. Israel was not the universal stand-in for the oppressed; Israel was God's particular people called to a particular vocation. Using the Exodus as a general liberation theology risks flattening the covenant story into a political program.

This is a serious concern, and it is important to hold it. The Exodus was not primarily a social justice manifesto. It was the foundation of a covenant relationship between God and a particular people through whom God intended to bless the world.

But the restriction does not hold when the New Testament itself refuses it. Paul explicitly uses the Exodus pattern — the cloud, the sea, the spiritual food, the spiritual drink (1 Corinthians 10:1-4) — to describe the Christian community's participation in the same story. The early church understood itself as living in the pattern of the Exodus, as recipients of a liberation that extended the original act of God into new history. And James and Matthew 25 and the entire Epistles' treatment of the poor make it unmistakable that care for the vulnerable is not a political opinion but a covenant obligation — for the church as it was for Israel.

The Exodus does not become less particular when the New Testament extends it. It becomes more demanding.

---

## Inside the House of Pharaoh

I have moved into the house of Pharaoh in ways I have not fully named. I have benefited from structures that the Exodus pattern would name as oppressive. I have preached liberation theology from a position of comfort, which is not a disqualification but is a reason for particular caution about whether my preaching has any purchase on reality.

The congregation I pastor lives primarily in safety and relative security. The people whose cry reaches God in the Exodus narrative are not, for the most part, in our seats on Sunday morning. The question the Exodus puts to me — to us — is whether we have structured our life around hearing that cry, or around not hearing it.

The church cannot be Moses and Pharaoh simultaneously. It cannot extract comfort from the wealth of the empire while claiming solidarity with the people the empire exploits. That split is not sustainable theologically. It eventually requires choosing.

> The church cannot be Moses and Pharaoh simultaneously.

What the Exodus demands is not simply that the church develop programs for the poor. It demands that the church form an alternative consciousness — a community that genuinely believes the cry of the oppressed reaches God, that God's response is liberation rather than comfort for the oppressors, and that the church's calling is to participate in that liberation rather than to maintain its own position within the existing order.

The burning bush is still burning. The cry from the brickfields is still rising. The question is whether there is anyone willing to take off their shoes, acknowledge the holiness of the ground under their feet, and accept the assignment.

God heard their groaning. He remembered the covenant. He was concerned.

The church that has no concern is the church that has forgotten the story it was built on.

Before there was a theology, there was a cry.

"And the people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help. Their cry for rescue from slavery came up to God. And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob. God saw the people of Israel — and God knew" (Exodus 2:23-25). Four verbs. Heard. Remembered. Saw. Knew. This is the first theological statement about who God is and how God operates — not a doctrine about divine attributes in the abstract but a record of divine response to human suffering in the concrete.

The Exodus is not just ancient history. It is the grammar of everything that follows.

---

## An Empire Built on Invisible Labor

The story begins in an empire. Pharaoh is not simply a bad king. He is the head of the most sophisticated civilization in the ancient Near East, a man who controls not just military force but the narrative — the official account of the world, who matters and who does not, what counts as a person and what counts as a resource. His system worked by making the labor of the enslaved invisible while making the monuments visible. The pyramids stood. The people who built them were counted as inputs, not as persons. The empire ran on the conversion of human beings into economic units.

> The content of liberation is concrete.

Moses's call begins with a burning bush and ends with a demand: "Let my people go." That demand is not primarily about theology. It is about the specific, material condition of specific, material people in a specific, material situation. God does not tell Pharaoh to improve his values. God tells him to release his captives. The content of liberation is concrete. The enslaved must actually go free. The land must actually be crossed. The sea must actually part. Redemption in the Exodus tradition is not a spiritual transaction that leaves material conditions unchanged. It is a disruption of the existing order at every level — economic, political, social, symbolic.

This is what Walter Brueggemann calls the "prophetic imagination" [cite — confirm]: the capacity to see the existing social order not as natural or necessary but as a constructed arrangement that can be imagined differently. Pharaoh's power depended on his subjects believing that the existing arrangement was simply the way things were. Moses's message was that the existing arrangement was not the way things had to be — that there was a God more powerful than Pharaoh who had a different plan for these people, who had heard a cry that Pharaoh had organized the whole apparatus of empire to suppress.

---

## The Church Receives the Exodus as Its Own

The New Testament church received the Exodus as its own story. Paul, writing to a community of mostly Gentile believers in Corinth, says flatly: "Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Corinthians 10:1-2). Our fathers. He appropriates the Exodus narrative for people who were not ethnically Israelite because the pattern it reveals is not about ethnicity. It is about the God who liberates. The Christian who claims this God claims the history of this God — including the history of what this God has done with the enslaved and what this God requires of those who follow him into freedom.

Luke 4 makes the same move. Jesus, reading from Isaiah 61 in the synagogue at Nazareth, announces his own program in language drawn directly from the Exodus and Jubilee traditions: good news to the poor, release to the captives, recovery of sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed (Luke 4:18). He does not treat these as metaphors. He treats them as descriptions of what the kingdom's arrival produces. When John's disciples ask from prison whether Jesus is the one who was to come, his answer is not a theological proposition — it is a list of concrete transformations: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news proclaimed to them (Luke 7:22). The evidence of the kingdom is the reversal of the conditions the Exodus pattern named as incompatible with the character of God.

---

## The Temptation to Spiritualize Deliverance

The church has always been tempted to spiritualize the Exodus — to make it a story about individual souls being freed from the slavery of sin, which is true as far as it goes but radically incomplete. The pattern the Exodus establishes is not only about interior liberation. It is about the God who enters history to disrupt arrangements of power that crush the vulnerable. The spiritual dimension and the material dimension are not in competition. The God who liberates souls from sin is the same God who heard the cry of those building bricks without straw, and he is not satisfied with a church that addresses the spiritual while ignoring the material, any more than he was satisfied with an Israel that offered sacrifices while consuming the poor.

This is the point Amos made to a prosperous Israel in the eighth century BC. This is the point Isaiah made to a confident Judah in Isaiah 58: "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house?" (Isaiah 58:6-7). This is the point Jesus made in Matthew 25, where the criterion of judgment is not doctrinal correctness but whether the hungry were fed, the stranger welcomed, the naked clothed, the sick and imprisoned visited.

> The Exodus demands a church that takes the cry of the oppressed as seriously as God takes it.

The Exodus demands a church that takes the cry of the oppressed as seriously as God takes it. Heard. Remembered. Saw. Knew. Four verbs that describe God's orientation toward human suffering. The church that represents this God inherits this orientation.

---

## What the Demand Looks Like Now

What does this demand look like concretely in the twenty-first century? The question is easier to avoid than it is to answer honestly.

Mass incarceration in America disproportionately affects Black men and poor communities at rates that have no parallel in the developed world [cite — confirm]. The United States imprisons more people per capita than any nation on earth. The carceral system functions, in many respects, the way the forced labor systems of antiquity functioned: it extracts productive years from people whose communities are already depleted, criminalizes poverty rather than addressing it, and produces generational damage that compounds over time. The church that reads Exodus and has nothing to say about mass incarceration has missed the point of the story it claims to be living inside.

Immigration enforcement separates families, detains children, deports people to countries they have not lived in since childhood. The same nation that produced the Statue of Liberty and the promise of refuge has periodically reorganized its immigration apparatus to function as an engine of fear for the most vulnerable people who arrive at its borders. Leviticus 19:34 is not ambiguous: "You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt." For you were strangers in Egypt. The Exodus is the reason for the command.

I am not proposing a partisan program. I am describing the pattern that the Scriptures themselves establish and demanding that we look at what that pattern requires of us. The specific policy questions are genuinely complex, require wisdom and prudence, and admit of disagreement among people who share the same theological convictions. But the pattern itself is not ambiguous. God hears the cry of the oppressed. God requires his people to hear it too.

---

## The Two Temptations of the Church

The church has two temptations in response to the Exodus demand.

The first is to spiritualize it so thoroughly that it makes no material claims. This is the temptation of comfort — to read liberation as a metaphor and thereby preserve the existing social arrangements from scrutiny. The enslaved who built Egypt are not available for metaphor. They were people whose bodies belonged to Pharaoh, whose children were subject to state-sponsored murder, whose cry God heard. A church that turns their liberation into a spiritual lesson and never asks about the people in its own time whose cry is similarly loud has not followed the God of the Exodus. It has domesticated him.

The second temptation is to make the Exodus a simple map from oppressor to oppressed and assume that the church always knows which side it is on. This is the temptation of self-righteousness. The history of the church includes chapters in which it played Pharaoh's role — providing theological justification for chattel slavery, blessing the conquest of indigenous peoples, organizing institutional opposition to the liberation movements that drew on Exodus imagery to describe their struggle. The church that reads the Exodus must read it with the self-implicating honesty that the text demands. We are not always Moses. We have sometimes been Egypt.

---

## A Theological Orientation, Not a Program

The demand the Exodus places on the church is not a political program. It is a theological orientation — a set of questions that the story requires us to ask and keep asking. Who is crying out in our time? Who has organized a system that converts people into resources and suppresses the cry of those being consumed by it? What would it mean for the people who bear the name of this God to hear that cry, descend to where it is rising, and act in a way that disrupts the arrangements that produce it?

These questions are not comfortable. The Exodus was not a comfortable story for Pharaoh. It was not entirely comfortable for Moses, who spent forty years in the desert before God was ready to send him. It was not comfortable for Israel, who built the golden calf before they reached the promised land and complained repeatedly that Egypt was better than the wilderness.

> The God who said "I have come down to deliver them" has not stopped coming down.

But the direction was always away from Egypt. The cry was always heard. The God who said "I have come down to deliver them" has not stopped coming down.

The church that is still in Egypt has not yet followed him out.

Read Acts 9 carefully. Paul has just been converted on the Damascus road. He is on fire, preaching in the synagogues, confounding the people who thought he was coming to arrest Christians. He arrives in Jerusalem and the church there wants nothing to do with him. They are afraid of him. The word on the street is that Saul of Tarsus destroys communities from the inside, and they are not persuaded that a vision on a road changes a man.

Then Barnabas does one specific thing. He takes Paul and brings him to the apostles. He vouches for him. He tells the story of Damascus in a room where no one wanted to believe it (Acts 9:27).

That is it. That is the whole act. Barnabas believed Paul when the church did not, and he said so out loud, in a room where the saying cost him something. Without that moment, there is no Galatian mission, no letter to the Romans, no Athens sermon. The theological architecture that has shaped Christian thought for two thousand years begins with one man willing to say: I know him. He is who he says he is.

> Every pastor I know who has lasted in ministry has a Barnabas in the story.

Every pastor I know who has lasted in ministry has a Barnabas in the story.

## What Barnabas Actually Did

Before we can talk about finding this person, we need to be clear about what Barnabas was doing. He was not a cheerleader. He was not someone who reflexively supported everyone in the room because conflict made him uncomfortable. He was someone who had paid close enough attention to Paul to have a formed opinion about him — who had observed something real and was willing to stake his own credibility on what he saw.

His name means "son of encouragement" (Acts 4:36), and the biographical note is introduced deliberately. This is not just his given name. It is a vocational description. The text wants us to understand that there are people whose primary contribution to the body of Christ is not their preaching or their administration or their theological innovation. It is the specific gift of seeing what others cannot yet see in a person and saying so at the moment when it matters most.

The encouragement Barnabas offered Paul was not generic affirmation. It was specific, costly, and public. He did not tell Paul privately that he believed in him and then stay silent when the apostles in Jerusalem raised their concerns. He took Paul into the room. The encouragement had weight precisely because it was witnessed and because it required Barnabas to be wrong with Paul if Paul turned out to be wrong.

That combination — belief specific enough to stake your reputation on it, offered in the room where the stakes are real — is what distinguishes a Barnabas from a flatterer. The flatterer agrees with you privately and says nothing when the room turns against you. Barnabas agrees with you and says so in the room.

## The Middle of Ministry

The pastors I know who have quit, who burned out quietly or collapsed publicly, almost universally share one thing: they were not accompanied. They may have had mentors in the early years. They may have had friends from seminary. But somewhere in the long middle of ministry — the decade after the early successes, when the novelty is gone and the weight of the work is fully apparent and the original enthusiasm has been worn down by the complexity of actual people in actual conflict — they lost the person who could hold both what they were capable of and what they were actually doing.

> The independent man in ministry is not strong.

I did not understand this for a long time. I thought that needing someone's belief in you was a kind of weakness — that a mature pastor should have sufficient theological conviction and internal stability to move without an external witness. I was wrong, and the wrongness cost me years I would like to have back. The independent man in ministry is not strong. He is brittle. He breaks in ways that accompanied men do not, because the breaks happen in the dark where no one sees them coming.

The isolation of pastoral ministry is structural, not incidental. You know things about the congregation that you cannot share. You carry confidences that create distance. You are in the position of caring for people whose care of you is complicated by the pastoral relationship. The asymmetry is real. The isolation it produces is not a character flaw. It is the predictable result of a role that requires you to give more than you receive in almost every relationship you have.

The Barnabas relationship is the corrective to this. It is the one relationship in which the asymmetry is not absolute — where you can receive as well as give, where you can be known rather than only knowing, where you can be believed in rather than only believing in others.

## The Shape of the Relationship

Barnabas and Paul's relationship was not without conflict. Acts 15:36–41 records a disagreement sharp enough to end their partnership — a dispute over whether to take John Mark on a second missionary journey, John Mark having turned back from the first. Barnabas wanted to give him another chance. Paul did not. The text says the disagreement was so sharp that they parted company.

This is essential to understand. The Barnabas you need is not a yes-man. A yes-man agrees with everything and protects the relationship by never raising the hard thing. A Barnabas believes in you while being capable of genuine disagreement — which means the belief is not conditional on agreement. He can see something in you that is worth believing in and simultaneously think you are wrong about John Mark. Those two things can coexist in the same relationship.

That kind of relationship is rarer than we admit. Most of what passes for pastoral accountability is either mutual encouragement that never rises to real challenge, or formal accountability structures that create compliance without intimacy. The Barnabas relationship requires both intimacy and honesty, and developing both simultaneously is a slow project.

## How It Gets Built

Finding this person is not a passive process. Barnabas did not appear because Paul was waiting. Barnabas was already in Jerusalem, already known to the apostles, already someone who had demonstrated the character to make his vouching mean something. The relationships that produce this kind of accompaniment are built before they are needed.

You do not find your Barnabas in a crisis. You find him in the ordinary Tuesday lunches and the phone calls that are about nothing in particular and the Sunday nights where you are exhausted and you call someone just to say that. The relationship that can hold you in the hard year is built in the easy years.

The practical implication is that this is not something to defer. Many pastors, pressed by the demands of ministry, treat personal relationships as the thing to get to when there is margin — which means they never get to it. The margin never appears. The relationship never forms. And when the crisis arrives, there is no one present with enough history to be useful.

I have had men in my life who did this for me. They believed in my calling before my calling had produced anything worth believing in. They sat across from me in the dark seasons and refused to let me conclude that the dark was permanent. They were not naive about my failures. They knew them — sometimes in more detail than I was comfortable with. They held the belief and the knowledge at the same time, and that combination — belief that survives knowledge — is precisely what makes it worth having.

> Mere affirmation does not survive knowledge.

Mere affirmation does not survive knowledge. The person who only knows your public self can only believe in your public self. The person who knows the full thing and believes in it anyway is carrying something different. That is costly for them to carry. It is irreplaceable for you.

## The Discipline of Being a Barnabas

The pastoral tradition tends to focus on receiving mentorship — finding the older, wiser figure who will invest in you. But Barnabas was not Paul's mentor in the conventional sense. He was a peer who believed in Paul's potential before Paul had demonstrated it. And one of the most important shifts in any pastor's formation is the shift from only looking for a Barnabas to also becoming one.

There is a young pastor in your network right now who is three years into ministry and making every mistake that three years of ministry produces. He may be gifted in ways he cannot yet see. He needs someone to see it first. The discipline of looking — of paying close enough attention to young leaders to form a real opinion about their potential, and then being willing to say it in the rooms where it matters — is not a supplement to your ministry. It is a substantial part of what your experience is for.

And there is something else: the discipline of offering it tends to make you more capable of receiving it. The pastor who has learned to see what is worth believing in young leaders has usually, in the process, learned something about what it means to be believed in. The giving and the receiving are not separate practices. They are the same posture, turned in different directions.

Find that person. Or better: be that person for someone younger than you, and trust that the discipline of offering it will make you capable of receiving it.

The ministry that lasts is always built on something that looks, from the outside, like ordinary friendship.

It is not ordinary. Nothing about it is ordinary.

A new pastor arrives with two things in abundance and one thing not at all. He has faith. He has calling. He does not have experience, and there is no way to acquire it except the slow way — in real time, in front of real people, while the stakes are real. That is the hard arithmetic of the first years.

I have watched the same mistakes recur across enough young pastors to believe they are not personal failings. They are predictable patterns. And a predictable mistake is a survivable one, if someone names it before it names you.

---

## Winning the Room Before Loving It

**The first is trying to win the room before you have loved it.**

The new pastor wants respect, and he wants it now. He reaches for the fastest lever — a bold change, a sharper sermon, a line drawn. The change may even be right. But a congregation does not grant authority to competence. It grants authority to love, demonstrated over time, in funerals and hospital rooms and the unglamorous attendance of ordinary weeks.

Lead the change before you have earned the trust and you will spend the trust you do not yet have. Most new pastors go into debt this way in the first year and spend the next three repaying it.

> But a congregation does not grant authority to competence.

The counterintuitive reality is that congregations are more ready for change than new pastors think — but only from people they trust. The old pastor who led the church for twenty-five years could propose something radical and get a hearing because twenty-five years of faithful presence had built the relational capital that made the proposal credible. The new pastor with eighteen months wants the same hearing. He will not get it, and pressing for it damages both the relationship and the cause.

The pattern in Scripture is patient. Moses spent forty years in the desert before he led the Exodus. Paul spent three years in Arabia after Damascus before his public ministry in earnest (Galatians 1:17-18). The urgency the young pastor feels is real. But urgency pressed too early against a community that has not had time to learn to trust you tends to produce exactly the resistance it was meant to overcome.

---

## Preaching to the Church You Wish You Had

**The second is preaching to the church you wish you had.**

It is easy to preach at the congregation in your head — the one that should be more committed, more theologically serious, more like the church you read about in books. It is harder to preach to the people actually in the chairs, with the marriages they actually have, the doubts they actually carry, the week they actually just lived.

The young pastor mistakes the first approach for prophetic courage. It is usually impatience wearing prophetic clothes. The pulpit is not where you correct the congregation for failing to be what you imagined when you took the call. It is where you feed the people in front of you what they can actually receive this week.

Eugene Peterson, in his memoir about his years as a pastor, describes the long discipline of paying attention to the actual congregation rather than the theoretical one — of learning to see who was actually in the room, what they were actually carrying, where God was actually working in lives that looked ordinary from the outside. [cite — confirm] That kind of attentiveness is harder than having a strong opinion about what the church should become. And it produces preaching that lands in a way that the corrective variety never quite does.

Real prophetic courage comes later, when you have sat with these people's grief and walked with them through enough to know exactly where the challenge is personal — not theoretical, not "the church" as an abstraction, but this man, this woman, this specific pattern that needs to be named. That kind of preaching can only come from inside the community. The preacher who stands outside it and corrects it has not earned it.

---

## Confusing Being Needed With Being Loved

**The third is confusing being needed with being loved.**

A new pastor is needed constantly, and the need is intoxicating. Every call answered, every crisis attended, every gap filled — it feels like love, and it is not. It is need. A congregation that needs you will still replace you. A man who builds his identity on being indispensable is building it on sand, and he will know it the first season the calls slow down.

This is the mistake underneath the mistake that produces pastoral burnout. The pastor who cannot stop filling every need is not simply overworked. He is feeding something — the sense that his presence is the thing that makes the ministry work, that his effort is what holds it together, that his availability is the measure of his faithfulness. These are not virtues when they are compulsive. They are the symptoms of a man who has not yet located his worth somewhere other than his usefulness.

> A congregation that needs you will still replace you.

Henri Nouwen's account of his own movement from "the university to the community" — his eventual choice to live at L'Arche with people who could not recognize his reputation and would never applaud his work — was a deliberate attempt to find identity in being loved rather than being needed. [cite — confirm] Most pastors will not make that move literally. But the internal movement Nouwen was describing — from productivity as the source of worth to belovedness as the source of worth — is the movement every pastor eventually needs to make, if they want to last.

Let yourself be needed. Do not let yourself be fed by it.

---

## The Damage of Leading Alone

**The fourth is leading alone.**

This is the one that does the most damage, because it hides as virtue. The young pastor carries everything himself and believes that carrying it by himself is what strength looks like — that asking for help is the admission of a man not quite cut out for the work.

The opposite is true. The pastors who last are not the ones who needed the least help. They are the ones who built, early and on purpose, the handful of relationships that could hold them: a mentor, a peer who is not in his system, someone who can ask how he actually is and expect an honest answer. "In an abundance of counselors there is safety," says Proverbs 11:14. The safety is not primarily institutional. It is personal — the safety of a man who does not have to pretend, who does not have to perform, who can name the thing that is actually hard without calculating the professional consequences.

Pastoral isolation is not the cost of leadership. It is the condition most likely to end it. The pastor who does not have at least one relationship in which he is genuinely known — not as the pastor but as a man who is struggling in specific ways and needs specific help — is a pastor who is one crisis away from a collapse that his congregation will not see coming.

The PCN network exists in part for this: not for professional development (though that happens), but for the basic human need of a man in a demanding, isolated role to be in a room with other men who know what he is carrying and will tell him the truth.

---

## Mistaking the Church for the Kingdom

**The fifth is mistaking the church for the kingdom.**

This one comes slowly, and it is the most dangerous because it looks the most like devotion. The new pastor pours everything into his congregation — and then the congregation becomes the whole horizon. His marriage thins. His own prayer life becomes sermon research. The work of the kingdom quietly shrinks to the size of one building's attendance figures.

He has not become more spiritual. He has made a smaller god out of a good thing, and the good thing cannot bear the weight.

Jesus sent the disciples out without him. Paul planted churches and left. The New Testament model for pastoral leadership includes a built-in reminder that the pastor is not the church, and the church is not the kingdom. The kingdom is bigger than any church, working in the city through actors and movements and individuals the pastor does not control and may not even know about. His job is not to contain the kingdom within his congregation but to participate faithfully in what God is doing through every structure God uses.

The pastor who equates the church's growth with kingdom progress and the church's struggles with kingdom loss has collapsed a crucial distinction — and will eventually lead from a place of scarcity, fear, and competition that is the opposite of the abundance the kingdom actually offers.

---

None of these are fatal. Every veteran pastor I respect made most of them, survived them, and learned to name them for the men coming up behind. That is most of what mentoring is — not strategy, but warning, handed from someone who paid for the lesson to someone who does not have to.

> The first call is the formation.

The pattern underneath all five is this: the first years of ministry are the years when a man's formation as a leader either takes or does not. The theological education was preparation. The first call is the formation. And formation requires being in the presence of failure long enough to learn from it rather than being destroyed by it.

That means the most important thing for a new pastor is not to have the right strategy or the right theology or the right network. It is to refuse to go through the formation alone. Find people who have been where you are going. Let them tell you what the road costs. Let them tell you the truth about what you are doing when you think you are doing something else.

Give yourself the grace you will need to give your people — the grace of a man who is allowed to be learning in public, because there was never any other way to learn this at all.

The congregation knows you are learning. They are hoping you will let them help.

The congregation learns what faith looks like from the pulpit. This is not an exaggeration — it is simply how communities form. What gets preached, repeatedly, shapes what the people believe is possible, what they think God is like, and what they understand Christianity to actually require of them. Which means that the patterns a preacher falls into — over months, over years — do more formative damage than any single bad sermon ever could.

I have preached these patterns. I am naming them from inside, not from above.

## The Pressures That Shape the Pulpit

Before the habits themselves: the conditions that produce them. The preacher is not lazy who falls into any of these patterns. He is, in most cases, someone who learned his craft under particular pressures — the pressure to keep people engaged, to avoid Sunday-morning conflict, to be liked enough to be trusted, to serve a congregation that responds well to certain things and noticeably less well to others. Over time, those pressures reshape what preaching becomes. What began as genuine pastoral care calcifies into something safer, shorter, and smaller. The damage accumulates in the congregation's bones before anyone notices it in the sermon.

Knowing the historical weight behind the pulpit helps name what is at stake. Augustine's *De Doctrina Christiana* — written in the late fourth and early fifth centuries — understood preaching as requiring three tasks: to teach, to delight, and to move [cite — confirm]. Delight is not the enemy of substance. But when delight becomes the primary purpose, teaching and movement atrophy. The congregation is pleased. It is not being formed. There is a very specific kind of congregational health that registers as contentment on Sunday and shows up as fragility on Tuesday. The patterns below are what produce it.

## The Clean Application Turn

**The first is the clean application turn.** The text does its work — raises the question, names the tension, maybe even lets the darkness gather — and then the sermon pivots too quickly to the resolution. Three steps. A practical response. The road home clearly marked. What this communicates to the congregation, over time, is that the Bible is primarily a problem-solving document, that faith is primarily about technique, and that anyone still living in the unreceived part of the promise is probably doing something wrong. Paul wrote Philippians from a Roman prison cell (Philippians 1:13), and the letter does not resolve his situation. It holds it. Paul can write "I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content" (Philippians 4:11) not because the prison opened but because the prison did not have the last word. Preaching that always resolves teaches people that unresolved lives are off the map.

The church has been down this road before. The prosperity gospel is the extreme form of the clean application turn — if you pray and believe correctly, the situation will resolve. But the milder version is everywhere, and it does the same theological damage at a lower dosage. Lamentations exists. Job exists. Psalm 88 ends with darkness, the last word unredeemed. The canon insists on the territory that quick resolutions foreclose. So must the pulpit.

## Therapeutic Substitution

**The second is therapeutic substitution.** The language of psychology is not wrong. But when the sermon consistently translates Scripture into psychological terms — your worth, your healing, your growth process — without also holding the demands of the text, it has shifted the organizing category from the kingdom of God to the self. The congregation begins to read the Bible primarily as a mirror rather than as a window onto something larger than themselves.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from Germany in the 1930s, named the danger of a Christianity so accommodated to the surrounding culture that it could no longer speak a word the culture had not already authorized [cite — confirm]. Therapeutic preaching is not the German church of the 1930s. But the structural problem is the same: when the sermon is shaped by what the surrounding therapeutic culture has already made acceptable, it cannot speak the word that that culture cannot hear — the word about repentance, about the demands of the kingdom, about the cross as something other than a metaphor for your healing arc. You cannot be formed by a mirror. Formation requires encounter with what is genuinely other.

## Intellectual Avoidance of the Costly Text

**The third is intellectual avoidance.** The text has a hard edge — a demand, a claim, a tension with the congregation's received politics or economics or family arrangements. And the sermon slides around it. It is not dishonest, exactly. It simply never arrives at the place where the text becomes genuinely costly. Over time, the congregation learns that the Bible is safe. That it will not ask anything they are not already prepared to give.

The prophets were not expelled from the sanctuary for being wrong. Amos 7:10–13 records Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, telling Amos to go preach somewhere else — not because Amos was theologically incoherent but because what he was saying was inconvenient to the existing arrangement. The preacher who slides around the inconvenient text is not being kind. He is being Amaziah. He is protecting a comfort that the text was sent to disturb. A faith that never costs anything eventually means nothing. The congregation did not come to hear what they already believe confirmed. They came, whether they know it or not, to hear the word that is alive and active and sharper than a two-edged sword (Hebrews 4:12).

## The Celebrity Proof-Text

**The fourth is the celebrity proof-text.** The sermon is built not from the biblical argument but from the accumulated authority of popular Christian voices — this well-known pastor said, that beloved author wrote. The congregation's faith becomes anchored to a personality rather than to the text itself. When that personality eventually falls — and some percentage of them always do — the faith built on their words falls with them.

The Bereans in Acts 17:11 are commended specifically because they tested Paul's preaching against the Scriptures themselves. Not because they distrusted Paul — they received the word eagerly. But they received it and then examined the Scriptures to see whether what Paul said was true. The congregation trained to defer to authority rather than to examine the text has been given a weakened faith. The current generation of young adults who have watched celebrity Christian culture implode — scandals, cover-ups, collapsed movements [cite — confirm] — can tell the difference between a sermon anchored in Scripture and a sermon anchored in a personality. The former will outlast the latter. The pastoral work is to build the faith that lasts.

## The Abandonment of Lament

**The fifth is systematic avoidance of lament.** The psalms of lament — and there are roughly sixty of them, constituting the largest single category in the Psalter [cite — confirm] — represent a theological territory that the American pulpit has almost entirely abandoned. Psalm 88 gives a full chapter of unanswered complaint, ending without resolution: *darkness is my closest friend.* Not as a setup for triumph. Simply as the psalmist's condition, named honestly before God.

The preacher who only celebrates, who frames every darkness as a setup for triumph, who cannot sit with genuine suffering and call it by name, creates a congregation ill-equipped to process their own lives when those lives refuse to resolve. Grief is not a phase. Doubt is not a failure. Anger at God has a scriptural tradition, and Job is not corrected by God for his complaints — he is honored for having spoken what is true in contrast to the friends whose theological tidy explanations were wrong (Job 42:7–8). The preacher who cannot give language to grief and doubt is leaving his people without a map for roughly half of what they will experience. When their lives enter the territory the sermons never described, they will conclude either that their faith is broken or that God has abandoned them. Both conclusions were produced by the pulpit's refusal to go where the canon actually goes.

None of these habits are chosen deliberately. They accumulate under pressure, in the direction of least resistance, shaped by what the congregation appears to respond to and what keeps Sunday morning from feeling like a confrontation. I understand the gravity of that. The pulpit is not a laboratory for the preacher's intellectual interests. It is a place of care.

> But care that shrinks the faith is not care.

But care that shrinks the faith is not care. It is management.

> They brought all of that into the room this morning.

The congregation is trying to live inside a world that is genuinely hard. A marriage that will not stabilize. A diagnosis that will not improve. A faith that once felt solid and now feels like it is held together only by habit. They brought all of that into the room this morning. And the question the sermon must answer is not whether they will feel better when they leave but whether they will have been given something true and large enough to carry that weight through the week.

That requires something of the preacher that is not primarily technical. The five habits above can be named, analyzed, and corrected at the level of craft. But the deeper correction is theological: the preacher who has himself lived in the unreceived promise, who has himself named grief honestly before God, who has himself found that the text cost him something — that preacher has been somewhere the congregation needs to go. He can lead them there because he has been there.

Eugene Peterson spent decades arguing that pastoral work is fundamentally a practice of attention — to the text, to the congregation, to the ways the text speaks into actual lives [cite — confirm]. The preacher who has cultivated that attention will not fall into these habits, not because he is more disciplined but because he is more present — present to what the text actually says, to what the congregation actually carries, and to the enormous distance between those two realities that only genuine preaching can close.

The sermon that takes that distance seriously will not be comfortable. It will not resolve everything. It will not make everyone happy. But it will be alive — sharp enough to divide, honest enough to stay in the darkness when the darkness is where the text goes, clear enough to say what it costs and what it promises.

That is what the congregation came for. Most of them know it, even if they would not say so. The preacher's job is to give it to them, even when — especially when — the easier thing would be to stay on the surface and leave everyone undisturbed.

Care that shrinks the faith is not care. It is management. The congregation you are trying to protect from difficulty will not thank you when difficulty arrives and they have nothing to hold. Give them something that will hold.

The prayer Jesus taught begins with bread. Not with theology. Not with the kingdom in abstract. *Give us this day our daily bread* (Matthew 6:11). It is the most material petition in the prayer — the one grounded in the irreducible physical requirement of survival. Before forgiveness, before deliverance from evil, before almost everything else: bread. The God who made the body and placed it in a world of grain and rain and soil does not consider the need for food beneath the dignity of prayer.

The theology of bread runs through the entire biblical narrative with a consistency that the church has largely managed to read past. Manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16). The ravens feeding Elijah by the brook (1 Kings 17:6). Ruth gleaning in Boaz's fields (Ruth 2). The feeding of the five thousand in all four Gospels — the one miracle mentioned by every evangelist, a detail that suggests they considered it load-bearing for what they were trying to say about Jesus. The Last Supper, with bread broken and given as the body that would be broken and given. The risen Christ on the Emmaus road, recognized not in the explanation of Scripture but in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:35). Bread matters to this story. It is not incidental.

## The Food Desert as a Theological Condition

Approximately 23.5 million Americans live in food deserts — areas where affordable and nutritious food is inaccessible due to distance, cost, or lack of transportation [cite — confirm]. The term "food desert" is a geographic designation, but it describes a theological condition: a community from which the provision of bread has been structured out by the decisions of corporations, governments, and investors who chose other neighborhoods for their grocery stores and left these ones without. The geography of food deserts tracks, with remarkable precision, the geography of racial segregation, concentrated poverty, and disinvestment. These communities are not accidentally underserved. They are structurally underserved — the result of accumulated decisions made by people who did not live there and did not expect to.

In the wilderness, Israel complained to Moses: *Would to God we had died in Egypt, where we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full* (Exodus 16:3). The complaint is not only ingratitude — it is a genuine crisis of provision that God takes seriously. The response is not a sermon on trusting Providence. The response is bread. *I will rain down bread from heaven for you* (Exodus 16:4). The provision is material before it is anything else. The theological lesson — trust the One who provides — cannot be taught to people who are starving. The bread comes first. The meaning of the bread is understood afterward.

> The church has largely inverted this order.

The church has largely inverted this order. We have become very good at providing the meaning while leaving the bread to others. The food pantry is the church's primary mode of engagement with food insecurity — charity that addresses the immediate hunger of individuals without asking why the neighborhood has no grocery store, without examining the agricultural policies that make processed food cheaper than fresh produce, without naming the decades of redlining and urban disinvestment that produced the geography of food access we now inhabit. The food pantry is not nothing. People eat. But the food pantry does not address what produced the food desert. It manages one symptom of a system the church has largely refused to examine.

## The Prophetic Tradition and the Systems of Hunger

The prophetic tradition is far less patient with this distinction than the church has been. Isaiah 58 — one of the most direct prophetic texts on the relationship between worship and justice — does not describe the acceptable fast as one that prays over food for the hungry and then distributes it. The fast God chooses is to *loose the chains of injustice* (Isaiah 58:6), to *share your food with the hungry* (v. 7), but also — and the context makes clear this is the structural dimension — to address the systems that produce the hunger. The Hebrew word behind "break every yoke" (v. 6) is a technical term for the economic bondage that the jubilee legislation was designed to address. The prophetic vision is not pastoral care for the hungry. It is structural change in the conditions that produce hunger.

Amos preached to the Northern Kingdom at a moment of relative prosperity in the eighth century BC — a moment when the wealthy were buying their winter and summer houses (Amos 3:15), when the merchants were waiting for the Sabbath to end so they could resume skimping on the measure and boosting the price (Amos 8:5). The poor were being sold for a pair of sandals (Amos 2:6). The sanctuary was full; the worship was lively; the injustice was systematic. God's response through Amos is not to commend the charitable giving of the wealthy but to reject their worship: *Away with the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps. But let justice roll on like a river* (Amos 5:23–24). The worship and the food insecurity of the poor are not separate issues. The God who hears *Give us this day our daily bread* also hears the silence of the congregation that sings but leaves the food desert intact.

## The Geography of a Seventy-Year Decision

The specific mechanisms that produce food deserts in American cities are worth naming, because the church tends to receive injustice as an abstraction until the mechanisms are made concrete. After redlining effectively locked Black Americans out of home ownership in most major American cities — a federal policy that lasted from roughly 1934 to 1968 [cite — confirm] — the disinvestment from those neighborhoods that followed produced predictable results: declining tax bases, deteriorating infrastructure, reduced services, and the exit of businesses, including grocery stores, that required spending power the neighborhood no longer had. The food desert is not a weather event. It is the current address of a seventy-year policy decision. The church that receives it as a natural condition to be charitably managed has accepted the premise that produced it.

## The Market Argument and Its Limits

The counter-position worth engaging honestly is the market argument: that grocery stores do not locate in low-income neighborhoods because the economics do not support them, and that policy intervention distorts markets in ways that produce worse outcomes than the market would otherwise produce. There is something to this — the economics of food retail are not simple, and failed supermarket initiatives in underserved neighborhoods are a real phenomenon. The argument that the church should focus on what it can do — food pantries, community gardens, local provision — rather than engaging complex policy debates it is not equipped to resolve has some force.

But the theological problem with this argument is that it accepts the existing market arrangement as morally neutral — as simply the way things are, rather than as the outcome of specific decisions by specific actors with specific interests. The market does not choose to exclude poor neighborhoods from fresh food access out of value-neutrality. It does so because the people who make market decisions do not live in those neighborhoods and are not accountable to those neighborhoods. That is a power arrangement. And the church's silence about power arrangements is never neutral — it always functions to ratify the existing arrangement.

## You Give Them Something to Eat

The feeding of the five thousand is worth sitting with, because the disciples' response to the hungry crowd is the response the church most often gives: *Send the crowds away, so they can go to the villages and buy themselves some food* (Matthew 14:15). It is not unkind. It is practical. The crowd is hungry. The crowd needs food. The disciples do not have food. The solution is to send the crowd where the food is. Jesus's response is the one that makes no logistical sense: *You give them something to eat* (v. 16). Not: address the structural reasons they do not have food. Not: organize a more efficient food distribution network. But also not: send them away. *You give them something to eat.* The disciples who do not know how to do this are standing in the presence of the One who does, and what he does with five loaves and two fish is not explained — only reported, in all four Gospels, with insistence that it happened, that it was enough, that there were twelve basketfuls left over.

I do not know how to eliminate food deserts. I am a pastor, not an urban planner. But I know that the community I serve includes people who live in the zones where fresh food is inaccessible, and I know that the community I serve includes people with resources, education, and influence who have not examined the structural conditions that produced those zones. The pastoral work is partly to refuse to let those two communities receive their common faith without letting it press them toward each other — to insist that *give us this day our daily bread* is a first-person plural prayer, not a first-person singular one, and that the *us* includes the neighbor in the food desert.

> The theology of bread does not end at the pantry.

The theology of bread does not end at the pantry. It begins there and pushes upstream — toward the policies, the corporate decisions, the investment patterns, the agricultural subsidies that have made it possible for some zip codes to have three grocery stores and others to have none. The church that prays for daily bread while leaving those questions unexamined is praying with its eyes closed to the room in which God has placed it.

The bread matters. It mattered enough to appear on the first page of the Lord's Prayer, on both sides of the Red Sea, in the wilderness, at the last table, and at every table in between. The church that takes this theology seriously will not be satisfied with managing access to bread one food pantry visit at a time.

It will want to know why there is a food desert in the first place. And it will not be comfortable with any answer that leaves the desert standing.

Begin with the table. Not the metaphor of the table — the actual table, the one where food arrives or does not arrive, where the question of who controls the conditions of that arrival is answered before the meal begins. The theology of the table in Christian tradition is rich and specific: the Eucharist, the eschatological banquet, the feeding of five thousand, the early church's common meals in Acts 2 that Luke reports with an attention to economic detail that most homiletical treatments quietly skip. That theology has mostly been read in one direction — upward, toward meaning, toward communion, toward the spiritual significance of breaking bread together. What it has rarely been pressed to address is the question underneath the meal: who decides what grows, where it grows, who can access it, and at what price?

Food sovereignty is the term that land rights and agrarian movements have used since at least the 1990s [cite — confirm] to name that question as a political one. It is the right of peoples to define their own food and agriculture systems — to determine what they grow, how they grow it, and how it is distributed — rather than having those systems imposed by the logic of global commodity markets and the interests of the corporations that dominate them. The concept emerged most prominently through Via Campesina, the international peasant movement, as a deliberate challenge to a food system that had been shaped by structural adjustment programs, free trade agreements, and agricultural policies that consistently benefited large producers at the expense of small farmers and subsistence communities in the Global South. [cite — confirm]

This history is not obscure. It is simply not taught in the contexts where most American pastors received their theological formation. And because it is not taught there, the church has largely missed that the question of food sovereignty is, at its root, a theological question about power, creation, and the image of God.

## The Gift of the Earth in Genesis

Start where the text starts. In Genesis 1, the first act of provision in the creation narrative is agricultural: "I have given you every plant yielding seed that is on the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit. You shall have them for food" (Genesis 1:29). The earth's capacity to produce food is narrated as a gift — distributed without means test, without market mechanism, without the mediation of a corporation's supply chain. The gift is to "every living thing on the face of the earth" (Genesis 1:30). The distribution logic is abundance and universality, not scarcity and exchange.

> This is not charity. It is law.

The law codifies this logic in ways the church has largely treated as archaeological curiosity. The Mosaic legislation in Leviticus 19 commands that farmers not reap to the very edges of their fields and not strip the vineyard bare — the corners, the gleanings, the fallen fruit belong not to the farmer but to "the poor and for the sojourner" (Leviticus 19:9–10). This is not charity. It is law. It is a structural limitation on the farmer's property rights for the sake of the neighbor who has no field of their own. Ruth gleaning in Boaz's field (Ruth 2) is not a heartwarming exception to the normal operation of the agrarian economy. It is the normal operation of the agrarian economy, functioning as designed, in service of someone who would otherwise have starved.

The Jubilee provisions in Leviticus 25 go further still: every fifty years, land returns to its original family. Debts cancel. Slaves are freed. The logic is explicit — the land belongs to God, not to any human owner, and therefore the indefinite accumulation of land at the expense of the dispossessed is a form of theft from both the poor and from God himself. "The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine" (Leviticus 25:23). This is not a program. It is a cosmological claim: the earth is not a commodity. It is the Lord's.

## Isaiah and the Concentration of Land

Isaiah's indictment in Isaiah 5:8 — "Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land" — is addressed to the political economy of land concentration in eighth-century Judah, where the expansion of latifundia by wealthy elites was displacing small farmers from the land their families had worked for generations. The prophet is not making a point about spiritual pride. He is naming a specific economic practice as an offense against the covenant community's responsibility to the land and to each other. The woe is structural.

I have not preached that passage as a text about agricultural policy. Neither have most of us. We have spiritualized it into a warning against greed in general, which is safe enough to not offend anyone and specific enough to do nothing.

## Jubilee Logic on a Hillside

The New Testament does not retreat from this. The feeding of the five thousand in Mark 6 — the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels, which should itself be a signal that the tradition considered it important — does not end with a spiritual lesson about relying on God. It ends with twelve baskets left over after everyone has eaten (Mark 6:43). The abundance is material. The distribution is universal and egalitarian: everyone sitting on the grass (Mark 6:39–40). Jesus does not run a means test. He does not create a private market for the bread. He blesses, breaks, and distributes. The logic is Jubilee logic, incarnated in a hillside meal.

The early Jerusalem community in Acts 2:44–45 and 4:34–35 practiced a distribution so radical that Luke pauses twice to describe it: they sold possessions and distributed to any as had need, and "there was not a needy person among them." This is not a blueprint for mandatory communism. It is a description of what happens when people who take the Jubilee logic seriously inhabit a community together. The table creates the economy, not the other way around.

## The Contemporary Food System Is Not Neutral

Against this background, the contemporary food system is not theologically neutral. A global food system that extracts grain from subsistence farming communities in sub-Saharan Africa to feed livestock for export markets in wealthier countries is doing something specific with the earth and with human bodies. A farm subsidy system that consistently advantages large commodity producers at the expense of small and mid-sized family farms is making a choice about who controls food production. A trade architecture that has repeatedly required developing nations to open their markets to subsidized agricultural imports while preventing those same nations from protecting their own farmers [cite — confirm] is an exercise of power over the most basic conditions of life — and it has a body count.

The church cannot be theologically serious about imago Dei — the full humanity of every person — and simultaneously indifferent to the conditions that determine whether that person can eat. The image of God is not a spiritual designation that floats above material existence. It is a claim about the full person, including the body that requires food, the family that requires land, the community that requires the capacity to feed itself.

## The Limits of the Counter-Argument

The counter-argument is worth taking seriously. It goes like this: the church is not a political movement, and the complexity of global agricultural policy exceeds the competence of most pastoral communities. The risk of the church becoming an advocacy organization for particular agrarian movements is real. The gospel is not reducible to economic policy, and the pastor who turns every Sunday into a political education session has misunderstood his vocation.

This is not wrong. The church is not primarily a policy lobby, and the pastoral vocation is not coextensive with the advocacy organizations that work these issues with greater expertise and accountability. But the counter-argument proves too much if it is used to justify a silence so total that the congregation never hears that food is a justice issue, never encounters the biblical material on gleaning and Jubilee and the feeding of multitudes in anything other than its spiritualized form, never learns that the choices embedded in their food system have consequences for the bodies and livelihoods of people who bear the image of God in communities they will never visit.

> Silence on this is not pastoral neutrality.

Silence on this is not pastoral neutrality. It is pastoral formation by default — forming the congregation in the assumption that the food system has nothing to do with the gospel, which is itself a theological position, and a false one.

What does faithfulness look like, concretely? It looks like a congregation that understands the connection between the Lord's Table and the kitchen table of their neighbor. It looks like preaching that handles the gleaning laws and the Jubilee provisions as live texts with a claim on the present rather than as historical curiosities. It looks like congregations that support local food sovereignty efforts — community gardens, food co-ops, advocacy for policies that protect small farmers and increase food access in low-income neighborhoods — not because these are the full answer to global agricultural injustice but because they are the nearest expression of the conviction that the earth is the Lord's and its produce is gift, not commodity.

The table the church gathers around each week is a table where a body was broken so that life could be distributed without means test to anyone who comes hungry. The logic of that table runs in a specific direction.

The question is whether the congregation is being formed to follow it past the sanctuary door.

The earth yields. The question has always been: who decides for whom.

There are approximately 400,000 children in the American foster care system on any given day [cite — confirm]. Most of them did not enter the system because their parents were evil. They entered because their parents were overwhelmed — by poverty, by addiction, by trauma, by the cascading failures of systems that were supposed to support families and didn't. The children bear the weight of those failures. They live in impermanence. Many of them will age out of the system at eighteen with no family, no safety net, and a statistical profile for homelessness, incarceration, and early death that should stop every congregation in this country cold.

It does not.

## The Orphans Within Driving Distance

The church talks about orphans. It has talked about orphans for centuries, because Scripture talks about orphans with a regularity and urgency that is impossible to miss. James 1:27 — *Religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world* — is quoted at every orphan care conference and stitched onto every mission trip t-shirt. It is not wrong to quote it. It is wrong to quote it and then treat the 400,000 children in the American foster system as a different category from the orphans the text describes.

They are not a different category. They are the orphans. They are the children without consistent parental protection, without a permanent family, without the belonging that every developmental framework identifies as necessary for human flourishing. They are the vulnerable ones Scripture is most consistently concerned about, and most of them live within driving distance of a church with a building and a budget and members with spare bedrooms and years of experience loving children.

The mandate is not finished. It has barely started.

> The mandate is not to support orphan care at a distance. It is to do it.

The church's engagement with foster care has been inconsistent and, in too many cases, programmatic in the worst sense — organized around the church's institutional interests rather than the child's actual needs. The "orphan care ministry" that hosts two fundraising events a year for an overseas orphanage while the elementary school two blocks away has fifteen kids in foster care has not misunderstood the mandate in degree. It has misunderstood it in kind. The mandate is not to support orphan care at a distance. It is to do it. To be the family. To take the child home.

## The Counter-Argument and Its Limit

Let me name the counter-argument fairly, because it is not nothing. Foster care is genuinely difficult. It requires licensing, training, ongoing supervision, and a level of disruption to ordinary family life that is not trivial to absorb. Children who have experienced trauma — and most foster children have experienced significant trauma — bring needs that exceed what most families, including most Christian families, are equipped to meet without substantial support. The foster parent who commits naively, without training, without community support, without honest knowledge of what is being undertaken, may do more damage than good, both to the child and to their own family. The cautionary literature on this is real and should be read [cite — confirm].

The counter-argument justifies better preparation. It does not justify non-participation.

## Building the Infrastructure of Care

The church that takes this mandate seriously needs to build more than a willing spirit. It needs to build infrastructure: certified adoption specialists who understand the foster care licensing process, ongoing support groups for foster families, respite care networks so that foster parents can receive rest without disrupting placement, financial support for the costs that licensing and placement and legal processes produce, a community culture in which foster parenting is understood as a shared congregational endeavor rather than an individual family's private decision.

This is the gap between the orphan care conference and the orphan care that the Scripture describes. The conference generates emotion and intention. The infrastructure sustains participation over the years that children actually need. Emotion that is not supported by structure produces burnout and withdrawal — the foster parent who entered with genuine commitment and lasted eighteen months before the weight of it exceeded what the congregation was prepared to share.

## Family as Covenant, Not Biology

The biblical materials on this are richer than the James 1:27 text alone. Psalm 68:6 — *God sets the lonely in families* — is a declaration about God's intent, and by extension about the shape of the community that bears God's character. The family is not primarily a biological arrangement in Scripture. It is a covenant arrangement. Ruth's commitment to Naomi is a commitment across the line of biology — *where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay* (Ruth 1:16) — and it is the covenant commitment of the outsider to the community that sets the entire story of redemption in motion.
