Boaz's willingness to act as kinsman-redeemer, to bring Ruth into his household and give her and Naomi protection and belonging, is the redemptive act of the narrative. The family is the instrument of justice. The household that opens its door is the place where the lonely are set in families.

Moses was raised in Pharaoh's household. Joseph was given a family in Egypt, however involuntarily, that positioned him to save the very family that had discarded him. The pattern of redemption running through the Old Testament is frequently a pattern of children finding families outside the biological family of origin — adopted into belonging, given the covenant relationship that their biological circumstances could not provide.

> God adopts.

The New Testament carries this forward. Paul's adoption language for salvation — *you received the Spirit of adoption to sonship; and by him we cry, "Abba, Father"* (Romans 8:15) — is not metaphorical decoration. It is a theological claim about what God does with the displaced. God adopts. God does not look at the spiritual orphan — the one without protection, without belonging, without a father's name — and organize a fundraising event. God takes the orphan in.

The church is meant to embody that reality in flesh. Not ideally or eventually. Now, with the children who are already in the system, already in the county, already waiting.

## What the Unfinished Mandate Requires

What does the church's unfinished mandate require?

First, it requires congregations to know the actual shape of foster care need in their county. How many children are in care? How many foster families are certified? What is the shortage? What are the specific barriers to participation in this community? The church that does not know the numbers in its own county has not yet taken the mandate seriously enough to investigate.

Second, it requires pastors to preach this explicitly and repeatedly. Not once, as a missions Sunday gesture, but as a recurring claim about what the Gospel produces in a community — the conviction that belonging is not optional for human flourishing, that children cannot wait, that the family of God has room and is obligated to make room. The average congregation that has heard the sermon once has not yet built the culture that produces sustained participation.

Third, it requires the willingness to address the systems that produce children who need foster care. Poverty is the primary driver of family disruption. Addiction is the presenting crisis in the majority of foster care placements, and addiction is downstream of poverty, trauma, and social conditions that the church can speak to and work against. A church that is serious about foster care should also be serious about the conditions that create the need for it — about housing stability, about addiction treatment access, about economic support for families under pressure.

Fourth — and this is the one most likely to be skipped — it requires the church to support the biological families of children in foster care, not just the children themselves. The goal of the foster care system is family reunification in the majority of cases. The foster parent who treats the biological parent as the villain in the child's story has misunderstood the system and may be undermining the reunification that is best for the child. The church that wraps its care around the child should also wrap care around the struggling parent — visiting, supporting, holding without judgment the person whose failure of capacity put the child in care.

This is harder and less rewarding than simply loving the child. It requires the kind of non-sentimental compassion that can hold complexity and resist the moralism that wants clean heroes and clean villains. But it is the comprehensive vision of the mandate: not just to care for the child in crisis but to work toward the restoration of the family, and where restoration is not possible, to provide what the family cannot.

The mandate is not finished. Four hundred thousand children are waiting. The church has the theology, the community structure, and in many cases the material resources to respond. What it has lacked, in most places, is the will to organize itself around this rather than around its own institutional interests.

> Bringing a child in disrupts the household.

The church has often chosen the comfortable form of obedience — the mission trip, the offering, the program that produces a report — over the form that disrupts the household and costs something daily. Bringing a child in disrupts the household. It disrupts the schedule, the budget, the quiet. It requires exactly the kind of extended, unglamorous, unspectacular faithfulness that does not generate platform stories. That is why most congregations avoid it while genuinely believing they care.

That is a matter of decision, not capacity. The decision is still available.

The map in the missions conference has not changed. It still shows the Western hemisphere as the sending base and the Global South as the receiving field — the arrows running outward from North America and Europe toward Africa, Asia, and Latin America, carrying the gospel from places of relative plenty to places of relative need. The map is not wrong as an artifact of history. It is increasingly wrong as a description of reality.

The future of missions is not being planned in mission headquarters in Colorado Springs or London. It is already happening in Lagos and Seoul and São Paulo and Nairobi. The church that does not understand this is not only missing an extraordinary moment in the history of Christianity. It is organizing itself for a missionary role that the global church has largely moved past.

**The Numbers, First**

Christianity is not a declining religion. It is declining in Europe and North America, which have dominated the Western imagination of what Christianity looks like. It is expanding at rates without historical precedent in sub-Saharan Africa, across Latin America, in South Korea, in China, in Iran. [cite — confirm] The majority of the world's Christians now live in the Global South — in Africa, Latin America, and Asia. The majority of the world's church growth is happening in those regions. The majority of the world's missionaries being sent across cultural lines are now being sent by churches in those regions.

## The Inversion of the Missionary Flow

Nigeria sends missionaries to England. South Korea sends missionaries to the Middle East and Central Asia. Brazil sends missionaries to the Portuguese-speaking world and beyond. The Philippines sends missionaries across Southeast Asia. China, despite active state opposition to religious expression, has a domestic church of tens of millions and mission movements that are reaching ethnic minorities and neighboring nations. [cite — confirm]

The direction of the missionary flow has not simply shifted. It has inverted. The once-receiving field is now the sending base. The regions that European and North American missions regarded as the mission field a century ago are now the most vital missionary-sending communities in the world.

> The direction of the missionary flow has not simply shifted. It has inverted.

**What Made This Possible**

The Pentecostal movement, often traced to the Azusa Street Revival of 1906 in Los Angeles, carried a set of theological convictions about the immediacy of the Spirit's work that proved extraordinarily transferable across cultural contexts. The expectation of healing, of direct encounter with God, of a faith that was experiential and corporate and available to anyone regardless of literacy or institutional connection — these convictions resonated in communities where the distance between daily precarity and the need for divine intervention was not abstract. When the gospel arrived in the Global South through Pentecostal and later charismatic streams, it arrived in a form that engaged the immediate and visceral concerns of people whose lives demanded more than doctrinal instruction.

## How Pentecost and African Theology Remade the Faith

The African church also received and transformed the gospel through the lens of African theological categories — concepts of community, ancestors, the spiritual dimensions of physical life, the corporate nature of personhood — that European Christianity had largely suppressed or ignored. The church that emerged was not simply European Christianity in African dress. It was something genuinely new: a Christianity that had passed through African intellectual and spiritual tradition and emerged changed, carrying insights about the God of Scripture that the European tradition had not fully seen.

The same is true of the Korean church. The theology of *han* — the Korean concept of grief, injustice, and collective suffering that is simultaneously a wound and a source of resilience — produced a Christian spirituality of prayer and lament that the comfortable Western church had largely lost. Korean Christians pray differently because they have suffered differently. Their missionary enterprise, which is now one of the largest in the world per capita of Christian population, carries a theology forged in persecution, division, and the experience of a church that knows the cost of faith is real. [cite — confirm]

**What the Western Church Is Missing**

The Western missionary enterprise has not processed the implications of this shift. Many mission organizations still operate on models developed in the colonial period — models that assume the Western church is the primary sending agency, that national churches are junior partners requiring supervision, that Western theological training is the credential that legitimates leadership. These models are not simply inefficient. They are theologically confused.

## The Colonial Models the West Has Not Outgrown

A church that insists on Western oversight of national leaders in countries where the church is larger, older in faith, and more deeply embedded in the culture than anything the Western mission organization can build — that church is practicing a patronizing arrangement it calls partnership but that the national church often experiences as control. The financial dependency that many mission relationships create — in which the national church's budget is underwritten by Western donors who therefore hold structural authority over its decisions — is not partnership. It is a funding arrangement with theological consequences.

> It is a funding arrangement with theological consequences.

The Western church also has much to receive from the global church that it has not been positioned to receive because it has organized itself as the sender. The church in the Global South has sustained faith under conditions of persecution, poverty, political instability, and social marginalization that the Western church has not faced in living memory. That sustained faith has produced theological resources — on prayer, on suffering, on community, on eschatological hope that is not merely theoretical — that the Western church badly needs.

I have been in rooms where Nigerian pastors spoke about prayer with a quality of expectation that made my own prayer practice feel anemic. I have heard Korean Christians describe fasting in ways that challenged my assumptions about what a spiritual discipline was for. I have read African theology that reframed questions I had inherited from Western systematic theology and revealed their cultural partiality. None of these are exotic curiosities. They are gifts the church has been trying to offer and the Western church has been too confident in its own frameworks to receive.

**What Partnership Actually Requires**

Genuine partnership — not the charity-and-control arrangement that has historically defined many mission relationships, but actual partnership — requires a willingness to enter the relationship as a learner as well as a contributor.

## What Genuine Partnership Demands

The Western church has financial resources the global church often lacks. Those resources are genuinely useful. But financial resources come with structural power, and that power without intentional accountability becomes dominance. The partner relationship must name that dynamic explicitly and build structures that prevent the financial reality from determining the theological agenda. The national church must own its mission. It must set its theological priorities without Western supervision. It must build its own leadership pipeline that does not require a Western institution to certify its validity.

This also means rethinking what Western missionaries do in contexts where the national church exists and is healthy. The role is not replacement — it is not the Western missionary pastoring the Nigerian church because he was sent with funding. The role, if there is one, is service: coming alongside a national church movement to offer specific capacities that are genuinely lacking, with full authority resting with the national leadership, with a clear endpoint, and with the conscious intention of building what is already there rather than building something parallel that the Western organization controls.

The model of the future is not the Western missionary to the Global South. It is the global church collaborating across its own regional and cultural contexts — Nigerians partnering with South Africans, Koreans partnering with Chinese, Brazilians partnering with Portuguese-speakers in Africa and Europe — with the Western church as one participant among many, learning to receive as well as to give, and discovering that the body of Christ is not organized around Western centers in the way it was organized a century ago.

**What the Pastor in Fenton Needs to Know**

I pastor a church in Fenton, Michigan. The world's mission does not feel immediate from here. But the global church is not abstract from Fenton. There are Nigerian families and South Korean families and families from the Philippines within an hour's drive of our church building. The global church is arriving in American cities and towns in the form of immigrants and refugees whose faith has been formed under conditions that the American church has not experienced. They are not mission objects. They are mission partners.

## Receiving the Global Church in Fenton

What they carry — the theology of suffering, the practice of prayer, the ecclesiology of community, the expectation of God's direct intervention in daily life — is something the American church needs and has often failed to recognize as such. The first move of a serious mission engagement in the current moment is not to organize another trip to the Global South. It is to sit down with the Nigerian pastor two towns over and to receive, with genuine humility, what he knows about following Christ that you do not.

> The future of missions is already there. It has been there for some time.

The future of missions is already there. It has been there for some time. The question is whether the Western church is willing to relinquish enough of its self-appointed centrality to notice.

Every generation gets misread by the church that is trying to reach it. Gen Z is being misread badly — and the misreading is costing churches the people they most need to keep.

The church's typical answer to losing young people has been, for thirty years, a version of the same thing: better production, more relevant music, a preacher who wears sneakers and speaks their language. Some of this helped, for a time, with certain generations. With Gen Z — roughly those born between the mid-1990s and early 2010s — it is landing wrong.

Not because young people today do not respond to quality. But because Gen Z has a highly developed sense of when they are being marketed to, and the church that reorganizes itself around attracting them tends to read to them as exactly that: a sales strategy dressed in theological language.

---

The Millennial adjustment happened first. Churches in the early 2000s responded to Millennial disengagement with what sociologists Robert Bellah and his colleagues, writing earlier in "Habits of the Heart" [cite — confirm], had already identified as the American tendency to reduce religion to therapeutic individualism: faith as a tool for personal fulfillment, community as a resource for personal growth, God as the guarantor of self-actualization. The Millennial-facing church softened its edges, reduced its theological demands, and produced experiences that were warm, low-commitment, and attentive to consumer preference.

## The Millennial Performance Handed Down

This worked, to a degree. For a decade or more, the churches that executed it well grew. They attracted people who wanted spirituality without severity, community without accountability, meaning without obligation. They created something that genuinely helped some people and also, over time, produced congregations with shallow roots and no capacity to endure difficulty.

Gen Z watched this from inside their parents' churches, and many of them identified, early and precisely, the gap between what was being advertised and what was actually on offer. They had grown up watching the same performance dynamics play out on social media — the curated presentation, the optimized surface, the gap between the image and the reality — and they had developed, as a survival skill, a fairly sophisticated ability to name when they were being managed rather than met. The church that had mastered the Millennial performance handed it to Gen Z, and Gen Z could see the seams.

---

What research on Gen Z's religious attitudes consistently shows [cite — confirm] is not a generation that has abandoned the desire for transcendence, community, or moral grounding. These are not people who are indifferent to meaning. They are people who have a profound suspicion of institutions that claim to offer meaning while demonstrating, through their behavior, something other than what they advertise.

## A Generation Trained to See the Seams

The scandals of the last two decades — financial, sexual, ecclesiastical — have not passed unnoticed by a generation that grew up with social media making institutional failures visible in real time. The Southern Baptist Convention's abuse cover-up revelations, the celebrity pastor collapses, the documented patterns of institutional protection of predators [cite — confirm] — these are not abstract historical events to a twenty-year-old. They are the content that appeared in her feed during the years she was forming her understanding of what institutions are and what they do with power.

> She is not uninterested in the church.

She is not uninterested in the church. She is skeptical of it for specific reasons that deserve specific responses, not more sophisticated marketing.

---

What they are looking for is not a more entertaining version of what their parents had. They are looking for something genuinely different from the consumerism that surrounds them everywhere else. They want a community that is actually a community — that knows its members, that bears one another's burdens in the Galatians 6:2 sense of the phrase, not merely as a tagline but as a practiced reality, a community that does not simply gather for a weekly event and disperse back into isolation. The church that has perfected the Sunday morning experience and done nothing about the Monday morning loneliness of its members will not hold Gen Z. Because they can identify that gap. They live in it.

## The Loneliness No Algorithm Can Repair

The loneliness among young adults in this era is not a minor pastoral challenge. Jean Twenge's research on generational shifts in psychological wellbeing [cite — confirm] and Jonathan Haidt's work on the decline of adolescent mental health [cite — confirm] both point to something measurable and serious: the generation that grew up with the most technological connection is, by a number of measures, the most socially isolated. They know the difference between connection and community. They have grown up in a world that offers the first at unprecedented scale and provides the second with decreasing reliability. What they are looking for, in some cases, is the real thing. The church that offers genuine community — that would notice if you were missing on a Wednesday and call on a Thursday, that would show up with a meal in a crisis, that would be present in the Tuesday of your life and not just the Sunday of your week — that church has something to offer that no algorithm can replicate.

> They know the difference between connection and community.

---

They also want, more than the church generally expects, intellectual honesty. This is the finding that most surprises pastors: Gen Z is not asking for faith made easier. Some of them are asking for faith that takes its hardest questions seriously — that does not treat doubt as a spiritual failure, that does not paper over the genuine difficulties of Christian intellectual claims, that can say "I do not know" without appearing to lose confidence in the whole structure.

## The Demand for Intellectual Honesty

The church that presents a version of Christianity that has been pre-sanitized of its complications — that has resolved the problem of evil into a formula, that has smoothed over the violence of certain Old Testament texts, that has made the claims of the resurrection sound less strange than they are — will lose the intellectually serious among Gen Z before the first month is out. Not because they are looking for excuses not to believe. Because they have grown up in environments where intellectual dishonesty is easy to identify, and they will not trust a community that seems to require it.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from Tegel Prison in 1944, described what he called "religionless Christianity" — a form of faith stripped of its bourgeois cultural trappings and expressed in terms that could be inhabited by people who had seen through the accommodations of institutional religion [cite — confirm]. He was not calling for less theology. He was calling for a theology embedded in actual human reality rather than protected from it. That is closer to what Gen Z is looking for than anything currently described as "Gen Z ministry." They do not need faith made comfortable. They need faith that can inhabit the actual conditions of their lives — the anxiety, the institutional distrust, the loneliness, the questions that don't resolve tidily.

---

The congregation that will retain young adults is not the one that has the best band or the most culturally current preacher. It is the one that has taken the hardest questions seriously, built genuine community across the week rather than just on Sunday morning, and demonstrated — in its actual life, not its marketing — that the gospel it announces is the thing it lives.

There is a concrete test for this. Ask: would a young adult in your church know who to call at 2 AM if they were in crisis? If the answer is no — if the best they could do is send a message to a general info account and hope someone sees it Monday morning — then the community your church offers is a Sunday morning community, not a body. That gap is what Gen Z notices. That gap is what makes the church, for so many of them, feel like one more institution performing care rather than actually practicing it.

The pastoral response to this is not a new program for young adults. Programs are what you build when you want the appearance of community without the cost of it. The cost of genuine community is what programs are designed to avoid — the time, the vulnerability, the willingness to be known and to know others, the sustained presence in each other's actual lives. Programs manage people. Community forms them.

---

I want to name one more thing the research consistently surfaces, because it runs counter to what most church growth literature assumes about young adults. Gen Z is not looking for a church that has made Christianity easy to swallow. A significant number of them are looking for a community that requires something of them — that has genuine convictions, that makes actual demands, that holds its members accountable to a way of life, not just a set of beliefs. The church that has reduced its expectations to accommodate consumer preference will not hold the young adult who is looking for something worth giving his life to. The church that asks for nothing will receive the loyalty that nothing commands.

## Community That Costs Something

This is not a counsel for harshness or legalism. It is a counsel for seriousness. There is a difference between a community that demands compliance and a community that calls its members toward a life genuinely shaped by the gospel — the selling of possessions and giving to the poor, the love of enemies, the willingness to be last. That kind of community is countercultural in the deepest sense. And that depth is, for a generation drowning in shallow, genuinely attractive.

Not to everyone. Not even to most. But to enough — to the ones who have already identified that the world the algorithm offers is not the world worth inhabiting, and who are looking for someone to say: there is another way, and it costs something, and it is worth the cost.

> The church that asks for nothing will receive the loyalty that nothing commands.

That is not a generational program. That is just the church being the church.

It has always been what young people needed. We have simply been too busy being relevant to notice.

The statistics exist. They have existed for decades. In the United States, approximately one in four women will experience severe intimate partner violence in her lifetime. [cite — confirm] Globally, the World Health Organization estimates that roughly 35 percent of women have experienced either intimate partner violence or non-partner sexual violence at some point in their lives. [cite — confirm] The numbers are not improving at any meaningful rate. They describe a pattern of harm so consistent, so widespread, and so embedded in the structures of intimate life that it cannot be understood as a series of individual failures. It must be understood as a system.

The church has not wanted to understand it as a system. The reasons are not hard to find.

To name gender-based violence as a system requires asking questions about the cultural soil in which it grows. It requires examining the theology of headship and submission as it has been taught and practiced, and asking whether some versions of that theology have provided ideological cover for the exercise of coercive control. It requires hearing survivors — women who have sat in our pews, who have come to us for pastoral care, who have been sent home to unsafe situations by pastors who prioritized the appearance of marital stability over the physical safety of the woman in front of them. It requires the church to consider whether its own institutional patterns of male authority, combined with its theological culture of forgiveness and reconciliation, have created conditions in which abusers thrive and victims are silenced.

## Naming Violence as a System

These are not comfortable questions. They have, in many ecclesiastical contexts, been treated as attacks on Scripture or on the family rather than as pastoral assessments of what the Scripture itself demands. That response is its own indictment.

The biblical witness on violence against the vulnerable is not ambiguous. The prophets are relentless on the defense of those who cannot defend themselves. Ezekiel condemns the leaders of Israel specifically for having used violence against the people in their care: "You have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, or bound up the injured. You have not brought back the strays or searched for the lost. You have ruled them harshly and brutally" (Ezekiel 34:4). The pastoral metaphor is explicit. Those who were given the authority of shepherds over the flock used that authority to harm rather than protect. This is a text about governance. It is also a text about every relationship structured by authority and trust — including marriage, including pastors and congregants, including every context where power differentials exist.

## The Prophets and the Limit on Power

The law of the Hebrew Bible contains specific provisions for the protection of women in conditions of vulnerability. The legislation in Deuteronomy about divorce, about the treatment of women taken in war, about the conditions under which wives could be put away — these texts require careful handling and their patriarchal assumptions must be acknowledged honestly. But running through the Mosaic legislation is a consistent thread: the law constrains the exercise of male authority. It does not simply authorize it. The law that protected the female slave, the captive woman, the divorced wife — imperfectly by our standards, but present against the backdrop of surrounding cultures that offered no such protection — was doing something specific: it was marking a limit on what the powerful could do to the vulnerable.

> These are not comfortable questions.

Proverbs 31 closes the book with a portrait of female excellence that the tradition has often read as a domestic ideal, but its closing verse makes the evaluative criterion explicit: "Give her the fruit of her hands; let her works praise her at the gates" (Proverbs 31:31). The gates were the place of public legal adjudication. The woman of Proverbs 31 is being praised in the space where justice is dispensed. Her excellence is not merely domestic. It is civic, public, recognized in the arena of covenant community life.

And then there is Tamar, in 2 Samuel 13. Her half-brother Amnon rapes her. Her father King David is enraged but does nothing. Her full brother Absalom tells her to keep quiet about it, and Tamar — who has just been violated — lives "a desolate woman" in her brother's house (2 Samuel 13:20). The text names this with a specificity that should disturb any reader who takes the Scripture seriously. It does not moralize the situation into resolution. It shows us the desolation. It names Absalom's eventual murder of Amnon as the consequence of institutional failure — the failure of a father-king who should have acted and did not. The text is not endorsing the silence. It is recording the cost of the silence, paid by Tamar, in her body and in her life.

## The Desolation of Tamar

I have sat across from women who told me what happened in their homes. I have also — and this is harder to say — been in conversations where the institutional pressure was toward keeping the family together, toward counseling rather than protection, toward the language of redemption before the conditions of safety were established. I participated in a pastoral culture that did not always ask first whether the woman in front of us was safe. That is not a neutral failure. It has a name.

The theological framework that has most damaged the church's response to gender-based violence is a misreading of the theology of suffering and sacrifice. When a woman in an abusive marriage is counseled to endure because suffering has redemptive value, when she is told that her cross is her marriage and Christ calls her to carry it, when the language of covenant faithfulness is deployed to prevent her from accessing safety — the church has weaponized the theology of the cross. It has turned an instrument of liberation into an instrument of captivity.

## When the Cross Becomes a Cage

The cross is not a template for absorbing the violence of the powerful. The cross is God absorbing the violence of the powerful so that the vulnerable do not have to. This distinction is not a minor adjustment. It is the difference between a theology that protects abusers and a theology that names abuse as the violation of the image of God in the person being harmed.

> The cross is not a template for absorbing the violence of the powerful.

Paul's instruction to husbands in Ephesians 5 — to love their wives "as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Ephesians 5:25) — places the weight of sacrifice on the one with authority, not on the one with less. The hermeneutic that has read this passage primarily as a warrant for female submission, while attending only minimally to the demands it places on the husband, has inverted the text. The sacrificial love demanded of the husband in Ephesians 5 is not a pleasant aspiration. It is a structural claim that the one with authority is required to use that authority for the benefit and protection of the more vulnerable party.

Repentance here is institutional, not only individual. The church that has protected its own reputation by silencing survivors, that has required reconciliation before safety, that has treated the leaving of an abusive marriage as a greater sin than the abuse itself, that has refused to name coercive control as an abuse of power — that church owes a specific and public acknowledgment of what it has done. Not as a therapeutic exercise. As truth-telling. As the precondition for genuine change.

## What Repentance Looks Like

What change looks like is specific. It looks like training — mandatory, recurring training for all pastoral staff in the recognition of domestic abuse and intimate partner violence, including coercive control, which leaves no visible marks and is among the most dangerous patterns. It looks like formal protocols for pastoral response that prioritize safety before reconciliation. It looks like the congregation becoming a community where survivors can speak and be believed, where the question "are you safe?" is asked before the question "how is your marriage?" It looks like the pulpit naming this from time to time without euphemism, not as a social program but as a covenantal obligation.

The woman who is unsafe in her home on Sunday night and sitting in a pew Sunday morning is not there by accident. She came, often, because the church has told her it stands for human dignity, for the protection of the vulnerable, for a vision of life together shaped by the love that gives itself up rather than taking by force.

Whether she finds that church or finds a different one depends on decisions that are within our authority to make.

> The desolate woman in 2 Samuel 13 is still waiting.

The church that becomes a place of genuine safety will not look primarily different on the outside. The worship will be recognizable. The theology will be orthodox. What will be different is the texture of trust — the sense that a person carrying a hidden weight can say what the weight is and not be sent home to carry it alone. That texture does not form through a policy. It forms through the repeated experience of being believed, protected, and held by a community whose stated theology and actual practice are the same.

The desolate woman in 2 Samuel 13 is still waiting.

We are not required to make her wait any longer.

The coffee shop opens first. Then the yoga studio. Then the artisan bakery with the brick-exposed walls and the chalkboard menu and the pour-over coffee that costs six dollars. The restaurant follows, with small plates and a wine list. The neighborhood begins appearing in city lifestyle magazines with words like "up and coming" and "revitalized" and "hidden gem." The people who have lived in that neighborhood for thirty years — who raised their children there, who buried their parents there, who know every family on the block — watch the rent double. Then triple. Some of them hold on for a few years. Most of them leave.

This is gentrification. Not as a slur. Not as a political talking point. As a description of a process that has reshaped American cities across the last four decades with measurable, documented effects on which communities get to stay in place and which are made to leave.

> The church has been largely quiet about it. That silence requires examination.

The church has been largely quiet about it. That silence requires examination.

---

## The Displacement That Came Before

Gentrification is not a natural weather event. It is the outcome of systems — investment decisions, zoning policies, tax structures, real estate speculation, city planning choices — that direct resources toward some neighborhoods and away from others in patterns that track with race and class. Richard Rothstein's *The Color of Law*, published in 2017 [cite — confirm year], documented how decades of explicit government policy — federal mortgage programs that excluded Black families, racially restrictive covenants enforced by courts, urban renewal projects that demolished Black neighborhoods and dispersed their residents — created the concentrated poverty that gentrification now "solves" by pricing out the people who survived it.

That is the point: the poverty and disinvestment that made these neighborhoods cheap enough to gentrify was itself the product of deliberate policy. The people being displaced now were first displaced into these neighborhoods by policies that excluded them from everywhere else. The gentrification completes the displacement that the original policies began.

That historical arc matters for how the church reads what is happening. This is not two parties in a neutral market transaction. It is the continuation of a long story of displacement in which the same communities keep losing.

---

## Inheritance and the Logic of Jubilee

The biblical tradition has a name for what is happening in the displacement of long-established communities. Micah 2:1–2 says: "Woe to those who plan iniquity, to those who plot evil on their beds! At morning's light they carry it out because it is in their power to do it. They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them. They defraud people of their homes, they rob them of their inheritance." The word translated "inheritance" is *nachalah* — the portion that roots a family to a place across generations, the land that carries their story and their belonging.

This is not metaphorical. The prophets understood that the displacement of families from their land was among the most serious violations a society could commit — because the land was the basis of livelihood, of community, of identity. The laws of Jubilee in Leviticus 25 were specifically designed to prevent the permanent alienation of family land, requiring that it revert to the original family in the fiftieth year. The permanent transfer of land from poor to wealthy families was understood as a structural corruption that needed to be architecturally corrected in the legal order. The Jubilee was God's answer to the market's tendency to concentrate land in the hands of those who could pay most for it.

The contemporary equivalent of this dynamic — real estate speculation pricing long-term residents out of neighborhoods their families have occupied for generations — maps precisely onto what the prophets named. The mechanism is different. The structure is the same.

---

## What the Market Cannot Quantify

Consider what is actually lost in displacement. The dominant narrative about gentrification frames it primarily in terms of economics: rising rents, increasing property values, improved "amenities." But what is actually being destroyed is something the market cannot quantify.

When a family is displaced from a neighborhood, they lose proximity to the informal networks — the neighbor who watches the children, the church community that knows their family's story, the relationships that provide emergency support when the car breaks down or the grandmother needs a ride — that make survival possible in conditions of economic fragility. The social capital that takes decades to build across a community is dispersed in a single lease-renewal cycle.

James 2:14–17 is direct: "What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone claims to have faith but has no deeds? Can such faith save them? Suppose a brother or a sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you says to them, 'Go in peace; keep warm and well fed,' but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is it?" The test of genuine faith is the material response to material need. And material need includes the need for stable housing, for community, for the ability to remain in place.

The church that holds services in a gentrifying neighborhood while remaining silent about displacement is offering, in effect, the James 2 benediction: "go in peace, be warm and well fed" — without addressing the structural forces that are making warmth and food and community increasingly inaccessible to the people in its neighborhood.

---

## The Silence That Suits Our Interests

The steel-man case for gentrification argues that neighborhood revitalization benefits communities that have suffered from disinvestment, that new resources and new residents bring amenities that benefit everyone, that the alternative to investment is continued decline, and that some degree of population change is inevitable and not necessarily harmful. Some advocates for "equitable development" argue that the question is not whether neighborhoods change but how to manage that change so that long-term residents can benefit from it rather than being priced out by it.

This is a serious argument and it deserves a serious response. Disinvestment is real and harmful. Neighborhoods cannot thrive without resources. The goal is not to freeze communities in poverty. The goal is to ensure that the benefits of investment flow to the people already there, rather than replacing them.

That framing — equitable development — is the right frame. But the church that uses the genuine complexity of the argument as a reason to say nothing has not engaged with the argument. It has used the argument as cover for a silence that suits its institutional interests. Many churches are in gentrifying neighborhoods. Some are among the institutions that are benefiting from rising property values. The church that says nothing about displacement while its own property values increase has its silence explained, at least in part, by its financial interests.

> It is practicing institutional self-protection and calling it prudence.

That is the harder thing to name. And the church that cannot name the ways its institutional interests shape its prophetic silences is not practicing prophetic discernment. It is practicing institutional self-protection and calling it prudence.

---

## Shalom and the Right to Remain

What does the biblical vision of shalom require here? Shalom is not simply the absence of conflict. It is the comprehensive flourishing of the whole community — the situation in which every family has what it needs to participate fully in the life of the community across generations. The *nachalah* — the inheritance, the rooted belonging — is part of shalom. A community characterized by shalom is one in which families can stay, can build, can belong, can pass something forward.

Displacement is the opposite of shalom. Not necessarily because the people moving in are bad, but because the system producing displacement treats the existing community as an obstacle to be priced out rather than a community to be invested in. The system does not see the long-term residents as bearers of the community's history and social capital. It sees them as temporary occupants of underpriced real estate.

Jeremiah's letter to the exiles in Babylon — "seek the peace and prosperity of the city to which I have carried you into exile" (Jeremiah 29:7) — is sometimes invoked in discussions of neighborhood investment, and rightly so. But the exiles Jeremiah was writing to were the displaced. They were the ones who had been taken from their homes. The command to seek the city's welfare was addressed to people who had already lost what they built. The church that reads Jeremiah 29 only as an instruction to invest in the city and never asks who has been displaced from it to make room for the investment has read selectively.

---

The practical question is where the church locates itself in this dynamic. Not abstractly — concretely, specifically, in the neighborhood it actually occupies.

Is the church's neighborhood gentrifying? If so, who is being displaced, and from what? What is the church doing with its platform and its presence to make the displacement visible? Has it spoken? If not, why not?

Is the church among the institutions whose property values are rising while the community's composition changes? What does it do with that? How does it use its resources not just to serve newcomers but to advocate for the people who are being priced out?

Does the church know the long-term residents of its neighborhood by name — not as a ministry category, but as neighbors? Does it know their stories, their histories, their vulnerabilities? A church that does not know who is being displaced from its neighborhood cannot advocate for them. And it cannot know them without paying the attention that genuine love requires.

The prophetic tradition is a tradition of naming what is happening to the most vulnerable people in your community. Not vaguely. Not in abstraction. Specifically. The names of the families who are leaving. The mechanisms that are driving them out. The institutions that could speak and choose silence.

The neighborhood belongs to God (Psalm 24:1). The land is the Lord's. The families who built their lives in it — who were often displaced into it by earlier policies of exclusion — have a claim rooted in something prior to the market. The church that cannot name that claim has reduced the gospel to a service for whoever currently occupies the pews, and has called the reduction faithfulness.

> The coffee shop is not the problem. The silence is.

The coffee shop is not the problem. The silence is.

Most feedback conversations accomplish one thing: they make the person giving the feedback feel that they have discharged an obligation. The conversation happens. The words are spoken. The file is documented. And the person receiving the feedback leaves the meeting confused, defensive, or privately unconvinced — and changes nothing.

I have given feedback this way. I have sat across from a staff member or a volunteer leader and said the right things in the right sequence and watched the person nod in all the right places and known, even as it was happening, that nothing would change. Not because the person was resistant, but because I had said what I needed to say rather than what they needed to hear.

This is not a small distinction. Most pastoral leaders are better at the former than the latter, for reasons that go deeper than skill.

## The Pastoral Discomfort with Correction

The pastoral tradition has a complicated relationship with correction. On one side is the prophetic heritage — Amos confronting Israel's injustice, Nathan confronting David, Paul writing to the Corinthians that he will come with a rod if they do not deal with the man living with his father's wife (1 Corinthians 5:3-5). The prophetic voice does not equivocate. It names the thing. On the other side is a pastoral temperament that bends toward mercy — toward wanting to protect people from pain, toward softening the hard edge, toward a kind of relational warmth that sometimes prevents rather than enables honest speech. Most pastors are, by constitution, more comfortable with the second than the first. The result is feedback that keeps the peace and changes nothing.

> The result is feedback that keeps the peace and changes nothing.

The church inherited its understanding of correction primarily from Paul, who modeled a complexity that is hard to imitate. When Paul writes to the Corinthians in 2 Corinthians 7:8-9, he says he does not regret the painful letter he wrote them, because it produced genuine repentance. The goal was not to wound. The goal was metanoia — the turning that leads to life. Paul's standard for whether correction was successful was not whether the person felt better afterward. It was whether they changed. That is a harder standard than most of us hold ourselves to.

The first failure of ineffective feedback is that it is abstract. "Your communication needs to improve." "You are not as present in meetings as you should be." These statements may be accurate. They do not tell the person what to actually do differently on Tuesday morning. Specific behavior is the only addressable unit of change. The feedback that changes anything is feedback that is concrete enough to act on: "When you send the meeting agenda the night before, people come unprepared. Send it by Thursday afternoon and watch what changes." The pastor who cannot name a specific, recent, observable behavior when giving feedback is not giving feedback. He is giving a general impression, and general impressions produce defensiveness, not growth.

## Why Abstract Feedback Changes Nothing

The second failure is that it arrives too late. Feedback delivered six weeks after the event it is responding to is not feedback. It is a record. The person being addressed has no access to the emotional and contextual reality that the feedback is responding to — it has faded, reinterpreted itself, been processed in a dozen different directions. The feedback that has the best chance of changing behavior is feedback given close enough to the event that the person can re-enter it, can access the specific situation, can actually imagine doing it differently.

Proverbs has a great deal to say about the relationship between words and their timing. "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver" (Proverbs 25:11). The word fitly spoken is the right word in the right moment — not just accurate in content but appropriate in timing and delivery. Timing feedback well requires the pastor to name what he observed in something close to real time — not necessarily in the moment, because some observations require reflection before they are ready to be shared, but close enough that the moment is still alive.

The third failure, and the one most costly to correct, is that the feedback lacks genuine care for the person receiving it. Feedback delivered as organizational maintenance — you are not meeting the job description, these are the requirements, this is being documented — communicates that the person is a function, not a person. Human beings do not change their behavior significantly in response to being treated as functions. They comply minimally and protect themselves. Behavior changes in response to someone who clearly cares about their actual growth and is willing to tell them hard things precisely because they believe those hard things will help.

## Restoration, Not Performance Management

Paul's counsel in Galatians 6:1 — "Brothers and sisters, if someone is caught in a sin, you who live by the Spirit should restore that person gently" — does not describe performance management. It describes pastoral intervention. The word Paul uses for *restore* — *katartizō* — is the word used for setting a broken bone or repairing a torn net. Painful, but aimed at making the thing whole and functional again. The gentleness is not softness. It is the posture of someone who is in the work for the other person's sake, not for the sake of institutional compliance.

There is a steel-man worth hearing here. Some pastoral leaders, taking the above seriously, make the opposite error: they become so focused on care and relationship that they cannot be direct. They circle the issue endlessly. They soften every hard truth until it no longer carries any edge. They confuse pastoral warmth with the avoidance of anything painful. This is not care — it is its counterfeit. The person who leaves the meeting not knowing that their leader has a serious concern about their performance has not been cared for. They have been managed. And they will eventually discover the problem, under worse circumstances, with less time to respond.

> Direct and caring are not opposites.

Direct and caring are not opposites. The most effective feedback I have ever witnessed held both without compromising either. It named the specific behavior, named its specific impact, named the expectation going forward, and then asked the person what support they needed to meet it. The care was not in the softening of the correction. The care was in treating the person as someone capable of change and worth the investment of honest speech.

The pastoral leader who wants to give feedback that actually changes behavior must practice three things.

## The Three Disciplines

First, the discipline of specificity. After every difficult observation, before the conversation: what specifically did you see, when did you see it, what specifically would different look like? If you cannot answer those questions concretely, you are not ready to speak.

Second, the discipline of proximity. Do not accumulate. Deal with what you observe in something close to real time. The conversation held thirty days after the event is helping no one. The conversation held forty-eight hours after the event, after you have slept on it and thought clearly about what you want to say, can change something.

Third, the discipline of investment. Ask yourself honestly: do I actually want this person to succeed? If the answer is yes, that investment will be audible. If the answer is no — if you are feeding a paper trail toward a termination decision rather than genuinely investing in someone's growth — then what you are doing is not feedback. It is documentation. Documentation has its place. It is not pastoral work.

The hardest feedback I have ever had to give was to someone I genuinely loved and whose failure was going to cost both of us something real. I gave it badly the first time — too much care, not enough directness. The message did not land. I gave it again, more plainly. The person heard it that time. It was not comfortable. It was not designed to be comfortable.

The goal was not comfort. The goal was restoration.

> The goal was not comfort. The goal was restoration.

That is usually how genuine pastoral correction works. You do not get credit for the attempt. You do not get credit for your intentions. You get the result, or you do not. And whether you get the result depends on whether you were willing to be both direct enough to actually name the thing and caring enough that the person knew you were on their side.

Most of us find one of those easier than the other. The work is to find both in the same conversation.

## The Feedback That Protects the Leader

There is a fourth failure that sits underneath the other three and rarely gets named: the leader who gives feedback primarily to protect himself. He speaks so that later he can say he spoke. He documents so that the termination is defensible. He delivers the message at the time and in the form that is most comfortable for him, not most useful for the person receiving it. This is not pastoral leadership. This is institutional self-protection dressed in the language of accountability.

The pastoral leader who wants to be taken seriously on this issue has to examine his own motives before he opens his mouth. Is the goal this person's growth? Or is the goal your record? Both may be legitimate in the end, but they require different conversations. The conversation aimed at growth treats the person as someone with capacity and worth and a future. The conversation aimed at documentation treats the person as a risk to be managed.

People know the difference. They have always known the difference. The conversation that treats them as capable of growth will be received as hard but caring. The conversation that treats them as a liability problem will be received as the preliminary to a firing, whether that is true or not.

Begin with the assumption that the person can change. Deliver the feedback accordingly. Then see what happens.

The global church is not somewhere else. We tend to picture it that way — believers in distant countries, with unfamiliar languages and harder lives, the subject of a missions slideshow and a line in our giving. Real, but remote. Theirs, not ours. That picture is a quiet heresy, and it impoverishes us more than it impoverishes them.

---

## Kinship Closer Than Blood

The New Testament will not allow the distance. Paul tells the Corinthians that they are members of a single body, and that "if one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together" (1 Corinthians 12:26). He is not speaking only of the people in one building in one city in the ancient world. He is speaking of the body of Christ, which has no nationality, which spans every tribe and tongue and language, which is one organism with one Head. The believer worshipping in a house church in a hostile country is not a stranger you support from a distance. He is your brother, closer kin in the only family that finally matters than your neighbors who do not share the faith.

> This reframes everything.

This reframes everything.

The persecuted church is not a charity. It is your family under fire. Hebrews tells you to "remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body" (Hebrews 13:3). As though with them. Not as distant beneficiaries of your concern, but as your own people, whose chains you are meant to feel in your own wrists. The command is not to send resources to people in difficult circumstances. It is to locate yourself inside their experience, because the body that is being imprisoned is the body you inhabit.

---

## The Missionary Frame and Its Distortions

The history of how Western Christianity has understood the global church is worth honest examination, because the errors are still producing consequences.

The nineteenth-century missionary movement — for all its genuine faith and genuine cost — operated largely within a framework that placed the Western church at the center: as the sender, the teacher, the mature tradition, and the recipient communities as the mission field, the immature, the ones who needed what the West possessed. The framework was not entirely wrong. There was real gospel. There was real sacrifice. William Carey, Hudson Taylor, David Livingstone — these were not frauds, and dismissing the missionary movement as merely colonialism fails the actual complexity.

But the frame was distorted, and the distortion produced consequences that the global church is still living with. Indigenous leadership was often undermined rather than developed. Western theology was often delivered as the universal form of Christianity rather than as one culturally situated expression of it. The ecclesial traditions and spiritual gifts of the receiving communities — traditions that in some cases were richer and more ancient than anything the Western missionaries carried — were treated as raw material to be evangelized rather than as the spiritual inheritance of communities who already knew something about God.

Lamin Sanneh, the Gambian-born scholar of world Christianity who taught at Yale, argued that the translation of the gospel into local languages carried within it the seeds of the frame's own correction: when you put Scripture into someone's mother tongue, you have admitted that their language is adequate to carry the revelation, and once you have admitted that, the claim of Western cultural superiority becomes theologically untenable. [cite — confirm] The translation was the decolonization, working slowly underneath the colonial assumptions of the movement that sponsored it.

---

## Where the Center of the Church Has Moved

The numbers tell a story that the Western church has been slow to absorb.

> The vitality is not here. It is there.

The center of global Christianity is no longer the North Atlantic. It is sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and parts of Asia. Philip Jenkins, in his landmark work on the future of global Christianity, documented the massive shift in the demographic center of the church that occurred through the twentieth century. [cite — confirm] The church is growing fastest, and often suffering most, in the very places the missions movement once treated as the recipients. The Christianity being practiced in the Global South is frequently more theologically conservative, more pneumatically alive, and more directly engaged with the suffering of poverty than what most Western congregations experience on a Sunday morning. The vitality is not here. It is there.

This does not mean Western Christianity is without contribution. It means the frame has reversed. We imagined ourselves the teachers. We are increasingly the ones who need to sit down and learn.

I have carried the provincial picture. I have prayed for the global church the way you pray for a cause rather than a family — briefly, at a distance, without really believing that their joys were mine to share and their suffering mine to feel. The repentance required is not primarily organizational. It is imaginative. It is the willingness to let the theological reality become emotionally actual: that I am bound, by something thicker than blood, to people I will not meet until glory, and that their faithfulness is part of my inheritance and their suffering part of my own body's pain.

---

## Insularity as Self-Harm

The theology Paul is working with in 1 Corinthians 12 is not metaphor. It is ontology. He is not saying the church is *like* a body. He is saying the church *is* the body of Christ — a real, organic unity in which the Spirit distributes gifts to each member for the good of the whole, in which the suffering of one part constitutes suffering of the whole organism, in which the provincial protection of any one part's interests at the expense of the whole is a self-wounding.

> We amputate a portion of our own inheritance.

That means the Western church's insularity is not only a moral failure. It is a form of self-harm. The gifts that the global church carries — its theologies of suffering, its practices of communal prayer and fasting, its clarity about the cost of discipleship, its experience of the Spirit's movement in conditions of material poverty — these are gifts to the body. When we treat the global church as the recipient of our resources while remaining closed to what it has to offer, we impoverish ourselves. We amputate a portion of our own inheritance.

---

What does it change, practically?

It changes how you pray. Not the blanket intercession for "the church around the world," but specific, named, located prayer — for the congregation in northern Nigeria navigating the violence between farming and herding communities, for the house church in a Central Asian city where gathering involves real risk, for the pastor in Haiti rebuilding for the fourth time. Prayer that has geography and names and the specificity you would use for family.

It changes how you give — not as a patron funding a project, but as one part of a body sharing resources with another part, because the organism does not thrive when its resources are permanently concentrated in one location.

It changes how you hold your own comfort. The member of your body who considers a week of genuine risk to be an ordinary week — who leads a church where attendance itself is an act of courage — will recalibrate what counts as hard in your own ministry. Not with guilt. With proportion.

And it changes how you understand the church itself. Not as your congregation with some international affiliates. Not as the Western tradition with a mission arm. But as a single, global, blood-bought people, spread across every language and nation, of whom your church is one small, beloved, accountable part — accountable to the whole body for how it uses its resources, for whether it is praying with the suffering members, for whether it has let the distance become an excuse to live as though the body that suffers on another continent is not its own.

Revelation 7:9 describes the end: "a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb." That gathering is what the church already is, in Christ, right now. The gathering on Sunday morning in one building is not the church. It is the church assembling as itself in one place — one expression of a body that extends to every corner of the globe and every generation of the faithful dead.

## The Collection as the Body Behaving Like a Body

The New Testament writers held this global scope as a non-negotiable feature of Christian identity. Paul's collection for the Jerusalem church — the project he described in Romans 15, 1 Corinthians 16, and 2 Corinthians 8-9 — was not a charitable program. It was a theological statement about the unity of the body. Gentile churches sending money to Jewish churches across the Mediterranean was Paul's evidence that the dividing wall had actually fallen, that the new humanity he described in Ephesians 2 was not a theological claim but a lived reality. The collection was the body behaving like a body.

What would it look like for a congregation to take that seriously today? Not as an annual missions offering, not as a line in the budget — but as a structural commitment to the truth that what happens to the church in one part of the world is happening to us? That the body in chains is our body? That the body rebuilding after the third earthquake is our family, not a worthy cause?

The rest of your church is already assembled. In prisons you are not in. In cemeteries you have not visited. In services conducted in languages you do not speak. In sanctuaries that do not have the heat on because the congregation cannot afford it, where the worship is more fully alive than anything you experienced last Sunday.

They are your family. They have been praying for you. The question is whether you will start praying as though you believed it was mutual.

There is a prayer meeting happening right now in northern Nigeria, or in a house church in Henan province in China, or in a village in Eritrea, where the people gathered are praying in full awareness that their faith may cost them something before the week is out. They are not praying for comfort. They are praying for courage. They are praying for each other's families in the event of arrest. They are praying, many of them, with the kind of specificity and desperation that is almost entirely absent from the prayer life of the average American congregation.

I have led prayer meetings in Fenton, Michigan. I know what they sound like. The comparison is not comfortable.

> The comparison is not comfortable.

The theology of suffering that emerges from the persecuted church is not an academic product. It is not developed in seminaries, though it is reflected in their finest theological thinking. It is developed in the experience of communities that have had no option but to discover what Paul actually means when he writes in Romans 8:18 that "the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed." They have not discovered this because they are more spiritual than American Christians. They have discovered it because they have had no comfortable alternative to the text.

---

## A Theology of Avoidance

The American church's theology of suffering is, by contrast, largely a theology of avoidance. We believe in a God who heals, who protects, who provides — and we are right to believe those things, because they are true. But we have often stopped the sentence there, at the part where God removes the difficulty, without proceeding to the part where God is present in the difficulty that does not get removed.

Hebrews 11 does not end with verse 33, where the heroes of faith conquered kingdoms and stopped the mouths of lions and received their dead back to life. It continues to verse 37, where others were sawn in two, and verse 38, where they wandered in deserts and mountains and caves, and verse 39, where none of them received what was promised.

Both halves of that chapter are the witness of faith. The American church preaches the first half with great enthusiasm. The second half makes us uncomfortable, because it does not fit the framework we have built for understanding what faithfulness looks like. We have built that framework in the context of a society in which the premium religious product is consolation, and in which suffering is primarily framed as a problem to be solved or at minimum explained — a pastoral emergency to be managed until it lifts, not a condition to be inhabited with faithfulness.

## The Laments That Do Not Resolve

The Psalms are more honest about this than most contemporary American preaching is. The lament psalms — which constitute roughly a third of the Psalter — do not resolve. Psalm 88 ends in darkness: "You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness" (Psalm 88:18). No resolution. No pivot to praise. Darkness is the last word. The Hebrew canon preserved that psalm. The canon made room for the prayer that does not get answered the way the pray-er hoped.

The American church has largely edited those prayers out. We rush to the resolution because unresolved suffering makes us theologically anxious — it raises questions about God's goodness, God's power, the mechanism of prayer, the relationship between faith and outcome. Rather than sit in the tension, we move toward the answer. Usually a specific kind of answer: the one in which God intervenes and the suffering ends.

---

## Both Halves of Hebrews 11

The church in the Global South — particularly in communities experiencing active persecution — has had to work with both halves of the Hebrews 11 text, because their experience includes both. They have seen the miraculous. They have also buried people for whom the miraculous did not come. Their faith has been formed in the tension between those two realities rather than in the avoidance of it.

This does not make suffering good. Lamin Sanneh, the great Gambian-born historian of World Christianity who taught at Yale for decades [cite — confirm], spent his career tracing how the gospel was received by communities who had no reason to expect that Christianity would align with their social comfort or political power. His work describes communities whose faith was forged in the absence of cultural support, in which the text spoke to people facing exactly the kind of extremity that the text addresses most directly.

The witness of those communities is not theoretical. It is not a chapter in a global theology textbook. It is the testimony of people — people with names, families, histories — who have found that God is present in conditions where the comfortable theology fails. Who have discovered that the prayer for removal of the cup was answered, for Jesus himself, by the cup's not being removed, and yet by the presence of the Father through what followed.

That is a different discovery than anything most American prayer meetings produce.

---

Philip Jenkins, in his account of the global South's Christian explosion, describes communities that read the biblical text of suffering without the hermeneutical filters that a culturally established church develops to soften the hardest passages [cite — confirm]. The passages about persecution, about the cost of discipleship, about the enemies of the cross — these are not metaphorical in communities that have literal enemies. They are read plainly, because the plain reading is the one that corresponds to the community's actual experience.

That plain reading produces a specific theological posture: not the expectation that faith produces safety, but the conviction that faith produces the capacity to remain faithful even when it does not produce safety. The distinction is everything. The first expectation — faith equals protection — is the expectation that collapses when the suffering arrives and does not lift. It is the expectation behind the "crisis of faith" that many Western Christians experience when life goes badly. The second conviction — faith equals the capacity for faithfulness within suffering — is the conviction that has sustained the church through every century of serious opposition.

> The distinction is everything.

Peter writes to communities who are already suffering: "Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed." (1 Peter 4:12-13) He does not tell them the trial will end. He tells them what to do with it while it is happening. He has a theology for the situation they are in. Most American pastoral theology has a theology for the situation in which the trial ends quickly.

---

## What This Means for the American Pastor

What this means practically for the American pastor is a question worth sitting with.

The first thing it means is that genuine relationship with the global church — relationship sustained over time, relationship that involves actual listening rather than project management — is not a nice addition to a well-rounded ministry. It is a theological necessity for any pastor who wants to preach honestly about suffering to people who suffer. The pastor whose theology of suffering has been formed entirely in comfortable circumstances will eventually face a congregant whose circumstances are not comfortable, and he will have words that are insufficient for what that person is carrying.

I have had that experience. I have sat with someone in a suffering that my theology could not hold, and I have watched myself reach for the platitudes — the God-is-in-control language, the Romans-8:28 application, the promise of eventual resolution — because I had not been formed by any tradition that could do better. I was not being dishonest. I was being inadequate. And the person across from me deserved more than my inadequacy.

The second thing it means is that we need to recover the lament tradition — not as a program or a series, but as a genuine liturgical practice. The community that cannot lament together cannot grieve together. The community that cannot grieve together will eventually find that suffering is an event to be managed rather than a human reality to be inhabited together. The church in Nigeria or the house church in Henan knows how to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15) because it has had to. We can choose to learn it.

The third thing it means is about the prosperity theology that has metastasized through significant portions of American Christianity. The persecuted church is not the church that believes its faithfulness will be rewarded with health and wealth and favor in this life. The persecuted church knows, from hard and recent experience, that faithfulness is sometimes rewarded with prison and death. Any theology that cannot account for those outcomes is not the theology of the New Testament. It is a theology that has been constructed to serve a comfortable audience, and it will shatter when the comfort is removed.

The church in the Global South holds the mirror up to this. Not because they have something we do not — they have less of almost everything by material measure. But because the conditions they have been formed in have forced them to read the text without the insulation we use to soften it.

---

## The Hope That Is Not Optimism

What that formation produces is a different quality of hope. Not optimism — which is a confidence that things will improve — but hope, which is a confidence that God is present regardless of whether things improve. The distinction is not semantic. It shapes how a community prays, how it sustains commitment across discouraging seasons, how it understands the death of its members, how it preaches to people who are suffering.

The American pastor who has access to this tradition through relationship with the global church — through genuine, sustained partnership rather than conference exposure — is receiving something that cannot be manufactured in a comfortable environment. He is receiving the testimony of people who have found God sufficient in conditions where nothing else was.

That testimony does not make suffering good. It does not make the persecution of the church in Nigeria or China or Eritrea acceptable. It demands our advocacy, our resources, our solidarity, our political voice where we have one.

But it also carries a word for us — for the comfortable church in the comfortable country — about what faith actually looks like when the scaffolding of cultural support and social acceptability and institutional favor is removed.

The word is: still faithful.

We need to hear that word more than we know. We need to hear it from people who have not said it theoretically, who have said it while standing in the ash, who say it still with nothing but the promise of the one who said it first.

> Still faithful.

Still faithful.

That is the whole of the tradition. And we have been too comfortable to fully receive it.

We have turned the parable of the Good Samaritan into a moral lesson about being helpful. This is one of the more impressive acts of domestication in Christian history.

The parable has been used to name hospitals, homeless shelters, and good deeds of all kinds — a word for the person who stops to help when others walk by. There is nothing wrong with that application except that it misses almost everything the parable is actually doing. Jesus is not teaching a lesson about helpfulness. He is answering a question with a story that was designed to be offensive — designed to expose the way his questioner's entire framework for organizing the world was wrong.

---

## The Lawyer Looking for the Edge of the Map

The setup requires attention. A lawyer — an expert in the Torah — asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life (Luke 10:25). Jesus asks him what the law says. The man answers correctly: love God with everything you have, and love your neighbor as yourself. Jesus tells him he has answered well.

But then comes the move that tells you everything about the man's actual concern: "And who is my neighbor?" (Luke 10:29). Luke adds the interpretive gloss that he said this "to justify himself." He is not asking in intellectual curiosity. He is asking because the commandment to love your neighbor has already landed, and he wants to know where the boundary is — how far out the obligation extends before he is free of it. He is asking for the line.

> He is asking for the line.

This is one of the oldest moves in the human moral playbook. We acknowledge the obligation in principle and then proceed to define the category of those to whom it applies as narrowly as possible. The question "who is my neighbor?" is the question of a man looking for the edge of the map. If he can locate it, he can love his neighbors and be righteous while remaining untroubled by everyone else.

Jesus tells a story in response. A man is beaten and left dying on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. A priest passes. A Levite passes. Both see the man. Both go to the other side. Then a Samaritan comes.

---

## Who the Samaritan Was to That Audience

To hear this as Jesus's audience would have heard it requires understanding who Samaritans were to first-century Jews.

The relationship between Jews and Samaritans was ancient and bitter.
