It originated in the aftermath of the Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom in the eighth century BCE, when the Assyrian policy of population transfer brought foreign settlers into the land who intermarried with the remaining Israelites and developed a mixed religious practice centered on Mount Gerizim rather than Jerusalem. By the first century, the animosity was deep and mutual. Jews traveling between Galilee and Judea would often take longer routes to avoid Samaria. The Samaritan woman in John 4 expresses the basic social reality: "Jews do not associate with Samaritans" (John 4:9).

This is not simply a story about crossing a cultural boundary to be kind. In the cultural imagination of Jesus's audience, the Samaritan is the enemy. Not just the stranger, not just the foreigner — the person from whom your community is separated by centuries of mutual contempt and competing religious claims. Choosing him as the hero of the story is not a gentle challenge to cultural preferences. It is a provocation.

---

## The Religion That Walks Past the Dying

The priest and the Levite are not villains for the sake of contrast. They are figures whose religious function made them plausible candidates to obey the law of neighbor-love. If the story is about obeying the commandment to love your neighbor, these are the people who should be doing it. Their failure raises a specific question: what kind of religion produces the capacity to walk past a dying man?

The answer embedded in the story is that a religion organized around boundary maintenance — around the careful demarcation of clean and unclean, obligation and non-obligation, neighbor and non-neighbor — produces exactly this capacity. The priest may have had legitimate ritual concerns about contact with a body that might be dead. The Levite may have had similar reasoning. Their religion gave them a framework for not stopping, and they used it.

This is the sharpest edge of the parable: it does not only challenge the lawyer's question about where the boundary is. It suggests that the very desire to locate the boundary — the instinct to ask "who is my neighbor?" as a limiting question rather than an opening one — is the symptom of a religious formation that has gone wrong somewhere fundamental.

---

## The Question Reversed

When Jesus concludes the story, he reverses the lawyer's question. The lawyer asked: "Who is my neighbor?" Jesus asks: "Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?" (Luke 10:36). The shift is significant. The question "who is my neighbor?" locates the moral agent at the center and asks which people in the world qualify for his attention. The question "who was a neighbor?" locates the suffering person at the center and asks which person responded to the obligation that the suffering created.

The first question allows you to define the circle. The second question does not. If the obligation is generated by the encounter with suffering, then the only answer to "who is my neighbor?" is: whoever you can help.

Kenneth Bailey, in his careful analysis of Middle Eastern cultural context in the parables, notes that the lawyer was forced into an extraordinary moment: he could not bring himself to say "the Samaritan" and instead answered "the one who showed him mercy" (Luke 10:37). [cite — confirm] Even in defeat, the boundary held in the language. Jesus tells him: go and do likewise. The "likewise" is not a commendation of charity. It is the command to cross the boundary the man's entire world was organized around maintaining.

---

## Justice, Not Charity

The parable is a justice argument, not a charity argument.

The distinction matters. Charity keeps the charitable person at the center and the suffering person as the recipient. It is a transaction in which the giver maintains control — the ability to define who qualifies, to determine the form and duration of the help, to feel good about the giving without being changed by it. The Samaritan in the parable does not exercise that control. He gets off his donkey. He touches the man. He puts him on his own animal. He takes him to an inn. He pays. He comes back. He absorbs the cost of someone else's suffering into the structure of his own life. That is not charity in the limited sense. That is a restructuring of existence around someone else's need.

The New Testament word used for the Samaritan's response in verse 33 is σπλαγχνίζομαι — the same word used throughout the Gospels for Jesus's own response to crowds, to lepers, to the sick and possessed. It means something visceral and prior to decision — a gut-level response to suffering that precedes the calculation of cost. This is not the compassion of careful moral reasoning. It is the compassion that has been so formed by attention to human need that the sight of it produces immediate physical response.

The parable is arguing that this kind of formation — a formation that crosses ethnic, religious, and social boundaries in response to suffering — is what it means to love your neighbor. Not the careful management of an obligation extended to a carefully defined circle. Not the charity that maintains the giver's control. The willingness to let someone else's emergency become your own.

---

The church has used this parable for two thousand years to justify programs of charitable service. That is not wrong. But it is incomplete.

> But it is incomplete.

The parable also asks the question that the lawyer was trying to escape: what is the system that put a man on the road to Jericho, and who profits from the fact that it keeps producing victims? The Samaritan addressed the immediate crisis. That was essential. But the prophetic tradition — the tradition the parable draws on — did not stop at the immediate crisis. Amos, Micah, Isaiah: they asked about the gates where the cheating happened, the courts where the poor had no advocate, the systems that made robbery profitable and victims routine.

The full extension of the parable's argument is not simply: be a Samaritan. It is: ask why the road from Jerusalem to Jericho requires a Samaritan.

That question does not reduce the obligation to stop and help. It extends it. The Samaritan still gets off his donkey. But the community that takes the parable seriously also asks why the road is designed the way it is, who benefits from the design, and what faithfulness requires in the space between the victims.

> He was talking about more than first aid.

Jesus told the lawyer to go and do likewise. He was talking about more than first aid.

The lawyer came with a boundary question. He left with a commission. The boundary he wanted to locate is the boundary Jesus refused to draw. The obligation, it turns out, extends to wherever your path intersects with suffering — and the only question left is what you will do when it does.

The question the lawyer asked is the one we all ask: "And who is my neighbor?" (Luke 10:29)

It sounds like a sincere request for clarification. It is not. The text tells us what it was: the lawyer, having already affirmed the two great commandments, "desiring to justify himself" asked the follow-up question. He was not confused about who his neighbor was. He was hoping for a definition narrow enough that he was already in compliance. A neighbor as someone who lives adjacent. A neighbor as someone who shares my ethnicity, my class, my religious tradition. A neighbor as someone I have explicitly chosen to be in relationship with. Any of these definitions would have left the man feeling satisfied that the law's demands on him were already met.

Jesus told a story instead of giving a definition. That is significant. A definition would have answered the question on the lawyer's terms. The story answers it on entirely different terms — and the terms matter more than the answer.

## The World the Parable Assumes

The road from Jerusalem to Jericho descended approximately 3,300 feet over seventeen miles through terrain that provided cover for bandits. [cite — confirm the geographical details] It was genuinely dangerous, genuinely isolated, a road where a man could be robbed and left for dead and no one would know for hours. The parable is not set in a hypothetical location. It is set on an actual road that every person in Jesus's audience would have walked or known.

The man who falls among robbers is unspecified. He has no name, no ethnicity, no religious identity. He is a person in need, and his need is total — he is stripped, beaten, and left half dead. He cannot advocate for himself. He cannot explain his background or establish his credentials. He is simply a body on the road, and the question of what his life is worth will be answered entirely by the choices of the next people who pass.

> He was not confused about who his neighbor was.

The first two who pass are not chosen arbitrarily. The priest and the Levite are figures of the highest religious standing in first-century Judaism — the ones most educated in the law's demands, most publicly associated with God's covenant community, most familiar with the texts that commanded care for the vulnerable. If anyone should have known what the law required, it was them. And they pass.

The reasons they pass are not given explicitly, which is more honest than explicit villainy would be. The priest may have been concerned with ritual purity — contact with a body that might be dead would have rendered him unable to perform his temple duties until he had completed a purification process that took time and cost social standing. The Levite may have calculated the same. These were not heartless men calculating self-interest crudely. They were people managing competing obligations within a religious system that had created categories that made the choice defensible.

That is the precise indictment. The religious system had generated categories of obligation that made it possible to step past a dying man while remaining, within the system's own logic, in compliance with the law. The priest did not violate a commandment by walking past. He honored the subset of commandments that governed priestly purity while violating the one that governed neighbor-love — and the system's categories made the first set visible and the second set invisible.

## The Samaritan and the Choice of the Protagonist

The Samaritan is not a random choice. In the ethnic and religious politics of first-century Judea, Samaritans and Jews maintained a hostility that was centuries old. The division traces to the Assyrian conquest and resettlement of the northern kingdom in 722 BC — when the Assyrians depopulated Israel and imported other peoples, the resulting mixed community developed a religious tradition that diverged from the Jerusalem tradition around the question of the correct place of worship (the Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim), among other things. [cite — confirm the Assyrian resettlement details] By the first century, the hostility was embedded. Jews and Samaritans did not associate (John 4:9). The disciples were shocked when Jesus spoke to the Samaritan woman at the well.

When a Jew in Jesus's audience heard "Samaritan" they heard: the wrong kind of person. Not the enemy exactly — that word might carry respect along with hostility. The wrong kind. The theologically deficient, the racially compromised, the one whose very presence in the story signals that something is going to be overturned.

And then this wrong kind of person sees the injured man, and the Greek text says something worth pausing on: he was *splanchnizomai* — moved in his viscera (Luke 10:33). The English translations say "had compassion," which is accurate but too soft. The Greek word points to the gut, the internal organs, the physical sensation of a body responding before the mind has completed its calculation. He felt it in his body before he decided anything. And then he decided: he bound the wounds, poured oil and wine, loaded the man on his own animal — which meant he walked — brought him to an inn, paid for his care, and promised to return and cover any additional expenses.

Every detail is costly. Every detail is specific. The Samaritan did not feel sorry for the man and continue on his way. He crossed every category that would have justified walking past.

## What Jesus Dismantles

Jesus does not then ask: "Which of these three was the true neighbor?" He asks: "Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?" (Luke 10:36). The shift matters. The first question would have confirmed the lawyer's frame: here are the candidates, tell me which one qualifies as a "real" neighbor. The second question dismantles the frame entirely.

The answer is not about identity. It is about action. The neighbor is not a category applied to persons based on their prior relationship to you. The neighbor is constituted in the act of neighborliness. The question is not "who is my neighbor?" — who qualifies for my care based on prior designation. The question is "to whom was this man a neighbor?" — who performed the neighborly act. The category is produced by the action, not the other way around.

The lawyer cannot say "the Samaritan." He says "the one who showed mercy." He cannot even speak the name of the category he has spent his life avoiding. And Jesus says: go and do likewise.

Go and do likewise is not an affirmation that the lawyer has understood correctly and now needs to execute. It is a displacement. The lawyer came to justify himself. He leaves with a command that will not be completed until he has stopped calculating whether the people in front of him qualify for his concern and started asking what their need requires of him.

## The Structural Argument

The parable is not about individual charity. It is an argument about the structure of moral obligation.

The question "who is my neighbor?" assumes that neighborliness is a category I apply to some people and withhold from others on the basis of prior relationship or shared identity. The parable deconstructs that assumption entirely. The neighbor is not a category I apply. The neighbor is the one in front of me who needs. My obligation is not defined by who they are. It is defined by what they face and what I have.

The church has spent centuries finding manageable definitions of "neighbor." We draw the lines at national borders, at zip codes, at church membership, at doctrinal agreement. Each of these definitions does for us what the lawyer was trying to get Jesus to do: it narrows the circle of obligation to a size we can already satisfy. It converts the command into a status we already hold.

The parable does not authorize any of those definitions. It authorizes one criterion only: need, encountered, and what you did about it.

The road from Jerusalem to Jericho runs through every neighborhood, through every policy debate, through every demographic category we have erected to manage the distribution of our concern. The man lying on it has no name and no ethnicity because Jesus did not want us to be able to ask whether he qualified. He lies there specifically so that the question cannot be the lawyer's question.

## The Honest Accounting

I have walked past on the other side. Not dramatically. Not with any clear moment of decision. But I have organized my life, my time, my resources, and my attention in ways that kept me on a road where I would not encounter the man who had fallen among robbers. I have lived in places and moved through schedules that made the question "who is my neighbor?" effectively answerable as "people like me." That is not neutrality. That is a choice. The parable names it.

The priest and the Levite were not bad people. They were people whose system had given them permission to walk past without being bad people, and they took the permission. The church does the same thing when it constructs programs that address the needs of the poor from a safe institutional distance, when it organizes ministry to the vulnerable in ways that do not require the minister to become personally inconvenienced, when it can report on its service projects without any individual member having had their life genuinely disrupted by the encounter.

The Samaritan's care cost him his animal, his time, his money, and his promise of return. Not proportionally. Not strategically. Not within a budget allocation for community service. He gave what the situation required until the situation did not require any more. That is the model.

The boundary Jesus will not let the lawyer draw is the one we keep trying to draw. Every generation finds its version of the priest-and-Levite calculation — the theological framework, the institutional structure, the political alliance, the cultural preference that makes the walk-past defensible. Every generation produces its version of the injured man on the road, stripped by systems that left him without protection and without advocate. And every generation has to answer the question that is not really the lawyer's question at all.

To whom was this man a neighbor?

Go and do likewise.

> The category is produced by the action, not the other way around.

The road is still the same road.

The Bible was not written in English. This is an obvious statement that carries non-obvious implications. The English Bible that most Christians read is a translation — an extraordinarily valuable translation, in many cases a masterwork of linguistic and theological precision, but a translation nonetheless. And every translation is a series of decisions about which range of meaning in the original language to bring forward and which to leave behind.

Most readers never see those decisions. They receive the English as the text, and the text feels self-evident, because language always feels self-evident to the person who grew up inside it. The English Bible has been part of the furniture of the church for so long that the distance between it and the original has become invisible. That invisibility has costs, and some of them are doctrinal.

## A Few Examples That Are Not Trivial

> And every translation is a series of decisions about which range of meaning in the original language to bring forward and which to leave behind.

Take love. English has one word and makes it carry everything — the love of God, the love of a marriage, the affection for a particular meal, the attachment to a city. The Greek of the New Testament works with a more differentiated vocabulary, and the distinctions are not decorative. When the risen Jesus questions Peter by the Sea of Tiberias (John 21:15-17), the text moves between *agapaō* and *phileō*, and readers have argued for centuries about whether the shift carries theological weight or is simply natural variation in Greek literary style [cite — confirm the debate; scholarly opinion is divided]. Whether or not that specific passage turns on the word distinction, the broader point stands: English flattens a range that the original could articulate, and the reader who does not know the range exists cannot even form the question.

More consequential than the love example is the problem of the second-person plural. English lost its plural "you" centuries ago, and the Bible has suffered for it ever since. When Paul writes to the Corinthians "Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you?" (1 Corinthians 3:16), every "you" in that sentence is plural in the Greek. He is talking about the community — the *ekklesia*, the gathered people — not the individual believer's personal interior. But generations of English readers, hearing "you" as singular because that is the only "you" English has, have read the text as a comment about personal piety, about being careful with your body, about individual holiness.

The communal meaning was not merely spiritually interesting. It was Paul's whole argument. He was writing to a fractured congregation, divided over personalities and party loyalties, and his point was that the community together was the temple, and that the factions were tearing down the structure where God had chosen to live. The individualized reading misses the pastoral emergency Paul was addressing. The Greek does not allow the miss. The English nearly requires it.

## The Hebrew Side

The Old Testament carries its own irreducible depths. *Hesed* — the covenantal faithfulness of God — is among the most important words in the Hebrew Bible and among the most stubbornly untranslatable. The King James rendered it "lovingkindness." The ESV often reads "steadfast love." The New Jerusalem Bible reaches for "faithful love." Each translation captures something and sacrifices something else. *Hesed* carries at once loyalty, loving commitment to a covenant relationship, reliability across time, and the specific tenderness of a love that will not break even when the other party has given it grounds to. No English phrase holds all of that together without losing some of it.

*Shalom* presents the same problem. The word is almost always rendered "peace," and peace is not wrong — but *shalom* is not merely the absence of conflict. It is wholeness, completeness, the state in which all relationships are rightly ordered, in which every person has what they need to flourish, in which creation is functioning as it was made to function. Read "peace" where the text says *shalom* and you have received a smaller promise than the one God made. The God who promises *shalom* is not promising the cessation of noise. He is promising the restoration of everything.

The prophet Isaiah uses the word in the famous passage of Isaiah 53:5: the suffering servant is chastised so that *our shalom might come*. Read through the English, it sounds like a promise of inner calm. Read through the Hebrew, it is a cosmic claim — that the world's fracture, from creation through history, is being addressed at the cross, and that what emerges on the other side is not merely the absence of tension but the restoration of all things to their intended order.

## What This Is Not

I am not arguing that the English Bible is unreliable. It is reliable. The canon of Scripture has been served by scholars across centuries whose work of translation has been conducted with extraordinary care and genuine faith. The central things — the death and resurrection of Jesus, the love of God, the way of salvation, the life of discipleship — are clear in any serious English translation, and God has seen to it that those who do not know Greek or Hebrew can know him fully. The original languages are not the gospel's locked safe. They are the gospel's texture.

> A little Greek is a dangerous thing, and the internet is full of people "correcting" their pastor with a half-understood word study, as though a single lexicon entry overturns the consensus of every translator and commentator in the room.

What the original languages offer is not access to a different gospel but a richer read of the one that is already there. They are the difference between hearing a symphony in a recording and reading the score — the recording is the thing, but the score shows you what was composed, and knowing both is worth more than knowing only one.

There is a guardrail here that is worth naming plainly, because the languages get misused. A little Greek is a dangerous thing, and the internet is full of people "correcting" their pastor with a half-understood word study, as though a single lexicon entry overturns the consensus of every translator and commentator in the room. That is not scholarship. It is the performance of scholarship, and the performance tends to serve the user's pre-existing conclusion rather than the text's actual meaning. The original languages, used rightly, make you more humble before the text, not less — more aware of how much careful labor stands between you and the Greek, more grateful for the community of scholars who have tended it.

I have misused them myself. I have landed on a Greek word that seemed to support a point I wanted to make, and given it more weight than the context warranted, and preached from that word as though the study settled the question when it only deepened it. The log I needed to remove from my own eye was visible enough in retrospect.

## Why Serious Readers Should Care

The history of doctrinal error is substantially a history of translation decisions and the interpretive communities that formed around them. Councils and controversies in the early church often turned on whether the Greek of the New Testament supported one reading or another — whether *homoousios* (of the same substance) or *homoiousios* (of similar substance) was the right word to describe the Son's relationship to the Father, and whether that difference of one iota was trivial or everything [cite — confirm Nicene Council, 325]. The church fathers who hammered out the Nicene Creed were doing Greek grammar in the service of pastoral survival. They knew that if they got the word wrong, they would give the congregation a savior who was merely very good, not God incarnate — and a very good savior cannot bridge the distance between God and the humanity that has broken his image.

That is not historical trivia. The same precision is required in every generation. When Paul tells the Galatians that Christ "redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13), the Greek word *ginomai* is not "bearing" but "becoming" — a distinction that matters for whether what happened at the cross was substitution in the fullest sense, Christ actually taking on the status of the cursed, or something softer. When Paul describes love in 1 Corinthians 13, the Greek word *agape* has a shape — not sentiment, not warm feeling, but the costly, chosen, persistent orientation toward another's good — that the English "love" cannot carry alone.

## The Practical Implication

You do not need to learn Greek or Hebrew to be a faithful Christian or a faithful preacher. Most believers who have never touched an interlinear have deeper Christian lives than many who have. The languages are not the gate.

> The score is richer than the recording.

But it is worth knowing the layer is there. It is worth reading commentaries that take the original languages seriously, so that the texture they provide reaches you even if you are receiving it secondhand. It is worth being a little more suspicious of confident readings that rest entirely on one English word, particularly when the doctrine seems too neat, the application too convenient, the hard passage too easily resolved.

And it is worth supporting the careful scholarship that tends this tradition — the translators, the commentators, the lexicographers who have spent their lives trying to render faithfully what was written in another language two millennia ago. They are doing something that matters. The depth they protect is not academic ornamentation.

The score is richer than the recording. The recording is still true. But there is more there than you have heard, and the more is worth knowing, because it belongs to the same God who gave you the text in the first place.

He was not being careless about the words. Neither should we.

Not everyone who has had an abortion is at peace with it. Some women grieve the loss for years — in silence, largely alone, because the culture around them is divided into two camps that together exhaust the available options while between them leaving out the most important one.

One camp says there is nothing to grieve. The pregnancy was a collection of cells. The decision was healthcare. Grief is an import from a moral framework the person has presumably rejected. To grieve is to concede the opposition's premise. So the grief must be managed, minimized, or explained away.

The other camp says the grief is the appropriate punishment for a moral failure. The grief is what you get. The grief proves what the camp already believed. To offer comfort in the midst of it would be to soften the lesson it was meant to teach.

Neither camp offers what the grief actually needs. And the church — which should be neither camp — has too often chosen one of them.

## What Grief Requires and Does Not Require

Grief does not require a clean moral category. That is the most important thing to understand about this particular grief, and the most consistently misunderstood.

> Grief does not require a clean moral category.

You can grieve a decision you believe was necessary. You can grieve a loss you believe was the right call. You can hold the complexity of having done the only thing you thought you could do and still mourn what that thing cost. Human beings are not required to be simple about their own pain.

The woman who grieved her abortion does not need to be assigned to a moral category before her grief is received. She is not asking whether her grief proves the pro-life position or the pro-choice position. She is not asking for a theological verdict. She is experiencing a loss — the specific, irreversible loss of a specific life that was part of her body and her future — and she needs a place to bring that loss that does not immediately convert it into evidence for someone else's argument.

Both camps want her grief for their purposes. The pro-life camp wants it as a confirmation of moral law. The pro-choice camp wants it managed away as a product of false consciousness. Both responses are a form of violence against the grief itself — a refusal to let it be what it is.

## The Psalms of Lament as Pastoral Theology

The Psalms of lament are not poems written by people who had everything sorted out. Psalm 22 opens with "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — a question directed at God that does not have a tidy answer and is not followed by one. The psalmist does not resolve the abandonment by the end of the poem; he moves through it, arrives somewhere different, but does not pretend the opening cry was not real.

Psalm 88 ends in darkness: "Darkness is my closest friend." There is no resolution. The psalm ends exactly where the psalmist is. The tradition of Scripture preserved this psalm not as a failure of faith but as its own legitimate form of it — the faith that brings what is real into the presence of God without demanding that God immediately make it presentable.

The lament tradition in Scripture is premised on the conviction that God can receive the full weight of what a person is carrying, including the parts that are tangled and contradictory and ugly. Lament is not the absence of faith. It is the form that faith takes when the situation does not admit of praise.

The grief of abortion is a form of lament. It carries the complexity of loss and choice and aftermath and unanswered questions. It does not resolve cleanly into gratitude or contrition. It is a real wound that deserves a real tradition for receiving it — and the church has one. It has just been reluctant to apply it here.

## What the Church Has Often Done Instead

The church has sometimes made the grief worse by making the silence more necessary. The pastoral pattern that has produced the most damage is not hostile rejection — it is the combination of public certainty about the moral category and private unavailability for the actual experience. The pastor who preaches clearly about the sanctity of life in the pulpit and has no infrastructure for the person in the pew who is carrying the grief of having violated it has not been pastorally consistent. He has been theologically consistent and pastorally absent.

> Lament is not the absence of faith.

I have been that pastor. I have preached the conviction without creating the conditions under which the person most implicated by the conviction could bring her actual life into the room. The sermon was right. The pastoral architecture around it was incomplete. That is a distinction worth naming, because it is available to be corrected in ways that the conviction itself is not.

The church has also sometimes weaponized the grief — used the documented psychological difficulty that some women experience after abortion as evidence for the anti-abortion argument, in a way that converts the person's suffering into a rhetorical instrument. This is a specific pastoral harm. The woman whose grief is appropriated to make a point about policy has not been served by the church. She has been used by it. The difference is not subtle.

## What She Actually Needs

What the woman grieving an abortion needs from the church is not a verdict. She has usually delivered one to herself already, often far harsher than any pastoral pronouncement could reach. The self-indictment that lives in the silence is not made gentler by an external one added to it.

She needs what the Psalms model: a place to be honest about the loss. A community that will not require her to tidy it up before she brings it in — that will not send her away to process it privately and return when she is ready to be coherent. She needs a God who is described, again and again, as "near to the brokenhearted" (Psalm 34:18) and a community that embodies rather than merely announces that nearness.

She needs time. Grief does not follow a schedule. The church's pastoral attention tends to peak at the moment of crisis and drop as the urgency fades, but grief has its own timeline, and the woman still carrying this five years later deserves the same presence as the woman who arrived yesterday.

She needs, eventually, the possibility of something like peace — not the peace that denies the loss, but the peace that the New Testament describes as "surpassing understanding" (Philippians 4:7), the peace that co-exists with the memory of what happened rather than requiring the erasure of it. That peace is not produced by a program or a counseling model. It is produced by years of honest relationship with God and with a community that knows the real story.

## The Counter-Position and Its Pastoral Cost

The counter-position is that extending pastoral care to the grief of abortion risks communicating that the church regards the abortion as a normal loss, like a miscarriage, rather than a moral act with consequences. That creating a space for grief without a theological frame around it produces a kind of grief that never arrives at repentance and therefore never arrives at genuine healing. That the pastoral instinct to comfort can short-circuit the prophetic instinct to name, and that the woman genuinely needs both.

This argument is not without merit. The grief of abortion is not identical to the grief of miscarriage, and treating them as equivalent collapses a distinction that matters. Repentance and healing are not enemies of each other; in the Christian tradition, they are the path to each other. A pastoral response that offers comfort while leaving the deeper question permanently unaddressed has not served the whole person.

But the argument fails in its sequencing. The person in active grief cannot receive a theological frame before she has been received. The attempt to lead with repentance when the person has not yet been welcomed produces defensiveness, not contrition. It confirms the silence she already knew was the safer choice. The pastoral wisdom of the New Testament — the father running toward the returning son before the son has delivered his prepared speech (Luke 15:20), Jesus asking the woman at the well about her life before naming its difficulty (John 4) — is about sequence. Welcome before instruction. Presence before direction. The theological frame has a place. It is not first.

> Welcome before instruction. Presence before direction.

## The Door That Is Still Closed

The church has not always been the place this grief can be brought. It has sometimes made the grief worse by making the silence more necessary. That is a failure worth naming — not to assign blame for the past, but because the people still carrying this in silence deserve to know that the door is open.

Not the door to a verdict. Not the door to a theology lesson. The door to the thing the Gospel actually offers: the presence of God with people in the middle of their worst moments, before they have cleaned themselves up, before they have composed themselves, before they have anything to offer except the weight they are carrying and the hope that someone in this building can actually hold it.

That door can be opened. It requires a pastor who has created the conditions for it. It requires a congregation that has learned, over time, what it means to receive hard things without immediately reaching for a category to put them in.

The grief is real. It is still being carried, in buildings all over this country, by women who have learned that silence is the price of belonging. They deserve better than that price.

That weight remains, unresolved, asking what you will do next.

The people who make abortion debates most uncomfortable are not the ideologues on either side. They are the women in the waiting rooms — the ones whose stories do not fit cleanly into anyone's framework.

The woman who is fourteen weeks pregnant and has just received a diagnosis that her child has no chance of survival outside the womb. The woman who is pregnant as a result of rape and is not sure what faithfulness looks like now. The woman whose continued pregnancy is a medical threat to her life. The couple who already have three children and are one financial crisis from losing everything, who are trying to figure out what love actually requires in the specific circumstances of their specific lives.

The easy answers do not reach these cases. And when pastors pretend they do — when confident theological declarations are handed to people whose situations the declarations were never designed to address — the people in those situations know immediately that they are not being seen.

## The Pharisees Had Clear Positions

The comparison is not flattering, and I offer it with awareness of what it costs. The Pharisees were not cynical or corrupt in their commitment to the Law. They were serious about it. They had worked out its implications with considerable care, and they were prepared to apply those implications with precision.

And Jesus, again and again, had time for the people whose situations embarrassed the positions. The woman with the bleeding disorder who had spent twelve years in the company of physicians — and who reached through the crowd and touched the hem of his garment in what was technically a violation of purity law (Mark 5:25-34). The man with the withered hand, whose healing Jesus performed on the Sabbath in full view of those monitoring his compliance with the rules (Mark 3:1-6). The sinful woman in the home of Simon the Pharisee, who wept on Jesus's feet while the host calculated the theological cost of permitting the display (Luke 7:36-50).

> The easy answers do not reach these cases.

Jesus was not indifferent to the Law. He said he came to fulfill it, not abolish it (Matthew 5:17). What he was indifferent to was the use of the Law as a barrier against the encounter with persons. The Law was made for human beings, he said, not human beings for the Law (Mark 2:27).

That principle has direct bearing on how the church handles the hard cases. The theological position exists to serve the person, not the other way around.

## What "Hard Cases" Actually Means

The hard cases are not hard because they present a challenge to the general pro-life position that cannot be answered. Many careful theologians have worked through the arguments about rape, incest, fetal abnormality, and maternal health risk with real rigor and have offered positions that deserve serious engagement.

The hard cases are hard because they require you to hold genuine moral complexity with real people attached to it. They are hard because the woman in front of you is not a hypothetical designed to test your position — she is a person who did not choose the circumstances she is in, who is being asked to bear a cost that is real and immediate, and who needs more than a verdict handed down from outside her situation.

The Greek word for mercy — eleos — is used in the Septuagint as the translation of the Hebrew hesed: covenantal faithfulness, loyal love, the kind of commitment that does not dissolve when the situation becomes complicated. Hesed in the Old Testament is the word used for God's commitment to Israel even when Israel has failed. It is the covenant love that does not evaporate when the conditions of the covenant are difficult to meet.

A church that is quick with a position and slow with eleos has the ratio backwards. The position may be correct. The timing is wrong. Presence before answers. Honest engagement with complexity before confident declaration. The humility to know that proximity to real suffering changes what you want to say.

## A Specific Scene

She came into my office after a service in which I had spoken about the sanctity of unborn life with the kind of clarity I thought the congregation needed. She was twenty-two years old and twelve weeks pregnant, and three weeks earlier she had learned that the pregnancy had resulted from an assault she had not told her family about.

She did not ask me what the church's position was. She knew what it was. She had sat in the third row and heard it. What she asked me — the question she managed to get out before she stopped being able to speak clearly — was whether God was still there with her. Whether he was still there in this.

> The Law was made for human beings, he said, not human beings for the Law (Mark 2:27).

I had prepared a sermon. I had not prepared for her. The gap between those two things is the gap this article is trying to name.

I said what I could. I do not know if it was enough. What I know is that the sermon I had preached twenty minutes earlier was not the thing she needed in that office, and that if I had led with the sermon, I would have lost her.

## The Counter-Position Deserves a Real Answer

The counter-position is this: hard cases are used rhetorically to undermine the general position. In reality, hard cases represent a very small percentage of abortions. Most abortions are not the result of rape or fetal abnormality; they are the result of an unwanted pregnancy in circumstances that could be addressed with genuine support. By focusing pastoral attention on the dramatic edge cases, you risk eroding the general conviction that protects the much larger number of unborn children whose situations are less dramatic.

This argument has statistical weight. The percentage of abortions that occur in the cases most frequently cited as hard — rape, incest, fetal abnormality, direct threat to maternal life — is genuinely small [cite — confirm]. The rhetorical deployment of hard cases to undermine the general principle is a real phenomenon, and the honest pastor needs to see it.

But the argument fails pastorally for two reasons. First, it treats the small number of hard cases as if the smallness of the percentage reduces the weight of the individual person's situation. The woman who conceived in rape is not a statistical edge case. She is a person. Her situation demands serious engagement regardless of how many people share it. Second, the argument assumes that pastoral engagement with the hard cases constitutes a compromise of the general principle — when in fact the ability to engage the hard cases honestly, with real presence and real care, is what earns the pastoral credibility to speak into any of the cases at all.

The church has often been willing to do the easy version of the pro-life commitment — the political declaration, the legislative position, the statement of principle — and very reluctant to do the costly version, which requires sitting with specific women in specific circumstances and offering something other than a verdict.

## What the Hard Cases Require

> I had prepared a sermon. I had not prepared for her.

Hard cases require presence before answers. They require the willingness to say "I am here" before the willingness to say "here is what I believe." They require the kind of pastoral self-knowledge that acknowledges: my position may be correct and still be harmful if delivered at the wrong moment in the wrong way without the relationship to carry it.

They require a community that has built the infrastructure of care before the crisis arrives — the relationships of trust, the culture of honest conversation, the network of practical support — so that when the woman in the hard case needs something, the church is not scrambling to construct a response from scratch.

They require training — not in debate, but in listening. The pastor who walks into the hard case having rehearsed his position is not prepared for what the person in front of him actually needs. The pastor who walks in having practiced the discipline of hearing without immediately constructing a response is beginning to be useful.

They require the theological humility to acknowledge that being in the middle of a situation and looking at it from outside are not the same epistemic position. I know what I believe about the sanctity of unborn life. I do not know what I would decide if I were the woman in the waiting room. That asymmetry is worth naming, not as a reason to abandon the conviction, but as a reason to hold it with the kind of care and humility that makes it possible to offer it to a real person in a real crisis.

The hardest thing about the hard cases is not that they are theologically unresolvable. It is that resolving them at a distance is easy, and sitting with someone in the middle of one is not. The church has often been very willing to do the first thing and very reluctant to do the second.

That is the problem worth naming — and then, harder still, worth doing something about.

The weight remains. It does not resolve itself by being named. It only becomes more demanding.

A woman in my congregation — I will call her Maria — worked two jobs, both without benefits. She knew something was wrong with her body for eight months before she could figure out how to pay to find out what it was. By the time she had the examination and the imaging, the cancer had moved from Stage II to Stage III. She asked me later, in one of the most precise sentences I have heard in fifteen years of pastoral ministry, "If I had been rich, would I have found this sooner?"

Yes. She would have. That is not a guess. It is what the data consistently shows.

The church has largely treated this as a political question, which means it has declined to treat it as a moral one. That is a category error with life-and-death consequences.

---

## The Geography of Who Gets Care

> If I had been rich, would I have found this sooner?

The distribution of healthcare access in the United States tracks with extraordinary consistency along the same lines as every other form of inequality: income, race, geography. Americans with employer-provided insurance or sufficient income receive healthcare at rates and quality comparable to the best in the world. Americans without consistent access — the uninsured, the underinsured, those in rural areas without nearby providers, those in communities of color with documented disparities in the quality of care they receive — receive healthcare that is intermittent, crisis-driven, and often catastrophically delayed.

As of the most recent data available, tens of millions of Americans remain uninsured or significantly underinsured [cite — confirm current figures]. Medical debt is the leading cause of personal bankruptcy in the United States [cite — confirm]. The infant mortality rate in the United States is significantly higher than in peer nations and shows marked disparities by race — Black infants in the United States die at rates more than twice those of white infants [cite — confirm]. Maternal mortality follows similar patterns, with Black women dying in childbirth at disproportionately high rates regardless of income level [cite — confirm].

These are not statistics about a distant population. These are facts about the people in your congregation's neighborhood, about the people whose children attend the same schools as your congregation's children, about people made in the image of God who are experiencing preventable suffering and preventable death because of how the healthcare system is structured.

---

## The Body God Made and Took On

The theological frame begins with the body. The Bible is not a Gnostic text. It does not treat the body as a temporary inconvenience to be escaped by the soul. Genesis 2:7 describes God forming the human being from the dust of the ground and breathing life into him — embodied life, physical existence, is God's creative act. The Incarnation (John 1:14) is the declaration that God valued embodied existence enough to take it on in the person of Jesus. The resurrection of Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15) is bodily resurrection — not the liberation of the soul from the body but the redemption of the whole person.

A theology that takes embodiment seriously cannot treat the health of bodies as a secondary concern. If the body is good — if God made it, took it on, and redeemed it — then the suffering of bodies from preventable, treatable disease is a matter of theological seriousness.

Ezekiel 34:4 indicts the shepherds of Israel with this: "You have not strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bound up the injured. You have not brought back the strays or searched for the lost." The failure to heal the sick is placed in the center of the prophetic indictment of failed leadership. Jesus's healing ministry — which occupies a significant proportion of the Gospel narratives — is not incidental to his proclamation of the kingdom. It is one of its primary demonstrations. When John's disciples ask Jesus whether he is "the one who is to come," Jesus responds: "Go back and report to John what you hear and see: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, those who have leprosy are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is proclaimed to the poor" (Matthew 11:4–5). Healing and good news are not separate categories. They are the same announcement.

---

## A Structural Choice With Moral Consequences

The specific form of the healthcare access problem in the United States is not the only imaginable way to structure medical provision. Every other wealthy nation in the world has organized its healthcare system differently and achieves better outcomes on most population-level health metrics at lower per-capita cost [cite — confirm general comparative finding]. The United States spends more per person on healthcare than any nation in the world and has worse outcomes on many markers — life expectancy, infant mortality, maternal mortality — than countries that spend significantly less [cite — confirm].

This comparison is not a political point. It is a factual observation about the consequences of structural choices. The way a society organizes its healthcare system is a moral choice. It reflects what that society believes about the value of human life and the obligations members of a community have to one another. The choice the United States has made — to organize healthcare primarily as a market commodity rather than as a common social provision — is a choice with moral consequences that are visible in the data.

The church should be equipped to say this. Not to prescribe a specific policy mechanism — there are genuine disagreements about which mechanisms best achieve universal access, and those disagreements deserve serious engagement. But to name the theological conviction that sits underneath the policy question: every person, as a bearer of God's image, has a claim on the care of their body. Their ability to exercise that claim should not depend on their income.

---

## The Steel-Man and What It Leaves Out

> The innovation is real and the access is unequal, and the people who pay the cost of the inequality are not the people making the argument.

The steel-man case against framing healthcare as a right or a justice issue goes like this: rights language applied to healthcare creates an entitlement to a service that has to be provided by other people's labor, which creates serious questions about compulsion and freedom. Market mechanisms, for all their flaws, have produced remarkable medical innovation; government systems tend toward rationing and inefficiency. The church's job is not to prescribe economic policy but to inspire individual generosity and to support charitable care for the sick. The church has been doing this through hospitals and clinics for centuries.

This argument deserves engagement. Medical innovation is a genuine good. Market mechanisms have produced it. Government systems have real weaknesses. The church's historic medical mission — from the hospitals founded by early Christian communities to the modern hospital systems bearing the names of saints and church orders — is a genuine contribution to healthcare access.

But notice what the argument leaves out. The question is not whether market mechanisms produce innovation. They do. The question is whether market mechanisms, as the primary organizing principle of healthcare delivery, produce equitable access. The evidence is that they do not. The innovation is real and the access is unequal, and the people who pay the cost of the inequality are not the people making the argument.

The church's charitable healthcare tradition is also genuine. And genuinely insufficient. The scale of the access problem in the United States cannot be solved by church clinics and charitable hospitals. The structural problem requires structural response. The church that points to its charitable contributions as a sufficient answer to a structural problem has confused category again.

---

## The Cries That Reach God's Ears

There is a passage in James 5 that does not get enough attention in healthcare discussions. James writes: "Now listen, you rich people, weep and wail because of the misery that is coming on you... Look! The wages you failed to pay the workers who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty" (James 5:1, 4). The withholding of wages — the failure to pay people what their labor is worth — is presented as a justice crime of sufficient seriousness that the cries reach God's ears directly.

The failure to ensure healthcare access to workers who cannot afford it is structurally similar. The labor of the working poor generates the wealth of the economy they work in. The system that extracts their labor and withholds from them the basic provision their bodies require — adequate healthcare — is doing something structurally related to what James 5 indicts. The cries are reaching God's ears. The question is whether they are reaching the church's ears.

---

## Why the Church Will Not Say So

Maria finished her treatment. The Stage III diagnosis required aggressive intervention — chemotherapy, radiation, surgery. She lost her hair. She lost months of work, which nearly lost her housing. A group from the congregation came together to help cover her expenses during treatment, which was beautiful. But what I remember is that she asked me, eight months in, whether her illness was God's will.

I told her no. And then I told her something harder: that the delay that turned a potentially manageable Stage II into a Stage III requiring everything her body had was not God's will either. That it was the consequence of a system organized in a way that left her without access to early detection. That God grieves what preventable suffering does to his image-bearers.

She sat with that for a while. Then she said: "Then why doesn't the church say so?"

The answer to her question is what I am trying to work out in this essay and in my own ministry. Why doesn't the church say so? Not because the theological case is unclear — the case for the dignity of every body, the obligation to heal, the prophetic indictment of systems that deny healing to the poor, is about as clear as biblical material gets. But because the political cost of saying so is high, and the institutional habit of the American church is to avoid political costs.

That habit has its own cost. The cost is measured in the people who did not get the early detection. In the cancers that were Stage III when they should have been Stage II. In the women who died in childbirth whose deaths were preventable. In the children who will carry the health consequences of untreated childhood illness into adulthood.

> Healthcare is a moral issue.

Healthcare is a moral issue. The church that treats it as a political question it is not qualified to address has chosen institutional comfort over prophetic faithfulness.

Maria is in remission. I am grateful for that. I am not at peace with how we got here.

Most people have two options they cycle between when conflict enters their marriage. Option one: engage with full intensity, let the argument expand until it has absorbed every grievance from the past six months, and end somewhere both people feel worse. Option two: avoid the conflict entirely, manage the surface, let the unaddressed thing burrow underground where it will surface again in three weeks wearing a different face.

Neither of these is conflict. The first is escalation. The second is suppression. Both are ways of not dealing with what is actually happening.

Healthy conflict looks different from both, and it is worth describing carefully, because most people have never seen it modeled. Not in their families of origin. Often not in their faith communities. Almost never in the culture at large, where conflict either becomes performance or gets resolved in the last five minutes of a thirty-minute episode.

## The Biblical Architecture of Conflict

Proverbs 15:1 — "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" — is not an instruction to be passive. The word translated "soft" in Hebrew is *rak*: gentle, tender, responsive to pressure. The proverb is describing the capacity to stay regulated in a moment of heat, which is one of the most demanding skills a human being can develop. It is not the instruction to have no answer. It is the instruction to shape the answer in a way that does not pour fuel on what is already burning.

James 1:19 adds the architecture: "quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger." This is a sequence, not a suggestion. It places listening before speaking and before anger. The person who does this in a conflict is not performing patience. They are refusing to let their nervous system override their values.

> Neither of these is conflict. The first is escalation. The second is suppression.

Both texts are describing something that has to be learned. Nobody does this naturally. The default human response to perceived threat — which is what conflict triggers — is some version of fight or flight. The fight version produces escalation. The flight version produces suppression. Neither produces resolution.

Matthew 18:15-17 provides Jesus's own framework for conflict within the community: "if your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone." The instruction is direct — go, tell, address. Not manage, not suppress, not wait and hope the situation resolves itself. The purpose of the direct conversation is stated in the same verse: "if he listens to you, you have gained your brother." The goal is restoration. Not victory. Not vindication. Restoration.

## What Research Shows About How Couples Fight

**The goal of conflict in a marriage is not to win. It is to be understood and to understand. Those two goals require entirely different strategies.**

John Gottman's forty years of research on couples produced a distinction that belongs in every premarital counseling curriculum [cite — confirm]. The difference between couples who stay together and couples who don't is not the absence of conflict. Couples who last fight as much as couples who don't — sometimes more. The difference is how they fight.

The couples who handle conflict well do several identifiable things. They attack the problem, not the person. They state what they need rather than cataloguing what the other person has failed to do. They take breaks when the nervous system is flooded, rather than continuing a conversation that has moved past the point of productive communication. And they repair — quickly, specifically, without requiring the other person to grovel.

The couples who don't handle it well use what Gottman calls the Four Horsemen: criticism (attacking character rather than behavior), contempt (communicating disgust or superiority), defensiveness (refusing to receive feedback), and stonewalling (shutting down entirely). These are not dramatic moves. They are ordinary habits. And they are learnable in reverse.

Contempt is the most corrosive. It carries within it the evaluation that the other person is beneath the contempt-holder — less than, not worth engaging. Gottman's research identified contempt as the single most reliable predictor of a marriage's end [cite — confirm]. Not conflict frequency. Not conflict intensity. The presence of contempt in how two people engage each other.

## The Historical and Theological Weight of This

The church has not always served married couples well in this area. The theological emphasis on forbearance — "bearing with one another in love" (Ephesians 4:2) — has sometimes been taught in ways that discourage legitimate conflict rather than shape it. The result is couples who have learned to perform peace rather than achieve it. They sit in the pew together every Sunday and will not look at each other in the parking lot.

> Contempt is the most corrosive.

Forbearance is not the suppression of legitimate needs. It is the patient willingness to engage those needs without explosion, to bring them into the relationship rather than performing as though they do not exist. The same letter that commands forbearance also commands "speaking the truth in love" (Ephesians 4:15) — a phrase that requires both things simultaneously, not alternating between them.

The household codes in Ephesians are not a description of a conflict-free marriage. They are a description of how two people oriented toward each other's flourishing handle the inevitable friction of two human beings living a shared life. Friction is built into the structure. What is not built in is the particular form friction takes.

## The Counter-Position Worth Hearing

Some pastoral and counseling traditions emphasize that the spiritual discipline of self-denial is the primary tool for conflict in marriage — that the husband who dies to self, the wife who chooses forbearance over expression, the couple who brings their grievances to prayer before bringing them to conversation are practicing the more excellent way. The concern is that a therapeutic framework for conflict management imports secular psychology into what is fundamentally a spiritual problem.

This concern is worth taking seriously rather than dismissing. There is a real way in which the therapeutic language of "flooding" and "repair attempts" can displace the theological language of repentance, forgiveness, and genuine self-offering. The question of whether a conversation needs a twenty-minute break for regulation or a twenty-minute prayer for humility is not always the same question.

The answer is that both are true and neither replaces the other. The neurological reality of flooding — that the human nervous system past a certain threshold of activation cannot engage in productive communication — is not a therapeutic construct. It is a physical fact that the Holy Spirit has not suspended. The person who insists on continuing a conversation when both people are past the point of productive engagement, because ending the conversation feels like spiritual failure, is not practicing faithfulness. They are practicing willfulness, and the conversation will produce damage rather than repair.

The disciplines of prayer, self-offering, and genuine repentance operate before and after the conversation. They shape the person who enters the room. They do not substitute for the concrete skills of staying in the room.

## The Specific Moves That Change Things

First: distinguish between the presenting issue and the underlying need. Most conflicts are not about what they appear to be about. "You never listen to me" is almost never a statement about the specific conversation happening right now. It is a bid for reassurance about being known and valued. Addressing the underlying need — "you matter to me, tell me what you actually need from this conversation" — often resolves what the argument never could.

Second: take the break before you need it, not after. The neurological threshold for flooding arrives faster than most people realize, and past it, nothing useful happens. Saying "I need twenty minutes" before you hit the wall is not avoidance. It is responsible self-regulation. The twenty minutes is not a rejection of the conversation. It is the preparation required to have it honestly.

Third: repair. Small, specific, quick. "That came out wrong. What I meant was..." The repair attempt does not need to be perfect. Research shows that the willingness to attempt repair matters more than the quality of the attempt. The couple that attempts repair badly is in better shape than the couple that waits for perfect repair and waits too long.

## Three Questions for This Week

What is the pattern of conflict in your marriage — does it escalate, avoid, or move between both? What triggers the escalation?

In your last significant argument, what were you actually trying to communicate underneath the words you used? Did your spouse receive that message?

> Conflict is not the problem in a marriage. Conflict is the curriculum.

Do you know your own early warning signs of flooding — the physical and emotional signals that tell you the nervous system is past productive engagement?

**This week:** the next time a low-stakes irritant comes up, practice the soft answer. Not capitulation — a regulated, honest, specific response. Notice what happens.

Conflict is not the problem in a marriage. Conflict is the curriculum. The couple that learns to fight well is building a skill that will serve them in every other area of the relationship. Safety grows where you know the hard conversation will not destroy what you have.

That safety is built in exactly the places it feels most threatened. Not by avoiding the hard conversation. By learning to have it without losing the person.

The call came on a Tuesday afternoon. A man in my congregation had reached the edge of what I could help him with — a combination of severe depression, marital collapse, and the kind of theological anger that makes pastoral care feel like fighting a fire with good intentions. He needed a therapist. He needed a marriage counselor with clinical training. He needed, eventually, a psychiatrist. And I needed to know exactly who to send him to.

I did not have that list. Not a real one. I had a few names, a general sense that there were Christian therapists in our city, and no clear understanding of whether any of them were actually skilled with what this man was carrying. I made calls. I got voicemails. I guessed.

That is not a referral network. That is pastoral improvisation, and it costs people.

---

## The Question That Builds a Real Network

> That is not a referral network. That is pastoral improvisation, and it costs people.

A healthy referral network begins with a different question than most pastors ask. The question most pastors ask is: "Who can I send people to?" The question that builds a real network is: "Who do I actually know well enough to trust with someone I care about?" Those two questions produce very different lists. The first produces a directory. The second produces a community.

The directory is easy to assemble and nearly useless in a crisis. When a family is falling apart, you do not want a name from a list — you want to call someone you have had lunch with, whose clinical approach you understand, whose faith you have some sense of, who will take the call and give you fifteen minutes of honest counsel about whether this family needs what they offer or needs to be directed somewhere else. That kind of relationship requires investment that has nothing to do with crisis management. It requires investment in the years before the crisis.

This is precisely what most pastors neglect, and the neglect has a specific shape. The years before crisis are filled with what seems more urgent: sermon preparation, committee meetings, hospital visits, the administrative weight of running a congregation. Relationship-building with therapists and social workers and doctors and lawyers in your community does not appear on the weekly to-do list. It has no deadline. It produces no visible outcome. And so it does not happen, until the Tuesday afternoon when you are holding a man's life in your inadequately prepared hands.

---

## What a Functioning Network Actually Looks Like

A functioning pastor referral network has a few distinguishing features.

It is built on genuine relationships, not professional transactions. The Christian therapist who is in your network because you send her clients and she sends you congregants is a transactional arrangement. The therapist who is in your network because you have met regularly, because she has challenged your thinking about mental health and faith, because you have prayed together and disagreed honestly — that is a relationship. Relationships are what you actually need at 9 PM when someone is in your office in crisis.

The difference between a transactional referral arrangement and a genuine relationship becomes visible in the hard moments. The professional contact you have met twice will tell you whether they have openings. The person who knows your congregation and your pastoral approach will tell you whether they are the right fit for this specific person — and when they are not, they will tell you that too, and point you to someone better. That level of honest counsel requires the trust that only accumulates over time and through the kind of conversation that goes beyond "here is my area of specialty and my fee schedule."

## Refer Beyond Your Own Theological Tribe

It includes people outside your theological tradition. The best referral for a congregation member struggling with addiction may be a counselor at a Catholic treatment center. The best referral for a grieving widow may be a licensed therapist who does not share your church's soteriology. The pastor who only refers within his own theological tribe will regularly have no good referral to make. And the person suffering the cost of that limitation is not the pastor. It is the person who needed help that was available — just not to them, because their pastor had not built the relationship that would have made the referral possible.

The kingdom is larger than your denomination. The professional community of mental health practitioners, physicians, social workers, and legal advocates in your city includes people of deep personal faith, people with no religious commitment, and everyone in between. The person who is best suited to help the teenager cutting herself in your youth group is not necessarily an elder at your church or a graduate of your theological tradition. She may be a licensed clinical social worker who has spent fifteen years working with adolescent self-harm, who treats her clients with a dignity that reflects the image of God whether or not she would describe it that way. Build the relationship. Make the referral.

It includes honest feedback loops. If you refer someone to a counselor and that counselor gives pastoral advice that contradicts the work you are doing — or worse, that is actively harmful — you need to know. A real referral partner calls you. He is not defensive about the feedback. He wants to know if the hand-off served the person well. That kind of accountability requires enough relational trust to make the difficult conversation feel safe. It also requires the humility to receive difficult feedback yourself — because the flow of information in a real network runs in both directions, and the therapist may sometimes have legitimate concerns about the pastoral care she is observing from the other end of the referral.

And it includes reciprocity. Not the transactional reciprocity of professional referrals — "I send you clients, you send me congregants" — but the theological reciprocity of people who regard each other as co-workers rather than competitors. The person who lands in the therapist's office with pastoral questions gets referred to a pastor. The person who arrives in a pastor's office with clinical needs gets referred to a therapist. Both of them are served well. Neither professional is protecting turf. Both are asking the same question: what does this person actually need, and who can best provide it?

---

## The Limits the Pastoral Ego Resists

> The pastor who understands his own limits is not a weak pastor.

The question of what a referral network requires pastors to acknowledge about their own limits is worth sitting with directly. Because the reason most pastors do not have a real referral network is not simply busyness. It is that building one requires admitting, in concrete relationships with people who will remember the conversation, that there are conditions you are not equipped to address — and that the admission of limitation is something the pastoral ego resists.

The pastor is trained, in his formation and in the expectations of his congregation, to be the person with the answer. People bring their heaviest problems to him. His capacity to receive those problems without panic has been understood as a sign of pastoral strength — the steady presence in the storm, the person who has seen enough suffering not to be destabilized by more of it. That steadiness is real and necessary. But it can calcify into a refusal to say the four words that would serve the person in the office far better than the pastoral steadiness: "I don't know. Let me find out."

The pastor who has a functioning referral network has already said those words, before the crisis. He has said them in the coffee shop, in the phone call, in the honest conversation with the therapist across town: "Here is what I can do. Here is where I run out. Where do you take things like this?" That conversation requires the very humility that Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 12 — the body that does not say to the hand "I have no need of you," the community of gifts in which each member contributes what only it can contribute.

The pastor who understands his own limits is not a weak pastor. He is a pastor who has thought carefully enough about care to know where his care should stop and someone else's should begin. That is a significant accomplishment, and it is rarer than it should be.

---

## The Slow Work Before the Crisis

Building this takes years. It requires being present for things that have no immediate payoff — attending the community mental health coalition meeting, making the lunch with the addiction counselor, sitting through the continuing education seminar on trauma that was held at the hospital and attended by no one from the local church. It requires being honest about your own limitations, which means first having to face them. It requires treating other professionals in your city — including ones with no religious affiliation — as people worth knowing rather than people to be evangelized at a professional distance.

## What the Pastors Connection Network Carries

The Pastors Connection Network exists, in part, because the most important referrals a pastor makes are often to other pastors. The colleague who has navigated the specific geography of your city's mental health resources, who knows which therapist has a six-month waiting list and which one can see someone this week, who has referred into the same systems you are now trying to enter — that colleague is an irreplaceable asset. The PCN conversations I have valued most have not been about preaching technique or church growth. They have been the ones where a pastor said, "I had someone in my office last week with a situation I had never seen before. Here is who I called," and someone else said, "Yes — or try this one instead." That is the referral network functioning at full capacity.

Most pastors have the referral network they have invested in building. The man who sat in my office on that Tuesday deserved better than what my negligence had prepared me to offer him.

I still think about that. I think about him every time I have coffee with someone I cannot yet refer to anyone.

The investment is slow. The payoff is invisible until the Tuesday afternoon when it is not.

Success in ministry does a thing no one warned you about. It closes doors.

The congregation grows. The platform expands. The speaking invitations arrive. The reputation circulates among other pastors — he is doing good work, you should hear him. And with every increase in visibility, there is a corresponding decrease in the number of people who will speak to you honestly, ask you hard questions, notice when you are not well, or tell you the truth when you would rather not hear it. Success creates a corona of deference that looks like community and functions like isolation.

I have felt it. The dinner table conversation where everyone is being careful. The elders who preface their concern with three compliments before getting to the point. The staff meeting where a problem exists that no one will name because the culture around you has decided, quietly and without anyone saying so, that your presence at the center of everything means your equilibrium cannot be disturbed. This is not cruelty. It is what happens when visibility becomes its own kind of wall.

The pain is not the pain of failure. That is a different wound with a different texture. The pain of the successful pastor is the pain of a man standing in a room full of people who need him, who are grateful for him, who would be genuinely distressed if he left — but who cannot know him. The distinction between being needed and being known is one that every pastor understands in theory and too many of us learn in the body, through the particular ache of standing at a reception after a strong sermon, shaking hands, receiving genuine warmth, and driving home with the deep animal certainty that no one in that room knows what it cost.

---

## Elijah Under the Broom Tree

> Success creates a corona of deference that looks like community and functions like isolation.

The Scriptures are not naive about this pattern. Elijah is the canonical case — the prophet who called down fire on Mount Carmel, who won the greatest public confrontation of his career, and who then fled into the wilderness and asked to die. First Kings 19 presents this sequence without embarrassment: the greatest triumph of his public ministry followed immediately by the deepest collapse of his private life. He sat under the broom tree and told God it was enough. He was done.

What strikes me every time I read that passage is how God responds. Not with a theological correction. Not with a reminder of what Elijah had just accomplished on Carmel. God's response was an angel touching him and saying: arise and eat. Twice. Sleep first. Then food.
