Then a long walk, forty days and forty nights, to Horeb — the mountain of God, the place where Moses had encountered the divine presence in another era of exhaustion. And then the question that God asks with a tenderness that still surprises me: "What are you doing here, Elijah?"

Not a rebuke. An invitation to speak. God wanted to hear what was wrong in Elijah's own words: I alone am left. I am the only one. The isolation of visible ministry had convinced him that his position was both unique and untenable — that he was carrying something no one else could see or share.

The steel-man version of that trajectory is worth hearing honestly. Perhaps the pain of successful ministry is simply the cost of a calling — that some degree of loneliness is intrinsic to the prophetic office, that Moses was alone on the mountain, that the weight of leadership is by nature heavier than what can be fully distributed. That is true as far as it goes. The calling does carry weight that cannot be redistributed to people who do not carry it. But Elijah's God did not tell him to push through. He told him to eat and sleep. He told him to find Elisha. The remedy for the prophet's depletion was provision and companionship, not a theology that sanctified the condition.

---

## The Invisible Formation Success Squeezes Out

Henri Nouwen wrote about the pastor's calling as a ministry of presence, but he was honest about what presence requires: a self that has been formed in solitude and genuine community, not just in public performance [cite — confirm]. The formation that sustains visible ministry is almost always invisible — prayer, friendship, accountability, the willingness to be weak with at least a few people who will not be damaged by the sight of it. And success, ironically, makes the invisible formation harder to maintain. There is always something to do, always someone who needs the visible you, and the interior work gets squeezed out by the demands of the platform.

This is the specific spiritual danger that the New Testament addresses when James writes that not many should become teachers, because teachers will be judged with greater strictness (James 3:1). The strictness is not primarily about doctrinal accuracy. It is about the peculiar pressure that public responsibility places on the interior life — the way that being watched continuously by people who need you to be a certain kind of person can gradually reshape you into a performance of that person rather than the person himself. The distinction is subtle until it isn't.

I have watched men I respect lose the interior life that made their public ministry worth having — not because they were unfaithful, not because they made large and obvious failures, but because the structure of their success gave them no room to maintain what mattered most. The speaking schedule was full. The book contract was signed. The church was thriving by every measurable indicator. And somewhere in all of that, the man who was doing the work stopped being cared for by anyone who was allowed to see him clearly.

---

## Needed but Not Known

There is a particular loneliness that belongs to the man whose public competence has become its own credential. The congregation sees a person who knows what to say in every situation — at the hospital bed, in the counseling room, from the pulpit — and they conclude, reasonably, that this person does not need what they need. That he has resources the rest of them are seeking. And in one sense he does. He has studied. He has prayed. He has learned, over years, how to hold the weight of other people's grief without being crushed by it.

But the capacity to hold another person's grief is not the same thing as having no grief of your own. The skill at pastoral presence does not make the pastor immune to the conditions that require pastoral presence. He marries and the marriage is hard. He parents and the children struggle. He ages and the body slows. He looks at his own life on a Tuesday afternoon and finds the same territory that his congregation finds — the distance between what faith promises and what experience delivers, the prayers that go unanswered, the doubts that return even after long seasons of resolution.

> But the capacity to hold another person's grief is not the same thing as having no grief of your own.

The difference is that the congregation is permitted to bring those things to him. He, increasingly, is not permitted to bring them to anyone.

This is not a complaint about congregational callousness. Most congregations genuinely love their pastors and would be grieved to know the cost. The problem is structural. The pastoral role creates an asymmetry — a one-directional flow of care — that is natural in its origins but becomes damaging over time if no counterstructure exists to balance it. Every pastor needs at least one relationship that runs the other direction: someone who is paying attention to the pastor's interior life, not because the pastor has something to offer, but because the pastor is a person who needs to be known.

---

## The Counterstructure Every Pastor Needs

Paul understood this. His letters are not only theological documents — they are the record of a man who needed and pursued genuine human connection. The personal greetings in Romans 16 are not filler. They are a window into a network of people who knew him, traveled with him, sheltered him, and shared his work in ways that went beyond the formal structures of his apostolic role. He asks for prayer — specifically that he will be delivered from those in Judea who do not believe, and that his service in Jerusalem will be acceptable to the saints, and that he will come to them with joy and be refreshed in their company (Romans 15:30-32). He wanted to be refreshed by their company. He was not ashamed to say so.

The church does not know how to care for its successful pastors. It knows how to celebrate them, resource them, promote them. It does not know how to ask: are you well? Not your ministry. You.

That question requires someone positioned close enough to ask it and trusted enough to hear the answer. It requires a relationship that was built on terms other than the pastoral role — a friend who knew you before the platform existed, or a fellow pastor who carries enough of his own weight that he does not need you to be invulnerable, or a counselor who is paid precisely to hold the space where you cannot perform. Most successful pastors do not have that person. They have built their ministry around others' need without building the structures that address their own.

---

## Depletion Dressed as Devotion

The wound is not theoretical. I know men who stepped away from ministry in their late forties after building something genuinely significant — not because they had done anything wrong, not because of scandal, but because they had been running at a pace that gave the public self everything and the private self nothing, and eventually the private self simply stopped. The tank was empty in a way that could not be filled by another strong Sunday. They needed something the platform could not provide.

The solution is not to work less. It is not to protect yourself from the demands of the calling. The calling is real and the demands are real and the work is worth doing. The solution is to be honest, first with yourself and then with at least one other person, about what the work is costing. To resist the temptation to perform wholeness for the people who need your wholeness to be real. To find the Elisha that the God of Elijah commanded be found — the person who walks the road with you, not who needs you to be ahead of them on it.

The pain of the successful pastor is survivable. I know this because I have survived parts of it and am still surviving others. But it requires being named. It requires the courage to say to someone who is allowed to hear it: this is what it actually costs, and I cannot carry it alone.

Name it first to yourself. Then find one person who is allowed to know. The ministry that costs you everything and gives nothing back in return is not the kind of self-emptying that Paul praises in Philippians 2. It is depletion dressed as devotion. And the people who need you most need you to know the difference.

The pneumatology we have actually practiced — as opposed to the one in our doctrinal statements — runs something like this: the Holy Spirit is the part of Christianity that feels good. The Spirit is the warmth in worship, the sense of presence in prayer, the emotional uplift that distinguishes a spiritual experience from a merely intellectual one. When people talk about being "moved by the Spirit," they mean moved emotionally. When a worship service is described as "Spirit-filled," the evidence is usually the intensity of the feeling in the room.

This is not entirely wrong. It is dangerously incomplete.

> It is dangerously incomplete.

The Spirit in the New Testament is not primarily a source of pleasant religious experience. The Spirit is the active, working presence of God in the world, accomplishing specific things that could not otherwise be accomplished — convicting the world of sin and righteousness and judgment (John 16:8), producing in believers the character of Christ (Galatians 5:22–23), interceding with sighs too deep for words (Romans 8:26), distributing gifts for the building of the body (1 Corinthians 12), guiding the church into truth (John 16:13). These are not emotional states. They are actions. The Spirit acts.

## The Reduction and Its History

The reduction of the Spirit to emotional experience has a traceable history. The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in the Protestant world were shaped by a series of revivals that put enormous weight on the felt experience of conversion. The Pietist movement in Germany and Scandinavia, reacting against the dry orthodoxy of Lutheran scholasticism, emphasized the necessity of a heartfelt, experiential faith — a warm personal relationship with God that could not be reduced to doctrinal assent [cite — confirm]. The Methodist movement in England, and the First Great Awakening in the American colonies, amplified this emphasis dramatically.

> The Spirit acts.

John Wesley's description of his Aldersgate experience in 1738 — "I felt my heart strangely warmed" — became paradigmatic [cite — confirm]. Jonathan Edwards, who carefully documented the physical manifestations of revival in his Northampton, Massachusetts congregation in the early 1740s, tried to hold emotion and orthodoxy together, arguing in *A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections* [cite — confirm] that genuine religious experience involved both the understanding and the affections, and that affections without transformation of character were suspect. But the revival movements he helped to generate often outran his careful theology. The warmth became the evidence; the transformation became secondary.

The evidential function of emotion created a problem that subsequent generations have had to manage. If the Spirit's presence is confirmed by the feeling, then the absence of the feeling suggests the absence of the Spirit. This produces a spirituality constantly chasing the next experience, measuring the health of one's faith by the intensity of one's feelings in a given worship service. It produces what C.S. Lewis called, somewhere in his correspondence [cite — confirm], the error of treating feeling as the measure of reality rather than as an unreliable servant of it.

By the twentieth century, the Pentecostal and charismatic movements had made glossolalia — speaking in tongues — the primary evidential sign of Spirit baptism [cite — confirm]. The Azusa Street Revival of 1906 launched a global movement built around this conviction, and the movement is now arguably the fastest-growing expression of Christianity in the world [cite — confirm]. I do not name this to dismiss it. I name it because even the most robust traditions of Spirit-emphasis tend, over generations, to reduce the Spirit to the dramatic and the emotional. The tongues become the evidence, and the long slow work of character formation — which is less spectacular and less immediately gratifying — recedes from view.

## What Paul Says About Formation

Paul's account of his own experience reads as an extensive counter-testimony to the emotional reduction. Second Corinthians 4 and 11–12 describe affliction, confusion, persecution, beatings, shipwrecks, sleeplessness, and abandonment by people he had trusted. He does not describe these as periods when the Spirit was absent. He describes them as periods of extraordinary spiritual formation in which the life of Jesus was made manifest in his mortal body (2 Corinthians 4:10–11). The formation was not comfortable. The Spirit was present through the discomfort, not despite it.

Romans 8 is the most sustained pneumatological passage in Paul's letters, and it is remarkably unsentimental. The Spirit helps us in our weakness (8:26). The Spirit intercedes for us when we cannot find words for prayer — not with eloquence but with groanings (8:26). The Spirit leads us as sons and daughters into the inheritance of Christ — but that inheritance includes sharing his sufferings in order to share his glory (8:17). This is not a picture of spiritual life as emotional uplift. It is a picture of the Spirit sustaining the community of the crucified through the weight of a world that is not yet redeemed.

The fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23 — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control — is largely not emotional. Joy is the closest to an emotional state, and even joy in the New Testament (*chara*) is closer to settled confidence in God's goodness than to subjective exhilaration. Patience (*makrothumia*) is the capacity to endure what is long and difficult without being destroyed by it. Faithfulness (*pistis*) is reliable consistency over time. Self-control is the governance of impulse by will. These are character qualities — durable orientations of the will and the habitual self — not feelings that come and go with the quality of last Sunday's worship set.

> That is pneumatological evidence. It is not the evidence we have trained ourselves to look for.

The formation of these qualities is the long, slow, often unglamorous work of the Spirit in a person's life, and it looks almost nothing like what we describe when we say someone is "Spirit-filled." The most Spirit-formed people I know are not the most emotionally expressive people in the room. They are often the quietest. They are the ones whose patience in difficulty, whose consistency in faithfulness, whose capacity to love people who are hard to love, marks them as something that the surrounding culture does not produce on its own.

That is pneumatological evidence. It is not the evidence we have trained ourselves to look for.

## The Counter-Position

The charismatic tradition is not wrong to insist on the experiential dimension of Spirit life. The Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead is not an abstraction, and a Christianity that has no felt encounter with the living God has become something less than what the New Testament describes. The Pentecostal critic of cold evangelicalism has a point: a faith that never crosses into felt experience is in danger of collapsing into mere cognitive assent.

The tradition of *sensus divinitatis* — the Reformers' conviction that God has planted an awareness of himself in every human consciousness — suggests that the longing for felt encounter with God is not a corruption of true religion but a genuine instinct of it [cite — confirm]. John Owen, the seventeenth-century Puritan theologian, wrote extensively about the internal operations of the Spirit in sanctification and prayer, describing experiences of divine love and communion that were affective as well as cognitive [cite — confirm]. The mystics of the medieval tradition — Bernard of Clairvaux, Meister Eckhart, Julian of Norwich — described encounters with the divine presence that were unmistakably experiential.

The question is not whether experience is valid but whether it is the primary or the exclusive category by which we evaluate the Spirit's presence. When it becomes that, we have made the Spirit answerable to our emotional needs rather than to God's purpose. We have turned pneumatology into spiritual self-care, and that is a different religion than the one in which a poor carpenter from Galilee promised his followers that the Paraclete would convict the world of sin (John 16:8) — not make them feel warm about it.

## What This Means for the Church

A church that has reduced the Spirit to feeling will evaluate its spiritual health by metrics of emotional intensity — whether people are crying during worship, whether the services feel alive, whether there is a quality of atmosphere suggesting something beyond the ordinary. These are not nothing. But they are not the primary evidence.

The primary evidence is transformation. The Spirit was given, Peter announces on Pentecost (Acts 2:38), for the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit — a gift inseparable from a life that turns in a new direction. The community of Acts 2:42–47, devoted to the apostles' teaching, to the breaking of bread, to prayer, to shared possessions, to welcoming strangers — that is the pneumatological community. The Spirit produced it. It would not have happened otherwise. Notice: Luke does not say that the community gathered to feel the presence of the Spirit. He says the Spirit produced a community capable of living a particular kind of life together.

That life is the evidence. The tongues were extraordinary and they were not the point. What happened after the tongues — in the street, in the homes, in the distribution of resources to those who had none — that is what Spirit-fullness looked like in Luke's telling.

I have led worship services that generated significant emotional response and produced almost no measurable transformation in the lives of the people in the room. I have also sat with people in hospital rooms and jail cells where no one was weeping from spiritual intensity, and where something was present that I can only describe as the Spirit — steady, specific, attending to the weight of what was happening with a presence that was not manufactured and could not be manufactured.

The Spirit is not a feeling. The Spirit is the power of the age to come invading the present age, making possible in human beings what is otherwise simply not possible — love for enemies, patience in affliction, generosity in scarcity, faithfulness in obscurity. That is not an emotional state. That is the life of God.

We should want that more than we want to feel good. They are not the same thing, and the confusion between them has cost us more than we have yet reckoned.

Paul said it plainly and we quote it without feeling its full weight: "If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins. Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ are lost. If only for this life we have hope in Christ, we are of all people most to be pitied" (1 Corinthians 15:17-19).

Most pastors. Of all people most to be pitied.

## The Line Paul Draws

He was not speaking hypothetically. He was drawing the line directly: either the resurrection is a historical event with cosmic consequences or the pastoral vocation is, at its core, a massive mistake. There is no middle position available. No version of ministry that affirms the resurrection as meaningful symbol while quietly treating it as something other than bodily, historical, and actual. The middle position is the one Paul calls pitiable. And I think more pastors than would admit it have quietly drifted toward it.

> The middle position is the one Paul calls pitiable.

Not through theological apostasy. Through something more common: the slow erosion of resurrectional confidence under the weight of pastoral experience. You sit with enough grief to know it is not easily resolved. You watch enough people walk away from faith to stop being confident that God reliably shows up. You bury enough church members — including ones whose faith was enormous and whose suffering was severe — to find the resurrection feeling more like comfort language than world-altering claim. You keep preaching it. You stop being shocked by it. The shock, it turns out, was doing more work than you knew.

## The Drift Toward the Pitiable Middle

The historical stakes of the resurrection are worth recovering. The first proclamation of the risen Christ took place in the city where the crucifixion had happened, within weeks of the event, in the presence of people who could have verified or falsified the claim. Peter's sermon at Pentecost (Acts 2:14-36) is not a call to spiritual experience. It is a piece of historical argument: this man was executed before your eyes; God raised him, and we are witnesses. The proclamation is testable in principle. The fact that the movement exploded rather than collapsed in that environment is not nothing.

The early Christians did not treat the resurrection as a spiritual category. They treated it as the explosive announcement that changed what was possible inside history. The fact that the Roman authorities moved to suppress the story — bribing the soldiers to say the disciples stole the body (Matthew 28:12-13) — indicates they understood that the claim, if believed, would be socially destabilizing [cite — confirm]. They were correct. The early church expanded across the Roman Empire not because it offered a better moral philosophy but because it proclaimed that the specific man Rome had executed was alive, that death had been defeated, that the future was permanently different from what it had been before that Sunday morning.

## The Historical Stakes of an Empty Tomb

N.T. Wright's exhaustive work on the resurrection demonstrates that the early Christian proclamation was distinctive precisely in its insistence on bodily resurrection — not spiritual survival, not the immortality of the soul, but the transformation of the body into the kind of body that belongs to the renewed creation [cite — confirm]. The resurrection in the Christian claim is not the departure of the soul from the world. It is the irruption of the new creation into the old. Jesus's resurrection is the first installment of a renovation that will encompass everything.

The pastor who genuinely believes this leads differently.

He sits at the deathbed and holds something more than professional composure. He presides at the graveside and means what he says — not as rhetorical consolation but as the statement of a truth he actually inhabits. He endures the seasons of apparent failure in ministry without losing his footing entirely, because his confidence is not in the trajectory of the congregation's attendance but in the God who raises dead things.

## Leading From the Resurrection

I have led from that confidence in seasons, and I have led without it in others. The difference is not primarily in what I said from the pulpit. The difference was in what happened to me when the week went badly, when someone I loved suffered, when the church felt like it was going backwards. Without the resurrection, those moments produce despair. With it — genuinely with it, not merely confessionally attached to the proposition — they produce something harder to manufacture: a grief that still hopes, a realism that does not collapse into nihilism, a willingness to keep going that does not depend on visible signs of progress.

The counter-position deserves a hearing. There are serious theologians who have argued that the resurrection's significance is primarily soteriological and existential — that what matters is not the brute historical fact but the meaning it carries, the encounter it enables, the community it founds. Rudolf Bultmann's demythologization program, which was enormously influential in the mid-twentieth century, moved in this direction: strip away the mythological container, preserve the kerygmatic content [cite — confirm]. The pastoral appeal of this position is real. It seems to protect the gospel from the precariousness of historical claims.

> Optimism is defeated by evidence.

The problem is that Paul's argument in 1 Corinthians 15 does not allow this move. Paul does not say: if Christ has not been raised as a powerful symbol of new life, your faith is futile. He says: if Christ has not been raised as a historical event, you are still in your sins and those who have died are lost. The claim is contingent on historical reality. Remove the history and you have not preserved the gospel. You have replaced it with something smaller.

## The Counter-Position and Its Limit

This is not the prosperity gospel's confident abundance. The prosperity gospel has no room for the cross. Resurrectional hope has plenty of room for the cross, because it knows what came after. The cross is real and devastating; the empty tomb is also real and changes everything about what the cross means. Both must be held, together, without letting either cancel the other.

The cross says: God is not absent from suffering. The resurrection says: suffering is not the last word. Together they produce the peculiar posture that Paul describes as "sorrowful, yet always rejoicing" (2 Corinthians 6:10). Not the forced joy that performs happiness in the face of pain. Not the despair that treats the suffering as final. The grief that carries hope. The hope that does not require the suffering to have been unreal.

That posture is what pastoral ministry runs on over the long arc. The congregation will not always be growing. The finances will not always be stable. The community will not always be healthy. There will be betrayals and departures and seasons when the effort seems to be producing nothing visible. What keeps a pastor in the room — what keeps him from the slow drift toward cynicism that eventually kills more ministries than any public collapse — is not optimism. Optimism is defeated by evidence. What keeps him is the operative conviction that God raises dead things, that the trajectory of history is not determined by current appearances, that the God who brought Israel out of Egypt and raised Jesus from the tomb is still active in the particular, unglamorous, sometimes discouraging circumstances of this congregation, this city, this year.

The pastoral vocation is sustained in the long run by this hope or it is not sustained at all. You can manage a congregation for a while on competence and charisma and genuine care. Ministry across decades requires something the competent manager does not have: the actual, operative belief that God raises the dead.

That belief is not an achievement. It is a gift. It comes through the Scripture, through prayer, through the repeated encounter with the living God in the ordinary practices of ministry — the Lord's Supper where Christ is genuinely present, the baptism where the water means what it says, the sermon where the ancient text addresses the present moment with uncanny precision. The belief must be regularly renewed, because pastoral experience — with its suffering and failure and complexity — will erode it if you are not attending.

Wendell Berry writes, in the agrarian tradition, about the importance of practicing resurrection — not as a one-time event but as a daily commitment to acts of renewal and return and repair that embody the conviction that the world is not finished [cite — confirm]. The phrase has become common enough to be abstract. But for the pastor, it names something specific: the practice of leading from the conviction of the empty tomb rather than the management of present appearances.

## Practicing Resurrection in the Long Arc

The tomb is still empty. Lead like you believe it.

Every deathbed you sit at, every marriage you counsel through the hardest season, every person you receive back after a departure — you are either bringing the resurrection into that room or you are not. You cannot fake it for long. Either you actually believe that God raises dead things, or you believe something smaller.

> The tomb is still empty. Lead like you believe it.

Go back to the text. Stay there until it shocks you again.

Somewhere in the last century, hospitality became a personality type.

You are either a "hospitable person" — someone who naturally loves hosting, who keeps a clean house and knows how to make guests feel welcome — or you are not, and the church mostly leaves you alone about it. The word appears on church websites as a gift of the Spirit for the few, a ministry for the kitchen volunteers, a season of life for people whose children are grown and whose table is large enough. It is optional. It is for those who feel called.

This is not the biblical account.

> This is not the biblical account.

## The Covenant Obligation

The Hebrew commands regarding the stranger are not addressed to a hospitality committee. They are addressed to the entire community, repeatedly, with the same theological grounding: you were a stranger in Egypt. You know what it means to be excluded, to have your presence treated as an inconvenience or a threat, to live at the mercy of people whose power over you was total. Therefore: do not do that to others.

Leviticus 19:33–34 is unambiguous: "When a stranger sojourns with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong. You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God." The grounding — "I am the LORD your God" — places the obligation in the character of God himself, not in the emotional preference of the host. The stranger is to be treated as a native, loved as the self. This is not courtesy. This is the covenant enacted toward the most vulnerable person in the community, the one without land or legal standing or family protection.

Deuteronomy 10:18–19 describes God's own character in terms of hospitality: "He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing. Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt." The command to love the sojourner flows directly from the description of God as the one who provides for sojourners. The community is to embody what God embodies. Hospitality is not a program the community runs. It is an expression of what God is like.

The hospitality of Abraham in Genesis 18 — running to meet three strangers, bowing to them, preparing food, standing near them as they ate — is presented in the text as a paradigmatic act of righteousness. The story does not say Abraham had the gift of hospitality. It says he saw the strangers and ran toward them, which is a posture, not a personality type. The running is the act of welcome before the identity of the guests is known. Hebrews 12:2 draws the explicit implication: "Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." The possibility that the stranger might be holy is built into the command, because the stranger has been created in the image of the holy God.

> Hospitality is not a program the community runs.

## What the New Testament Commands

By the time Paul writes to the Roman church, the vocabulary has intensified. The word he uses — *philoxenia* — means literally "love of the stranger" (Romans 12:13). Not tolerance. Not accommodation. Love. He places it in a list alongside blessing those who persecute you and weeping with those who weep — not as a lesser item, but as a posture so fundamental that its absence is the absence of the gospel operating in a community.

The letter to the Hebrews reinforces this with the explicit rationale about angels, which is more than superstitious sentiment. The point is that the stranger arrives carrying something you do not know about yet — a dignity, a need, a gift, possibly a word from God — and the posture of welcome is the posture that makes receiving it possible. The posture of exclusion forecloses what God was bringing through the one who came.

First Peter 4:9 addresses the specific community situation of the early church, scattered and sojourning under Roman pressure: "Show hospitality to one another without grumbling." The "without grumbling" is significant. It acknowledges that genuine hospitality is costly and can generate resentment, and then commands it anyway. This is not hospitality as pleasant social performance. This is hospitality as discipline — the deliberate extension of welcome across the cost of it.

The early church gathered in homes precisely because the home is the primary site of hospitality. When the church moved into basilicas and cathedrals, beginning in the fourth century after Constantine's settlement [cite — confirm], it did not simply change architecture. It changed the social grammar of welcome. The private home says: I am letting you into my life. The public building says: you may enter the facility. These are not the same posture. One is intimate. One is institutional. The church that only has institutional hospitality — programs for inclusion, diversity initiatives, welcome teams in branded shirts — has not yet practiced what the New Testament demands.

## The Social Architecture of Exclusion

I have stood in my own church and watched people walk in the door alone and leave alone, and I have told myself that we were a welcoming congregation because we had greeters at the door. We had a hospitality team. We had a system. What we did not have, in those moments, was hospitality — because hospitality is not a system. It is a posture of the self toward the other that says: you are not a visitor here. You are kin.

There is a difference between greeters and welcomers. Greeters acknowledge your arrival. Welcomers attend to your presence — notice whether you are standing alone, find out where you are in life, invite you into a conversation that is not about the church's program but about you. The greeter is a function. The welcomer is a person practicing a discipline. We have built extensive systems for the former while leaving the latter largely to chance.

> Affinity is pleasant. Hospitality is costly.

The people most likely to be turned away from the social reality of the church — even when they are present in the building — are the homeless, the mentally ill, the recently incarcerated, the undocumented, the poor who do not dress for the building they are entering. These are precisely the people the prophets name when they describe the test of faithful community. The widow, the orphan, the stranger. The ones without advocates. The ones whose presence makes the comfortable congregation slightly less comfortable.

The church that welcomes only the people who look like it is not practicing hospitality. It is practicing affinity. Affinity is pleasant. Hospitality is costly. The difference between them is the willingness to let someone who is not like you occupy your space, sit at your table, make demands on your time — and to receive that not as a burden but as the arriving of something holy.

## The Table as Theology

The risen Christ, in the Gospel of Luke, makes himself known at table (Luke 24:30–31). Not in the synagogue. Not in a formal teaching setting. At a table, in the breaking of bread, with strangers who did not recognize him until the meal. The host becomes the guest; the guest becomes the host. The meal is the site of recognition.

This is not coincidental. The Gospel of Luke is the gospel of meals — Jesus eating with tax collectors (Luke 5:29–30), eating with Pharisees (Luke 7:36, 11:37, 14:1), feeding the multitude (Luke 9:12–17), dining with Zacchaeus (Luke 19:1–10), sharing the Last Supper (Luke 22:14–20), and finally making himself known in the breaking of bread at Emmaus (Luke 24:30–31). The table is the recurring site of revelation and reconciliation in Luke's account. To eat with someone is to be made vulnerable to them, and it is in that vulnerability that the presence of God is recognized.

Stefan, a Congolese refugee who attended a church I know [cite — confirm], said that what he noticed first was not whether the church had a welcome process. He noticed whether anyone ate with him. Anyone can shake your hand at the door. The question is who sits down. The question is who shares the meal.

That is the right question. And it is not asked often enough, because the answer is uncomfortable. It requires not only the formal structures of inclusion but the personal willingness to actually sit with someone whose story is different from yours, whose English is limited, whose trauma is visible, whose presence at your table changes the dynamics of your comfortable gathering.

## Hospitality as Prophetic Act

The church that practices genuine hospitality is not running a program. It is making a theological claim about who belongs in the kingdom of God. Every meal shared across social boundaries is an enactment of the kingdom vision — the feast of Isaiah 25:6, where the Lord spreads a banquet for all peoples; the parable of Luke 14, where the poor and the crippled and the blind and the lame are brought in from the streets because the invited guests declined. The meal is not merely social. It is eschatological. It anticipates and enacts the future God is building.

This is why hospitality is a justice issue, not merely a courtesy issue. The structures that determine who feels welcome in a given space are not neutral. They are political. They reflect decisions about who belongs and who does not, whose presence is assumed and whose requires explanation. The church that addresses hospitality only at the individual level — asking individual congregants to be friendlier — while leaving unchanged the institutional structures, the location, the programming assumptions, the implicit social codes of its gathering, has not yet arrived at the full demand of *philoxenia*.

The full demand is a community whose orientation toward the other is so fundamental that strangers arriving at the door feel not that they have entered a facility but that they have been welcomed into a family. That is not produced by greeters alone. It is produced by a community that has practiced, over time, the costly discipline of making room — of allowing its own comfort to be disturbed by the presence of the one who was not expected.

He is still doing this. The stranger at the door is still, potentially, the stranger at Emmaus. The risen Christ is still making himself known at tables where the welcome was genuine enough to hold him.

The question is whether we are setting the table.

The church mobilizes for human trafficking with a coherence it rarely displays around other forms of exploitation. Conferences fill. Awareness campaigns spread. Youth groups raise money for rescue organizations. And much of this is genuinely good — the trafficking of human beings for sexual and labor exploitation is among the most direct violations of human dignity imaginable, and the church is right to oppose it.

But there is something else present in the church's response to trafficking that deserves examination. It is not enough to ask whether we oppose trafficking. We must also ask which trafficking we oppose, whose trafficking we name, and whose exploitation we walk past on the way to the rescue conference.

## The Full Shape of the Problem

Human trafficking in the United States takes two primary forms: sex trafficking and labor trafficking. Sex trafficking receives the overwhelming majority of the church's attention. Labor trafficking — the coerced and exploitative use of human labor through debt bondage, document confiscation, threats of violence, and systematic deception — is considerably less prominent in evangelical awareness campaigns, despite affecting large numbers of workers in agriculture, domestic work, construction, and manufacturing. [cite — confirm current figures]

The theological stakes are the same in both cases. A person trapped in labor trafficking has been stripped of the agency God built into them as image-bearers as surely as a person trapped in sex trafficking. The mechanism is different. The violation of imago Dei is identical.

> The mechanism is different. The violation of imago Dei is identical.

Why, then, the asymmetry? The question is worth pressing not to diminish the importance of fighting sex trafficking but to interrogate what the asymmetry reveals about whose suffering we are trained to notice and whose we are trained to manage.

Labor trafficking touches supply chains. It runs through the agricultural fields where produce is harvested, the factories where goods are assembled, the construction sites where buildings rise, the domestic work arrangements in homes that look, from the outside, like normal employment. The products of labor trafficking sit in grocery stores and on kitchen tables and in church fellowship halls. The person who has been trafficked for their labor may have produced something we purchased last week, in a transaction that passed through legitimate-seeming commercial channels. Our outrage is selective partly because our implication is much harder to contain if we widen the frame.

## What the Bible Says About Exploitation

The prophetic tradition in Scripture does not distinguish between types of exploitation based on how disturbing they are to examine. Jeremiah 22:13 is direct: "Woe to him who builds his palace by unrighteousness, his upper rooms by injustice, making his own people work for nothing, not paying them for their labor." The sin named is the extraction of labor without just compensation — the building of wealth on someone else's exploitation. Amos spent most of his ministry condemning economic systems that ground the poor into dust, selling "the needy for a pair of sandals" (Amos 2:6). James 5:4 addresses labor exploitation with unusual directness: "Look! The wages you failed to pay the workers who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty."

The text is not interested in whether the exploitation was accomplished through formal coercion or through market structures that left workers no viable alternative. What it names is the system that takes from the vulnerable what is rightfully theirs and transfers it to those who already have enough. That system has many forms. Human trafficking in its rawest form is simply the extreme end of a continuum that runs through wage theft, predatory contract arrangements, debt bondage through payday lending, and the full range of labor practices that extract human value without returning adequate compensation. The prophets named the whole continuum. The church has tended to name only the extreme end, and only the version that allows us to feel entirely outside the system we are condemning.

## The Selective Frame and What It Costs Us

Selective outrage is not morally neutral. It is a form of moral positioning that maintains the appearance of prophetic witness while protecting the positions and arrangements that benefit us.

> The rescue narrative is clean. The supply chain narrative is not. We choose the clean narrative.

The church that rallies around sex trafficking and stays quiet about agricultural labor trafficking is not simply choosing its battles. It is revealing something about whose vulnerability activates its instincts and whose does not. The women and girls exploited in sex trafficking are real people whose suffering is real and whose rescue matters. And the migrant workers confined to debt bondage on farms that supply national grocery chains are also real people whose suffering is real and whose liberation matters. The question is why one group's suffering fills evangelical conferences and the other's barely registers.

Part of the answer is social distance. Sex trafficking maps onto narratives of individual victimization and rescue that are theologically familiar and emotionally accessible. Labor trafficking maps onto economic systems, supply chains, regulatory policy, and consumer behavior — all of which implicate the church's members in ways that sex trafficking does not. The rescue narrative is clean. The supply chain narrative is not. We choose the clean narrative.

Part of the answer is political alliance. In the American evangelical world, the political affiliations that dominate make it relatively comfortable to condemn sex trafficking — it fits within a shared moral framework — and relatively uncomfortable to condemn labor exploitation of migrant workers, because that conversation touches immigration policy, agricultural industry lobbying, and the supply chain practices of companies whose executives may be in the pews. Prophetic witness that stops at the edge of political discomfort is not prophetic witness. It is politics with a theological wrapper.

## The Counter-Position Taken Seriously

There is a real argument on the other side. Organizations that focus specifically on sex trafficking argue that concentration of resources on a single, clearly defined target is more effective than spreading awareness across multiple forms of exploitation. A diffuse campaign is a weak campaign. Focused attention, they argue, saves more lives than distributed attention. This is not a dishonest position. It reflects genuine strategic thinking about how change happens.

But strategic focus does not require theological silence about the wider pattern. A church can direct its practical resources toward a specific form of intervention while still forming its people's moral imagination around the full scope of exploitation the text condemns. The problem is not that churches focus on sex trafficking as a ministry strategy. The problem is that the narrowness of the focus becomes the narrowness of the moral vision — that what we campaign against becomes the full extent of what we see. And what we do not see, we do not interrogate.

The prophets were not selective in this way. Amos moved from indicting sexual exploitation to indicting economic exploitation to indicting the legal corruption that protected the wealthy to indicting the religious ceremonialism that dressed all of it in spiritual legitimacy. He did not separate these sins into categories of the actionable and the awkward. They were all the same sin: the use of power to take what belonged to the vulnerable.

## A Honest Self-Accounting

I have been moved by anti-trafficking campaigns. I have given money to rescue organizations. I have preached the horror of sex trafficking with genuine anger. And I have not asked, with the same rigor, who picked the tomatoes at the bottom of my grocery bag, or whether the supply chain behind the shirt I am wearing moved through factories where workers were held in debt bondage, or what the labor conditions were in the manufacturing that built the things in my home.

That is not a small inconsistency. It is a structural one. My outrage is calibrated to the forms of exploitation I can condemn without examining my own economic life. That calibration is exactly what the prophets refused. Amos preached to people who brought their offerings to Bethel and were certain of their own righteousness. They opposed the sins they could see in others. They could not see the sins built into the arrangements that sustained their comfort.

Isaiah 58 names the form of religion that is energetic about its visible practices and blind to its structural ones: "You fast and quarrel and strike with a wicked fist." The people were performing their religious obligations while the systems around them ground down the poor. God's response was not to commend their visible devotion. It was to name the form of justice that their fasting was designed to avoid.

## What Faithfulness Requires

> The question is whether we have.

Not abandoning anti-trafficking work. The rescue of the person trapped in sexual exploitation is urgent and right. The work of the organizations doing this work deserves support.

But faithfulness requires that the church's moral attention be as wide as the text's — which means naming labor trafficking alongside sex trafficking, examining the supply chains our consumer lives run through, asking what the labor conditions are behind the goods we purchase cheaply, and being willing to apply the same prophetic energy to the exploitation that implicates us as to the exploitation that does not.

It requires being honest about what our outrage actually covers. The church that is loud about one form of human exploitation and silent about others has not taken the full measure of the evil it claims to oppose. It has found a version of opposition that costs very little — no reexamination of purchasing habits, no uncomfortable political positions, no renegotiation of supply chain relationships, no naming of the people in our own congregations who benefit from exploitative labor arrangements.

Selective outrage is not nothing. But it is less than what the prophets demanded. Less than what the text requires. Less than what the people in the labor trafficking camps, the fields, and the factories deserve from a church that claims to speak for the God who hears the cry of the exploited and asks whose cry we have decided to hear.

Every human being trapped in exploitation — by sex traffickers or by labor traffickers, by the dramatic violation or the slow grinding of systemic extraction — bears the image of the God who said: the wages you withheld are crying out against you. The Lord Almighty heard them.

The question is whether we have.

In the ancient Near East, a king would place images of himself throughout the territories he governed. The image — the *tselem* — functioned as a claim of sovereignty: this territory belongs to the one whose image stands here. Stone figures of Pharaoh or Nebuchadnezzar in distant provinces announced that the power at the center reached this far. The image was not decorative. It was jurisdictional.

Genesis 1:26–27 enters this cultural world and overturns its logic entirely. The whole earth is God's territory. God's image — *imago Dei* — is not placed in stone in strategic locations. It is breathed into every human being, without qualification, without exception, without condition. Every person, in this account, is a living marker of divine sovereignty — not a representative of a political ruler but the bearer of the living God's own likeness, set in the middle of creation as its steward and crown.

This is not primarily a statement about human dignity, though it grounds human dignity. It is primarily a statement about God's sovereignty. And its implications run farther than most preaching ever reaches.

> The prohibition against murder is grounded in theology, not merely in social utility.

## The Logic of the Doctrine

If every human being bears the image of God, then every act of violence against a human being is an act against the image of the One whose claim extends over all creation. Genesis 9:6 makes this explicit in the context of law: "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image." The gravity of the crime is not merely that a life is ended. It is that an image of God has been destroyed. The prohibition against murder is grounded in theology, not merely in social utility.

Expand that logic. Not just murder. What about the slower violences — the poverty that shortens lives by decades, the incarceration that strips agency and dignity across years, the medical neglect of communities without insurance, the housing conditions that expose children to lead and mold and chronic stress? If these things diminish or destroy the people who bear God's image, what does the *imago Dei* doctrine demand of us in response?

The tradition has pressed this logic further than most contemporary preaching does. John Calvin, writing in the Institutes, argued that when we meet a neighbor in need, we have no business asking whether they deserve our help, because we see on their face the image of God and that is sufficient basis for action. [cite — confirm Calvin reference] The image is not a spiritual compliment we extend to people we already respect. It is an ontological status that precedes and overrides every category we impose upon people to justify our indifference toward them. The person sleeping under the bridge, the person convicted of a violent crime, the person whose immigration status is contested — they bear the image of God as fully as the person in the front pew who tithes faithfully. The doctrine does not recognize our sorting categories.

## The New Testament Radicalization

Jesus does not soften this logic. He radicalizes it. In the Sermon on the Mount, he extends the prohibition on murder to the prohibition on contempt: "Anyone who says to a brother or sister, 'Raca,' is answerable to the court" (Matthew 5:22). The word *raca* is a term of dismissal — the kind of word you use when you are communicating that someone does not deserve your serious attention, that they are beneath the dignity of genuine engagement. Jesus treats this as a violation nearly as serious as the violence that follows when contempt goes to its logical end. The contempt is where the violence begins, and the contempt is already a violation of the *imago Dei* in the person being dismissed.

> The contempt is where the violence begins, and the contempt is already a violation of the *imago Dei* in the person being dismissed.

Matthew 25 takes this further, to the place where the doctrine becomes almost unbearable in its demands. "Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me" (Matthew 25:40). The person who is hungry, thirsty, a stranger, without clothing, sick, imprisoned — in each case, Christ says: this is where I am. To encounter that person's need and to walk past it is not merely a missed opportunity for charity. It is a failure to recognize Christ. The *imago Dei* has become, in the Gospel's account, identification. God is not merely the one in whose image the vulnerable person was made. God is the one present in that person's vulnerability, in a way that makes the encounter with their need an encounter with the divine presence.

This is not comfortable theology. It was not meant to be. The text does not invite us to feel good about the dignity of people like us. It demands that we see the dignity of people we have sorted into categories of lesser concern.

## The Consistency the Doctrine Requires

The *imago Dei* doctrine, consistently applied, prohibits a selective compassion that treats some people's suffering as worthy of prophetic attention and others' suffering as a matter of personal responsibility. It is common in American evangelical culture to affirm the *imago Dei* in the abstract while maintaining social arrangements that systematically deny it in practice — through housing patterns that concentrate poverty in some communities while protecting wealth in others, through criminal justice practices that treat the same crimes differently depending on the race and class of the accused, through political positions that advocate for the unborn while showing indifference to the conditions that will shape the lives of those born into poverty.

These inconsistencies are not incidental. They reveal a functional doctrine of human worth that is considerably narrower than the Genesis account warrants. If the *imago Dei* applies uniformly, then the death of a child from a preventable disease in a poor neighborhood carries the same theological weight as the death of a child from any other cause. The bearing of God's image is not diminished by poverty, by race, by disability, by age, by criminal history, by immigration status, or by any other category human societies have constructed to manage the distribution of dignity.

Disability theologians have pressed this point with particular sharpness in recent decades. The church that speaks of the *imago Dei* while designing worship spaces that exclude people in wheelchairs, programming that ignores sensory needs, and community that implicitly communicates that people with cognitive disabilities are objects of care rather than contributors to community — that church has believed the doctrine insufficiently. The image of God in the person with Down syndrome is not a diminished image. It is the full image. The church's practice must reflect that, not as an accommodation but as recognition of what has always been true.

## The Steel-Man Objection

The serious objection deserves a serious hearing: doctrine and policy are different things, and *imago Dei* does not automatically resolve contested questions about how best to structure social arrangements. This is true. The doctrine does not settle debates about the best mechanism for addressing poverty, the most effective approach to criminal justice reform, or the correct policy on immigration. Reasonable people who affirm the *imago Dei* fully can disagree about which policies best serve the flourishing of image-bearers.

But the objection cannot be used to soften the doctrine into irrelevance. While the *imago Dei* does not generate a specific legislative program, it does generate certain prohibitions and certain requirements. It prohibits treating any human being as expendable. It prohibits arrangements that systematically discard people — through poverty, through dehumanizing institutional treatment, through the legal stripping of legal standing — as if their image-bearing were conditional on their social usefulness. The distance between the doctrine's general claim and specific policy may be debated. The prohibition against contempt is not.

The church that can name the *imago Dei* on Sunday morning and spend the rest of the week in comfortable indifference toward the people whose image-bearing it has just affirmed has not applied the doctrine. It has invoked the language without bearing the cost.

> That is not comfortable theology. It is the foundation of all the other theology that follows.

## What It Demands Next

I have said "every person bears the image of God" in sermons. I have not always followed that sentence to where it leads. It is easier to affirm the doctrine than to reckon with what the doctrine requires of me when I pass the man sleeping in the parking garage or vote on policies that will affect the conditions of people I will never meet. The doctrine is not comfortable if you take it seriously. It is costly. It demands that people I would rather categorize as problems be seen instead as bearers of the same image I claim for myself.

The image cannot be erased. Genesis does not provide a mechanism for the loss of the *imago Dei* — not through sin, not through poverty, not through conviction, not through the categories any society constructs to manage the distribution of moral concern. Every person who has ever lived, and who is living now, and who will live — bears the image of the God who placed it in them before they had done anything to deserve it or forfeit it.

That is not comfortable theology. It is the foundation of all the other theology that follows. Get it wrong — narrow it, qualify it, apply it selectively — and everything else in the moral architecture of the faith tilts with it.

Get it right, and the woman at the shelter, the man in the cell, the child in the underfunded school, the refugee at the border — they are not problems to be solved. They are the image of the God you worship, and what you do to them is the question that will be waiting for you.

What it demands next is the harder question. One the doctrine will not let us defer indefinitely.

There is a sentence that sits near the foundation of everything the Christian tradition claims about human beings, and most of us have heard it so many times that we have stopped hearing it at all.

"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). The imago Dei. The image of God. We use it in seminary courses and ethics papers and statements of belief. We invoke it in discussions about human dignity and in arguments against abortion and in sermon series about identity and worth. And in using it that much, in that many contexts, for that many purposes, we have domesticated it until it no longer functions as the claim it actually is.

The claim it actually is would be unsettling if we heard it fresh. Let me try to say it plainly.
