That word welcome, in its full sense, does not mean making someone comfortable within your existing structures. It means changing your structures enough to actually include them. The church that welcomes people of different cultural backgrounds into a service whose aesthetic, liturgical structure, preaching style, community rhythms, and decision-making processes are entirely shaped by one cultural tradition has not welcomed them. It has extended a polite invitation to assimilate.

> That reading is not less theological than mine. It is more textually complete.

This is not unity. This is majority culture extending a conditional invitation.

## The Counter-Position Worth Engaging

The Ephesians passage is the most sustained biblical treatment of cross-cultural unity in the New Testament. Paul writes about the dividing wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile — not a metaphorical wall, but the literal stone barrier in the Jerusalem temple that marked where Gentiles could not pass, on penalty of death [cite — confirm]. Christ has demolished that wall (Ephesians 2:14). He has created "in himself one new man in place of the two" (Ephesians 2:15). The key phrase is "one new man" — not the Gentile being absorbed into the Jewish community, not the Jew being absorbed into the Gentile community, but something genuinely new, a third thing, a community that does not exist before the work of Christ creates it.

Most cross-cultural church conversations are not aiming at the third thing. They are aiming at one community graciously accommodating the presence of another. That is generosity. It is not the "one new man" that Paul describes.

---

## The Work Is the Staying

The formation that my cross-cultural partnerships produced in me was real, and it ran in specific directions.

My understanding of grief changed. The West African tradition my colleagues carried included a way of communal grief — extended, public, physically present, sustained across weeks — that was almost entirely foreign to how I had been formed to grieve and to pastor grieving people. The "move through it and forward" framework I carried was not biblical. It was cultural. The psalms of lament last longer than a week. The book of Lamentations does not resolve. The early church's practice of extended mourning, preserved in Eastern Christian traditions, is closer to the African pattern than to the efficient, processed, ready-to-move-on approach I had been applying to the pastoral care of grieving people.

My understanding of authority changed. The cultures I was in relationship with carried a deep respect for elder wisdom — not deference to age as such, but reverence for the kind of authority that comes from having lived long enough to carry the community's memory and to have earned trust through sustained faithfulness. That authority was consulted before major decisions. It was not bypassed because the decision seemed obvious. The pastor who makes decisions without consulting the community's wisdom carriers has not streamlined the process. He has damaged a relationship and signaled that he does not actually need what they carry.

My preaching changed. Not my theology. But my understanding of which aspects of the text the people in front of me most needed to hear. I had been preaching from a position of cultural security — the assumption that my hearers' primary context was middle-class white evangelical American culture, with its specific anxieties and its specific assumptions about God and success and personal flourishing. My brothers from other cultural traditions read the same texts and heard different words landing — the words about God's presence in suffering, the words about the enemy's impotence against the one who walks with God, the words about the God who sees the oppressed and acts on their behalf. These were not different texts. They were the same texts read from different positions in the social order.

That reading is not less theological than mine. It is more textually complete. The prosperity of the majority culture reader has been editing out the passages that most directly address the experience of people for whom prosperity is not the presenting context.

---

There is a counter-position worth engaging. It says: the emphasis on cultural difference can itself become an obstacle to unity. The church is called to transcend cultural divisions, not to perform them. The preacher who is always contextualizing the text for specific cultural communities is fragmenting the congregation rather than unifying it. The gospel has a universal claim that transcends cultural particularity, and the church that makes too much of cultural difference risks being more sociological than theological in its self-understanding.

This is a genuine concern. The gospel is not a cultural artifact. Christ is not the property of any ethnicity. The New Testament's most dramatic claim about the community of faith is that it crosses lines that human beings treat as ultimate — there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female (Galatians 3:28). That is a real theological claim with real social consequences, and it must not be surrendered in the name of cultural sensitivity.

But the claim that the gospel transcends culture cannot become the claim that culture does not matter. The gospel has always been received in cultural contexts, and the way it is received reflects the assumptions of those contexts. The insistence that a particular cultural form of Christianity is simply Christianity, without the modifier, is not the affirmation of the gospel's universality. It is the particular culture's failure to recognize itself as a culture.

What Paul describes in Ephesians 2 is not the erasure of Jewish and Gentile particularity in the name of a new uniformity. It is the creation of something in which both particulars are held, transformed, and surpassed. The Jew does not stop being Jewish. The Gentile does not stop being Gentile. But neither one's cultural inheritance determines the community's life. Both are placed under the lordship of the one who has made peace between them.

---

That kind of unity formation cannot happen at a diversity conference. It cannot happen through reading. It happens in relationship sustained long enough to produce genuine trust and genuine friction — because trust without friction is politeness, and politeness is not unity.

What homogeneous churches miss is not the aesthetic variety of diverse worship. What they miss is the theological depth that comes from encountering the same God through genuinely different eyes.

I became a different pastor through those relationships. The certainty did not disappear — it never does, entirely, for people constituted the way I am. But it acquired a companion it had not had before: the genuine awareness that the person across the table from me might be right about something I am wrong about, and that the only way I am going to find out is by staying in the room long enough for the friction to happen, and by not leaving when it does.

That staying is the work. Not the conference attendance, not the curriculum, not the well-intentioned programs that perform diversity without producing it.

The work is the staying.

I needed to learn to stay.

I am still learning it.

The text is not ambiguous. It never was.

Leviticus 19:33-34: "When a stranger sojourns with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong. You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the Lord your God."

> The treatment of the stranger is not a secondary application of the law. It is a direct expression of the character of the God who gave it.

That last phrase — I am the Lord your God — is not ornamental. It appears throughout Leviticus 19 as a divine signature, an assertion of authority. When the Lord signs a command with his own name, he is not offering a suggestion. He is binding the covenant community to a standard inseparable from who he is. The treatment of the stranger is not a secondary application of the law. It is a direct expression of the character of the God who gave it.

The church that has spent recent years debating the ethics of immigration while treating Leviticus 19 as a historical curiosity has made a theological error of the first order.

## The Memory at the Center

The command does not stand alone. It is rooted in a specific historical memory: you were strangers in the land of Egypt. This is not analogy. This is the mechanism of the command. Israel is commanded to protect the stranger because Israel knows from inside what it means to be a stranger — to be powerless, to be subject to the decisions of a host society that can exploit or expel at will, to have no legal standing, no advocate, no protection except whatever the powerful choose to extend.

> You do not get to be Israel without being obligated by what it means to have been a stranger.

God took note of what Egypt did to Israel in that condition. God intervened. The entire narrative of Exodus — the deliverance, the wilderness, the law at Sinai — flows from that intervention. And then God commands: because you know what that is, because you were in that place, you will not be Egypt to the stranger in your land.

The Hebrew word for stranger in these texts is *ger* — a person living outside their native land, resident among a foreign people. The ger had no tribal belonging, no family network, no inherited claim on the land's resources. The law protected the ger explicitly and repeatedly because the ger was structurally without protection. Leviticus 19, Deuteronomy 10, Deuteronomy 24, Exodus 22 — the command recurs so often that its repetition is itself a theological statement. God keeps returning to it because Israel kept needing to be reminded. The pressure to treat the stranger as less than the native was always present. The command against it was equally persistent.

The American church exists in a country whose founding mythology borrowed heavily from the Exodus. Puritan settlers identified themselves explicitly with Israel fleeing Egypt, with the Atlantic as their Red Sea, with the New World as Canaan. That metaphor has been deployed again and again in American religious history. But if the church has borrowed that metaphor, it has also inherited the command at its center. You do not get to be Israel without being obligated by what it means to have been a stranger.

## What the Law Encoded

Leviticus 19 is remarkable for how much it encodes in one chapter. Within forty-six verses, God commands the leaving of field edges for the poor and stranger (verse 9-10), honest weights and measures (verse 35-36), love of neighbor as oneself (verse 18), and love of the stranger as oneself (verse 33-34). The chapter treats care for the vulnerable not as a supplement to religious practice but as its core substance. The commands come interspersed with the divine signature, binding each to God's own identity.

The prophets understood this. Jeremiah 22:3 summarizes the prophetic demand: "Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow." The resident alien appears again. He always appears. In Ezekiel 22, among the catalog of Jerusalem's sins that have brought judgment, one of the charges is: "The stranger living among you suffers extortion" (verse 29). Not an afterthought. Evidence for the prosecution.

Zechariah 7:10, Malachi 3:5, Isaiah 1:17 — the prophetic witness is consistent. The treatment of the stranger is not one justice concern among many equal concerns. It is a recurring, foregrounded test of covenant faithfulness. God cares about this with the intensity of someone who was once in the stranger's position and has not forgotten it.

## What Every Crisis Reveals

Every border crisis — and this one is not the first — reveals what the church actually believes about the stranger, as opposed to what it preaches about him.

The debate around immigration policy involves genuine complexity. Nations have responsibilities for order and security that are not illegitimate. A careful reader can hold those concerns alongside the commands of Leviticus 19 and does not have to choose between them entirely. I am not arguing that open borders are the obvious and only faithful policy position, or that every element of border enforcement is categorically wrong.

What is not defensible is the silence. What is not defensible is the church that has weeks of internal discussion about worship style, budget priorities, and children's programming, and has had no serious conversation about the families separated at the border, the asylum seekers in detention, the undocumented worker in the congregation who is afraid of what the next executive order means for her children. The silence is a position. It is just a position we have not been honest enough to name.

I have been part of congregations that practiced that silence. I have contributed to it. The deacon meeting where someone raised the question and the room went very quiet, and we moved on to the next agenda item — I was in that room. That silence is not neutrality. It is a choice about whose discomfort matters more.

## Two Evasions That Fail

I have watched the American evangelical church, in recent years, perform elaborate theological gymnastics to avoid the plain reading of texts like Leviticus 19. The gymnastics usually take one of two forms.

> We were strangers once. We were not forgotten.

The first is dispensationalism applied to ethics: that was Israel's theocratic law, it does not apply to a secular nation-state, we live in a different covenant era. This move fails for at least two reasons. First, the New Testament does not abandon the logic of Leviticus 19. Jesus quotes Leviticus 19:18 — "love your neighbor as yourself" — as one of the two greatest commandments (Matthew 22:39). The parable of the Good Samaritan expands the definition of neighbor to include precisely the person the religious establishment had decided to walk past. The stranger is still in the text. The command has not been retired. Second, the principle underlying the command — you were once powerless, therefore you will not exploit the powerless — is not a theocratic novelty. It is a moral logic rooted in the character of God that runs from Genesis to Revelation.

The second evasion is the separation of justice and politics: I care about the immigrant as a person, but immigration policy is a political question and the church should not be political. This fails because the prophets were relentlessly political in the specific sense that they named what political and economic systems were doing to the poor and the stranger. Avoiding politics was not an option available to Amos or Isaiah or Jeremiah. When Amos denounced the merchants who could not wait for the Sabbath to end so they could get back to cheating the poor with false scales (Amos 8:5), he was making a political claim about economic practice. When Isaiah condemned those who "join house to house" and "add field to field" until they alone inhabit the land (Isaiah 5:8), he was addressing a policy of land consolidation. The prophets did not have a category for prophetic witness that was non-political in its application.

The church that separates its love for the immigrant person from its engagement with the systems that determine how that person is treated has made a theological choice to operate at the level of charity rather than justice. Charity is good. It is insufficient.

## The Word That Remains

Love him as yourself. Not love him as you would a distant beneficiary of your charitable giving. Not love him as you would a mission project with clear boundaries and funding cycles. As yourself.

That standard is demanding. It requires asking what I would want, what I would need, what I would be owed, if I were in his position. It means asking those questions about the man who fled violence in Central America with his family, who crossed a border because the legal channels had been closed or made inaccessible, who is now living in my city, working, attending my church or one near it, afraid every time a vehicle moves slowly past. What would I want, in that position?

The answer to that question does not resolve every immigration policy debate. Reasonable people applying the same Scripture can disagree about the mechanisms of border management, the structure of asylum processes, the pathways to legal status. But it tells me where to start. It tells me that silence in the face of his vulnerability is not an option Leviticus 19 leaves open. It tells me that the community God gave his name to protect him has an obligation that precedes and exceeds every policy preference.

I grew up without a father to advocate for me. I know something about what it means to be without protection in a social context that is organized around the assumption of protection you do not have. I did not have to cross a border to know that. I grew up speaking English in Michigan. The man at the border has less than I had. The command reaches him. It reaches me.

We were strangers once. We were not forgotten.

The command is: do not forget.

The book of Deuteronomy commands that the law be read aloud to the entire assembly — men, women, children, the foreigners living in the town — at the Feast of Booths every seven years (Deuteronomy 31:10-13). Not summarized for the educated. Not read to the leadership who would then explain it to the rest. Read aloud to everyone. The reason given is explicit: *so they can listen and learn to fear the Lord your God and follow carefully all the words of this law.* The word of God was not to be the property of specialists. Access to the word was the condition for faithful life, and access required comprehension, and comprehension required a community committed to ensuring that every member of the community could receive it.

This is not a minor textual footnote. It is the theological architecture beneath a claim the church has not always honored: that access to the written word — to the capacity to read, understand, and participate in the traditions of meaning that constitute a community's life — is not a privilege for the capable but a condition for full human dignity. Literacy is a justice issue. The church that has not understood this has missed something foundational in its own Scripture.

## The History of This Question Is a History of Power

The history of this question is a history of power.

> Literacy is a justice issue.

In medieval Europe, the restriction of Scripture to Latin — a language the vast majority of the population could not read — was not accidental. It was structural. The church that controlled the text controlled the interpretation of the text, and the interpretation of the text controlled the community's understanding of God, authority, sin, and salvation. John Wycliffe's insistence in the late fourteenth century on translating Scripture into English was not primarily a linguistic project. It was a justice project — an argument that the word of God belonged to the plowman as much as to the priest, that the capacity to read and interpret it was not a clerical monopoly but a human right [cite — confirm]. Wycliffe was condemned for this. The institutional church understood exactly what was at stake.

William Tyndale understood it too. His English translation of the New Testament, completed in 1526, was burned by church authorities and cost him his life — he was strangled and burned at the stake in 1536. His reported last words, *Lord, open the King of England's eyes*, are the words of a man who understood that access to the written word was bound up with access to power, and that the powerful did not give up that control without cost [cite — confirm]. The Reformation's democratizing impulse — the priesthood of all believers, the accessibility of Scripture — was premised on literacy in ways that the Reformers understood and the institutions they challenged feared.

In the American South before the Civil War, teaching enslaved people to read was illegal in most slaveholding states [cite — confirm]. This is the clearest possible evidence that literacy is power. The enslaved person who could read could read Frederick Douglass's *Narrative*. Could read the Bible without a white minister's interpretation of it. Could read the forged passes that allowed movement. Could read the advertisements for escaped slaves that described what they were running from. The prohibition was not about pedagogy. It was about control, and the people who enforced it understood exactly what they were controlling.

> The connection between literacy and liberation was not metaphorical. It was material.

Nat Turner could read. Frederick Douglass, who described in his autobiography the moment he understood that literacy was the path from slavery to freedom, later said: *Once you learn to read, you will be forever free* [cite — confirm]. The connection between literacy and liberation was not metaphorical. It was material.

Today, in the United States, approximately 54 percent of adults read below a sixth-grade level [cite — confirm]. This figure is not distributed evenly. It is concentrated in communities of poverty, in communities of color, among populations that have been systematically underfunded by the school systems that property-tax-based funding models favor. The child in the underfunded district does not get worse education because the community values education less. She gets worse education because the system was designed — not by accident but by a series of policy choices stretching back generations — to concentrate educational resources where wealth already exists.

## Illiteracy as Systemic Sin

This is systemic sin in the technical sense: an arrangement of institutions and policies that produces unjust outcomes regardless of the individual intentions of the people operating within it. Most of the teachers in underfunded schools are working as hard as or harder than their counterparts in well-funded schools. Most of the parents in those communities want their children to learn to read. The system produces illiteracy not because anyone inside it is malicious but because the system was built to produce this result and has not been fundamentally changed.

The church's response to this has been mostly charitable and occasionally substantive, but rarely prophetic. There are after-school tutoring programs, literacy ministries, reading circles attached to congregations across the country. They are doing real good and the people running them are often among the most faithful people I know. But they are addressing the symptom without addressing the system that produces it. The child who learns to read in a church basement program in a neighborhood with an underfunded school will return the next morning to that school. The symptom has been addressed. The cause is still operating.

## Naming the Cause Beneath the Symptom

Prophetic witness requires the willingness to name the cause.

The cause is a public school funding model that ties educational quality to neighborhood wealth, that produces — by design — unequal educational outcomes for children who had no choice about where they were born. The cause is a political economy that has consistently underinvested in the communities with the least political power and overinvested in the communities with the most. The cause is a historical inheritance of segregation — both residential, produced by redlining and discriminatory housing policy, and educational, produced by the school funding model that maps onto those residential patterns — that continues to shape outcomes decades after the legal instruments of segregation were dismantled.

James 2:14-17 asks the question directly: *What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone claims to have faith but has no deeds? Can such faith save them? Suppose a brother or a sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you says to them, 'Go in peace; keep warm and well fed,' but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is it?* The church that runs reading programs while supporting politicians and policies that perpetuate the inequality producing illiteracy has said *go in peace* without addressing the need. It has faith without deeds, in precisely the sense James condemns.

This is not an argument that every pastor should become an education policy advocate in the specific legislative sense. It is an argument that the church that takes seriously the Deuteronomy vision — that the word should be accessible to every member of the community, that full human participation in the life of God's people requires the capacity to receive it — has a theological stake in the conditions that make literacy possible or impossible.

## The Image of God and the Capacity to Read

The imago Dei claim carries this. If every person bears the image of God, then the capacity for every person to participate fully in the written traditions of human civilization — to read contracts, to access medical information, to engage with Scripture directly rather than through filtered summary, to participate in democratic processes that require reading to engage — is not a nice-to-have. It is a condition for the full expression of the dignity that the image of God confers.

The church that has historically cared about Scripture should care, with equivalent intensity, about the conditions that make Scripture accessible. Not only in translation — though the translation project remains vital in many parts of the world. But in the literacy that makes translation useful. The word can be in the language of the people and still be inaccessible if the people cannot read it.

## Recovering the Sunday School Tradition

In the nineteenth century, the Sunday school movement in England and America — begun not primarily as a religious education program but as a literacy program for children of the industrial poor who worked six days a week and had Sunday free — was one of the church's most significant justice contributions [cite — confirm]. Robert Raikes, who launched it in Gloucester in 1780, was responding to what he observed in the streets: children without education, without access to the traditions of meaning that might give their lives structure and dignity, moving toward a predictable adulthood of poverty and institutional neglect. The Sunday school taught them to read. And it taught them to read using the Bible, which was the text those communities had. The program was both charity and justice — addressing the immediate need of the individual child while building the infrastructure for a community in which literacy would be possible.

That tradition is worth recovering — not in the form of the Sunday school, which has evolved into something else, but in the spirit of a church that understands literacy as a theological imperative rather than a social service, that sees the relationship between the word of God and the capacity to read it as something more than incidental, that is willing to address not just the immediate gap but the systems that produce it.

> The word was given to be read.

The word was given to be read. The community was commanded to ensure that everyone could receive it. What that costs and who pays it is not a minor question. It is a question about what the church actually believes is at stake in the person sitting across from it who cannot read.

David wrote Psalm 22 from a place no one who had not been there could fully identify. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, so far from my cries of anguish?" He was not performing grief. He was reporting it. And the first movement of that psalm is solitary in a way that only someone who has carried weight in the dark can recognize — a man calling out and hearing nothing return, surrounded by people who do not understand what he is holding.

That is not only a spiritual portrait. It is a leadership portrait.

## The Structural Loneliness of the Role

The loneliness of leading a congregation is structural. It is built into the role itself, not a symptom of doing it wrong. You hold information people gave you in confidence — the couple whose marriage is collapsing under the surface of their Sunday smiles, the elder whose son is in serious trouble, the woman in the third row who told you something she has never told another person. You carry that knowledge into every room. You make decisions that affect people's lives, and you often cannot explain why you made them without breaching the trust that made you worth telling in the first place. You see the institution from above and below and inside simultaneously, in a way that no individual member sees it, and the full view is not something you can share over lunch or unload in a board meeting or process in a sermon.

This is not complaint. This is description. Leadership requires the willingness to bear weight that cannot be distributed.

> Leadership requires the willingness to bear weight that cannot be distributed.

But I have come to understand something harder: the loneliness that is structural is one thing. The loneliness that is self-imposed is another, and it is the more dangerous kind.

## The Self-Imposed Isolation That Destroys

I have watched men in ministry seal themselves off — not because the role demanded it, but because they decided that asking for help was a vulnerability they could not afford, that admitting struggle was inconsistent with the authority they needed to lead. They confused the necessary aloneness of decision-making with a total isolation that was not required by anything except their own fear of being known. They built a persona that performed competence, maintained it for years, and one day were not fine — and no one around them had any idea it was coming, because they had made absolutely sure no one would.

The result is almost always the same. A man who seemed fine, who was producing results and delivering sermons and meeting with people, and then one day was not. The congregation was blindsided. The family was blindsided. The man himself was, in some sense, the last to know how close to the edge he had been walking, because he had been too busy performing health to notice its absence.

## Jethro's Word From Outside

Moses carried the disputes of an entire nation alone until his father-in-law Jethro came from Midian and saw it and told him plainly: "What you are doing is not good. You and these people who come to you will only wear yourselves out. The work is too heavy for you; you cannot handle it alone" (Exodus 18:17–18). That assessment came from outside Moses. Moses was too close to see it. He had been doing it this way long enough that the doing-it-alone had become invisible to him, the water he swam in. He needed someone positioned differently — someone with no stake in his performance, someone who loved him without needing him to be impressive — to name what the situation required.

Jethro's advice was not theological. It was organizational: appoint capable leaders, delegate the ordinary disputes, reserve yourself for the extraordinary ones. But behind the organization was a more fundamental claim — that the pretense of handling everything alone was not faithfulness. It was unsustainability dressed as dedication.

> It was unsustainability dressed as dedication.

The pastoral tradition has never held up total self-sufficiency as a virtue. The elders of Acts 20 gathered together, not as isolated leaders in isolated churches but as a network of people who carried related weight. Paul wrote to his communities and received reports from trusted colleagues about what those communities were actually experiencing. The epistles are not the product of a solitary genius — they are the product of a man in constant correspondence, constantly informed by Epaphroditus and Timothy and Titus and the household of Chloe, constantly accompanied by a network of co-laborers who told him the truth about what was happening on the ground. Paul's authority was not compromised by his dependence on that network. It was expressed through it.

## The New Testament Network of Co-Laborers

The tradition that produces the isolated pastor-hero is not the New Testament. It is a cultural inheritance — partly American, partly masculine, partly peculiar to the clergy class — that equates need with weakness and self-disclosure with inadequacy. It is the tradition that produces men who go twenty years without telling anyone the truth about what their ministry is costing them, and then leaves the profession in a condition of spiritual and emotional exhaustion that could have been interrupted if anyone had known.

I know this from the inside. I know what it is to walk into a Sunday service carrying weight from the week that I have told no one about, and to preach the words I believed and to feel the distance between what I was saying and what I was living. Not hypocrisy exactly — I believed it. But a kind of unsustained solitude that had become the default mode of my interior life. That default is not heroic. It is a slow withdrawal from the kind of connection that would have made me a better pastor and a more grounded human being.

Eugene Peterson, whose work shaped my understanding of pastoral ministry more than any other, wrote repeatedly about the pastor's need for friends who are not parishioners — people outside the pastoral relationship whose connection to you is not mediated by role or need or institutional expectation. [cite — confirm Peterson's specific treatment of this in *The Contemplative Pastor* or similar] The pastor who has only pastoral relationships has surrounded himself with people he must always, in some sense, perform for. He has no one who knows him without the title. And a man who is never known without the title eventually loses the ability to find the person underneath it.

That person is the one who can lead sustainably. The persona can lead for a while — often impressively, convincingly, long enough to build something substantial. But it runs on borrowed energy, and when the energy runs out, what is left is either collapse or a quiet, grinding diminishment that looks like leadership from the outside and feels like nothing much from the inside.

## Friends Who Are Not Parishioners

You are not called to carry this alone. You are called to lead well, and leading well requires honesty with at least a small circle of people about what it is actually costing you. A spiritual director who meets with you regularly and asks the questions you will not ask yourself. A peer pastor who carries the same kind of weight and will tell you when you are losing your way. A therapist who understands what ministry does to the interior life over time. The specific form matters less than the substance: someone who knows what you are actually carrying, not the performance you present on Sunday morning.

The peer network is the particular gift that the Pastors Connection Network was built to provide — not an organization of pastors performing success at each other, but a community of pastors telling the truth to each other. The difference matters enormously. Success performance is everywhere. Truth-telling is rare, and rare things have extraordinary value.

The loneliness of leadership is real. It is also, in significant part, a choice. The choice to remain alone with the weight is not protection and it is not dedication. It is, at its root, a form of pride — the belief that the need for companionship and accountability is a sign of inadequacy. The pastor who cannot be known is not protecting his congregation. He is protecting an image of himself. And the protection eventually becomes the thing that breaks him.

Psalm 22, the psalm of desolation that Jesus quoted from the cross, does not end in isolation. It moves — slowly, at great cost — from the cry of the forsaken to a community of witnesses: "For he has not despised or scorned the suffering of the afflicted one; he has not hidden his face from him but has listened to his cry for help" (Psalm 22:24). The voice that cried into silence was heard. The isolation was real, and it was not the final word.

It is not the final word for you either. But you have to be willing to say the thing out loud to someone who is actually in the room.

> Find the people who can hold what you are holding.

Find the people who can hold what you are holding. Not to fix it. To witness it. To stand with you in it long enough for the weight to be shared rather than performed.

That is often enough. And it is not as available as it should be, which is why the isolation continues — not because the company is absent, but because the asking for it requires the kind of courage that the role trains you to avoid.

The question is whether you will pay that cost, or whether you will wait until a larger one is due.

For a certain kind of marriage — and it is more common than anyone likes to admit — the children were the project. Not deliberately, not consciously, but functionally. The marriage organized itself around them: their schedules, their needs, their crises, their milestones. The couple was competent co-parents. What they were to each other beyond that had been deferred, for years, until the kids were launched.

And then the kids are launched. And the house is quiet. And the two people standing in it look at each other and realize they have been living with a stranger for the better part of a decade.

This is not a tragedy. But it is a reckoning.

## The Developmental Crisis Nobody Prepared For

The empty nest season arrives as a developmental crisis for couples who have used parenting as the primary container for the marriage. Without the shared project, the question that was never answered surfaces: Who are we to each other when we are not doing something together?

> Parenting together is not the same as being married. The empty house reveals the difference.

Genesis 2:24 describes the original covenant: "Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh." The word translated "hold fast" — dabaq in Hebrew — means to cling, to cleave, to remain in proximity by active intention. The text does not describe something automatic. It describes something that requires continuous, willed decision to maintain.

Children do not produce that cleaving. They can occupy the space where it would otherwise need to happen. The couple that has been dabaq through two decades of parenting will land in the empty house with something between them. The couple that has been parallel parenting in proximity will land there with very little.

**Parenting together is not the same as being married. The empty house reveals the difference.**

## What the Research and the Tradition Both Confirm

> This is not a failure of love. It is a failure of attention.

The pattern of marital satisfaction declining during the child-raising years and then either recovering or not in the empty nest is well-documented in longitudinal research on marriage [cite — confirm]. What is less well-documented, because it is harder to measure, is the particular texture of the recovery that happens in some marriages and not others.

The marriages that recover are not necessarily the ones that were happiest during the parenting years. They are the ones where the partners had maintained enough genuine interest in each other — enough curiosity, enough small investments of attention — that when the parenting project concluded, there was something to return to. Not a preserved version of the early marriage. Something new: the marriage of two people who have been through things together and are willing to discover who they have become.

The marriages that do not recover are typically the ones where the interest was allowed to atrophy entirely — where the partners became so functionally competent in their co-parenting roles that they stopped being curious about each other's interiors, stopped having conversations that were not about logistics, stopped growing in ways that included rather than excluded the other.

> Rediscovery is the right word, not reconstruction.

The Song of Songs carries within it the most striking portrait of this kind of sustained attention in the biblical canon. "Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave" (Song of Solomon 8:6). The jealousy described here is not possessiveness. It is the fierce refusal to be replaced by other concerns — including the very real and legitimate concerns of child-rearing. The seal upon the heart is a continuous, not incidental, claim.

## The Crisis, When It Comes

The crisis is not always dramatic. Sometimes it is just a creeping awareness — over weeks, then months — that there is no organic conversation anymore. That the kids were the subject, and now there is no subject. That the easy physical affection that used to come from proximity has faded because the proximity was always child-adjacent and now the child is not there.

I have sat with couples in this season who were not unhappy in any specific way and who could not articulate what was wrong. What was wrong was the absence of what had never been built — a marriage that existed independent of the parenting project. They had been so committed to doing right by their children that they had deferred doing right by each other for twenty years.

This is not a failure of love. It is a failure of attention. The love was real. The intention was good. What was missing was the sustained practice of treating the marriage as its own thing — not just the platform from which the parenting happened, but a relationship with its own interior life that required tending.

## The Counter-Position Worth Engaging

There is a parenting philosophy — and it has real theological resonance — that argues that the most important thing a couple can do for their children is to model a loving, sacrificial marriage. On this view, the investment in the marriage is itself the investment in the children, not a competing priority. This is true as far as it goes.

But the position can be, and often is, used in the other direction — to justify the marriage as primarily instrumental, primarily about what it produces in the children. If the marriage is good because it is good for the kids, then when the kids leave, the justification leaves with them. The couple is left without the habit of valuing the marriage for its own sake.

The covenantal theology of marriage in the Hebrew and Christian traditions resists this instrumentalization. Marriage in Genesis 2 precedes the children. The covenant of dabaq is made before the commandment to be fruitful and multiply. The sequence matters. The marriage is not the means to the family. The family is one of the things that grows from the marriage. When the children are launched, the marriage remains — not because it was successful at producing children, but because it was a covenant that precedes and outlasts that particular season of its expression.

## What the Empty Nest Actually Requires

Rediscovery is the right word, not reconstruction. The people in the empty house are not strangers who are starting from scratch. They are two people who have been through things together, who know each other at a depth no new relationship can offer, who have built something real even if they haven't always built it toward each other.

What the season requires is curiosity. Who is this person now, at fifty-two or fifty-eight or sixty-three? What are they interested in that I have not asked about? What have they become through the parenting years that I watched from a distance but never actually engaged with? This is not a technique. It is the basic posture of wanting to know someone — the posture that was presumably present at the beginning of the marriage and that, in the best cases, never fully left.

It also requires honesty about what got lost. Some couples in this season discover, with grief, that the emotional intimacy was sacrificed along the way — that the habit of talking about real things atrophied while they were managing logistics. Rebuilding it requires the courage to bring the real things back into the room. They are still there. They have just not been addressed in a while.

The grief is real and deserves acknowledgment. Something was lost — years of potential closeness that were spent on other things. The couple that pretends this loss doesn't exist, that jumps directly to the exciting possibilities of this new season, will find the grief surfacing anyway, usually in the form of conflict or withdrawal. Naming it is not defeat. It is the beginning of building something on honest ground rather than managed optimism.

## The Opportunity Hidden in the Disruption

Paul's description of marriage in Ephesians 5 — "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Ephesians 5:25) — is not primarily about the parenting years. It is about the whole of the covenant. The self-giving that it describes does not end when the children leave. It simply no longer has the same clear object and the same clear structure. The empty nest asks: what does this self-giving look like now, when the shared project has changed?

For some couples, the answer is a new shared project — ministry, service, a business, travel, the care of aging parents. The shared project was never the problem. The problem was when the shared project became the entire substance of the marriage. The couple who replaces child-rearing with a new project, without ever asking the deeper question of who they are to each other when no project is present, has not rebuilt the marriage. They have rescheduled the reckoning.

The deeper opportunity is to build the kind of marriage that the parenting years either established or deferred — the marriage of two people who are genuinely interested in each other's interior lives, who find each other worth knowing, who choose each other not because of the shared project but because of the person. That is not a guarantee that the empty house will feel like freedom rather than loss. It is a guarantee that the work you do in the parting is real.

## Three Questions for This Week

If your children left tomorrow — or if they already have — what would the marriage be about? What do you and your spouse genuinely share beyond co-parenting?

What is something about your spouse that you are currently curious about that you have not asked?

When did you last do something together that had nothing to do with the children, the house, or logistics — something you did because you enjoy each other's company?

**This week:** one date with no agenda beyond presence. Not a difficult conversation about the marriage. Not logistics dressed as quality time. Something you both actually enjoy, done together.

The couple that invests in the marriage during the parenting years — not instead of parenting well, but alongside it — arrives at the empty nest with something between them. The couple that defers that investment arrives at the same house asking what they deferred it for.

It is not too late to begin. In most cases, it is exactly on time. But it is not automatic. It is a choice, made deliberately, in the direction of the person standing across from you — the person who signed the same covenant you did, who has been through what you have been through, who is still there. Turn toward them. The rest follows from that.

It is possible to love someone deeply and look at them one morning and realize you do not know who this person is anymore. Not because they have been deceptive. Not because there was a dramatic rupture. But because ten or fifteen or twenty years have passed, and the person you married and the person sitting across the table from you have diverged in ways that feel significant.

Sometimes the change is growth — they have become something more than who they were, and the marriage is struggling to accommodate it. Sometimes it is regression — an old wound has reopened, an addiction has taken hold, a depression has altered the personality in ways that feel permanent. Sometimes it is gradual drift — two people becoming more themselves, and discovering that more-themselves are not as compatible as the twenty-five-year-old versions were.

The situation is real in all three forms. And it requires different responses depending on which one is actually happening.

## The Disorientation Named Honestly

> You cannot reconnect with the person you thought you married. You can only connect with the person who is actually there.

The Psalms have a word for the disorientation of finding that the ground has shifted without warning. Psalm 46:2 describes the mountains being cast into the sea — not as catastrophe only, but as the condition under which faith is still possible. "Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way." The *therefore* is important. The writer is not describing the absence of the disruption. They are describing the presence of a ground that holds even when the recognizable terrain does not.

The person you no longer recognize is still in a covenant with you. That covenant does not require you to pretend the change is not happening. It does require you to bring the change into honest engagement rather than quiet resignation.

**You cannot reconnect with the person you thought you married. You can only connect with the person who is actually there.**

I have sat with people who were grieving their spouse while their spouse was still alive. Not because of betrayal, but because illness — physical or psychological — had altered someone so fundamentally that the person they had built their life around was, in some real sense, gone. They were still present. But they were different. And the grief of that is its own category, with no clean name and very few people who can hold it without immediately trying to fix it.

There is also the subtler version — the one that does not announce itself as grief. The spouse whose political convictions have shifted so dramatically that shared conversation is strained. The partner whose faith has dissolved or intensified to the point where the worldview that once connected them no longer does. The person who survived something and came out the other side as someone neither of them fully knows yet.

> The covenant's task is not to arrest that development. It is to remain in relationship across it.

In all of these: the relationship to the changed person requires a renegotiation that most couples do not know how to initiate.

## The Historical Pattern of People Who Changed

The New Testament is populated by people whose transformation was, from the outside, disorienting. Peter, the fisherman who denied Jesus three times, becomes the preacher of Pentecost. Paul, who had been Saul, who had supervised murders, arrives in Damascus transformed and spends years rebuilding trust with people who had every reason to remain terrified of him. The early church's constant struggle was to integrate people whose conversions had genuinely altered them — to receive transformation rather than simply demanding continuity.

2 Corinthians 5:17 says "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." The Greek carries an urgency: *kainē ktisis* — not a modified version of the old, but something genuinely new. That newness was disorienting to the communities receiving transformed people. The former persecutor is now your brother. The former idol-worshipper has brought the old practices to repentance. The new creation does not simply occupy the old social position.

> Pastoral care that cannot tell the difference between personal transformation and genuine harm — and that counsels endurance in both cases — is not faithfulness. It is negligence dressed as theology.

In marriage, transformation presents the same challenge in an intimate register. The converted spouse is not the same person their unbelieving partner married. The spouse who finally gets sober after ten years of alcoholism is genuinely different from the person who was drinking. The spouse who survives cancer is not simply restored to their previous self. Change, even the best kind, requires a renegotiation of the relationship. That renegotiation is not a threat to the covenant. It is the covenant being worked out across the actual arc of two human lives.

## The Counter-Position Worth Hearing

Some pastoral traditions argue that the emphasis should fall not on adjusting to who your spouse has become but on holding them to who they committed to be — that the covenant establishes an identity that is not purely subject to individual evolution, that the marriage itself is a formative institution that shapes both people toward a shared identity rather than simply accommodating divergent ones.

There is something real in this. Marriage is not only a response to who the other person is — it is also a commitment that helps form who they are becoming. The covenant has a shaping function, not just a relational one. Two people who take their covenant seriously will be changed by it in ways that tend toward convergence rather than divergence, because they are both oriented toward something larger than their individual self-realization.

But the argument breaks down when it is used to deny the reality of genuine change — when it requires a spouse to relate to who their partner was rather than who they are, or when it treats the legitimate evolution of a person over decades as a violation of the covenant's terms. The covenant was not made with a static person. It was made with a human being who would grow, suffer, be altered by what they survived, and arrive at fifty or sixty as genuinely different from the person at twenty-five.

The covenant's task is not to arrest that development. It is to remain in relationship across it.

## Ruth's Covenant with a Changed Naomi

Ruth 1:16 — "where you go, I will go" — is a declaration of covenant commitment made in circumstances where the future is genuinely unknown. Naomi is not the same woman she was in Bethlehem. She has buried her husband and both sons. She has described herself, in verse 20, as *Mara* — bitter. "I went away full, and the Lord has brought me back empty." She is telling Ruth: do not commit to me as I once was. Commit to what is left.

Ruth's declaration is not romantic idealism. It is eyes-open covenantal faithfulness. She is committing to follow a grief-altered, self-described bitter woman into an uncertain future. She does not require Naomi to return to her previous self before she renews the bond. She commits to the Naomi who is actually there.

That is the model for a marriage in which one person has changed. Not the pretense that the change did not happen. Not the demand that the changed person return to who they were. The decision to recommit — with full acknowledgment of who they have become — to the person who is actually there.

## The Honest Question That Has to Be Asked

There is also the version of this question that has to be asked in some situations: has the change produced something that is genuinely harmful? Addiction is not a character evolution. Abuse is not growth. There are versions of "you are not who I married" that are not simply about incompatibility but about danger — and pastoral wisdom names that difference rather than flattening it under the language of covenant endurance.

A woman who says "I don't recognize my husband anymore" because he has become violent is not facing a growth gap that requires better curiosity. She is facing a safety crisis that requires direct intervention. Pastoral care that cannot tell the difference between personal transformation and genuine harm — and that counsels endurance in both cases — is not faithfulness. It is negligence dressed as theology.

The covenant does not require a person to remain in proximity to their own destruction. The same God who spoke the covenant at Sinai also built provisions for protection, for justice, for the vindication of the vulnerable, into the same law.

## The Work of Re-Learning

What is required, in the cases that are not about danger, is something that is at once very simple and very hard: curiosity without nostalgia. The person in front of you is not who you married. That is not only a loss — it may also be an invitation. Who are they now? What do they need that the person they were at thirty did not need? What have they become through the years you have been together that you have not actually engaged with?

This is not a technique. It is the basic posture of wanting to know someone — of remaining genuinely interested in the actual person rather than the remembered version of them.

## Three Questions for This Week

What specifically is different about your spouse from who they were when you married? Is that change growth, regression, or something more neutral?

Have you grieved what has changed — honestly, not just in private — and has your spouse been invited to grieve alongside you?

Are you relating to the person they actually are now, or to the person you expected them to remain?

**This week:** one conversation that begins with genuine curiosity about who your spouse currently is. Not who they were. Not who you need them to be. Who they are.

Every long marriage contains this reckoning at some point. The people who made it to fifty years together did not do so because they married the right person and the person stayed right. They did so because they kept choosing the actual person — again and again, across all the versions — rather than the version they had first chosen.

That is what covenant looks like over a life. Not the preservation of a fixed portrait. The ongoing choice of the living person.

The United States has the highest maternal mortality rate among wealthy nations. By a significant margin. A woman in America is more than twice as likely to die from a pregnancy-related cause as a woman in Canada, more than three times as likely as a woman in Sweden [cite — confirm]. Black women in America die from pregnancy-related causes at roughly three times the rate of white women — a disparity that persists even when controlling for income and education [cite — confirm]. These deaths are not medical mysteries. They are, in substantial measure, preventable. They are the consequence of a healthcare system that has systematically underinvested in maternal care, that has closed labor and delivery units in rural hospitals, that provides inadequate prenatal care to low-income women, and that produces outcomes that track along racial and economic lines with striking consistency.

The American church that calls itself pro-life has been largely silent about this.

Not totally silent. Not every congregation. Not every pastor. But as a matter of broad ecclesial culture — the institutions, the publications, the advocacy organizations, the political energy that the American evangelical pro-life movement has generated and sustained for fifty years — the silence about maternal mortality is glaring.

## The Asymmetry at the Center of the Movement

The question is why. And the answer to that question is a diagnosis.

> It has achieved political coherence at the cost of theological coherence.

---

## What the Law and the Prophets Already Knew

The pro-life movement as it has functioned in American evangelical culture has been organized, almost entirely, around the moment of abortion — the legal right to end a pregnancy. This focus has generated enormous political energy, produced legal changes of historic magnitude, and constituted the primary political identity of a large portion of American evangelical Christianity for two generations. Whatever one believes about the underlying questions, the movement's capacity for sustained political engagement has been remarkable.

But the human life at the center of that engagement has a mother. And that mother's life, in the framework that has dominated the American pro-life movement, has consistently received less attention than the life she carries. This is not a minor theological inconsistency. It is a fundamental asymmetry that reveals the actual operating logic of the movement — an operating logic that is more coherent as a political strategy than as a consistent theology of human life.

A theology of human life that treats the unborn with absolute moral seriousness while treating maternal mortality as a policy question beyond the church's concern has not achieved theological consistency. It has achieved political coherence at the cost of theological coherence. The life of the mother is as sacred as the life of the child. Both bear the image of God. Both matter in the same way, for the same reason. A pro-life commitment that is not also a maternal care commitment has made a selection among lives that the theology of the imago Dei does not permit.

## The Racial Disparity as Theological Scandal

---

The biblical tradition does not make this selection.

## The Counter-Argument and Where It Fails

The law of Moses is distinctive in the ancient Near Eastern context for the specific protections it extends to pregnant women and to mothers. Exodus 21:22-25, whatever its specific application in debates about fetal life, establishes that harm to a pregnant woman carries consequences — the law is attentive to her vulnerability in ways that other ancient legal codes are not. The Psalms include multiple images of God as the one who formed the person in the mother's womb, who was present to the created life from before birth — but those texts do not exist in isolation from the broader tradition that also insists on care for the widow, the orphan, and the vulnerable person who has no one to advocate for her.

> The vulnerability is real. The absence of advocacy is real. The theological problem is real.

The widow in the New Testament is the paradigmatic figure of vulnerability — the person without protection in the social order, without income, without status, dependent on the decency of the community for her survival. The church's care for widows is described in Acts 6, organized and structured and taken seriously enough that the appointment of deacons was organized specifically to ensure it was being done adequately. Paul's instruction to Timothy about widows (1 Timothy 5) is detailed and specific, addressing the different circumstances of widows in ways that demonstrate the tradition's serious engagement with the reality of vulnerable women.

## What a Fuller Pro-Life Witness Would Require

A church that is attentive to that tradition and not attentive to the death of women in childbirth has failed to read its own material carefully.

---

The racial dimension is not separable from the theological one.

## The Decision the Church Has Not Yet Made

That Black women in America die from pregnancy-related causes at three times the rate of white women is not a coincidence. It is the outcome of specific systems — the legacy of a medical culture that, until very recently, treated the pain reports of Black women as less credible than those of white women [cite — confirm]; the disproportionate closure of labor and delivery units in communities of color where hospital economics made the units unprofitable; the inadequacy of prenatal care access in communities where poverty and insurance gaps intersect; the chronic stress of living in a society where your racial identity marks you for differential treatment in every institutional context you move through.

These are not mysteries. They are outcomes that have been studied, documented, and named. They are the application of the same logic that the prophets condemned — the logic of the social order that assigns value to human beings according to their proximity to power, their economic productivity, their social standing. The prophet Amos did not catalog abstract injustices. He named specific economic and legal practices that produced specific suffering for specific people (Amos 2:6-7, Amos 8:4-6). The contemporary prophetic tradition owes the same specificity.

> Both of them bear God's image. Both of them matter.

The church that professes concern for human life from conception and says nothing about the racial disparity in maternal mortality has made a choice about whose life matters enough to generate its energy. That choice requires theological justification that I have not seen provided.

---

The counter-argument deserves a direct hearing.

The argument is this: the unborn child has no political voice, no capacity to advocate, no access to any system of protection except the legal one. The pregnant woman is a person with full legal personhood, with the capacity to vote, to organize, to advocate for her own care. The urgency of protecting the unborn is therefore distinctive in a way that makes the comparative energy allocation defensible: the most vulnerable, those with no voice at all, deserve the most concentrated advocacy.

There is something to this argument. The relative vulnerability of the person who cannot speak at all is a real moral consideration. Advocacy for those with no voice is a genuine calling, and the tradition that insists on it is reading its Scripture.

But the argument does not survive examination of the actual maternal mortality data, because the women who are dying in childbirth are not, in most cases, dying because they lack political voice in the abstract. They are dying because the specific systems that serve them — the rural hospital that closed its labor and delivery unit, the insurance plan that does not cover adequate prenatal care, the medical provider whose implicit bias shaped his clinical judgment — are failing them. And the political voice they theoretically possess has not produced adequate correction of these systems, because the political coalition most energetically organized around the sanctity of human life has not organized around these specific failures.

The vulnerability is real. The absence of advocacy is real. The theological problem is real.

---

What would a genuinely comprehensive pro-life engagement with maternal mortality look like?

It would involve the same kind of sustained public advocacy that the movement has generated around abortion law. It would name specific policy failures — the Medicaid coverage gaps that leave low-income pregnant women without prenatal care, the rural hospital closures that have eliminated labor and delivery capacity in underserved communities, the inadequacy of postpartum care that allows preventable deaths in the weeks after delivery.

It would involve direct engagement with the racial disparity — not as an incidental detail but as a central moral scandal. The fact that where you live and what you look like determines whether you survive childbirth is not a secondary concern. It is a justice indictment that the biblical tradition is equipped to name and that the church, if it is serious about the imago Dei, must name.

It would involve the local congregation asking: what do the pregnant women in our community need, and are we providing it? Not the middle-class pregnant women whose insurance is adequate and whose prenatal care is excellent. The women without insurance, the undocumented women who fear that seeking care will generate consequences, the women in the county where the hospital closed its birthing unit four years ago.

---

I have preached the sanctity of human life. I believe it. The unborn child matters. That conviction is not the problem.

The problem is what the conviction does not include — the lives it does not name, the deaths it does not mourn, the systems it does not challenge because challenging them would require a political energy directed at targets other than the ones the movement has chosen.

Pro-life is a claim about which lives matter. The church that makes that claim is accountable for its full application. Not its convenient application. Its full one.

The woman who dies in childbirth matters. Her death is not a policy footnote. It is a theological indictment of every framework that named her child's life as sacred and fell silent about her own.

Both of them bear God's image. Both of them matter.

The church that knows this and does not say it has not yet decided to be pro-life in the fullest sense.

That decision is still available. Make it.

Ask the average pastor how his church is doing, and he will tell you a number. Attendance, usually. Sometimes giving. Sometimes both, in a ratio that signals whether things are moving in the right direction. These are the metrics the denomination wants, the metrics that appear on the annual report, the metrics that determine whether a pastor is perceived as effective. They are also, largely, the wrong metrics.

Not because they do not matter. They do — an empty room is a real problem, and a church that cannot fund its operations is a church in genuine crisis. But attendance and giving are lag indicators. They tell you what happened, not what is happening. They measure the output of a system whose real activity is largely invisible to any spreadsheet.

The church growth movement that reshaped American evangelicalism in the latter half of the twentieth century made a contribution that was genuine and a distortion that was significant. The genuine contribution was the insistence that the gospel ought to reach people and that failing to reach people should be examined rather than excused. The distortion was the reduction of "reaching people" to a headcount, and the consequent elevation of attendance as the primary measure of faithfulness. The pastor who filled seats was the pastor who was succeeding. The pastor whose seats were not filling was the pastor who had something to learn. This framework is so embedded in the average pastor's self-evaluation that it operates unconsciously — the Sunday morning number is not just a data point. It is a verdict on the week.

That verdict measures the wrong things.

## The Verdict the Numbers Cannot Render

The first question a pastor ought to be able to answer honestly is this: are people in this congregation becoming more like Jesus? Not more committed to the church's programs. Not more knowledgeable about the Bible's content — though that matters too. More like Christ — more generous with their material resources, more patient in conflict, more willing to extend mercy to people who have not earned it, more honest about their own failures. This is formation. It is the stated purpose of the church's existence — "to equip his people for works of service, so that the body of Christ may be built up until we all reach unity in the faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God and become mature, attaining to the whole measure of the fullness of Christ" (Ephesians 4:12-13).

> They measure the output of a system whose real activity is largely invisible to any spreadsheet.

Formation is almost never measured, because it is very difficult to measure, and the difficulty is not a reason to stop asking. The pastor who wants to assess his congregation's formation does not need a survey instrument. He needs to know his congregation well enough to answer the question from direct observation — whether the people he has been preaching to for five years treat their money differently, handle conflict differently, respond to suffering differently than they did when they arrived. If he does not know his people well enough to answer that question, the attendance numbers are irrelevant. He does not actually know how his church is doing.

## Formation as the First Measure

A second honest question is whether the people in this congregation actually know each other. Not know of each other. Know each other — their names, their children, their anxieties, the specific weight they carry that is not visible on a Sunday morning. The early church in Jerusalem is described in Acts 2:44-45 as a community that held goods in common and distributed to anyone who had need. That kind of generosity requires a level of mutual knowledge that is not produced by sitting in the same room once a week. It requires community that has gone deeper than attendance.

## Whether the People Actually Know Each Other

Acts 2:42 describes the community as devoted to four things: the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer. The fellowship — koinonia — is not a program. It is a quality of mutual life that makes it impossible for someone to have a need that goes unmet because no one knows about it. The church that reports healthy attendance but where the families who are struggling keep their struggles private, where the marriages in crisis are managing their presentation, where the person in financial collapse is tithing because they are terrified to admit the truth — that church has numbers but not koinonia. It has an audience, not a community.

## The Question of Being Sent

A third question is harder: are people being sent from this congregation into the world with a genuine sense of vocation? The church that produces spiritually formed, deeply connected members who stay inside the church's walls and serve only its programs has not completed its mission. The measure of a healthy church is not only what happens inside its gathering, but what its people carry into their work, their neighborhoods, their families, their civic lives.

> It has an audience, not a community.

The New Testament does not describe the church as an end in itself. The gathering in Acts 2 is immediately followed by the scattering in Acts 8 — the persecution that sends believers throughout Judea and Samaria and, in Luke's framing, begins the fulfillment of the Great Commission. The pattern is: gather, be formed, be sent. The church that gathers and forms but does not send has stopped at the second movement of a three-movement piece. It is producing Christians who are theologically informed and relationally connected but whose formation never makes contact with the world the gospel is sent to.

## The Honest Case for the Numbers

The steel-man of the numbers-driven approach is real and should be heard. Without adequate attendance, no pastor long remains to form anyone. Without adequate giving, programs that serve the vulnerable cannot be sustained. Institutional viability is not nothing — it is a precondition for everything else. The church that is so focused on formation and fellowship that it fails to reach anyone new has become a private club with good theology. Growth matters. Mission matters. The congregation that has stopped caring whether anyone outside its current membership encounters the gospel has lost something essential.

This is true. And it does not refute the argument being made here. The question is not whether a church should want to grow. The question is whether the growth metrics are measuring growth in the right things. A congregation that grows in size while declining in generosity, in mutual accountability, in its engagement with the world outside its walls — that congregation is not growing in any sense that the New Testament would recognize. A congregation that grows in formation, deepens in genuine community, and increases in the number of its members who are living out their faith in their neighborhoods and workplaces — that congregation may or may not be growing in attendance, but it is growing in the things that matter.

The pastor who reports good numbers to his board while privately knowing that his congregation is unchanged, unformed, and barely acquainted with each other is reporting on the wrong things. He is also, likely, carrying a private weight that the numbers cannot address — because the numbers look right and something still feels wrong, and he cannot say what it is to people who are reading the spreadsheet.

What feels wrong is that the metrics he is using cannot see what he is actually responsible for.

The metrics the New Testament offers for congregational health are qualitative, relational, and slow to develop. Formation takes years. Community takes sustained investment. Vocation develops through the long process of integrating faith with work and life. None of these are measurable in the way that Sunday attendance is measurable, and none of them will appear on the annual report.

But they are what the church is for.

## Beginning the Conversation With a Story

Name what you are measuring. Then ask whether those measurements are capturing the right thing. If they are not, change the measurements first — and be willing to defend to your board why the new measurements matter, which requires being able to articulate what the church is actually for.

That conversation, between a pastor and his governing board, about what success actually means, is one of the most important conversations most churches have never had.

> The shepherd who knows his sheep by name.

It is not too late to have it.

Here is what that conversation might begin with. Not "our attendance is up seven percent" and not "our attendance is down." Begin with a story. Tell the board about a specific person in the congregation who is different this year than they were a year ago — who is more generous, who is more honest, who handled a crisis differently, who reached out to a neighbor in a way they would not have done before. That story is a data point. It is a different kind of data point than a headcount, but it is evidence of the same thing the headcount is supposed to measure: whether the gospel is doing anything real.

Then ask the board to bring their own stories. The board member who only knows how to read the spreadsheet will struggle with this. Good. That struggle is the beginning of the conversation the board actually needs to have about what it is governing and why.

The church is not a business. The board that governs it as though it were a business — measuring inputs and outputs, tracking attendance as a performance indicator, optimizing the organization for growth — is applying a framework to the thing that the thing was not designed to fit. The church is an organism. Organisms are measured by their health, not their size. Health is not always visible from the outside. It requires the kind of sustained, inside knowledge that comes from genuine pastoral attention.

That is what the pastor is for. Not the attendance counter. The shepherd who knows his sheep by name.

*He has shown you, O mortal, what is good. And what does the Lord require of you? To act justly and to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God.*

We have printed this on coffee mugs. We have put it in church lobbies in hand-lettered calligraphy. We have used it as a caption for photographs of mission trips. And in doing all of that, we have managed to receive the most demanding verse in the prophetic canon as a kind of spiritual aesthetic — something beautiful to aspire toward when we are feeling generous, something that captures the spirit of what we are trying to do, something that sits nicely in the lobby while the rest of the building operates on entirely different terms.

## The Verse Set Inside a Lawsuit

The text is not interested in being a caption. It was not written for lobbies. It was written in the context of a lawsuit.

---

> He is filing a complaint.

Stand Micah 6 in its full context and the aesthetic reading becomes impossible.
