Naming those templates in the room that day did not resolve the pattern immediately. But it changed the question. They stopped asking "why are you doing this to me" and started asking "what are we each bringing to this."

> They stopped asking "why are you doing this to me" and started asking "what are we each bringing to this."

That is what the work of examining the template makes possible.

## Three Questions for This Week

What is one pattern in your marriage that you recognize from your parents' marriage — something you either replicated or overcorrected for?

What did you conclude about yourself, about love, or about marriage from what you watched? Are those conclusions still running, unchallenged, in your current relationship?

Have you ever talked with your spouse about both of your families of origin — not to assign blame, but to understand the templates each of you brought into the marriage?

**This week:** one conversation with your spouse about what each of your families of origin modeled. No blame, no defensiveness — just curiosity about the templates you are both running from.

Ezekiel's corrective stands: the son does not have to carry the father's iniquity. But the son who has never looked at the father's iniquity is almost certainly carrying it anyway.

See it clearly. Name it honestly. Then decide — deliberately, consciously, with your spouse — what you are choosing instead.

That is what renewal of the mind looks like in a marriage. Not the erasure of what was formed. The decision about what to keep.

The mission trip model that most American churches inherited was built on a set of assumptions so deep they were almost invisible: that the primary resource in the mission equation flows from here to there, that the expertise originates in the West and is received abroad, that the goal is to plant something that looks, when the team flies home, like a smaller version of what they left. Underneath all of it was a single organizing premise: we have what they need.

That premise is not evil. It is not even entirely wrong. American churches have resources — financial, educational, infrastructural — that many churches in the Global South still lack. The problem is not that the resources flow. The problem is the posture that comes with them. And that posture, when it goes unexamined, produces exactly the opposite of partnership.

> we have what they need.

Genuine partnership with a national pastor looks different from what most American churches practice. Understanding how different requires a brief honest account of the history that shaped the current arrangement.

## The Inheritance of Empire

The modern Western missionary movement — from William Carey's arrival in India in 1793 through the great expansion of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries [cite — confirm] — carried the gospel with genuine faithfulness to places where it had not arrived before. It also carried the assumptions of empire. The missionary was usually white, educated, and situated within colonial administrative structures that his very presence reinforced. He built institutions — schools, hospitals, churches — modeled on their Western equivalents. He trained indigenous leaders in Western modes of thought and organization. In many cases, he functioned as an agent of cultural disruption that went far beyond the theological content of what he proclaimed. The gospel and the colonizer traveled on the same ships. The church that exists today in much of Africa, Asia, and Latin America carries both inheritances.

This is not a reason to regret the missionary movement entire. The global church that now constitutes the majority of Christianity worldwide [cite — confirm] exists partly because of that movement. But it is a reason to ask, with genuine humility, what assumptions the American church still carries into its partnership arrangements — and what those assumptions cost the people on the other side of them.

## The Pastor Who Corrected Me

The national pastor I am thinking of — and I am thinking of a real relationship, though I will not name him — leads a congregation in a context I do not understand from the inside. He speaks languages I do not speak. He navigates political pressures I have never faced. He shepherds people through losses that my suburban congregation in Michigan will, in most cases, not experience. He understands the theological tradition his community emerged from — the ways the gospel was preached to his people, the ways it was used against them, the ways they have reshaped it to speak into their own life — with a depth and nuance I cannot access from the outside.

When I arrived in his world and began talking about what we could do together, the first thing he did — graciously, without embarrassment — was explain to me that I had misunderstood what his community needed. The project I had imagined would not serve his congregation. The structure I had proposed replicated a pattern he had spent years trying to move away from. He was not ungrateful. He was honest. And in his honesty was the beginning of what actual partnership requires.

## Listening Before Proposing

Actual partnership begins with listening rather than proposing. It requires a willingness to spend a significant amount of time understanding the context — the history, the cultural dynamics, the theological tradition, the specific challenges the pastor is navigating — before offering anything. Not because Western resources and perspectives have nothing to contribute. Because the pattern in which Western resources arrive with Western agendas and produce Western-shaped outcomes, regardless of what the receiving community actually needs, has been documented too thoroughly to ignore [cite — confirm].

The listening is not simply strategic — a smarter approach to accomplishing the same goal. It is theological. The body of Christ is not a body in which one part provides and the other parts receive. Paul's description in 1 Corinthians 12 is of mutual dependence, in which the parts that appear less honorable are actually indispensable (1 Corinthians 12:22–23). The American church that arrives in a Global South context with the posture of a provider has already decided that it is the stronger member — has already arranged the relationship in a way that contradicts the ecclesiology it claims to hold.

> The listening is not simply strategic — a smarter approach to accomplishing the same goal. It is theological.

## What Genuine Partnership Requires

What does genuine partnership require in practice?

It requires a long relationship before significant resource transfer. The short-term mission trip model — two weeks in country, a project completed, a check written, and home — is almost structurally incapable of producing genuine partnership. Partnership requires the kind of knowledge that only develops over time: knowing the pastor's theological commitments, his community's history, what has been tried before and failed, what would be received as support and what would be received as intrusion. A single visit does not produce this knowledge. A decade of correspondence and mutual accountability might begin to.

It requires accountability structures that flow in both directions. Most Western partnership arrangements involve accountability from the national pastor to the Western donor — reports submitted, photos provided, outcomes documented. Genuine partnership inverts and equalizes this: the Western church is also accountable to the national pastor, who has the standing to challenge the assumptions the Western partner brings. This is uncomfortable for institutions accustomed to holding the financial power. It is theologically necessary.

It requires genuine deference on questions of contextualization. The national pastor knows how the gospel should be proclaimed and embodied in his context with a depth of knowledge the Western partner cannot match. When those two perspectives conflict — when the Western partner thinks the church should look or sound different than it does — the burden of proof is on the outside perspective, not the inside one. The Incarnation argues for this: God did not bring a universal model into the world. God entered a particular language, a particular culture, a particular body. Contextual faithfulness is not a compromise of the gospel. It is the mode in which the gospel has always arrived.

There is a real counter-concern here. The argument for genuine cross-cultural accountability includes the observation that theological error can be embedded in contextual practice in ways that are difficult to see from inside the context. Some partnerships have sent resources to national pastors who held theological positions the Western church would have challenged if it had known about them. Deference is not the same as abdication. The partnership involves genuine mutual theological accountability — and that requires the Western partner to have done enough theological work to have a real position, held with real conviction, not just the posture of endless openness.

But the imbalance in most existing partnerships runs heavily in the direction of Western assumption rather than Western deference. The correction needed is not more Western oversight. It is more genuine listening — and the discipline of letting the national pastor's knowledge of his context override the Western partner's categories for understanding it.

## Receiving More Than We Bring

The PCN network has given me access to pastors around the world who are leading faithfully in contexts I would not understand without them. The most important thing those relationships have given me is not the satisfaction of having contributed something. It is the correction of my assumptions about what the global church looks like and what it needs. I arrived thinking I was bringing something. I received something more.

That is what genuine partnership produces. Not a better-run mission trip. A rearranged understanding of who is rich and who is poor in the economy of the kingdom — which turns out to run differently than the economy I was formed in.

The Macedonian churches in 2 Corinthians 8 gave "beyond their ability" (v. 3) to support the Jerusalem collection — churches that were themselves in "extreme poverty" (v. 2). Paul describes their giving not as charity toward the worse-off but as a participation in grace. The categories of who gives and who receives are scrambled in the kingdom economy. The American church that arrives in the Global South assuming it knows which category it occupies has not yet understood this.

The national pastor who told me I had misunderstood what his community needed was not refusing partnership. He was inviting me into one. The real kind — the kind in which I came home changed, not just the kind in which the project got done.

> He was inviting me into one.

Those are not the same thing. Partnership worth the name produces the first. The second is easier to report and impossible to sustain.

What I brought home from that conversation — and from the years of relationship that followed — is a different understanding of what the global church is. It is not a collection of mission fields organized around Western sending churches. It is a body. Paul's body metaphor in 1 Corinthians 12 is not primarily about the local congregation. It is about the whole — the community of people in every nation who have been incorporated into Christ. That body has parts that are suffering, parts that are leading, parts that are carrying wisdom the Western church desperately needs, and parts that have material resources the Global South can use. The question is not who gives and who receives. The question is whether the arrangement is actually mutual.

Genuine partnership requires the Western church to be willing to be the learner more often than it is accustomed to. The churches in parts of the world where Christianity is growing fastest are growing in contexts of persecution, poverty, and political marginalization — contexts in which faith is not a leisure activity but a survival practice, in which the promises of the gospel about the last being first and the mourning being comforted are not inspiring aspirations but necessary lifelines. Those churches understand things about the gospel that the comfortable Western church does not. The partnership that flows only in the direction of Western resources to Global South projects is wasting the most important resource the Global South has to offer.

## The Whole Body Before the Throne

The theological correction runs through Revelation 7:9 — the vision of the great multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language standing before the throne. That is the church. Not the Western church with a missions budget, distributing its resources to the parts that need them. The whole body, every part necessary, every part honored, every part contributing what the others cannot provide without it. The partnership that approximates that vision requires the death of the premise that the primary resource flows from here to there. It does not. The kingdom is richer than that. The partners we are not listening to are carrying things we have not yet received.

That is what genuine partnership actually looks like. It is not a project model with a recipient. It is a relationship with a teacher. The distinction changes everything about how you show up.

The congregation I stood before had people who despised each other's politics. Not quietly, the way polite people manage these things — but openly, with the specific contempt that comes from years of algorithm-fed outrage. They were in the same pews. They took communion from the same table. And after the service, some of them could barely bring themselves to shake hands.

I am not describing a church that failed. I am describing almost every church in America right now.

> I am describing almost every church in America right now.

The political division in the American church is real, and it is deep, and it did not arrive from nowhere. It arrived from a decades-long drift in which the church allowed its primary identity categories to be supplied by the political culture rather than by the theological tradition. When Christians are sorted by political affiliation more reliably than by theological conviction — when exit polling shows that church attendance predicts voting behavior more consistently than doctrinal confession does [cite — confirm] — the church has a deeper problem than its policy disagreements. It has allowed itself to be colonized by a foreign framework for what matters most.

## The Cost of Careful Neutrality

The standard pastoral advice when this topic comes up is to avoid politics from the pulpit, to stay in the safe center, to speak in broad enough terms that no one feels targeted. I understand the impulse. I have felt it. But that posture has a cost that pastors rarely name: it trains the congregation to believe the Gospel is compatible with any political allegiance, that following Jesus requires no specific reordering of loyalties, that the Kingdom of God is a spiritual reality with no purchase on Monday morning.

The congregation that hears that for long enough will eventually organize its life around something else. And in this cultural moment, that something else is politics.

Here is the harder truth: the politically divided congregation is often a symptom of Gospel-thin preaching, not a management problem to be handled with careful neutrality. The pastor who has never preached the Sermon on the Mount to its actual economic edge. Who has never asked the congregation to examine their spending against the parable of the rich young ruler. Who preaches eternal salvation every week but rarely asks what it would look like to live, right now, as if the Kingdom of God is real and present and making claims on the household budget and the community's obligations to the poor.

That pastor has not avoided politics. He has chosen a politics — the politics of the status quo — by declining to disturb it.

> That pastor has not avoided politics. He has chosen a politics — the politics of the status quo — by declining to disturb it.

This is not a comfortable thing to say, and I include myself in the indictment. There have been seasons of my ministry when I softened the political edges of the Gospel to keep the peace — when I knew the text demanded more than I was willing to preach. That is not neutrality. It is cowardice dressed in pastoral language.

## A Lord Who Relativizes Every Allegiance

The Gospel is not politically neutral. This needs to be said carefully, because it can be misused in both directions. The Kingdom of God is not the Democratic Party platform, and it is not the Republican Party platform, and the pastor who identifies it with either has committed theological error of a serious kind. But the Kingdom of God is also not content to leave the political order undisturbed. It is, from its first announcement by Jesus in Luke 4 — good news to the poor, release to the captives, recovery of sight to the blind, liberation for the oppressed — a declaration that the existing arrangement is subject to revision by the incoming reign of God.

The first-century listeners who heard that announcement understood immediately that it was political. The authorities who crucified Jesus understood it was political. The early church that proclaimed Jesus as Lord — a title that belonged, in Roman imperial theology, to Caesar — understood it was political. The claim was not that Christianity was one political option among others. The claim was that there is a King whose rule supersedes every earthly political claim and whose character defines justice in ways that earthly powers may conform to or resist, but cannot supersede.

This is the framework. Not a party. Not a platform. A Lord whose kingship relativizes every other claim to ultimate loyalty.

The church that preaches this clearly will frustrate people on both sides. That is, historically speaking, a reliable sign of faithfulness. It frustrated Herod and it frustrated the Pharisees. It frustrated the Roman authorities and the Jewish establishment simultaneously, which is one of the more remarkable things about Jesus's ministry and a reasonable benchmark for whether the contemporary church is actually preaching him.

> The church that preaches this clearly will frustrate people on both sides.

---

## Preaching the Whole Counsel Without Flinching

What this requires in practice is not the avoidance of political topics but the consistent proclamation of what Scripture actually says about power, about the poor, about the neighbor, about the stranger, about the use of wealth — and the willingness to let those texts land where they land, regardless of who is sitting in the room.

A congregation that has heard the Sermon on the Mount preached straight for five consecutive years will not agree on every policy question, but it will have a common framework that transcends party. They will know that the blessed are the poor in spirit, not the culturally powerful. That the merciful receive mercy. That those who hunger and thirst for justice — not merely personal righteousness but the social ordering that reflects God's character — will be satisfied. They will have absorbed a vision of the human community that is simply incompatible with contempt, with indifference to the vulnerable, with the logic of the strong having no obligation to the weak.

That framework is the work. Building it is slower than conflict management. It requires preaching the uncomfortable texts rather than the confirming ones. It requires the kind of consistency that does not let either side off the hook — the texts that make conservatives uncomfortable and the texts that make progressives uncomfortable, in the same year, without flinching at either.

Some practical notes. The pastor who addresses only the justice texts that challenge the right and never the identity texts that challenge the left has taken a side, whatever his intentions. The pastor who challenges wealth from the pulpit but never addresses the breakdown of the family has taken a side. The credibility of prophetic preaching depends on its consistency — on the congregation's lived experience that the pastor is not a partisan who invokes Scripture selectively, but a preacher who actually believes the whole counsel of God has something to say to everyone.

## The People You Will Lose

You will lose some people. Let me be honest about that.

Some people have fused their political identity so completely with their spiritual identity that any prophetic challenge to one feels like an assault on the other. They have built a coherent worldview in which the party they support is the faithful party and the party they oppose is the apostate one, and they have recruited sufficient Scripture to defend the coherent worldview without much difficulty because Scripture can be recruited to almost anything if you work at it. Preaching the Kingdom seriously to such a person does not feel like a return to Scripture. It feels like the pastor taking the other side.

You cannot pastor that out of them in a single series. Sometimes you preach the text, they experience it as partisan, and they leave. That is painful. It is also not a failure of your leadership. It is the normal cost of preaching the Kingdom in a nation that wants a chaplain.

The question is not whether you will lose people by preaching the whole Gospel. You will. The question is what you are building with the people who stay. A congregation formed on the steady proclamation of the Kingdom — who have had their categories stretched by sustained engagement with what Jesus actually taught — that congregation is building something. Not agreement on every policy question. But a common center that is stronger than their differences.

---

## The Unity That Preaching Cannot Manufacture

The relational dimension matters more than the preaching, and this is easy to underestimate.

Brené Brown has written that shared vulnerability is the precondition for genuine connection, and whatever one makes of her broader project, this observation is pastorally exact [cite — confirm]. The politically divided congregation cannot be argued into unity. It can, in some cases, be loved into it — loved through the slow work of relationships that refuse to honor the political boundary as a final one. That work begins with the pastor but cannot be confined to him.

Consider who you actually eat with. Whether your relationships model across-the-aisle connections in practice or only in principle. Whether the congregation has experiences — shared service to the poor, shared engagement with the community, shared suffering through grief — that create the common ground that preaching can build on but cannot manufacture by itself. The unity that transcends political division is not primarily a cognitive achievement. It is a relational one, grown through time and shared life and the repeated, costly choice to remain in relationship with people who organize their politics differently than you do.

This is the long work. There is no sermon series that accomplishes it in six weeks. But it is the work the Gospel requires, and the pastor who does it faithfully is doing something more durable than conflict management. He is building the thing that conflict management cannot build: a community that knows what it shares is more permanent than what divides it.

---

Name the Gospel explicitly and often. Call the congregation to primary loyalty to Christ above every other allegiance, and then trust the Spirit to do what only the Spirit can do.

That last part is not a resignation from leadership. It is the recognition that the Spirit's work in forming a people is not finally contingent on the pastor's program management skills. You preach. You stay faithful. You love across the divide. And you hold the long view that the Kingdom of God is coming and that the community that has organized itself around that coming has chosen the most durable thing available.

That is not political neutrality. That is the Gospel. They are not the same thing. Do not confuse them. Do not let the congregation confuse them. Preach into the confusion with patience and with conviction that the one who said "on this rock I will build my church" (Matthew 16:18) was not joking about the foundation.

The church was not built on a party platform. It will not fall because one party wins and one loses. It will stand or fall by whether it is actually organized around the King.

Keep preaching the King.

There is a pastoral failure we do not discuss, because discussing it is uncomfortable, and because the person most likely to leave when it becomes uncomfortable is also the person most likely to have funded the building.

I have committed this failure. I am still capable of it.

The wealthy congregant is not a problem to manage. He is a soul for whom Christ died, carrying the particular burden that Jesus named directly and without softening in Mark 10:23 — "How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God." The disciples were astonished. They had assumed the opposite. Wealth looked like favor. It looked like evidence of righteousness, the visible sign of God's blessing on a life well-ordered. Jesus was not gentle in correcting them. He pressed: harder than a camel through the eye of a needle. The disciples asked each other who could possibly be saved. That is the right response. That is the response that takes the text seriously.

Most of us do not take it seriously. We take the wealthy member seriously — as a donor, as a board member, as a person whose opinion carries weight in elder meetings and capital campaigns — and we call that pastoral care. It is not pastoral care. It is institutional management.

> It is not pastoral care. It is institutional management.

## What the History Tells Us

The church's accommodation of wealth is not a recent development. Constantine's conversion in the early fourth century [cite — confirm] changed the social composition of the church overnight. The community that had been primarily composed of the working poor, slaves, artisans, and women on the social margins became, within a generation, the preferred religion of the empire's upper classes. The social pressure that had functioned as a filter — the cost of following Christ in a hostile culture — was removed. Wealth and power entered the church without being required to submit to the same scrutiny that poverty and vulnerability had.

Chrysostom, the fourth-century bishop of Constantinople, stood against this with a directness that eventually got him exiled. His sermons on Matthew and on the letters of Paul are extended prophetic indictments of wealthy Christians who built elaborate houses while the poor of Constantinople went without food and shelter [cite — confirm]. He preached that the wealthy had no right to their wealth while anyone in the city was hungry. He named the donors in his congregation and the gap between their giving and their assets. The wealthy responded by engineering his removal. The empress herself pressed for his exile. He died in 407 on a forced march to the Black Sea. His consistency cost him everything.

Most of us are not Chrysostom. Most of us have made the trade he refused.

## What Care Actually Requires

The steel-man case for the approach we take is this: wealthy congregants are humans with real griefs, real marriages, real anxieties, real fear of death. They deserve pastoral presence in those moments. The CEO sitting across from me at the hospital bed of his dying mother is not his balance sheet. He is a son who is about to lose his mother, and he needs the same word of the Lord that anyone needs. He needs presence, Scripture, prayer, the assurance that death is not the last word. That is not wrong. That is exactly right.

But pastoral care is not only crisis response. It is formation. It is the long, patient work of shaping a soul toward the kingdom. And the kingdom, as Jesus described it, makes specific demands on the accumulation of wealth that pastoral care must eventually name. Not once. Not as a disclaimer slipped into a stewardship sermon. As a recurring, patient, self-implicating conversation that comes from a pastor who is inside the same struggle.

Because I am inside the same struggle. I am not rich by the standards of my wealthy congregants. By the standards of the world's population, I am extraordinarily comfortable. The question of what wealth does to the soul is not a question I ask from the outside. It is a question I ask as someone who has felt the pull — the pull toward security, toward comfort, toward the accumulation of margin that insulates me from the kinds of dependency that are actually central to the kingdom life Jesus described.

## What the Prophets Saw That We Are Afraid to Name

Amos did not comfort the wealthy of Samaria. He addressed them: "Woe to those who lie on beds of ivory and stretch out on their couches, and eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the stall, who sing idle songs to the sound of the harp and like David invent for themselves instruments of music, who drink wine in bowls and anoint themselves with the finest oils, but are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph" (Amos 6:4–6). The ruin of Joseph was the suffering of the poor. The comfortable had ceased to feel it. Not because they were monsters. Because comfort produces a specific kind of insulation from the suffering that happens outside its radius.

The prophetic job was not to expel the wealthy. It was to awaken them. To break through the insulation. To make them feel, again, what comfort had anesthetized. That is a pastoral act. It is the most demanding pastoral act — more demanding than hospital visits, more demanding than marriage counseling, because it requires the pastor to name something the wealthy person has arranged their entire life to avoid hearing.

> The prophetic job was not to expel the wealthy. It was to awaken them.

Jesus's encounter with the rich young ruler in Mark 10 is the paradigm. The man had kept the commandments. His life was, by external measure, morally ordered. He was earnest. Jesus "looked at him and loved him" (v. 21) — the text is explicit about the affection before the demand. Then: "Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." Something specific. Something costly. Something that went to the center of what the man's wealth had become: his security, his identity, the evidence he had accumulated that his life was working. The man went away sorrowful. He did not stay to argue. He went away.

Jesus did not chase him. He did not soften the word. He let the man go.

## What We Refuse to Say

The wealthy in our congregations generally know that Jesus said hard things about money. They have read Luke 12:15 — "one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions." They have heard it preached around the edges. What they have rarely experienced is a pastor willing to sit with them and ask: What is this doing to your soul? What does your wealth cost the people downstream from the decisions your wealth makes possible? Is the kingdom of God actually the organizing center of your financial life, or is your financial life a separate sovereignty that coexists peacefully alongside your religious practice?

Those questions are not comfortable. They are also not optional if you believe the Sermon on the Mount is binding on the community you are forming.

I know a pastor — a good man, a careful man — who has spent fifteen years serving a congregation with several families of significant wealth. He has never once had a direct conversation with any of them about money and discipleship. He tells himself they know. They do not know. They have never been told. They have been prayed over, counseled in marriage difficulty, eulogized when they lost parents, and handed the offering plate on stewardship Sunday. They have not been pastored in the place where the hardest work of discipleship is required.

He is afraid. I understand the fear. I have lived it. The fear is specific and real: he might leave; he might pull his pledge; the building campaign might fall short; the conflict might become public; the congregation might choose sides. Those are real possibilities. They are not theological reasons to remain silent.

## What Complicity Looks Like

Pastoral care that does not include prophetic challenge is not pastoral care. It is what the prophets called false peace — speaking smooth words to those who have not been reached by grief (Jeremiah 6:14). The prophet who assures the wealthy that their wealth is a sign of God's blessing while the poor of the congregation struggle with medical debt has spoken a false word. He has not pastored. He has performed.

The prosperity gospel is the most visible form of this failure — the explicit theological claim that wealth is God's reward for faith, that abundance is evidence of righteousness. But the failure is not limited to congregations that name the prosperity gospel explicitly. It operates wherever pastors preach about generosity without examining the structural sources of wealth, wherever the stewardship campaign focuses on what donors give without asking what the rest of their financial lives look like, wherever the wealthy are celebrated for their philanthropy without being asked about their supply chains, their wage practices, their investment portfolios.

The word of God for the wealthy congregant is not "give more to the building campaign." It is what Jesus gave to the rich young ruler: something specific, something costly, something that goes to the center of the question that wealth always raises — what does it mean to hold loosely what the world says you have earned?

## The Hardest Sentence in the Text

Some will leave. The rich young ruler left. He "went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions" (Matthew 19:22). Jesus did not chase him. He did not soften the word. He did not call after him to say that the requirement was merely illustrative, that the principle was the thing, that actual divestiture was not really what was meant.

He let the man go.

> The wealthy congregant needs to be loved enough to be told the truth.

That is the hardest sentence in the text. Not because it is harsh. Because it refuses the consolation that the pastoral instinct reaches for — the assurance that there is always a way to say the hard thing in a soft enough register that no one leaves. Sometimes there is not. Sometimes the word is what it is, and the person it reaches will respond as the rich young ruler responded, and the pastor's job is to have spoken it truly and to let the Spirit do what the Spirit does.

The wealthy congregant needs to be loved enough to be told the truth. That love is more demanding than the management of the relationship that keeps the pledge coming. It requires the pastor to care more about the soul than the budget — which is itself a test of whether the pastor believes what he preaches about where treasure actually is.

The congregation that produces that love has made a different trade than the one most of us have made. It has traded the comfort of the wealthy for their formation. The formation is far more valuable. It is what the pastoral office was actually created to produce.

Most of us have not made it. The text keeps asking whether we are ready to begin.

There is a cowardice that dresses itself as respect. You do not press on certain areas. You keep the conversation in safe waters. You visit when called, offer what is asked, and take careful note of the check in the offering plate. You are professionally warm and spiritually incurious about the one domain of this person's life that Jesus spent more time on than almost any other.

We call this pastoral care. The Gospels would not recognize it.

> We call this pastoral care. The Gospels would not recognize it.

---

## The Hard Word That Love Required

Jesus was not afraid of wealthy people. He ate with them. He was moved by them. He loved them specifically — the rich young ruler is the only person in the Synoptic Gospels of whom Mark says Jesus, looking at him, loved him (Mark 10:21). The love was not a dismissal. The love was the reason for the hard word that followed. "Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." The man went away sorrowful. He had many possessions. And Jesus, watching him leave, did not soften the conclusion: "How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God" (Mark 10:23).

The disciples were astonished. They had a category for wealth that Jesus was now explicitly dismantling — the assumption, inherited from a certain reading of the Deuteronomic tradition, that prosperity was a sign of divine favor and poverty a mark of divine discipline. Jesus dismantles it with an image so stark that interpreters have been retreating from it ever since: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God (Mark 10:25).

There is no metaphorical exit from that sentence. No ancient gate called "the needle's eye" that camels could pass through with some effort. Jesus means what he says. Wealth is dangerous. It is spiritually dangerous in a way that requires the specific pastoral attention he gave to no other condition. And the danger is not primarily external — not a matter of what the wealth does to others, though that is real — but internal. It is what wealth does to the soul of the one who holds it.

> There is no metaphorical exit from that sentence.

---

## The Pressure of Money on the Pulpit

This is the pastoral challenge with the wealthy congregant, and it is harder than most pastors acknowledge.

The challenge begins with access. Wealthy people in most congregations occupy a structural position that makes honest pastoral relationship genuinely difficult. They have resources the church needs. They sit on boards. They write checks that fund staff positions. They are known in the community in ways that carry social weight. The informal dynamics of a congregation's financial life create a kind of protective distance around the wealthy — not always out of deliberate calculation, but out of the accumulated weight of small decisions: who gets visited when the schedule fills, whose input is sought when decisions are made, whose discomfort prompts a quick recalibration.

I have been in conversations where I adjusted my pastoral approach because of what I knew about the family's financial situation. I have softened a line I intended to press. I have let a question die that deserved to live. The rationalization is available: this is the pastoral art, reading the room, timing the word for when it can be received. Sometimes that rationalization is correct. Often it is not. Often it is the pressure of money on the pulpit, operating below the level of conscious decision.

The prophet Micah named a version of this with unsparing specificity: "Its priests teach for a price, its prophets practice divination for money; yet they lean on the Lord and say, 'Is not the Lord in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us'" (Micah 3:11). The worst version is when the financial relationship is explicit and transactional. But the subtler version is when the financial relationship is simply present — present enough to shape what the pastor is willing to say and not say. The prophets called this corruption. We tend to call it wisdom.

> The prophets called this corruption. We tend to call it wisdom.

---

## The Patronage the Apostles Confronted

The ancient church was not naïve about this dynamic. The Epistle of James confronts it in terms so direct they are still startling: "For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing comes into your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in, and if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, 'You sit here in a good place,' while you say to the poor man, 'You stand over there,' or, 'Sit down at my feet,' have you not made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?" (James 2:2-4). James is not describing an extreme case. He is describing the default of unreformed human social behavior in religious settings.

The default runs deep. Luke Timothy Johnson, in his work on the social world of the early church, traces how the patronage system of the Roman world shaped — and often distorted — the earliest Christian communities. [cite — confirm] The wealthy patron was a figure of enormous social power in that world. His (almost always his) favor was worth cultivating. His displeasure had consequences. The temptation for leaders of new communities was to accommodate these dynamics rather than confront them, which is precisely why James and Paul spend so much time confronting them.

The theology underneath the accommodation is worth naming. It is a functional prosperity theology — not the explicit variety of the television preacher who promises financial returns on faith, but the structural variety, the quiet assumption that the wealthy congregant's success represents a kind of divine approval that the church should not disturb. It protects the wealthy from the word they most need to hear: that their wealth is a spiritual emergency, not an occasion for congratulation.

---

## The Material Demand of the Kingdom

Jesus's teaching on wealth is more sustained and more demanding than almost any other single topic in the Synoptics except the kingdom of God itself. The parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31) is not primarily about the afterlife. It is about the moral demand that proximity to suffering places on the wealthy. Lazarus was at the gate every day. The rich man knew he was there. The failure was not dramatic cruelty. It was the more common failure: the capacity to remain comfortable in the presence of suffering, to integrate that suffering into the background of a life organized around one's own comfort, and to continue in that life without the disruption the suffering should produce.

The parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14-30) has been domesticated by centuries of application to "using your gifts for God." But the economic context is specific and the judgment is specific: the servant who buried his master's money out of fear is condemned not for theft but for non-use. And in the broader narrative of Matthew 25, the criterion for final judgment is not theological correctness but what you did with the suffering in front of you: the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick, the imprisoned (Matthew 25:31-46). These are not spiritual categories. They are material ones.

---

## What Faithful Care Actually Looks Like

What does faithful pastoral care of the wealthy congregant actually look like?

It begins with honest theological conversation about wealth — not as a rebuke, not as a fundraising strategy, but as the pastoral work of helping a person inhabit their faith in the part of their life that Jesus found most spiritually urgent. The question is not whether they tithe. The question is what wealth is doing to their soul: their capacity for trust, their relationship with anxiety, their ability to take risks for the sake of the kingdom, their posture toward the poor people whose lives are affected by the economic decisions they make as employers and investors and citizens.

It means that the prophetic word cannot be withheld on the basis of the check in the offering plate. This does not mean attacking the wealthy from the pulpit. It means treating them as the full adults they are, capable of receiving the word Jesus gave the rich young ruler — given with love, given directly, and not softened because the love makes the truth too awkward.

And it means the pastor must examine his own relationship with the wealthy people in his congregation. Not to manufacture suspicion. But to ask: is there a conversation I have been avoiding? Is there a topic I have consistently not addressed because of who is in the room? Have I given this person the pastoral care I would give anyone else — the genuine attention to where they are spiritually struggling, including in the place where Jesus most clearly identified their struggle?

The rich young ruler walked away. That was a possibility Jesus accepted. The alternative — softening the word so the man would stay — would have been the pastor's failure, not the man's freedom.

We preach about sacrifice to people who have little. We owe the same sermon to people who have much. Their souls are on the table at that moment just as much as anyone else's, and the silence that protects our institutional ease is not pastoral wisdom. It is a form of abandonment dressed in the language of tact.

Jesus taught with authority, and the crowds were astonished — "not as the scribes" (Matthew 7:28–29). The scribes had credentials. They had lineage and training and the full institutional weight of the synagogue behind their words. They held the recognized positions, possessed the formal qualifications, had been through the approved processes of authorization. What they did not have, and what Jesus had, was the kind of authority that does not require the institution to enforce it. It arrived before the argument did. It was present in the room.

We have spent a great deal of energy in the church debating the source of pastoral authority — biblical, ecclesiastical, congregational, charismatic — and the debate is not without merit. But it tends to skip the most observable fact about how authority actually functions in a congregation: people follow leaders they trust, and trust is built the same way it has always been built. Slowly. Through kept promises and honest presence and being found reliable when it costs something.

## What Positional Authority Can and Cannot Do

Positional authority is real. The office of pastor carries weight in the text and in the tradition. The elders who lead well are worthy of double honor (1 Timothy 5:17). The congregation is to obey its leaders and submit to their authority (Hebrews 13:17). This is not merely courtesy language. Leadership structures matter and the pastoral office carries genuine theological weight.

> But positional authority alone can compel attendance. It cannot compel following.

But positional authority alone can compel attendance. It cannot compel following. A congregation can sit in the pews, vote the right way, serve on the right committees, and not be following you in any meaningful sense — not actually moving in the direction you are calling them toward. They are present without being persuaded. They are compliant without being committed.

I have led that way. I know what it produces. It produces a church where the pastor is the center of everything and the congregation is the audience, where vision is issued and received rather than built and owned, where people measure the institution by whether the pastor delivers rather than whether they belong to something they believe in. It looks like a functioning church from the outside. From the inside, it is waiting to fracture along whatever fault line appears first.

The church that follows its pastor because he has the title is an institution. The church that follows its pastor because they know him is a community. The difference between those two things is the difference between a pastor who leads until the moment of crisis and a pastor who can lead through crisis because the people around him have enough history with him to know, in their bones, that he is for them.

## The New Testament Pattern

The pastoral letters in the New Testament are striking for how relational they are. Paul does not write to churches as an executive issuing directives to subsidiary offices. He writes as a man who loves the people he is writing to, who names them by name, who is anxious about them and proud of them and sometimes desperate about them.

> The authority was the relationship, demonstrated through years of shared life and real cost and genuine care.

The letter to the Philippians opens with Paul's expression of deep personal affection: "I thank my God every time I remember you" (Philippians 1:3). The letter to the Thessalonians speaks of Paul's care like a nursing mother who cares for her children (1 Thessalonians 2:7). The letter to Philemon is an appeal based entirely on personal relationship — Paul does not command Onesimus's release; he asks, as the man who led Philemon to faith, for a gift freely given rather than a compliance compelled (Philemon 14). His authority in those churches was real — he defended it vigorously when it was challenged — but it was not separable from relationship. The authority was the relationship, demonstrated through years of shared life and real cost and genuine care.

This is not accidental to Paul's theology. In 2 Corinthians 1:24, he tells the Corinthians: "Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy." The phrase "lord it over" is the same construction Jesus uses in Mark 10:42-45 when he contrasts the leadership of the Gentile rulers with the leadership of the kingdom: "Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant." The authority of the kingdom is not the authority that stands above and compels. It is the authority that stands alongside and serves. It is the authority that is earned by the quality of the service, not granted by the quality of the credential.

## The Good Shepherd Model

"I am the good shepherd," Jesus said. "The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep" (John 10:11). The sheep follow him "because they know his voice" (John 10:4). Not because he has a title. Because they know him. That knowing is built through proximity, through care that costs something, through the experience over time that this person is for me rather than for the institution.

> Not because he has a title. Because they know him.

The contrast in John 10 is with the hired hand, who runs when the wolf comes because the sheep are not his own — because the relationship is transactional rather than covenantal, because what he values is the wage rather than the welfare. The sheep do not follow the hired hand with the same confidence because the hired hand's behavior in the moment of crisis reveals what the normal times concealed: that his commitment to them was contingent on cost.

The congregation knows this about their pastor long before the crisis arrives. They know it in the accumulation of small moments — whether the pastor appeared when it was inconvenient as well as when it was easy, whether he kept the promise he made on Tuesday when no one was watching, whether his care for them costs him anything real or whether it is exercised within the comfortable limits of a professional role. The crisis just reveals what was always there.

## What Relational Authority Requires

Relational authority is more demanding than positional authority, because it cannot be granted by a vote or maintained by a document. It must be earned continuously. A pastor can have twenty years of track record and squander it in a single season of unavailability or dishonesty or decisions that communicate that the institution matters more than the people. Trust accumulates slowly and departs quickly.

The pastor who has been operating on positional authority will often not realize how thin the relational foundation has become until the moment of crisis when he needs people to follow him somewhere hard and discovers they will not. Not because they dislike him. Because they do not know him well enough to trust him with something that costs them.

The counter-position has genuine weight: the pastor cannot be personally available to every member of a congregation of any substantial size. The pastoral relationship has institutional dimensions that are not in themselves a failure of relational care. A pastor of two thousand people cannot know every family the way a pastor of forty can. The structures of formal pastoral authority exist precisely because congregational size makes purely relational authority impractical.

This is true. But the conclusion it suggests is not "therefore positional authority is sufficient." It is "therefore the pastor must be even more intentional about where relational authority is actually built — with the leaders who lead the leaders, with the people whose trust multiplies through the structures of congregational life, with the communities within the community where the real pastoral work happens." Size changes the strategy. It does not change the principle. The principle is that people follow who they trust, and trust is built through personal presence that costs something.

## The Specific Work

The answer is not complicated, but it is demanding. Be present. Keep your word to people who cannot advance your career. Show up in the Tuesday-afternoon moments when no one is watching and nothing is being built. Know the names and the losses and the fears of the people in your congregation well enough that your care for them is evident rather than performed.

That kind of knowing takes time you feel like you cannot spare. It is time that does not produce a sermon, does not advance a program, does not generate the output a ministry culture tends to count and report. It is time spent in hospital waiting rooms and at gravesides and across kitchen tables in conversations that have no agenda except the pastoral relationship itself. It looks, from the outside, like inefficiency. It is actually the work. The sermon is built from what happens in those rooms. The vision is trusted or distrusted based on whether the people to whom it is offered have enough history with the pastor to believe he is seeing the same thing they are.

The congregation that follows you into the hard seasons — the seasons of financial difficulty or staff failure or theological recalibration or genuine conflict — is the one that knew you in the ordinary ones. They follow because they have accumulated enough experience of your trustworthiness to extend it into territory they cannot yet see. That extension is relational. It cannot be manufactured in a sermon or generated by a vote or produced by any credential the institution can grant.

It is built slowly, in the Tuesday afternoons, one kept promise at a time. By the time you need it, it is either there or it is not.

Build it before you need it.

That kind of authority takes years. Begin.

Charles Spurgeon preached to thousands of people at the Metropolitan Tabernacle on Sunday mornings and spent significant portions of his life unable to get out of bed [cite — confirm]. He wrote about his depression with the specificity of a man who was not performing vulnerability for an audience — he wrote about it because it was real, because it was sometimes disabling, because it returned when he had done nothing to invite it back. He called it a "fainting fit." He did not call it a faith problem. He knew better.

## The Tradition of Preachers in the Dark

The tradition of preachers who have wrestled with what we now call depression is not a footnote. It is a primary document. Spurgeon. William Cowper, the hymn-writer, who experienced episodes of such severity that he twice attempted to take his own life and spent years in an asylum, and who wrote "God moves in a mysterious way, His wonders to perform" from inside a darkness most of his readers never knew he inhabited. Martin Luther, who described periods of such terror and abandonment that he believed himself condemned — what he called Anfechtung, a word that has no exact English equivalent but that includes something of what we would recognize as severe depression and spiritual crisis. The prophet Elijah, who after the defeat of the prophets of Baal sat under a juniper tree in the wilderness and asked God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4). The author of Psalm 88, who ends without resolution, without the familiar turn back to praise, with simply this: "darkness is my closest friend."

These are not spiritual failures. These are the testimonies of people who took God seriously enough to tell the truth about what it cost.

---

## A Modern Confusion With a Specific Genealogy

The theological confusion that identifies depression with lack of faith is not an ancient confusion. It is largely a modern one, and it has a specific genealogy.

> These are not spiritual failures. These are the testimonies of people who took God seriously enough to tell the truth about what it cost.

It grows, in the American context, from a broad cultural narrative that equates Christian life with emotional wellness — that maps the abundant life Jesus promises in John 10:10 onto the categories of positive psychology and middle-class flourishing. In this frame, depression becomes diagnostic evidence of something wrong in the spiritual life: sin unrepented, prayer insufficiently urgent, trust inadequately formed, faith not big enough to claim the promise.

This is not the theology of the Psalms. The Psalms contain lament as a primary genre — prayers of abandonment, prayers of accusation, prayers that name darkness and do not exit it within the psalm's own frame. Psalm 13 opens "How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?" Psalm 22 opens with the words Jesus quoted from the cross: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" These are not failures of faith. They are exercises of faith — the specific faith that brings the full weight of the actual experience to God, rather than the curated version.

The theology that equates depression with faithlessness is not the theology of the Psalms. It is not the theology of Paul, who wrote from prison, who had a thorn in the flesh that was not removed despite repeated petition (2 Corinthians 12:7-9), who catalogued his suffering in 2 Corinthians 11 without euphemism. It is not the theology of Jeremiah, who cursed the day of his birth (Jeremiah 20:14). It is a theology of the Sunday morning marketing department. It is a theology that has confused the hope of the resurrection with the present experience of the resurrection, and that confusion has done real damage to real people who needed the Psalms and got cheerfulness instead.

---

## The Weight Underneath the Performance

Depression in ministry is not rare. And it does not present the way the pastoral culture expects it to present, which is part of why it goes unaddressed.

The pastor does not, in most cases, stop functioning when he is depressed. He continues to preach. He continues to perform the ritual of pastoral care. He continues to appear, from the outside, to be doing the job. The depression is the weight underneath the performance — the gray that drains the color from everything, the inability to feel the things he speaks about, the private doubt that what he is doing means anything, the 3 a.m. hour when the voices are loudest and sleep is furthest.

The specific pressures of pastoral life create conditions in which depression is not a surprising outcome. Sustained exposure to grief and trauma — funerals, hospital visits, the slow weight of other people's suffering carried repeatedly without adequate processing — depletes the emotional resources that sustain resilience. The isolation of visible leadership means the pastor's peer relationships are structurally different from those of people around him — he is the one people come to with their worst, and he has few relationships in which he can be the one who goes to someone else. The entanglement of identity with congregational performance creates a particular kind of anxiety that never fully disengages. The absence of genuine community — despite being surrounded by people at all times — is one of the more specific features of pastoral depression, and one of the more under-discussed.

> The depression is the weight underneath the performance — the gray that drains the color from everything, the inability to feel the things he speaks about, the private doubt that what he is doing means anything, the 3 a.m. hour when the voices are loudest and sleep is furthest.

And then there is the biology. Depression is a clinical reality that involves brain chemistry, neurological function, genetic predisposition, and the kinds of factors that respond to correct doctrine about as well as a broken leg responds to correct doctrine. To say this is not to reduce human beings to their neurology. It is to take seriously what we know about how human beings are made — that we are embodied creatures, that our spiritual lives are lived in bodies, that the body's health and the soul's experience are not fully separable, and that therefore the body sometimes needs clinical attention that supplements rather than replaces the spiritual.

---

## The Mask That Makes It Harder to Name

The practical reality for pastors dealing with depression is that the professional mask makes it harder to name.

You continue to function, continue to preach, continue to pray for others' healing while secretly doubting whether healing is available for you. The congregation cannot tell. The elders cannot tell. And the shame that accompanies the depression — the certainty that a man of faith should not feel this, that if he really believed what he preaches he would not be lying awake at 3 a.m. wondering if any of it is true — keeps him from seeking the help that would make naming it possible.

The shame is the specific pastoral version of the problem, and it is worth treating as its own obstacle. A depressed lay person can, in many churches, speak about their struggle and receive some measure of support. A depressed pastor faces the additional layer of anxiety about what disclosure would mean for his position, his authority, his congregation's confidence in his leadership. The fear is not irrational — pastoral culture has not always responded well to pastoral vulnerability. But the cost of the silence is usually higher than the cost of the disclosure, because the silence allows the depression to deepen while the reasons for secrecy remain.

What the depressed pastor needs is not, first of all, a better theology of suffering, though that may help. What he needs first is a safe relationship — one person, outside his professional responsibilities, who knows what is actually happening and will not use it against him. A counselor. A trusted peer pastor. A physician who understands that the presenting symptoms have a biological dimension and will not address only the spiritual. A spouse who has been invited into the reality rather than protected from it.

---

## Prayer Is Not the Only Resource

Here is the counter-argument, stated honestly: doesn't faith in God's sovereignty include trust that God can and does heal depression? Isn't there something to the tradition of prayer and spiritual battle and the authority of the believer that is worth bringing to bear here?

Yes. Fully yes. The spiritual resources of the tradition are real, and the pastor who is depressed and prays, who confesses, who reads Scripture as an act of faith when faith itself feels like performance — that practice is not irrelevant. It is not sufficient by itself, but it is not irrelevant. The Psalms were not written to be analyzed as literature. They were written to be prayed, and the pastor who prays Psalm 88 when he is in Psalm 88 is doing something that matters.

But the argument that prayer is the only resource — that medication represents a failure of faith, that professional counseling replaces rather than supplements the spiritual — is a theological position with a very thin biblical basis and a very long history of leaving suffering people without the help they need. The tradition that insists on prayer while denying the reality of clinical depression has a problem with the Psalms. It has a problem with Elijah. It has a problem with the incarnation's insistence that God's engagement with human suffering is material and physical and specific, not merely spiritual and abstract.

---

## What the Naming Breaks

The practical implications are direct.

If you are a pastor reading this who is depressed, the first step is to say so — to someone. Not to the congregation, necessarily, but to someone. A counselor. A physician. A trusted peer. Name it. The naming breaks the isolation, which is itself part of the condition. Do not measure your faith by whether you feel it. Feelings are not the foundation. The foundation is the God who met Elijah under the juniper tree and said, before anything else, "arise and eat."

> It is not a faith problem. It never was.

If you lead pastors — if you are a denomination executive, a bishop, a network leader, a PCN board member — build the structures that make disclosure possible without threatening a man's livelihood. The pastor who fears that admitting depression will cost him his call will not admit it until the concealment costs more than the disclosure. Most of the time, that moment arrives too late.

It is not a faith problem. It never was.

The prophets knew this. Spurgeon knew this. The author of Psalm 88 knew this, and wrote it down so that every generation after him would have a prayer that does not demand recovery by the final stanza.

The darkness is named in the canonical record. The tradition holds it.

So does the God of the tradition.

My sons know things about ministry that the congregation does not know, because they have watched it from a distance of about three feet. They were in the kitchen when the difficult phone calls came in. They were in the car when the elder board meeting's aftermath was visible on my face. They watched me leave for hospital visits on birthdays and return from conferences tired in a way that Sunday's sermon did not show. They have the data of proximity, and they will draw conclusions from it for the rest of their lives.

The question "what are your kids seeing?" is not sentimental. It is theological.

## The Household as a Diagnostic Test

The pastoral vocation, in the theological tradition that takes it seriously, is not just a job a man does. It is a shape that a life takes. The Pastoral Letters to Timothy and Titus are explicit about this: the bishop must manage his own household well, with all dignity, keeping his children submissive (1 Timothy 3:4-5). Paul is not adding a domestic footnote to a professional checklist. He is identifying the household as a diagnostic test. The household management reveals whether the character is real or performed, whether the theology has been internalized or merely processed. And the first people to know the answer to that question are the children.

The children are always watching. What they are watching for — though they could not name it this way — is whether the man who preaches on Sunday is the same man who eats breakfast on Tuesday. Whether the faith that gets articulated from the platform is the faith that operates in the kitchen when no one outside the family is present. Whether the grace he extends to grieving strangers extends also to the people he comes home to. The children are the most rigorous theologians in the household, because they are conducting the experiment under uncontrolled conditions, and they are keeping very good notes.

## The Particular Burden of the Pastor's Kids

The PKs — pastor's kids — carry a particular burden that most congregations underestimate. They have the calling loaded onto them without their consent. The congregation expects something of them by virtue of parentage. They are watched in a way that other children are not. The PK who misbehaves in the pew is not just a child misbehaving in a pew; the congregation reads it as a reflection on the pastor, and the pastor knows they are reading it that way, and the child knows the pastor knows, and the whole arrangement creates a pressure that no child should carry alone.

Eugene Peterson, who spent decades thinking about what pastoral formation actually requires, drew a distinction between the pastor's congregation and the pastor's family that was, in his view, the difference between sustainability and collapse [cite — confirm]. The congregation gets the office. The family gets the man. The two are not the same, and a man who does not protect that distinction — who performs the pastoral role at the kitchen table, who brings the platform self home and leaves the actual self outside, who turns every family conversation into a teaching moment or a sermon illustration — will eventually find that his children have concluded the actual man does not exist. That they have been pastored all their lives and never actually known their father.

## The Wound of the Gap

This is the wound that research on pastor's kids returns to repeatedly [cite — confirm]. Not the missed events, though those leave marks. Not the fishbowl visibility, though that creates real pressure. The primary wound is the gap — the distance between the public man and the private one, when that distance is large enough to feel like deception. The child who discovers that the man in the pulpit was a performance, that the warmth and wisdom the congregation received were not available at home, does not easily recover that faith. Not in the father. Often not in the institution the father represented. Sometimes not in the God the institution was supposed to represent.

> The children are the most rigorous theologians in the household, because they are conducting the experiment under uncontrolled conditions, and they are keeping very good notes.

I have not always been the same man at home as at church. The gap has been smaller in some seasons than others. My sons are old enough now to tell me when it is larger than it should be, and when they do, it lands with the weight it deserves. They are not wrong. The gap is real. And the ministry of closing it — slowly, repeatedly, across the years of a family's life together — is among the most important ministry I do, because it is the ministry that shapes the people closest to me.

What does it mean to pastor your own children well?

## What It Means to Pastor Your Own Children

It means they know, from direct experience, that the faith is real in the private life, not just the public one. That you pray when you are alone, not just when you are performing the pastoral function. That the Scripture you open Monday morning is opened to speak to you, not to produce a sermon for Sunday. That the God you describe from the platform is the God you actually lean on at midnight when you are afraid.

It means you ask for forgiveness, specifically, when you have wronged them — not a generic pastoral acknowledgment of imperfection, but an actual apology for an actual failure, offered to an actual person who was actually hurt. This is harder than it sounds, because the pastoral identity can produce a reflexive paternal authority that makes genuine apology feel like loss of standing. It is not. The father who repents to his child is not losing authority. He is modeling the thing the Gospel claims is central — that we are all inside the need for forgiveness, not outside it, and that saying so to the people who are watching is not weakness. It is the most convincing evidence they will ever receive that the faith is real.

> It means they know, from direct experience, that the faith is real in the private life, not just the public one.

It means you protect their experience of childhood from the congregation's expectations, which can be voracious. The congregation's hunger for the pastor's family to be a visible embodiment of the church's values is not malicious. But it is real, and if it is not managed by the pastor himself, it will consume the family. Your children are not the congregation's illustration. They are people who did not choose the visibility and deserve the privacy to grow up without performing for an audience.

It means you are curious about who they are becoming, not anxious about whether they are representing you well. The pastor who reads his children primarily as a reflection of his ministry success will produce children who are performing rather than forming. The pastor who is genuinely curious — who asks questions he doesn't already know the answers to, who listens to the answer rather than framing a response, who is interested in the actual person rather than the person he wishes were there — gives his children something rarer than the children of public figures often receive: the experience of being seen.

## Vocation as Whole-Life Faithfulness

The theological tradition that most clearly names this is the tradition of vocation as whole-life faithfulness. Luther's insistence that the common life was not spiritually inferior to the religious life — that the father feeding his child was doing holy work, that the mother nursing her infant was doing holy work, that the ordinary materials of household life were the primary theater of Christian formation — was a revolutionary claim in the sixteenth century and has not been fully absorbed by the pastoral culture that descended from it [cite — confirm]. The pastor who treats the congregation as the real ministry and the family as the supportive context has not escaped the medieval hierarchy Luther was opposing. He has simply moved the sacred location from the monastery to the pulpit.

The household is a call. The children are a congregation. Not in the sense that reduces them to objects of ministry rather than subjects of relationship, but in the sense that they are people in your care who are being formed by what they see in you. The formation is happening whether you intend it or not. The question is only what kind.

The PK who grows up knowing that his father's faith was real — tested in the ordinary materials of family life and found genuine — has received something no congregational program can supply. He has watched a man believe it on a Tuesday. He has evidence from the inside of the life that the sermon was not a performance but a report. He carries that evidence with him through the seasons when his own faith is under pressure, and it is more durable than the sermon he watched from the pew, because it is not doctrine. It is data. He was there.

The PK who grows up knowing that the sermon and the kitchen table were different countries lives with that knowledge for the rest of his life. Some of them eventually forgive it. Some of them leave the faith entirely, and when researchers ask why, the private gap is often part of the answer.

Your children are your first congregation. Not because they have rights over your ministry, but because what they see will form them in ways that outlast everything you preach.

> Your children are your first congregation.

What they are seeing is the question that matters most.

The Mosaic law was not neutral on the question of lending money to the poor.

Exodus 22:25: "If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not be like a moneylender to him, and you shall not exact interest from him." Leviticus 25:35–37 extends the prohibition and ties it explicitly to the memory of Israel's own bondage: you were in Egypt, you know what it is to be crushed by systems that extract from the vulnerable. Deuteronomy 23:19 is categorical: "You shall not charge interest on loans to your brother, interest on money, interest on food, interest on anything that is lent for interest." These are not suggestions offered as pastoral guidance to those who feel led in that direction. They are commands embedded in the economic structure of the covenant community, because God understood something American Christianity has largely forgotten: the capacity to extract interest from the desperate is the capacity to trap them permanently in dependency. It is the mechanism of bondage wearing the clothing of a transaction.

Payday lending — short-term loans at annual percentage rates that commonly exceed 300% and sometimes approach 600% [cite — confirm] — is not a new concept. It is usury with modern paperwork. The person who borrows $200 to cover a gap between paychecks and repays $260 two weeks later, only to need another loan immediately because the $260 came out of the rent money, is not experiencing a free-market service. They are in a trap designed by people who understood exactly what they were building.

I have not said this from a pulpit. I have preached about personal financial responsibility — the dangers of debt, the virtue of savings, the discipline of the tithe. I have not named the industry that profits specifically from people who cannot practice those virtues because they are already underwater. That silence was not neutrality. It was a choice about whose interests it served.

## The Biblical Architecture Against Usury

The Hebrew word for interest that these passages prohibit is *neshek* — literally, a bite. The image is deliberate. The word pictures interest on loans to the vulnerable as something that consumes the person from whom it is taken, the way a predator's bite begins the process of death. The legislation is built around that image because the legislators understood what high-interest lending does over time: it does not merely inconvenience the borrower. It devours them.

Ezekiel places lending at interest alongside murder and adultery in his catalog of sins that defile the covenant community (Ezekiel 18:13). Not peripheral offenses. Defiling ones. The person who lends at interest to the poor is placed in the same category as the person who commits violence — because the moral logic of the community regards both as acts that destroy the human beings God has made.

> It is usury with modern paperwork.

The Psalms make the connection to character. Psalm 15 asks who may dwell on God's holy mountain, and the answer includes: one who "lends money without charging interest" (Psalm 15:5). The absence of extractive lending is a mark of the righteous person. Not an external legal requirement alone, but a disposition of the heart toward the neighbor — a refusal to treat the neighbor's desperation as an opportunity for profit.

Nehemiah, when he returned to Jerusalem and found that wealthy Jewish landowners were charging interest to their poor countrymen during a famine — some of them forcing them to mortgage their fields, their vineyards, their children into debt slavery — was "very angry" (Nehemiah 5:6). He did not immediately forgive. He assembled a great meeting, named the sin publicly, and demanded that the wealthy return the fields, the vineyards, the houses, and the hundredth part of the money they had been taking (Nehemiah 5:11). Correction in this account is structural. It requires the return of what was taken, not merely the stopping of the practice.

## What the Industry Is

Payday lending is a $30 billion annual industry in the United States [cite — confirm]. It operates through approximately 23,000 storefronts — more than the number of McDonald's locations in the country [cite — confirm]. The industry's location strategy is explicit: payday lenders cluster in low-income communities, near military bases, in predominantly Black and Hispanic neighborhoods [cite — confirm]. This is not because poor people have worse access to banks and therefore genuinely need emergency credit — though that is true. It is because the business model requires clients who are financially desperate enough to pay 400% interest, and those clients are concentrated in specific ZIP codes.
