It emerged in a country where the equation of God's blessing with material prosperity had deep roots in the Puritan work ethic, in the providentialist interpretation of American economic success, in the frontier mythology of individual effort producing individual reward.

## Faith Performed as Extraction

What happened in the second half of the twentieth century is that this theology, fully formed in the American context, was exported globally through the same missionary networks and media platforms that carried American evangelical Christianity around the world. It arrived in sub-Saharan Africa, in Latin America, in Southeast Asia — in communities experiencing genuine poverty, genuine desperation, genuine longing for God's intervention in conditions of material suffering. And it arrived with the implicit guarantee that the right kind of faith, expressed in the right kind of giving and declaring and believing, would produce material deliverance.

**Who Bears the Cost**

> The people who give those fifty-dollar seed gifts are not foolish.

The prosperity gospel requires a performance of faith — particularly a performance of generosity that flows toward the ministry conducting the performance. The prosperity preacher who tells his congregation that their seed gift of fifty dollars will return a hundredfold harvest is not being generous. He is extracting resources from people who cannot afford to give them, on the basis of a promised return that the theology guarantees but the evidence does not support, and the extraction makes him wealthy while leaving the congregation, on average, where it began.

The people who give those fifty-dollar seed gifts are not foolish. They are desperate. And the prosperity gospel specializes in people who are desperate. It reaches into communities where healthcare is unaffordable, where the job market has hollowed out, where generational poverty has closed the doors that middle-class optimism keeps open, where the longing for a breakthrough is not self-deception but the rational response of a person who has tried the available secular options and found them insufficient. The prosperity gospel meets that longing with the claim that God has prepared a specific and material deliverance — and that the obstacle between you and that deliverance is the size of your faith and the boldness of your giving.

## What Jesus Said About Money

This is not good news for the poor. It is a mechanism for extracting the resources of the poor under the cover of divine sanction. When the breakthrough does not come — and for the majority of the congregation, it does not come in any materially measurable sense — the theology provides its own explanation: insufficient faith. Inadequate giving. Some blockage in the spiritual plumbing of the believer's inner life. The promised return is always deferred, and the deferral is always the fault of the person who believed and gave and did not receive.

The poor person who gives her seed gift and does not receive the hundredfold return is left not only without her fifty dollars. She is left with a theological framework that tells her the failure was hers, that her poverty is the evidence of a faith deficit, that God has material abundance prepared for everyone who truly believes and that her continued economic suffering is the judgment on her spiritual condition. This is cruelty dressed as comfort. It deserves to be named plainly.

> These are not outliers in the teaching of Jesus.

**What the Bible Actually Says**

## The Redistribution Mandate Removed

Jesus spoke about money more than about any other single subject except the kingdom of God. He did not speak about it the way the prosperity gospel speaks about it. He spoke about it as a spiritual danger — specifically, as the primary competitor with God for the human heart's allegiance (Matthew 6:24). He told the rich young ruler to sell everything he had and give it to the poor, because the wealth was the obstacle to eternal life (Mark 10:21-22). He told the parable of the rich fool who built bigger barns to store his growing surplus and was called a fool by God that very night (Luke 12:16-20). He told the parable of the rich man who feasted while Lazarus lay at his gate and ended in torment while Lazarus was comforted in Abraham's bosom (Luke 16:19-31).

These are not outliers in the teaching of Jesus. They are his consistent instruction about wealth: it is spiritually dangerous, it tends to blind its possessor to the claims of God and neighbor, its accumulation is not a sign of divine favor but a potential sign of spiritual peril, and its proper use involves radical generosity toward the poor rather than multiplication for personal benefit.

The Hebrew prophets were, if possible, even more direct. Amos condemned the wealthy of Israel who "sell the innocent for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals" and who "trample on the heads of the poor as on the dust of the ground" (Amos 2:6-7). Isaiah pronounced woe on those who "add house to house and join field to field till no space is left and you live alone in the land" (Isaiah 5:8). Micah condemned those who "covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them. They defraud people of their homes, they rob them of their inheritance" (Micah 2:2).

> This is cruelty dressed as comfort.

The prosperity gospel's reading of Scripture requires a systematic inversion of this tradition. It requires treating the warnings about wealth as if they were promises of wealth, treating the commendations of the poor as if they were temporary conditions on the way to material improvement, treating the prophetic indictments of economic exploitation as irrelevant to the church's relationship with its members' financial lives. This inversion is not a matter of emphasis or interpretation at the margins. It is a fundamental misreading of what the Bible says about money, poverty, and the character of God.

**The Counter-Argument, Honestly**

The most honest version of the prosperity gospel's defense goes something like this: God does bless his people. The Old Testament is full of examples of God's material provision for those who are faithful — the patriarchs, Solomon, the returning exiles. The claim that God cares about material flourishing and that faith produces it is not invented from nothing.

This is true as far as it goes, and it is worth taking seriously rather than dismissing. God's provision is real. God does care about the material flourishing of his people. The Hebrew vision of shalom is not merely spiritual. It includes enough food, safe housing, meaningful work, community stability — the conditions under which human beings flourish as the creatures they are.

What the prosperity gospel does with this real biblical material is detach it from its context. The material blessings in the Hebrew narrative are embedded in a covenant structure that is equally emphatic about the obligations of the blessed toward the poor. Deuteronomy 15, the chapter that promises abundance to the obedient, also commands the cancellation of debts every seven years and insists that "there should be no poor among you" — because the prosperity of the covenant community was to be distributed, not hoarded (Deuteronomy 15:4). The tithe in the Hebrew system was not primarily a mechanism for funding the temple. It was a redistributive mechanism: every third year's tithe went to "the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow" so that they could eat and be satisfied (Deuteronomy 14:28-29).

The prosperity gospel takes the promise of God's provision and removes the redistribution mandate that was always attached to it. What remains is a theology of individual accumulation dressed in the language of divine favor — a theology that, by design or consequence, benefits the wealthy at the expense of the poor and calls it the blessing of God.

**The Verdict**

The prosperity gospel is not a harmless error for which enthusiastic teachers should be gently corrected. It is an active harm, extracting resources from the poor, leaving them with a theology that blames them for their poverty, and providing theological cover for wealth extraction by presenting it as spiritual leadership.

The church that tolerates prosperity theology in its network — that platformizes its teachers, shares its platforms, avoids naming its errors in the name of evangelical comity — is participating in the harm. Silence on the prosperity gospel is not theological neutrality. It is complicity with a system that Jesus, in almost every economic teaching he gave, would have condemned.

He reserved his most severe words not for the obviously sinful but for the religiously respectable who used their religious authority for economic advantage. "Woe to you, teachers of the law and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You devour widows' houses" (Matthew 23:14). The charge was not theological imprecision. It was economic exploitation conducted under religious cover. It had a name. It still does.

There is a theology buried in the way most pastors manage their time, and it is not the theology they would preach. The preached theology says that the covenant of marriage is the primary human relationship — the one that images the covenant between Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25-32), the one that demands the same sacrificial, self-emptying love the cross required. The practiced theology, the one visible in the actual calendar, says that the congregation's need is an emergency and the marriage is a standing arrangement that can absorb the remainder.

The remainder is never enough. It has never been enough.

**The Silence That Looks Like Stability**

The marriage does not announce its deterioration the way a congregational crisis does. A staff conflict sends an email. A grieving family calls at midnight. A financial crisis appears on the treasurer's report and produces an emergency elder meeting. But the marriage just grows quieter. The conversations get shorter. The space between the two people living in the same house gradually expands — not with hostility, most of the time, but with a careful, weary distance that neither person is naming because naming it would require the kind of sustained attention the schedule never permits.

## The Quiet That Looks Like Stability

The quiet is easy to mistake for stability. I have made that mistake. I have come home from the work of caring for other people's marriages with nothing left for my own, and called it faithfulness.

It is not faithfulness. It is a theology of availability applied to the wrong things, in the wrong order.

> It is a theology of availability applied to the wrong things, in the wrong order.

**The Structural Problem**

## A Subsidiary Ministry

The pastor who preaches the sanctity of marriage while systematically denying his own marriage the presence, attention, and genuine care that sanctity requires is not being hypocritical in the ordinary sense. He believes what he preaches. The problem is structural. The systems around him reward congregational availability and provide no natural correction for marital neglect. There is no elder meeting called when a pastor's wife has not had a real conversation with her husband in three weeks. There is no accountability structure that names the slow withdrawal of the man's best energy from the person who has most right to it.

The elder who calls at ten on a Thursday night does not know that the pastor's wife has been waiting to talk since Tuesday. The church does not see the marriage the way it sees the ministry. The congregation observes the pastor's public role — the sermons, the hospital visits, the board meetings, the counseling appointments — and assesses his health on the basis of what is visible. What is invisible is the marriage, and the marriage is where the real depletion registers first.

There is a version of evangelical pastoral culture that has, without fully intending to, turned the pastor's family into a subsidiary ministry. The family is the thing the pastor does after he has done the real thing. The wife and children receive what is left after the congregation has taken its share. This is not articulated, because articulated it would be obviously wrong. But it is practiced constantly. The family knows it is practiced. They rarely say so, because the calling is real and they honor it, and saying so would feel like undermining something sacred.

## The Cross Has No Footnote for Ministry

But the quiet honoring is not evidence that all is well. It is often evidence that the pastor's wife has stopped expecting anything different.

**The Full Weight of the Text**

Paul's instruction in Ephesians 5 is not a metaphor that gets weaker when it encounters the demands of ministry. He says that husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). The verb is *gave himself up* — the same verb Paul uses for the cross, the total self-offering that withheld nothing. The model is not calibrated availability. It is the kind of love that treats the other's flourishing as the organizing principle of the relationship.

> There is no neutral position.

There is no footnote in that text that exempts the pastor during capital campaigns or sermon series or seasons of congregational growth. The command stands regardless of what else is standing alongside it.

## What the Calling Has Cost Her

This is why the protection of the marriage must be active, not passive. Active protection means specific, scheduled, non-negotiable time that the congregation does not have access to and that cannot be interrupted except by genuine emergency. Not "date night when we can manage it" — the phrase that sounds like a commitment and is actually a surrender to circumstance. One night per week that does not move for board meetings. One night that does not yield to the member in crisis. One morning each week that belongs to the marriage and not to the ministry.

This will feel selfish the first time the pastor enforces it. The phone will ring. The need will be real. The sense of obligation will press. But the marriage that is protected in ordinary weeks develops the resilience to survive the extraordinary weeks — the weeks when the crisis is genuine and the absence is actually required. The marriage that never receives protected time develops no such resilience. It is always running on whatever is left.

**What She Has Actually Lost**

Protection also requires honest conversation — the kind that is harder than any congregational conversation, because the stakes are more personal and the vulnerability required is the kind that cannot be managed from a position of authority.

## The Theology You Live

The pastor's wife who has been in ministry for ten years has likely absorbed things she has not named. The lonely Sundays when the church members got warmth and attention and she got the exhausted man at the back of the service. The congregational projections — the saint's wife who must always seem stable, appropriately spiritual, supportive of the pastor's vision without visible needs of her own. The expectations about hospitality, about presence at every event, about her children's behavior, about her own public persona. The specific loneliness of being married to a man whose best self, the patient self, the attentive self, the generous self, gets deployed for others most of the week.

Most pastoral spouses carry this quietly. The calling is real, and they honor it, and the church is full of people who are genuinely changed by the ministry their husband's life makes possible. None of that makes the carrying light.

The question worth asking — regularly, not once, not during a conflict, but as a practice — is: what has the ministry cost her this year? Not in a managed pastoral way, as though it were a counseling check-in. But genuinely. With enough patience to hear a real answer, which will take longer than feels comfortable, and enough courage to receive it without defending.

> Both are possible.

**The Stakes**

I have watched marriages collapse in ministry. I am not speaking hypothetically. I have sat with pastors whose marriages ended after fifteen years, after twenty years, after building something for the congregation that cost them the thing they cannot rebuild. The aftermath is not just personal. The congregation pays. The children pay. The pastor's witness pays. The slow erosion of a pastoral marriage is not a private failure. It belongs to the congregation's story in ways they will only understand after the fact.

The congregation will survive a pastor who protects his marriage. It will not survive — not whole, not without significant damage — a pastor whose marriage collapses and takes the church's trust with it. The church that loses a pastor to an affair, or to a divorce driven by years of neglect, does not simply process that as a personnel matter. It processes it as a theological crisis: if the man who taught us about covenant could not keep his own, what exactly were we learning?

That crisis is preventable. Not by perfection — no marriage is without its seasons of struggle, and the pastoral marriage carries its own specific difficulties that a protected schedule cannot entirely remove. But by treating the marriage as what Paul says it is: the primary covenant, the one that images something divine, the one that cannot be relegated to the remainder of the week without theological consequence.

**Choosing Both**

It is possible to pastor a congregation faithfully and to be present to your wife and children in ways that matter. I am not offering a hopeful aspiration. I have seen it done by men who decided, deliberately, that the theology they preached required something of their actual lives.

The decision is not made once. It is made every week when the schedule is built. It is made every Thursday night when the phone rings at ten. It is made every time the elder meeting runs over and the question is whether to call ahead or to simply arrive late. The accumulation of those small decisions, over years, is either the slow protection of the marriage or its slow erosion. There is no neutral position.

The pastor who treats his marriage as structure rather than remainder — as the foundation the ministry is built on rather than the thing left after the ministry has taken its share — is practicing the theology he preaches. His congregation can see the difference, even when they cannot name it. His children will know the difference when they are adults. His wife will know it every week.

The marriage is not what comes after the ministry. The ministry is what comes out of the marriage — out of a man who is loved and known at home, who practices covenant fidelity in the daily domestic decisions before he preaches it on Sunday, who is accountable to someone who has no illusions about who he is and stays anyway.

That man has something to offer the congregation that the man running on performance and neglect does not.

Build it in. Protect it. Decide that the theology you preach is also the theology you live. The congregation deserves a pastor who actually believes what he says about marriage. Your wife deserves the man you were before the ministry grew large enough to consume him.

Both are possible. Both require choosing.

There is a psalm that most congregations have never heard preached. It is eight verses long. It opens in a courtroom where the defendant is God — or rather, where God is the judge and the defendants are gods, divine beings who have been given authority over the nations and who have exercised that authority corruptly. It is a strange, unsettling text, and its strangeness is precisely why it matters.

Psalm 82 opens: "God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment" (Psalm 82:1). The Hebrew is explicit: God stands in the *'adat-'el*, the assembly of the divine beings, and renders a verdict. The beings assembled are not metaphors for human rulers, though many interpreters have tried to make them so. They are the *elohim* who have been assigned governance of the nations — a cosmology attested elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible (Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in the Dead Sea Scrolls tradition; Daniel 10) and in the wider ancient Near Eastern understanding of how divine powers administered human affairs. [cite — confirm] The psalm is working with that cosmology and exploding it from within.

The indictment is specific. These divine governors have failed at their governing function, and the failure is named in terms of who has been harmed: "How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute. Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked" (Psalm 82:2–4).

## The Specificity of the Charge

The list is worth sitting with. The weak. The fatherless. The afflicted. The destitute. The needy. These are not incidental groupings. They are the specific population that appears repeatedly throughout the Hebrew prophetic tradition as the measure of a society's justice — the people whose vulnerability reveals whether the governing powers are operating in alignment with the character of the God who made them. The divine council is indicted not for failing in some abstract governance task but for failing the specific people whose protection is the defining purpose of just governance.

I grew up without a father. I do not read "the fatherless" in that list as a rhetorical category. I read it as a description of a specific form of social vulnerability that governance structures either protect or exploit. The psalm names the exploitation of the fatherless as cosmic treason.

> The psalm names the exploitation of the fatherless as cosmic treason.

The verdict follows the indictment: "They have neither knowledge nor understanding, they walk about in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken" (Psalm 82:5). This is the causal logic the psalm is pressing. When the governing powers fail to protect the vulnerable, the foundations shake. Not as metaphor. As structural reality. The stability of the created order depends on the just treatment of the weakest members of the community. The corruption of governance toward the wicked and away from the poor does not merely harm individuals. It destabilizes the architecture of the world. The cosmos is not neutral about injustice.

## When the Foundations Shake

The sentence is then passed: "You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you; nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince" (Psalm 82:6–7). The authority delegated to these powers is revoked. The tenure of divine governance that failed the weak is ended. And the psalm closes with a petition that is, given what precedes it, explosive: "Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations" (Psalm 82:8).

This is not a prayer for divine intervention in a private matter. It is a political declaration: the failed governors have forfeited their authority, and the God who stands in defense of the weak and the fatherless is now claimed as the rightful ruler of every nation.

Jesus quotes Psalm 82 in John 10:34 in a context that New Testament scholarship has increasingly recognized as a claim to divine identity — he is not merely citing the text as precedent but positioning himself as the one the psalm's closing petition had requested. [cite — confirm] The one who rises to judge the earth, who inherits the nations, who takes governance from the powers that have walked in darkness — that one has arrived. This changes the pastoral weight of Psalm 82. It is not only a text about ancient Near Eastern cosmology or a historical artifact of Israelite religion. It is a text that the New Testament reads as inaugurated. The justice it demands has been launched in the person of the one who said in Luke 4 that he had been anointed "to proclaim good news to the poor" and "liberty to the oppressed."

> The justice it demands has been launched in the person of the one who said in Luke 4 that he had been anointed "to proclaim good news to the poor" and "liberty to the oppressed."

Which means the church that reads this text cannot do so from a neutral position. The powers named in Psalm 82 are generic enough to name any governing structure — any system of economic, political, or social authority — that consistently delivers for the powerful and consistently fails the weak. The logic of the indictment does not require the governor to be a supernatural being. It requires the governor to have authority and to exercise it in ways that walk in darkness — that show partiality to the wicked, that neglect the fatherless and the destitute, that leave the needy in the hand of those who would exploit them.

## The Plain Reading of the Text

The application to contemporary systemic injustice is not a liberal innovation or a conservative threat. It is the plain reading of the text.

The counter-argument from those who resist systemic analysis of injustice goes like this: the church should focus on individual sin and individual transformation, not on systems. Systems are too abstract. Social change is too slow and too politically entangled. The gospel transforms persons, and transformed persons change cultures from within. There is truth in this — genuine truth, worth holding. Individual repentance is not optional. Transformed hearts do change communities. The reduction of justice work to political organizing without the accompanying call to personal metanoia is a real theological error.

But Psalm 82 does not give us the luxury of that reduction in the other direction. The psalm is not addressed to the hearts of individuals. It is addressed to governing powers — to the structures and systems through which authority is exercised. The indictment is systemic: the entire council has failed in its governing function. The solution is not merely the conversion of individual council members. It is the replacement of the corrupt governance structure with the direct rule of the God who defends the weak. The psalm is thinking categorically, structurally, about how power is organized and for whose benefit.

## A Standard That Is Covenantal, Not Partisan

The prophetic tradition that preceded and followed Psalm 82 shares this structural analysis. Amos 5 does not merely indict greedy individuals. It indicts the system that "trample the head of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the afflicted" (Amos 2:7). Micah 6:8 does not call for personal spiritual disciplines as an alternative to justice. It names justice — *mishpat* — as the required disposition alongside mercy and humility. Isaiah 10 pronounces woe on those "who decree iniquitous decrees, and the writers who keep writing oppression, to turn aside the needy from justice and to rob the poor of my people of their right" (Isaiah 10:1–2). The decrees are the problem. The legislative structures are the subject of the indictment. The scribes who write the policies are named alongside the powerful who benefit from them.

The church that inherits this tradition and then refuses to apply it to contemporary governing systems because that would be "getting political" has performed an act of hermeneutic cowardice that the tradition itself does not support.

What Psalm 82 requires is not that the church become an arm of a particular political party. Both major parties in the American system have at various points exercised the kind of governance the psalm indicts — showing partiality to the powerful, failing the fatherless, leaving the needy in the hands of those who exploit them. The psalm's standard is not partisan. It is covenantal. It measures governance by one question: is the system protecting and providing for the weakest members of the community, or is it not?

> We know.

That question can and should be applied by a congregation across the full spectrum of policies that affect the vulnerable — tax policy, housing policy, immigration enforcement, child welfare, criminal justice, food access, medical care. The congregation that learns to ask the psalm's question will not become a single-issue voter bloc. It will become a community capable of prophetic discernment that is accountable to something older and more demanding than party loyalty.

The foundations of the earth are at stake when the weak are abandoned. That is not rhetoric. It is the psalm's own structural claim.

The God who arises to judge the earth judges the church too. We have been entrusted with the same governing responsibility — not over nations, but over our own practices of power, our own institutional decisions about who receives our care and whose suffering we acknowledge and whose we ignore. The council assembled in Psalm 82 walked in darkness because they did not know, did not understand. Ignorance does not protect them from the verdict.

We know. The question is whether knowing has changed what we do.

Arise, O God. Judge the earth.

And let the church that prays that prayer be ready to be judged with it.

Psalm 88 ends without resolution.

That is unusual. Most lament psalms move through darkness toward some form of trust — they end with a declaration of confidence, a memory of God's past faithfulness, a choice to keep worshipping in spite of the darkness. Psalm 88 does none of that. It begins with a cry to God and ends with the words "darkness is my closest friend." There is no turn. There is no uplift. The darkness is the last word.

The church has generally not known what to do with Psalm 88. We quote Psalm 23 at funerals. We sing Psalm 100. We return to Psalm 51 for confession. Psalm 88 sits in the collection, rarely preached, rarely sung, rarely prayed — because it does not go where we expect the Psalms to go, and its refusal to go there makes us uncomfortable.

But the Psalter is not a collection of devotional verses arranged for our comfort. It is the prayer book of the people of God, assembled over centuries, including the full range of what happens when human beings try to talk to God honestly. The fact that Psalm 88 is in the canon is a theological statement: this is also what prayer looks like. This is also what faith sounds like when it has nowhere left to go.

> The darkness is the last word.

## The History Behind the Collection

The Psalter took its final shape over roughly a thousand years of Israel's life with God. The earliest psalms may reach back to the wilderness period. The latest reflect the experience of Babylonian exile — Psalm 137's anguished cry "by the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept" (Psalm 137:1) is the cry of people who have watched Jerusalem burn, who have been marched hundreds of miles from home, who are singing the Lord's songs in a foreign land because their captors have demanded entertainment.

> They did not sanitize.

The Psalter was assembled as the prayer book for the Second Temple community returning from exile — people who came back to a land that was not quite the land they had expected, to ruins they had to rebuild, to a form of worship that had to be reconstructed from memory and imagination. They needed prayers for every condition of the human heart before God: celebration, thanksgiving, orientation, disorientation, rage, grief, accusation, trust, exhaustion, and praise. The editors included all of it. They did not sanitize.

That editorial decision is itself a form of pastoral theology. The community that will say all of this to God is a community that believes God can receive all of it. The God of the Psalter is not fragile. He is not offended by honest complaint. He does not require the worshiper to approach in a particular emotional register before the prayer counts. Every form of the interior life — including the forms the church has been uncomfortable with — is admitted to the conversation.

## What the Psalms Actually Are

> The accusation is a form of faith.

Walter Brueggemann's distinction between psalms of orientation, disorientation, and new orientation [cite — confirm] is the most useful framework I know for understanding why the Psalter is structured the way it is. Psalms of orientation celebrate the goodness of God in a world where things are working. Psalms of disorientation — the laments, the complaints, the expressions of abandonment — name what it is like when the world has fallen apart and God seems absent or hostile. Psalms of new orientation describe what it is like to have come through darkness to a different kind of trust: not the naive trust of orientation but the hard-won trust of someone who has been in the darkness and survived it.

The church has been very comfortable with orientation psalms and new orientation psalms. It has been systematically uncomfortable with disorientation psalms — the ones where God is accused of sleeping, of forgetting, of turning his face away. We have treated those psalms as embarrassing ancestors of a more mature faith, the raw expressions of people who had not yet learned to trust properly.

This is exactly backwards. The laments are not evidence of immature faith. They are evidence of honest faith — of people who believed in God enough to bring their grief and their accusation to him rather than collapsing into silence or turning away. The person who cannot bring anger to God has not matured beyond the lament psalms. She has lost access to part of her own interior life that God already knows is there.

Psalm 44 accuses God of sleeping: "Awake, Lord! Why do you sleep? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever" (verse 23). This is not the prayer of someone who has given up on God. It is the prayer of someone so convinced that God matters, so committed to the relationship, that she will not pretend the unanswered prayer is fine. The accusation is a form of faith. The silence would be the abandonment.

## What We Have Lost by Aestheticizing Them

The King James Bible's translation of the Psalms is genuinely beautiful. That beauty has been, in certain respects, a problem. When Psalm 22 becomes a text we admire for its poetry — "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" — we have placed it at aesthetic distance from the person in the hospital room who is praying the same prayer without the archaic diction and without any sense that this psalm belongs to her.

She should know it belongs to her. That is precisely what it is for.

Eugene Peterson spent years rendering the Psalms into contemporary English for what became The Message [cite — confirm], not because the original translations were inaccurate but because through familiarity and liturgical distance they had become texts people admired rather than prayers people prayed. He wanted to give people the Psalms as working documents — as tools for the interior life rather than exhibits in the museum of religious literature.

The imprecatory psalms are where this becomes most acute. Psalm 137, which ends with a brutal image of infant deaths as an expression of the Babylonian exiles' grief and rage, is genuinely difficult. We do not sing it. We do not pray it. We explain it in footnotes. But it is in the canon, and its presence there is the canon's acknowledgment that the grief of people who have lost everything — who have watched their city burned and their families destroyed and their children taken — can produce a darkness that Scripture does not sanitize. The psalm does not endorse the image it contains. It names what grief at that depth sounds like. The naming is itself an act of pastoral care.

I have sat with people whose grief was of that depth. Whose loss was not metaphorical. Whose anger was not performing but actual, directed at God with the full force of someone who had believed and been devastated. The impulse of the American evangelical church is to move quickly in those rooms toward comfort and resolution, to offer the psalm of orientation before the person is ready for it, to skip the lament and go straight to the new orientation. I have done this. I have been the pastor who rushed the prayer toward resolution because the unresolved darkness made me uncomfortable. What I was communicating in those moments, without intending to, was that this person's honest condition was not acceptable in the presence of God — that they needed to adjust before they could pray properly.

The Psalter says otherwise.

## What Is Actually at Stake

Thomas Merton observed that the Psalms are in some sense the prayers of Christ himself — that when we pray the Psalms, we are praying in the voice of the one who learned them and prayed them before us [cite — confirm]. The cry of dereliction from the cross is Psalm 22. That is not incidental. Jesus, at the moment of maximum suffering, prayed the lament psalms. He had learned them in the synagogue at Nazareth. He prayed them when nothing else was left. The church that has excised the lament psalms from its prayer practice has, in a specific sense, excised from its prayer practice the prayers that Jesus prayed on the cross.

The Psalms also contain declarations of trust that only make sense coming from the other side of lament. Psalm 46's "God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble" (verse 1) lands differently if you have prayed Psalm 44's accusation first. The trust has weight because it has been tested. The orientation of Psalm 23 — "Even though I walk through the darkest valley" — is not the orientation of someone who has never been in the valley. It is the orientation of someone who has been there and has found God there.

The church that only uses the trust psalms and skips the accusation psalms is producing a thin form of faith that is not equipped for the actual conditions of human life. People who pray only psalms of orientation are not prepared for the conditions that call for psalms of disorientation. When those conditions arrive — and they will — they discover that their prayer vocabulary does not include what they are experiencing, and they conclude that either their experience is wrong or their faith is insufficient. Neither is true. Their prayer education was simply incomplete.

## How to Pray Them Again

The most important thing is to read the whole collection, including the parts you have skipped. Particularly the parts you have skipped.

The next most important thing is to understand that the Psalms are permission. Permission to be angry at God. Permission to accuse. Permission to say that you cannot find him, that the prayers are not being answered, that the darkness is lasting longer than you were told it would. The permission is not the end of the prayer. It is the beginning of the kind of prayer that goes somewhere real, because it starts somewhere real rather than starting where we think prayer is supposed to start.

Pray Psalm 88 in a season when you have no resolution to offer. Pray Psalm 22 when you are sitting with someone who has none. Pray Psalm 137 with honesty about what grief at the level of total loss actually feels like, even if the specific circumstances differ. Pray Psalm 44 when the prayers have not been answered and the silence is piling up.

The Psalms are not poetry, though they are also poetry. They are not history, though they are also history. They are the voice of people in extremity, talking to God, and they are the record that God accepted that conversation — that the conversation counted, that the cry was heard even when the answer was slow or strange or not what was asked for.

Pray them. All of them.

Especially the ones that end in darkness.

The photographs from multi-ethnic Sunday services are real. The warmth in those rooms is real. No one who has experienced genuine worship across racial lines would dismiss what happens there. It is a glimpse — a real glimpse — of something the New Testament insists is central to the church's identity: that the dividing wall of hostility between peoples has been broken down in Christ (Ephesians 2:14). That is not a minor theological claim. Paul names it as the demonstration — the visible, material, social demonstration — that the powers of division and enmity have met something they could not overcome.

But a photograph of diversity is not reconciliation. A moment of warmth is not reconciliation. Reconciliation is a specific theological movement — from estrangement to restored relationship — and it has a specific requirement that the American church has largely tried to satisfy without meeting.

The requirement is repentance.

## The Requirement Is Repentance

Not acknowledged wrongdoing. Not regret about how things turned out. Not the careful wording that expresses sadness without any agent who caused the sadness. Repentance — the Hebrew *shuv*, the Greek *metanoia* — is a turning. A turning away from the patterns that produced the estrangement, toward a different way of being that demonstrates in practice that something has actually changed. Without the turning, what you have is apology without amendment. The relationship does not change. The power arrangements do not change. The systems that produced the injury continue to produce it. Only the language about them has shifted.

And that, precisely, is the shape of what the American church has mostly offered.

> Without the turning, what you have is apology without amendment.

The history is not disputed among historians who have examined it. American Christianity — Protestant and Catholic — has a documented record of institutional choices made consistently across centuries in the service of racial hierarchy: white churches that provided theological justification for chattel slavery, drawing on Scripture with a confidence matched only by their misuse of it; that remained largely silent during the lynching era, which took between 4,000 and 5,000 lives in the American South between 1877 and 1950 [cite — confirm these figures]; that organized opposition to school integration in the 1950s and 1960s in the name of biblical principle; that used the structures of religious affiliation to protect social arrangements that the prophets would have recognized — without difficulty — as the exploitation of the weak by the powerful. The documentation exists. It is not a polemical construction. It is the record.

## The Record Is Not Disputed

The response to that record that the American church has most commonly attempted is reconciliation-without-turning. Diverse programming, cross-cultural preaching events, statements of acknowledgment, partnerships that are more symbolic than structural. Worship teams that reflect diversity. Guest preachers from communities that have been historically excluded. Language that expresses sorrow without specifying what the sorrow requires. These things are not nothing. They are not nothing. But they ask the people who were harmed to do the emotional labor of performing reconciliation for the benefit of the institution that harmed them, and they leave the institutional structures unchanged.

Genuine repentance would require something harder and more specific.

It would require white congregations to ask — honestly, without the retreat into abstraction that makes the question painless — what they have materially benefited from through the historical arrangements they now apologize for. The wealth that passed through hands kept in order by the threat of violence. The land. The educational advantage. The social standing. The ability to build equity while redlining prevented their neighbors from doing the same. These are not ancient grievances without contemporary relevance. They are the mechanisms by which the gap between white and Black family wealth in America came to be approximately ten to one, [cite — confirm current figures] a gap that was not produced by individual choices and cannot be closed by individual choices, because it was produced by coordinated institutional action over generations.

Acknowledging the gap and asking what restoration might require is not a political move. It is a theological move — it is what Zacchaeus did (Luke 19:8). It is what Leviticus 6 requires of the person who has defrauded another: restitution plus a fifth. It is what the Jubilee laws in Leviticus 25 were designed to accomplish at the structural level — the periodic correction of the accumulations of advantage that market economies reliably produce. The theology of restoration is not new. It is woven through the canon.

## Diagnostic Questions, Not Accusations

It would also require those same congregations to examine their present structures — not their histories but their present realities. Who holds power in this congregation? Who makes the decisions that determine the congregation's direction and resource allocation? Whose cultural preferences shape the worship, the programming, the aesthetics, the social norms? Whose comfort is protected when conflict about these things arises? Whose interpretation of the faith is treated as the default, requiring no defense, against which other interpretations must prove themselves?

These are not accusatory questions. They are diagnostic ones. A congregation that examines them honestly will often discover that the answer is, across the board: the same demographic that has historically held power in American institutions. That is not surprising. It is the predictable result of institutional history. What would be surprising is a congregation that saw this and responded with something other than defensive assertion that the current arrangement is simply the result of who showed up.

> That is not neutral.

I am not writing about other churches. I am writing about my own failures in this territory, which are real. I have been in rooms where reconciliation language was fluent and structural change was absent. I have been part of conversations that produced warmth and produced nothing else. I have preached texts about unity across difference without examining the ways my own congregation's culture was organized around the comfort of people who were already comfortable there. I have called this hospitality when it was closer to invitation-without-change — the message that you are welcome to join what we have built and to find your place within it, rather than the message that your presence changes what we are.

## The Standard Was Always an Actual Turning

That is not neutral. It is complicity in a milder register, and the mildness does not make it innocent. It makes it harder to see.

The New Testament's vision in Galatians 3:28 — neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female, all one in Christ — was not describing a feeling shared at a gathering. It was describing an economic and social reality that was, in the communities Paul was writing to, visibly and practically true: the wealthy sharing meals with the poor, the educated with the uneducated, the Jew with the Gentile, in ways that violated every social expectation of first-century Mediterranean culture. The church was scandalous precisely because the reconciliation was actual. It changed who sat at whose table. It changed who was treated as family. It changed the material arrangements of daily life.

That is the standard. Not a better photograph. An actual turning.

Willie James Jennings, in *The Christian Imagination*, argues that the failure of Western Christianity to produce genuine multiracial communion is not a peripheral failure — it is a failure at the center of the church's understanding of itself. [cite — confirm Jennings's argument] The church that produced racial hierarchy did not produce it despite its theology. It produced it by deploying a theology that separated the spiritual from the social, the interior from the structural, in ways that made the gospel compatible with any existing arrangement of power. That is the theological problem that reconciliation language without structural change reproduces in updated form.

## What Actual Turning Looks Like

The word for reconciliation that costs nothing is not reconciliation. The word for warmth without turning is not healing. The word for diverse photographs that cover unchanged power structures is the one already named: marketing.

Until the turning, the language is something other than what it claims to be. And the people who have been waiting for the turning — who have extended grace and good faith across decades of reconciliation conversations that produced warmth and produced nothing else — those people are not wrong to be skeptical. They have simply been paying attention to what the institutions have actually done, which is the only reliable guide to what the institutions actually intend.

What does actual turning look like? It looks like the congregation that examines its elder board and asks not "why don't more people of color want to lead here?" but "what about how we operate makes it difficult for people who are not from our culture to hold authority here, and what are we willing to change?" It looks like the denomination that moves from a statement acknowledging its history with slavery to a specific, material commitment — funded, accountable, with a timeline — to address the educational and economic disparities its predecessor churches helped create. It looks like the pastor who names from the pulpit that his tradition carries a specific debt, and invites his congregation into the discomfort of asking what payment looks like, rather than smoothing the discomfort in the interest of institutional peace.

> Repentance is specific.

These are not hypothetical demands. They are what repentance has always looked like. The Zacchaeus moment in Luke 19 did not require extended discernment about what justice asked. Zacchaeus announced, without prompting, that he would give half his possessions to the poor and repay fourfold anyone he had defrauded. The specificity was the repentance. Vague contrition is not a turning. It is the preparation for a turning that never arrives.

The church is not incapable of this. It has done harder things. The communities that organized the underground railroad, the congregations that defied the Fugitive Slave Act at risk to their members, the white ministers who marched across the Edmund Pettus Bridge and absorbed the consequences — these were real, costly, specific acts of institutional turning. [cite — confirm] They were insufficient to undo the whole history, but they were not nothing. They were the beginning of the kind of witness that produces credibility.

Repentance is specific. It names what it is turning from, describes what it is turning toward, and demonstrates the change in action. It is costly exactly in proportion to the harm it is addressing.

Nothing less will do what reconciliation requires. And anything less, however warmly expressed, is asking the people who were harmed to settle for the appearance of a thing they were promised and have not yet received.

The rich young ruler walked away sad (Mark 10:22). Jesus let him go.

This moment tends to make us uncomfortable, so we soften it. We note that Jesus loved him (Mark 10:21), which is true. We point to the broader context about things being possible with God, which is also true. What we do less readily is sit with the plain sequence of events: a wealthy, morally serious, spiritually seeking young man asked Jesus what was required, Jesus told him to sell what he had and give it to the poor, and the man left. And Jesus did not call after him with a more accommodating answer. He watched him go and then told his disciples: it is very hard for the wealthy to enter the kingdom of God.

Very hard. Not impossible, but the disciples' astonishment — "Then who can be saved?" — tells us they heard this as a radical narrowing of expectation. Jesus had just made a theological statement about the relationship between accumulated wealth and the kingdom, and the statement was not comfortable.

The American church has worked very hard to make it comfortable again.

> The American church has worked very hard to make it comfortable again.

Not explicitly. No one gives a sermon titled "the rich young ruler was wrong to leave." But the theology gets reconstructed through emphasis — through what gets said and what does not, through whose stories are told from the stage, through whose comfort level shapes the ministry culture. A congregation that measures its success by the quality of its facilities and the income level of its zip code has made choices about which demographic it is optimized to reach. Those choices are theological, even when they are not named as such.

## The Principled Defense

There are articulate defenses of ministry that disproportionately engages the wealthy. Wealthy people have resources that multiply ministry impact. A congregation with financial stability can fund missionaries, support benevolence, sustain programs that serve the poor. The wealthy need the gospel too, and it would be reverse snobbery to treat their souls as less valuable. To deliberately avoid reaching successful people out of some romantic preference for the poor would be its own error. These arguments are not frivolous.

> The road paved with pragmatism arrives, eventually, at a destination that is not the one the gospel describes.

But they have a tendency to become cover for something less defensible: the decision to build ministry cultures that are comfortable for people with disposable income, located in areas accessible to the affluent, structured around programming sensibilities that reflect middle and upper-class assumptions, staffed by leaders whose personal financial situation insulates them from the daily precarity that shapes the lives of the poor. None of this is consciously chosen as anti-poor policy. It is the accumulated effect of a thousand small decisions, each of which felt pragmatic rather than theological.

The road paved with pragmatism arrives, eventually, at a destination that is not the one the gospel describes.

## The Shape of Jesus's Ministry

Jesus's ministry did not look like what the comfortable church has built. He was based in Galilee, not Jerusalem — a provincial region associated with economic marginality and limited cultural prestige [cite — confirm]. His primary audience was peasant farmers, fishermen, people living at subsistence level under both Roman taxation and the temple tax system. The twelve he chose were not drawn from the educated class. When he described the scope of his mission in Luke 4:18, borrowing from Isaiah 61, the list was specific: the poor, the captive, the blind, the oppressed.

These are not metaphorical categories. They are social descriptions of people at the bottom of every hierarchy in the ancient world. Jesus did not come primarily to people who had other good options and were wondering which way to optimize their lives. He came to people for whom the good news was genuinely, materially news — who had nothing else to try, nowhere else to go.

Luke's Gospel preserves the starkest account of this orientation. In Luke 6:20–26, Matthew's "poor in spirit" becomes simply "poor" — the literal poor, those who literally hunger, those who literally weep. And the woes are addressed to the literally rich, the literally full, the literally comfortable. Luke is not spiritualizing. He is quoting a Jesus who said things that made the established order uncomfortable, and the reason this Jesus gets softened in so many sermons is precisely because his comfort level with the poor makes us uneasy about our own.

Paul makes an observation about the Corinthian church that reads as almost sociological: "Not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth" (1 Corinthians 1:26). The church at Corinth was disproportionately poor, low-status, marginalized. Paul does not treat this as a problem to solve. He treats it as a revelation of God's logic — that God chose the foolish to shame the wise, the weak to shame the strong, the low and despised to bring to nothing the things that are (1 Corinthians 1:27–28). This is not accidental. It is the sign of what kind of movement this is and who it was built around.

> The cross is not efficient.

## What the Historical Record Shows

The reforming movements in church history that most faithfully embodied the gospel's priorities have consistently been movements that moved toward the poor rather than the wealthy. The early Methodist movement in eighteenth-century England deliberately engaged the coal miners, mill workers, and urban poor of an industrializing society that the established church had largely abandoned [cite — confirm]. William Booth founded the Salvation Army in the slums of East London in 1865 [cite — confirm], not in the drawing rooms of the middle class. Dorothy Day and the Catholic Worker movement planted their houses in the poorest neighborhoods of American cities, not in the suburbs where the giving was reliable [cite — confirm].

These movements did not avoid the wealthy. They did not treat the wealthy as beyond reach. But their gravitational center was at the bottom of the social order, not the top, and that center shaped everything — their vocabulary, their priorities, their institutional culture, their willingness to bear costs that a prosperity-oriented church would never accept.

The revivalism that shaped American evangelicalism moved in a different direction. Charles Finney's anxious bench was pitched to farmers and merchants in upstate New York [cite — confirm], not to the urban poor. Dwight Moody's revivals were sustained by the donations of wealthy industrialists like Cyrus McCormick and Jay Cooke [cite — confirm]. The arrangement was not corrupt. But it created dependencies that shaped what could and could not be said, and what populations were and were not centered in the ministry's imagination.

By the twentieth century, the megachurch movement that came to define evangelical success had largely completed the orientation toward the suburban middle class. The mega-facilities that became the flagship of American Christian witness were built in the fastest-growing, wealthiest suburbs — not by accident, but by deliberate demographic targeting. The prosperity gospel that emerged from this environment was not an aberration. It was the logical conclusion of a trajectory that had been building for a century.

## The Cost to Witness

I have made decisions about where to focus ministry energy that followed the logic of resource efficiency rather than the logic of the cross. I have considered which neighborhoods offered the best growth potential, which demographics were most likely to give, which partnerships would enhance the church's reputation. That is not entirely wrong — stewardship requires thinking about resources. But when it becomes the primary logic, it has displaced something essential.

The cross is not efficient. It reaches down rather than up. It spends toward the lost rather than the found, the marginal rather than the central, the ones who cannot reciprocate rather than the ones who can write a check.

The practical consequence of the church's orientation toward the comfortable is a credibility problem among the poor. The people most likely to have no other advocate — the incarcerated, the undocumented, the homeless, the addicted — tend to have the most precisely calibrated sense of whether an institution is actually on their side or is performing concern while protecting its donors. They have long memories for the times the church showed up and the times it didn't. They notice the difference between the church that comes to their neighborhood when there is a photo opportunity and the church that is there every Tuesday regardless.

That credibility is not recovered easily. It is built, or not built, in the thousand small decisions about where to locate, who to staff, what to fund, whose voices to center in the church's public witness. The rich young ruler walked away, and Jesus let him go. But Jesus stayed — in Galilee, among the poor, with the people the religious establishment had already written off.

I have not consistently done the same. I have made the easier calls more often than I want to admit, and the accumulated result is a ministry that reflects my comfort more than his priorities.

The hard thing about the rich young ruler story is not what Jesus said. It is what it reveals about the cost of saying nothing. The ruler walked away sad. Jesus watched him go. And then, in the silence after the departure, he turned to the disciples and told them the truth about money and the kingdom.

We have been qualifying that truth ever since. The qualifications are understandable. They are also the reason the poor continue to find the church — with its enormous resources and its enormous silence — more comfort to the comfortable than to them.

There is a congregation in nearly every American city that understands itself to be doing the work of the kingdom by bringing wealthy, educated, culturally influential people into the church. The strategic logic is coherent: if you can reach the people with resources and influence, they will fund the mission and shape the culture. Leaders matter. Resources matter. A church that influences the powerful has, in theory, outsized kingdom reach.

I have heard this argument from serious people who genuinely love God. I have made versions of it myself. It contains real truth, and the truth in it has made it possible to ignore the theological problem at its center for most of American church history.

The theological problem is Jesus.

---

## What Jesus Said About Wealth and the Kingdom

He was not subtle about this.

"It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God" (Matthew 19:24). The disciples, who shared the common cultural assumption that wealth was a sign of God's blessing, were "greatly astonished" and asked who, then, could be saved. Jesus did not retract the statement. He deepened it: "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible" — which is not a soft landing for the wealthy. It is an acknowledgment that the barrier is real and formidable.

Luke records that Jesus read from Isaiah at the synagogue in Nazareth to announce what his ministry would be: "good news to the poor," "freedom for the prisoners," "recovery of sight for the blind," "freedom for the oppressed" (Luke 4:18). He did not say "good news to the influential, which will eventually improve conditions for everyone." He named the poor first, specifically, as the primary recipients of the kingdom announcement.

> These are not metaphors.

The Beatitudes in Luke are more explicit than Matthew's version: "Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God" (Luke 6:20). And then: "Woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort" (Luke 6:24). These are not metaphors. They are social and economic categories, and the reversals they announce are genuine reversals. The kingdom puts these categories upside down.

The comfortable church has never quite known what to do with any of this.

---

## How the Money Shaped the Preaching

The American church's orientation toward wealth has historical roots that predate the contemporary megachurch. The Protestant work ethic, as Max Weber [cite — confirm] traced it, created a cultural logic in which material success was read as a sign of election — God's favor made visible in earthly prosperity. This was always a theological distortion, but it was an extraordinarily useful one for the emerging commercial culture of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. It sanctified accumulation. It made the successful man spiritually respectable and the poor man spiritually suspect.

The late-nineteenth and early-twentieth century saw this logic reach full flower in the Gospel of Wealth — most explicitly articulated by Andrew Carnegie [cite — confirm] — and in the parallel phenomenon of wealthy industrialists becoming prominent figures in and donors to the mainline Protestant churches. The church that was home to the Carnegie and Rockefeller families was not in a strong institutional position to prophesy against Gilded Age exploitation of labor. It was too dependent on the same.

Historian Richard Hofstadter [cite — confirm] and others have documented the degree to which American Protestant Christianity was shaped by the commercial class that dominated it financially. When the money in the room comes from a particular direction, the preaching tends to follow. This is not a conspiracy. It is an institutional logic that operates below the level of conscious decision: the pastor who offends his major donors loses his major donors, and the institution that depends on them cannot survive that loss. The financial pressure produces doctrinal outcomes over time.

The twentieth-century megachurch replicated and amplified this pattern. The churches that grew most dramatically in the suburban expansion of the postwar decades were churches that spoke the language and addressed the concerns of the middle and upper-middle class — the nuclear family, professional success, personal fulfillment, therapeutic wellbeing. The people who came to these churches in the largest numbers were the people for whom this message was most immediately relevant. The people for whom it was least relevant — the poor, the economically marginal, the incarcerated, the homeless — were not, structurally, the target.

---

## The Steelman for Reaching the Powerful

The logic of targeting the wealthy for kingdom impact has a steelman worth addressing honestly.

Billy Graham's ministry reached presidents and cultural leaders because he understood that influence multiplies through networks — that a converted executive shapes more lives than a converted laborer, not because the executive's soul is worth more, but because his reach is wider [cite — confirm]. The argument is pragmatic and not, in its pure form, theologically corrupt. The New Testament does not exclude the wealthy from the kingdom. Zacchaeus was a tax collector and wealthy, and Jesus sought him out. Nicodemus was a member of the ruling council, and Jesus engaged him at length. Joseph of Arimathea, who provided the tomb, was described as a rich man (Matthew 27:57). The church has had influential, wealthy members since its earliest days.

> The problem is not that the wealthy are welcome in the church.

The problem is not that the wealthy are welcome in the church. The problem is the organizational logic that makes reaching the wealthy the church's *primary* strategic orientation — that positions the poor as a ministry category rather than the theological center, that measures kingdom success in donor networks and cultural influence rather than in proximity to the people Jesus named first when he described his mission.

The difference between including the wealthy in a community organized around the poor and the marginalized, versus organizing the community around the wealthy and adding a charity program for the poor — that difference is not trivial. It determines who sits at the center of the church's life, whose concerns shape the preaching, whose presence defines the culture. It determines whether the poor are guests or neighbors. It determines whether the church's relationship to wealth is prophetic or dependent.

---

## Amos and the Church That Does Not Grieve

There is a passage in Amos that most wealthy congregations have not heard preached in its proper context. Chapter 6 opens: "Woe to you who are complacent in Zion, and to you who feel secure on Mount Samaria, you notable men of the foremost nation, to whom the people of Israel come!" (Amos 6:1). The notable men. The foremost nation. The people come to them. This is the church that has influence, that is respected, that sits at the tables of cultural power. And Amos's word to them is *woe* — because their comfort has made them indifferent to the suffering around them: "You do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph" (Amos 6:6). The ruin is happening. The notable men are not grieving it. They are lying on beds of ivory and singing songs to the sound of the harp.

The church organized around reaching the powerful is always in danger of becoming the church that does not grieve the ruin.

---

I have not been immune to this. I have felt the appeal of the growing church, the influential church, the church with the capacity to project its voice into the culture. I have felt the pull of a budget that allows real ministry to happen, funded by the generosity of people who have the resources to fund it. This is not entirely wrong. Ministry requires resources, and resources require givers, and the church that refuses to welcome givers because they are successful has made an error in the other direction.

But I have also sat across tables from pastors of small, underfunded, predominantly poor congregations whose theological clarity about the kingdom was sharper than anything I encountered in the places with the larger budgets and the more impressive reach. They knew something about the kingdom that the megachurch pastor does not easily know, because they are living in closer proximity to the people Jesus named first.

The institutional suspicion that greets the pastor who orients his church around the poor is real. It comes from boards who wonder about sustainability. It comes from denominational structures that measure success in attendance and giving. It comes from peer culture among pastors who define effectiveness in the metrics that wealthy churches produce. The pastor who turns toward the poor, in the American church environment, is not rowing with the current.

He is rowing against the current. The current is money.

---

## Who the Guest List Is Built Around

The question is not whether the church should exclude the wealthy. The question is whether the church has allowed wealth and its presence to become the organizing principle of its life and mission — whether the arrangement of the congregation, the tone of the preaching, the strategic choices about location and programming, have all been calibrated around the comfort and retention of people with resources, while the people Jesus named first remain somewhere over there, in the mercy ministry budget, not quite at the center.

Luke 14 contains the dinner party passage where Jesus instructs the host: "When you give a luncheon or dinner, do not invite your friends, your brothers or sisters, your relatives, or your rich neighbors; if you do, they may invite you back and so you will be repaid. But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed" (Luke 14:12-14).

He did not say refuse the rich. He said orient the table differently. He said the metric of kingdom faithfulness is who you invite when there is nothing to be gained.

The church that gathers only people who can give back to it has understood giving as transaction. The church that invites the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind — that church is describing something else. It is describing the kingdom of God.

That table is available. The question is who we are building our guest list around.

Trust, once broken, does not rebuild on a timeline. That is the first thing to understand, and the thing the person who broke it most needs to hear. There is no fixed duration. There is no moment when the betrayed partner is obligated to arrive at healed. Anyone who tells a betrayed spouse to "get over it" or "move on" or implies that continued hurt is a form of unforgiveness — is confusing trust with willpower.

Trust is not a decision. It is a conclusion the nervous system reaches based on accumulated evidence. You cannot decide to trust someone who has given you reason not to. You can decide to remain in the relationship while trust is being rebuilt. That is a different thing, and the difference matters enormously.

> Trust is not a decision.

This distinction is pastoral mercy dressed as neurological fact. The betrayed person who cannot "just trust again" is not spiritually weak. They are functioning exactly as designed. Bessel van der Kolk spent decades documenting what trauma does to the nervous system's ability to read safety [cite — confirm], and betrayal — especially in the most intimate relationship of a person's life — registers as trauma. The path forward is not willpower. It is evidence over time.

## The Biblical Architecture of Trust Repair

Proverbs 25:19 says trust in an unfaithful person in a time of trouble is like a broken tooth or a foot that slips. The writer is not being harsh. They are being accurate. A broken trust placed under weight will fail again. The question in a marriage recovering from betrayal is not "should we trust" — it is "what has to be rebuilt before trust can bear weight again?"

The answer is almost always the same: three things, in order. Acknowledgment. Changed behavior. Time. And the order is not negotiable.

**Acknowledgment without changed behavior is an apology. Changed behavior without acknowledgment is performance. Neither one is repair.**

Acknowledgment means the person who broke trust names specifically what they did, without softening it with context, without distributing the blame, without pivoting to their own pain. "I lied to you about this for this long and it was wrong" is acknowledgment. "I wasn't getting what I needed and I made a bad choice" is something else. The second statement may be true, but it is not acknowledgment. It is explanation. Explanations, in the early stages of trust repair, are received as minimization — because they redirect attention from the wound to the wound-maker's context.

The distinction matters because the betrayed person's nervous system is not reading the content of the apology. It is reading whether the person doing the apologizing understands the weight of what happened. Full acknowledgment communicates: I see what I did. I see what it cost you. I am not minimizing either.

Changed behavior is the acknowledgment made real over time. It is the open phone. The answered question. The willingness to be inconvenienced by accountability without resentment. The person rebuilding trust does not get to decide when they have done enough. The person whose trust was broken is the one keeping score — and that is appropriate, not punitive.

> You cannot rush a nervous system with sincerity.

Time is the third element because the nervous system takes time to update. You cannot rush a nervous system with sincerity. You can only provide consistent evidence and allow the conclusion to form at its own pace.

## The Historical Arc of This Problem

The pastoral tradition has not always served betrayed spouses well. For much of church history, the pressure has been toward rapid forgiveness and the restoration of outward marital function — driven by a theology of marriage permanence that, in practice, sometimes functioned to protect the person who broke trust rather than to genuinely serve the person who bore the cost of the breaking.

Augustine's theology of marriage as a sacramental bond that cannot be dissolved [cite — confirm] shaped the Western church's reflexive resistance to acknowledging how devastating betrayal is to the fabric of the relationship. The emphasis fell on keeping the institution intact. The person holding the wound was expected to prioritize the institution over their own condition. This produced generations of marriages that looked intact from the outside and were empty on the inside — two people performing covenant while one of them was still bleeding.

The Protestant tradition corrected some of this with its recognition of legitimate grounds for divorce, but the pastoral practice of many Protestant churches retained the emotional logic of the older position: minimize the disruption, prioritize reconciliation, treat the betrayed person's prolonged grief as a spiritual problem rather than an appropriate response to a real wound.

Neither tradition has served betrayed people as well as the Scripture itself does, which gives us Job sitting in ashes for seven days while his friends are silent (Job 2:13), gives us the lament psalms' unflinching exposure of pain without resolution, gives us Jesus at Lazarus's tomb weeping even when he knows what is about to happen — because the grief is real and requires genuine acknowledgment before the resurrection.

## What the Church Often Gets Wrong

Two pastoral errors are common. The first is rushing forgiveness into trust. Forgiveness is a gift the betrayed person can give before trust has returned — it releases them from the corrosive weight of bitterness. But forgiveness is not the same as trust. You can forgive someone and still require changed behavior before trusting them. The two are parallel tracks, not a sequence.

Colossians 3:13 calls believers to "forgive each other as the Lord has forgiven you." The model of divine forgiveness does not mean the absence of consequences — throughout the Old Testament narrative, forgiven people still lived with the results of their choices. The prodigal son is restored, but the years in the far country are not undone. Forgiveness cancels the debt of bitterness the betrayed person would otherwise carry. It does not cancel the requirement for demonstrated change before intimacy is restored.

The second error is treating the betrayed person's ongoing hurt as a spiritual problem. When a spouse who has been lied to or cheated on remains cautious, asks hard questions, struggles with triggers — this is not unforgiveness. This is an accurate nervous system doing its job. The pastoral response is not to correct them. It is to sit with them in it.

Jesus said in Matthew 10:16 to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Wisdom, in the aftermath of betrayal, looks like requiring evidence before extending trust. That is not bitterness. That is faithfulness to the marriage you are trying to save.

## The Counter-Position Worth Hearing

There is a position in some pastoral counseling traditions that the demand for ongoing behavioral evidence amounts to the betrayed spouse holding power over the marriage in a way that prevents genuine healing. The argument is that genuine forgiveness must include the restoration of trust as an act of will — that to require evidence indefinitely is to make the betrayed person the judge of the marriage rather than a participant in its healing.

This position has enough pastoral concern in it to deserve a direct answer. It is true that prolonged, weaponized suspicion can itself become destructive — that a person can use their wound as a weapon in ways that prevent genuine repair even when genuine repair is being offered. This happens. It is worth naming.

But the solution is not to require the betrayed person to trust before trust has been earned. The solution is to distinguish between appropriate caution and weaponized suspicion — a distinction that a skilled counselor can help a couple work through. The concern about power imbalance does not disappear by removing the betrayed person's legitimate right to require evidence. It disappears when the person who broke trust provides the evidence consistently enough that the need to demand it diminishes.

## A Concrete Pastoral Scene

I sat with a couple in which the husband had maintained a secret email correspondence with a former girlfriend for the better part of three years. Nothing physically happened. He described it as "just talking." His wife, who discovered it, did not experience it as "just talking."
