The threshold of legal personhood, the specific circumstances under which the competing claims of the woman and the unborn should be adjudicated, the exact developmental moment at which all the implications of the Imago Dei attach — these applications require wisdom, context, and the kind of careful reasoning that proof-texting shortcuts.

The church owes the people in its pews — and the people watching from a distance, deciding whether the church is worth trusting — an honest account of what Scripture actually establishes versus what has been claimed in Scripture's name. The conflation of those two things has produced both bad theology and bad pastoral practice: people who abandon a conviction because it was overstated, and people who defend a position with more certainty than the texts actually warrant. Both failures damage the people the argument is meant to serve.

The conviction is biblical. Some of the certainty claimed in its name is not. Knowing the difference between those two things is not an act of theological weakness. It is what honest interpretation requires.

> The conviction is biblical. Some of the certainty claimed in its name is not.

And honest interpretation is the only kind that can actually serve the people whose lives depend on getting this right.

There is a number that marriage researchers use: fewer than ten times a year. Below that threshold, the clinical language is "sexless marriage." The research suggests it describes somewhere between fifteen and twenty percent of marriages at any given time, and that the actual number is likely higher, because this is not a topic people report accurately [cite — confirm].

It is also not a topic most pastors address. The silence from the pulpit on this specific subject is near-total, which means the couple experiencing it has nowhere in their faith community to bring it. They carry it alone, each in their own interpretation of what it means, each accumulating a story about the marriage and the other person that may or may not be accurate.

The conversation that does not happen is not only costing them intimacy. It is costing them the chance to understand what the absence is actually about.

> The conversation that does not happen is not only costing them intimacy. It is costing them the chance to understand what the absence is actually about.

## The Biblical Vision That Makes the Silence Indefensible

Song of Solomon 7:10 — "I am my beloved's and his desire is for me" — is a statement of mutual desire as the natural condition of a covenant marriage. The biblical vision of sex in marriage is not merely permissive; it is expectant. The entire arc of Song of Solomon treats erotic desire as a gift embedded in the creation order, not a concession to human weakness. The church's historical discomfort with the book's frankness has sometimes led to allegorical readings that evacuate its most immediate content. But the most straightforward reading is also the most theologically productive: God made human beings with bodies, with desire, with the capacity for pleasure in each other, and that making is called very good (Genesis 1:31).

Paul's instruction in 1 Corinthians 7:3-5 is explicit and anatomically frank in a way that surprises first-time readers: "The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control."

The instruction is mutual — notice that the authority runs in both directions, a genuinely countercultural statement in a Greco-Roman context where the husband's authority over the wife's body was assumed and the reverse was not. The implied baseline is regular, mutually engaged sexual intimacy. Paul treats its absence not as a neutral condition but as a vulnerability that requires specific justification and a defined endpoint.

**The body keeps honest what the conversation has avoided. What a couple is not doing in the bedroom is usually connected to what they are not saying in the kitchen.**

## The Historical Weight of Church Silence

The church's silence on this topic has deep roots. The patristic period produced a theology of sexuality in which the body was a problematic inheritance from the fall rather than a gift from creation. Augustine's influential treatment of concupiscence — the disordered desire that marks fallen sexuality — cast a long shadow over the tradition's capacity to affirm sexual desire within marriage as genuinely good [cite — confirm]. The shadow persists. Many Christians who have grown up in churches that preached purity culture have internalized a view of the body as primarily dangerous rather than primarily good — a site of temptation rather than a vehicle of covenantal connection.

This formation does real damage to marriages. A person who has spent their formative years learning to manage and suppress sexual desire in order to be holy does not automatically reverse that training when they receive a marriage certificate. The suppression continues. The body that was managed as a spiritual liability is now expected to function as a relational gift. That transition is harder than any pre-marital curriculum adequately prepares couples to make.

The history here is not uniformly negative. John Calvin's theology of marriage as a genuine good, Martin Luther's robust affirmation of sexual intimacy within the covenant, the Puritan tradition's surprising frankness about marital sexuality — all of these represent genuine corrections within the tradition [cite — confirm]. But they have not fully displaced the older suspicion of embodied desire that the patristic period installed.

## The Causes Are Not Monolithic

> The biblical vision of sex in marriage is not merely permissive; it is expectant.

The gap between that vision and what many marriages are actually experiencing is real. And the gap is not primarily a moral failure. It is almost always a symptom of something else.

Sometimes it is medical — hormonal shifts, chronic illness, medication side effects, pain conditions that are being treated as personal failure rather than physical reality. Testosterone decline in men and estrogen decline in women, the sexual side effects of antidepressants and blood pressure medications, the genuine physical disruption of chronic pain or illness — these are not spiritual problems. They are physical conditions that deserve medical attention without shame.

Sometimes it is psychological — unprocessed trauma, depression, anxiety, the crushing exhaustion of a season of life that has stripped every margin. The connection between mental health and sexual desire is direct and well-documented. A person in the grip of clinical depression does not have low desire because they do not love their spouse. They have low desire because the condition suppresses the neurological systems that generate it.

Sometimes it is relational — resentment that has migrated from the emotional to the physical, the body refusing what the heart cannot yet offer. This is perhaps the most common form, and the most important for couples to understand: the absence of sexual intimacy in this case is not the problem. It is the symptom of an unaddressed relational problem. Addressing the physical without addressing the relational produces at best compliance without desire, which is not the biblical vision.

Sometimes it is the slow default of two people who got busy and kept intending to reconnect and kept not doing it until the gap became its own obstacle. Inertia is a real force in marriages. The couple who went three months without intimacy during a particular season of stress often discovers that the three months became a year before they noticed, and that the year has now built its own awkwardness around reengaging.

## The Counter-Position Worth Hearing

Some pastoral counselors argue that the explicit clinical discussion of sexual frequency — the setting of targets, the therapeutic language of "desire discrepancy," the behavioral interventions — reduces what should be an expression of intimate covenant love to a performance metric. The concern is that treating sexual intimacy as a goal to be achieved by technique misses the relational soil in which genuine desire grows.

This concern has real weight. The couple who has a better technique but no better emotional connection has not solved the actual problem. Desire is not primarily mechanical — it is relational, and the relational conditions for desire are built or eroded by everything that happens outside the bedroom as well as within it.

But the concern should not produce pastoral silence. The couple sitting in private shame about something that pastoral care and good clinical support can address is not served by the preacher's discretion. They are abandoned by it. The pastoral responsibility is not to be clinical about something intimate — it is to name the reality enough to give permission to the couple to address it, with whatever support they need.

## What the Conversation Needs to Include

It needs honesty about which person is experiencing more distance from desire — and why. It needs the other person to receive that honesty without defensiveness, which is one of the hardest things to do in a long marriage. It needs both people to distinguish between "I do not want intimacy with you" and "I do not have access to desire right now," because those are very different situations with very different implications.

It also needs to include the possibility of professional help — medical, therapeutic, or both — without shame. The couple who has not had sex in eighteen months is not beyond help. They are, in most cases, a few honest conversations and a competent counselor away from a path forward.

What the conversation almost never needs: performance pressure, comparison to other couples, or the implied accusation that the lower-drive partner is withholding something they owe. Desire cannot be compelled. It can be cultivated — in an environment of safety, kindness, and the genuine belief that the other person sees you as a whole person and not a need-delivery system.

Do you know what is actually driving the distance? Is it relational, physical, psychological, or some combination? Have you asked your doctor or a counselor?

Does the lower-drive partner feel safe enough to tell the truth about what they actually need in order for desire to return? Does the higher-drive partner know what that safety requires of them?

The group flew fourteen hours, built a wall for three days, tore it down because it was not structurally sound, and then flew home with photographs and a renewed sense of purpose. The local construction workers who could have built the wall correctly in one day were not hired. The money spent on flights and lodging would have funded six months of local wages. The photographs were beautiful.

That story is not a caricature. It is a real pattern that has been documented extensively in the literature on short-term missions [cite — confirm], and the fact that it is still happening at scale inside the American church says something significant about the purposes the short-term trip actually serves — and for whom.

## Who the Trip Actually Serves

The honest question, the one that most pastors and youth pastors do not want to ask before they start the fundraising campaign, is this: who does this trip primarily benefit? The answer, more often than the church admits, is the participants.

That is not necessarily a damning answer. Formation of the trip participants is a legitimate purpose. The young person who returns from two weeks in another country having encountered poverty and faith at a depth that is not available in suburban America has been changed. That change has value. It may produce decades of giving, advocacy, and genuine cross-cultural relationship. It may produce a missionary. The formation of the American church for global awareness and generosity is a real need, and short-term trips are one tool for meeting it.

The question is whether that formation can be accomplished without extracting a cost from the communities the trips are ostensibly serving.

## How the Short-Term Trip Became an Institution

The short-term mission trip as an institution in the American church is relatively recent. The modern form emerged in the late 1970s and 1980s, as air travel became affordable and as the church growth movement began to emphasize experiential engagement with global Christianity [cite — confirm]. By the 1990s the short-term mission trip had become a standard feature of youth ministry calendars, and by the early 2000s an estimated 1.5 million Americans were participating in short-term mission trips annually [cite — confirm]. The industry built around equipping, placing, and organizing those trips has become significant. The evaluation of whether the trips serve their stated purposes has lagged considerably behind the growth.

The most rigorous critics of short-term missions — including Robert Lupton in *Toxic Charity* [cite — confirm] and the broader conversation in international development about "voluntourism" — are not arguing that trips are always harmful. They are arguing that the design of the trip determines its effect, and that most trips in the American church are designed around the participants' needs rather than the host community's needs. Those are not the same thing, and treating them as though they are is the most common and most damaging error in short-term missions practice.

The trip designed around participants' needs asks: what can these people usefully do for one week? What will be meaningful to them? What story will they carry home? The trip designed around the host community's needs asks: what does this community actually need, in what timeframe, at what skill level, and is a short-term team the right instrument for meeting it? Those questions lead to very different trips, and very different outcomes.

## Designed Around the Participants or the Host

The answer, developed by practitioners and researchers in international development over the past thirty years, is that it depends entirely on how the trip is designed and what relationship it exists within [cite — confirm]. The trip that serves the mission is embedded in a long-term partnership with a national church or ministry that identifies the need, directs the work, and retains authority over the outcome. The trip that serves the trip is designed from the sending church's end, around the availability and capacities of the participants, and arrives in the host community with a predetermined agenda that may or may not correspond to what is actually needed there.

The former requires relationship before the trip. It requires that the pastor or ministry leader in the host community have a genuine voice in the design — what tasks, what timeline, what preparation, what follow-up. It requires that the trip participants arrive with the posture of learners rather than rescuers. That posture shift is not easy to produce. It requires pre-trip preparation that most sending churches do not invest in — not just logistics and fundraising, but the theological reorientation from "we are going to help" to "we are going to serve under the direction of people who know more than we do about what is needed here."

## When Help Becomes a Wound

The trip that produces dependency — where the community learns to orient its development calendar around the annual arrival of American volunteers rather than around building its own capacities — is doing harm regardless of the good intentions involved. Sustained dependency is not a gift. It is a wound delivered with warmth and enthusiasm. When the medical team comes every year to provide care that the local clinic could provide if it were staffed and supplied, the annual trip becomes an argument against investing in the local clinic. Why build permanent capacity when Americans will provide it for free each summer?

> Sustained dependency is not a gift. It is a wound delivered with warmth and enthusiasm.

The pastoral question is not whether to do short-term trips. It is whether to design them in a way that serves the people in the host community rather than primarily serving the participants' need for a significant experience. That design question requires asking the host community — not the trip organizers — what they actually need, and being willing to hear that what they need is money rather than presence, local labor rather than foreign volunteers, sustained partnership rather than annual visits.

There is a legitimate counter-argument here that deserves honest engagement. Some practitioners of short-term missions contend that the critics overstate the harm and understate the formational value — that the American church's engagement with global mission would collapse without the visceral, personal experience that trips provide, and that a congregation of people who have stood in a community experiencing poverty and met believers of deep faith under difficult conditions gives differently, prays differently, and advocates differently than a congregation that has only read about those things. This is not wrong. The experience is irreplaceable in the way that all direct encounter is irreplaceable. The question is whether there are ways to design that formational encounter that do not extract a cost from the communities that host it.

The trip that serves both the participants and the host community is possible. It is not the norm. It requires:

A pre-existing long-term relationship between the sending church and a national ministry, where the national leader has genuine authority to shape what the team does.

A fundraising model that raises significantly more than the cost of the trip — ideally two to three times — so that money stays in the community after the team leaves and continues work the team started.

A post-trip engagement structure that converts the experience into sustained action: ongoing giving, advocacy, correspondence with the national partners, and the commitment to return not annually for a fresh formational experience but periodically as part of a deepening relationship.

## What I Should Not Have Sent

I have sent groups on trips I should not have sent them on. The budget, the enthusiasm, the formational opportunity for the participants — all of those were real, and none of them guaranteed that the people we visited were actually served. In some cases they were served. In other cases we were building walls that needed to be torn down, spending resources on travel that the host ministry needed for operations, and producing in ourselves a sense of accomplishment that did not correspond to what we had actually accomplished.

James 1:27 defines pure religion as visiting orphans and widows in their affliction and keeping oneself unstained from the world. The first part of that definition is active — go to where the need is, be present, be involved. The second part is harder — keep yourself unstained from the world's way of doing things, including the world's way of helping, which turns the vulnerable into objects of the helper's need for significance.

The trip that keeps itself unstained is the trip that is genuinely oriented toward the people it is serving rather than toward the story the participants will bring home. That trip is more difficult to design, less immediately satisfying to the participants, and more likely to produce lasting good.

> The trip that keeps itself unstained is the trip that is genuinely oriented toward the people it is serving rather than toward the story the participants will bring home.

It is also less common.

That is a question worth sitting with before the next fundraising campaign begins.

## A Theology of Mission for Whom

The pastor who is willing to ask that question honestly — not to stop the trips, but to stop designing them for the wrong person — will likely find that the conversation with his congregation about missions design is more formative than most of the trips themselves. The conversation that says, "We have been doing this primarily for our own formation, and we need to decide whether we are willing to redesign it around the actual needs of the people we go to serve," is a theological conversation about who the mission is for. That conversation, done honestly, does more to form a genuine theology of mission in a congregation than a hundred trips can do.

It also requires the humility to tell the story honestly when you come back — not only the inspiring version, but the version that includes the question marks. The teams I have seen come home with the most durable formation were the teams whose leaders refused to package the experience into a tidy narrative of impact. The team that came home saying, "We are not sure what we accomplished, but we met people, and we were changed by what we met" is the team that is ready to go back differently.

Most teams do not come home saying that. Most come home with the wall story and the photographs.

> The work of redesigning short-term missions for integrity begins with the willingness to tell the honest version.

God speaks to the shepherds of Israel who have fed themselves on the flock rather than feeding it. Who have not strengthened the weak. Not sympathetically. With fury. "I am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep at their hand" (Ezekiel 34:10).

## The Ancient Failure of the Shepherds

The scandal of abuse in Christian institutions is not a modern problem with a modern cause. It is the ancient failure of shepherds who served themselves, and the ancient pattern of structures that protected the shepherd's position over the sheep's life. What is modern is the scale of documentation, the courage of survivors who refused to stay quiet, and the public accounting that has followed. The reports on Sovereign Grace Ministries, the Southern Baptist Convention abuse investigation that surfaced hundreds of documented cases over twenty years, the investigations across multiple Catholic dioceses — [cite — confirm] these are not peripheral events in the history of the church. They are the same event: institutionalized protection of abusers and systematic silencing of those they harmed.

I have to say something before I continue arguing.

I have served on committees. I have participated in conversations where the primary concern, before anyone named the harm done to a person, was what this would mean for the church's reputation and the ministry's continuation. I knew, in those rooms, that something was wrong with the priorities. I did not name it with the directness the moment required. I know what it is to choose institution over person while telling yourself you are managing the situation wisely. That was not wisdom. That was complicity with a pattern I am here naming as sin.

## How Institutions Protect Themselves

The structural argument deserves to be made plainly. Institutions protect themselves. This is not a characteristic peculiar to religious institutions — every organization develops self-preservation instincts that can override its stated purpose. But the church faces a particular corruption when it operates this way, because its stated purpose is the care of the vulnerable, and the one against whom its institutional instincts are activated is precisely the person its purpose requires it to protect. The abuser is a threat to the institution's reputation. The victim is also a threat to the institution's reputation. The institution's response — historically, repeatedly, documentably — has been to manage both threats, which in practice means removing the abuser quietly and pressuring the victim to silence.

That management is theological error of the most serious kind. It treats reputation as a value higher than the truth. It treats the institution's survival as a value higher than the person's dignity. It treats the abuser's continuity as a pastoral concern more urgent than the survivor's justice.

The gospel cannot survive that logic. A community organized around a God who took on flesh and suffered and was vindicated against the powers that killed him cannot simultaneously be an institution that sacrifices the suffering to protect the powerful. Not without losing the capacity to proclaim what it claims to believe.

> They are the same event: institutionalized protection of abusers and systematic silencing of those they harmed.

---

## The Weaponization of Grace

There is a particular theological distortion that enables this pattern, and it deserves to be named directly. It is the weaponization of grace.

The logic runs like this: we are all sinners. The abuser has sinned. He is also a brother in Christ. Grace requires that we forgive. Forgiveness requires that we not destroy a man's ministry. Therefore the institutional response to abuse is to offer private correction, require private repentance, and manage the situation in a way that allows ministry to continue while protecting the victim — through confidentiality agreements, through the subtle pressure of Christian community, through appeals to forgiveness as the measure of a survivor's spiritual health.

This is not grace. It is the counterfeit of grace, deployed in the service of institutional self-protection.

Paul's letter to the Corinthians addresses a case of sexual immorality within the congregation with a directness that should disturb any pastor who has been tempted toward managed transitions and quiet arrangements. "Purge the evil person from among you" (1 Corinthians 5:13). Paul is quoting Deuteronomy, and he knows it. The continuity between the testaments on this point is not accidental. Communities that harbor the predator in order to protect the institution's reputation are not acting in grace. They are acting in the same cowardice the Deuteronomic law was designed to prevent.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in *Life Together* about the difference between the community that tells people what they want to hear and the community that is willing to name the truth at cost. He called cheap grace the deadliest enemy of the church — not because it was graceless but because it was grace without cost, reconciliation without genuine confrontation with the wrong that required reconciliation. [cite — confirm] What passes for pastoral sensitivity in many abuse cases is cheap grace of the most cynical variety: absolution for the powerful, silence for the powerless, and the institutional reputation intact.

The survivor who approaches a church leadership team expecting to be heard and protected, and instead finds herself encouraged toward forgiveness as a precondition of being believed — that woman has not been treated with grace. She has been managed. The church has protected itself at her expense and called it ministry.

---

The historical record here is not obscure. It requires only the willingness to look.

## The Documented Pattern Across Traditions

The pattern of institutional self-protection in the face of clergy abuse has been documented across traditions — Catholic, Southern Baptist, non-denominational evangelical, charismatic networks, independent churches. [cite — confirm] The particulars differ. The mechanism is identical: the institution's need to protect its reputation, its leadership, and its financial stability overrides the institution's theological commitment to justice and the protection of the vulnerable. The hierarchy closes ranks. The survivor is isolated. The abuser is moved, counseled, quietly retired, or given a reference that does not disclose what the institution knows.

This has happened not because these institutions were staffed by uniquely wicked people. It has happened because institutions, by their nature, develop survival instincts, and because the culture of deference to pastoral authority that many Christian communities have cultivated creates conditions where abuse can operate without detection and disclosure can be punished by the very community that should receive it.

Power without accountability is not just a management problem. It is a theological problem. The New Testament model of leadership is not the unchecked authority of a singular figure but the shared accountability of a plurality of elders, the congregation's capacity to name and address sin among its members, and the structural principle that no one in the community is above the truth. When the senior pastor is above accountability — when the board exists to affirm his vision rather than to genuinely oversee his conduct, when the staff are financially dependent on his approval, when the congregation has been formed to conflate loyalty to the pastor with loyalty to God — the conditions for abuse are already present, waiting only for a person willing to exploit them.

> Power without accountability is not just a management problem. It is a theological problem.

---

What justice requires here is not complicated, though it is costly.

## What Justice Actually Requires

Mandatory reporting. Not discretionary reporting, not prayerful discernment about whether this rises to the level requiring outside intervention, not the pastoral judgment call made by the same institution that has an interest in the outcome. Mandatory. To civil authorities. Before internal processes begin, not after they have already shaped the narrative.

Independent accountability structures with genuine authority — not advisory bodies that report to the leaders they are supposed to oversee. If the body investigating abuse reports to the senior pastor, it is not an accountability structure. It is a loyalty performance.

Survivor-centered processes rather than institution-centered ones. This means asking first what the person who was harmed needs, not what the institution needs in order to manage the situation. It means the survivor's account is received before it is evaluated. It means the burden of proof is not placed on the person with less power.

Named accountability, not managed transitions to other ministry contexts. The pastor who abused and is moved to another congregation without disclosure is not being given a second chance. He is being given a new supply of victims. This is not pastoral generosity. It is the creation of conditions for the harm to continue.

None of these requirements are uniquely demanding in light of what the church claims about the God it serves. They are the minimum institutional integrity that basic decency would require, even apart from the theological framework that makes the failure so catastrophic.

## The Courage to Say It Out Loud

What God requires of the church — and what the church has failed to provide — is the courage to say out loud what it already knows in private. The church knows that abuse happens in its spaces. It knows that its structures can enable rather than prevent it. It knows that the patterns of deference and silence that have served the institution have not served the people in its care.

The silence is not neutral. The silence is participation in the harm.

> The silence is not neutral. The silence is participation in the harm.

Naming it is the beginning of something that might, over time, look like faithfulness. Not comfort. Not reputation. Not managed stability.

Something that might, at cost, look like the shepherd who goes after the one who was lost, rather than the shepherd who counts heads on Sunday morning and calls it care.

The sheep who was taken were not lost. They were taken. The shepherd who says otherwise has not yet faced Ezekiel 34.

The therapeutic version of sin works like this: sin is the things you do that hurt yourself or others. The solution is awareness, accountability, and better habits. The gospel, in this reading, is primarily information about what constitutes sin and motivation to do better. Jesus shows us what right behavior looks like and provides inspiration and community to pursue it.

This is not wrong exactly. It is so inadequate that it produces a Christianity that cannot explain why people who are aware of their failures, who are accountable to communities, who are genuinely trying — still cannot change the things that matter most. Why the man who preaches against anger loses his temper with his children on the way home from church. Why the woman who has confessed envy a hundred times still finds it rising in her chest when someone she resents succeeds. Why, after years of spiritual formation, the pride that drives so much of what I do is still there — disguised, perhaps, wearing the clothing of pastoral dedication or theological seriousness, but recognizable to anyone paying careful attention, including me.

Paul knew the problem from the inside. Romans 7 is his autobiographical account: "I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate" (Romans 7:15). He is not describing a person who lacks information about the right behavior. He is describing a person who knows precisely what the right behavior is and finds himself unable consistently to do it — not from laziness or lack of effort, but because there is something wrong at a level that effort cannot reach.

## Sin as Disorder Before It Is Behavior

The Hebrew word for sin — chatta't — can mean a missing of the mark, but the broader canonical picture of sin is not reducible to that archery image. Genesis 3 does not present the first sin as a simple behavioral failure. It presents it as an act of disordering — of placing the self in the position of God, of reaching for the knowledge of good and evil, of deciding that the creature's judgment should override the Creator's word. The disorder is ontological before it is behavioral. The wrong action is the expression of a disordered self, not merely a bad choice made by an otherwise healthy self.

This is why Jeremiah can say that the human heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick (Jeremiah 17:9) — not that certain hearts are this way, but that this is the universal condition, the description of the interior from which human beings generate their lives in the absence of intervention. This is why the psalmist, in Psalm 51:5, traces his sin not to a particular bad decision but to the condition from which he emerged: "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me." Not blame toward the mother. An acknowledgment that the problem runs deeper than any particular act.

Jesus, in Mark 7:21-22, locates the source of all defilement inside the person — in the heart — rather than in external contact with the unclean. "For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person." He is not describing a list of behaviors that certain people with particular weaknesses practice. He is describing the interior from which all human beings, without intervention, generate their lives.

Not actions. Interior. The source is the heart.

> Not actions. Interior. The source is the heart.

## Augustine and the Bondage of the Will

Augustine articulated this with a precision that shaped Western theology for more than a thousand years, and whose insight remains the most honest account I have found of the actual human condition. His concept of the will's bondage — the phrase non posse non peccare, the inability not to sin — described not a person who lacks freedom in the ordinary sense but a person whose will has been so disordered that even its best efforts at righteousness are directed by something other than the pure love of God [cite — confirm]. The will functions. It chooses. But the chooser is bent, and bent-ness produces bent choices even when the bent person is trying to be straight.

The steel-man case against this position is worth sitting with honestly. Pelagius argued in the fifth century that if sin is a condition of nature rather than a behavior, then it cannot properly be our fault, and if it is not our fault, then God's judgment of it is unjust [cite — confirm]. If we cannot do otherwise, we cannot be held accountable for what we do. This is not a frivolous argument. It has an internal logic that the church has never entirely dismissed. The councils that condemned Pelagius did not dismiss his concern for human accountability. They answered it.

The Augustinian answer was this: the bondage of the will is itself the consequence of a choice freely made. The condition is not imposed from outside by a God who then judges us for what he imposed. It is the result of what the human being, using genuine freedom, did with the freedom given. The fire burned because humans lit it. The chains are real, but the chain-making was an act of will. We are accountable for the condition because we produced it — not any individual descendant of Adam who is personally responsible for the original act, but a species that has consistently, comprehensively, without exception in any historical generation, chosen what Genesis 3 describes: the self in the position of God.

But more importantly than the philosophical response: the Pelagian account does not fit the experience of people who have actually tried to change. I have tried to change. I have watched people try to change who are more disciplined than I am, more aware, more accountable. The things that need changing most deeply — the pride that shapes even my most apparently generous acts, the fear that masquerades as caution, the desire to be seen that drives even my most apparently humble service — do not yield to effort and awareness. They yield to something that comes from outside the self. That is not a theory. That is what I have observed in thirty years of following Christ and pastoring people who are trying to do the same.

## Why the Shape of the Problem Determines the Solution

Why does this matter for salvation? Because the shape of the problem determines the shape of the solution.

If sin is primarily behavioral, the solution is primarily behavioral — education, motivation, spiritual disciplines, community accountability, sustained effort over time. These are not worthless. They address real things. But they address symptoms while the condition remains. You can change the behaviors and still be the same person. You can stop the particular acts that are most visible and still be operating from the same disordered interior that produced them. Anyone who has watched a religious community that emphasizes behavioral compliance without dealing with the interior knows the result: people who have gotten better at hiding what they are while remaining what they are.

If sin is ontological — a condition of the will and the self, not merely a catalog of misbehaviors — then the solution must address the self at its root. Paul calls this new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). John calls it being born again, born from above — the generation of a new life that the flesh cannot produce from within itself (John 3:3-8). The language is deliberately biological. It is not language about improved performance. It is language about a different kind of being.

> The difference between a Christianity that addresses behavior and a Christianity that addresses being is the difference between a new coat of paint on a condemned building and actual reconstruction.

This is not a minor theological distinction. The difference between a Christianity that addresses behavior and a Christianity that addresses being is the difference between a new coat of paint on a condemned building and actual reconstruction. The condemned building may look better from the street. It is still condemned.

## What the Cross Accomplished

The gospel actually announces something different from behavior modification. In the death of Jesus, something was accomplished — not just demonstrated. The cross is not primarily a moral example. It is, in Paul's language, the place where "him who knew no sin" became sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). Not that we would now try harder to be righteous. That we would become what we were made to be, from the inside, by the agency of the Spirit who applies what the cross accomplished.

---

## The Pastoral Consequence of Getting This Wrong

The practical consequence of getting this wrong is visible in the pastoral experience of most churches.

The congregation that understands sin primarily as behavior will try to address it primarily through accountability — accountability groups, confession, public commitments to do better. These structures are not useless. But they are regularly experienced as exhausting and ultimately ineffective in precisely the areas that matter most, because what they address is the expression of the condition while the condition itself remains. The person commits again and again to stop the behavior, and the behavior returns, and each failure produces shame, and shame produces hiding, and hiding prevents the honest reckoning with the interior from which the behavior grows.

The congregation that understands sin as a condition will understand why the disciplines of formation — prayer, Scripture, communal worship, service — are not primarily techniques for improving behavior but practices that create the conditions in which the Spirit can work at the level of the will itself. They are not causes of the new birth. They are, in Eugene Peterson's language [cite — confirm], the means by which we practice the life we have been given — the way the new creation, given from outside, is exercised into an actual new manner of living.

I have tried both, in my own life and in the churches I have served. The congregation that focuses primarily on behavior produces people who are exhausted by the effort and secretly convinced that they are failing what the gospel requires. The congregation that grasps the depth of the condition — and therefore grasps the depth of what the gospel addresses — tends to produce people who are honest about their failures, who understand that honesty as part of the work rather than evidence of its absence, and who are, over long years, genuinely different rather than merely more disciplined.

---

## Sin Is What We Are

Sin is what we are. Not the worst of us — all of us. Not only in our most dramatic failures, but in the orientations that drive even our best moments.

Salvation is what God does about what we are. And what God does is not primarily announce the rules more clearly or increase the motivation to follow them. What God does, in the incarnation and the cross and the resurrection and the ongoing work of the Spirit, is make something new where something old had been. Slowly, not without suffering, not without the long work of formation, not without honest reckoning with what is still being changed — but genuinely new.

That is harder to believe than the behavioral account. It removes the sense of control that the behavioral account preserves. It requires admitting that the problem is deeper than any strategy you can devise can reach. It requires trusting that what God has promised, God will do — which means living in the tension between the condition being addressed and the completion not yet arrived.

I have not arrived. I am not where I was. That difference is not the result of my sustained effort. It is the result of a grace that met me in the condition I was in, which was worse than I admitted for years, and that is still meeting me there.

> That is the only account I have found that is honest about the problem.

That is the only account I have found that is honest about the problem. It is also the only one that offers a solution commensurate with the problem's actual depth.

Burnout almost never arrives as an event. We picture it that way — a collapse, a breakdown, a dramatic morning a man cannot get out of the car. But the collapse is only the last frame. What precedes it is a slow burn, months or years long, so gradual that the man living it cannot feel the temperature changing. He is the frog in the warming water, and the warming is the whole danger.

It does not look like exhaustion at first. It looks like productivity. The early stages of a slow burn are often a pastor's busiest and most admired season — more meetings, more output, more visible faithfulness. The decline hides inside the achievement, which is exactly why no one intervenes. You do not pull a man off the field while he is scoring. So the erosion proceeds underneath the success, unseen by the congregation and, for a long time, by the man himself.

I know the early frames because I have lived in them.

## Acedia and the Noonday Demon

The theological tradition that shaped the pastoral office was not naive about this. The Desert Fathers, those fourth-century monks who fled to the Egyptian wilderness not because they hated the world but because they recognized the degree to which the world's rhythms could hollow a man without his noticing, developed a rich vocabulary for what they called *acedia* — a kind of spiritual torpor that settled over a person not in moments of dramatic crisis but in the ordinary middle of the afternoon [cite — confirm]. The noonday demon, they called it: not the dramatic failure of apostasy, but the slow drift toward meaninglessness that came when the disciplines that kept the soul alive were quietly abandoned in favor of more visible forms of industry. The monk who was always busy but never formed. The man who could produce without receiving, output without input, for years — until the day there was nothing left to produce.

The pastoral tradition carried this forward. Richard Baxter, writing his *The Reformed Pastor* in 1656, addressed it directly: "Take heed to yourselves, lest you be void of that saving grace of God which you offer to others, and be strangers to the effectual working of that gospel which you preach." Baxter's concern was spiritual, but the mechanism he described is also psychological. The man who handles sacred things professionally — who reads Scripture for sermons rather than for formation, who prays for an audience rather than before God — gradually loses access to the interior life that the sacred things were meant to sustain. The tools wear the craftsman down rather than building him up, because the craftsman stopped being a student and became only a tradesman.

Three centuries later, the sociologist Robert Bellah and his colleagues documented what they called the "therapeutic culture" of modern American life [cite — confirm] — a culture that had lost the vocabulary of calling and vocation and replaced it with a language of professional fulfillment and personal satisfaction. This matters for ministry because it means that many pastors entered the work without a framework for understanding why the depletion they were experiencing was not a failure of professionalism but a theological problem. When you believe the work is fundamentally about your output and your impact, and the output starts to feel hollow and the impact starts to feel uncertain, the only remaining question is whether you are doing enough of it. The answer is always more. And more is not the answer.

## What the Slow Burn Took First

The first to go was not my schedule but my interior life — the prayer that became preparation, the Scripture I now only read professionally, looking for sermons instead of being addressed by God. Then went the margin: the unhurried conversation, the walk with no agenda, the capacity to be interrupted without resentment. Then the small joys flattened. Things that used to move me did not. I called it maturity. It was numbness, and numbness is one of the body's last warnings before the system protects itself by shutting down.

> Learn the signs while they are still quiet, because the loud sign is the one that ends ministries.

Learn the signs while they are still quiet, because the loud sign is the one that ends ministries.

## Learning to Read the Gauges

Watch for the slow conversion of people into tasks — when the family in crisis becomes an item on the list rather than a soul to love. This is perhaps the most reliable early warning. Ministry begins with the conviction that people are the point; it drifts toward the management of people as problems to be solved and demands to be handled. When a man stops seeing the person behind the pastoral need, something in him has already closed.

Watch for cynicism, which arrives disguised as discernment: the new, reflexive suspicion of everyone's motives, the eye-roll where compassion used to be. Cynicism and discernment have the same surface appearance — both involve a clear-eyed assessment of human nature. What distinguishes them is love. Discernment is assessment in the service of care. Cynicism is assessment in the service of self-protection. The cynical pastor is a man who learned, somewhere in the slow burn, that hope was too expensive, and has been billing himself as wise ever since.

Watch for the disappearance of delight. A man losing himself slowly does not usually feel sad first. He feels flat. The music that used to move him doesn't. The text that used to arrest him slides past. The congregation that he once could not believe he was permitted to serve has become, on the worst days, a crowd of demands and a source of criticism. The flatness is not depression in the clinical sense, necessarily. It is the absence of the thing that animated the work — and its absence is already the slow burn's most serious symptom.

Watch for the secret fantasies of escape. Not dramatic ones — not the sudden departure, not the resignation letter — but the quiet Tuesday thought that it would be a relief if it all simply stopped. That thought is not treachery. It is a symptom. The man having it is a man whose reserves are so depleted that the only rest he can imagine is a rest that removes the source of the demand altogether. That is the slow burn's voice, and it sounds like reason.

> None of these are moral failures. They are gauges, and a gauge is not an accusation; it is information.

None of these are moral failures. They are gauges, and a gauge is not an accusation; it is information. The tragedy is not that pastors run low — every faithful life runs low sometimes. The tragedy is the silence around the gauges, the long habit of ignoring the warning lights because the engine is still running and the schedule is still full.

## The Distorted Doctrine of Vocation

The deeper theological problem underneath the slow burn is a distorted doctrine of vocation. The pastor who burns out slowly has usually, somewhere beneath his stated theology, come to believe that the work depends on him — that the church's health is a product of his faithfulness, that his output is the primary mechanism by which God works in the community, that rest is something he can afford when the work is done. This is not a conscious heresy. It rarely gets named from a pulpit. But it shapes behavior, and its shape is exhaustion.

Paul's letter to the Corinthians offers a corrective that is so direct it is easy to miss: *I planted the seed, Apollos watered it, but God has been making it grow. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow* (1 Corinthians 3:6-7). This is not pastoral modesty. It is a theological claim about causation. The growth is not your work. You are a participant in something that was already underway before you arrived and will continue after you are gone. The man who has genuinely internalized this can rest without guilt. The man who has not will burn out in the gap between the growth he believes is his responsibility and the growth he is actually capable of producing.

## Unwinding the Burn by Small Reversals

The remedy is not a single dramatic rescue. A slow burn was built over months, and it is unwound the same way — by small, unglamorous reversals, repeated. A real day of rest, kept when the calendar protests. A return to prayer that has no sermon attached. A few people allowed close enough to notice the flatness and name it. Honest attention to the body, the sleep, the marriage, the ordinary creaturely things a depleted man is most tempted to neglect and most needs. The Sabbath commandment is not primarily a productivity strategy. It is a declaration that you are a creature and not an engine, and that creatures have limits, and that limits are not failures of faith. God built the rest into the structure of the week before sin entered the story. The need for it is not a symptom of the fall. It is an architecture of the creation.

There is a counter-argument worth naming honestly. The great cloud of witnesses includes figures who ran at a pace that seems to contradict the slow-burn argument — men and women of enormous output, sustained for decades, who appear to have carried crushing loads without the kind of depletion I am describing. Some of this testimony is accurate. Some of it is the hagiographic tendency to omit the breakdown, the year away, the unnamed cost. The cases that deserve weight are the ones that show genuine sustainability — figures like Eugene Peterson, who served the same congregation for nearly thirty years and then spent the second half of his life writing about why unhurried ministry is not a luxury but the only kind that actually forms people [cite — confirm]. Speed and volume are not the same as faithfulness. The congregation that is formed by a man who has been sustainably fed will receive something different from the congregation formed by a man running on fumes. The difference compounds over decades.

And under all of it, the slow relearning of the truth the busyness buried: that you are a creature and not an engine, that the church is held up by Christ and not by your stamina, that the God who rested on the seventh day did not think less of his work for resting and will not think less of you.

## The Warning That Arrives While There Is Still Time

If you are reading this and recognizing yourself in the early frames — the prayer gone professional, the people gone flat, the quiet fantasy of escape — that recognition is not failure. It is the warning arriving while there is still time to heed it.

Most pastors get the warning. Fewer stop. Be one of the ones who stops — now, while it is still a slow burn, and not yet the morning the engine will not start. Because that morning is not the crisis that ends the ministry. It is the end of what the ministry was quietly becoming long before the engine quit.

> The slow burn was always the thing to fear. Not the collapse. The long warmth you stopped feeling was the temperature.

The slow burn was always the thing to fear. Not the collapse. The long warmth you stopped feeling was the temperature.

The story we tell about failed marriages involves revelation. A discovery, a confession, a moment where something hidden becomes visible and the marriage cannot survive the exposure. We tell that story because it makes sense. It has a cause. It has a before and an after. It is legible.

The more common story does not have any of that. It has no single moment. No confession. No dramatic rupture. It has a slow, barely-perceptible drift — two people becoming less connected over months and years, neither of them intending it, both of them managing the surface while the depth quietly empties. And one day one of them says the words that shock the other, because from the outside nothing appeared wrong: I am not sure I am in love with you anymore.

The drift is the more dangerous story precisely because it is invisible. You can see a crisis and respond to it. You cannot easily see a drift until the gap has become too wide to close without significant effort.

> The drift is the more dangerous story precisely because it is invisible.

## The Little Foxes

The Song of Solomon contains a line in chapter 2 that reads like a warning about exactly this: "Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that spoil the vineyards, for our vineyards are in blossom." The vineyard is the relationship at its most alive. The little foxes are not lions. They are small, and that is the point. Nobody ignores a lion in the vineyard. People ignore little foxes — until the vineyard is ruined.

The little foxes in a marriage are the small uncorrected defaults: the phone that comes to the dinner table and stays. The conversation that gets deferred and never returned to. The affectionate gesture that used to be automatic and quietly stopped. The question about the other person's interior life that nobody has asked in months. Each one is inconsequential. Together, over time, they produce the drift.

**The drift does not announce itself. It accumulates until the distance requires explanation — and by then, one person has already found a private explanation of their own.**

## The Historical and Social Pattern

The second half of the twentieth century produced a significant change in the social meaning of marriage in the United States. Before the 1960s, marriage was largely understood as a functional institution — an economic and social arrangement in which the stability of the unit was the goal and individual fulfillment was a bonus rather than a requirement. The psychological revolution of the mid-century, combined with the economic changes that made individual independence more feasible, shifted this understanding dramatically. Marriage became a primary vehicle for personal self-realization. The expectation of emotional intimacy, personal growth, and mutual fulfillment rose to levels that the institution had never previously been asked to carry [cite — confirm].

This is not entirely a bad development. Marriages that function as joyless institutional arrangements at the expense of their members are not models to recover. The genuine goods of intimacy and mutual flourishing that the revised expectations pointed toward are real goods.

But the shift created a new vulnerability that the previous model did not have. When marriage is primarily a vehicle for personal fulfillment, the drift of disconnection is experienced not just as loss but as failure — as evidence that the marriage is not working, that the right person was not chosen, that something fundamentally broken cannot be repaired. Couples who might have tolerated a functional distance in an earlier era now interpret it as grounds for exit.

The church's response to the cultural shift has been inconsistent. In some traditions, the theological emphasis on covenant permanence has been taught in ways that simply ignore the drift — that counsel endurance without addressing the actual condition of the relationship. In others, the absorption of therapeutic culture has produced a version of Christian marriage counseling that is barely distinguishable from secular self-actualization. Neither has served couples well.

## What the Drift Actually Feels Like From the Inside

I have noticed a consistent pattern in couples who come in late. Not late as in after betrayal, but late as in after one of them has privately concluded that the marriage is over — and they are only in the room because of obligation, not because they believe something can change. The other spouse is often genuinely bewildered. From where they were standing, the marriage was fine. It was functional. There was no crisis.

What they did not see was that their spouse had been sending signals — bids for connection, bids for conversation, bids for a different quality of attention — for years, and those bids had gone unanswered, and the private conclusion had been reached quietly and maintained privately until the weight of it was too much to carry alone.

Gottman's research identifies "bids for connection" as the basic unit of emotional intimacy in a relationship — small invitations to turn toward each other rather than away [cite — confirm]. Partners who consistently turn toward each other's bids build emotional capital. Partners who consistently miss or deflect them drain it. The account can run dry without either person noticing — until the day one of them realizes the account is empty and has been empty for some time.

The disconnect is real: one person experienced a long slow emergency, and the other experienced nothing unusual. That asymmetry is the product of drift. One person was tracking the marriage closely enough to feel it going wrong. The other was not tracking it at all.

> Covenant without investment is not faithfulness. It is possession.

## The Counter-Position and What It Gets Wrong

Some pastoral counselors argue that the focus on emotional intimacy and connection as the primary measure of marriage health is itself a symptom of the therapeutic revolution — that marriages ordered by covenant commitment rather than emotional satisfaction are more durable, and that teaching couples to prioritize the maintenance of feeling-connection puts the marriage's foundation on subjective experience rather than objective commitment.

The concern is understandable. A marriage that is only as strong as the emotional experience of connection will not survive the seasons when connection is hard to feel. Covenant commitment is the infrastructure that holds the marriage together when the emotional weather is poor.

But the covenant does not excuse the neglect of the relationship it protects. The same husband who would invoke covenant permanence to resist his wife's request for divorce but who has not initiated a genuine conversation about her interior life in three years is using theology as a substitute for faithfulness rather than an expression of it. Covenant without investment is not faithfulness. It is possession.

Malachi 2:14 describes God as "witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant." The accusation in that text is not infidelity in the usual sense. It is the faithlessness of treating a covenant partner as something other than a companion — the reduction of the wife to a legal status while the actual relationship of companionship was abandoned.

The drift is precisely that kind of faithlessness. Not the dramatic violation. The slow abandonment of the companion.

## The Discipline That Prevents It

Drift prevention is not romantic. It is structural. It looks like regular intentional check-ins — not state-of-the-union conversations that carry the weight of everything unaddressed, but the small regular questions: How are you actually doing? What is something you need from me that you have not told me? Is there something between us that we have not named?

Hebrews 3:13 says "encourage one another daily, as long as it is called 'today,' so that none of you may be hardened by sin's deceitfulness." The instruction is for the community, but the pattern is applicable: daily. Not annual. Not when the relationship is in crisis. The regular tending that prevents the hardening.

The couple that builds this practice does not always have significant conversations. Most days the answer is "I'm fine, everything is okay." But the practice creates the condition under which the honest answer — the harder answer — can arrive before it has aged into a private conclusion.

## Three Questions for This Week

When did you last ask your spouse how they were actually doing — not as a formality, but as a genuine question you waited to hear the answer to?

Is there a gap that has been growing in your marriage that neither of you has named? What is keeping you from naming it?

What are the little foxes in your marriage right now — the small uncorrected defaults that are costing you more than they appear to?

**This week:** one genuine check-in. Not "how was your day." Something like: "Is there anything between us that you have been carrying that I should know about?" Then listen to the full answer.

The marriages that end in drift do not fail for lack of love. They fail for lack of attention. Attention is not a feeling. It is a practice.

> The marriages that end in drift do not fail for lack of love. They fail for lack of attention.

The vineyard is in blossom. Catch the foxes now, before the harvest that depends on it is already gone.

The dominant assumption in American Christianity is that growth is the direction of health — that the small church is a church that has not yet succeeded, or a church that used to succeed and is now failing. The megachurch is the aspiration. The small church is the consolation prize.

This assumption is worth examining, because it is not as biblical as we tend to treat it.

## The Metrics Borrowed From the Corporate World

The metrics that define success in American church culture were largely borrowed from the corporate world in the latter half of the twentieth century. Church growth as a formal discipline emerged in the 1960s with Donald McGavran's work at Fuller Seminary [cite — confirm], and while the movement contained genuine missional insight — that the gospel ought to reach people and that reaching more people is, in principle, better than reaching fewer — the metric it handed to the average pastor was a headcount. You are succeeding if the number goes up. You are failing if it does not. A small church is, by this definition, either pre-success or post-failure. It does not appear as a category of its own.

## The Church Began as Small Gatherings

But the early church did not think this way. The church began as a movement of small gatherings — house churches that met in the homes of people like Nympha (Colossians 4:15), Priscilla and Aquila (Romans 16:5), and Philemon. These were not staging grounds for eventual large congregations. They were the thing itself. The primary unit of Christian community in the ancient world was small enough that everyone knew the names of the sick, the new converts, the ones who were struggling, the ones carrying unusual grief. That kind of knowledge is not incidental to community. It is what community is.

> This is accountability without a program. It is simply what happens when a community is small enough to see each other.

The small church, by its nature, cannot hide. The person who misses two Sundays gets a phone call, because there are only enough people present that an absence is visible. The elder who is struggling financially cannot be anonymous in the prayer request, because the community is small enough that the prayer request is not a form but a conversation. The family in crisis cannot manage its presentation as carefully, because the people watching them also know their children and have eaten dinner in their home. This is accountability without a program. It is simply what happens when a community is small enough to see each other.

I have served in communities like this. The intimacy is real, and so is the difficulty. The small church cannot produce anonymity, which means that both the help and the conflict are closer and more personal than anyone who has only served in larger congregations might anticipate. People leave for that reason. Grievances have nowhere to hide. And yet that same condition — the inability to be unknown — is also what creates the kind of pastoral care that large churches build entire staff departments trying to replicate.

The large church has genuine strengths. Resources, specialized programming, the capacity to reach people the small church cannot reach, a critical mass that makes certain kinds of community possible. None of this is nothing. But the large church also faces a structural problem that the small church never has to solve: how do you create genuine community at scale? The small group strategy, the parish model, the care team infrastructure — these are all attempts to manufacture inside a large institution something that exists organically in the small church. They can work. They require constant maintenance. The small church simply lives in the thing that larger institutions labor to approximate.

Paul's theology of the body in 1 Corinthians 12 — that every member is necessary, that there is no member the body can say it does not need — describes a community where every member is actually visible. That description fits the small church more naturally than it fits an auditorium of two thousand. "The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you,' nor again the head to the feet, 'I have no need of you'" (1 Corinthians 12:21). The ear does not feel expendable in a twenty-person gathering. It often does in a crowd.

## The Pastoral Character Proximity Produces

There is a second thing the small church gets right that goes largely unacknowledged: it develops pastoral character in its leader that comfort rarely produces. The small-church pastor who has been doing ministry for fifteen years in a congregation of seventy people has counseled marriages, buried members he baptized as children, navigated the complicated relationships of three-generation families with competing loyalties, preached through seasons when attendance dropped by a third and there was no budget for a consultant or a conference. He has been made by those experiences. He has learned things about the human soul and the nature of genuine pastoral care that do not appear in church growth literature because they are not scalable. They are personal. They are the product of proximity and time.

Eugene Peterson spent most of his pastoral ministry at a single congregation in Maryland — Christ Our King Presbyterian in Bel Air — and what he learned there shaped everything he eventually wrote about the pastoral vocation. His insistence that pastoral work is essentially local, particular, and slow grew directly from the experience of a non-large church that required him to know his people by name and by history. Peterson's work on *spiritual direction as the primary pastoral act* — on the pastor as the person who helps particular people pay attention to what God is doing in particular lives — is almost impossible to practice at institutional scale. It is entirely possible in a congregation of one hundred.

## The Steel-Man of the Growth Metric

The steel-man of the growth-metric approach is fair and should be heard: a church that cannot reach new people is not fulfilling the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19). A church that exists only for its existing members has become a private club with a liturgy. Growth matters. Mission matters. A church that has stopped caring whether anyone outside its current membership encounters the gospel has lost something essential.

This is true. It does not refute the argument being made here. The question is not whether a church should want to reach people. The question is whether the size of the congregation is the primary measure of whether it is doing so. A small church that has been faithfully present in its neighborhood for forty years, that has buried three generations, that has fed families during lean times and counseled marriages through crisis and sent its young people out into the world with a genuine faith that holds — that church is not a failure. It may be the most faithful institution in the county.

## What the Small Church Teaches About Money

There is also the matter of what the small church teaches about money. In a congregation of sixty, the financial contribution of every member is visible in its effects. When the family who tithes faithfully gives, the furnace gets replaced or the food pantry gets stocked or the missionary gets supported. The connection between giving and impact is direct. The theology of stewardship in a small church is necessarily concrete: your money does that specific thing. In the large church, individual giving disappears into an institutional budget whose allocations are made by a finance committee and communicated in a pie chart. Both are legitimate. Neither produces the immediate, visible connection between an individual's faithfulness and a community's capacity that the small church makes available.

Jesus told a parable about a woman who had ten coins, lost one, and swept the whole house searching for it — and when she found it, called her neighbors together to rejoice (Luke 15:8-9). The parable assumes a community where a single coin is visible in its absence. That is a small-community economy. Not every community is small, and Jesus was not prescribing a church size. But the economy of visibility that the parable assumes — where one matters, where loss is noticed, where recovery is communal — describes something that does not happen at scale without enormous structural effort.

The pastor of the small church is not leading a failed institution. He is the steward of a community that has something the market cannot produce and that the large church often has to work very hard to recover. He is doing something that the metrics of American Christianity are not built to see, which is why he spends so much energy defending the worth of what he is doing to people who read the wrong numbers.

What he is doing is community. Not as a program. As a practice. As the thing itself.

> That is not nothing. That is actually the point.

That is not nothing. That is actually the point.

## The Only Church That Will Ever Serve

There is one more thing worth naming: the small church is, in most of America, the only church that will ever serve certain communities. The rural county where there is no megachurch campus, the urban neighborhood where the building is aging and the demographics have shifted, the town that is not on a growth trajectory and never will be — these communities are served by small churches or they are not served at all. The pastor who treats his small church as a failure has misread the territory he is actually standing in. He may be the only sustained institutional presence for the gospel in a five-mile radius.

> That is not a consolation. That is a calling.

That is not a consolation. That is a calling.

The pastor of the small church is not a lesser version of something larger. He is the whole thing in a concentrated form — closer to his people, more accountable to his context, less protected by the institutional buffer that scale provides, and therefore, when he does it well, more genuinely pastoral than the model he is being told to aspire toward.

The word solidarity carries freight it did not earn in every room where it is spoken.

In some rooms it sounds like a union hall. In some rooms it sounds like a protest slogan. In American evangelical Christianity it has acquired, through a process of cultural association, the smell of progressive politics — which means that the word itself, before the argument is made, has already been sorted by many listeners into "not our category, not our language, not our concern." The sorting happens fast and almost entirely without examination.

The irony is severe. The concept the word describes is one of the most thoroughly biblical claims about the character of God and the calling of the church that the tradition contains. We did not get the word from the Left. The Left borrowed it from a history the church should recognize as its own.

---

## The God Who Comes Down

The Greek word in its New Testament vicinity is sympatheo — to suffer with. Paul uses it in Hebrews 4:15 to describe the nature of the high priest Jesus: "We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin." This is a claim about the kind of God the incarnation reveals — not a God who administers human suffering from outside but a God who enters it, who bears it, who knows from the inside what it weighs.

The entire arc of the Old Testament prepares for this. The God of the Exodus is a God who descends to see, descends to hear, descends to act. "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings, and I have come down to deliver them" (Exodus 3:7-8). Three movements: see, hear, come down. The God of Scripture is not neutral between the oppressor and the one being crushed. He takes a position. He moves toward the one in need. He does not stay in a position of safety while managing the suffering from a comfortable distance.

That is solidarity. And it is not borrowed from any political tradition. It is the shape of God's activity through the whole canon.

> That is solidarity. And it is not borrowed from any political tradition. It is the shape of God's activity through the whole canon.

Isaiah 57:15 says this with the kind of precision that stops me every time: "For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: 'I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite.'" The God who inhabits eternity dwells specifically, particularly, with the contrite and lowly. Not primarily with the powerful. Not most naturally at home with the institutions that bear his name while accumulating the security that his name commends them to surrender. He dwells with the lowly.

The incarnation is the logical completion of this pattern. The Word became flesh and dwelt — the Greek is eskenosen, pitched a tent — among us (John 1:14). Not among us in the sense of proximity. Among us in the sense of full human embodiment, in the conditions of poverty and marginality, in a province occupied by an empire, born in a stable because the established places were full. God did not send a message about human suffering. God entered human suffering, in the body, in the class and social position of those at the bottom of every list that the powerful keep.

---

## Solidarity Beyond Charity

Solidarity, as a theological virtue, means this: to stand with people in conditions you did not create and do not fully share, not as a manager of their problem but as a participant in their reality. This is different from charity. Charity typically moves from a place of security to a place of need with a gift in hand. Charity is good. The tradition praises it and the Scriptures command it. But solidarity is more demanding than charity in every respect.

Charity can be anonymous. You can write a check and never know whose life it touches. Solidarity requires presence. You have to actually go there, to the place where the need is, and let the conditions of that place become conditions you know in your body rather than in your mind.

Charity gives from where you are. Solidarity goes to where they are. The distance matters. The willingness to close the distance, to let your social position be visible in proximity to those whose social position costs them — that is what solidarity adds to charity. Not instead of giving. In addition to giving, the willingness to be seen standing next to the person the world has sorted into the category of expendable.

> Charity gives from where you are. Solidarity goes to where they are.

Charity addresses need. Solidarity addresses the loneliness of being in need — the particular weight of carrying a condition that no one around you seems willing to share or even witness.

Paul names the theological logic in Philippians 2: "Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others."
