He grounds it immediately in the christological hymn that follows — Christ, who was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but made himself nothing, taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of human beings (Philippians 2:6-7). The downward movement of Christ is the template for the movement the church is called to make. Not to manage the needy from a distance. To move toward them, which means moving away from the securities that distance provides.

---

I have not done this consistently. I am better at charity than at solidarity — which means I have helped from a position that protected my own comfort and social location while occasionally distributing from my surplus. That is not the same as standing with. It is closer to standing near, which preserves the option to move away when proximity becomes costly.

## The Steel-Man and Its Misreading

The steel-man version of the resistance to solidarity is worth sitting with. The argument goes like this: charity is sustainable because it operates from strength; solidarity, by compromising your own position, eventually leaves you with nothing to give. The person who gives away too much cannot keep giving. Better to maintain your position and give generously from it than to sacrifice the position and have nothing left. This is not a cynical argument. It has a logic.

But the argument misreads what solidarity actually is. Solidarity is not self-destruction. It is not the erasure of every distinction between your condition and the condition of the people you are standing with. Paul did not become a slave. He called himself one, he lived as one in terms of his freedom of movement and his dependence on others' hospitality — but the call to solidarity is not a call to pretend you have resources you do not have. It is a call to stop pretending that your resources insulate you from the obligation of presence.

The argument also misreads what the early church actually did. The observers of the ancient world who noted the unusual practices of Christian communities were not describing congregations that had bankrupted themselves. They were describing communities that shared across class lines in ways that had no precedent in the social arrangements of the empire [cite — confirm] — communities where Greek and Jew, slave and free, shared the same table and the same Lord, where the distinction between who was inside the circle of concern and who was outside had been redefined by the practice of baptism. They were describing a community that had concluded, from its theology, that no one in the room was expendable.

That practice was not a program. It was a theology worked out in the body — the theology of a God who had refused, definitively and publicly, to remain at a safe distance from human need.

---

## Constantine and the Cost of Distance

The centuries that followed complicated the picture. Constantine's embrace of Christianity in the fourth century made it safe and then powerful, and power predictably creates distance. By the time John Chrysostom was preaching in Constantinople in the late fourth and early fifth centuries [cite — confirm], the church had become wealthy enough that his sermons against the wealth of the church sound, to our ears, almost outrageous. He called the person who keeps more than he needs while others starve a thief. Not a theologically confused person. Not a spiritually underdeveloped person. A thief. He was not considered a radical. He was considered orthodox, standing squarely in the tradition of the prophets and the apostles.

What Chrysostom understood was what Amos had understood before him: that the presence of great wealth alongside great poverty in the community of God is not a neutral fact about economic arrangements. It is a theological statement about who the community believes God to be. The God who dwells with the contrite and lowly does not quietly bless the structures that produce the contrite and lowly without remedy.

This is why the comfortable American church's ease with economic inequality is not simply a failure of generosity. It is a theological displacement — a substitution of a different god for the one the Scriptures announce. The God of Amos and Isaiah and Chrysostom and the early church is not comfortable with the arrangements we have made. The God who came down to deliver the enslaved is not satisfied with a church that prays for the vulnerable while maintaining a safe distance from their conditions.

---

## The Three Demands of Solidarity

Solidarity as a theological virtue requires three things that charity does not.

First, proximity. You cannot practice solidarity with people you do not know, in conditions you have not witnessed, from neighborhoods you have never entered. The incarnation is not metaphorical here. God actually went there. The people who have embodied solidarity most fully in the history of the church — Dorothy Day, Desmond Tutu, Oscar Romero [cite — confirm] — are people who put themselves physically in the proximity of suffering and let the proximity teach them what they could not have learned from a distance.

Second, willingness to be changed. Charity can be practiced without being affected. You can give and remain exactly who you were before the giving. Solidarity is more dangerous than that. Standing with people in conditions you did not create will eventually challenge your assumptions about how the world works, about who is responsible for what, about what "deserve" means in the economy of the kingdom. You will find that the people the comfortable church has categorized as problems are, in fact, people — and that the people the comfortable church has categorized as successful have, in many cases, benefited from arrangements that required someone else's deprivation.

Third, willingness to be seen. Solidarity means letting your proximity to the marginalized be visible. This is the cost that the comfortable church most reliably avoids. To stand publicly with people whose condition makes the powerful uncomfortable is to accept some of their social costs. Jesus did this in ways that attracted explicit criticism — eating with tax collectors and sinners, touching the unclean, being found in the company of those whom the religious establishment had correctly identified as beneath association. His proximity was not accidental. It was the argument.

---

The political language has borrowed the word solidarity. We should not let the borrowing become our excuse to abandon the original. The church does not need to baptize any political movement to practice what the word describes. What the church needs is to recover the theology it has always held: that the God revealed in Scripture is a God of downward movement, that the church that follows him is called to the same movement, and that the distance we have maintained from the suffering of our neighbors is not prudence. It is a theological problem.

> It is a virtue rooted in the character of God, demanded by the prophets, embodied by the incarnation, and practiced by the early church at a cost that included their blood.

Solidarity is a virtue. It is a virtue rooted in the character of God, demanded by the prophets, embodied by the incarnation, and practiced by the early church at a cost that included their blood. We did not invent it and we cannot afford to surrender it. Your condition is my concern — not because I have surplus to give, but because you are my neighbor and the God I follow went to where you are.

That is the claim. It is not a political position. It has always been theology.

Nobody warned me that the job itself would become the thing standing between me and God.

That is the particular irony of pastoral ministry — that the constant demand to speak about God, pray about God, lead people toward God can systematically crowd out the quiet space where God actually addresses you. The week that ends in Sunday begins again immediately on Monday, and somewhere in the relentless forward momentum of ministry, the disciplines that should anchor you get reclassified as things you do when the real work slows down. The real work never slows down. And so the anchor drags.

## The Professionalized Soul

There is a structural reason for this that deserves naming. The pastor's spiritual life has been professionalized. Prayer is sermon preparation. Bible reading is exegesis. Silence is the moment between meetings. The practices that were designed to form the person have been instrumentalized in the service of the program, and what gets lost is exactly the thing they were designed to produce: a man who knows the difference between his own voice and God's.

Dallas Willard spent a career arguing that spiritual disciplines are not a performance category — something you do to become the kind of person God applauds — but a training category, practices that put the body and soul in position to receive what God is already giving [cite — confirm]. The athlete does not lift weights to impress the coach. He lifts weights so that the body can do in the game what it cannot do untrained. The pastor who neglects spiritual disciplines is not simply missing a devotional habit. He arrives at the most demanding work there is without the formation the work requires. He performs with untrained muscles.

> He performs with untrained muscles.

The result is familiar to anyone who has spent time inside pastoral ministry: the man who can speak compellingly about the peace of God and who cannot access that peace in his own chest during the difficult conversation. The man who preaches the grace of God and who cannot extend it to himself when he fails. The man whose congregation trusts his spiritual depth, and who knows — as they do not — that the depth is thinner than the voice that announces it.

## The Gap Between Proclamation and Practice

I have a confession: I taught spiritual disciplines before I practiced them. I preached about Sabbath during a season when I was taking none. I counseled congregation members toward fasting while treating it as an occasional discipline for crisis moments rather than a regular rhythm. I knew the theology. I was not living inside it. And the gap between what I proclaimed and what I practiced was slowly producing in me a kind of spiritual sourness — the low-grade cynicism that develops when a person stops believing that what he says is actually true for him.

That is the particular danger of the pastoral version of this failure. The layperson who neglects spiritual disciplines suffers privately. The pastor who neglects them suffers publicly, in the most important ways — in what he does not say, in what he cannot see, in what he has no interior resources to offer when the congregant in front of him needs something more than his professional competence.

The tradition offers more here than most contemporary ministry culture has retained. Consider what has been tested and found sufficient across centuries.

## What the Tradition Has Tested

Fasting. Not as punishment or performance, but as the deliberate reordering of the body's demands in service of attention to God. Jesus assumed his followers would fast (Matthew 6:16-17). The tradition from the Didache through the medieval church through the Reformers through the Wesleyan revival treated fasting as a normal dimension of Christian formation [cite — confirm]. The pastor who fasts regularly is training himself in a specific and necessary capacity: the ability to say no to an appetite in the service of something more important. That capacity turns out to be essential in a vocation that is full of appetites competing for attention.

Extended prayer. Not the three-minute invocation before a meeting. Not the pastoral prayer on Sunday morning that is as much performance as address. The extended prayer — an hour, two hours, a morning — in which you sit in the presence of God long enough for the noise to settle and for something other than your own agenda to become audible. Evagrius Ponticus in the fourth century called pure prayer "the conversation of the intellect with God" [cite — confirm]. The intellect does not arrive at that conversation instantly. It requires time to stop being loud.

Solitude and silence. The desert fathers relocated to the Egyptian wilderness in the third and fourth centuries not because they had renounced the world but because they understood that the noise of the social world made it nearly impossible to hear what was required to be heard. Their experiment was too extreme for most contemporary pastors. The insight behind it is not. Every pastor needs a regular and protected encounter with the silence that is not the silence between phone calls but the silence in which God is audible.

The examen — the daily practice, rooted in Ignatian spirituality, of reviewing the day with God, noticing where grace was present and where you resisted it [cite — confirm]. This is ten minutes before sleep. No journal required, no program. A simple question put to God: where were you today, and where did I miss you? What was I most alive in? What did I carry that I should have set down? The practice accumulates. Over months it begins to show you your own patterns — the recurring sites of resistance, the persistent areas of unawareness — with a clarity that no amount of professional reflection produces.

Sabbath kept as more than a day off. Not the pastor's "day off" that is saturated with the mental activity of ministry — the sermon outline forming, the difficult conversation replaying, the calendar anxiety humming below everything. The Sabbath in its biblical sense is a weekly declaration that the world does not depend on your effort. That God was sustaining the creation before you started working and will sustain it after you stop. The Sabbath is God's standing argument against the pastoral messiah complex. To keep it seriously is to practice, once a week, the surrender of the illusion of indispensability.

The practical question is always the same: where do you find the time? Ministry does not build free hours into the schedule. The calendar fills from the outside. What does not get scheduled does not happen.

> The disciplines that survive in a pastor's life are the ones he has decided are load-bearing, not ornamental.

This means the disciplines require what the entire pastoral vocation requires: the conviction that they are necessary, not optional. That fasting is not something you do when you feel spiritually ambitious. That silence is not available only in retreat settings. That the examen can be ten minutes before sleep, a truthful accounting of the day before God, without a journal and without a program. The disciplines that survive in a pastor's life are the ones he has decided are load-bearing, not ornamental.

## Grace Training, Not Achievement

The counter-position worth engaging honestly: there is a version of spiritual discipline culture that becomes one more form of achievement-orientation, one more arena in which the pastor measures himself against an ideal and finds himself insufficient. The Pharisees were not undisciplined. They were disciplined in the service of self-justification, and Jesus did not find the combination impressive (Matthew 23:23). Discipline without the grace-orientation that Willard called "grace training" produces something harder and colder than the thing it was meant to form. The disciplines are means, not ends. They form the kind of person who is available to God, not the kind of person who has earned access to God.

That caveat taken seriously: what the disciplines produce, accumulated over time, is not dramatic. It is not the spiritual experience worth reporting. It is something harder to measure and more essential: a man who knows the difference between his own voice and God's voice, who has enough interior space to listen before he speaks, who has sat with his own sin in God's presence often enough that he does not need to pretend otherwise from the pulpit. The congregation needs that man more than they need the man who has read every book on leadership.

Not every discipline will fit every temperament or season. This is not a prescription for one method. It is an argument for the seriousness of the project — that tending your own soul is not self-indulgence but faithfulness, that the disciplines are not interruptions to ministry but its foundation.

You will not drift accidentally into a healthy interior life. Nobody does. The drift goes the other direction — toward management, toward productivity, toward a version of ministry that is impressive and hollow. The hollowness takes years to be visible from the outside. It is felt from the inside long before that.

The congregation will eventually inherit whatever you have actually cultivated. Not what you preached. What you cultivated.

## What the Metrics Do Not Measure

There is a dimension of this that the current culture of ministry evaluation has made harder to see. Ministry health is measured in the metrics of growth and engagement — attendance, budget, programs launched, staff hired, services added. None of these are bad data points. But they are data points about outputs, not about formation. A ministry can produce impressive outputs while the man at the center is hollowing out. The outputs will eventually reflect the interior, but there is usually a significant lag. Churches have been led by hollow men for years, and the congregation only encounters the hollowness when it becomes undeniable.

The spiritual disciplines are the work of maintaining what the metrics do not measure: the interior life from which everything else eventually flows. Thomas à Kempis wrote in the *Imitation of Christ* that "what doth it profit thee to enter into deep discussion concerning the Holy Trinity, if thou lack humility?" [cite — confirm]. The question is not rhetorical. He is pointing at the specific danger of the theologically sophisticated man who has mastered the vocabulary of the interior life and has not developed one — who can speak with precision about prayer and has not prayed seriously in months.

I know this from the inside. There are seasons when the sermon is producing in me nothing that I am not already producing — when the preparation is craft rather than encounter, when the pulpit is a performance space and not a place of address. Those seasons do not always look bad from the outside. They feel hollow from the inside. And the cure is not more preparation. The cure is the slow, unglamorous return to the disciplines that put me back in a position to receive what God is giving, rather than performing what I have accumulated.

> The well does not refill on its own. You have to go back to the source.

The well does not refill on its own. You have to go back to the source. The source is not the library or the conference or the podcast about ministry strategy. The source is what it has always been: the silence that is not comfortable until you have stayed in it long enough, the Scripture that addresses you rather than providing material, the prayer that begins with an honest accounting of what is actually true.

Go back. Go regularly. The congregation is waiting to receive what you find there.

The pastor chose this life. He felt the call, pursued the training, said yes to the church. His spouse said yes to *him* — and somewhere in that yes, often without fully reckoning the cost, said yes to a life she did not choose the way he did. That asymmetry sits underneath a great deal of quiet ministry-marriage pain, and most pastors are too close to it to see it.

The research on ministry marriages consistently finds that pastor spouses report higher rates of loneliness, higher rates of depression, and lower rates of marital satisfaction than their peers in comparable non-ministry households [cite — confirm]. These are not people who are unhappy with their faith or their calling. They are people who are carrying a structural burden that their husbands have not named clearly enough to help them bear. The silence around that burden is its own form of harm.

So let me try to say what a pastor's spouse often wishes he knew, and rarely finds the words to tell him without it sounding like an accusation.

---

## The Glass House She Did Not Build

She lives in a glass house she did not build. The congregation watches the pastor's family — the marriage, the children, the home — and forms opinions, and the spouse feels the watching constantly. She cannot have an ordinary bad day in public. She cannot let the kids be ordinary kids without wondering who is drawing conclusions about the pastor's household. She carries a scrutiny the pastor at least signed up for. She did not, and it is wearying in a way he can forget because for him it comes with a calling that gives it meaning. Her suffering is the same suffering, minus the meaning the calling attaches to it for him.

> Her suffering is the same suffering, minus the meaning the calling attaches to it for him.

This dynamic has theological weight. In 1 Timothy 3, the qualifications for an overseer include the management of his own household — *He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?* (1 Timothy 3:4-5). The passage is about the pastor's character and competence, not about making his family a permanent public exhibition. But the way it has been read and applied in church culture has often turned the pastor's family into a performance that the congregation evaluates continuously — a living credential, permanently on display.

The spouse who is performing that credential, rather than simply living her life, is doing a kind of work the congregation does not see and the pastor too often fails to acknowledge. It is real work. It is costly. And the fact that it is invisible does not make it less exhausting.

---

## Sharing You With Everyone

She shares you with everyone, and the sharing is presented to her as holy. The needs of the congregation are real and they are endless, and they have a way of always outranking her. The crisis call comes during dinner and he takes it — and it is the right thing, and it is also the hundredth time — and she is left holding the meal and the children and the unspoken sense that she is competing with God's work for her own husband, a competition she is not allowed to win and not allowed to name.

The theological framing that surrounds pastoral availability — the pastor as the man who is always there, always ready, always present for the flock — can be beautiful in its portrait of genuine shepherd-heart. It becomes corrosive when it is not balanced by the equal theological truth that the pastor's first pastoral responsibility is to the people under his own roof. He was a husband and a father before he was a pastor to anyone else, and those roles do not become less sacred when the ordination certificate arrives. They become more visible, which is a different thing.

I write this as a confession, not a lecture, because I have made my spouse carry versions of this and called the carrying *partnership* when it was really just cost I was offloading. The hardest thing to see, from inside the calling, is that my yes obligated her to a yes she never fully got to give — and that the least I owe her is to stop pretending the weight is symmetrical when it is not.

---

## The Spouse Who Has No Pastor

She often has no pastor. Everyone else in the building has someone to go to with their burdens: the pastor. She is married to him, which means the one person everyone else confides in is the one person she cannot fully confide in about the thing that is hardest — the ministry itself, his exhaustion, the church politics, the wound a board member left, the way a congregant treated her. Her natural confidants are the very people she must be careful around. The result is a particular loneliness: surrounded by a congregation, belonging fully to none of it.

> The result is a particular loneliness: surrounded by a congregation, belonging fully to none of it.

There is a historical precedent for this isolation that the church rarely names. The pastor's wife in American evangelical and Baptist traditions has occupied a peculiar social position since at least the nineteenth century — expected to be simultaneously a model of piety, a servant of the congregation, and an invisible support structure for her husband's ministry. The role was never chosen; it was assumed. Women who married ministers in the 1800s found that the congregation's expectations for their time, their hospitality, their leadership of women's societies, their personal holiness, and their public deportment were exhaustive and uncompensated [cite — confirm]. Those expectations evolved over time, but they did not disappear. They became more covert, which made them harder to name and therefore harder to refuse.

The woman who enters a ministry marriage today carries the inheritance of that history even if she has never read it. The expectations arrive through cultural osmosis — through what people assume when they shake her hand after a service, through what is left unsaid in the women's Bible study, through the subtle ways the congregation signals what a good pastor's wife looks like. She may not be able to articulate where the pressure comes from. She feels it every week.

---

## Staff She Never Applied to Be

She frequently feels like staff she did not apply to be. The unspoken expectations arrive anyway — that she will play piano or lead worship, host small groups, coordinate the women's ministry, model biblical femininity, appear at every significant congregational event with a smile that is genuine, not performed. Her gifts may lie elsewhere entirely. But the role came attached to the marriage, and declining it feels like failing him in front of his people.

The response to this from well-meaning congregations is often some version of *but she doesn't have to do anything* — which is technically true and practically false. She does not have to in the sense of contractual obligation. She does have to in the sense of social pressure that the pastor, who is the one the congregation is invested in pleasing, is often too embedded in the system to feel on her behalf.

What she actually needs is for him to name the expectations clearly and to tell the congregation explicitly that she is not staff, that her role in the church is her own to define, and that the congregation's perception of him as a pastor is not diminished when his wife is simply his wife rather than his unpaid co-pastor. Most pastors never say this because they have never thought it through carefully enough to say it. The assumption runs on autopilot, and so does the cost to her.

---

## What She Actually Needs

What does she need from him? Less than he fears and more than he is giving.

She needs him to see the asymmetry — to stop assuming she experiences this life the way he does, that her relationship to the call is the same as his, that her loneliness is the same as his tiredness. It is not the same. He is tired because he is giving. She is lonely because she is giving in a context that does not even have language for what she is giving.

She needs a pastor of her own — someone outside the congregation she can be honest with, and his active help in finding one. Not permission; partnership. He should be the one making phone calls, identifying options, clearing time in the schedule, making the conditions in which genuine pastoral care for her is possible, not leaving it to her to solve alone after she has already carried the invisible weight of the household and the ministry's social obligations.

She needs the freedom to not be the unpaid associate minister — to define her own role in the church, or to step back from a role that was assumed onto her rather than asked of her. This is his responsibility to communicate to the congregation, not hers. He is the one with standing. He should use it.

She needs some part of him that the congregation cannot have, reliably and not as leftovers. The husband who is fully present at every hospital visit and staff meeting and weekend event and arrives at home as a residual person — distracted, depleted, already composing next week's sermon in the back of his mind — is not protecting his marriage. He is borrowing against it, and the debt compounds.

And she needs to hear, out loud and often, that her sacrifice is seen — because the congregation will never fully thank her, and the applause that sustains him does not reach her at all. She lives in the wake of his visibility, and visibility has a wake.

---

The pastoral imagination that has always spoken of the church as a family has often failed to protect the actual family at the center of it. The man who cares for five hundred people while failing to see the one person who sees him most clearly — who knows him past the pulpit, who carries the weight the congregation never sees — has made a theological error in the arrangement of his loves.

> The called one owes her more than gratitude. He owes her sight.

You were called. She came with you, into a house she did not build, to share you with a thousand people who will never know what it cost her. The called one owes her more than gratitude. He owes her sight.

Ask her what she wishes you knew. Then be quiet long enough to actually hear it. What she says will be the most useful theological education you receive this year.

The church staff that cannot keep good people has usually decided, usually without knowing it, that the mission matters more than the people serving it. Not in any document. Not in any stated value. In the daily accumulation of small decisions: the email sent at eleven on a Sunday night that expects a response, the week off that never quite materialized, the meeting scheduled over someone's standing personal commitment, the feedback that is always corrective and never affirming, the sense that the pastor is pleased when things go well and disappointed in the person when they do not.

> This is how cultures are actually built. Not by the vision statement. By what happens between the meetings.

This is how cultures are actually built. Not by the vision statement. By what happens between the meetings.

I have been that pastor. Not intentionally. But I have looked at the pattern of who left and why and seen in it a reflection of assumptions I carried without examining them — that commitment to ministry was demonstrated by availability, that the people who stayed late cared more than the people who went home, that excellence in the work was its own reward and the person providing it should find that sufficient. These assumptions are common among pastors who came to ministry with genuine calling and genuine zeal. They are also, quietly, brutal — because they treat the people on staff as instruments of the mission rather than as participants in it.

## Instruments or Image-Bearers

I want to say that more carefully. Not merely inefficient. Theologically wrong.

The distinction matters. If the problem were merely efficiency, the solution would be better management — adjusted compensation, clearer org charts, upgraded sabbatical policies. You could fix it with a consultant and a calendar audit. What I am describing is something beneath that, a failure of theological imagination about what persons are. The church that burns its staff members through the grinder of relentless missional urgency has not simply made a management error. It has violated the imago Dei in the people it was meant to serve alongside. It has treated the image-bearers in the building as fuel rather than as ends.

That is not a small error. That is a theological one.

---

## The Witness of Paul and Nehemiah

Paul told the Thessalonians that he had been gentle among them "like a nursing mother caring for her own children" (1 Thessalonians 2:7) — that his ministry among them was not simply proclamation but the giving of his own life. He stays in that maternal image deliberately. It is not accidental tenderness. It is a specific kind of attention: close, physically present, responsive to what the person in front of him actually needs rather than what the program requires. That posture extends to the people a pastor leads, not only the congregation he serves.

Nehemiah is another witness. In the account of the wall's reconstruction, what is striking is how often Nehemiah attends to the people doing the work — not just to the work itself. He posts guards at the exposed sections so the workers are not alone (Nehemiah 4:13). He feeds people at his own table (Nehemiah 5:17). When the nobles are exploiting their workers financially, he calls them out publicly (Nehemiah 5:7) — not because it threatens the project's timeline, but because it is wrong to use people that way. The mission is real and urgent. And the people are not expendable.

> He is a good project manager who has made people into project components.

Most pastoral leaders know Nehemiah as a leadership text. We use it to teach vision, communication, perseverance under opposition. We do not use it nearly enough to teach this: that the leader who cannot protect his people's dignity while pursuing the mission is not actually a good leader. He is a good project manager who has made people into project components.

---

## The Conditions That Retain People

The structural conditions that retain good people are not mysterious, but they require the pastor to be honest about what is actually happening — which is harder than it sounds.

Sustainable workloads. This means the pastor himself has to be willing to say that there is too much and something has to come off. Most ministry leaders are constitutionally resistant to this admission because reducing the load feels like reducing the faithfulness. It does not. It feels like the Sabbath command. God did not give Israel the Sabbath because he was concerned about agricultural productivity. He gave it because a people who cannot stop working have started to believe that the world depends on them. That belief is not faith. It is a subtle form of idolatry dressed in the clothing of dedication.

The pastor whose staff is chronically overloaded has, consciously or not, decided that the mission's demands outweigh the limits of embodied human beings. He is wrong. And the people he has made that decision about will eventually tell him so — not usually directly, because the power differential makes directness costly — but through their resignations, through their disengagement, through the slow erosion of the energy they once brought to work they once loved.

Clear expectations. People cannot thrive in an environment where the standard is invisible. "Excellence" is not a job description. "Passion for the mission" is not a performance review. The staff member who does not know what successful performance looks like will spend enormous emotional energy managing anxiety rather than doing work. That anxiety accumulates over months and years into a kind of chronic fatigue that looks from the outside like disengagement and is actually exhaustion from a different cause.

Genuine affirmation. Not flattery. Specific acknowledgment of specific contributions, given often enough that it does not feel like an event. I have watched myself fall into the pattern of silence when things are going well and comment when something is wrong. Over time, that pattern teaches the people around me that my attention means there is a problem — and that when they have done something genuinely well, no one is watching. That is not the culture I want. It is the culture I accidentally built by neglecting the specific discipline of noticing and naming what is good.

Genuine development. The pastor who cares whether his staff are growing — not just performing — invests time and attention in that growth even when it is not immediately productive. This is counterintuitive in seasons of urgency. But the staff member who is growing in their craft, their theological depth, their leadership capacity, is far more likely to remain. Not because they have become more valuable to the institution, but because they have become more fully themselves in it.

---

## The Abuse of the Language of Sacrifice

There is a counter-position worth taking seriously. The minister's life has always demanded irregular hours, personal sacrifice, availability to crisis. Paul's own ministry demonstrates this — prison, beatings, sleepless nights, the daily pressure of his care for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:23-28). The history of Christian ministry is not a history of people who went home at five. The saints and servants who shaped the church were not people who prioritized self-care over availability.

That witness is real and it deserves respect. It is also regularly abused.

The difference is not whether sacrifice is ever appropriate — it is. The difference is between sacrifice that is freely given by a person who has been given the conditions for genuine choice, and sacrifice that is extracted by a culture that treats exhaustion as evidence of commitment. Paul's suffering was not extracted by Barnabas. It was the result of his own response to his own calling, in relationship with communities that also suffered, in the context of a mission that cost everyone something. The cross is at the center of this faith. It cannot be domesticated.

> But the cross that Paul carried was not put there by a senior pastor who sent emails at midnight.

But the cross that Paul carried was not put there by a senior pastor who sent emails at midnight.

The abuse of the language of sacrifice — using the vocabulary of calling and mission to make excessive labor demands seem like faithfulness — is one of the most common forms of manipulation in church staff culture. Pastors who do this are not usually doing it deliberately. They have usually been shaped by the same culture themselves and have never had anyone help them see what it looks like from the receiving end.

I have been shaped by it. I have practiced it. These words are self-implicating.

---

## The Sabbath Applied to the Staff Meeting

Building a staff culture where good people remain requires that the pastor see the people around him — actually see them, not as ministry capacities to be deployed but as persons whose inner lives, families, physical limits, and flourishing matter to God and should therefore matter to the person who leads them.

This is the Sabbath command applied to the staff meeting. Exodus 20:10 does not permit the household's workers to be required to labor on the day of rest. The command was given to a people who had just come out of a system in which unlimited labor extraction was normal — where persons were categorized as labor and their limits were irrelevant to the logic of production. The Sabbath command was a categorical refusal of that logic. It said: not here. Not among God's people. Not to anyone in your care.

That principle does not expire in Exodus. It runs through the prophets, through the wisdom literature, through the teaching of Jesus — who noticed that the disciples were hungry and made time for them to eat (Mark 6:31), who saw that they were weary after ministry and called them to rest. The one who built the church knew that the people building it were not machines.

Build the culture you would want to work inside. Not the culture that is most productive by the ministry's metrics. Not the culture that extracts the most from the most committed people. The culture in which a person who is genuinely called, genuinely gifted, and genuinely devoted to the work can remain for twenty years and emerge more whole than when they arrived.

Then build it before you have to. Because the culture you have is already communicating something to every person on your staff. It is telling them what they are worth to you. It is telling them whether their limits matter, whether their families count, whether the mission is something they are invited into or something they are consumed by.

They are listening. They are drawing conclusions. Some of them have already made the decision you have not yet been told about.

Start now. Build the thing you actually believe about the people God has given you to lead.

That is not a management strategy.

That is pastoral faithfulness applied internally.

It was a Tuesday afternoon when I finally admitted it to myself. I was preparing a sermon on grief — Psalm 22, the one Jesus quoted from the cross — and I was not praying. I was workshopping. I was testing the lines. I was listening to how the material would land in the room on Sunday morning and editing accordingly. The sermon was about a man's abandonment by God, and I was producing content about it. The distance between those two things had opened without my permission, and I had not noticed because the sermons were still good. People were still moved. The machine was running.

> It works for a long time before it destroys you, and during the time it is working, you have almost no way to know the difference from the inside.

That is the particular danger of performance-driven ministry. It works for a long time before it destroys you, and during the time it is working, you have almost no way to know the difference from the inside. The congregation cannot tell. The metrics cannot tell. Your own emotional experience cannot tell, because the performance generates its own adrenaline, and adrenaline is a reasonable counterfeit of joy if you do not inspect it too closely.

This is not a modern problem. It is a problem as old as the office.

## A Problem as Old as the Office

Jeremiah carried it. The prophet who wept over Jerusalem, who dictated laments to Baruch, who told God he did not want to speak anymore and found the word burning in his bones like fire — Jeremiah 20 gives us the anatomy of a man who could not tell the difference between his calling and his crisis, who had been performing faithfulness so long that he no longer knew where the performance ended and the person began. The Pastoral Letters to Timothy understood it: Paul does not say simply *be competent*. He says *watch your life and your doctrine closely* (1 Timothy 4:16). The doctrine first, then the life. The sequence matters. The interior first, then the public work. You cannot reverse the order and keep the goods.

The Reformers had a phrase for the opposite condition: *coram Deo*, before the face of God. Life lived in conscious awareness of the divine presence, not as an emotional experience but as an ontological reality — everything done before an audience of One. Luther's early polemic against indulgences was not primarily ecclesiological; it was a protest against a system that had made religious performance profitable, that had given people a way to satisfy the demand of God without being changed by the encounter with God. The indulgence was performance made sacramental. And Luther knew it, in part, because he had watched himself do the same thing in a different register. He had performed his way through the monastery for years, flagellating himself toward holiness while missing the Gospel that made holiness possible. The Reformation came from a man who had been performing for God and finally stopped.

## Coram Deo and the Convert's Intensity

I came to faith from atheism, which means I entered the pastoral ministry with a convert's intensity — the kind that can look like earnestness but is sometimes closer to a man still performing for an audience he secretly fears does not exist. I had something to prove. I had left a whole framework of meaning and rebuilt it around the Gospel, and the ministry was, for the first several years, partly an argument I was still making to myself. Preaching was convincing. Prayer was a kind of self-reassurance. The pastoral work was real, but underneath it was a man still not entirely sure he was allowed to be there, still earning the right.

## How Performance Creeps In

Performance creeps in through the smallest doors. It begins, often, with a good Sunday — a sermon that connected, a response that gratified, a moment in the room where you felt the thing you entered ministry hoping to feel. And then, imperceptibly, you begin to aim for that feeling rather than for the truth that produced it. You begin to construct the sermon not from Scripture outward but from the desired emotional landing backward. You begin to measure the week by how the congregation felt on Sunday rather than by whether you prayed on Monday. The craft — which is a real thing and matters — starts to replace the conversation with God that the craft is supposed to serve.

Eugene Peterson, in his long argument for what he called the contemplative pastor, put it this way: the pastor's most important work is not visible to the congregation and produces no immediate results [cite — confirm]. It is the slow, unhurried work of being shaped by prayer and Scripture before either is used to shape anyone else. Peterson was drawing on a tradition that runs from the Desert Fathers through the medieval mystics through the Puritan tradition of the pastor as a man of God first and a professional second — a tradition that American evangelical pragmatism has largely gutted in favor of measurable outcomes. We know what a healthy attendance curve looks like. We are considerably less certain what a healthy pastor looks like on a Monday morning in his study.

> Here is what the performance costs that no one names clearly enough: it costs you the interior life that makes the external work worth doing.

Here is what the performance costs that no one names clearly enough: it costs you the interior life that makes the external work worth doing.

A man can preach the resurrection and not believe it — not the way you believe something that has reorganized your life, but believe it the way you believe a fact you rehearse rather than a reality you inhabit. The performance keeps the words in order while the faith that animated them slowly depletes. The congregation hears a sermon. The preacher knows, somewhere beneath the craft, that he is reading from a script that used to be a letter. The script is accurate. But there is a difference between a letter and a script, and the man at the lectern is not always able to say which one he is holding.

## The Long Road of Recovery

The recovery did not come with a single crisis or a dramatic confrontation. It came slowly, the way the drift had come. It began when I started meeting weekly with two other pastors who had made a specific commitment to tell each other the truth. Not pastoral colleagues sharing sermon illustrations. Two men who agreed, explicitly, that the pastoral face was not allowed in the room. We prayed for each other with the specificity that requires actual knowledge of actual circumstances. We named what was happening inside the work, not just in the work. It was ordinary and it was essential.

The second thing was a decision to re-order the week so that sermon preparation was not the week's first priority. Prayer was. Not prayer in the professional sense — the pastoral prayer, the staff meeting invocation — but the unscheduled, unproductive, honestly formative sitting with God that has nothing to do with Sunday. Eugene Peterson called it the pastor's first responsibility, the formation of the pastor's own soul. I had known this. I had not been doing it. The reorganization of the week felt like loss at first and then felt like coming back to myself.

The third thing was harder. I had to ask whether the image I was projecting from the platform was the same person who existed Monday through Saturday. Not whether I was lying — I was not. But whether the pastoral persona had developed its own internal logic that was not fully accountable to the actual man. There was a gap. Smaller than I feared, larger than I had admitted. Closing it required years, not a weekend.

There is a steel-man for the performance argument. The pastor's role is partly liturgical in the sense that the sermon has a structure, the public self must be ordered enough to bear the congregation's projections without shattering. You are not simply yourself on Sunday morning. You are also a vessel, a representative, a person inhabiting an office. The Reformers understood this — Calvin insisted that the preacher's authority came not from his personality but from the Word he was called to proclaim. The office confers a dignity that does not depend on the individual's interior state on a given Sunday. These things are real and not spiritually corrupt in themselves.

## The Vessel Must Be Full

But the vessel must be full of something. The representative must be representing something real. The office must be inhabited by an actual man whose interior life is not a performance. When the performance consumes the person, there is nothing left to offer but a better and better-crafted emptiness. The congregation may not be able to name what they are receiving, but they will feel it. The word for what they are feeling is the word they use when someone says *I love you* and you suspect they are rehearsing rather than meaning it. They are receiving something technically correct and essentially hollow.

Bonhoeffer, writing from Tegel Prison in the last years of his life, asked what it means for a man to know God not at the margins of life — in crisis, in extremity — but at the center, in the ordinary materials of Mondays and meals and the body's needs [cite — confirm]. That question is the pastor's question at every point. Not whether you can perform godliness under pressure. Whether you inhabit it when no one is watching, when the sermon is three days away, when the phone is quiet and the calendar is clear and there is nothing to produce.

That Tuesday afternoon with Psalm 22, I put the outline down. I sat with the text the way you sit with something that is going to address you, not the way you sit with something you are going to use. The sermon that came from it was different. I cannot tell you that the congregation knew the difference. I know I did. The gap between the man and the work was a little smaller. That is what recovery looks like — not dramatic, not sudden, not visible from the platform. A little smaller. Again and again. Until the sermon is a letter and not a script, and the man at the lectern is reading his own name.

> Stop performing. Not today, not all at once. But begin.

Stop performing. Not today, not all at once. But begin. One honest conversation. One un-workshopped prayer. One week where the sermon is a letter to God before it is a communication to the congregation.

That is where pastoring starts. And it is a long road back from the place most of us have already gone.

I will tell you something I am not proud of. For years I kept a private scoreboard. The church across town grew, and something in me tightened. Their building project went up, and I found a reason it was unwise. Their pastor was kind to me at the lunch, and I went home and explained to myself why his kindness was a strategy. I would not have called it competition. I called it discernment. It was envy wearing a collar.

> It was envy wearing a collar.

The competitive spirit in ministry is quiet, and that is what makes it dangerous. It does not announce itself. It hides inside legitimate things — a desire to reach people, a longing to see the work flourish, a healthy attention to whether you are being faithful. It borrows the language of zeal and it means something closer to fear. Fear that there is not enough — not enough people, not enough room, not enough significance — and that the brother down the road is taking your share.

That fear has a long history in the church, and naming the history helps.

## The History Beneath the Scoreboard

The American church inherited a model of congregational success shaped less by the New Testament than by the market logic of the frontier. When circuit riders competed for converts in the early nineteenth century, the theological framework was revivalism and the practical metric was decisions. Charles Finney's "new measures" — the anxious bench, the protracted meeting, the direct appeal for public commitment — were innovations designed, consciously or not, to be more effective than what the next denomination was doing [cite — confirm]. The competition was dressed in the language of harvest, but the underlying logic was institutional. More converts was better. More converts than the Methodists was better still.

That logic did not disappear when the frontier closed. It migrated into the church growth movement of the late twentieth century, which imported the language of market strategy and demographic analysis and consumer preference into the work of building congregations. The result was a pastoral culture shaped by competitive growth metrics — attendance, giving units, square footage, platform visibility — and a generation of pastors whose sense of vocational health was indexed to those metrics more than they knew. I was one of those pastors. The scoreboard I was keeping was not an aberration. It was the ecosystem.

Here is the theology underneath the competition: a functional belief that the kingdom of God is a zero-sum market. That the family who joins the church across town is a family that cannot join mine. That the pastor whose platform grows at my city's expense has taken something from me. That the town is not large enough for both of us to be faithful.

## The Kingdom Is Not a Market

It is a strange thing to believe while preaching the gospel I preach. The kingdom of God is not a market. The other church is not my competitor; it is, if the creed I recite on Sundays is true, the same body, serving the same Lord, advancing the same kingdom in the same town. When they reach a family I never could, the kingdom gains. When their doors stay open through a hard year, the gospel has a witness on a corner where mine does not stand. I knew all of that. I preached all of that. And I kept the scoreboard anyway, because the heart can hold a doctrine and disobey it at the same time, and a pastor's heart is not exempt.

What broke it was not an argument. It was a funeral.

## What Broke It Was a Funeral

A pastor I had quietly measured myself against lost a child, and I sat in his sanctuary, in the back, and watched a man I had been competing with stand at the front of the worst day of his life. There was no scoreboard in that room. There was a brother, and grief, and the same Lord we both served holding both of us up. I drove home and I could not find the rivalry anymore. It had never been real. I had built it out of my own fear and then lived inside it as though it were a fact.

Grief has a way of stripping the constructed things down to what actually holds. What held in that room was not institutional. It was the unity that Paul describes in Ephesians 4 — one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father (Ephesians 4:4-6). The oneness is not aspirational. It is the already-given reality that we are called to *keep*, to guard, to preserve — not to create. The competition was a denial of something that was already true. I was fighting over territory in a kingdom that was never divided.

## The Brothers the Competition Costs

Here is what the competition costs, and it is more than character. It costs you the brothers.

A pastor's loneliness is real and well-documented, and one of its quiet engines is this: the men who could most understand your work are the very men you have decided to compete with. You isolate yourself from your only true peers and then wonder why no one understands. The pastoral work is not fully legible to the congregation — they experience it but do not see behind it. The pastoral work is not fully legible to the denomination — they track metrics but not the interior. The pastoral work is legible to other pastors, because they are doing it too, because they have felt the same weight on the same kinds of Sundays. And if you have made them rivals, you have cut off the relationship that could most honestly hold you.

> And if you have made them rivals, you have cut off the relationship that could most honestly hold you.

The Pastoral Connection Network was built on a recognition of exactly this: that the pastor's isolation is not an inevitable feature of the role but a structural problem that requires a structural solution. Men who should be brothers have been made strangers by competition, geography, and the habits of professional self-protection. The network is an attempt to reverse that — to build, deliberately and with some effort, the kind of relationship where the scoreboard is not allowed. I know what the network can produce, because I have been inside it and I have watched men find, in middle age, the pastoral friendships that the competition kept them from building in their thirties.

## The Steel-Man and Its Corruption

The steel-man for the competitive approach goes like this: healthy competition between churches raises the quality of ministry across the board. When churches compete for the same population, each is incentivized to be more effective, more relevant, more excellent in its programming and preaching and pastoral care. The market produces quality. The congregation benefits.

The argument has a partial truth in it. The churches I have been inside that were most serious about excellence in preaching were often led by pastors who had excellent peers they were measuring themselves against. Excellence does not emerge in isolation. The standard matters.

But the competitive framework corrupts the goal. When the goal of the excellent sermon is to attract more families than the excellent sermon down the road, the sermon is no longer primarily an address from God to the congregation. It is a competitive product. The pastoral care that is driven by retention strategy is no longer primarily about the flourishing of the souls being cared for. It is institutional maintenance dressed in pastoral language. The corruption is not obvious, but it is real, and it shows up in what the pastor actually worries about when he lies awake at three in the morning.

So I stopped, as best a man can stop a thing that grows back. I started praying for the church across town by name, and meaning it, which is harder than it sounds. I started telling the truth at the pastors' lunch instead of managing my image at it. When their work flourished, I made myself say, out loud to God, *good* — and kept saying it until some of it became true in me.

I started sending families to that church when it was clear they belonged there better than they belonged with me. This was the hardest part. Not the prayer and not the honesty — those were interior changes that cost something but cost it privately. Sending a family across town is a public act with a public cost. The congregation notices the departure. The scoreboard takes a hit. But the family needed what the other church could give them, and my commitment was to them, not to the number. The commission to make disciples does not include a territorial clause.

The town does not need two pastors quietly at war for the same hundred families. It needs a few who have laid the scoreboard down — who can stand in each other's sanctuaries on the worst days, who can send a family across town when that church can serve them better, who measure their ministries by faithfulness and not by the comparison that was always going to leave them empty.

Jesus prayed that his people would be one, so that the world would believe (John 17:21). He tied our unity to the gospel's credibility. The watching town is not most persuaded by the church that wins. It is persuaded, if it is persuaded at all, by the unlikely sight of churches that could compete and refuse to. The unity is the witness. The competition is its undoing.

I still notice the scoreboard. I would be lying if I said otherwise. The machine was built over years and it does not dismantle in a season. But I notice it now as a symptom rather than a fact — a flag that tells me fear is operating, that the kingdom logic has been temporarily displaced by market logic, that I need to pray for the brother whose success triggered the tightening.

> The brother across town was never the rival. The fear was.

Lay it down. The brother across town was never the rival. The fear was. And the fear was lying to you the whole time.

The Hebrew word is *ger* — the resident alien, the one who lives among the people of Israel without belonging to the kinship networks that provide protection and standing. Not a visitor passing through. Not an enemy combatant. The *ger* is the person who has come to live among you, who has made a life in the community, who is present and vulnerable, who has no one at the city gate to advocate for him in the legal disputes that determined whether you kept your land, your freedom, and your family.

In the ancient Near Eastern world, the city gate was where commerce was conducted, where legal disputes were adjudicated, where the elders sat to render judgment (Ruth 4:1-11). To have advocates at the gate was to have standing in society. The widow had lost hers when her husband died. The orphan had never had any. The *ger* — the resident alien — arrived without the kinship connections that made advocacy possible. He was present but not protected. In the community but not of it in the way that generated legal standing.

It is for this person that the law of Israel makes repeated, detailed, insistent provision.

## The Shape of the Law

Leviticus 19:33-34 states: "When a foreigner resides among you in your land, do not mistreat them. The foreigner residing among you must be treated as your native-born. Love them as yourself, for you were foreigners in Egypt. I am the Lord your God." This is not a general hospitality principle. It is a specific legal command with a theological rationale: you know what it means to be the stranger. You lived it in Egypt. That memory is the basis of the obligation.

Deuteronomy returns to this command so many times that it cannot be read as incidental. The tithe every third year includes provision for the *ger* alongside the widow and the orphan (Deuteronomy 14:29). The gleaning laws require that the edges of the field be left unharvested so that the *ger* can eat (Deuteronomy 24:19-21). The Sabbath rest applies to the *ger* as well as to Israel's own people (Deuteronomy 5:14) — which means the alien worker receives the same weekly rest that the Israelite landowner receives, a provision that directly limits the economic exploitation of vulnerable labor. The stranger is woven into the fabric of the covenant community's economic and social life, not as an object of charity, but as a participant with legal standing and legal protections.

The rationale is always the same: you were foreigners in Egypt. The Exodus is not merely a theological event. It is the founding memory that shapes Israel's ethical obligations for the rest of her history. The people who were enslaved in a foreign land, who were vulnerable and powerless, who had no advocate at the gate — those people were liberated by God. And because God liberated them, they are obligated to never become the kind of community that treats the *ger* the way Egypt treated them.

> Justice rooted in memory.

This theological logic is among the most demanding in the entire Old Testament. It is not asking Israel to be generous to strangers out of benevolence. It is asking Israel to remember its own history with enough clarity that the sight of a vulnerable stranger activates the same obligation God demonstrated toward them when they were in that position. Justice rooted in memory. The obligation flows from the story, and the story is not allowed to be forgotten.

## The Prophetic Indictment

When Israel forgets, the prophets name it. Ezekiel 22:7 includes the mistreatment of the foreigner in a list of sins that constitute the grounds for Jerusalem's destruction: "In you they have treated father and mother with contempt; in you they have oppressed the foreigner and mistreated the fatherless and the widow." The *ger* is mentioned in the same breath as the widow and orphan — the other figures without advocates at the gate. Jeremiah 7:6 places doing wrong to the foreigner alongside shedding innocent blood as conditions of God's continued presence in the temple. Zechariah 7:10 commands: "Do not oppress the widow or the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor."

The prophets are not speaking abstractly. They are naming specific economic practices that stripped the *ger* of resources and left them without recourse — the wage theft, the land encroachment, the debt arrangements that turned vulnerability into permanent servitude. The law of Moses was attempting to build a society structurally unlike Egypt. The prophets are pointing to the places where Israel has, over centuries, rebuilt the Egyptian arrangements under a different name.

> To be the community of God, in this account, is to share that positioning — to place yourself at the gate in behalf of the one who cannot place themselves there.

The God of the Old Testament is consistently described as the protector of those who have no human protector. Psalm 146:9 is a brief but total statement: "The Lord watches over the foreigner and sustains the fatherless and the widow, but he frustrates the ways of the wicked." God is positioned at the gate, on behalf of those who have no one else there. To be the community of God, in this account, is to share that positioning — to place yourself at the gate in behalf of the one who cannot place themselves there.

## The New Testament Extension

The New Testament does not retire this obligation. Jesus's parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37) takes the boundaries of the *ger* obligation and pushes them past any kinship or ethnic category entirely: the neighbor is not defined by who they are but by who is in front of you in need. And Revelation's vision of the renewed Jerusalem includes "every nation, tribe, people and language" gathered before the throne (Revelation 7:9). The stranger at the gate of the earthly community is, in the eschatological vision, invited to the center of the heavenly one.

Matthew 25 brings this full circle: "I was a stranger and you invited me in" (Matthew 25:35). Not "you contributed to a relief fund that served strangers." Not "you voted for policies that technically improved conditions for strangers." You invited me in. The personal, particular, costly hospitality that the Levitical law envisioned — where the stranger is your native-born, where you love them as yourself — is the thing Jesus names as the criterion of judgment. The encounter with the stranger is the encounter with Christ. The welcome or refusal is rendered, in this account, to him.

## The Steel-Man Position

The serious objection deserves engagement: national sovereignty requires the ability to regulate borders, and the biblical category of the *ger* does not map cleanly onto contemporary immigration debates that involve complicated questions of legal process, national security, and economic impact. Reasonable people who take Scripture seriously disagree about the specific policies that should govern immigration. The text does not resolve those debates automatically.

This is true. The Levitical law was written for a covenant community, not for a modern nation-state, and direct application requires careful work.

But the objection is used, most commonly, to do something the text does not permit: to move from the complexity of policy to silence about the person. Whatever the correct immigration policy is, the person who has arrived — the *ger* who is present in the community, working, living, raising children — is protected by this sustained biblical concern. The law's specific provisions are translatable even when its specific mechanisms are not. The *ger* must be treated as your native-born. The foreigner must not be mistreated. You must love them as yourself.

The complexity of immigration policy does not release the church from the obligation to the immigrant in front of it. The complexity is real. The obligation is also real. The church that uses the one to avoid the other has made a choice that the text will not ratify.

## What the Church Has Done

I have watched the church in America decide, in recent decades, that its response to the question of strangers and immigrants is primarily a political position rather than a biblical one. I have made that calculation myself — weighing the political complexity against the textual clarity and concluding that the complexity was reason enough to stay quiet. That is not neutrality. It is a choice, and it has a cost that I have not always been willing to name.

The churches in my denomination have people in their pews who hold strong opinions about immigration enforcement. They have people whose families include undocumented members. They have people who came here as strangers and built lives. They have people who are afraid of the stranger and people who are the stranger. Navigating that pastoral reality is genuinely hard, and I do not want to pretend it is easy.

But the text is not hard to read. Leviticus 19:33-34 is not ambiguous. Deuteronomy 24:19 is not ambiguous. Ezekiel 22:7 is not ambiguous. The theological rationale — you were foreigners in Egypt — is not a complex hermeneutical puzzle. It is a direct appeal to a founding memory that the church has largely allowed to be overwritten by political identity.

The memory that Israel was commanded to maintain — that they had been the *ger*, that they knew the vulnerability from the inside, that God had been their advocate when they had no other — is available to the church in a different form. The church exists because God chose the stranger. Abraham left his country and kindred and went to a land he did not know (Genesis 12:1). Israel spent four hundred years as the stranger in a foreign land. Jesus was a refugee in Egypt (Matthew 2:13-14). The disciples scattered after the resurrection and took the gospel to nations that had not asked for it, making themselves strangers in service of the God who had welcomed them.

The church is not a settled community that receives strangers as a courtesy. It is, in its deepest identity, a community of strangers — people who confess that they have "no permanent city" (Hebrews 13:14) and who look for the city that is to come. The welcome of the stranger is not a program the church considers alongside other options. It is a recognition of what the church itself is.

The stranger is at the gate. The text is clear about what is required. The question is whether the community that claims to live by that text will remember what it was when it had no one at the gate to advocate for it.

> The stranger is at the gate. The text is clear about what is required.

The obligation has not changed. The gate is still the same gate.

You cannot make a compelling case for the value of a human life and then decline to fund what that life requires to survive.

This is not a rhetorical point. It is a logical one. If the argument for protecting the unborn is grounded in the Imago Dei — in the conviction that every human being bears the image of God and therefore possesses intrinsic worth — then that argument does not expire at delivery. The image of God is not a prenatal condition. It is a permanent one.

> This is not a rhetorical point. It is a logical one.

The church has sometimes spoken as though the protection of life before birth and the support of life after birth are separate concerns, pursued by different kinds of people with different political orientations. That separation is not biblical. It is a product of American political sorting, and the church has been far too willing to accept it.

## What the Scriptures Say About Life After Birth

Deuteronomy 15:11 is not a suggestion: "There will always be poor people in the land. Therefore I command you to be openhanded toward your fellow Israelites who are poor and needy." The openhanded command is not qualified by whether the poor person made good choices or by whether their poverty was deserved. It is absolute, and it is addressed to the whole community as a community obligation, not only as an individual aspiration.

Proverbs 19:17 makes the theological stakes explicit: "Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord." The language is astonishing. To care for the poor person in front of you is to be in a transaction with God — not a metaphorical one, but a real one in which God is the debtor. The Proverbs do not offer this as an exaggeration. It is a claim about the identification between God and the person in need.

Matthew 25:40 extends this identification into the New Testament: "Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me." The "least of these" in Matthew 25 are not abstract. They are hungry, thirsty, naked, sick, imprisoned. They are specific human beings in specific circumstances, and the test Jesus describes is not ideological affiliation or theological correctness. It is material response to material need.

The child who is born into poverty is hungry, thirsty, and in need of the community's material response. The infant whose mother cannot afford prenatal care, whose family has no stable housing, whose neighborhood has no adequate healthcare — that child is in exactly the category Matthew 25 is describing. The church that was passionate about that child's right to be born and then withdraws from the community's responsibility to support the child's life has not been pro-life. It has been pre-natal.

## The Imago Dei Does Not Expire

The theological argument for the sanctity of unborn life is the same argument that demands material support for the lives already born. If the ground of the argument is that every human person, regardless of their size, their developmental stage, their economic contribution, their cognitive capacity, bears the image of God — then the argument that covers the embryo also covers the infant, the toddler, the child in the underfunded school, the teenager in the juvenile justice system, the adult in prison.

The image of God does not come with conditions. It is not contingent on productivity or viability or social utility. It is a permanent feature of what it means to be human. And the church that uses the Imago Dei to defend the unborn but then treats the born poor as a separate category — as a political issue rather than a theological one — has not actually applied the argument it claims. It has applied it selectively, which is to say it has not applied it at all.

> The image of God does not come with conditions.

This is an indictment that lands on me before it lands anywhere else. I have been quicker to preach the sanctity of the unborn than to examine what my congregation's budget says about its actual commitment to the lives of those who have been born into hardship in our community. The gap between the conviction I articulate and the resources I deploy is a gap that requires honest examination.

## What the Credibility Gap Costs

The credibility of the pro-life argument depends, in no small part, on whether the people who make it are willing to pay for it. This is not cynicism. It is the ordinary epistemology of moral argument: the person who calls you to a sacrifice they are not willing to make themselves has a credibility problem that is not rhetorical. It is substantive.

The watching world — including the people most likely to be persuaded by a pro-life argument — has noticed the gap. The political scientist who observes that the states with the strongest abortion restrictions also have the weakest social safety nets is making a sociological observation [cite — confirm]. But it lands as a moral one. The church that is loudest about protecting the unborn in the womb and quietest about funding what those children need after birth has demonstrated something about what it actually believes. Not what it says it believes. What it believes.

The pro-choice argument gains its most powerful traction from exactly this gap. When the argument is made that pro-life legislation forces women to carry pregnancies to term without adequate support for what comes after — and when the churches that advocate for that legislation have not demonstrated a credible commitment to filling that support gap — the argument is not easily answered. The church's response cannot be purely theological. It must be material.

## What the Counter-Argument Gets Right

There is an honest counter-position: the church is not the government, and the demand that congregations solve systemic poverty before they earn the right to advocate against abortion is a form of rhetorical hostage-taking designed to produce paralysis rather than action. No other advocacy position is held to this standard. Anti-trafficking organizations are not required to solve poverty before they can oppose trafficking. Civil rights organizations were not required to solve structural inequality before they could oppose segregation.

This argument is partially correct. The demand for perfect consistency before any advocacy is permitted is unreasonable and is often deployed strategically to silence positions that the person making the demand opposes. The church should not accept the premise that its pro-life advocacy is invalid until it has solved poverty.

But the counter-argument does not discharge the obligation. It establishes that the obligation does not need to be fully met before advocacy is permitted. It does not establish that the obligation does not exist. The church can advocate for the unborn and simultaneously — not sequentially, but simultaneously — advocate for and fund the material support that makes life after birth possible. The failure to do the second does not invalidate the first. But it does narrow the argument's moral reach in ways the church should care about.

## What Material Support for Life After Birth Actually Looks Like

The obligation is specific. It looks like adoption and foster care ministries that are as organized, funded, and publicly celebrated as the political advocacy for the unborn. It looks like material support — diapers, food, rent assistance, childcare — for the women in the congregation who chose life without a support system. It looks like advocacy for the healthcare and childcare policies that determine whether a single mother can survive with a newborn. It looks like congregations that track the outcomes for the children they helped bring into the world, and remain present for those outcomes.

It looks like a church willing to ask the uncomfortable question: of the women in our congregation who have given birth in the last five years, how many of them had genuine material support from this community beyond a baby shower? How many of them know they can call someone here at midnight when the situation is impossible? How many of them are still connected to this congregation, or did the community's attention evaporate when the urgency did?

Those questions are harder than a political position. They require more than a vote. They require the kind of long, slow, material investment that does not generate a testimony at the denominational gathering.

They are also the questions that determine whether the pro-life conviction is real or performed.
