The richest exploration of this problem in Scripture may be Ecclesiastes, where Qohelet catalogues every possible way that a person can spend their time — work, pleasure, wisdom, accumulation, achievement — and returns again and again to the verdict: vapor. Not because those things are worthless, but because they cannot answer the question of what a life is for. The answer to that question does not emerge from better time allocation. It requires the fear of God, which is what Qohelet arrives at in the final chapter (Ecclesiastes 12:13): "Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the duty of all mankind." Not efficiency. Orientation.

Until you ask what God actually wants from your day, you will keep sacrificing what is eternal on the altar of what feels urgent. The urgent is usually clear. The eternal requires discernment, which requires quiet, which requires the willingness to stop.

## The Practical Shape of a Theology of Time

A theology of time is not a productivity philosophy with Sabbath added. It is a different orientation from the beginning. It asks, before it asks how to organize the day, what the day is for — what kind of person you are trying to be and what kind of presence you are trying to offer to the people and the work and the God that constitute your actual life.

It builds in rest not as reward for completion but as the declaration that your identity precedes your productivity. It limits commitments not because you are lazy but because the alternative to limits is eventually a self that has been spent entirely on other people's urgencies and has nothing left to bring to the moments that are yours to steward.

It treats the question of what to do with your time as a spiritual question — not the final spiritual question, but one whose answer flows from the deeper question of who you are before God and what you are here for.

That question does not have a productivity system that answers it. It has prayer, and honest self-examination, and the willingness to sit with silence long enough for the silence to say something.

Your calendar is a theological document. What it says about your actual beliefs — about what matters, what can be sacrificed, what will never be given time — is the truest account of your working theology.

That account deserves examination.

What it reveals is the weight you carry out of this.

The question should not require a theological case. That it does — that, in 2026, the church finds itself in a position where making a theological argument against the deliberate infliction of pain on human beings to extract information is necessary — is itself a symptom worth diagnosing. The symptom is not primarily political. It is a failure of theological formation so thoroughgoing that the most basic implications of Christian doctrine have become contested terrain.

Let me begin where Christian theology must always begin on questions of human treatment: imago Dei.

## The Image of God in the Tortured Body

Genesis 1:26-27 establishes something that the rest of Scripture never revises: human beings, every human being, bear the image of God. This is not a merit-based designation. It is not restricted to the innocent, the cooperative, the friendly. It is a statement about the ontological status of human beings as such — not what they have done or failed to do, not what they know or refuse to reveal, not what nation they belong to or what cause they serve. Every person who has ever been strapped to a chair or submerged in water or subjected to sleep deprivation or exposed to extremes of temperature or had their body broken by another person — every one of them bore the image of God when it happened.

> Every person who has ever been strapped to a chair or submerged in water or subjected to sleep deprivation or exposed to extremes of temperature or had their body broken by another person — every one of them bore the image of God when it happened.

Torture, defined precisely, is the deliberate infliction of severe suffering — physical, psychological, or both — upon a person in order to coerce a response. The coercion may target information, a confession, compliance, or simply the capitulation of the person's will. In every case, the torturer is using the image of God as an instrument. He is taking the God-bearing creature and treating her as a thing — a system to be broken, a source to be mined, a problem to be solved by the application of sufficient pain. The imago Dei is not destroyed by this; the theologians are right that it is indelible. But it is treated as if it does not exist. And the theological verdict on that treatment is not difficult to locate.

## The Incarnation and the Location of the Lord

The second pillar of the theological case is the Incarnation. In becoming human, God entered the condition that makes torture possible. Jesus of Nazareth had a body that could be struck, pierced, exhausted, broken. The accounts of his crucifixion in the Gospels describe not a dignified execution but a process of systematic state torture — the flogging before crucifixion, the crown of thorns, the cross itself as an instrument designed to maximize suffering and extend dying. When the church says "we believe in the crucifixion," it is confessing, among other things, that God has occupied the position of the torture victim. He has been there. He is there still — Matthew 25:31-46 makes explicit the logic: what is done to the least of these is done to him. The person undergoing torture in a black site or a detention facility — whatever she has done, whatever she knows, whatever threat she represents — she is, in the calculus of Matthew 25, the one to whom the crucified God is present.

The theological implications of this for the church's stance on torture are not ambiguous. The church that is silent about torture, or that hedges its position with calculations about national security, has not merely failed a political test. It has failed to acknowledge the location of its Lord.

## The Ticking Bomb and the Logic of Exception

The counter-argument that any honest treatment of this subject must engage is the argument from extreme necessity. It runs as follows: "Suppose you have captured a person who has information about an imminent attack that will kill thousands of innocent people. Are you really arguing that no amount of suffering inflicted on this one person is permissible to prevent that mass killing?" This is the "ticking bomb" scenario, and it has been deployed with considerable effectiveness in post-September 11 debates about enhanced interrogation [cite — confirm]. It deserves a direct answer, not dismissal.

The answer has two parts. The first part is empirical: the ticking bomb scenario has almost never accurately described real interrogation situations [cite — confirm]. Professional interrogators with decades of experience in intelligence gathering have consistently reported that coercive interrogation produces unreliable information — that the person being tortured will say whatever he calculates will stop the pain, which is not reliably the truth, and that rapport-based interrogation techniques produce better information in real situations [cite — confirm]. The scenario that makes torture seem obvious is a fiction of television dramas, not an accurate description of the actual conditions under which interrogation occurs. Real intelligence work is slow, uncertain, and fundamentally incompatible with the logic of emergency that the ticking bomb scenario depends on.

> moral principles that apply "except in extreme circumstances" are not principles. They are preferences.

The second part is theological: moral principles that apply "except in extreme circumstances" are not principles. They are preferences. The absolute prohibition on torture in the Christian tradition — articulated in the Geneva Conventions, in Catholic social teaching, in the statements of mainstream Protestant denominations — is not an absolute because the tradition failed to think about hard cases. It is an absolute because the tradition understood that the moment you build in the exception, the exception becomes the rule. Every torturing regime in modern history has operated under the conviction that its particular circumstances were exceptional enough to justify what it was doing. The Nazis had their exceptional circumstances. The Khmer Rouge had theirs. The logic of emergency exceptionalism, once admitted, has no natural stopping point.

Augustine, in the early fifth century, wrote about the judge who tortures the accused to discover whether he is guilty — and noted the bitter irony: the judge inflicts certain suffering on the accused in order to prevent uncertain suffering, and if the man is innocent, the judge cannot give him back what the torture took [cite — confirm]. Augustine was not opposed to capital punishment. He was not what we would now call a pacifist. But he saw clearly that torture corrupts the administration of justice at its foundations, because it treats the presumption of guilt as a license for what amounts to punishment before judgment.

## What Torture Does to the Torturer

That corruption is not merely institutional. It is personal and pastoral.

The person who tortures — the one whose hands do it, who gives the order, who signs off on the policy — does something to themselves in the doing. The church has always understood that sin distorts the sinner, not merely the sinned-against. The soldier who learns to inflict systematic suffering on another human being, who trains himself to be unmoved by screaming and weeping and the breaking of a body, has not merely performed a function. He has formed himself. He has become something. The pastoral literature emerging from those who have worked with veterans of enhanced interrogation describes the moral injury — a concept the field of trauma psychology has developed to describe the damage done to the self by participation in acts that violate one's own moral understanding — as serious and lasting [cite — confirm]. These are not people whose consciences were unaffected by what they did. They are people who discovered, too late, that the act requires the actor to cross a threshold that cannot be uncrossed.

The church's silence on this is not political caution. It is pastoral negligence. The same community that has people in it who have been asked to torture, and who carry the weight of having done so, needs to have a theological vocabulary that takes seriously both the gravity of what was done and the possibility of the forgiveness and healing that the gospel announces. That vocabulary requires being clear about whether torture is something the church believes God condemns. If the church cannot say that clearly, it has nothing to offer the man in the back pew who cannot sleep.

## The Silence of the American Church

I came to faith from atheism, and one of the things that drew me toward Christian theology was its refusal to treat the question of what we do to bodies as merely political. The Christian tradition insists that bodies matter — that the resurrection of the body is not a metaphor, that what happens to a body in history has eschatological weight, that the God who made a body his own is not indifferent to what bodies undergo. A faith built on those convictions cannot be neutral about the deliberate destruction of a body's integrity in order to extract its secrets.

The silence of the American church on torture — a practice that was officially authorized and documented in the recent history of this country — is a theological failure of the first order. It is not a gray area. The image of God, the Incarnation, and the Matthew 25 logic together produce a case that does not require a close reading of policy documents. It requires the church to say, clearly and without qualification, that the deliberate infliction of severe suffering on a human being made in the image of God is something that the God of Scripture hates.

> He hates it. The church should say so.

He hates it. The church should say so.

And then it should ask — as I ask of myself — where its silence has made it complicit in what it refused to name.

Breathe.

You just did something that Genesis 2:7 traces to the act of God. "Then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature." The Hebrew word is *neshama* — breath, soul, the animating force of a life. Every breath connects the living creature to the Creator who breathed it into existence. Respiration is, in this sense, a theological act. The air you breathe is not a resource. It is a gift. And the gift is being poisoned.

That is not a political claim. It is a statement about what is happening and who bears the cost.

---

## The Uneven Distribution of Dirty Air

The body of research on air pollution and its effects on human health is not contested science. Fine particulate matter — PM2.5, the particles small enough to penetrate deep into lung tissue — is associated with increased rates of cardiovascular disease, stroke, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and premature death. The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes approximately seven million premature deaths per year globally [cite — confirm]. In the United States, communities near highways, industrial facilities, and petrochemical plants bear the highest exposure to particulate matter, ground-level ozone, and chemical emissions. Those communities are disproportionately Black, Latino, and low-income. [cite — confirm]

This is not coincidence. The siting of industrial facilities and highways in communities of color follows patterns established by the same kinds of policy decisions that produced redlining — decisions about whose neighborhoods were valuable enough to protect and whose were available for uses that the protected neighborhoods would not tolerate. The result is that the air quality in a given zip code correlates strongly with the racial composition of that zip code. Children in those communities have higher rates of asthma. Adults have shorter lifespans. The health burden of dirty air is distributed along lines that should be recognizable to anyone who has spent time reading the prophets.

---

Amos 4:1 addresses the women of Bashan who crushed the poor and demanded more from their husbands. The oppression Amos named was economic and structural — the accumulation of luxury by those whose comfort depended on the suffering of the poor. The mechanism was trade, lending, taxation. In 2026, the mechanism includes the siting of refineries and chemical plants in communities that lack the political power to prevent it, the failure to regulate particulate emissions from truck traffic concentrated on highways that were built through communities of color, and the persistence of lead-contaminated infrastructure in cities where the replacement cost is treated as excessive.

> The prophetic vocabulary does not change when the mechanism changes.

The prophetic vocabulary does not change when the mechanism changes. The people bearing the cost are still the poor. The people setting the conditions are still the powerful. The question the prophet asks is still: what does the LORD require?

## Mishpat and the Child in Flint

Micah 6:8 is the most compressed answer Scripture gives: do justice, love mercy, walk humbly with your God. The justice Micah has in mind is not a general disposition of fairness. It is *mishpat* — the active establishment of right order in relationships and institutions, the restoration of those who have been damaged by the corruption of that order. To do mishpat is to name the specific injustice and to act against it. The child in Flint, Michigan whose development was damaged by lead-contaminated water — damaged not by accident but by official decision to use the Flint River as a cost-saving measure and to ignore the evidence that the water was unsafe [cite — confirm] — that child is a mishpat claim. The church in Flint that did not raise its voice in that child's defense was not being apolitical. It was failing to do justice.

---

## The Image of God at the Fence Line

The theological case for clean air as a justice concern begins with imago Dei — the affirmation of Genesis 1:26-27 that every human being is made in the image of God. The imago Dei is not primarily a statement about human cognition or spiritual capacity. It is a statement about dignity — the inherent worth of every person that cannot be reduced to their utility, their productivity, or their economic value to the people around them. To damage a person's health through preventable environmental exposure is to treat the imago Dei as expendable when it lives in a body that lacks political protection.

The specific targets of the prophetic witness — the widow, the orphan, the stranger, the poor — are not simply people who need charity. They are the people the social order has most thoroughly failed, the people whose imago Dei is most systematically denied by the structures of the world they live in. They are the people who live near the fence lines of chemical plants. They are the people who breathe the air that the rest of us made dirty and then arranged not to live near.

The New Testament does not abandon this concern. Paul's letter to the Romans includes the famous declaration that "creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption" (Romans 8:21) — that the redemption God is working toward is not only the salvation of individual souls but the liberation of the whole created order from the decay that sin introduced. The present condition of creation is described as groaning (Romans 8:22) — a labor pain that points toward a birth rather than toward a death. The church that reads this text and concludes that the material world is dispensable has misread it.

## When Clean Air Is Called Politics

There is a pastoral objection worth addressing directly: the charge that environmental justice is a political cause that the church has no business endorsing.

This charge contains a real concern. The church has been weaponized by political causes in both directions, and the pastor who cannot distinguish prophetic faithfulness from partisan alignment has lost the ability to speak to either. The warning is legitimate.

> The church that will not speak for her has confused neutrality with faithfulness.

But the charge proves too much. The question is not whether the church should endorse a policy platform. The question is whether the church should care about the child who cannot breathe. That question has an answer that does not require a party registration. Jesus placed a child in the center of the disciples' argument about greatness (Matthew 18:1-4). He said that whoever receives a child in his name receives him, and whoever causes a child to stumble would be better off drowned (Matthew 18:5-6). The child with asthma in the neighborhood near the highway is not a political abstraction. She is a child. The church that will not speak for her has confused neutrality with faithfulness.

The steel-man version of the objection goes further: perhaps clean air is a genuine concern, but the church should pursue it through prayer and charity rather than through policy engagement, because the church's proper sphere is the spiritual rather than the political. This view has a long pedigree in American Christianity — the pietist tradition that locates the church's primary work in the transformation of individual souls, trusting that individual transformation will eventually produce social change.

That tradition has genuine insight. The transformation of individual hearts is irreplaceable. No policy can do what genuine conversion does. But the prophets did not make the distinction. Amos and Micah and Isaiah addressed the political and economic structures of their day with the same authority they addressed individual sin. They did not have a category for spiritual concerns that were separate from the conditions under which the poor lived. The God who breathed life into the human creature through the breath is not indifferent to the condition of the air that creature now breathes. The two are not separable.

---

## The Older Framework of the Whole Canon

The environmental justice movement has deep roots in communities of faith. The term "environmental justice" itself was shaped significantly by the work of Black churches in Warren County, North Carolina in 1982 [cite — confirm], when those communities led a protest against the siting of a PCB landfill in a majority-Black county. The connection between environmental harm and racial injustice was named by people of faith because they had the theological vocabulary for it: the poor, the vulnerable, the people the system treats as expendable.

The church does not need to adopt an environmental justice framework from the secular left. It has a better one — older, more comprehensive, more theologically grounded. It is the framework of the whole biblical canon, from the creation mandate of Genesis 2 to the restored creation of Revelation 22, in which the tree of life stands beside the river of the water of life and its leaves are for "the healing of the nations" (Revelation 22:2).

The tree is still there. The nations still need healing. The air they breathe still matters to the God who breathed life into the first human being and has not stopped breathing.

---

What does the theology of clean air ask of the church?

At minimum, it asks for the willingness to see — to look at the map of air quality in your city, to notice where it is worst, to ask who lives there and why. It asks for the courage to name the connection between environmental harm and racial and economic injustice, to call it what the prophets would have called it.

It asks for the willingness to stand alongside the communities that bear the worst of it — not as paternalistic helpers but as members of the same body, whose health is bound up with theirs, whose flourishing depends on theirs, because the body of Christ is one body and when one part suffers, the whole suffers (1 Corinthians 12:26).

> Every breath you take is a gift.

Every breath you take is a gift. The child whose breath comes harder than yours is a daughter of the same Creator.

What are we going to do about that?

There is a command in Deuteronomy that the American church has treated as an artifact of ancient Near Eastern labor regulations — an interesting historical detail with no particular claim on contemporary economic practice. It reads: "You shall not oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers or one of the sojourners who are in your land within your towns. You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets (for he is poor and counts on it), lest he cry out against you to the Lord, and you be guilty of sin" (Deuteronomy 24:14-15).

The specificity of this text is worth dwelling on. Not a general principle about being fair to workers. A specific command about daily wage payment, grounded in a specific explanation — "he is poor and counts on it" — and attached to a specific consequence: his cry reaches God, and you bear guilt for it. The legislator of Deuteronomy is describing an economy in which day laborers had no cushion, no savings, no capacity to wait until Friday for money they needed to feed their households on Tuesday. The wage on the same day, before the sun sets, was not a courtesy. It was the margin between eating and not eating.

That economy is not as distant from our own as we have preferred to believe.

The theology of fair wages is not a minor theme in Scripture. It runs through the law, the prophets, the wisdom literature, the epistles, and the recorded words of Jesus with a consistency that should be embarrassing to any tradition that claims Scripture as its final authority and has nonetheless found a way to treat wage justice as a political topic rather than a theological one.

## Withholding Wages as Theft With Another Name

Start in the law. Leviticus 19:13 prohibits both robbery and the withholding of wages — placing them in the same sentence, as equivalent violations. The connection is not rhetorical. The law understands that withholding earned wages is a form of taking what belongs to someone else. It differs from theft only in its legal form, not in its moral substance. The worker who has performed the labor and not received the agreed payment has been robbed — the verb in the Hebrew, `ashaq`, carries the sense of extortion, of taking by power and position what belongs to another. This is not a matter of business negotiation. It is a matter of theft with a different name.

## The Prophets and the Cry That Reaches God

> It is a matter of theft with a different name.

The prophets intensified this. Malachi, in a passage the church reads primarily as a promise about tithing, includes among those who will face divine judgment "those who oppress the hired worker in his wages" (Malachi 3:5). Malachi places wage theft in the same list as sorcerers, adulterers, and those who swear falsely. The company is instructive. These are not the gray areas of ancient ethics. These are the violations that drew the sharp edge of prophetic condemnation. And wage theft — the oppression of the hired worker in his wages — is among them without qualification.

Jeremiah, in one of the most pointed indictments in the prophetic corpus, turns his attention to Jehoiakim, king of Judah, who was building himself a magnificent palace: "Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms by injustice, who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing and does not give him his wages" (Jeremiah 22:13). The word translated "for nothing" is `hinnam` — gratuitously, without payment, without cause. Jeremiah is naming something specific: the king who extracts labor without compensation to fund his own grandeur. The grandeur does not impress Jeremiah. The extraction damns him.

James 5 carries this into the apostolic tradition with a force that should have been difficult to misread: "Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts" (James 5:4). The language reaches back to Deuteronomy 24 — the cry that reaches God. The wages kept by fraud cry out. The God who hears is named with a specific title: "Lord of hosts," the God of armies, the God of power. James is not making a pious wish that things were different. He is announcing that the God of the universe has specific interest in whether people receive what they have earned.

> The church has read these texts for centuries.

The church has read these texts for centuries. It has not, in the main, understood them as applying to the structure of wages in a modern economy.

## The Partition Between the Spiritual and the Material

The reasons for this are complex, but one of the most important is a theological partition that the Reformation helped produce and that American Christianity has deepened: the partition between the spiritual and the material, between "religious" questions (salvation, prayer, worship, personal ethics) and "secular" questions (economics, wages, the organization of labor). On this partition, the Deuteronomy texts about wages become ancient Near Eastern labor codes that have been superseded; the James 5 text becomes a warning about individual greed rather than a word about systemic wage structures; and the prophets become spiritual advisors whose economic critiques were addressed to specific historical situations with no contemporary applicability.

This partition is theologically incoherent, but it has been remarkably durable. It has allowed the American church to develop a robust theology of individual sin (the man who cheats his neighbor) while maintaining a nearly complete silence on the structural arrangements that determine how millions of workers are compensated for their labor.

Those arrangements deserve naming. The federal minimum wage in the United States has not been raised since 2009 [cite — confirm]. In many states and industries, workers earn wages that make it functionally impossible to afford housing, food, and healthcare simultaneously, regardless of how many hours they work. Wage theft — defined as the failure of employers to pay legally required wages, overtime, or benefits — costs American workers tens of billions of dollars annually [cite — confirm]. These are not abstract economic statistics. They are the specific contemporary form of what Deuteronomy 24 addresses: workers who are poor and count on their wages, and do not receive them.

## The Free-Market Answer and Its Missing Substance

The counter-argument from the church's comfortable wing runs predictably: "The Bible is not an economics textbook. It doesn't specify a minimum wage. Free markets determine wages more efficiently than biblical commands can. We should address the spiritual roots of greed rather than legislate outcomes." This argument has the form of theological seriousness. It does not have the substance.

It does not have the substance because it treats the scriptural witness as a source of spiritual principles rather than specific demands. Deuteronomy 24 is specific. It names day laborers. It names the sun going down. It names the cry that reaches God. That specificity was not accidental — the law was addressing specific people in specific situations of vulnerability, because law that addresses only spiritual principles and never specific situations protects no one.

And it does not have the substance because the free-market account of wages depends on assumptions — perfect information, equal bargaining power, genuine mobility of labor — that the people who mow the fields and work the warehouses and staff the call centers simply do not possess. The bargaining power between an employer who can afford to wait and a worker who cannot afford not to work is not a negotiation between equals. This is not a radical economic claim. It is an observation about power that Deuteronomy and Jeremiah and James made before any formal economics existed.

## What Fair Wages Require of the Congregation

The church that is serious about the theology of fair wages will need to think concretely. That thinking might include paying everyone employed by the church at a wage that allows dignified living in the local economy — which more churches do not do than do [cite — confirm]. It might include speaking from the pulpit about the specific conditions of wage-earning in the community the church serves — acknowledging that some families in the congregation work full-time and cannot make rent, and that this is a theological problem, not a personal failure. It might include joining coalitions of workers and advocates working for wage standards that would bring local employment practices into alignment with what Deuteronomy 24 requires.

None of this is comfortable. The theology of fair wages will create friction in congregations that include business owners and employers — people who are not necessarily acting in bad faith but who have absorbed, along with their business education, a set of assumptions about wage determination that has very little overlap with what James 5 describes. The pastor who addresses this directly will receive pushback. Some of it will be sophisticated pushback. It will deserve honest engagement.

But the pastor who avoids the topic because the topic creates friction has made a choice: the comfort of the employed is worth more than the cry of the laborer that reaches the ears of the Lord of hosts. That is not a neutral pastoral decision. That is a theological position, whether or not it is acknowledged as one.

> The worker counts on his wages. Before the sun sets.

The worker counts on his wages. Before the sun sets. The specificity is not incidental. It is the whole point.

The God who wrote the specificity into the law of Israel has not since revised his interest in what happens to the person who cannot afford to wait.

Borders are very old human technology. The first thing Cain does after killing Abel is build a city — a bounded space, defined by walls, organized around his survival rather than around the image of God in his brother (Genesis 4:17). The biblical narrative does not look back on that founding moment with uncritical approval. From the beginning, the technology of the boundary is entangled with the problem of the person excluded.

This does not mean borders are inherently illegitimate. The Old Testament envisions a world of nations — the table of nations in Genesis 10, the division of peoples, the various territorial arrangements that God ordains through history. The nation of Israel has borders. The texts are realistic about political geography in ways that make any simple "borders are sin" argument misread the material.

But the tradition also insists, from within that same political realism, that the God of Israel is not bound by any border, that the justice God requires does not stop at any political line, and that the treatment of the person who stands at or crosses the border is one of the most consistent tests of a people's faithfulness. The theological question is not whether borders exist. The theological question is what they mean and what they are permitted to do to the human beings they divide.

---

## The Sojourner and the Memory of Egypt

The Hebrew Bible uses three words for the outsider: ger (the resident alien or sojourner), nokhri (the foreign national), and zar (the stranger who may pose a threat). The distinctions matter. The ger — the person who has left their homeland and is living among Israel — is the subject of the most intensive legal protection in the Mosaic code. The command to care for the ger appears more than thirty-five times in the Torah, more frequently than almost any other single ethical command.

"You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 22:21). The logic is not appeal to abstract principle. It is appeal to memory — the memory of what it felt like to be on the other side of the border, vulnerable, without status, without rights, dependent on the decency of those who had the power to help or harm. Israel's own experience of displacement is supposed to produce a specific kind of moral imagination: the capacity to see the current stranger through the lens of your own remembered strangeness.

This is not merely sentiment. It is built into the legal code. The gleaning laws of Leviticus 19 require the landowner to leave portions of the harvest specifically for the poor and the sojourner (Leviticus 19:9-10). The Sabbath rest commanded in Deuteronomy explicitly includes the sojourner within your gates (Deuteronomy 5:14). Leviticus 19:34 is unambiguous: "You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt." The love command is not confined to the insider community. It is extended across the border to the one who has crossed it.

> The love command is not confined to the insider community.

---

## The New Testament and the Crossed Border

The New Testament deepens this in ways that make any nationalism that claims Christian support theologically difficult to sustain.

The parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37) is, on one level, exactly about borders — ethnic, religious, cultural — and the capacity of those borders to determine who counts as a neighbor. The lawyer's question is a border question: "Who is my neighbor?" — meaning, where does my obligation stop? Jesus's answer, in the form of a story, does the precise opposite of drawing the border: it places the compassionate act in the most ethnically charged figure available to his audience, and makes the measure of "neighbor" not ethnic proximity but the willingness to cross the distance to help.

The Pentecost narrative in Acts 2 is deliberately constructed to reverse the Babel narrative of Genesis 11. At Babel, the diversity of languages produces dispersion and division. At Pentecost, the diversity of languages is not overcome by a single tongue — everyone hears in their own language. The Spirit does not dissolve difference into uniformity. The Spirit creates communion across difference. This is the eschatological vision the church is supposed to be enacting: not a community where everyone becomes the same, but a community where the divisions that once defined who was in and who was out have been reorganized by the new humanity in Christ.

Paul's formulation in Galatians 3:28 — "there is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" — is often reduced to a spiritual claim with no political content. But the Jew/Gentile distinction in the first century was precisely a border claim, enforced by real legal and social mechanisms that determined who had access to the covenant community and on what terms. Paul is not saying the distinction doesn't matter. He is saying it no longer determines access. The border has been crossed by the reconciling work of Christ, and the community that gathers around that work must embody, in its actual practice, the reality that the border no longer holds.

---

## What a Nation May Do and What the Church Must Be

None of this produces a simple Christian immigration policy, and anyone who claims it does is collapsing a complex political question into a proof-text. The church has always recognized that nations have legitimate interests in security, in the coherence of their communities, in the ordered management of their borders. These are not wicked interests. They are the interests of governors whom Paul himself describes as servants of God for good (Romans 13:4).

But the question of what a nation may legitimately do at its border is not the same as the question of what posture the church must take toward the human beings who stand at the border. Those are different questions, and confusing them is how Christian nationalism does its most damaging theological work. The political question of immigration policy is a question about which reasonable people can hold different views while remaining committed to justice. The pastoral question of how the Christian community is to regard the stranger, the sojourner, the displaced person — that question has a much clearer biblical answer.

The counter-argument, stated honestly, is this: national sovereignty is a God-given structure of order, and the church that advocates for open borders is undermining the stability that makes human flourishing possible. There is something to this. Order is a good. Stable governance is a good. The collapse of institutional structures does real harm to real people, and the church must not be naive about that harm. Walter Brueggemann's distinction between the prophetic tradition and mere utopianism is relevant here [cite — confirm]: the prophets were not naive about power; they engaged it.

> The imago Dei does not expire at the border.

But the argument that national sovereignty licenses any treatment of the person who has crossed or is seeking to cross the border goes well beyond what any serious theological tradition can sustain. The family separation, the detention without adequate care, the deportation of people who have built their lives in a country for decades — these are not neutral administrative questions. They are actions being performed on people who bear the image of God. The imago Dei does not expire at the border. It does not depend on documentation. It is not revocable by state action.

---

## The Idolatry of a Sanctified Nationalism

The American church, in the current political climate, is being asked to choose between its nationalist commitments and its theological ones, and many are choosing nationalism while insisting they are choosing theology. This is not a new temptation. The church in Germany in the 1930s faced a version of it, and the Barmen Declaration's famous insistence that Jesus Christ "is the one Word of God whom we have to hear, and whom we have to trust and obey in life and death" was written precisely to name the theological idolatry of a nationalism that had claimed divine sanction [cite — confirm].

Bonhoeffer's willingness to stake the theological claim against the political one — and to do it at personal cost — is instructive not as a prescription for identical action in different circumstances, but as a model of what theological integrity requires when the political culture presses the church to organize its life around something other than the Gospel. The church that allows its vision of the neighbor to be determined by the border rather than by the character of God has made the border into a theological category that the biblical text refuses to give it.

---

## The Congregation That Sees the Stranger

The specific pastoral question for the pastor who is reading this is simple but costly: do the people in your congregation who have come from somewhere else — who are immigrants, documented or otherwise, or who are refugees, or who are ethnically identified with nations your country regards with suspicion — do they experience your church as a place that sees them? Not as a demographic the church is trying to reach, not as a ministry category, but as people whose full humanity is honored, whose stories are considered, whose children are safe?

That is the minimum. The minimum is not the maximum. The maximum involves the kind of advocacy that is costly — speaking publicly about policies that harm vulnerable people even when the political cost is real, building relationships with advocacy organizations that work on these questions, asking the congregation to examine the gap between what it preaches about the imago Dei and what it advocates for in the public square.

God's justice transcends borders. That is not a liberal position. That is the position of the God who called Abraham to leave his borders and become a blessing to all nations, who identified Israel's own story with the story of displacement and commanded them to honor the memory in how they treated the stranger, who sent his Son not to a nation but to the world, and who is, even now, gathering from every tribe and tongue and people and nation the community that will stand before the throne.

> The border is not the final word. The King is.

The border is not the final word. The King is.

The word is found early in the Exodus story, in the episode most preachers move past on their way to more dramatic material. God rains bread from heaven — manna, the substance with no prior reference, a word that means roughly "what is it?" — and the instruction accompanying it is specific and strange: each household is to gather as much as it needs for that day. No more. The household that gathers more and tries to store it will find it rotten by morning. On the sixth day, gather two portions, because the seventh belongs to rest and no manna will come. The system is designed against accumulation.

This is not an efficiency arrangement. It is a theological statement about the nature of provision — about who owns the supply, who determines the portion, and what happens to communities built around the refusal to trust that enough will come again tomorrow. Exodus 16 is not a food-distribution logistics story. It is the first extended act of formation for a people who have been enslaved in an economy built on surplus extraction — pharaoh's logic — and who must now learn a different logic for a different kind of life.

They struggle with it. They keep trying to store extra. They find it corrupted. The lesson requires repetition because the lesson is fighting against something deep in them, something the years in Egypt had written into their instincts: the person who controls tomorrow's supply is safe, and the person who trusts today's provision and has nothing left by nightfall is vulnerable. Pharaoh's formation goes down a long way.

> So does ours.

So does ours.

## The Logic of Accumulation Against the Manna

The civilization that produced the contemporary American church has been running on a different account of provision than Exodus 16 describes. The Industrial Revolution, with its logic of scale and accumulation, produced in the nineteenth century a new kind of wealth — not the aristocratic landholding wealth that had defined European society for centuries, but a mobile, abstract, endlessly compoundable wealth that measured success not in the size of the harvest but in the rate of the return. The cultural formation that accompanied this new economy was correspondingly different: the virtuous person was not the one who received enough and rested but the one who reinvested, leveraged, expanded, compounded. The parable of the talents in Matthew 25:14-30 was read not as a story about faithfulness to what has been entrusted but as a warrant for the investment logic that governed the Gilded Age. That reading required ignoring the context in which the parable appears — which is a sustained discourse about the reversal of the powerful and the vindication of the vulnerable — but the reading was convenient and it stuck.

We inherited it. I inherited it. The pastor who grew up in suburban American Christianity absorbed, alongside the theology, an entire account of what flourishing looks like that has almost nothing to do with manna and almost everything to do with the quarterly return.

The theologian who has done the most rigorous work on how modern economic formations shape desire and imagination is James K.A. Smith, whose work on cultural liturgies traces the way that practices and environments form us before ideas do [cite — confirm]. Smith's argument is that the mall, the stadium, the market are not merely neutral spaces where pre-formed people make choices — they are formative environments that train desire, that habituate us toward certain ends, that produce in us a particular vision of the good life. The good life, in the formation of consumer capitalism, is an expanding life: more space, more options, more accumulated capability. Enough is a resting point on the way to more. It is never a destination.

Against this formation, the Scriptures offer something comprehensive and strange: a theology of enough.

## A Prayer That Refuses Both Poles

The manna story is the earliest statement, but it is not alone. Proverbs 30:7-9 contains one of the most remarkable prayers in the biblical literature: "Two things I ask of you, Lord; do not refuse me before I die: Keep falsehood and lies far from me; give me neither poverty nor riches, but give me only my daily bread. Otherwise, I may have too much and disown you and say, 'Who is the Lord?' Or I may become poor and steal, and so dishonor the name of my God." The prayer refuses both poles. Not poverty. Not wealth. Enough. The wisdom here is that both poverty and riches create conditions hostile to covenant faithfulness — poverty through desperation, wealth through the particular blindness that comes with comfort.

Jesus returns to this territory repeatedly, in a way that the church has consistently tried to soften. The Sermon on the Mount's teaching on anxiety — "do not worry about your life, what you will eat or drink, or about your body, what you will wear" (Matthew 6:25) — is not addressed to the desperately poor. It is addressed to people with enough options to have something to worry about. And the argument is theological before it is practical: the God who clothes the grass of the field and feeds the birds of the air is not indifferent to your need. The anxiety that drives accumulation is, at its root, a failure of trust. The accumulation does not resolve the anxiety — it reseeds it, because the horizon of enough under accumulation logic is always just beyond what is currently possessed.

> He had become rich toward himself and poor toward God.

The parable of the rich fool in Luke 12:13-21 is perhaps the sharpest statement. The man's crops are abundant. His response is entirely reasonable by any standard the contemporary church has absorbed: expand the barns, store the surplus, rest secure. God calls him a fool. Not because he was dishonest or violent or openly unjust. Because he organized his entire existence around the logic of accumulation and called it security — and he was about to discover that the logic was wrong at the most fundamental level. The grain in his expanded barns would do him no good. He had become rich toward himself and poor toward God.

## What It Means to Be Poor Toward God

What does it mean to be poor toward God? I have lived in that territory. I recognize it from the inside. It is the state of having so organized your desires around what you control that the very concept of dependence on anything beyond yourself has atrophied. The person poor toward God is not necessarily the person who has rejected belief. He may attend church faithfully, may give generously by percentage, may have his theology entirely correct. But the underlying formation — the deep grammar of his life — is the grammar of accumulation and control. He has never genuinely sat with the manna question: what if tomorrow's provision belongs to tomorrow, and my task today is to receive what today requires and trust the rest?

## Provision for Need and Accumulation as an End

There is a serious counter-argument here, and it deserves honest engagement. The counter-argument goes: "This reasoning, taken seriously, would produce irresponsibility. It would counsel against retirement savings, against insurance, against the prudent planning that protects families from catastrophe. Are you really arguing that accumulation is sinful?" No. The theology of enough is not a theology of improvidence. The ant in Proverbs 6 stores food in summer for winter's use, and is commended for it. Joseph's seven years of Egyptian surplus savings in Genesis 41 protected an entire region from famine. Prudent provision is not the same as the endless expansion of appetite that the manna prohibition targets.

The distinction is between provision for need and accumulation as an end in itself — between the barn that holds enough and the barn that must always be expanded because the question of enough can never be answered. The theology of enough does not prohibit saving. It prohibits the making of accumulated wealth into the organizing principle of a life, the thing that produces security, the ultimate hedge against the vulnerability of being a creature in a world you did not make and do not control.

## The Barn the Church Has Built

The practical question for the church is not primarily about individual financial practice, though it reaches there. It is about institutional practice. American churches hold enormous collective wealth — in endowments, in buildings, in investments [cite — confirm]. That wealth is almost always justified as necessary infrastructure for mission. And some of it is. But some of it is the barn. Some of it is the accumulation that protects the institution against a vulnerability that the institution, in its formation, has learned to fear more than it fears the judgment of the God who asked the rich fool whether he had made provision for the moment his soul would be required of him.

The theology of enough is not comfortable to sit with. It asks questions that have no comfortable answers: How much of what you hold is need and how much is anxiety made solid? What would it mean, actually, to give as though tomorrow's provision were not your problem? What would it mean for the church to operate with a budget that had no cushion, that trusted the God it preaches?

I am not certain I know how to live this. I am certain that the church I grew up in never taught it — not because the teachers were dishonest, but because the formation that surrounded us had made it unthinkable. We were shaped by the same cultural liturgies as everyone else, and those liturgies produce people for whom enough is always one barn-expansion away.

> The manna spoiled when they tried to store it.

The manna spoiled when they tried to store it.

That was not punitive. That was pedagogical. The God who provided it was teaching them something about the nature of the economy they were being invited into — an economy of trust rather than control, of today's provision rather than tomorrow's security, of community whose members could not individually hoard because the system itself was designed against hoarding.

The kingdom of God is not the American economy. The sooner the church remembers this, the more it will have to say to a world that is discovering, with increasing desperation, that the American economy does not answer the deepest questions of what it means to have enough.

There is a building in most American cities that sits on land whose story it does not know. It has a mortgage, a tax bill, a property line. It may even have a plaque marking the year it was built. What it almost certainly does not have is a reckoning with the full history of the ground beneath it — who lived there before, how the title passed from one hand to another, what was taken, what was paid, what was never paid at all.

The church is one of those buildings. And the theology we have inherited has not given us much help in reading the land we stand on.

## Tending the Earth as Liturgy

The Bible begins with land. Not with individual souls and their private transactions with God, but with the earth — *ha'aretz* — declared good, filled with creatures, entrusted to humanity for cultivation and care (Genesis 1:28-31, 2:15). The first command is not a moral law. It is a vocation: tend this. Keep it. The original human task is not primarily religious in the narrow sense. It is agricultural, ecological, custodial. The human being is set into the garden to serve it — the Hebrew *abad*, to serve, is the same word used for the service of the Levitical priests. Tending the earth is liturgy.

> These are images of the earth healed, not the earth abandoned.

The fall has a land dimension. When the first human beings fracture their relationship with God, the fracture extends immediately into the soil: "cursed is the ground because of you" (Genesis 3:17). The rupture between humanity and God produces a rupture between humanity and the earth. The biblical vision of redemption is therefore not the evacuation of souls from a material world that is simply discarded. It is the restoration of the whole system — the repair of the relationship between the Creator, the human creature, and the created world. The prophetic vision of shalom is explicitly ecological: mountains dripping with sweet wine, threshing floors full of grain, vats overflowing with wine and oil (Joel 2:24). Isaiah's vision of the new creation includes wolves and lambs together, children playing over the serpent's den (Isaiah 11:6-9). These are images of the earth healed, not the earth abandoned.

---

## Land as Gift and the Logic of Jubilee

In the Hebrew covenant, land is not property in the modern sense. It is gift. It is trust. The Torah's land theology is revolutionary and remains largely unabsorbed by the contemporary church: the land belongs to God, not to the people who occupy it. "The land shall not be sold permanently, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me" (Leviticus 25:23). The Jubilee ordinance that follows from this premise — the return of land to its original families every fifty years, the cancellation of debt, the release of those held in bondage — is precisely a structural mechanism for preventing the permanent accumulation of land in the hands of the wealthy at the expense of the poor. The land cannot be finally sold because it was never finally the seller's to sell.

The prophets returned to this again and again because the accumulation of land was exactly what the wealthy of Israel were doing. "Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land" (Isaiah 5:8). Micah indicted those who devised wickedness in the night and implemented it in the morning — who coveted fields and seized them, houses and took them away (Micah 2:1-2). The prophetic indictment of land accumulation is not incidental to the prophetic witness. It is central.

The church has largely read these texts as spiritualized allegory or as specific historical instructions for ancient Israel, neither of which applies to modern property law. But the theological premise — that the earth is God's and that human ownership is always a form of stewardship, always conditional, always accountable — does not depend on the specific legal mechanisms of Levitical law. It is a claim about the nature of creation, not a piece of agricultural legislation.

---

## Naboth's Vineyard and the Inseparability of Theft

Land theft is as old as the covenant people's temptation to acquire it. The story of Naboth's vineyard in 1 Kings 21 is among the most pointed land texts in Scripture. Ahab, the king of Israel, wants Naboth's vineyard for a vegetable garden. He offers to buy it or to trade for it. Naboth refuses: "The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers" (1 Kings 21:3). Naboth is not being stubborn or irrational. He is operating within a theological framework in which the ancestral land is a covenant inheritance, not a commodity to be traded at the king's convenience.

Jezebel solves the problem by arranging Naboth's judicial murder and confiscating the land. Elijah is sent to confront Ahab in the vineyard itself, the specific scene of the crime: "Have you killed and also taken possession?" (1 Kings 21:19). The question is one of the most compact prophetic indictments in Scripture. The murder and the land theft are named together as a single act. The prophet does not address one without the other.

> In the biblical imagination, land acquisition and violence are inseparable.

This is the pattern. In the biblical imagination, land acquisition and violence are inseparable. Land is not an abstraction. It is the site of human life — the place where children grow up, where the dead are buried, where the family practices its vocation and maintains its economic security. To take the land is to take all of that.

---

## The Specific History Beneath the American Church

The American church stands on land with a specific history. The continent was occupied before European settlement. The displacement of Indigenous peoples from their land was accomplished through a combination of treaty, military force, disease, and legal mechanisms — and the church was implicated in that displacement in multiple, documented ways. The doctrine of discovery — the fifteenth-century papal principle that gave Christian nations the right to claim territory inhabited by non-Christian peoples [cite — confirm] — provided the theological cover for centuries of colonial land seizure. The residential school system that forcibly removed Indigenous children from their communities and attempted to eliminate their cultures was operated in significant part by Christian denominations. [cite — confirm]

This is not ancient history. Many of those residential schools operated into the twentieth century. [cite — confirm] The land on which many American church buildings stand was taken from Indigenous communities within recorded history, in some cases within the lifetimes of people still living.

The same structural pattern repeated itself in the dispossession of Black land ownership in the South during and after Reconstruction — a period when Black families, having been prohibited from owning property for generations, acquired land only to have it taken by legal manipulation, by violence, and by the system of convict leasing that effectively re-enslaved formerly free people. [cite — confirm] The church watched, and in many cases participated.

---

None of this means that the contemporary church must hand its building back to someone. It means the contemporary church must know the story it is standing in. The pastor who leads a congregation on ground with this kind of history and never names it is not being neutral. He is choosing not to look.

Walter Brueggemann, in *The Land: Place as Gift, Promise, and Challenge in Biblical Faith* [cite — confirm], argues that land is one of the most important and underexamined categories in biblical theology — that the biblical story is fundamentally a story about land, about the promise of it and the betrayal of it and the hope of its restoration. The exile is not primarily about individuals losing God's favor. It is about a community losing its land and being forced to reckon with what the land meant. The return from exile is not primarily about individual spiritual renewal. It is about coming home to a specific place.

The American church has tried to be a community without a place — or rather, a community that occupies a place without owning its history. That is not an option the Bible gives us. The God of Israel is the God who met his people at specific places — Bethel, Sinai, Jerusalem — and who named those places as sites of encounter and accountability. The land remembers what the people have done on it. The prophets were certain of that.

---

## What a Theology of Land Asks Today

What does a theology of land ask of the church today?

It asks for honesty about the ground we stand on and the history that put it in our hands. It asks for the theological seriousness to take Leviticus 25 and Isaiah 5 and Micah 2 as words addressed to us, not just to ancient Israel. It asks for engagement with the Indigenous communities whose land we occupy — not as a program, but as a long-term relationship built on acknowledgment and accountability.

It asks for the courage to say, in the language of the psalmist: "The earth is the LORD's, and everything in it" (Psalm 24:1). Not as a worship chorus. As a claim that reorganizes our relationship to the ground beneath our feet.

> The land is not ours. We are stewards of it.

The land is not ours. We are stewards of it. We are accountable for what happens on it and what we do with it.

That accountability has not yet been fully faced.

It is waiting.

There is a persistent assumption in large portions of the American church that protest is somehow un-Christian. That marching in the street, raising a voice against injustice, confronting power publicly — these are activities of the secular left, not the people of God. The Christian response to injustice, under this assumption, is prayer, charity, and the quiet transformation of hearts one at a time. Public demonstration is, at best, a distraction. At worst, it is worldly politics contaminating the church's spiritual mission.

The biblical tradition will not sustain this assumption. It cannot be made to sustain it without significant surgery.

---

## The Prophets as Public Demonstration

The prophetic tradition in the Hebrew Bible is, from beginning to end, a tradition of public protest. Elijah confronted Ahab directly: "Is that you, you troubler of Israel?" (1 Kings 18:17–18). Amos stood in the royal sanctuary at Bethel — the religious center of the Northern Kingdom, the king's chapel — and delivered an oracle of judgment against the nation's economic exploitation of the poor (Amos 7:10–17). Isaiah walked through Jerusalem naked and barefoot for three years as a living acted oracle against the military alliances that Israel's leaders were relying on instead of God (Isaiah 20:2–3). Jeremiah wore a wooden yoke in public, smashed a clay jar in the valley of Ben Hinnom, and stood at the temple gate delivering messages that the temple leadership had specifically ordered him to stop delivering (Jeremiah 7:1–2, 19:1–13, 28:1–17).

> They are exactly what we call protest.

These are not quiet, private, politically cautious activities. They are public demonstrations — embodied, disruptive, confrontational. They are exactly what we call protest.

The prophets were not politely appealing to the conscience of those in power. They were publicly naming what was wrong and publicly demanding change, in spaces designed to maximize the visibility of their message. Amos chose Bethel, the royal sanctuary, not the desert. Jeremiah chose the temple gate. They understood that prophetic witness requires public platform — that the injustice named only in private is functionally unnamed.

---

## Jesus and the Overturned Tables

Jesus inherited this tradition and extended it. The cleansing of the temple — described in all four Gospels, which means it was considered among the most important events of the final week — is an act of public protest by any reasonable definition. Jesus entered the temple courts, overturned the tables of the money changers, drove out those selling animals for sacrifice, and prevented people from carrying merchandise through the courts (Mark 11:15–17). He cited two prophets simultaneously — Isaiah ("a house of prayer for all nations") and Jeremiah ("a den of robbers"). He was doing what Jeremiah had done: standing in the temple courts and delivering a public indictment.

This action precipitated his arrest and execution. The chief priests and scribes, Mark tells us, "heard this and began looking for a way to kill him" (Mark 11:18). The cleansing of the temple was not a minor disruption. It was a political provocation of sufficient seriousness to move the authorities to act. Jesus knew that. He did it anyway.

The Palm Sunday entry into Jerusalem is also a public, politically charged demonstration. Riding a donkey into Jerusalem while crowds waved palms and shouted "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!" (Mark 11:9) is a direct parody of the Roman imperial procession — Pontius Pilate entered Jerusalem around the same time from the west, with horses and soldiers, the full military display of imperial power [cite — confirm the parallel entry argument attributed to Marcus Borg and John Dominic Crossan]. Jesus entered from the east, on a donkey, attended by the poor and the sick. It was a public statement about what the kingdom of God looks like compared to the kingdoms of this world. It was protest through embodied sign-act.

---

## The Church at Its Most Prophetic Moments

The long history of the church at its most prophetic moments is a history of public witness. Bartolomé de las Casas, in the sixteenth century, publicly denounced the colonial enslavement and genocide of indigenous peoples before the Spanish court and in his writings at a time when such denunciation cost him the approval of his own institution and threatened his freedom [cite — confirm]. The Confessing Church in Germany, under the leadership of Karl Barth and Dietrich Bonhoeffer, issued the Barmen Declaration in 1934 as a public repudiation of the Deutsche Christen — the German Christians who had accommodated National Socialism — at a moment when that repudiation placed signatories at real personal risk [cite — confirm year and signatories].

Bonhoeffer wrote later from prison that the church is called to speak for those who cannot speak for themselves, and that the church that remains silent when the state violates the dignity of human beings has abandoned its calling [cite — confirm specific work]. This is not a peripheral observation in Bonhoeffer's theology. It is central to it. The church's refusal of public witness in the name of political neutrality is not, for Bonhoeffer, a failure of strategy. It is a failure of faith.

The American civil rights movement was organized and led primarily by Black pastors and theologians — Martin Luther King Jr., Fred Shuttlesworth, Ralph Abernathy, C.T. Vivian, Fannie Lou Hamer — who understood their marches, their sit-ins, their public confrontations with law enforcement as acts of prophetic witness rooted in the biblical tradition [cite — confirm]. They prayed before they marched. They sang hymns on the way to jail. They understood the movement as a form of worship.

The white churches that criticized them for "mixing religion and politics" were repeating, almost word for word, the charge Amaziah leveled at Amos: "Get out of here, you seer! Go back to the land of Judah... Prophesy there, but never again prophesy at Bethel, for this is the king's sanctuary" (Amos 7:12–13). The protest was theologically grounded. The criticism of the protest was the position with the weak theological foundation.

---

## The Steel-Man Case for Caution

The steel-man case for caution about protest deserves engagement. It goes like this: the church can be co-opted by political movements that use the language of justice but serve partisan rather than genuinely prophetic ends. History contains examples of churches that marched and rallied for causes that turned out to be wrong. The church's credibility depends on its willingness to evaluate causes on theological grounds rather than simply aligning with whatever movement claims justice language. Prophetic witness requires discernment, not just volume. Not every protest is a just protest.

This is correct. The church has been co-opted before and will be again if it is not careful. The prophets themselves warned against false prophets — against those who cried "peace, peace" when there was no peace, or who told the people what they wanted to hear (Jeremiah 6:14, Ezekiel 13). Discernment is real. Theological evaluation is real. The church should not march for every cause that borrows prophetic language.

But the answer to the danger of uncritical co-optation is not silence. It is discernment. The church is called to evaluate causes on theological grounds and then, having done that evaluation, to act with conviction. The danger of prophetic witness being co-opted does not establish the safety of prophetic silence. Silence is also a position. It also serves some interests and abandons others.

The church in 1930s Germany that remained silent about National Socialism was not being theologically cautious. It was being complicit. The church in 1960s Alabama that remained silent about the systematic terror of racial apartheid was not exercising discernment. It was choosing the comfortable side. The appearance of theological caution often disguises a choice to protect institutional relationships and social standing.

> I have made this choice.

I have made this choice. I have been quiet when speaking would have cost me something I valued. I know what that silence feels like from the inside, and I know what it is worth.

---

## Protest Rooted in the Character of God

The theology of protest, properly understood, is rooted in the character of God. The God of the Exodus does not observe Israel's suffering from a distance and maintain political neutrality. Exodus 3:7–8 is explicit: "The Lord said, 'I have indeed seen the misery of my people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their slave drivers, and I am concerned about their suffering. So I have come down to rescue them.'" God hears. God is concerned. God acts.

The church is the body of Christ — called to continue, in its historical embodiment, the ministry Jesus announced in Luke 4:18–19. "He has sent me to proclaim freedom for the prisoners and recovery of sight for the blind, to set the oppressed free, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor." The proclamation is not only verbal. Jesus followed it with action — healing, feeding, confronting, overturning tables. The body of Christ is called to do the same.

Protest, in this frame, is not a departure from the church's spiritual mission. It is one form the spiritual mission takes when the spiritual mission encounters systemic injustice. It is the church saying, with its body and its voice and its presence, what God has been saying throughout Scripture: the oppression of the vulnerable is unacceptable to the God who made them.

---

## The Selectivity of the Comfortable Protest

There is a form of protest the church has generally been comfortable with: the protest of individual moral failure. The church has protested abortion clinics. It has protested various expressions of human sexuality it considers sinful. It has been willing to show up publicly, in numbers, when the cause falls within the categories its cultural formation has identified as the church's proper concerns.

The same churches that showed up for those protests have often been absent from protests against mass incarceration, police violence, wage theft, housing displacement, and environmental contamination of poor communities. The selectivity is not theologically neutral. It reflects a set of choices about which sins are worth public protest and which are not — and those choices track, with uncomfortable consistency, with the class and racial interests of the people in the pews.

Amos did not protest the sexual ethics of the ruling class. He protested the economic ethics. "They sell the innocent for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals. They trample on the heads of the poor as on the dust of the ground" (Amos 2:6–7). The prophetic tradition's central concern, measured by sheer weight of the textual evidence, is economic justice and the treatment of the vulnerable. The church that inverts this hierarchy has reorganized the prophetic tradition around its own comfort.

---

The theology of protest is not a theology for everyone else. It is a theology for the church — for the communities that claim to follow the one who overturned the tables, who wept over Jerusalem, who stood in the temple courts and delivered the indictment.

It requires the courage to be seen. To be associated. To be criticized. To be told, as Amos was told, to go somewhere else. The prophet who was comfortable in the sanctuary was not a prophet. He was a chaplain to the status quo.

There is enough status quo chaplaincy in the American church already. The prophetic tradition calls for something harder, costlier, more public, and more faithful.

> The tables are still waiting to be overturned. The gate is still the place to stand.

The tables are still waiting to be overturned. The gate is still the place to stand.

The Hebrew prophets did not speak primarily about preventing future wrongdoing. They spoke about reckoning with what had already been done. Amos does not say: let us create conditions where injustice is less likely. He says: let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream (Amos 5:24). The image is not a committee. It is a flood.

We have reduced justice to prevention when the tradition demands repair.

> We have reduced justice to prevention when the tradition demands repair.

The word the prophets use most often for what God requires is not "reform." It is restoration — the return of what was taken, the healing of what was broken, the re-establishment of relationship where relationship was severed. This distinction matters because prevention and repair are not the same moral claim. Prevention says: do not do this again. Repair says: account for what was done. The first lets the past remain in the past. The second refuses to let the past be past until it has been addressed.

## The Covenant Structure of Repair

The Jubilee laws in Leviticus 25 are perhaps the most radical economic legislation in the ancient world, and they are built around the logic of repair rather than prevention. Every fifty years, land returned to its original families (Leviticus 25:13). Debt slaves were released (Leviticus 25:40–41). Accumulated economic advantage was reset. The text is explicit about the theological basis: "The land is mine," God says, "and you are but aliens and my tenants" (Leviticus 25:23). No permanent dispossession is possible in a system built on that premise, because the foundation of ownership is always conditional on the covenant, and the covenant insists that what the poor need cannot simply become permanent wealth in the hands of those who took it from them.

The Jubilee was not aspirational. It was calendrical — written into the liturgical structure of Israel's life, meant to recur with the same regularity as Sabbath and harvest festivals. Whether it was ever fully practiced is a matter of historical debate [cite — confirm]. That it was commanded — that it was inscribed in the covenant as the baseline expectation of a faithful community — is the theological claim. The God who commands the Jubilee is not satisfied with individuals who are personally generous toward the poor. He requires systems that do not permanently concentrate advantage. He requires that the damage of dispossession not become permanent simply because it becomes old.

The prophets understood this. When Micah condemns those who "covet fields and seize them, and houses and take them away" (Micah 2:2), he is not primarily warning about future coveting. He is indicting the accumulated result of past coveting — the parcels already seized, the families already displaced, the ancestral inheritance already in someone else's possession. The indictment points backward. The required remedy points forward but must account for what has happened.

## What Augustine and Aquinas Knew

The Christian theological tradition has resources here that it has largely failed to deploy. Augustine's doctrine of sin includes not just the acts we commit but the disorder those acts create in the world — a disorder that does not resolve on its own because sin damages the structures in which human life is embedded, not merely the individual hearts that chose to sin [cite — confirm]. The world is disordered by our sin. The sin can be forgiven without the disorder being repaired, and a forgiveness that only addresses the sin while leaving the disorder intact is not the full restoration the gospel envisions.

Thomas Aquinas argued, in his discussion of commutative justice in the *Summa Theologiae* [cite — confirm], that restitution is a precondition of genuine justice — that having wronged someone creates an obligation to repair the wrong, not merely to stop doing it, and that this obligation is not discharged by repentance alone. The grace that forgives the sinner does not automatically restore what the sinner took. These are related but distinct. Forgiveness addresses the relationship between the wrongdoer and God. Restitution addresses the material damage done to the wronged person. To conflate them is to offer forgiveness as a substitute for repair rather than as the foundation of it.

Luther preached grace freely given, and grace is freely given — nothing I am arguing here disputes that. But Luther's tradition also produced in the same century a rigorous Lutheran social ethic under figures like Johannes Bugenhagen [cite — confirm], who worked to establish systematic care for the poor in Lutheran cities precisely because the forgiveness of individual sins did not automatically resolve the social conditions that left the poor poor. The cross forgives the sinner. The community of the cross is supposed to repair the damage.

## The American Church's Evasion

I have preached about justice for fifteen years, and most of what I preached was about stopping harm. I preached against racism and I preached against poverty and I did not preach about what is owed to those who have already suffered under both for generations. I named the injustice. I did not name the debt. Those are not the same sermon.

> Divine love without divine restitution is not the full gospel.
