The American church has repeatedly confused forgiveness with repair. We have told survivors of abuse: God forgives your abuser, and closed the door on the question of what the abuser owes. We have told communities fractured by decades of redlining and deliberate economic exclusion that God loves everyone equally, and then wondered why that message lands as an insult. It lands as an insult because it is incomplete. Divine love without divine restitution is not the full gospel. It is half of it, strategically selected to comfort the people who have the most to lose from full accountability.

The history is specific. Between 1934 and 1968, the Federal Housing Administration's redlining policies systematically denied mortgage loans in Black and minority neighborhoods while subsidizing homeownership in white suburbs [cite — confirm]. The effect was to prevent an entire generation of Black families from building the home equity that constitutes the primary form of wealth accumulation for American households. The families who were excluded did not simply fail to accumulate wealth. Wealth was structurally withheld from them by government policy, often with the institutional cooperation of banks, real estate agencies, and communities — including many churches that blessed the white flight and the segregated suburbs as God's provision. The wealth gap between white and Black American families that persists today [cite — confirm] is not a natural fact. It is the accumulated compound interest on that structural theft.

To say that God loves everyone equally in response to that history is to offer a truth that, in isolation, functions as a mechanism for avoiding the harder truth: that love without repair is not the love the prophets described.

## The Parable as Economic Narrative

The story of Zacchaeus is instructive here (Luke 19:1–10). When Jesus arrives at his house and the people grumble about him entering the home of a sinner, Zacchaeus stands and makes a declaration: half of what he owns he will give to the poor, and anyone he has defrauded he will repay fourfold. Jesus does not generate this response by delivering a lecture about structural injustice. He generates it by presence — by arriving at the door of the man everyone had agreed to exclude. And what emerges from that encounter is not simply a changed heart. It is a changed ledger.

Salvation came to this house, Jesus says. Not that Zacchaeus understood correct doctrine about the atonement. That salvation came. And salvation, in this house, looked like math. It looked like fourfold restitution to anyone who had been defrauded. The specific number is significant: it is the number the Mosaic law required for the theft of livestock (Exodus 22:1). Zacchaeus is applying the Torah's logic of repair to his own life, and Jesus names it as salvation. Not as a supplement to salvation. As salvation.

## What Repair Actually Requires

The theology of repair is not primarily a political program, and I am not arguing for a single policy position. I am arguing that the church must have the theological vocabulary for this conversation — that when we arrive at the hard questions of what repair looks like, we arrive with the full tradition, not just the convenient half.

The truth-and-reconciliation process that South Africa attempted after the end of apartheid, beginning in 1995, was not perfect [cite — confirm]. Many of its limitations were the result of insufficient commitment to the repair dimension — the process produced testimony and some limited amnesty but did not produce the structural economic repair that the full tradition demands. Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who chaired the commission, was clear that reconciliation without the restoration of dignity and material loss was an inadequate substitute for justice [cite — confirm]. His clarity came from a theological tradition shaped by the prophets who knew the difference between stopping harm and repairing it.

The God who requires mishpat and tsedaqah is not satisfied with gestures. He is satisfied with justice, which is to say: with the world made more fully right than it was. That is a higher bar than we have typically set for ourselves. It is also the bar the full tradition sets, and there is no credible way to preach the prophets while quietly setting it aside.

> That difference is not small. It is the difference between a gospel that confronts the powerful and a gospel that consoles them.

I have preached about the damage. I have not always preached about the debt. That difference is not small. It is the difference between a gospel that confronts the powerful and a gospel that consoles them.

The damage is older than we are. That does not make it ours to ignore.

We are the generation standing in the rubble. The question is not whether we caused all of it. The question is what we do now that we are here.

The word arrives with immediate weight. In most evangelical conversations I have witnessed, reparations is treated as a political position — one side of a culture war argument — before it is treated as anything theological. This is itself a diagnosis. That the first response of the church to a question this theologically freighted is to reach for political category rather than biblical category tells us something about which text we have been formed by.

The Bible has a great deal to say about restitution. More, in fact, than most American Christians realize. And the biblical account of restitution is not vague. It is specific, structural, and demanding.

## What Leviticus Requires of the Wrongdoer

---

Begin with Leviticus 6. When someone defrauds another — withholds wages, takes by force, deceives in a transaction — the restoration required is full restitution of the principal plus twenty percent (Leviticus 6:5). Not apology. Not acknowledgment. Twenty percent more than what was taken, paid back to the person from whom it was taken. The law assumes that the harm done by economic exploitation is real and measurable and that the spiritual relationship between the wrongdoer and the wronged cannot be restored without material restoration. "He must make restitution in full, add a fifth of the value to it and give it all to the owner on the day he presents his guilt offering" (Leviticus 6:5). The moral accounting and the material accounting are inseparable.

> The moral accounting and the material accounting are inseparable.

Zacchaeus, in one of the most structurally significant conversion accounts in the New Testament, demonstrates exactly this understanding. When he encounters Jesus, the first words out of his mouth after announcing his change of heart are material: "Look, Lord! Here and now I give half of my possessions to the poor, and if I have cheated anybody out of anything, I will pay back four times the amount" (Luke 19:8). This exceeds the Levitical requirement. And Jesus's response — "Today salvation has come to this house" — connects the salvation announcement directly to the restitution pledge. The two are not separable in the narrative. The salvation is manifested in the economic turning.

The church that preaches salvation while remaining indifferent to restitution has separated what the New Testament holds together.

## Forty Acres and a Broken Federal Promise

---

The specific historical question of African American reparations has a concrete American beginning. In January 1865, General William T. Sherman issued Special Field Order No. 15 [cite — confirm], distributing approximately 400,000 acres of coastal land in South Carolina and Georgia to formerly enslaved people — roughly forty acres per family, the origin of the "forty acres and a mule" promise. President Lincoln endorsed the order. By June 1865, approximately 40,000 Black families had been settled on this land [cite — confirm]. Within months of Lincoln's assassination, President Andrew Johnson reversed the order, returned the land to the former Confederate owners, and displaced the Black families who had begun to farm it.

This is not ancient history approached through a haze of moral uncertainty. This is a documented federal promise made to people who had been subjected to 250 years of chattel slavery — forced, unpaid, brutal labor that produced enormous wealth for white landowners and for the American economy more broadly — followed by a documented federal revocation of that promise within the year. The theological question of restitution does not require speculative reconstruction. It requires reading the historical record.

> The theological question of restitution does not require speculative reconstruction. It requires reading the historical record.

The economist Thomas Piketty [cite — confirm] and others have documented how intergenerational wealth transfer functions — how the family that had land in 1865 used it to build equity, which funded education, which opened economic opportunity, which became assets transferred to the next generation. The family from whom the forty acres were rescinded entered the period of Reconstruction without land, without legal protection adequate to their situation, into a sharecropping system that was in many cases designed to recreate the economic conditions of slavery without its formal legal status. The compounding effect of that dispossession across generations is measurable and has been measured [cite — confirm].

## The Question of Inherited Possession

---

The counter-position is important to take seriously, because it is held by thoughtful people who are not motivated by racial hostility.

The argument runs something like this: collective guilt is theologically incoherent. The biblical tradition holds individuals accountable for their own sins, not for the sins of their ancestors. The person alive today did not own slaves and should not be held financially liable for what others did. The practical mechanics of reparations — who qualifies, how much, administered by whom — are unworkable. And the deeper problem is that reparations treats race as the primary category of human identity, which is itself a form of racial essentialism that the church should resist.

These are real concerns. The theological point about collective guilt deserves careful engagement, because it is not nothing.

But notice what the argument quietly assumes: it frames reparations as punishment of the innocent for sins they did not commit. This is the wrong frame. The biblical model of restitution is not about punishment. It is about the correction of an ongoing condition. If I steal your land and then die, my children who inherited the land have not committed the original theft. But they are in possession of something that does not belong to them. The question of what they owe is not a question about their guilt for their father's crime. It is a question about their possession of property that was wrongly acquired.

## Teshuvah and the Limits of Lament

The land in coastal Georgia that was redistributed to Confederate landowners after 1865 was, and remained, property that had a prior claim on it. The families who cleared it and would have farmed it had been promised it by the federal government as partial compensation for 250 years of uncompensated labor. That promise was broken. The breaking of it produced conditions that compounded economically across generations. The theological question is not whether descendants should be punished for their ancestors. The theological question is whether the ongoing possession and benefit of wrongly distributed wealth creates an obligation of restitution — and the biblical record, from Leviticus to Zacchaeus, says yes.

---

The Hebrew concept of *teshuvah* — turning, return — describes the full movement of genuine repentance: not only interior contrition but exterior action, not only acknowledgment but the material correction of what was wrong. The rabbis taught that teshuvah was incomplete without repair — without actually fixing, to the extent possible, the damage done. This is not a fringe position in the tradition. It is the tradition. Repentance that remains only interior is, in the rabbinic understanding, not yet complete repentance.

## What Restitution Asks of the Church

The American church's engagement with its racial history has been heavy on acknowledgment and light on teshuvah in the full sense. Denominational resolutions. Formal apologies. Lament services. Statements. These are not nothing. But they do not, by themselves, constitute the turning that includes material repair. And the communities most affected know the difference between being lamented and being compensated. They have been lamented before.

Desmond Tutu [cite — confirm] observed that when a man has stolen your land and built his house on it, his offer to pray with you about the situation does not constitute justice. Justice requires addressing the land. The prayer, disconnected from the land, is not a spiritual supplement to justice. It is a substitute for it.

---

What would a theology of reparations actually look like in practice for the church, rather than for the federal government?

It begins with honest historical reckoning. The Southern Baptist Convention was founded in 1845 in defense of slaveholding [cite — confirm]. The Presbyterian Church's southern branches were explicit defenders of slavery as a divinely sanctioned institution. Many of the most prominent seminaries of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries were built on land worked by enslaved people and funded by slaveowners' donations. These are facts, not interpretations. A church that does not know its own history cannot repent of it.

It continues with material commitment — not as a symbolic gesture, but as a structural redirection. What percentage of the church's endowment and annual giving is directed toward historically Black institutions, toward communities that bore the weight of the economic extraction that built the church's own wealth? Not as charity. As restitution. The category matters. Charity is voluntary, surplus-dispensing, and morally praiseworthy. Restitution is obligatory, debt-paying, and morally required.

> The debt is real. The history is documented. The theological framework is available.

It includes advocacy for public policy that addresses the material conditions created by centuries of documented theft. The pastor who preaches Zacchaeus without asking what federal policy today creates the conditions for restitution or prevents it has stopped the sermon a verse too soon.

---

I am inside this indictment. My tradition benefited from the same historical arrangements I am describing. I have preached repentance and been slower to ask about repair. I have been moved by lament services and returned to the same structures unchanged.

The theological case for reparations is not a political position borrowed from the left. It is an extension of what the Bible actually says about what justice requires when something has been taken. Leviticus 6 knew it. Zacchaeus knew it. The prophets knew it. The question is whether the twenty-first-century American church, which inherited institutions built on the labor of enslaved people, will finally know it too.

The debt is real. The history is documented. The theological framework is available.

What is missing is not the argument. It is the will.

That is a pastoral problem. Which means it is also a preaching problem. Which means it lands, finally, here — at the pulpit, where the text says what it says, and the preacher decides whether to let it land.

In 2020, the pastoral question that should have been theological became political almost immediately. Masks or no masks. Vaccines or conscience. Gathering in person or following government guidelines. The churches that handled the pandemic well — meaning the churches that protected their most vulnerable members while maintaining community, that held the tension of institutional responsibility and congregational care — were mostly the churches that had already thought theologically about the health of their neighbors before the crisis arrived. The churches that handled it poorly were often the churches for whom public health had never been a theological category at all.

That failure did not begin in 2020. It was the accumulation of decades of theological thinning — the gradual privatization of the gospel into personal salvation and individual morality, the slow evacuation of the social dimensions of Christian responsibility, the training of congregations to interpret biblical language about the body and health and community in exclusively spiritual terms, while the material conditions of their neighbors' lives remained outside the frame.

**What the Body Means in Scripture**

> The gospel is addressed to whole persons.

The Hebrew tradition does not permit the body-soul separation that Greek philosophy introduced into Christian theology and that American evangelicalism has often pressed further than either the Greek philosophers or the early church intended. The Hebrew understanding of the human person is integrated and indivisible — not in the therapeutic sense that word has acquired in recent culture, but in the sense that the body is not a vehicle for the soul, not a temporary housing to be escaped, not less important than the spiritual self. The word *nephesh* in the Hebrew Bible, often translated "soul," refers to the whole living person — the self as embodied, hungry, thirsty, breathing, vulnerable. When the psalmist says "my soul thirsts for God" (Psalm 63:1), the thirst is not metaphor. It is the whole person, including the body, reaching for the living God.

## Health as a Crisis of Testimony in 2020

This matters for public health because it means that the church cannot care for the "souls" of its neighbors while remaining indifferent to the conditions that shape their bodies. The gospel is addressed to whole persons. Whole persons live in bodies that can be healthy or sick, in neighborhoods that can be clean or toxic, in systems that can support or undermine their flourishing. The God who created the body cares about its conditions.

The New Testament is not less material than the Hebrew Bible. Jesus healed bodies. He fed crowds. He touched lepers when touching them was a public health risk to himself. The early church, in Acts 2 and 4, organized itself around shared material resources precisely because the flourishing of the community required it. The deacons appointed in Acts 6 were appointed to manage food distribution — a public health function in a community where food insecurity was a real and present threat to the most vulnerable members. This is not a minor subplot in the New Testament story. It is the structure of the early church's common life.

> Seeking the city's welfare is a public health mandate. It is not optional.

**What Public Health Actually Is**

Public health is not primarily the government telling people what to do. It is the organized effort of communities to protect and improve the health of their populations — to identify the conditions that produce disease, injury, and premature death and to change them. John Snow mapping cholera cases in London in 1854 to identify the Broad Street pump as the source was public health. [cite — confirm] The sanitation reforms that reduced infant mortality in industrial cities through the late nineteenth century were public health. The elimination of smallpox through international vaccination campaigns was public health. The reduction of tobacco-related deaths through decades of public education and policy change was public health.

## The Selective Reading of Leviticus

None of these interventions were primarily about individual choices. They were about the conditions in which people live — the water they drink, the air they breathe, the information available to them about health risks, the systems that distribute health-protective resources to some communities and not to others. Public health is the recognition that health is not simply the outcome of individual decisions but the product of environments and systems that individuals do not fully control.

This recognition is theologically legible. The prophets understood that communities are environments that produce outcomes for the people who live in them. Isaiah's vision of the restored city in Isaiah 65:20-22 includes people who live out their full years, who build houses and inhabit them, who plant vineyards and eat their fruit — the vision of a community whose conditions support human flourishing rather than cutting it short. The Jeremiah 29:7 command to "seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile" uses the word *shalom* — the comprehensive well-being that includes health, safety, material sufficiency, right relationship. Seeking the city's welfare is a public health mandate. It is not optional.

## The Imago Dei in an Untreated Body

**What the Church Has Gotten Wrong**

The evangelical church in the United States has, in large segments, treated public health as a government intrusion on personal freedom rather than as a theological responsibility rooted in the love of neighbor. This position has required a selective reading of Scripture that magnifies the texts about individual liberty while minimizing the texts about communal obligation.

> The theology produced the public health outcome.

The most obvious example: the book of Leviticus, which evangelical churches tend to approach selectively, contains extensive public health legislation. The regulations about infectious disease — covering isolation of infected persons, inspection protocols, requirements for cleaning or destroying contaminated materials — were not merely ritual purity requirements. They were community health practices designed to prevent the spread of disease in a densely settled community (Leviticus 13-14). The logic was that the health of one person was a matter of communal concern because community members shared physical space, water, and food sources. Individual behavior had community consequences. The community had legitimate interest in regulating behavior that affected its health.

## Individual Liberty Dressed in Theological Language

The early church understood this logic when it organized care for the sick at personal risk to caregivers. During the Antonine Plague of the second century and the Plague of Cyprian in the third, Christians became known in the Roman world for caring for the sick — including non-Christians — when others fled. Rodney Stark, in his sociological study of early Christian growth, argues that this practice was both theologically motivated and practically significant: Christian communities had higher survival rates partly because they organized care for the sick rather than abandoning them. [cite — confirm] The theology and the public health outcome were not competing interests. The theology produced the public health outcome.

**The Justice Dimension**

## Narrowing Theology to a Size the Bible Rejects

Public health and justice are not separable. The burden of preventable disease, injury, and premature death in the United States is not distributed randomly. It follows the lines of race and income with a consistency that is not incidental. Black Americans die of preventable conditions at higher rates than white Americans in almost every disease category. [cite — confirm] Poor communities have higher rates of uncontrolled asthma, diabetes, and hypertension than wealthy communities. Communities adjacent to industrial facilities with high pollution outputs — which are disproportionately communities of color — have elevated rates of childhood asthma and cancer. [cite — confirm]

This distribution is not the result of different individual choices across racial and economic groups. It is the result of different exposures — to environmental toxins, to food environments, to healthcare access, to the chronic stress of economic precarity and racial threat. It is the result of systems that distribute health risks and health protections unequally.

The church that preaches the equal dignity of all persons before God while remaining silent about the systems that produce unequal health outcomes has not finished its sentence. The imago Dei — the divine image carried by every human being — is not an abstraction that floats above material conditions. It is a claim about the person in their full embodied existence. The person whose childhood asthma is untreated because her family cannot afford healthcare carries the image of God in a body the church has declared sacred in principle while declining to protect in practice.

**What the Pandemic Revealed**

COVID-19 did not create the church's failures around public health. It exposed them. It revealed how thoroughly the theology of much of American Christianity had been shaped by the individualism of American culture rather than the communal obligations of the biblical tradition. The churches that insisted on gathering in person when the medical consensus was clear that gathering would spread disease and kill the most vulnerable among them were not being faithful to Scripture. They were being faithful to an American ideology of individual rights that had been dressed in theological language.

I am not interested in scoring partisan points on this. I am interested in the theological error, which belongs to all of us in different ways. The privatization of faith — the reduction of Christianity to personal salvation, individual morality, and private spiritual practice — has left the church without categories for thinking about the communal and structural dimensions of human flourishing. When a question arises that requires those categories, the church defaults to whatever the surrounding culture offers. In much of American evangelical culture, what the surrounding culture offers is a framework of individual liberty in which the community's claim on the individual is always presumptively suspect.

That framework is not the framework of Leviticus, or the prophets, or the early church, or the New Testament at any point. It is a framework the church has absorbed from a specific cultural context and has failed to critically examine.

**What the Church Should Be Doing**

The church that takes public health seriously as a theological matter will do several things. It will ensure that its own community practices support the health of its most vulnerable members — the elderly, the immunocompromised, the people for whom a communicable disease is not an inconvenience but a genuine threat. It will speak prophetically about the conditions that produce unequal health outcomes in its city — the food desert two miles from the church building, the industrial facility polluting the air in the neighborhood that cannot afford to move, the lack of healthcare access that means the family across town is managing its diabetes with emergency room visits rather than primary care.

And it will resist the cultural framework that treats the health of its neighbors as a private matter — outside the church's concern, outside the scope of the gospel, best left to individual choice and market mechanisms. That framework has a name. It is not Christianity. It has been confused with Christianity for long enough.

The God who made bodies cares about their conditions. The church that does not care about the conditions that shape the bodies of its neighbors has narrowed its theology to a size the Bible does not recognize.

The conventional wisdom about church planting runs in a single direction: a sending church, large enough to absorb the cost, releases a team and a planter and carries the financial weight of the first several years. That model works. It requires a church large enough to give away tens of thousands of dollars annually while absorbing the departure of key families and volunteer leaders. It requires a pastor secure enough in his own ecclesiological identity to raise up a leader he is willing to release. And it is unavailable to the vast majority of churches in America, which are under two hundred people, run close to the financial edge already, and led by pastors who are doing everything alone.

What happens when three churches that cannot afford to plant alone decide to plant together?

That is not a theoretical question. The Pastors Connection Network has seen versions of this arrangement take shape in communities across the Midwest, and what those arrangements reveal about the nature of the church is at least as interesting as what they reveal about church planting strategy.

## When No Single Authority Can Be Assumed

The first thing that happens when small churches attempt a collaborative plant is that every assumption about ownership has to be renegotiated. A single sending church knows who is in charge. The lead pastor of the sending church carries the authority, and the planter is accountable to him. Three churches sharing a plant means three pastors, three governing structures, three sets of expectations about what success looks like — and no obvious single authority. The negotiation of that shared governance is difficult and revealing. It is also, ironically, precisely the kind of difficulty that the church needs to practice.

> The practice is uncomfortable. It is also formative.

Paul's description of the body in 1 Corinthians 12 is not a description of how organisms work under a single organizational head. It is a description of how differently gifted communities need each other — how the eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of you" (1 Corinthians 12:21). Three small churches bringing different strengths to a shared plant begin to practice that interdependence in ways that the single sending church never has to. The practice is uncomfortable. It is also formative.

## What Each Small Church Brings to the Table

Consider what typically differentiates small churches from each other in the same city. One church brings financial stability but no young families — it is aging in place, giving faithfully, and aware that it does not have the demographics to sustain itself indefinitely. One church brings young families but no financial margin — it is growing but scraping. One church brings a neighborhood presence in exactly the place where the plant needs to take root but no capacity for anything beyond its own Sunday morning. Together they have something. Separately they have nothing but good intentions and a common problem.

The plant that emerges from that collaboration carries a different genetic material than the plant that emerges from a single strong sender. It is accountable to multiple bodies. Its planter navigates three sets of pastoral relationships instead of one. The governance is more complicated. The decision-making is slower. And the congregation that forms — if the collaboration holds — has been planted into a posture of inter-church dependence from its origin. That posture is very hard to teach to a church that has never practiced it. It is the native disposition of a church born from a collaborative act.

There is also something the collaborative plant does to the sending churches themselves. The church that releases a family or a tithe-unit or a key volunteer toward a shared plant has made a theological statement about its own purpose. It has said, with its budget and its people, that the gospel advancing in this city matters more than its own institutional stability. That is not a small thing. Most small churches are functioning in a moderate degree of self-protective anxiety — wondering whether they have enough, whether they will survive another decade, whether the next pastor will stay. The church that gives away something it cannot easily afford in order to participate in a shared mission has reoriented itself. The anxiety does not disappear, but it has been interrupted by an act of genuine faith.

## The Steel-Man of the Sending Model

This is not metaphorical. It is practical and observable. The churches that participate in collaborative plants tend to describe a renewal of their own sense of purpose that neither could generate alone. Being part of something larger than yourself is not just a spiritual principle. It is a sociological one — communities that are organized around something beyond their own survival tend to be healthier than communities that are organized around their own continuation.

The steel-man of the conventional sending model is legitimate and should be heard. Clear authority produces clear accountability. When one church sends and one pastor is in charge, decisions get made cleanly, conflicts get resolved through a single chain of authority, and the planter knows exactly who he answers to. Three-way governance produces real friction — three sets of expectations about worship style, about theological emphasis, about ministry priorities, about what "success" looks like in year three. That friction can be generative, but it can also be paralyzing. The collaborations that fail tend to fail along exactly these lines: a governance vacuum that nobody wanted to fill, theological differences that were papered over in the early enthusiasm, the gradual calcification of the partnership into a transactional arrangement where the churches are contributors rather than co-laborers.

What makes these collaborations survive is harder to name precisely. The arrangements that hold seem to share one characteristic: the pastors involved have submitted to something larger than their own church's brand. They have decided, at some level, that the plant succeeds if the gospel advances — not if their particular congregation gets credit for it. That posture is not natural to most pastoral leaders, who have significant ego invested in their own congregation's identity and are doing ministry in contexts where comparative success is visible and constantly evaluated.

## The Friendship That Holds Collaboration Together

The posture requires friendship. Not professional collegiality — actual friendship between pastors, the kind that requires regular conversation, shared meals, honest disagreement, and the willingness to say the hard things that institutional partners do not say to each other. The Pastors Connection Network exists, in part, because that kind of friendship between pastors does not happen by accident. It requires structure — a regular gathering, a committed group, the expectation that real things will be said rather than managed presentations of pastoral competence. Collaborative church planting requires the same kind of relationship between the sending churches' pastors.

It also requires humility about failure. Some collaborative plants do not survive. The governance collapses. The planter leaves after two years. One of the sending churches withdraws its support when a key family moves away and the giving drops. The shared vision that animated the early partnership turns out to have had different practical implications for different churches, and the differences were not negotiated honestly at the beginning. That failure is painful. It does not prove that collaboration was a mistake. It proves that collaboration is hard enough to require more than good intentions and enthusiasm to sustain it.

The three churches that plant together and survive have learned something about the body of Christ that cannot be taught in a church planting conference. They have discovered that something they believed abstractly — that the church is one body with many members, that no single congregation constitutes the whole — is actually true in a way that costs something and requires real discipline. They have practiced the theology of the body rather than merely reading it.

Ephesians 4:3 commands the church to "make every effort to keep the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace." The language is not passive. Every effort. Not hope for unity, or appreciate unity, or acknowledge unity as a good in principle. Make every effort to keep it. The collaborative church plant is an attempt to do exactly that — to act, at real cost and with real difficulty, on the claim that the church is one body.

## Practicing the Theology of the Body in Public

That is not a small act. In a church culture that has learned to compete and to brand and to measure success by the growth of individual institutions, a collaborative plant is a counter-testimony. It says that the mission matters more than the credit. It says that the gospel advancing in this city is worth more than the name on the sign.

The three churches that plant together are practicing something the American church desperately needs to recover.

> The capacity was created by the commitment, not the other way around.

They are practicing it in public, with their money and their people.

> Act first, and discover what becomes possible.

That witness is worth more than the church they started.

There is a final word for the pastor who reads this and thinks his church is too small, too limited, too financially marginal to participate in planting anything. The churches in this account did not have excess capacity. They had commitment to something larger than themselves and enough trust between their pastors to try. The capacity was created by the commitment, not the other way around. The resources came because the decision came first.

This is the pattern of most of what God asks the church to do. Not: accumulate enough first, then act. Act first, and discover what becomes possible. The widow's jar of flour that does not run out (1 Kings 17:14-16) does not fill up before Elijah arrives. It fills as they eat from it, one meal at a time. The collaborative plant that waits for the conditions to be right before it begins will wait forever. The collaborative plant that begins with commitment and genuine relationship and the willingness to figure it out together will discover that what it needed was present all along — distributed across three congregations, none of whom had enough alone.

Pilate's question has outlasted his empire.

"What is truth?" (John 18:38). He asked it and walked away without waiting for an answer, which is the gesture of a man who has concluded the question is unanswerable — or that the answer is irrelevant to the business of governance. Two thousand years later, the question is everywhere again, with the same implication: not that truth doesn't exist but that it cannot be reliably known, that claims to truth are performances of power, that the appropriate posture is skepticism toward every assertion made by every institution that has the standing to make assertions.

That skepticism did not appear from nowhere. It was produced.

The institutions that built the architecture of public trust in the modern West — universities, media, government, medicine, and yes, the church — have in various ways earned the distrust they now receive. The church specifically has offered the watching world a sustained demonstration that proclaimed moral authority and actual moral behavior can diverge dramatically, that the institution designed to speak for the God who is truth has been capable of systematic concealment when the truth was inconvenient. The abuse crises, the financial scandals, the institutional self-protection dressed as pastoral care — none of this was invented by the church's critics. All of it was documented, reported, covered up, and documented again. The skepticism is not irrational. It is a reasonable response to available evidence.

> The skepticism is not irrational. It is a reasonable response to available evidence.

This is the situation in which the church is asked to speak. Not from a position of unquestioned cultural authority. From a position of damaged credibility, in a culture that has been taught by long experience to treat truth claims as power claims and to look for the agenda behind every assertion.

## Two Failures, One Problem

The temptation in that situation is one of two moves, both of which are failures.

The first move is to double down on assertion — to speak more loudly, more confidently, with greater institutional force, as if the credibility problem can be solved by volume. This produces the church that has an answer to every question and certainty about every controversy, that confuses dogmatism for conviction and combativeness for prophetic witness. It does not produce truth-telling. It produces a performance of truth-telling that the watching world correctly identifies as performance.

The second move is the mirror image: a retreat into epistemic humility so total that the church has nothing to say, every question becomes too complex for any answer, and the distinctiveness of the gospel is dissolved in endless qualification. This is not honesty. It is cowardice dressed as sophistication.

I have been in both places. I have preached with a certainty calibrated to manage congregational anxiety more than to tell the truth. I have also softened claims because the cost of making them clearly felt too high. Neither posture was honest. One was fear wearing the clothes of confidence. The other was fear wearing the clothes of nuance. Fear is a poor guide to truth in either direction.

## The Historical Weight of the Question

The church is not the first community to face a culture that treats truth as a construction. The early church preached in a Hellenistic world where competing philosophical schools had been arguing about epistemology for four centuries. The Sophists, in the fifth century before Christ, had already established a market for persuasion that did not depend on correspondence to reality — what mattered was the argument that worked, the rhetoric that moved, not the claim that was accurate [cite — confirm]. The Apostle Paul entered that world and said something that sounded, to educated Greco-Roman ears, like intellectual suicide: "For the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom" (1 Corinthians 1:25). He was not abandoning reason. He was refusing to conduct the conversation entirely on the sophist's terms.

The Gnostic challenge of the second and third centuries was, in part, a challenge about the nature of truth: is it available to all people in common, or is it esoteric knowledge reserved for those with the spiritual capacity to receive it? The church's answer — canon, creed, and community — was institutional: here is the shared text, here is the common confession, here is the embodied community that holds and demonstrates what we believe is true. Irenaeus of Lyons, writing in the late second century against the Gnostics, argued that the church's claim to truth was grounded not just in argument but in continuity of testimony — bishops in succession from the apostles, communities whose common life demonstrated the coherence of the gospel [cite — confirm].

The church's answer to the post-truth moment cannot be thinner than its answer to Gnosticism was. It cannot be mere assertion, and it cannot be mere demonstration. It requires both.

## The Claim That Has Not Been Softened

> This is either the most important claim in human history or it is nothing. There is no comfortable middle.

Jesus made a claim about himself so total that it either demands everything or explains nothing: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). Not a true teacher among true teachers. Not one reliable guide among several. The truth — the reality against which all other claims are measured. That claim has not been softened by subsequent scholarship or qualified away by careful theology. It stands, as demanding as it ever was.

The Greek word here is *aletheia* — the same word at the root of Pilate's question, the word that in classical usage meant disclosure, the removal of concealment, reality as it actually is. Jesus does not say he has the truth or teaches the truth or points toward the truth. He identifies himself with it. The Logos of John 1, through whom all things were made, through whom the universe has its order and coherence, became flesh and dwelt among us. The Christian claim is that truth is not an abstraction but a person, and that person entered the material, historical world and was witnessed, recorded, and passed down.

This is either the most important claim in human history or it is nothing. There is no comfortable middle.

## Witness as the Argument

What the moment requires is something harder than either loud assertion or polite retreat: a church that speaks from demonstrated integrity, that earns the right to be heard by being what it claims before it says what it believes. When Paul wrote to Titus about what the church's life should look like, the purpose was always witness — the community living in a way that made the teaching "attractive" (Titus 2:10). The life was the argument. The speech carried weight because the practice gave it weight.

This is not a new strategy. It is the oldest one. The early church in the Roman Empire did not win its place through political power or superior rhetoric. It won it — to whatever extent it won it — by being a community that crossed the class lines the Empire maintained absolutely, that cared for sick and dying people during plagues when the healthy had fled, that included women and slaves and foreigners in positions of genuine dignity. The argument was embodied before it was articulated. Tertullian recorded the pagan observation: see how they love one another [cite — confirm]. That was the evidence. The evidence preceded the assertion.

Lesslie Newbigin, writing in the second half of the twentieth century as Western Christianity faced the challenge of post-Enlightenment secularism, argued that the local congregation is the hermeneutic of the gospel — the interpretive framework through which the gospel either becomes credible or remains abstract [cite — confirm]. The church does not just deliver a message. The church *is* the message's demonstration. A congregation that practices forgiveness makes the claim of forgiveness credible. A congregation that crosses economic and racial lines makes the claim of reconciliation credible. A congregation where suffering people are met with genuine presence makes the claim of a God who is present to suffering credible.

> The argument that holds is the life that cannot be explained except by what it believes.

The church that has not been that community cannot simply speak its way into credibility. It has to become the community first.

## The Counter-Position Answered

The honest counter-argument is this: the claim that the church must earn credibility before speaking sounds like it delays the gospel's proclamation indefinitely, given how much the church has failed. By that standard, no church is ready to speak. The gospel is not the church's record. The gospel is Christ's record. And Christ's record does not depend on our consistency.

This is true, as far as it goes. The gospel's truth is not contingent on the church's performance. But the church's credibility as a witness to that truth is. Paul understood this — why else would he devote such sustained attention in letter after letter to the moral life of the communities that bore the name of Christ? Not because their behavior constituted the gospel, but because their behavior either commended or undermined their proclamation of it.

The gospel is not the church's to own. But the witness is.

## What Remains

The culture's loss of confidence in truth is not primarily a philosophical problem. It is a crisis of testimony — of institutions and communities that have claimed to speak truthfully and demonstrably have not. The church is among those institutions. Its path forward is not to out-argue the skeptics. It is to become a community where people who have been told by everything else that truth is a function of power discover a different kind of community — one where confession is possible, where real things are named, where forgiveness is offered and received and therefore actually real rather than merely claimed.

That community is the argument.

Not a loud one. Pilate walked away from the loud argument too.

I have five sons watching what my life argues for. The congregation I serve is watching. The skeptic who sat in the back pew twice last year and has not returned is watching, in the sense that whatever she concluded about whether this community is real is still shaping whether she returns. I cannot think about the post-truth crisis as an abstract cultural problem. It is what I face every Sunday, every pastoral conversation, every deacon meeting where the question underneath every other question is: do we actually believe what we say we believe, or is this another institution performing what it claims while concealing what it does?

The question is Pilate's question. The answer has to be the life. Specifically, the life of the community that has been formed by the one who stood before Pilate and said nothing, having already said everything.

The argument that holds is the life that cannot be explained except by what it believes.

The night before he died, Jesus prayed for unity.

Not for agreement on every doctrinal question. Not for a single worship style or a unified political position or a cultural consensus that would make the church legible to the empire. He prayed that his followers would be one "as you, Father, are in me, and I in you" — and the purpose he named was not institutional efficiency but witness: "that the world may believe that you have sent me" (John 17:21). The unity is not an organizational achievement. It is an argument. It is the thing that makes the claim credible in a world that has every reason to be skeptical of grand theological assertions.

## Sameness Mistaken for Unity

We have, on the whole, not produced that thing. We have produced a different thing — a tendency to mistake sameness for unity, to create communities held together by shared cultural markers, shared political assumptions, shared worship aesthetics, shared levels of education or income — and to call the result the body of Christ. What we have built is a club. Clubs are comfortable. They are not arguments. They confirm what their members already believe about the world, and the world watches them and learns nothing.

> Clubs are comfortable. They are not arguments.

The New Testament church was not a club. Acts 2 describes a community that would have been sociologically implausible in first-century Jerusalem — Parthians and Medes and Elamites, residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and parts of Libya, visitors from Rome, Cretans and Arabs (Acts 2:9–11). This was not diversity as a program or as an institutional commitment. These groups did not naturally gather. They had histories of competition, mutual suspicion, and ethnic distance that went back generations. What gathered them was not shared background or shared social location. It was a shared encounter with a risen Lord, and the claim that encounter made on every other organizing principle of their lives.

## What Baptism Does to the Social Order

Including the organizing principles they most valued.

Paul's letter to the Galatians was written to a community that was fracturing along exactly the lines that come most naturally to human beings — ethnic and religious identity. Some in the Galatian church were insisting that Gentile believers adopt the covenant markers of Jewish identity, particularly circumcision. This was not a fringe position; it came from people who believed, sincerely, that they were protecting the integrity of the gospel. And Paul said — with a force that shocks the reader who encounters it without warning — that they were not protecting the gospel. They were destroying it. "There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). Not a sentimental aspiration. A description of what baptism does to the social order and to the identity categories the social order depends on.

The passage does not mean that the differences cease to exist. Paul knew perfectly well that Gentiles remained Gentiles and Jews remained Jews after baptism. The differences remained. What changed was their organizing power — their capacity to function as the primary categories by which people were included or excluded, valued or dismissed. In Christ, those categories are relativized. Not erased. Relativized — placed under something larger than themselves, something that determines their ultimate weight and reach.

## The Cost of Uniformity Purchased by Absence

This is a costly claim. It was costly in the first century, when it produced the scandal of Jew and Gentile eating at the same table and wealthy and poor being addressed without distinction. It is costly now, when it asks a congregation to remain in relationship with the member whose conclusions they find difficult — to share the table with someone whose politics or aesthetics or secondary theology produces friction, because the ground on which we stand together is more fundamental than the things we dispute.

> This is not witness. This is performance.

I have attended churches that achieved unity by achieving uniformity. Everyone agreed on the contested questions, the worship had one sound, the congregation occupied a tight band of the cultural spectrum. And in every case — without exception — the uniformity had been purchased at the price of someone's absence. The people who complicated the picture had left, or had learned to keep their complications private. The community was unified because it was not actually diverse, and the appearance of unity was maintained by the quiet removal of everyone who would have made it harder.

## Which Things Belong to the Center

This is not witness. This is performance. The world does not look at a room of people who all think the same things and feel the same things and come from the same places and conclude that the resurrection must be true. There is nothing there that cannot be explained by sociology. A community that holds together across genuine difference — that stays in the room with the person it disagrees with, that works out the tension rather than eliminating the one who produces it — that is harder to explain. That is the thing that requires an account.

The honest counter-argument holds that doctrinal clarity requires some exclusion, that a community with no real center cannot hold, that the language of unity-without-uniformity can become a way of refusing to name error. This is not wrong. The unity I am describing is not theological indifferentism. Not the claim that all positions are equivalent or that the center of the faith is too thin to generate any real conviction. The gospel is a specific thing: the death and resurrection of Jesus, the forgiveness of sins, the reconciliation of human beings to God, the coming of the Kingdom that is already and not yet. That center is not negotiable, and the church that trades its specificity for a vague inclusiveness has abandoned the thing that makes it capable of being any particular community at all.

The question is which things belong to the center and which things belong to the secondary ring where genuine Christians have disagreed across centuries without destroying each other. The church's history of fracture is in large part a history of treating the secondary ring as though it were the center — of splitting over baptismal mode and church governance and worship style and political alignment, as though the truth about these things were as critical as the truth about the resurrection. Every split has come with theological justification. Almost none of them have been worth what they cost.

## The Table That Holds People Across Difference

James K.A. Smith argues that what forms communities is not primarily shared beliefs but shared practices — the liturgies of daily life that shape desire and identity before explicit theology gets to them. [cite — confirm Smith's argument in *Desiring the Kingdom*] If that is right, then the question of unity-without-uniformity is not primarily a question of how to manage doctrinal disagreement. It is a question of whether the community's shared practices — worship, communion, service, prayer — are thick enough to hold people across the differences they bring to those practices. The practice of sitting at the same table, over time, does things to the people sitting there that argument alone cannot do.

The Lord's Supper was, in the New Testament context, a shared meal that included people from every level of the social hierarchy — and Paul's fierce rebuke in 1 Corinthians 11 is precisely about the failure to eat together across those lines. The wealthy were eating their own food and getting drunk while the poor went hungry, and Paul said this practice made the Lord's Supper not the Lord's Supper at all. The practice was invalidated by the exclusion. The unity the practice was meant to enact required actual sharing across actual difference — bodies at the same table, eating from the same loaf.

Genuine unity costs more than uniformity. It requires staying in the room with the person you would prefer to have leave. It requires the theological confidence to say: the ground on which we stand is larger than the questions we disagree about, and I am not going anywhere. It requires the willingness to be changed by the encounter — to discover that the person you disagreed with has something that you need, that your picture of the faith is smaller than the faith itself, that the community you have built is impoverished by the absence of the people who would have complicated it.

> That work is the witness.

The church that can produce that kind of unity is the church that has something to say to a fractured world. Not because it has solved the problem of difference — no institution has — but because it is visibly trying to hold together what everything else is tearing apart, and the effort itself is an argument about what is ultimately real.

The prayer of John 17 is not answered once and then preserved. It is answered continuously, by people who have decided that the prayer matters more than their comfort with the people who share it.

That work is the witness. The world is watching, and it has been watching for a long time, waiting to see whether the church means it.

Drive past your church building at eleven on a Tuesday morning and count the people within a mile radius who will have no meaningful contact with the gospel this week. Count the apartment complex where recent immigrants from Somalia live in quiet and considerable isolation. Count the truck stop twenty minutes outside town where men sleep in their cabs because they cannot afford a room. Count the nursing facility with eighty residents, three of whom have a visitor more than once a month. Count the county jail.

Then tell me where the unreached people groups are.

## The Geography of Mission in Scripture

---

The missionary tradition in American Christianity has a specific geography: far away and difficult to get to. The maps with the red circles over the 10/40 Window [cite — confirm] — the band of latitude between ten and forty degrees north encompassing the most densely non-Christian populations on earth — form the visual imagination of global mission, and they are not wrong. Those populations deserve the church's attention and resources and prayer. The 7,000-plus people groups worldwide with no indigenous evangelical church, the communities that have no access to Scripture in their language, the places where naming the name of Christ requires a willingness to die for it — these represent genuine missionary urgency, and the church's commitment to them is not a mistake.

> he is not describing a continent. He is describing a posture.

But the geography of mission in Scripture is more complicated than that. When Paul writes in Romans 15:20 that he makes it his ambition to preach the gospel where Christ has not already been named, he is not describing a continent. He is describing a posture. The ambition is to go where the good news has not landed — not to define that location from a conference in Colorado or to assume that "not yet reached" means "not yet reached by someone from somewhere far away."

## The Immigrant Community at the Strip-Mall Mosque

There are populations within your city — possibly within your zip code — where the gospel has not, in any meaningful sense, landed. Not because there are no church buildings nearby. But because the church buildings are not inhabited by those populations, do not speak their languages, do not operate on their schedules, do not exist in their social world, and have never seriously tried to.

---

The immigrant community is the most obvious and most neglected example. American cities have experienced significant demographic change from immigration in the past three decades [cite — confirm], and the communities that formed in strip-mall mosques and apartment complexes and informal networks of mutual aid are not, by and large, communities in conversation with the local evangelical church. They are not in conversation with us partly because we have not sought them, partly because the cultural and linguistic distance requires significant investment to cross, and partly because the crossing will cost us something and we have quietly decided the cost is not worth bearing.

## The Incarcerated the Church Walks Past Daily

That last part deserves honesty. The cultural distance is real, and navigating it requires more than good intentions. It requires learning. Language learning, or at minimum the humility of entering a linguistic environment where you are the one without competence — where the tables are turned and the person who arrived last is the most capable in the room. It requires the willingness to be a guest in someone else's social world before extending an invitation to your own. It requires the renegotiation of what "church" looks like when the congregation is primarily first-generation immigrants with different assumptions about time, space, authority, community, and the relationship between faith and ethnicity than the church you built for people who look like you.

The congregations doing this well are not the ones with the best cross-cultural training programs. They are the ones whose pastors went first — who walked into the apartment complex uninvited and began meeting people, who showed up at the cultural festival and stayed long enough to have an actual conversation, who found the community leader and asked what the community needed rather than announcing what the church planned to offer.

## The Elderly Isolated as a Mission Field

---

The incarcerated population is another unreached group that the church walks past daily. The United States incarcerates people at a rate that is extraordinary by global standards [cite — confirm] — roughly two million people at any given time, with millions more cycling through pre-trial detention each year. The county jail in your community holds men and women who are, in many cases, more genuinely open to the gospel than anyone sitting in your Sunday morning congregation — because the conditions of their lives have stripped away the comfortable alternatives. They have time. They have stripped-down conditions that make the fundamental questions unavoidable. They are often cut off from the social networks that make it possible to avoid direct engagement with the state of their own souls.

The church that has a jail ministry carried by one or two volunteers who visit on Thursday evenings has done something. The church that has integrated the formerly incarcerated into its actual community — that has understood reentry as a mission field requiring the same sustained investment as a church plant in another country, that has people from the congregation serving as mentors and employers and friends to people coming out of incarceration — that church is rare. The gap between what the church offers and what the Scripture requires of it on this question is among the widest in American Christianity. Matthew 25:36 is not ambiguous: "I was in prison and you came to visit me." The Matthean logic is not "I was in prison and you started a Thursday evening program." It is "you came."

## Every Town and Every Place

---

The elderly isolated are not usually discussed in missionary terms at all. They are understood as a pastoral care challenge rather than a mission field. But the eighty-year-old in the nursing facility who has never been asked what she believes about God — who was raised in a nominally religious household, who attended church at Christmas for a few decades, who has never made any kind of personal faith commitment, and who has now been alone with her thoughts for three years — she is unreached. The pastoral imagination that sees her only as someone to visit, rather than someone to whom the gospel has not yet come, has missed what the text requires.

The same is true of the homebound, the deeply depressed, the people whose social circumstances — poverty, disability, mental illness, histories that make them difficult to be around — have resulted in a practical exclusion from the social world in which Christianity primarily operates in America. The gospel was announced first to shepherds — Luke 2:8 places the first proclamation not in the temple or among the respectable but in a field at night among workers whose occupation rendered them ritually impure and socially marginal by the standards of first-century Judaism. The first recipients of the announcement were not in a position to spread it effectively through respectable social networks. They were exactly the kind of people who are nowhere near your Sunday morning attendance count.

---

Jesus sent the seventy-two out in Luke 10 and told them to go to every town and place where he was about to go. Every town. Every place. Not the strategically significant ones. Not the ones with high potential for multiplication or favorable demographics or existing relationships with the sending church. Every place.

> They are the mission. They have always been the mission.

The missiology that limits the missionary imagination to the far away is a distortion that serves the institutional church's preference for distance. Distance is comfortable in a specific way: it allows the church to feel missional without requiring it to cross the social and cultural boundaries that are genuinely proximate. The neighbor who is a different ethnicity, who is behind bars, who is dying in a facility with no visitors — they require a different kind of crossing than the church member who buys mission calendars and prays for distant people groups. The crossing required is personal and costly and cannot be delegated to a professional missionary who is working somewhere else.

The unreached people nearest to you are not a consolation prize for the churches that cannot afford to go far. They are the mission. They have always been the mission.

> That is not faithfulness. That is a deferral dressed as strategy.

---

Let me make this concrete. In Fenton, Michigan — the small city where I pastor — there are populations within walking distance of our building who have had no meaningful engagement with the gospel in their lifetimes. Recent immigrants. The incarcerated at the county level. The elderly in facilities nearby. The families whose economic circumstances have placed them outside the social world the church inhabits.

These are not populations I have fully reached. I have not invested in all of them with the seriousness the text requires. I have had the convenient thought that the farther mission was more urgent, that the global commitment justified a degree of local neglect, that starting closer to home would have to wait until the infrastructure was better positioned.

That is not faithfulness. That is a deferral dressed as strategy.

The commitment to global mission and the commitment to the unreached at your gate are not in competition. The tradition of the church has understood since Acts 1:8 — "Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth" — that the geography of witness is concentric, not exclusive. The word "and" appears twice. Not "or." Not "eventually." The Jerusalem and the ends of the earth are simultaneous callings, not sequential ones.

The distance that matters is not geographic.

It is the distance between the church you have built and the people God has placed in its shadow. Whether you close that distance is a theological question, not a logistical one. The logistics are solvable. The will is the question.

Who is within a mile of your building right now, waiting for something the church claims to carry?

Nehemiah did not arrive in Jerusalem with a plan.

He arrived in the middle of the night, alone, and rode around the rubble of the walls before he said a single word to anyone about why he was there (Nehemiah 2:12–15). He did not call a meeting. He did not call a press conference. He looked at what was broken. He walked the perimeter of the destruction in the dark, alone with the God who had sent him, taking the full measure of what the situation actually required before he opened his mouth.

And when he finally gathered the leaders, his first move was not proclamation. It was disclosure: "You see the trouble we are in" (Nehemiah 2:17). Not the trouble I have diagnosed and come to fix. Not the trouble I have received a vision about. The trouble we are in together. He named the shared reality before he named the shared calling. The vision came out of the community's grief, not over it.

## The Move Most Vision-Casting Skips

This is the move that most pastoral vision-casting skips. The skipping is costly, and it tends to be invisible to the one doing it.

A pastor attends a conference. He reads a book. He sits with God in sustained prayer over several weeks and comes home with a clarity about where the church should go — a clarity that is real, genuinely Spirit-formed, and that he has enough pastoral confidence to trust. And then he presents it. In a sermon, in a leadership meeting, in a document with a mission statement and a five-year plan. And what he gets back is polite interest that deepens, over months, into polite resistance, and the resistance eventually becomes a quiet movement of key people toward the exits.

## Compliance That Looks Like Movement

The problem was not the vision. The problem was the process.

> The problem was not the vision. The problem was the process.

The congregation was never inside the grief that produced the vision. They did not sit with the same question. They did not name the same brokenness. They were presented with conclusions from a discernment process they were not part of, and they were asked to commit their energy and resources to a destination they did not help choose. Some will follow out of trust — genuine, appropriate trust, the kind that a congregation should have for a pastor it has come to know over time. But trust has a different quality when it is exercised in the absence of understanding. It is trust that says: I believe you believe this, and I will follow for now. It is not trust that says: this is ours, and I am not going anywhere.

Many will follow at half-speed. They will wait to see if the plan survives contact with reality, preserving in their interior life enough of the old vision to return to it if the new one fails. They will not say this. They will attend meetings and vote the right direction and nod in the right places. But you can feel the difference between a congregation that has claimed a vision and a congregation that is accompanying the pastor's vision. One produces initiative. The other produces compliance. Compliance can look like movement for years. It rarely endures the cost that genuine vision eventually requires.

## Living Into the Questions That Produced the Vision

I have done this. I have arrived with the vision folded in my pocket, convinced that the clarity of my calling was sufficient warrant for leading people toward it without the messy, slow process of bringing them inside the question. I was not wrong about the calling. I was wrong about what shared ownership actually requires, which is different from a presentation of conclusions.

James K.A. Smith, in his work on liturgical formation, argues that we are not primarily thinking creatures who adopt ideas but desiring creatures whose loves are shaped by practice — that the community's shared life forms the imagination before rational argument can reach it. [cite — confirm Smith's specific argument] That has implications for how vision works in a congregation. A community whose loves have been formed by a particular set of practices, a particular understanding of who they are, does not adopt a new vision by hearing it. They adopt it by living into the questions that produced it. They need to have sat in the same darkness, named the same brokenness, felt the same weight before the vision arrives as answer. Otherwise the answer lands in soil that has not been prepared for it.

The practical shape of this is slower than most pastors want it to be. It means spending considerable time asking questions before offering answers — listening to the congregation's own diagnosis of the church's condition, what they see, what they grieve, what they believe is missing or broken. It means building a small group of honest voices early in the process, people who will tell you what the congregation actually thinks rather than what the congregation says in front of the pastor, and taking what they tell you seriously enough to let it reshape the plan. It means resisting the pressure — and there is always pressure, both internal and external — to arrive with answers faster than the community has had time to form the questions.

## Decision Without Democracy in Nehemiah

None of this means abandoning leadership or treating vision as a democratic process where the majority gets what the majority prefers. Nehemiah made decisions. He was not running a committee. When the wall-builders were threatened by Sanballat and Tobiah, he did not call a congregational vote about whether to arm the workers. He decided, and the workers trusted him because they had been inside the process long enough to trust the decision-maker (Nehemiah 4:16–18). The authority to decide was not derived from the congregation's consent to every particular. It was derived from the congregation's ownership of the shared enterprise.

The key observation in Nehemiah 3 is geographic: each family group rebuilt the section of wall nearest their own house. They were not executing the leader's vision on the leader's terms. They were rebuilding their own street, their own neighborhood, the wall that stood between their children and the rubble. The vision had been organized to include them not as workers implementing a plan but as neighbors protecting what they already owned. They were not following Nehemiah's dream. They were doing their own work inside a shared framework.

That is the outcome the process needs to produce. Not a congregation that can articulate the pastor's vision correctly but a congregation that has internalized the vision as its own — that says "we believe this" rather than "he believes this" and "our church is going here" rather than "the pastor has a plan." The pronoun shift from "he" to "we" is not cosmetic. It is the actual measure of whether the vision has been received or merely tolerated.

## The Pronoun Shift From He to We

The vision that lasts is the one the community can speak in the first person plural.

> The vision that lasts is the one the community can speak in the first person plural.

That pronoun is not created by a sermon. It is not created by a document or a branding exercise or a well-produced video. It is created by the slow, unglamorous, time-consuming work of bringing people into the question before you offer them the answer — of sitting with them in their grief about the present state of the church, honoring what they see and what they feel, and then, together, naming what you believe God is inviting you toward. That process produces ownership that no presentation can purchase.

The pressure on pastors to produce vision quickly and communicate it compellingly is real and in some ways legitimate. Congregations do need direction. Drift is not neutral. A community without a clear sense of where it is going tends to organize around the preservation of its past, which is its own kind of failure. The pastor's calling includes the calling to see ahead and to say clearly what he sees.

But the seeing must be done with the community, not for it. The saying must come after the listening, not before. And the plan, however clearly it has been received, must be offered into the community's own hands to shape and own, not deposited as a finished product for them to implement.

Buildings require builders who believe the work is theirs. Walls get rebuilt fastest when the families rebuilding them are rebuilding their own street.

The vision that does not include the community in its formation is a plan. Plans get executed. Visions get owned. The difference between a church that executes a plan and a church that owns a vision is the difference between an organization and a community. One of those things can be built in three years. The other takes most of a pastoral lifetime.

Nehemiah knew this. He looked at the rubble first, alone, before he said a word. He counted the cost honestly. And then he went to the people who would have to bear it and said: you see the trouble we are in. Not the trouble I'm here to fix. Ours. Together.

> But the seeing must be done with the community, not for it.

That is where the work begins — and where most pastoral visions, however clear and genuine and Spirit-formed, fail before they start.

The homeless man sleeping under the interstate overpass three blocks from my church does not come to our Sunday services. This is not because he has not been invited. It is because the social distance between where he is and where we gather on Sunday morning is too great to be bridged by an invitation.

I have known this for years. I have mostly not said it from the pulpit.

The people Jesus spent the most time with — the tax collectors, the prostitutes, the lepers, the demoniacs, the Samaritan woman at the well, the man in the tombs among the Gerasenes who cut himself with stones — were not the kind of people who showed up at synagogue. They were excluded from the formal religious community. Some of them were legally impure and could not enter. Some of them were socially marked in ways that made their presence unwelcome. And Jesus went to them. He did not wait for them to figure out how to cross the threshold into the respectable gathering. He crossed the threshold into their world.

This is not a minor strategic difference. It is a theological one. The God who became flesh in a feeding trough in an occupied province, who was born to refugees who fled across a border into Egypt, who grew up in Galilee of the Gentiles — this God did not arrive through official channels. He arrived among the people the official channels had already abandoned.

The church has built many programs to reach vulnerable people. Food banks, clothes closets, holiday toy drives, addiction recovery groups — these are genuine goods, and I am not dismissing them. But they are structured around an assumption: the vulnerable need to come to where the church is. They need to make the journey to our building, to enter our space, to participate on our terms.
