The model is attractional, even when the programs are labeled outreach.

> Jesus did not operate on an attractional model.

Jesus did not operate on an attractional model. The Sermon on the Mount was delivered to a crowd that had followed him into a field because there was something in him that drew people who had nothing else to try. His ministry was characterized by going — into the synagogues, yes, but also into the countryside, into the cemetery, into the home of a tax collector, into the social space of a Samaritan village where no self-respecting rabbi would have stopped. He went where the need was, and the need was not primarily inside the religious gathering.

## The Architecture of Absence

Why are the most vulnerable people in your city not in your pews? Several reasons, and most of them are design choices.

The building is inaccessible — architecturally, socially, culturally. The gathered congregation is, in most cases, economically and culturally homogeneous in ways that signal to the poor and marginalized that this is not a room built for them. The service is structured around the assumptions and capacities of middle-class participants. The social rituals of hospitality — the coffee hour, the greeting, the small talk — require a kind of social fluency that people in genuine crisis do not have at nine on a Sunday morning.

> These are design choices. Every design choice is a theological statement about who the church is for.

These are design choices. Every design choice is a theological statement about who the church is for.

When Nehemiah surveyed the broken walls of Jerusalem in the fifth century B.C., he began not with a capital campaign but with a census — a careful accounting of who was in the city and who was absent (Nehemiah 7). The gaps in the wall corresponded to the gaps in the community. You could read the social fractures of the city in the architecture of its neglected defenses. Every church building tells the same story. Where are the gaps? Who is missing, and why? That question is not administrative. It is prophetic.

The prison population in the United States exceeds two million people [cite — confirm]. The vast majority of those two million have families, most of them poor, living in the communities around your church. They are one of the largest unreached populations in the country, and they are geographically proximate to every congregation in America. Most churches have no sustained engagement with them — not because the need is invisible, but because meeting the need requires going somewhere that makes middle-class Christians uncomfortable. It requires walking through a metal detector, sitting in a room with people who did things we would rather not think about, and offering the gospel in a context where it cannot be packaged with comfortable programming.

The same is true of the shelter network, the addiction recovery houses, the transitional living facilities for people exiting incarceration, the apartment complexes where the working poor live three families to a unit. These are not distant mission fields. They are within walking distance of most American churches. The distance is not geographical. It is social. And social distance can be crossed.

## The Shape of Jesus's Ministry

Luke's Gospel is the one that preserves most clearly the pattern of Jesus's ministry in relation to the excluded. In Luke 4:18, quoting Isaiah 61, Jesus describes his mission: good news to the poor, release to the captives, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed. These are not metaphorical categories. They are social descriptions of people at the bottom of every hierarchy in the ancient world.

Luke 7:34 records that Jesus's enemies accused him of being "a friend of tax collectors and sinners." This was not a compliment. Tax collectors were collaborators with Roman occupation, people who had bought the right to extract money from their own neighbors and were despised accordingly. "Sinners" was a broad category that included people in occupations considered ritually polluting — tanners, who worked with dead animals; shepherds, whose work made Sabbath observance nearly impossible; women whose sexual history placed them outside the boundaries of respectable community. Jesus ate with these people. In the ancient world, table fellowship was an act of social identification. To eat with someone was to say: I am willing to be associated with you in public. Jesus made that statement repeatedly, and the religious establishment found it scandalous.

We should find our own version of it equally scandalous. Not the fact of association, but its absence.

Luke 14 describes a dinner where the host, after the invited guests make excuses, sends his servant to bring in "the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame" from the streets and alleys (Luke 14:21). When there is still room, he sends the servant out again to the roads and country lanes to compel people to come in, "so that my house will be full." This is not a church growth strategy. It is a description of what the kingdom feast looks like — and it requires the host to go where the guests are, rather than waiting for the guests to arrive.

## The Counter-Argument

The honest objection deserves to be named. A congregation that sets out to serve the most vulnerable will face real challenges: safety concerns, resource constraints, the difficulty of building a sustainable community across vast social distances, the risk of creating a congregation that is a social services provider rather than a worshiping body. Some of these concerns are legitimate.

But they tend to be invoked selectively. The same congregations that cite safety concerns when asked about engaging the homeless are, in many cases, running elaborate and expensive ministries that serve people who are already comfortable. The safety concern is real; the question is whether it is being applied consistently or whether it functions as a socially acceptable way of protecting the congregation's demographic homogeneity.

The deeper concern — that engagement with the most vulnerable will distort the church's primary calling to worship and formation — is also worth addressing honestly. The church is not a social service agency. Its primary gathering is for worship, proclamation, and the formation of people in the gospel. But the gospel being proclaimed shapes who shows up to hear it. A gospel that announces good news to the poor will draw the poor. A gospel that doesn't mention them will draw people who are comfortable without it.

The New Testament church in Acts 2 is remarkable not primarily because of the spectacular events of Pentecost but because of what followed: a community that shared possessions, sold property, and distributed to anyone in need (Acts 2:44–45). The early church was multiclass in composition and radically redistributive in practice. Not because redistribution was the point. Because when the poor and the wealthy heard the same gospel and gathered at the same table, the practical logic of their belonging required it.

## What It Would Require

> I am not arguing for a program. I am arguing for a posture.

Going to the most vulnerable in your city — not merely offering programs for them to come to — requires sustained commitment of the kind that doesn't produce visible metrics on Sunday morning. It requires volunteers who will show up at the shelter on Tuesday. It requires pastoral staff whose job descriptions include the county jail. It requires a budget allocation that reflects the belief that the people outside the building matter as much as the people inside it.

It requires the courage to let the congregation's identity be shaped by its engagement with the excluded rather than by its reputation in the suburbs.

The early Methodists in eighteenth-century England went into the coal mines and the mills and the slums of industrializing Britain precisely because John Wesley understood that the people who most needed the gospel were not the people who had the leisure and the social confidence to enter a church building [cite — confirm]. He took the gospel to the spaces where the poor already were — and the result was a revival that transformed not just individual lives but the social fabric of a nation.

I am not arguing for a program. I am arguing for a posture. The posture that asks, on Sunday morning: who is not here? Why are they not here? What would it cost us to go to them? And then, having asked, to be willing to hear an answer that requires something.

The most vulnerable people in your city are on the streets and in the shelters and in the county jail and in the apartments where the heat has been cut off. The church that takes Luke 14 seriously knows where to find them.

The question is whether it will go.

That question does not resolve easily. It sits there every Sunday morning, in the gap between who is present and who is not, waiting for someone to take it seriously enough to act.

The man pushing the cart along the highway median at noon on a Wednesday is not going to find you. He does not have a car. He may not have a phone. He has learned, through the repeated experience of being handled and dismissed, to distrust the kind of institution that has a nice sign out front. He is not outside the church because he is indifferent to God. He is outside because the church he encountered treated him as a problem to be managed rather than a person to be known.

This is not a theory. It is the church's institutional history, and it is still operating today.

The most vulnerable people in your city — the homeless, the working poor, the undocumented, the recently incarcerated, the woman in the apartment above the nail salon who is one lost shift away from not making rent — are not in your pews. Not accidentally. The church's architecture, its culture, its economic assumptions, its programming calendar, its location in the neighborhood it chose when it could afford to choose — all of these are signals, and the vulnerable read them accurately. *This is not for you.* They don't always say it that way. They say it by not coming.

This is a theological problem before it is a pastoral problem.

## The Hearing That Precedes the Covenant

The biblical witness about who God's concern runs toward is not ambiguous. It is among the most consistent data sets in the entire canon. In the Exodus narrative — the event that defines Israel's theological identity — God hears the cry of slaves before they have a theology, before they have a temple, before they have anything to offer except their suffering (Exodus 3:7). The hearing precedes the covenant. God is present to the oppressed not because they have earned presence but because oppression itself is an offense against the God who made them. The entire Sinai law code is structured around this: the widow, the orphan, the stranger appear not as charitable recipients but as the test of the community's faithfulness. *You shall not oppress a stranger; you know the heart of a stranger, for you were strangers in Egypt* (Exodus 23:9). The remembering is commanded because it shapes behavior. The community that forgets what it was rescued from will re-enact the oppression it was rescued from. Israel proved this several times. The church has proved it too.

> The community that forgets what it was rescued from will re-enact the oppression it was rescued from.

The prophets named the failure with a precision that should unsettle every congregation that has built its programming around the comfortable. Amos directed his indictment not at pagan nations but at the covenant community — the people who brought their tithes, attended their festivals, sang their songs, and kept their religion entirely separate from the economic arrangements that crushed the poor at the gate (Amos 5:21-24). The prophetic critique is not that Israel was irreligious. It was that Israel was religious in ways that cost nothing, that made no contact with the social arrangements the religion was supposed to transform. God had given them a law that was, by ancient Near Eastern standards, a radical redistribution mechanism — gleaning laws, Jubilee, remission of debts, no interest charged to the poor. And they had made the religion work without any of it.

The American church stands in that line. Not because it is evil. Because it is comfortable, and comfort has its own institutional momentum.

## The Institutional Momentum of Comfort

Here is what comfort produces, ecclesially: congregations whose members are economically similar, whose programming serves the already-churched, whose evangelistic imagination runs toward the unchurched who look a great deal like the churched. The working poor are not hostile to God. Research consistently shows that religious practice is more common in low-income communities than in affluent ones [cite — confirm]. What the working poor are hostile to is the particular form of church that signals, in a hundred quiet ways, that they will need to dress differently, speak differently, and assume a kind of economic stability they do not have before they fully belong. The church's insularity is not an absence of evangelism. It is evangelism directed toward people who already share the church's cultural assumptions.

This is where the counter-argument has real weight. Some churches have, with genuine integrity, planted themselves in the hardest neighborhoods, adjusted their entire economic model to serve communities without resources, and paid the institutional cost of that commitment. There are pastors in cities across this country who have spent twenty years in the same block of a neighborhood that was never going to give them the growth metrics that would make them visible in the evangelical world. They are not famous. They are not platforms. They are doing what Jeremiah told the exiles to do: seeking the welfare of the city they were sent to, not the city they wished they inhabited (Jeremiah 29:7). Their witness is real and it is costly and I am not dismissing it.

But they are not the majority of the church's institutional weight. The majority of American church resources — buildings, budgets, staff, attention — is concentrated in a band of the population that is not the most vulnerable. That is not an accusation. It is an observation with theological implications.

What does it require, practically, to reorient toward the people who are not in the pews?

## The Movement of the Kingdom Is Toward

First, it requires going to them rather than waiting for them to come. The mission does not originate with the church's doors. Jesus did not wait in Capernaum for the sick to find him. He moved through the towns. He was in the places that the religious infrastructure had written off — the tax collector's house, the Samaritan well, the graveyard where the demoniac had been chained (Mark 5). The pattern is consistent enough to be a theological statement: the movement of the kingdom is toward the excluded, not from them toward the center. The church that is always waiting for the excluded to find the door has reversed the direction of the movement it claims to be part of.

Second, it requires listening before programming. The church's first instinct, confronted with a community's need, is to design a ministry to address it. The ministry becomes the church's project, organized around the church's assumptions about the need, run by the church's volunteers, measured by the church's metrics. This is how food pantries become the church's act of benevolence toward the poor rather than a relationship between neighbors. It is how after-school programs become evangelistic pipelines rather than genuine investments in children. The vulnerable people outside the pews do not need more programs. They need the church to know their names, to understand the actual conditions of their lives, and to let that knowledge change the church rather than simply adding a service line to the church's portfolio.

> The vulnerable people outside the pews do not need more programs.

Third, it requires institutional honesty about why the vulnerable are not there. Not guilt — guilt that does not lead to changed behavior is just a feeling the comfortable church uses to feel less comfortable without actually becoming different. Honesty. Why is the parking lot arranged the way it is? Why is the dress culture what it is? Why are the small group times set when they are? Why is the financial ask structured the way it is? These are not trivial questions. They are the questions that reveal whether the institution has been shaped by the people it claims to serve or by the people it has been most successful at retaining.

## The Table That Fills With the Excluded

Luke 14 contains a parable that should be read at every building committee meeting and every programming retreat. The great banquet from which the invited guests excuse themselves, and the host who sends his servants into the streets and alleys to bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, the lame (Luke 14:21). The table gets full. It gets full with exactly the people who had been excluded from the original invitation list. The parable is not primarily about eschatology, though it has eschatological dimensions. It is about who belongs at the table and what happens when the original invitation is declined. The church that is waiting for the comfortable to accept its invitation may be missing the entire point of the table.

The most vulnerable people in your city are not indifferent to the Gospel. They are indifferent to the church's current form, and they have reasons. They have been told, in ways more persuasive than any sermon, that what the church offers is not for them. Changing that requires more than a targeted program. It requires the church to examine what it has become — for whom it has been shaped, whose presence it has optimized its existence around — and to ask whether that is the church Jesus described or a comfortable institution that has learned to use Jesus's language.

That examination is not pleasant. It implicates me. The churches I have led have been more accessible to the comfortable than to the vulnerable, in ways I was not always aware of and in ways I was sometimes aware of and chose not to address because addressing it would have cost something I was not ready to spend.

## Whether We Will Find Them

The question is not whether the vulnerable should find us. They are not required to find us. The question is whether we will find them — as the shepherd found the sheep, as the woman found the coin, as the father ran toward the son who was still a long way off (Luke 15). The running is always toward. That is the theological direction. The church that has reversed it and is sitting still, waiting for the excluded to close the distance, may be waiting for something that the Gospel does not promise will happen.

> The running is always toward.

Go. Know names. Be changed by what you find. That is not a program. It is a posture. And it is the posture the most vulnerable people in your city have not yet seen from most of the churches in it.

Water appears on the first page of the Bible. Before the earth had form, before light, before any living thing — the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters (Genesis 1:2). Water is architecturally present at the beginning of creation and architecturally present at the end: the river of the water of life, flowing from the throne of God through the new Jerusalem (Revelation 22:1–2). Between those two appearances, water carries more theological weight than almost any other material substance in the canon. The parting of the Red Sea. The wilderness thirst. The rock that Moses struck. The Jordan crossing. Jesus's baptism, his conversation with the woman at the well, the water and blood from his side at the cross, the command to baptize in the name of the Father and Son and Spirit.

Water in Scripture is never merely water. It is the medium of deliverance. It is the sign of covenant. It is the substance through which God names his people and the substance through which God's enemies drown. It is what the psalmist cries out for in Psalm 42:1 — *as the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul pants for you, my God* — which means that the desire for actual water and the desire for God are allowed to rhyme in the same sentence, the physical thirst a window onto the spiritual one.

This is why the current global water crisis is a theological issue and not merely a logistical or environmental one.

## Why Water Is Never Merely Water

More than two billion people lack access to safe drinking water [cite — confirm]. In some regions, women and children walk hours each day to reach water sources that are contaminated. People die of waterborne disease at rates that the wealthy world long since ceased to regard as imaginable. The communities most affected by water insecurity are, with remarkable consistency, the poor, the colonized, the politically marginalized — the same communities that appear in Scripture as the specific objects of God's concern.

The church has largely received this reality as a humanitarian concern — something for NGOs and mission agencies, the province of people with technical expertise. That framing is not wrong. Technical expertise matters. Clean water requires engineering. But the theological framing matters too, and its absence explains why the church has engaged this issue with such inconsistency.

## Who Controls the Water Controls the Life

The biblical account of water is inseparable from the biblical account of power. Who controls the water controls the life that depends on it. Pharaoh's Egypt sat astride the Nile — the great agricultural engine that made empire possible. The Exodus is partly a story about what happens when the God who made water in the beginning refuses to let his image-bearers remain enslaved to those who control it. Moses is not striking a rock for theological reasons only. He is demonstrating that the God of Israel can provide in the wilderness what Egypt provided in the valley — that the empire does not control the conditions of life, that the Source lies elsewhere.

The Samaritan woman at the well in John 4 is standing at a water source that is itself entangled in the long history of ethnic and religious division in that region. Jesus asks for a drink from a woman he was culturally forbidden to address, at a well that marked a contested heritage. His conversation with her — the offer of living water, the honest engagement with her actual situation, the revelation that he is the Messiah — takes place at the intersection of water, power, and exclusion. It is not an accident. The gospel enters through the door that material conditions open.

The Flint water crisis — in which the city of Flint, Michigan changed its water source in 2014 and exposed tens of thousands of residents, predominantly Black and low-income, to lead contamination — put the theological stakes in immediate terms [cite — confirm]. An American city, within reasonable driving distance of where I preach, watched its children's futures get altered by a failure of governance that followed the exact lines of race and poverty that run through every other form of injustice in this country. The people who were poisoned were not poisoned by accident. They were poisoned because their suffering was treated as less costly than the alternatives.

## Flint and the Lines of Race and Poverty

> Charity tends the wound. Justice asks who inflicted it.

The church's response was mostly charity — bottled water collections, donation drives. Not nothing. But charity does not name the structural reality. Charity does not ask who made the decision and why they made it and whether the same decision would have been made in a different zip code. Charity tends the wound. Justice asks who inflicted it.

Jeremiah 2:13 records God's indictment of Israel: *My people have committed two sins: They have forsaken me, the spring of living water, and have dug their own cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water.* The image is not only spiritual. It is economic and political. Israel's pursuit of alliances with Egypt and Assyria — the great water-powers of the ancient Near East — over against trust in the God who provides, is being named here as both theological betrayal and political foolishness. The broken cisterns are human-made systems of security that fail precisely because they locate provision in the wrong place.

Contemporary water privatization is worth naming here, because it raises exactly the question Jeremiah was raising. When water systems are transferred from public to private control, the logic of profit replaces the logic of provision. Communities that cannot pay market rates for water lose access. This is not a neutral technical arrangement. It is a theological one: it locates control of a basic condition of human survival in the hands of those who will profit from it. The church that has nothing to say about this arrangement is Jeremiah's audience — sitting comfortably beside the broken cisterns, having forgotten who made the water in the beginning.

## The Broken Cisterns of Privatized Provision

The steel-man for the other side deserves honest engagement. The argument runs: water systems require massive infrastructure investment, and private capital can accomplish what public institutions often cannot. Market mechanisms, the argument continues, actually allocate scarce resources more efficiently than government administration. This is not entirely false. There are water systems in the Global South that have improved under private management [cite — confirm]. Technical solutions to water problems are not inherently unjust.

But the theological question is not only about efficiency. It is about what happens at the bottom of the market — to the people who cannot pay, to the communities whose political marginalization means they receive last attention and worst quality. The efficiency argument cannot answer that question, because efficiency optimizes for different goals than justice does. Justice is not efficient. Justice is obligatory. And the test of any water system, on biblical terms, is not whether it runs well for the people who can afford it. It is whether it serves the widow, the orphan, the stranger — the ones Leviticus 19 and Deuteronomy 24 and Zechariah 7:10 and the entire prophetic tradition name as the measure of the community's faithfulness.

Isaiah 55:1 is an invitation that begins with water: *Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you who have no money, come, buy and eat!* The eschatological vision is of provision without price — not because provision is free, but because the provision comes from the One who does not require payment for what he made. That vision stands in judgment on every arrangement in which water is controlled by those who charge more than the poor can pay.

I am not arguing for a particular policy framework. I am not equipped to design water infrastructure. But I am arguing that the church cannot receive global water insecurity as merely a technical problem to be solved by technicians. The same Lord who hovered over the waters at creation, who parted the sea for the enslaved, who struck the rock in the wilderness, who offered living water to the woman at the well, who turned water into wine and walked on water and rose from a tomb that could not hold him — that Lord has something to say about who gets clean water and who dies from the lack of it.

> The church's voice is not the engineer's voice.

The church's voice is not the engineer's voice. But the church's voice is the one that refuses to let the question of water become purely technical. The one that says: these are image-bearers dying of thirst. The one that asks which political and economic arrangements are producing this death. The one that names injustice even when the injustice is distributed so widely and operates so quietly that naming it feels like aggression against the beneficiaries.

## The Water That Connects

Every Sunday I pour water into a baptismal. The act is theological — death and resurrection, the old washed away, the new given. I have done it for men and women who will walk out of the church into a world where, depending on where they live and what they earn, that water either flows freely or is a daily negotiation with scarcity.

The water connects. The theology and the material reality are not separate domains. The God who is the spring of living water has an interest in how his image-bearers access the water he made. The church that says otherwise has separated the gospel from the world the gospel enters.

> That is not an accident the church can afford to miss.

Water is the first substance named in the Bible. It is the last gift in the vision of the restored city. Between those two moments, billions of people are thirsty. That is not an accident the church can afford to miss.

You know things about your congregation that nobody else knows. You know whose marriage is barely hanging on while they hold hands in the third row. You know who is in recovery and who has relapsed. You know which respected family is coming apart behind the door, which volunteer is drowning in debt, which pillar of the church confessed something on a Tuesday that you will carry to your grave. You are the keeper of a city's worth of secrets, and you can tell no one. That is the job. It is also a wound almost no one names.

## The Weight of What Accumulates

The weight of confidential knowledge is one of the least-discussed burdens of pastoral ministry, and one of the heaviest. It is not the weight of any single secret. It is the accumulation — years of them, layered, each one trustworthy and unspeakable, until the pastor is walking around as the local archive of everyone's worst hour.

He smiles at the potluck knowing what three of the families there are actually enduring. He preaches hope on Sunday morning while holding the private knowledge of how much quiet despair is sitting in the chairs. He congratulates the couple on their anniversary knowing what the marriage has cost. He cannot unburden it to his friends because they are also his congregants. He often cannot fully unburden it to his spouse because it is not his to tell. So it stays in, and it compounds.

This is real, and it is not a complaint against the calling. The confidence is sacred. The ability to hold it is part of what makes a pastor safe to confess to. The privilege of being trusted with people's true lives is one of the genuine gifts of the work. But a gift can also be a load, and pretending the load is weightless is how pastors end up carrying it alone until it bends them.

## What It Does to You Over Time

The pastoral literature almost never addresses this directly, and the silence has costs. The accumulation of unspeakable knowledge does something to a person over time. The direction it takes depends partly on character and partly on whether the pastor has found any way to process the weight.

One direction is cynicism. The secret knowledge curdling into a low view of the people you are also called to love. The pastor who has heard too many confessions without any outlet for the weight of hearing them can arrive at a place where his pastoral knowledge feels like disillusionment — where the gap between the congregation's public presentation and their private reality has become, in his experience, simply the evidence of universal hypocrisy. That pastoral knowledge, meant to deepen compassion, has produced contempt instead. This is a spiritual emergency, and it often presents as weariness or world-weariness, something much quieter than contempt, something that is easy to mistake for wisdom.

The other direction is numbness. The dissociation between what is known and what can be said creates a kind of internal pressure that the only defense a tired soul can manage is to stop feeling it. The pastor becomes the person who goes through the pastoral motions — sits with the grieving, prays with the sick, counsels the troubled — without the interior engagement that makes those motions genuine. He is present in body and absent in soul. He has stopped metabolizing the suffering he encounters because the cost of metabolizing it, without any outlet, has become too high.

> I have felt both of these.

I have felt both of these. I have felt the cynicism of knowing too much about people I was supposed to love, and the numbness of learning to hold what I knew at a distance so that it would not destroy me. Neither is the man I want to be in the pulpit. Neither is the man the congregation deserves.

## The Priestly Image That Changes the Frame

There is an image in Exodus 28 that I have returned to more than once when the weight has been heavy. The high priest of Israel wore the names of the twelve tribes on his breastplate when he entered the presence of God — "Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel on the breastplate of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place, to bring them to regular remembrance before the Lord" (Exodus 28:29). The priest carried the people with him into the presence of God. He was not the terminus of what he carried. He was the bearer. His job was to take what he held and bring it before the One who could actually do something with it.

The pastor is not finally the one who holds the congregation's sins and sorrows. He is the one who carries them to the one who can. That reframing does not make the weight lighter immediately. But it changes the nature of what the weight is. The secrets are not yours to solve, to fix, to contain, to manage. They are yours to carry into the presence of God and release there.

A great deal of pastoral exhaustion is the result of forgetting this — of becoming the container rather than the conduit, holding what was always meant to be passed up. The priest who tried to carry the names of the tribes without bringing them before God would eventually be destroyed by the load. That is not the design. The design is bearing and releasing, bearing and releasing, not bearing and accumulating.

> The secrets are not yours to solve, to fix, to contain, to manage.

## What Stewardship of the Secrets Looks Like

First: you need at least one outlet that does not violate the trust. A confessor of your own — a spiritual director, a counselor bound by their own confidentiality, a peer pastor in another city with no overlap to your congregation — where you can lay down the weight of carrying without betraying the content. You do not need to name names to say: I am holding more sorrow than I can metabolize alone, and it is affecting how I preach, how I love my family, how I show up in the pastoral relationships I am supposed to be present in. That sentence, spoken to the right person, is not gossip. It is survival, and it is permitted.

The reason most pastors do not make this arrangement is not that they have calculated it and found it unnecessary. It is that making the arrangement requires admitting that the weight is affecting them, and that admission feels like weakness, and the pastoral role has made weakness feel like failure. It is not failure. It is the honest acknowledgment of what carrying what you carry costs, and that acknowledgment is the beginning of being able to carry it without it destroying you.

Second: take the secrets to God deliberately and regularly, as their actual keeper. Not in the vague sense of "I have mentioned this in prayer." In the deliberate, named sense of the high priest carrying the names of the tribes: Lord, I am holding what belongs to you. I am bearing it as a conduit, not as a container. Take it. Let it rest with you rather than with me. I am a bearer, not a vault.

This practice is not mystical avoidance of the weight. It is the theological grounding that makes the weight bearable — the regular return to the conviction that the congregation does not finally belong to you, that what they have entrusted to you was always his to hold, and that your pastoral faithfulness is the act of bringing what you carry before him, not the act of carrying it until your back breaks.

Third: let the weight make you tender rather than hard. The knowledge of how much people are suffering behind their composure is a terrible gift. But it is a gift. It can keep you from ever again preaching to your congregation as though their lives were simple, as though the choices were obvious, as though the people in the chairs were the performance they present on Sunday morning. You know they are not. You know whose Sunday morning smile is costing them something they cannot name. Let that knowledge soften the sermon rather than sour the soul.

## What You Are Carrying It For

> You carry what others cannot see.

There is a reason the calling carries this weight. It is not accidental, and it is not merely the cost of doing business. The pastor who knows what his congregation actually endures — who has been trusted with the real, unedited version of his people's lives — is the pastor who can preach to them as though they are real, not as though they are the version they present. He can look out at the room and speak to what is actually there, because what is actually there is not hidden from him.

That specificity of pastoral knowledge is, when it is rightly held, one of the greatest pastoral gifts there is. The congregation does not know that the pastor knows. They experience it as something else — as a preacher who somehow seems to understand what their actual life feels like, a pastor who does not talk over their heads at an imaginary congregation but speaks into the room where they actually live.

You carry what others cannot see. That is the calling, and it is heavier than the people in the chairs will ever know. Do not carry it as though you were its final resting place. Bear it. Bring it. Release it. Hand it up. It was always his to hold.

That is the priestly work. And it begins not with what you can say, but with what you carry before God in the silence.

James 5 begins with a warning, and it is not addressed to the poor. *Now listen, you rich people, weep and wail because of the misery that is coming on you* (James 5:1). The letter does not ease into this. It arrives at full force in the first sentence of the chapter, and what follows is not a balanced treatment of wealth's complications or a careful exploration of money's mixed effects on the spiritual life. It is a sustained, specific, theologically grounded condemnation of the wealthy who have built their comfort on the exploitation of workers. It is among the most economically direct passages in the New Testament, and the American church has spent considerable energy not reading it.

The most common homiletical approach to James 5 is to treat it as a warning about the spiritual dangers of wealth in general — the idolatry of money, the false security of accumulated assets, the spiritual blindness that prosperity can produce. These things are real, and James addresses them. But the text does not stay at the level of spiritual danger. It names a specific crime: *The wages you failed to pay the workers who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty* (James 5:4). This is not a metaphor for spiritual displacement from God. It is a description of an economic practice — withholding wages — that God identifies as a sin requiring urgent response.

## The Specific Crime the Text Names

The practice James condemns was familiar in the first-century economy in which he wrote. Day laborers — workers without permanent employment or institutional protection — were paid at the end of each day. This arrangement is encoded in Deuteronomy 24:14–15, which commands: *Pay them their wages each day before sunset, because they are poor and are counting on it.* The daily wage was, for most of these workers, the margin between eating and not eating. To hold it back was not simply to delay a financial transaction. It was to use the power differential between employer and worker — the employer's ability to wait, the worker's inability to — as an instrument of further extraction. The employer who withheld wages was not only keeping money that belonged to the worker. He was forcing the worker's desperation to compound daily, increasing his own power while decreasing the worker's capacity to resist.

James writes this into a context of significant economic stratification in the early church. The letter is addressed to dispersed Jewish Christian communities in which class differences were real, visible, and apparently tolerated in the community's practice in ways James finds intolerable. James 2 addresses the same structural problem from the side of worship: the wealthy visitor gets the good seat, the poor man stands by the wall, and the community that has arranged its liturgical space around the power hierarchy of the surrounding culture has denied the faith in the very act of assembling (James 2:1–4). James 5 addresses the same problem from the side of economic life: the wealthy who have accumulated their resources by exploiting workers, and who presumably sit in those good seats, have their wages crying out against them before the Lord Almighty.

The ears of the Lord Almighty. This is not a small claim. The Hebrew behind the title — *Yahweh Sabaoth*, Lord of Hosts — is the title used when God acts in history to right what has been wronged, to intervene against the powers that have arrayed themselves against the vulnerable. When the prophets invoke *Yahweh Sabaoth*, something is about to happen. James is invoking it here in the context of unpaid wages. The God who hears the cry of the oppressed (Exodus 3:7) hears the cries of the harvesters. The theological claim is that wage theft is not a private economic matter between employer and employee. It is a matter that rises before the God who governs history.

## The Ears of the Lord Almighty

The application to the American economy in 2026 is direct, and the church's silence on it is conspicuous.

Wage theft — the failure to pay workers what they have legally and contractually earned — is among the most pervasive economic crimes in the United States. The Economic Policy Institute has documented that minimum wage violations alone cost workers billions of dollars annually [cite — confirm]. When overtime violations, tip theft, illegal deductions, and off-the-clock work requirements are included, the scale dwarfs all property crimes combined [cite — confirm]. The workers most affected are the ones who least have the power to challenge the arrangement: undocumented workers who fear immigration enforcement, workers in industries where retaliation is common, workers who do not know their legal rights, workers whose economic desperation mirrors exactly the first-century day laborers James was addressing.

> It is also, on the plain reading of James 5, a theological emergency.

The church has largely treated wage theft as an economic policy debate. It is that. It is also, on the plain reading of James 5, a theological emergency.

The text expands beyond wages in the verses that follow. *You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened yourselves in the day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the innocent one, who was not opposing you* (James 5:5–6). James moves from the specific economic crime to the broader condition it reveals: a life organized around the extraction of comfort at the expense of others, ending in a judgment so severe he describes it in terms of slaughter. The luxury and self-indulgence are not condemned merely as spiritual risks to the wealthy person. They are condemned as the fruit of the worker's unpaid wages — the direct causal connection between what the employer has and what the worker has not.

## The Move the Church Refuses to Make

This is the move the church consistently refuses to make. It will address wealth as a spiritual condition — the idol that competes with God for the heart, the anxiety that excessive accumulation produces, the generosity that God's people are called to practice. These are real and worth addressing. But James is addressing something structurally prior: the wealth that was built by taking what belongs to the worker. The luxury that rests on the foundation of the withheld wage. The generosity question cannot be asked without first asking how the wealth was accumulated. James asks it. The church has preferred not to.

The counter-position that must be engaged is the argument that James 5 addresses first-century economic conditions that are qualitatively different from contemporary capitalist markets, and that applying it directly to modern employment relationships requires a contextual leap that the text does not authorize. Contemporary labor law provides protections James's workers lacked; the state regulates wages in ways the Roman Empire did not; the employer-employee relationship is framed by contract and regulated by enforcement mechanisms that the day laborer had no access to.

## When the Mechanism Changes but the Structure Does Not

This argument has some force. The specific mechanism James addresses — the daily withholding of cash wages from agricultural day laborers — is not the most common contemporary form of wage theft. The forms are more varied: misclassification of employees as independent contractors to avoid wage obligations, algorithmic scheduling that produces fewer hours than workers were promised, mandatory off-the-clock training, tip pooling arrangements that redirect gratuities to management [cite — confirm]. The technical forms have changed.

> The theological structure has not.

The theological structure has not. The wealthy using the power differential between themselves and workers to extract additional value from those who cannot easily resist it — this is exactly what James condemns. The sophistication of the mechanism does not change the theological character of the act. The wages crying out before the Lord Almighty are crying out in 2026 as surely as they were crying out in the first century. The ears that hear have not changed.

James does not offer policy prescriptions. He does not tell the early church what labor laws to advocate for, what enforcement mechanisms to demand, how to organize workers for collective bargaining. He speaks the prophetic word: this is what you are doing, this is what it costs those you are doing it to, these are the ears into which their cry has risen, this is what is coming. The prophetic function is to name reality in light of God's character and God's commitments. What the community then does with that naming — how it translates the prophetic word into pastoral practice, congregational accountability, civic engagement — is the community's ongoing work.

But the prophetic word must first be spoken. The congregation that has never heard James 5 applied to the actual conditions of its economic life has not been fully formed by the canon it claims to hold. The pastor who has found a way to preach about spiritual attitudes toward money without addressing the workers whose wages are crying out has chosen a narrower gospel than the letter offers.

## The Prophetic Word Lands on the Preacher First

I am in this. The congregation I serve includes people who own businesses. It includes people who have benefited from economic arrangements they did not design and perhaps did not question. It includes me — a man who pays the staff of a church and has not always asked hard enough questions about whether what I am offering is adequate. The prophetic word lands on the preacher first. James is not addressing someone else's congregation.

*The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty.* The church's response to those cries should be something more than silence. It should be something more than teaching wealthy congregants to manage their anxiety about money. It should be, at minimum, the willingness to read James 5 where it actually goes, to name what it names, and to let the congregation sit with the implication that the God who hears the workers has an opinion about how his people treat them.

> That is not politics. That is Scripture.

That is not politics. That is Scripture. The difference matters, and the church that cannot make the distinction has not protected itself from political capture. It has ensured it.

The Jubilee was God's economic reset button — a radical vision of economic justice built into the law of Israel. Every fifty years, debts were forgiven, slaves were freed, and land was returned to its original owners. It was a theological statement about the limits of accumulation and the priority of liberation.

Leviticus 25 is the kind of text that gets skipped in Bible reading plans. It is detailed, it is agricultural, and on the surface it seems to address a land tenure system so foreign to our own that application appears impossible. So we move on. And in moving on, we miss one of the most radical economic visions in the entire canon of Scripture.

## The Structure of the Thing

The Jubilee arrived every fiftieth year, following seven cycles of seven sabbath years. In that year, land that had been sold reverted to its original family. Debts were cancelled. Israelites who had sold themselves into indentured labor to pay their debts were freed and allowed to return home. The trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement — the day of national cleansing — and the fiftieth year began with restoration as its governing logic.

The institution was not isolated. It was embedded in a broader structure. The sabbath year, occurring every seventh year, already built debt release and land rest into the economic calendar (Deuteronomy 15:1-11). The gleaning laws required landowners to leave the edges of the field unharvested for the poor (Leviticus 19:9-10). The prohibition on charging interest to a fellow Israelite was absolute (Leviticus 25:36-37). The Jubilee was the apex of this structure — the once-per-generation reset that prevented the gradual, generational accumulation of wealth in fewer and fewer hands from becoming permanent.

The theological rationale is stated explicitly in Leviticus 25:23: "The land must not be sold permanently, because the land is mine and you reside in my land as foreigners and strangers." The Jubilee rests on a claim about ownership. The land belongs to God. Not to Israel in the national sense. Not to individual Israelites in the proprietary sense. To God, whose tenants Israel was.

This means that what we call property rights — the permanent, transferable, absolute ownership of land — did not exist in the same form within the Israelite covenant. What existed was stewardship: the use of land entrusted to you for a season, under conditions established by the owner, to be returned when the time came. The Jubilee was not charity. It was not the wealthy being generous. It was the owner enforcing the terms of the tenancy.

> The Jubilee was not charity.

## What the Jubilee Was Not

It is worth clearing the ground of two misreadings that have made this text easier to dismiss.

The first misreading is that the Jubilee was a utopian fantasy that was never intended to be practiced. There is a version of this argument that notes the absence of clear historical evidence for Jubilee observance in Israel and concludes that the institution was always more aspirational than actual — a prophetic ideal rather than a legal requirement. Scholars debate the question of whether the Jubilee was ever consistently practiced [cite — confirm scholarly debate; views vary significantly]. What is not in question is that God commanded it, that it appears in the same legal code as the prohibitions against murder and theft, and that the prophets' denunciations of debt slavery and land accumulation read precisely as indictments of a community that was not observing it. The absence of consistent practice does not reduce the institution's authority. It is evidence of the same disobedience the prophets were naming.

The second misreading is the fully spiritualized one — that the Jubilee was always primarily a metaphor for spiritual liberation, and that its material and economic content was always meant to dissolve into the language of freedom from sin. This reading has the advantage of making the text comfortable, which is usually a sign that something has gone wrong. The Jubilee in Leviticus 25 involves real fields. Real families. Real liberation from real debt. These are not illustrations of a spiritual principle. They are the content. The spiritual and the material are not competing levels of meaning in this text. They are unified.

## Jesus and the Jubilee

Luke 4 makes the connection between the Jubilee and Jesus' ministry explicit. Jesus reads from the Isaiah scroll in the Nazareth synagogue: "The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim freedom for the prisoners and recovery of sight for the blind, to set the oppressed free, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor" (Luke 4:18-19, quoting Isaiah 61:1-2). He then closes the scroll and says: "Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing" (Luke 4:21).

The phrase translated "the year of the Lord's favor" is a direct reference to the Jubilee. The Greek of Luke follows the Greek translation of Isaiah, which was in turn rendering the Hebrew *yôbēl* — the Jubilee year, the year of liberation [cite — confirm the Greek term and LXX translation]. Jesus announces his ministry in Jubilee language. Liberation of the captive. Restoration of sight. Freedom for the oppressed. The year of the Lord's favor.

> The Jubilee is not merely Old Testament background to the Gospel.

This announcement was not primarily metaphorical. The congregation at Nazareth would have heard Jubilee language as economic language, because for them it was. And the immediate response to Jesus' sermon in Luke 4 is rage — the congregation drives him out of town (Luke 4:28-29). Whatever Jesus said next, after the promising opening, was not received as merely spiritual encouragement. Something in his application of the Jubilee to his own ministry hit close enough to home that the hometown congregation tried to throw him off a cliff.

The Jubilee is not merely Old Testament background to the Gospel. It is the shape of what Jesus came to do. Not a literal implementation of ancient land law — the Gentile mission alone required something more universal than the specific economic structures of agrarian Israel — but the pattern: liberation of the bound, return of what was lost, freedom for those whose debt had consumed them, the cancellation of what could not be paid.

## What This Demands

The question the Jubilee presses on the contemporary church is not whether to implement Leviticus 25 directly. The question is whether the church has anything to say to the conditions of permanent, generational indebtedness that characterize the lives of millions of people in contemporary society — where student debt follows young adults for decades, where medical debt determines whether families keep their homes, where the gap between those who inherit wealth and those who do not has widened to levels not seen in generations [cite — confirm current statistics if used; the general pattern is well-documented].

The Jubilee says that accumulation has limits and that debt can become a form of bondage. It says that a society in which the distance between the wealthy and the poor only ever increases is a society that has abandoned the covenant structure God built. It says that liberation is not merely a spiritual category — that God is concerned with the material conditions that determine whether people can participate in the fullness of community life, or whether they are locked into a permanent subordination from which there is no visible exit.

I have preached these texts and felt how much weight the comfortable congregation wants the word "metaphor" to carry. They want the Jubilee to mean something about spiritual freedom that does not require them to think about the economic conditions of their neighbors. The text will not allow the metaphor to do all the work. There were real fields. Real families. Real liberation. The year of the Lord's favor required something of the years before it.

We are in those years now. The Jubilee does not recur every fifty years in the new covenant; it arrived in Christ and is being worked out in the life of a community that takes its shape from what he announced in Nazareth. But the shape has not changed: good news to the poor, freedom for the captive, the year of the Lord's favor.

That year has obligations. They are not metaphorical.

> The trumpet has sounded.

Paul closes his second letter to the Corinthians with the most explicit new covenant statement of Jubilee logic in the New Testament: "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). He makes this statement not as a theological aside but as the theological ground for the collection he is gathering for the poor believers in Jerusalem — the practical, financial transfer of resources from those who have to those who do not. The movement is from the cross directly to the offering plate. The Jubilee is not only the background of Jesus' announcement in Nazareth. It is the pattern by which the church is supposed to organize its economic life with one another.

The church that reads 2 Corinthians 8-9 carefully will find that Paul is not appealing to the generosity of the Corinthians. He is appealing to the example of Christ's self-impoverishment for their sake, and saying: let that pattern define how you relate to those who have less. The trumpet has sounded. The year of favor has been proclaimed. What remains is the community that lives inside it.

I have five sons. That fact is not incidental to anything I write. It is the weight that keeps my theology honest. Abstract arguments about intergenerational responsibility become very concrete when you can put five names to the generation that will inherit what you leave behind.

The Scripture's concern for those who come after is not a modern environmental sentiment grafted onto an ancient text. It is structural. The Hebrew word for covenant — *berith* — carries a temporal depth that extends past the parties present at its making. When God makes a covenant with Abraham in Genesis 15 and 17, the covenant is explicitly extended to his descendants for generations. The law given at Sinai is given to a generation who will die in the wilderness, for the sake of the generation that will enter the land. Deuteronomy is Moses's long sermon to the children of the people who heard the thunder at Horeb. The audience is already once-removed. The obligations are not diminished.

The Deuteronomic vision of faithfulness is explicitly generational: "These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up" (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). The covenant shapes parenting. It shapes pedagogy. It shapes the structure of daily life, because the stakes are multigenerational and the consequences of forgetting are borne not just by those who forgot but by those who follow.

## The Category the Church Has Avoided

The application of this to climate and to accumulated injustice is uncomfortable for segments of the church, and I want to acknowledge why before making the argument.

The discomfort is partly political. Climate change has become a partisan category in the American context, and any church that touches it risks being heard as aligning with one political party rather than making a theological claim. I understand the wariness. I have felt it. I have also come to believe that the wariness has caused us to surrender the theological category to the political one, which is exactly backwards. The question of what we owe to those who come after us is not a Democrat question or a Republican question. It is a question that Moses asked, that the prophets asked, that every serious theology of covenant has always required an answer to.

The discomfort is also partly economic. The cost of addressing climate change falls, at least in the short term, on people and industries that are part of many congregations' social and economic world. Coal country churches, agricultural congregations, families whose livelihoods are tied to industries whose practices are implicated — these are real pastoral constituencies, and simplistic moralism that ignores their economic reality is not faithfulness. It is cruelty dressed in prophetic language.

I want to steel-man the case for the current approach: maintain political neutrality on contested policy questions, minister to all sides, focus on what Scripture clearly says and leave the contested applications to individual conscience. That is not without wisdom. The church that takes strong institutional positions on every contested political question quickly becomes a partisan organization rather than a community of witness.

> It is the weight that keeps my theology honest.

But the prophets did not maintain neutrality when the contested policy question was whether Israel would honor the covenant. They named what the generation in front of them was doing to the generations behind them. They named it specifically, with grief and without apology. Elijah named what Ahab's land-seizure policy was doing to Naboth's family (1 Kings 21). Amos named what the merchant class's economic practices were doing to the poor. The claim that prophetic witness must stop at the threshold of contested policy is a claim the prophets themselves did not accept.

## What the Prophets Said About Time

Isaiah's vision of redemption is consistently multigenerational. "You will be like a well-watered garden, like a spring whose waters never fail. Your people will rebuild the ancient ruins and will raise up the age-old foundations; you will be called Repairer of Broken Walls, Restorer of Streets with Dwellings" (Isaiah 58:11-12). The image is of a people who receive something broken, repair it, and pass it forward. The broken walls were left by the generation before. The restoration is for the generation after.

Psalm 78 is a long meditation on intergenerational faithfulness and failure. "We will not hide them from their descendants; we will tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the Lord, his power, and the wonders he has done" (Psalm 78:4). And immediately following: the story of how every generation that forgot what God had done produced consequences that fell on the generation following. The Psalm is not a comfort. It is a warning. Forgetfulness compounds.

The language of stewardship in Genesis 1 and 2 — the command to tend and keep the garden — is language of responsibility extended through time. The Hebrew *shamar*, to keep or guard, is the same word used of the cherubim guarding Eden (Genesis 3:24) and of the Levites guarding the tabernacle (Numbers 1:53). The gardener does not exhaust the soil. The gardener guards it and passes it forward. The creation does not belong to any generation. It is entrusted to each generation for the sake of the next.

## Inherited Injustice

Systemic racism is the same category of problem, and it belongs in this essay alongside the environmental question because both are fundamentally about what we pass down.

The wealth gap between white and Black families in America is not the product of different choices made in the present tense by different people. It is the accumulated consequence of policy decisions made over generations — the systematic exclusion of Black veterans from the GI Bill's benefits, the redlining of mortgage markets that denied Black families the wealth-building mechanism that built the white middle class, the discriminatory application of New Deal programs that explicitly excluded categories of work dominated by Black laborers [cite — confirm]. The effects compound across time. A family excluded from the housing market in 1950 does not simply recover when the exclusion ends in 1968. The equity they did not build, the inheritance they cannot pass down, the educational investments they cannot make — these extend across three generations and more.

> The effects compound across time.

The generation that did not make those decisions inherits their effects and the obligation to address them. This is not guilt for what your grandfather did. It is responsibility for what you have received and what you will pass on.

Nehemiah understood this. When he arrived in Jerusalem and saw the ruined walls, he did not say: I did not tear those walls down, I bear no responsibility for rebuilding them. He said: "I and this people have sinned" (Nehemiah 1:6). He implicated himself in the failure of a generation before his own because he was the one standing in front of the ruins, with the capacity to address them, and the question of what he would do with that capacity was the question in front of him. The historical guilt was distributed. The present responsibility was his.

## What This Looks Like for the Church

The church that takes intergenerational responsibility seriously will not look like the church that operates primarily within a single generation's preferences and horizons. It will make decisions differently.

It will ask, before building a new facility: does this serve the mission of the next generation of this community, or does it serve our preference for comfort and our need for an institutional monument? It will ask, before remaining silent about environmental policy: are we being neutral, or are we protecting the interests of people in this room at the cost of the people who will inherit the damage? It will ask, before treating racial justice as too politically contested to address: are we protecting ourselves, or protecting arrangements that compound inherited disadvantage for children who had nothing to do with the choices that created them?

These are not comfortable questions. They are the questions that Moses was asking when he preached Deuteronomy to a generation that would inherit promises made before they were born and face consequences for choices made by their parents.

## What I Owe My Sons

When I think about what I am leaving for my five sons, I do not think primarily about financial assets or career opportunities or even theological inheritance, though I care about all of those things. I think about whether they will inherit a world where the poor are still crushed by systems we refused to examine, where the earth is more depleted than it needed to be because we chose convenience, where the injustices that were visible in our generation are still unaddressed in theirs because we were too comfortable to speak.

I have done things that belong to that category. I have been silent when silence was easier. I have benefited from arrangements I did not examine. I have let pastoral wariness about political controversy function as a reason to avoid the kinds of conversations that would have required something from me and from the congregation. That is not a confession I make to feel better. It is a statement of where the obligation begins.

The Deuteronomic tradition teaches that the most dangerous word in any generation is the word "forget." Forget what God did. Forget what it cost. Forget who you were before the rescue. Forget who is still in the condition you were delivered from. Forgetting is not neutral. It is the mechanism by which every generation produces the injustice that the next generation inherits.

The question before us is not whether we will leave a legacy. We will. Every generation does, in the decisions it makes and the decisions it refuses. The question is what kind — what we built, what we failed to build, what we repaired, what we damaged further, what we had the capacity to address and chose not to.

The ones who come after us will inherit the answer to that question.

They are coming. They are already here in some cases, carrying the consequences of choices made before they understood the choices.

> It begins with me. It ends with the ones who come after.

It begins with me. It ends with the ones who come after.

The distance between those two points is the measure of what faithfulness requires.

My sons will inherit the world I am making. That sentence has the power to stop a man, or it should. Not the abstract world — the specific consequences of specific choices made in specific decades. The soil that will grow or not grow their food. The atmosphere that will be warmer or cooler by the degree we have now determined. The debt that will arrive on their doorstep in the form of public fiscal obligation. The institutions that will be weakened or strengthened depending on what this generation chose to do with them. The social trust that will be available or depleted depending on what we modeled about what human beings owe each other.

I have five sons. That is not an abstraction. Their futures are downstream from decisions I am making now, decisions my congregation is making now, decisions the church as an institution is either making or refusing to make. The question of what we owe the generations that follow us is therefore not merely philosophical. It is personal in the most specific sense of the word.

---

## The Intergenerational Conscience the Church Misplaced

The biblical tradition carries an explicit intergenerational conscience that the modern church has largely misplaced. When Moses delivers the law in Deuteronomy, he frames it repeatedly in terms of what it will mean for children not yet born. *You shall teach them diligently to your children* (Deuteronomy 6:7). *When your son asks you in time to come...* (Deuteronomy 6:20). The covenant at Sinai was structured to create an intergenerational community — not a contract between living parties who would renegotiate it when circumstances changed, but a commitment that the present generation would carry forward and transmit, intact and alive, to those who came after.

Psalm 78 is among the most sustained expressions of this intergenerational responsibility in the entire canon. It opens with this:

*We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the Lord, and his might, and the wonders that he has done. He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers to teach to their children, that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and arise and tell them to their children, so that they should set their hope in God* (Psalm 78:4-7).

> The children not yet born have a claim on the living.

The chain is explicit: each generation responsible not only to receive what it has been given but to pass it on to those who cannot yet speak for themselves. The children not yet born have a claim on the living. That claim is not sentimental. It is structural — built into the covenant community's self-understanding as a people who exist across time, not merely in the present moment.

## The Land You Steward for a Season

The prophetic tradition extends this beyond spiritual inheritance. When God addresses Israel's land use practices, the language is consistently intergenerational. The jubilee system in Leviticus 25 was designed, among other things, to prevent the permanent concentration of land in the hands of the wealthy — because the next generation had a claim on the land as inheritance, not only the present generation as property. You did not own the land in the modern sense; you were its steward for a season, and what you did with it in that season would either preserve or destroy the next generation's inheritance. *The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me* (Leviticus 25:23). This is an explicit limit on present-generation rights in the name of intergenerational obligation.

---

The environmental question is where this theology has the most urgent contemporary application, and it is also the place where the American church has been most resistant to speaking clearly. Climate change is real, it is largely human-caused, and the consequences are being distributed unjustly — falling hardest on the poorest communities, in the Global South and in poor communities domestically, communities that have contributed least to the problem and have least capacity to adapt to it [cite — confirm]. By the projections of current science [cite — confirm], the most severe consequences will be borne primarily by people not yet born, and by those born into circumstances that provide the least protection from what is coming.

## The Most Voiceless Constituency

This is the precise category the biblical tradition identifies as requiring prophetic response: the vulnerable, the voiceless, those who have no representative in the room where the decisions are being made. The unborn generations are the most voiceless constituency in the history of political discourse. They cannot vote. They cannot lobby. They cannot picket. They cannot even know, yet, what is being decided on their behalf. If the church has any calling to speak for those who cannot speak for themselves — and the tradition is unanimous that it does (Proverbs 31:8-9) — then the generation not yet born has the most comprehensive claim on that voice.

The counter-position from within evangelical Christianity tends to take one of two forms. The first questions the scientific consensus, arguing that the church should not build its prophetic program on contested empirical claims. The second argues that environmental concern is a distraction from the more urgent spiritual mission of the church, and that the emphasis on creation care comes at the expense of proclamation of the gospel.

Both deserve honest engagement. The first ignores the overwhelming scientific consensus that has developed over three decades of increasingly sophisticated research [cite — confirm] — a consensus that is essentially unanimous among the relevant scientific communities. The church's commitment to truth requires following evidence where it leads, and the evidence here is not genuinely contested among the people equipped to evaluate it.

The second argument poses a false choice. The proclamation of the gospel is not undermined by the church's engagement with creation care — it is amplified by it. The credibility of the church's witness to the coming kingdom is directly tied to the seriousness with which the church takes the world God made and pronounced good. A gospel that saves souls while being indifferent to the soil those souls will be buried in is not the gospel of the God who created the heavens and the earth, who called creation good before humanity was part of it, and who declares in the final vision of Scripture not the escape from earth but its renewal: *Behold, I am making all things new* (Revelation 21:5).

---

## The Debt We Hand the Unborn to Repay

The debt question is the economic equivalent of the environmental one. The practice of continuous deficit spending — at every level of government, and in most households — is a mechanism by which the present generation consumes resources that will have to be repaid by the next. This is not a partisan claim; it is an accounting identity. What we borrow, they will repay. The political arrangements that make intergenerational wealth transfer acceptable — that allow the present to tax the future to fund its own consumption — are a structural form of the injustice the prophets condemned: the powerful extracting from the powerless.

> The present generation is powerful relative to the unborn.

The present generation is powerful relative to the unborn. The unborn have no voice in the fiscal decisions being made on their behalf. This is exactly the configuration the prophetic tradition was designed to address. *Woe to those who add house to house and join field to field, until there is no room for anyone else, and you live alone in the midst of the land* (Isaiah 5:8). The logic of endless accumulation at the expense of future space, future possibility, future inheritance — this is what Isaiah was condemning, and its modern equivalents are not hard to find.

---

There is a form of short-termism built into democratic systems and market economies that the church is not required to replicate. The elected official thinks in four-year cycles. The publicly traded company thinks in quarterly earnings reports. The consumer thinks about this month's budget. None of these time horizons extends to the generation that will be born in 2050 or 2075 or 2100. None of the incentive structures built into these systems rewards decisions that sacrifice present gain for future flourishing.

The church's time horizon is explicitly longer. We serve the God who covenanted with Abraham about a people not yet born (Genesis 12:1-3), who made promises to David about a kingdom that would outlast every human dynasty (2 Samuel 7:16), who holds human history within a purpose that extends from creation to new creation. That extended vision is not a pious addition to the church's agenda. It is the fundamental form of its witness to the world: we are accountable to someone who sees all the consequences, including the ones that will not arrive for fifty years.

## The Institution That Asks What We Bequeath

This should make the church uniquely equipped to speak for the future — to be the institution in public life that consistently asks the question no one else is structurally incentivized to ask: *What are we bequeathing?*

I think of my sons. I think of what they will face, not abstractly but specifically — the particular shape of the world they will inherit depending on whether my generation made the choices this moment required, or whether we managed our discomfort and called the management wisdom. The men who planted trees they would never sit under understood something the present moment resists: you owe a debt to the future that no present comfort can discharge. The debt is real. The ones who will arrive to collect it do not exist yet, which is precisely why the people who do exist bear the responsibility.

This is the weight of being human beings in time — made, as the theologian Miroslav Volf has argued, for the long arc of history, not merely the brief present tense we inhabit [cite — confirm]. The children not yet born are waiting for us to act like it.

> That is not a comfortable thing to sit with. It is not meant to be.

That is not a comfortable thing to sit with. It is not meant to be.

No one who came to ministry out of a calling to care for people imagined that one of the most pastorally demanding acts they would ever perform would be firing a staff member. And yet it is. Because the person on the other side of that conversation is a person — someone with a mortgage and a family and an identity that is probably substantially wrapped up in the role you are about to remove them from — and how you carry out that conversation will shape what they believe about the church, and possibly about God, for a long time afterward.

This is why pastors avoid it too long. Not because they are cowardly, though sometimes that is part of it, but because the pastoral instinct is toward care — and care, misapplied, can become a refusal to tell the truth.
