## When Care Becomes a Refusal to Tell the Truth

> The mercy that never speaks is not mercy. It is avoidance.

Pastoral care that withholds necessary truth is not care. It is a kind of cowardice that hides behind compassion's language while doing something compassion would not permit: leaving a person in a role where they are failing, or in a situation that is damaging them and others, because the pastor cannot bear the grief of the necessary conversation. The mercy that never speaks is not mercy. It is avoidance.

---

Before the question of when, there is the question of whether — whether the situation actually requires termination, or whether it requires a different kind of intervention.

## The Prior Question Too Many Pastors Skip

Not every personnel failure is a firing offense. A staff member who is struggling with a specific area of performance, who has not received clear feedback, who has not been held to an articulated standard, who has not been given a defined opportunity to improve — that person has not been given a fair chance to succeed. The pastoral leader who releases someone without having done the harder work of honest feedback and genuine support has not acted with integrity. He has protected himself from the discomfort of a development conversation and called it a leadership decision.

This is the prior question that too many pastors skip over. The months of private frustration, of vague dissatisfaction, of complaining to a spouse or a trusted elder that something is not working — those months often substitute for the direct, honest, early conversation that might have prevented the ending. If you have been noticing a problem for six months without naming it clearly to the person who has the problem, the problem is partly yours. You did not give them the information they needed to change. You deprived them of the chance to succeed by withholding the feedback that would have made success possible.

This matters before any termination conversation, because you need to be honest with yourself about whether you did that prior work. If you did not, the first step is not termination. It is the development conversation that should have happened months ago.

---

The situations that do require termination are clearer than pastors sometimes make them.

## The Situations That Genuinely Require It

When someone's behavior violates the ethical or theological standards of the community — involves dishonesty, moral failure, or conduct that directly harms others — and the violation is ongoing rather than genuinely repented of, that is a termination situation. The clear failure to repent is the critical element here, because repentance and restoration are themselves Christian goods. A staff member who has failed morally but who responds with genuine accountability and a willingness to do whatever the restoration process requires is in a different situation than a staff member who is defensive, who minimizes what happened, who manages the information rather than responding to it.

When a staff member is actively damaging the culture — creating division, undermining trust, poisoning the relationships that the team depends on — and every reasonable intervention has failed to produce change, that is a termination situation. This category is harder, because culture damage is less visible than individual moral failure and the person causing it often has defenders who see only their gifts. But a staff member who is toxic to the team, whatever their individual gifts, is doing damage that exceeds the value of those gifts. The leader who cannot act on this because the person in question is talented or popular or has been there a long time has misunderstood his accountability.

When the role itself no longer exists, or is being restructured in a way that the current person is genuinely unable to fill, that is a termination situation that is often handled with more honesty than the others because it feels less personal. This is the one pastors typically find easiest. It still deserves the same care.

---

When the decision is made, the conversation must be honest and direct.

## The Conversation That Must Be Honest and Direct

This is where pastoral instinct most often fails. The desire to soften the blow — to leave the person with hope that is not real, to imply that the door is not closed when it is, to attribute the termination to circumstances rather than to the actual problem — is understandable, and it is harmful. The person being released deserves to know the truth. Not every detail, not with cruelty, but clearly.

They will construct a narrative of what happened either way. Giving them an accurate account allows them to grieve honestly, to learn from the experience, to process it without the distortion of false information. Giving them a false one — or a carefully incomplete one designed to avoid discomfort — leaves them confused, possibly angry in ways that are ultimately directed at the wrong target, and likely to repeat the same patterns in the next role.

> It insists on both simultaneously.

Paul's instruction to speak truth in love (Ephesians 4:15) does not offer a choice between truth and love. It insists on both simultaneously. The termination conversation that is all love and no truth leaves someone unable to understand what happened. The conversation that is all truth and no love causes unnecessary damage to someone who is already losing something significant. The discipline is the both-and: clear enough to be understood, warm enough to be humane.

Some specifics. Do not have the conversation on a Friday afternoon before a long weekend, leaving the person with nowhere to turn for two days. Do not have it over email or through an intermediary if you are the person who made the decision. Do not begin it with excessive softening that delays the actual news — the human brain, once it senses the weight in the room, cannot process anything else until the main thing is named. Say it early in the conversation: "I need to let you know that I am ending your employment here." Then give the clear reasons. Then the severance terms. Then be quiet and let them respond.

Let them be angry or hurt. This is appropriate. Do not rush to explain or defend yourself — you have said what needed to be said, and now the pastoral work is to be present to the response, not to manage it. If they raise questions you need to answer, answer them honestly. If they raise accusations that require response, respond to them directly, without defensiveness if possible. You are not trying to win an argument. You are trying to end an employment relationship with integrity.

---

The pastoral care does not end with the conversation.

## The Care That Does Not End With the Conversation

What happens to the person after they leave matters — whether the severance is genuinely generous, reflecting the church's stated belief about human dignity rather than its minimum legal obligation; whether the public communication about the departure is honest without being exposing; whether the pastor makes himself available for a follow-up conversation if the person needs to process what happened.

The church is not simply an employer. It is, or is supposed to be, a community that holds a particular vision of human worth and of how people should be treated in hard moments. The termination that is legally clean but pastorally cold betrays that vision. The person who is released deserves to experience the church's care even as they experience the church's decision. Both things are possible. It requires more from the pastor, but both things are possible.

There are things to avoid. Do not allow other staff to hear about the termination through the grapevine before the terminated person has had the conversation. Do not say more to the congregation than is necessary — they need to know the person is no longer on staff, and in most cases they do not need the reasons. Do not allow the terminated person to be spoken of unkindly in the aftermath, by you or by anyone else, even when the reasons for the termination were genuinely serious.

---

I have released people from staff. It has never been easy. The ones I handled with the most integrity were the ones where I told the truth, did it directly, provided what I could for the transition, and did not leave the person wondering what had actually happened. They could grieve. They could be angry. But they knew. And several of them, in the months afterward, told me that the clarity — painful as it was — allowed them to heal in ways that the vague and managed exit does not.

The ones I am least proud of are the ones where I delayed too long, softened the truth too much, and left the person without the clear accounting they deserved. The extended vagueness was not kind. It was self-protective. I told myself I was protecting them, but I was protecting myself from their grief. That is not pastoral care. It is pastoral cowardice in pastoral clothing.

> The ministry is not served by the compassion that cannot act.

The ministry is not served by the compassion that cannot act. The person on the other side of the conversation deserves the difficult gift of your honesty, your directness, and your genuine care — all three, simultaneously, in the same conversation.

Do it clearly. Do it with care. Do not do it later than it should be done.

The moment it is necessary is the moment it should happen.

Patriotism is not a sin. Let that be said first, clearly, and without apology. The love of a particular place, a particular people, a particular inheritance — this is not idolatry. It is not wrong to weep at a flag, to feel the weight of what your nation's better moments have cost. The love of the proximate — the people placed near you by birth and history — is a kind of love the tradition has long recognized as ordered and right.

But there is a point where patriotism stops being love of country and starts being faith in country, and that crossing is one of the defining spiritual catastrophes of American church history. We have been crossing it for more than two centuries without noticing what we were doing, because the crossing is gradual, and gradual crossings are the hardest kind to name.

The Kingdom of God is the organizing center of Jesus's entire proclamation. Not America, not democracy, not Western civilization — the Kingdom. The Sermon on the Mount is not a speech about good governance. The Lord's Prayer is not a civic liturgy. When Jesus says "Thy kingdom come," he is not describing a project that requires congressional approval or a movement that belongs to one nation's story. He is announcing a sovereignty that stands over all other sovereignties, judges all other sovereignties, and will, in the end, outlast all other sovereignties. That is the thing we have quietly, incrementally, comfortably replaced with "God Bless America."

The replacement did not begin with malice. It began with gratitude — genuine, understandable, earned gratitude for a nation that provided unusual freedoms and unusual stability, that allowed the church to build and preach and organize without the kind of state persecution that had characterized Christian life in most of Christian history. That gratitude is appropriate. But gratitude, when it is not held under something larger than itself, curdles into entitlement, and entitlement hardens into theology. By the early twentieth century, the equation was already structural: many American pulpits preached a gospel in which the blessings of democracy and the blessings of Christ were assumed to be the same blessings, aimed at the same people, advancing the same project.

Robert Bellah wrote in 1967 about what he called American civil religion — the set of beliefs, symbols, and rituals that function as a national faith, drawing on but not identical to Christianity, in which America plays a special role in God's purposes, its founding documents treated as quasi-sacred texts, its wars interpreted as providential, its prosperity as divine favor. [cite — confirm Bellah's 1967 essay "Civil Religion in America"] That analysis was correct then. It has deepened since. The civil religion and the church have become harder to distinguish in large sectors of American Christianity, not because Christians are hypocrites but because the merger was slow enough that no single generation had to make a conscious choice for it.

I swam in that water. I preached in it, with more confidence than I had earned, telling the story in which the American experiment was the continuation of God's purposes rather than one more chapter in the long, unfinished history of nations rising and falling under his gaze. I was wrong. The wrongness was comfortable enough that I had little incentive to notice it. When the comfort of a theological position and the comfort of your social location align, you do not feel the weight of the error. You feel at home.

Here is what the replacement has cost the church, concretely.

When the Kingdom of God is the organizing principle of Christian life, the Sermon on the Mount operates as public ethics. The poor have a claim on you that your voting bloc does not. The stranger matters as much as the citizen — because the Kingdom makes no distinction between them, and Jesus's own account of judgment in Matthew 25 describes a God who identifies himself with the hungry, the stranger, the naked, the sick, the imprisoned. Not the powerful. Not the comfortable. The ones at the bottom of every social hierarchy. That is where Jesus locates himself in the final accounting.

But when patriotism becomes the practical savior — when the survival of American freedom becomes the thing we are actually working for, the prize the church is positioned to protect — the Sermon on the Mount becomes inconvenient. You spiritualize it. You defer it to the afterlife or the individual interior. You give it a private domain that does not touch the public square where the real decisions are made. The enemy's dignity cannot be honored if the enemy is what we are defending ourselves against. The poor have no special claim if the whole framework is about protecting what you have built.

The prophets of Israel never made that move. Amos did not tell the wealthy of Samaria that their economic predations were a private matter between themselves and God, outside the scope of the nation's public life. Isaiah did not suggest that the oppression of the poor was a question of personal morality that had nothing to do with the structure of the kingdom. Micah did not separate mishpat — the public establishment of right order — from the daily life of the nation. The prophets assumed that God had opinions about how the community organized itself, and that those opinions had consequences, and that the consequences were not requests. The whole prophetic tradition is premised on the claim that the God of Israel is sovereign over the nation, judges the nation, and is not obligated to protect the nation if the nation violates the covenant.

The American church, when it chose nationalism as its organizing principle, lost access to the prophets. Not formally. We still read them. But we read them as poetry about ancient Israel, sealed off from any analogical claim on our own national life. We have domesticated the fire.

The strongest counter-argument is worth honoring. Ordered love, as Augustine argued, begins with what is nearest — family, community, nation — and works outward. [cite — confirm Augustine on ordered love] The claim that Christians should have no particular attachment to their nation confuses universal love with abstract indifference and ends up serving neither God nor neighbor. And the specific goods of the liberal democratic order — freedom of speech, freedom of worship, procedural protections against tyranny — are genuine goods that Christians have benefited from and that deserve gratitude and some degree of defense. These are not nothing.

They are real goods. They are not ultimate goods. And the moment we treat proximate goods as ultimate goods, we commit the oldest error in the human story — idolatry. The error is not loving your country. The error is loving your country with the kind of love that belongs only to God, trusting your country with a trust that belongs only to God, and organizing your public life around the survival of your country in a way that crowds out the organizing claim of the Kingdom. When the flag is in the sanctuary, when the worship service includes pledges to the republic, when the church's political witness is indistinguishable from the platform of one of its parties, something has gone profoundly wrong at the level of what the church actually believes.

Lesslie Newbigin, writing after decades as a missionary in India and watching the European church from outside, identified the fundamental crisis of Western Christianity as the privatization of faith — the removal of the gospel from its claim on public life and public order, which he traced in part to the church's accommodation to whatever order it happened to inhabit. [cite — confirm Newbigin's argument in *The Gospel in a Pluralist Society*] The American version of that accommodation is nationalist Christianity — the church that has identified its survival with the nation's survival and its health with the nation's health, and that therefore cannot speak a prophetic word to the nation without undermining its own institutional position.

That is not the church Jesus prayed for in John 17. That is not the community that Acts 2 describes — a community that cut across every national and ethnic line, that had no nation to protect because its Lord had already been executed by the most powerful nation in the world, and whose hope was not the preservation of an existing order but the coming of a new one.

I came to faith from atheism. I had no inherited loyalty to any version of Christian nationalism; I came in as an outsider, and I can still see the shape of the thing when I stand back from it. What I see is a church that has let the flag and the cross become confused — not through bad intention, but through the long, slow substitution of a proximate good for the ultimate one.

The Kingdom of God does not need America. America, like every nation, needs the Kingdom. Not to be blessed by it in the sense of preserved and prospered — but to be judged by it, corrected by it, and called, at least in its best moments, toward the justice and mercy that are not American values first and Christian values second but the character of the God who made every nation and will outlast them all.

The Lord's Prayer is not addressed to the republic. It is addressed to a Father whose name is to be made holy, whose Kingdom is to come, whose will is to be done — on earth as in heaven. That prayer is either the organizing center of everything we do, or it is a liturgical habit that doesn't cost us anything.

Which one it is, is showing.

Sometimes the crisis is not in the congregation. It is in the man at the front.

A marriage coming apart. A depression that will not lift. A grief too large to preach around. A failure that is about to become public. The pastor faces a question no class prepared him for: what do you do when the person whose job is to hold everyone else together is the one falling apart?

I have been closer to this question than I like to admit. And what I know now — what I did not know in the middle of it — is that the question itself is formed by a wrong assumption. The assumption that the man in the pulpit is supposed to be the person who holds everyone else together. That the pastoral function is to be the non-anxious presence, the steady center, the rock on which the congregation leans. That if he is the one falling, something has gone catastrophically wrong.

That assumption is a theological error. And it will kill you if you believe it.

---

The first instinct when the crisis arrives is almost always concealment, and the instinct is understandable. We have trained pastors to be the strong ones. The culture of professional ministry has specific expectations about composure, about the managed presentation of emotional stability, about the pastoral persona that is available and steady and never visibly overwhelmed. To let the congregation see the collapse feels like a dereliction — as though the man's whole authority depended on appearing intact.

So he performs wellness over an open wound. He preaches strength he does not have. He structures his public face around the management of an image while the real man bleeds out behind it. He learns to preach about suffering from a safe theological distance that protects the congregation from the knowledge that the preacher is suffering. He prays with people whose problems are smaller than his, and does not say so. He counsels marriages while his own is under water, and calls this normal, and keeps going until he cannot.

The performing is not a neutral choice. It has costs that accumulate before they become visible.

It costs the man himself first — the sustained cognitive and emotional work of maintaining a performance across every public context while managing an internal reality that contradicts it. This is exhausting in ways that compound over time. The man who performs wellness for long enough begins to lose track of what he actually feels, because the performance has colonized the space where genuine emotional experience used to live.

It costs the congregation second, in a way that is less obvious but more theologically serious. A pastor who must appear unbroken to keep his standing is quietly teaching his people that the Christian life is the management of an image — that grace is for the congregation but the pastor must be self-sufficient, that the gospel of weakness made strong (2 Corinthians 12:9-10) applies to everyone except the man explaining it. The congregation absorbs that lesson whether or not he ever says it. And they take it home, and apply it to their own suffering, and conclude that real faith means not letting your collapse show.

This is not the gospel. This is the prosperity theology that smuggled itself into the pastoral office.

---

Paul wrote about his own weakness with a specificity that the pastoral tradition has often glossed over. "I have been in labor and toil, in many sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure. And apart from all these external things, there is the daily pressure of my anxiety for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant?" (2 Corinthians 11:27-29). This is not a rhetorical performance of vulnerability designed to authenticate his authority. This is a man naming what pastoral ministry actually cost him. The anxiety was real. The weakness was real. He wrote about it in a letter to a congregation he was fighting to keep.

He also wrote, in that same letter, about a thorn in the flesh — something so significant that he pleaded with God three times to remove it, and God declined (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). The reason given: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." This is not a consolation prize. It is a theological claim about where divine power operates. It does not operate through the performance of invincibility. It operates through acknowledged limitation. The man who is honest about what he cannot do creates the space where God can do what only God can.

The pastor who hides his weakness does not protect his congregation. He deprives them of the testimony that matters most: that the Gospel is true when it is tested, not only when it is proclaimed.

---

There is, of course, wisdom in how and what you disclose. This requires more than a blanket call to transparency.

Not every detail belongs in front of the congregation. Some crises are not only the pastor's — they involve his family, and the members of his family who have not chosen public life deserve their privacy. A marriage in crisis cannot be fully disclosed from the pulpit without exposing the other person in the marriage to a congregation that will carry that information in ways neither of them can control. The pastoral crisis that involves sin must be handled through the appropriate structures of accountability rather than through public disclosure that can substitute for genuine repentance and restoration.

Discernment matters. The question is not "how much do I tell?" but "how do I stop pretending in ways that allow the people I lead to see that I am a man under the same grace I preach?"

That distinction matters. The pastor does not owe the congregation the details of his crisis. He owes them the truth that he has one, and that he is being a Christian in it — that he is doing the things he has told them to do, rather than doing the things the pastoral performance culture has told him to do. He is not performing composure. He is letting himself be carried. He is in the room where real things are happening to him, and he is bringing those real things to the God he preaches on Sunday.

The congregation watching their pastor honestly walk through a hard season is not losing confidence in the Gospel. They are, for perhaps the first time, seeing evidence that it is real. That it holds the weight of an actual life. That the man who preaches it on Sunday is not exempt from needing it on Monday.

---

Elijah in 1 Kings 19 is the textbook for what this looks like from God's side. Elijah has just experienced one of the most dramatic prophetic victories in the Old Testament — the confrontation at Mount Carmel, the fire coming down, the prophets of Baal defeated — and he immediately collapses. He runs. He sits under a juniper tree and asks God to take his life. "It is enough," he says. "I am no better than my fathers." He falls asleep.

God's response is not rebuke. God does not tell him to recover his composure and get back to work. God lets him sleep. Then an angel wakes him and says, not "pull yourself together," but "arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you" (1 Kings 19:7). The acknowledgment is direct: this is too much. The provision is direct: food, water, rest. The invitation back into ministry is extended after two rounds of sleep and eating, not before.

The God of Elijah is not the God of the pastoral performance culture. He does not require the prophet to pretend he is fine. He meets him where he has collapsed. He provides for the practical need. He asks, gently, "What are you doing here?" — and then he listens to the answer, even when the answer is a long complaint that is only partially accurate. And then he re-commissions him.

This is the pattern. The man who collapses, brought to God honestly, is the man God re-commissions. Not the man who manages the collapse into invisibility and keeps going on empty.

---

Practically, what does this look like?

It means getting help before you need it and certainly when you need it. It means having people in your life — outside the congregation, not subject to your pastoral authority, not dependent on your professional function — who can hold what is actually happening. It means being willing to take time away, to see a counselor, to let the elders carry more than usual, to be honest with the board about the level of your struggle when honesty is required. It means trusting that the institution you have given your life to can survive knowing you are human.

Some of this trust will be betrayed. Some congregations and boards, when the pastor is honest about a significant personal struggle, will respond not with support but with pressure, or with the first serious questioning of his fitness. That is a real risk. The culture of pastoral invincibility did not grow without reason — vulnerability has been used against pastors in genuinely damaging ways.

But the alternative — the man who keeps going behind the mask until the mask no longer fits, who breaks in public what he refused to name in private — is worse. The managed collapse is more damaging than the honest one. The congregation can handle more truth than the pastoral culture assumes. And the pastor who lets himself be held, in controlled and pastoral ways, usually discovers that what he feared would destroy his standing actually deepened it.

---

I was loved for my function. That was the fear underneath the concealment. If the function faltered, the love would go.

The healing, when it came, came partly through discovering that the fear was a lie. The people who actually loved me wanted the man, not the performance. And letting them see the broken version did not cost me my ministry. It deepened it. They had heard me say that we are saved by grace and not by strength. Now they watched me need it.

The man in the pulpit will fall apart. Not might. Will.

The only question is whether he does it hiding or held.

Choose held. It is the truer sermon.

And it is the only one that will keep you.

It starts as something you cannot quite name. A slow awareness that the conversations you are having with your spouse are not the conversations you are having anywhere else. That the person you have become does not map cleanly onto the person you were when you made your vows. That you have moved — in your faith, your understanding of yourself, your capacity for self-awareness — and the distance between where you started and where you are now is not the same distance your spouse has traveled.

This is one of the loneliest positions in a marriage. And it is one of the least talked about. Not because it is rare. Because naming it feels like an accusation. To say "I have grown and you haven't" sounds like arrogance dressed as self-awareness. So people carry it quietly, or they drop hints that land as criticism, or they slowly withdraw into the parts of their lives where they feel understood — and the marriage quietly hollows.

## The Language Worth Having

The New Testament gives us a word worth sitting with here: sunergos — a co-laborer, one who works alongside. Paul uses it repeatedly for his closest ministry companions in Romans 16:3, Philippians 2:25, and elsewhere. The image embedded in it is not sameness but shared direction. What makes two people sunergos is not that they are at the same place; it is that they are moving the same way.

That distinction matters. The question in a marriage where one person has grown is not "why hasn't my spouse caught up" — it is "are we still moving in the same direction, and am I willing to do the slow work of bringing them with me rather than leaving them behind?"

The answer to that question determines whether what is happening is a growth gap or a growing apart. They feel the same. They are not the same.

**Growing faster than your spouse is not the problem. Growing in a direction that no longer includes them is.**

## The Pastoral Reality

A woman I'll call Sarah came to faith seriously in her mid-thirties — the kind of faith that reorganized her priorities, her relationships, her sense of what her life was for. Her husband was not hostile to her faith, but he did not share it. They had been married for eleven years. The woman who had made those vows was a different person than the one now sitting across from him at dinner.

She described the gap not as theological but as dimensional. "He is a good man," she said. "He just doesn't want to go anywhere. And I can't stop going."

What she needed to hear — and eventually did — was that her growth had introduced an obligation, not just a gap. Growth that does not remain in relationship is not spiritual maturity; it is spiritual isolation with better vocabulary.

This is the part that the books about spiritual growth rarely say clearly. The growth becomes a problem not when it happens, but when the person who has grown begins to use the growth as a category that places them above the one who hasn't. Superiority is not the same as depth. The person who has genuinely wrestled with hard things and come out different should have, among the things they came out with, a more honest accounting of their own limitations — not a measuring stick for their spouse.

## The Historical Arc of the Problem

The marriage covenant in the biblical tradition was never premised on two people being at the same place spiritually or intellectually. Ruth and Boaz were at very different places in terms of their formation and their social position when the covenant was made. Hosea's marriage was built on a disparity so profound that it became a theological metaphor for God's relationship to Israel. Priscilla and Aquila, in Acts 18, appear to have had different gifts — she is sometimes listed first, which in ancient convention often signified greater standing in the relationship's given context.

What these portraits share is not equivalence but covenant — the decision to remain bound to another person, to continue moving in the same direction even when the pace is unequal, to extend to the other person the same patient investment that the relationship itself has required from the beginning.

The problem arises not from difference but from what difference does to the posture of the one who is ahead. Philippians 2:3 says: "in humility count others more significant than yourselves." This is one of the most demanding verses in the New Testament, and it is particularly demanding in the context of a marriage where one person has done significant interior work and the other has not. The person who has done the work has access to evidence that they are more self-aware, more emotionally present, more spiritually developed than their partner. The temptation to count that evidence and draw the obvious conclusion is real. The instruction is to not.

## The Counter-Position Worth Engaging

There is a view — not uncommon in certain Christian circles — that interprets the 1 Corinthians 7 passage about the believing spouse and the unbelieving spouse to mean that significant spiritual disparity in a marriage is grounds, or at least permission, for dissolution: "But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved" (1 Corinthians 7:15). On this reading, the person who has grown spiritually is in a position analogous to the believer married to an unbeliever, and the distance between them is sufficient cause for departure.

This reading requires more than the text can bear. Paul is describing a specific case — a pagan spouse who chooses to leave the marriage upon their partner's conversion to Christianity. He is not providing a general principle that any significant spiritual gap justifies dissolution. The verse that follows is even clearer: "For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?" (1 Corinthians 7:16). Paul's actual prescription is to remain — and to remain with the specific intention that the covenant relationship might itself become the means of the other person's growth.

The growth gap, then, is not a problem to be resolved by departure. It is a situation in which the one who has grown has a particular responsibility — not superiority, not distance, but the patient presence that Paul describes when he says in Galatians 6:2: "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ."

## What Growth Actually Requires of the Person Who Has Done It

Genuine growth produces humility, not hierarchy. The person who has done real work on themselves knows how much they did not know, how many blindspots remain, how much of what they now see was invisible to them five years ago. If growth is producing impatience with a spouse who hasn't arrived yet, something else is happening. The growth is being wielded as a weapon rather than offered as invitation.

Proverbs 31:26 says wisdom's words are kind. Kindness is not the soft option — it is the harder one. It is easier to perform growth than to bring someone with you through it.

What the partner who has grown owes the marriage: continued investment, honest naming of the gap without contempt, patient invitation rather than ultimatum, and a genuine willingness to examine whether their own growth has produced in them something the other person would actually want to pursue. I have sat with people who described their spiritual growth in terms that would repel anyone listening carefully — a constant performance of depth, an impatience with anyone who didn't speak the same language, a spiritual sophistication that had somehow produced less warmth rather than more. That is not growth. That is acquisition without integration.

What the partner who has not grown owes the marriage: honesty about whether they are unwilling or simply uninvited. The two look identical from the outside. They are not identical in their implications. The person who is genuinely uninterested in growth requires a different kind of conversation than the person who has not been invited into the growth that their partner is experiencing. Many spouses who appear to have stopped growing are actually waiting to be included — waiting for an invitation that has not come because the growing partner has assumed the gap is permanent rather than simply uncrossed.

## What This Looks Like Over Time

The couples who survive this do not erase the gap. They build a bridge across it — with enough patience and enough honesty and enough refusal to let the silence become permanent. They stay curious about each other in a direction that the growth gap itself can illuminate. The growing partner learns from the one who seems less developed: often the person who has not engaged in formal therapeutic or spiritual formation carries a kind of practical wisdom, a groundedness, a capacity for ordinary fidelity that the more sophisticated partner has bypassed in their upward movement. The less visibly developed partner learns from the one who has done the work: that growth is possible, that the interior matters, that the conversation can go deeper.

## Three Questions for This Week

If you are the one who has grown: has your growth made you easier or harder to be married to? Would your spouse's answer match yours?

If you are the one who feels left behind: is the distance about direction or pace? Are you resisting the same destination, or just the pressure to arrive faster?

For both: when did you last learn something from each other? What would need to be true for that to happen again?

**This week:** one conversation where the person who has grown asks to be taught something — not performed humility, but genuine curiosity about what the other person knows that they don't.

The gap does not close by being ignored. It does not close by one person waiting for the other to catch up. It closes, slowly, by two people who are still choosing each other — who are willing to do the patient, unglamorous work of building a bridge rather than standing on their respective banks and watching the distance widen.

It is harder than leaving. It is also more worth it.

By Thursday afternoon the dread has arrived. The text is open. The commentary stack is there. And nothing comes — not the electricity that used to arrive, not the sense that this passage is hunting you, that it needs to be preached. Just words. Just obligation. Just the crushing awareness that Sunday is three days away and you have nothing that will cost you anything to say.

Every honest preacher knows that chair. The question is not whether you will sit in it, but whether you will tell yourself the truth about why you are there.

---

Stale preaching is not primarily a craft problem. It is a soul problem — and most preachers try to fix the craft because the soul examination is harder to bear. They buy a new commentary. They switch series. They try a different structure. They discover a preacher they envy and borrow his moves. None of it works for long, because the real problem is not what is in the books. The real problem is that somewhere in the accumulated weight of ministry — the funerals, the board meetings, the pastoral emergencies at ten o'clock on a Saturday night, the decade of Sunday mornings in the same room — the preacher stopped being a person before God and became a professional before a congregation.

The difference is audible from the third row. A sermon produced by a man who is processing the text publicly, for people who need it, sounds different from a sermon produced by a professional who is executing a performance. The congregation cannot always name the difference, but they feel it. There is a quality of weight that comes from the preacher who is genuinely wrestling — who is speaking from the middle of a question he has not fully resolved, who is offering what the text has cost him rather than what the text yields under efficient extraction. When that quality is absent, the words remain grammatically correct and theologically defensible and existentially thin.

The history of Christian preaching is instructive here. Augustine's sermons in Hippo were famous for their rawness — he often preached from a text he chose that morning, with his congregation responding aloud, interrupting, questioning [cite — confirm]. It was not efficient. It was alive. John Chrysostom, preaching in Antioch and later in Constantinople in the late fourth century, was called "the golden-mouthed" not because of his technique but because of the sense his hearers had that he was preaching from a place of genuine conviction about what he was saying [cite — confirm]. The craft was there, but the craft was in service of something that came from elsewhere. When craft becomes the primary thing — when the preacher is executing a method rather than opening a wound — the congregation notices, even without the vocabulary to say what they are noticing.

---

The Psalms model something the modern pulpit has mostly forgotten. The poets of Israel did not write from composure. They wrote from the middle — from inside the confusion, the grief, the bewilderment that God was silent. Psalm 22 opens not with a sermon point but with a cry: *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, so far from my cries of anguish?* (Psalm 22:1). This is not a rhetorical device. It is a man in genuine distress asking a genuine question about whether God is present. The psalm does not resolve the question quickly. It holds the tension for twenty verses before arriving at any kind of confidence, and even then the confidence is hard-won, not simply assumed.

The preacher who has not spent time in that territory — not as a rhetorical exercise but as a genuine description of his own inner life — has nothing to offer the congregation member who sits there in exactly that condition every week. There is one in the third row right now. One in the back who has not slept in three months because of a diagnosis. One near the exit whose marriage is ending. They do not need a man who has managed the text into a clean three-point structure. They need a man who has been in the dark and is willing to say so.

When preaching goes stale, the first and most important question is not *what technique can I recover* but *when did I stop going to the dark places?* When did I start reading the text only as material to be processed for Sunday rather than as a message addressed to me, specifically, about my own life with God? The preacher whose personal devotional life has become indistinguishable from his sermon preparation is a preacher who has stopped eating and started cooking. He handles food all day. He is starving.

---

The structural problem underneath stale preaching is often isolation. Elijah, exhausted after Carmel, did not need a vision or a new strategy. He needed sleep, bread, water, and someone who said *the journey is too great for you* (1 Kings 19:7). What he received was presence. The preacher who preaches to community without living inside community of his own will eventually run out of the kind of deep knowing that makes preaching land somewhere other than the surface.

Preaching is always, on some level, the articulation of what has been lived. When a pastor is living his whole life inside the church building — managing, administering, counseling, troubleshooting, performing the pastoral presence that the congregation expects — and has no life outside that frame that is genuinely his own, the preaching will eventually reflect the deprivation. There is nothing coming in that is not immediately being processed for consumption. The well cannot give what it is not receiving.

This is why the ancient practice of *lectio divina* — the slow, prayerful reading of Scripture as a reader rather than as a preacher — is not a luxury. It is a survival requirement. Not reading to find next week's sermon. Reading because God might say something to you, specifically, today. Eugene Peterson argued consistently across his career that the pastor who had no life before God apart from ministry preparation was not a pastor but a religious professional, and that the distinction mattered for the congregation as much as it mattered for the pastor himself [cite — confirm]. The congregation gets what the pastor is. When the pastor is empty, the congregation gets emptiness dressed in competence.

---

Steel-manning the drift is important here: there are legitimate explanations for a season of staleness that have nothing to do with spiritual failure. Grief does this. Protracted conflict does this. The kind of exhaustion that accumulates across fifteen years of sustained giving without adequate replenishment does this too. Sometimes the well is not polluted. It is simply empty. And an empty well needs to be filled, not blamed.

But even that diagnosis points to the same answer. The filling does not happen through ministry productivity. It happens through the kind of sustained, unhurried encounter with the living God that the ministry machine is designed, inadvertently, to prevent. The meeting is never done. The email never goes to zero. The need is never fully met. And so the pastor who waits for his schedule to clear before he will seek God — before he will take the retreat, before he will sit with the text without an agenda, before he will let himself be prayed for rather than always being the one who prays — will wait forever, and slowly die in the waiting.

The most practically urgent thing a preacher can do when his preaching goes stale is to stop trying to fix the preaching and start asking what has happened to the preacher. Trace the moment when the obligation arrived and the encounter left. When did Sunday become primarily a performance event rather than a moment of genuine witness? When did the text stop being the place where God addresses you and become the material from which you construct addresses to others?

Go back to that moment. Not with self-condemnation — self-condemnation is another form of productivity, another way of staying busy in the soul's house rather than opening the windows. Go back to it with curiosity. Something changed. Name what it was. Was it a loss? A conflict? A season of success that subtly shifted your identity from servant to performer? The sermon preparation cannot carry you forward until the preacher himself is moving in the right direction.

---

There is also the community question, which the isolated pastor never asks. The stale preacher almost always preaches into a vacuum — he does not know what is actually happening in the lives of the people he is preaching to. He knows the aggregate, the demographic, the general categories of suffering that his congregation contains. He does not know the specific person in the third row who is going to hear the passage he is preaching on Sunday. He has stopped making hospital visits and started managing systems. The pastoral texture of his ministry has thinned, and the preaching has thinned with it, because preaching at its best is always a response to the actual people actually present, and you cannot respond well to people you do not know.

This is not a call to emotional exploitation — the sermon that mines pastoral encounters for illustrative material without the parishioner's knowledge is a violation of trust, not an example of good preaching. It is a call to sustained presence among the people being served, so that the preacher knows from the inside what the congregation is carrying, and can speak to it with the specificity that distinguishes prophetic preaching from generic religious content.

The verdict: you cannot give what you have stopped receiving. The fix is not more preparation. The fix is more exposure — to text you are reading for yourself, to people who know you past your title, to the God who called you into this work in the first place.

The sermon that matters next Sunday is not built in the study on Thursday. It is built in the accumulated faithfulness of a life before God across the whole week. When that faithfulness is present, even a preacher who is uncertain and unpolished will find that what he says carries weight — not because he performed it well, but because it is true, and truth has mass.

The fire is not gone. But you may need to stop running long enough to find where it went.

There is a season in a marriage when you look at your spouse across the table and the feeling you have is not warm. Not hostile — just neutral. The chemistry that was once effortless now requires effort, and effort applied to romance feels like a contradiction in terms. The feeling that used to arrive uninvited no longer arrives at all.

This is the season most couples never discuss with anyone. It feels like a verdict on the marriage, and they are afraid of what that verdict is. So they perform contentment in public and carry the quiet flatness in private, waiting for something to change or for the reason they are still doing this to become clear again.

The question that lives in this season is a real one: Is a marriage without romance still a marriage worth keeping? And the answer depends entirely on what you think romance is for.

## What the Culture Taught Us to Expect

The modern assumption is that romance is the marriage — that the covenant is the container for the feeling, and when the feeling goes, the container has lost its reason to exist. This is not a Christian idea. It is a Romantic-era idea — a product of the late eighteenth century, crystallized by Rousseau and Goethe and their literary descendants — with enough cultural saturation that most people cannot see it as an idea at all. It just feels true.

The Romantic movement placed the individual's inner experience at the center of moral authority. Feeling became the measure of the real. A love that felt powerful was genuine; a love that did not feel powerful was counterfeit or dead. Marriage entered this framework as the permanent institutional expression of a feeling that was, by its nature, impermanent — which meant that marriage as an institution was set up to fail from the moment the Romantic framework defined what success required.

We are still inside this story. The divorce rate is not primarily a product of immoral people making selfish choices. It is primarily a product of people who genuinely believe what their culture has taught them: that the feeling is the marriage, and that when the feeling fades, the marriage has ended, even if the legal arrangement has not caught up yet.

## What the Scripture Actually Offers

The Hebrew of Song of Solomon uses a word — *dodi*, my beloved — that carries both sensory delight and covenantal commitment woven together. The erotic poetry of the text is not the church's embarrassment. It is its argument: that physical and spiritual love are not opposed, that embodied delight is part of what covenant is for. But even there — in the most unambiguously romantic text in the canon — the love is particular, directed toward a specific person, shaped by a specific history. "His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me" (Song of Solomon 2:6). This is not a song about the experience of romance in general. It is a song about a specific person in the presence of a specific other.

The covenantal logic of the Hebrew Scriptures runs counter to the Romantic logic at every point. Ruth's declaration to Naomi in Ruth 1:16 — "where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay" — is not a description of feeling. It is a declaration of will, made in the teeth of circumstances that warranted departure. The covenant holds precisely when the feeling does not compel it.

In the New Testament, Paul's instruction to husbands in Ephesians 5:25 — "love your wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" — does not appeal to romantic feeling as the motivation for marital love. It appeals to a pattern of costly self-giving that is independent of emotional state. Christ did not go to the cross because it felt natural. He went because he was committed. That commitment is the model for marital love, and it is a commitment that survives the seasons in which feeling does not arrive uninvited.

The question is not whether romance dies. It does. The question is whether what comes after it is worth staying for.

## A Steel-Manned Counter-Position

Before I answer that question too quickly, the counter-position deserves its full weight. There is a version of covenant-theology that has functioned as a trap rather than a gift — that has told people (often women, disproportionately) to stay in marriages that were not merely romantically flat but actively harmful, citing covenant obligation as the reason. The theological argument for the permanence of marriage has been used to cover abuse, to suppress legitimate need, and to insist on the form of covenant fidelity while the substance of it was long gone.

I am not arguing for that. Covenant fidelity is not the same as the obligation to remain in a dangerous situation. The question I am addressing is not "should I stay in a marriage that is harming me" but "should I stay in a marriage where the romance has faded and I am not sure it will return." These are not the same question, and conflating them has done enormous damage.

The covenant argument for staying is a powerful one. But it is not an argument for staying at any cost, under any conditions, regardless of what staying requires of the one who stays. It is an argument that the presence or absence of romantic feeling is not, by itself, an adequate reason to leave a marriage that is otherwise intact. That is a narrower claim, and it is the one worth defending.

## The Covenant That Holds When Feeling Fades

A covenant is not a feeling. It is a commitment made in the presence of witnesses and God. It is a promise to remain even when the promise becomes hard, even when the other person disappoints you, even when you disappoint yourself.

The modern marriage culture has inverted this. We treat the feeling as the covenant and the covenant as the feeling. We ask marriage to do what only romance can do — produce the constant sense of being chosen, delighted in, pursued. And when marriage cannot do that (because it is not marriage's job), we conclude that the marriage has failed.

A marriage that lasts long enough will move through seasons. The season of effortless attraction gives way to the season of chosen commitment. The season of discovery gives way to the season of depth. The season of romance gives way to the season of covenant.

This is not a tragedy. This is maturity. And maturity has its own beauty, though it is not the beauty the Romantic tradition taught us to want.

## A Concrete Scene

I know a couple who have been married for thirty-one years. In their eighteenth year, they reached a period that lasted nearly two years in which neither of them would have described what they felt as love — not in the way the word had meant at the beginning. They were exhausted by children and debt and a period of ministry that had taken more than it gave. They were civil. They were functional. They were not intimate in any of the ways that matter.

They did not leave. They did not perform happiness they did not feel. They stayed, and they stayed honestly — which meant they told each other the truth about where they were, which was harder than leaving would have been. The honesty was the turning point. Not a dramatic revival of romantic feeling. Just two people deciding that the covenant was a reason to keep returning, even when returning did not feel like anything.

The woman told me: "I stopped waiting for the feeling to justify the commitment. I let the commitment carry us until the feeling came back. And it did come back. But it came back as something different. Deeper, I think. Less exciting and more true."

## What Happens When You Stop Waiting for the Feeling to Return

The couples who move through this season well do something counterintuitive: they stop waiting for the feeling to return and start building something else. They invest in the marriage not because they feel like it, but because they committed to it. They choose each other daily, not because the choice is easy, but because the alternative — the dissolution of something sacred — is worse.

They discover that commitment, lived out consistently over time, produces something the initial romance never could: a deep, textured, resilient love that has survived disappointment and chosen to stay anyway. This is the love that can hold you when everything else falls apart. This is the love that knows you — not the version of you that you present on good days, but the actual you, with all your failures and fears and contradictions — and chooses you anyway.

The theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in a letter from prison that it is not your love that sustains your marriage but the marriage that sustains your love [cite — confirm]. He was onto something. The structure holds the content until the content can stand on its own. The covenant provides the container in which the deeper love — the one that is less exciting and more true — is slowly formed.

## Three Questions for This Week

What did you think romance was for when you got married? What do you think it is for now?

If the feeling never returns to what it was, would you stay? What would that require of you?

What is one way you could choose your spouse this week — not because you feel like it, but because you committed to?

Tell your spouse one specific thing you appreciate about them that has nothing to do with romance — something you have discovered about their character, their faithfulness, their presence in your life.

## The Weight of What Remains

The couples who last are not the ones for whom romance never fades. They are the ones who discover that something deeper than romance can grow in its place. They are the ones who learn that covenant, kept faithfully through the seasons, becomes its own kind of beauty — less like a fire, more like a foundation, the kind of thing you do not notice until everything else is shaking and it does not move.

The flatness in your marriage right now may not be a verdict. It may be an invitation. An invitation to stop relying on the feeling to carry the commitment, and to let the commitment carry you until the feeling finds its new form.

Not romance. Something better. Something that stays.

You were never designed to carry the weight of ministry alone — and the Gospel you preach proves it. You know how to shepherd. You've sat with people in hospital rooms at midnight. You have driven across town to sit with a family that just got the worst phone call of their lives. You have stood at graves in February and said the words that hold people together when nothing else will.

So let me ask you a question, and I want you to sit with it before you answer: Who shepherds you?

Most pastors I talk to go silent when I ask that. Some give an answer — naming a spouse, a mentor, a close friend — and when I probe it, what I find is that the relationship they are describing is one where they process the work of ministry. The logistical difficulties. The difficult people. The institutional frustrations. But not the interior of their own souls. There is a difference. The person who listens to you talk about your board is not necessarily the person who is watching your soul.

## What the Gospel You Preach Actually Says

You were never designed to carry the weight of ministry alone. The Gospel you preach says so, clearly and without qualification. It says that the human self in isolation is not the design — it is the fracture. "It is not good for man to be alone" (Genesis 2:18) is not a comment about marriage, at least not exclusively. It is a description of the structure of human existence. We are made for dependence on God and for interdependence with one another. The pastor who has constructed a ministry life in which he is the one who gives care and never the one who receives it has not achieved spiritual maturity. He has reproduced in himself the very isolation the Gospel came to address.

Paul asked for prayer. Repeatedly. The man who wrote "I can do all things through him who strengthens me" (Philippians 4:13) also wrote "pray for us" (1 Thessalonians 5:25) and "I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf" (Romans 15:30). He was not performing humility. He was naming a real dependence. The apostle to the Gentiles, the man who planted churches across the Mediterranean, publicly named his need for the prayers of the people he served. The relationship was mutual, not hierarchical. He gave them the Gospel and they gave him their prayers, and neither one was optional.

The pastor who cannot ask for prayer — who cannot name his own need to the people he leads — has confused professional distance with spiritual strength. They are not the same thing.

## What the Role Does Over Time

The loneliness of pastoral leadership is structurally produced. The congregation needs you to be the strong one, the settled presence in the storm, the person with answers. That role creates a relentless pull toward the management of appearances — toward performing stability even when the interior is not stable, toward projecting competence even when the situation is genuinely difficult.

This does not happen suddenly. It develops slowly, across years. As the weight of holding confidences separates you from the community. As the role creates distance that feels like maturity but is actually isolation. As the fear of appearing weak makes you progressively less willing to name what is actually happening inside you. As the performance becomes so practiced that you begin to lose track of the difference between the performance and the person.

And then one day you look up and you realize that you have no one. No one who knows the actual state of your marriage, not just the pastoral-care version of it. No one who knows that you have been carrying the same doubt for three years. No one who would notice if you stopped praying, because no one is close enough to see. The isolation is comfortable in the way that numbness is comfortable — you stop feeling the lack because you have adapted to it.

I have been in that place. I have sat in my study after a Sunday morning where everything went well — the service was strong, the people were encouraged, the feedback was warm — and felt something close to despair, because the performance of pastoral health and actual pastoral health are two entirely different things, and I had been performing long enough that I had lost track of which one I was doing. The congregation received something that looked fine. I was not fine.

## What Ezekiel 34 Names

Ezekiel 34 is the prophet's extended indictment of the shepherds of Israel — the leaders who have failed the flock. He describes them as shepherds who have fed themselves and neglected the sheep, who "have not strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bound up the injured" (Ezekiel 34:4). The passage is usually preached as a warning to pastors about neglecting their congregations. That reading is correct and important.

But there is another side of the passage that is less often addressed. The God who indicts the failed shepherds also promises: "I myself will tend my sheep and have them lie down, declares the Sovereign Lord. I will search for the lost and bring back the strayed. I will bind up the injured and strengthen the weak" (Ezekiel 34:15-16). The shepherd image runs in both directions. The congregation needs the pastor to shepherd. The pastor needs God to shepherd him. The failure mode Ezekiel is describing — the shepherd who consumes what the flock provides without tending the flock — is the failure mode of a man who has stopped receiving what he needs, which is why he is taking what he should be giving.

The pastor who is not being shepherded will eventually become one of two things: a consumer or a hollow man. The consumer takes from the congregation what was meant to be given to them — attention, affirmation, the emotional supply that comes from being needed — because he has no other source of nourishment. The hollow man goes through the motions without the interior life that the motions are supposed to express, because the interior life has not been tended by anyone.

## What Shepherding the Shepherd Requires

It requires someone who will not treat you primarily as a pastor. A peer, a spiritual director, a counselor who has no stake in the church's success, a friend whose relationship to you predates the ministry and exists outside it. Someone who will ask the real question — "How are you, actually?" — and wait for the real answer. Not "how's the church going" but "what is actually happening in you right now."

It requires that you stop protecting the image long enough to answer that question honestly. Not for the sake of emotional processing. For the sake of your soul. The pastor whose interior life has not been named and witnessed by another human being in years is a pastor whose interior life is likely deteriorating in ways that will eventually show up in the pulpit, in the marriage, in the slow erosion of the capacity for genuine pastoral care.

David had Nathan. Nathan was the one who walked into the room after David's worst decision — the arranged death of Uriah, the taking of Bathsheba, the abuse of a position of power so comprehensive that it reads as the full catalogue of what unchecked power does — and said: "You are the man" (2 Samuel 12:7). The prophet named what the king could not see about himself because the king had no one close enough to tell him. Nathan was not an enabler. He was not a flatterer. He was not someone who needed David to remain strong. He was the one who told the truth.

You need a Nathan. Not someone who needs you to be well so that their own faith is stable. Someone who will look at you clearly and say what they see.

The Psalms gave David a space to name what was actually happening inside him — the rage, the grief, the abandonment, the hope, the despair, the vindication — in all its violence and darkness, and put it before God. The fact that those prayers are in the canon is not incidental. God received them. He did not require David to perform stability before he would listen. He received the real thing, including the parts that were not edifying.

You are permitted to do the same. The God who received Psalm 88 — which ends without resolution, without comfort, with the speaker still in the dark — is the God who will receive your actual interior life and not only the version you have edited for public consumption.

## Who Is That Person for You

Who is that person for you right now? If you can name someone immediately, without hesitation — someone who knows you well enough to see you, who has the relationship with you to tell you the truth, who is not dependent on your performance remaining strong — then you have something worth protecting. Protect it.

If you cannot name anyone, that is the most important pastoral problem you currently have. More important than the difficult elder. More important than the declining attendance numbers. More important than the budget. The ministry that is running on the fumes of a depleted interior will eventually stop, and the stopping will be more damaging than anything the difficult elder or the budget shortfall could produce.

The shepherd needs shepherding. The Gospel you preach has always known this. The question is whether you have the honesty to apply to yourself the same truth you preach to everyone else.

You know how to sit with people in their hardest moments. This is one of yours. Sit with it.

The church in America has a history that is not primarily the history of courage and faithfulness, though it contains that. It is, in significant stretches, a history of silence in the face of injustice — a silence that was often theological, often institutional, and almost always served the interests of the church's own comfort and cultural position more than the interests of the people the silence abandoned.

That is the sentence I would prefer not to write. It is also the sentence the church would prefer not to hear. That preference — the preference to tell the flattering half of our story and call the omission discretion — is itself a form of the problem.

So let us be specific, because specificity is where the reckoning gets real.

The silence during chattel slavery: when the dominant theological tradition not only failed to oppose the institution but provided the biblical justifications for it. Theologians wrote careful treatises. Pastors preached from the text to defend the buying and selling of human beings made in God's image. The denominational machinery split not because the church chose conscience over culture, but because it chose culture over conscience — and the fractures along those lines persist in American church life to this day. Albert Barnes, writing in 1846 [cite — confirm publication details], catalogued the rationalizations and found them wanting. But Barnes was the exception. The majority held the comfortable position.

The silence during Jim Crow: when the white church largely acquiesced to a system of racial terror and legal apartheid that its own theology should have made intolerable. The cross stood in front of churches whose members rode in the night, or who knew the riders and said nothing, or who considered their silence the better part of wisdom. Emmett Till was fourteen years old. The murderers were acquitted in sixty-seven minutes. The churches in that county held services the following Sunday and the text was not Micah 6:8 and the application was not repentance.

The silence during the civil rights movement: when the majority of white evangelical and mainline churches were not on the side of the movement but were, at best, uncomfortable bystanders and, at worst, active opponents of the very justice the prophets had announced. Martin Luther King Jr. wrote his Letter from Birmingham Jail not to the Klan but to the clergy — the white moderates who preferred order to truth, who found his methods too disruptive, who kept asking him to be patient. [cite — confirm exact letter recipients.] That letter is one of the most theologically precise documents produced in twentieth-century American Christianity, and its primary audience was the church that would not move.

This is not comfortable history. It is not the history the church tells about itself in its promotional materials. But it is the history — and the church that refuses to reckon with it honestly is a church that has chosen comfort over truthfulness, which is itself a continuation of the pattern.

---

Here is where I need to be careful, because this kind of reckoning gets weaponized in both directions.

Some use the history to indict the faith itself, as though the failures of the church disprove the gospel. They do not. They prove, rather, that the gospel was not applied — that the institution substituted cultural allegiance for theological conviction and called the exchange faithful. The standard by which we can name these things failures is the gospel itself. A Christianity capacious enough to produce Harriet Tubman and Dietrich Bonhoeffer [cite — confirm Bonhoeffer's explicit anti-racism work] and the abolitionist wing of the church is not the problem. The problem is what happens when that Christianity gets domesticated, when it makes peace with the systems it was always supposed to confront.

Others refuse the reckoning entirely. They hear any honest account of the past as an attack on the faith, and they retreat into the flattering half of the story. They point to the abolitionists — correctly — and then stop there, as though the abolitionists' courage excuses the majority's silence. It does not. Courage in some parts of the church does not baptize cowardice in the rest.

Both evasions miss the same thing: the capacity for repentance that is the church's greatest asset and most consistently abandoned gift. We cannot repent of what we will not name.

---

And it is ours to name. Not theirs. Ours.

This is the part the comfortable Christian wants to skip. It is easy to condemn the slaveholding preacher across the distance of a century and a half — it costs nothing, and it allows me to locate myself on the right side without examining whether I am actually on it. I would almost certainly not have been the brave exception. The people who defended the indefensible were not monsters. They were ordinary believers who let their culture, their comfort, and their economic interest read the Bible for them. They had prayer lives and family devotions and genuine piety in other respects. Their failure was not a failure of religion but a failure to let religion mean what it meant — a failure to let the God of Exodus be more determinative than the comfort of empire.

That is not a nineteenth-century disease. It is the permanent temptation of the church in every age, and I am not outside it. I know what it is to let the cost of a sermon suppress the text it should have come from. I know what it is to preach around the thing that would cost something. The mechanism has not changed.

---

The biblical pattern is unambiguous and worth sitting with longer than we usually do.

The prophets in Israel were not sent primarily to the pagan nations. They were sent to the people of God — to a worshiping community whose songs God could not tolerate because their hands were full of injustice. "When you come to appear before me," God says through Isaiah, "who has required of you this trampling of my courts?" (Isaiah 1:12). "Your hands are full of blood" (Isaiah 1:15). The indictment falls on the faithful, not the faithless.

Amos is even harder. He speaks directly to religious people who kept the feast days and offered burnt offerings — people who had a rigorous liturgical life — and God tells them: "I hate, I despise your feasts, and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies" (Amos 5:21). Why? Because justice was not rolling down like waters. Because the poor were being ground down while the worshipers sang. The religious performance and the social indifference were not separate problems. The second made a mockery of the first.

Jesus did not soften this. The harshest judgment in Matthew 25 is not pronounced on the overtly wicked but on those who saw the stranger, the hungry, the imprisoned — and passed by. Not malicious. Not cruel. Simply absent. "I did not know you" is the verdict, and it comes after a lifetime of apparently religious activity (Matthew 25:44-45).

Ezekiel catalogued the sins of Sodom and found, at the head of the list, not the sexual immorality that dominates our cultural memory of that story, but this: "Behold, this was the guilt of your sister Sodom: she and her daughters had pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy" (Ezekiel 16:49). Excess and ease, combined with the failure to aid those in need. That indictment has more purchase on contemporary American Christianity than most of our pulpits have been willing to admit.

---

Consider a steel-manned version of the counter-position.

The argument goes: the church should not become a political organization. Conflating the gospel with any particular social agenda distorts the church's primary mission, which is the proclamation of salvation through Christ. History shows that churches that lead with social reform eventually lose the gospel altogether, and the progressive mainline denominations stand as evidence. Better to stick to what the church knows — worship, Scripture, the sacraments — and let political engagement remain the work of individual Christians.

That argument has real weight. The social gospel movement of the early twentieth century did produce churches that traded away theological substance for progressive politics, and those churches are dying, not because justice killed them but because the gospel departed before justice arrived. The concern about politicization is not paranoia; it is the memory of a real catastrophe.

But the argument proves too much. It assumes that the church's choice is between the gospel and justice, when the Hebrew prophets and the New Testament make them inseparable. Jesus does not present the kingdom as a spiritual reality floating above the material conditions of human beings. He announces it in a world where the poor are crushed, where the widow is ignored, where the prisoner is forgotten — and he says the kingdom's arrival changes that. Not as a secondary application of a spiritual gospel. As constitutive of what the gospel is.

The churches that traded the gospel for progressive politics did not fail because they cared about justice. They failed because they stopped believing in the resurrection, the unique authority of Scripture, the reality of sin — and justice untethered from those convictions becomes simply the politics of the moment wearing clerical vestments. The answer to that failure is not to abandon justice. The answer is to recover the full theology that makes justice coherent — the theology in which human beings have dignity because they bear God's image, in which injustice is offense against a holy God, in which the arc of history bends toward a kingdom not built by human effort alone.

---

A concrete scene, because the history can remain abstract in ways that protect us.

A pastor in the 1950s South, by all accounts a good man — kind to the families in his congregation, faithful to his visiting schedule, a good preacher, a loving husband and father. He knows what is happening. He has seen the signs on the water fountains. He has heard the stories. He reads his Bible; he knows what Micah says. But there are powerful men in his congregation who built their businesses on the existing order, and there are families whose sons are on the county police force, and there are deacons who have made it clear that the church is not the place for this. And so he preaches. He preaches faithfully on many things. He is not a bad man. He never preaches a word of support for the system. He simply never preaches a word against it either.

And the people in his congregation, the ones without property and without protection, go to bed each Sunday night knowing that the man who opened the Bible this morning does not think they are worth the risk of a hard sermon.

I know that pastor's calculation because I have made versions of it.
