A person formed in the Reformed tradition and a person formed in the Pentecostal tradition will read the same chapter of Acts and notice different things, weight different emphases, find different centers of gravity. Neither is simply wrong. Both are reading from inside a tradition that has selected for certain things and against others.

We read against our enemies. The passages most weaponized in American culture-war Christianity are the ones that address behaviors associated with the opposing tribe. The passages that address the behaviors most characteristic of the tribe doing the reading receive considerably less attention. This is not unique to one side. It is the universal human tendency to read the prophets' indictment as aimed at someone else.

---

The honest counter-position deserves a full hearing.

The argument runs: if every reading is conditioned by the reader's context, then there is no authoritative reading — only competing interpretations, none more valid than another. This leads to interpretive relativism, in which the text means whatever the reader brings to it, and the church loses any capacity to say that some interpretations are wrong. The result is the kind of theological drift that has characterized the progressive churches — where Scripture gets reinterpreted until it endorses whatever the current cultural consensus holds, and the prophetic distance between the gospel and the culture collapses entirely.

This is a serious argument and it names a real danger. The solution to the problem of conditioned reading is not to abandon the claim that the text has a meaning that exists independent of the reader. It is to pursue that meaning with all available tools — careful exegesis, attention to historical context, the witness of the broader tradition, the correction of the community, the illumination of the Spirit — while holding the results with the honesty that any finite reader is still a finite reader.

The tradition is not useless. The creeds were not written by people who had stopped caring what the text actually said. The councils of the early church — wrestling with the nature of Christ, the Trinity, the relationship between the testaments — were doing exegetical work, even when they were also doing political work. The tradition is the cumulative reading of the church across time, and it has real authority — not as a substitute for the text but as a correction of the individual reader's inevitable distortions.

The Reformation's *sola scriptura* was not a claim that each individual reader could determine the text's meaning in isolation. It was a claim that the text stood in judgment over the tradition, that tradition could not add to Scripture what Scripture did not authorize. Even that claim required a community to apply it — the community of Reformed interpretation, accountable to the same text, correcting each other's readings over centuries.

The answer to conditioned reading is not epistemic humility that dissolves into relativism. It is the specific humility of a reader who knows they are conditioned and seeks, by every available means, to be corrected — by the text's own internal logic, by the witness of the historically marginalized whose reading of the same text looks different from the majority reading, by the accumulated wisdom of the tradition, by the willingness to be wrong.

---

The practical implication is not abstract.

Read the parts of the Bible that make you uncomfortable. The parts that are addressed to someone who looks like you in your position of relative comfort, who is doing something that people in your position typically do, and who is told by the prophet or the apostle that it is not acceptable. Those passages are not aimed at your enemy. They are aimed at you. Read them slowly. Read them with the assumption that they mean what they say before you begin finding the reasons they must mean something else.

Read with people who are unlike you. The tradition of reading that has been formed entirely within one culture, one class, one racial or national community is a tradition that has consistently filtered out the things that community preferred not to see. The Black church's reading of Exodus is not less valid than the white evangelical reading of Romans. It is, in many ways, more dangerous — more accurate to the raw experience of the text because it has been read by people for whom the experience of bondage and liberation is not metaphorical.

Read with the honest question: what would I need to give up if this passage means what it appears to mean? If the answer to that question is something you are not willing to give up, you have identified the lens.

---

The Pharisees were not bad people. They were people who had confused their reading of the text with the text itself — who had so thoroughly identified their interpretive tradition with divine authority that when the thing the text was pointing toward arrived, they could not see him.

That is not a first-century problem. It is the permanent temptation of every community of faith that has lived with the text long enough to feel at home in it. The familiarity is a gift. It is also a danger.

The Bible does not change. But our interpretation of it does. And the room you are reading it in — right now, today, in this particular moment of American history, inside whatever fears and hopes and cultural formations have shaped you — that room is shaping what you see.

You are not the exception to this. Neither am I. The question is whether we will be humble enough to know it — and honest enough to let that knowledge do something.

The departure of young adults from the American church was so consistent and so well-documented over the first two decades of this century that it began to feel like a settled trajectory — that the demographic math was simply pointing in one direction and would continue to do so indefinitely. The Pew Research Center and Barna Group both tracked the decline with enough precision to generate an entire industry of church-response strategies: contemporary worship, shorter sermons, better coffee, relevance-speak from the pulpit. [cite — confirm] Most of those strategies failed to reverse the trend, which should have told us something about the nature of the problem.

Recent data suggests the picture is more complicated. [cite — confirm] Some young adults are coming back. The question worth asking is why — and what that means for the churches they are entering.

The return is not driven by what the church was doing to attract them. That is the first important thing to understand. The young adults returning to faith communities in meaningful numbers are not returning because a congregation's marketing got better or because the worship service became more accessible. They are returning because something in their lives — a birth, a death, a marriage, a crisis, a sustained encounter with mortality or meaninglessness — pressed them against questions that the secular alternatives in their lives could not adequately answer. The return is, in many cases, a return to questions they left behind, not a return to the institution they remembered.

The secular alternatives they encountered in their twenties were not without substance. This matters for the reception the church offers. Many of the young adults who left the church did not leave because they found the gospel intellectually indefensible. They left because the version of Christianity they were handed could not hold the weight of the questions they were carrying — questions about suffering, about justice, about the integrity of the church's own institutional conduct, about whether the faith was actually doing the work it claimed in the lives of the people who held it. The church they left was, in many cases, not the church that had engaged those questions seriously. It was the church that had managed them away.

When they return, they carry the full weight of what they have lived through in the years since. They have watched parents' marriages dissolve. They have sat with dying friends. They have encountered institutional corruption in places they trusted. They have felt the specific texture of contemporary meaninglessness — the peculiar emptiness of a life organized around consumption and productivity that nevertheless cannot explain why any of it matters. They are not coming back for nostalgia. They are coming back because they have run out of secular answers to questions that will not stop being asked.

This creates both an opportunity and a danger for the church. The opportunity is that these returning adults are not looking for the same thing they were offered before. They left partly because the version of Christianity they encountered could not sustain serious engagement with life's hardest realities. They are coming back, many of them, specifically because they have now lived enough of those realities to know they need something with more weight. They are not satisfied with consumer experience. They will not be satisfied with the version of Christianity that is primarily a community of pleasantness with Jesus-shaped decoration.

The danger is that the church, encountering a return of young adults, will immediately try to reproduce what produced the previous engagement — more accessible services, stronger programming for their demographic, contemporary music, a pastor who speaks their cultural language. If these returning adults came back looking for depth and encounter what they find is a more polished version of the superficiality they left, they will leave again, faster than before, and this time with much less likelihood of return. The second departure is harder to come back from than the first.

The parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11–32) is usually read as a story about an individual's restoration. But it contains a portrait of the kind of reception that makes return possible — and the kind that makes it impossible. The father does not redesign the estate to look like the far country. He does not pretend the departure never happened. He does not present the son with a list of conditions for reentry. He runs. He embraces. He throws a party. He restores the relationship at full cost to himself without waiting for the son to prove his rehabilitation.

And there is the elder brother, who cannot receive the return because he is counting what it cost and who is getting what. The elder brother is not a villain. He is a person whose years of faithful work have produced a measuring posture that makes genuine welcome impossible. The church that greets the returning young adult with an implicit accounting of what he missed, what he owed, what he must now demonstrate before he belongs — that church is the elder brother, and the returning son will read the reception accurately.

What the returning young adult needs is not a redesigned worship service. It is a community capable of holding who she actually is now — who has lived through the secular alternatives, who carries real questions and real doubts and real disappointment, who does not need to be convinced that life is hard but who needs to know whether the gospel has anything to say about life as it actually is.

The intellectual dimension of this is underestimated. A significant portion of the young adults who left the church left because they encountered — in college, in graduate school, in the literature they read, in the conversations they had — serious intellectual challenges to Christian belief that the church had not prepared them to engage. The problem of evil. The relationship between faith and neuroscience. The historical criticism of Scripture. The moral record of Christianity across its history. These are not simple questions, and the church that dismissed them as threats to be avoided rather than challenges to be engaged honestly forfeited the trust of the people carrying them.

The church that will keep the returning young adult is the one that can hold the conversation about those questions seriously — not to provide clean answers to every hard problem, but to demonstrate that the faith is not afraid of the questions, that the intellectual tradition of Christianity has engaged these challenges with real rigor, and that doubt can coexist with commitment without one destroying the other.

I have watched people come back and leave again within six months because the community they found was warm but shallow. I have also watched people come back and stay, and what kept them was almost never the music or the building. It was the experience of being genuinely known — known in the specific texture of who they were now, not who they had been before they left. It was the experience of a community that had some idea what to do with questions, with grief, with the person they actually were rather than the person the church wished they had become.

The theological substance this requires is not novel. It is the same substance the church has always had, when it has had the courage to offer it without the protective coating of palatability. Augustine's *Confessions* — the record of a life trying to satisfy its hungers in every possible direction before arriving at the one place the hunger could be addressed — has been reaching exactly this person for sixteen centuries. [cite — confirm] Pascal's articulation of the *God-shaped hole* has named the specific texture of secular meaninglessness in terms that map precisely onto the experience of the returning young adult. [cite — confirm] The tradition is not thin. The church's presentation of the tradition has sometimes been.

What does this require from the church in practice? It requires preachers who take intellectual objections seriously from the pulpit, who name the hard questions rather than managing them away, who demonstrate that faith and inquiry are not opposites. It requires small communities where depth is possible — where someone can say "I'm not sure I believe this" and receive engagement rather than alarm. It requires the patience to hold the returning person in the ambiguity of their re-entry, not requiring that they perform certainty they do not have before they are fully welcomed.

The returning young adult is not a demographic opportunity. She is not a sign that the church's strategy is working. She is a neighbor who went to a far country and came back. She is hungry, and she has been traveling a long time, and she does not need the church's congratulations for the return.

She needs what the father gave: the embrace before the explanation, the table before the accounting, the robe and the ring before the conversation about what happened.

The question is what she finds when she arrives.

Make it worth the walk home.

When Jeremiah wrote to the exiles in Babylon, he did not tell them to keep their distance from the city until the rescue came. He told them to build houses, plant gardens, marry, raise children — and to "seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare" (Jeremiah 29:7). Seek the shalom of Babylon. The place of captivity was also the place of calling.

This is the instruction that most of us have not fully received.

The word Jeremiah uses — *shalom* — carries more weight than the English "welfare" can hold. It does not mean simply the absence of conflict. It means the comprehensive flourishing of a community: right relationships, just structures, material provision, the kind of order in which people and creation can thrive together. The exiles were being instructed to invest themselves in the comprehensive flourishing of the city that had conquered them. Not to assimilate — Jeremiah's letter opens with commands that presuppose maintained identity. But to serve. To be present. To let their welfare be bound up with the welfare of the people around them.

That is the posture that missional theology, at its best, has tried to recover. And it is the posture that most American churches, in practice, have not adopted.

There is a particular version of Christian mission that locates the real work somewhere else — in the Global South, in the unreached people groups, in the countries where missionaries go and churches pray for and support financially. None of that is wrong. The global mission of the church is real and costly and necessary. What is wrong is the proportion — the amount of missiological imagination we pour into distant places relative to the amount we invest in the specific block where the church building sits.

I have sat in churches that sent teams to Africa while their immediate neighborhood had no Christian presence with any relationship to the people who actually lived there. I have sat with pastors who could name unreached people groups in Southeast Asia but could not name the dominant ethnic community within six blocks of their congregation's front door. I have been that pastor. I have been more conversant with global statistics than with the actual human beings whose daily life takes place in the shadow of our steeple.

The global mission does not excuse the local one. It actually depends on it. The New Testament pattern of mission is centrifugal — moving outward from the community where discipleship is practiced to the communities adjacent to it and then beyond. Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). The ends of the earth are the culmination of the movement, not the substitute for the beginning. A church that skips Jerusalem and Judea for the ends of the earth has confused the direction of the arrow.

The historical pattern is instructive here. The remarkable expansion of the early church through the cities of the Roman Empire — Antioch, Corinth, Ephesus, Rome — happened not primarily through strategic missionary deployment but through the daily life of ordinary Christians whose neighbors noticed that they lived differently. Rodney Stark has argued, controversially but with evidence, that the early church's growth was substantially powered by its response to urban crises — the epidemics of the second and third centuries that drove wealthy Romans to flee the cities while Christians stayed to care for the sick and bury the dead [cite — confirm]. Whether or not one accepts all of Stark's argument, the basic pattern is well attested in early church sources: the church was present where others were absent. It was in the city. It was in the suffering. It was seen.

The local mission is harder than the distant one in a particular way. Distant mission allows a kind of abstraction — you send money, you pray for names, you support work you will never see and people you will never know. That abstraction is not nothing. But it can also insulate you from the specific, demanding, human work of loving your actual neighbors — who are complicated, who may not be interested in what you are offering, who know things about your neighborhood that you do not, who have needs that your current programming is not designed to address.

The counter-position deserves honest engagement: there are genuine reasons why the local can feel more elusive than the distant. The church that is embedded in a middle-class suburban neighborhood may be genuinely limited in its capacity to address urban poverty across the city. The distance is real. The cultural gap is real. Parachuting into a community you do not inhabit with solutions developed by people who do not live there can cause real harm, and some churches have learned to stay in their lane as a form of humility, not evasion.

True. And insufficient. The call to seek the shalom of the city does not require you to solve everything from a distance. It requires you to be actually present to the people God has placed around you — however proximate they are, however complex the relationship. You do not need to understand everything before you begin. You need to show up. You need to be a neighbor, in the sense that Jesus meant when he told the story of the man who stopped at the roadside: not the one who had the best theory of neighbor-hood, but the one who was actually there.

The work of loving your city begins with knowing it. Not knowing about it — the demographics and the statistics and the economic profile — but knowing it the way you know a person: slowly, through presence, through repeated encounters that build the kind of familiarity where real conversation becomes possible. It begins with the question that Nehemiah asked when he arrived in Jerusalem: what is the actual condition of this place? Not what I assume the condition to be, but what I see when I stop performing activity long enough to look (Nehemiah 2:11-13).

In most American cities, what you will see when you look is a profound isolation. Neighbors who do not know each other. Communities fractured along economic lines that the church building often reinforces rather than crosses. People in genuine need with no relationship to any institution with the capacity to help. And in the midst of that, a congregation that has the theological resources, the community structure, and the social presence to be a genuine force for human flourishing — if it is willing to direct those resources outward rather than inward.

The mission field is not abstract. It is the homeless man outside your building who sees the congregation arrive and depart each Sunday without eye contact. It is the apartment complex three streets over where no one from the congregation has ever been. It is the school where the neighborhood's children spend their days, where the teachers are desperate for partners. It is the small business owner who serves the neighborhood but does not know a single person in the church. It is the family that moved in eight months ago and has not spoken to a neighbor.

These are not secondary mission concerns while the real work happens elsewhere. These are the first call.

Leslie Newbigin spent decades arguing that the local congregation is the hermeneutic of the gospel — the primary way the world encounters what the good news is [cite — confirm]. The congregation does not primarily demonstrate the gospel by what it says. It demonstrates the gospel by what it is: a community of people who love each other across lines the world does not cross, who serve the neighborhood without requiring payment, who are present when presence is costly. The argument is not verbal. It is enacted.

That enactment begins with the decision to be actually present to the place you are in. To know it. To serve it without requiring it to come to you. To seek its shalom with the same seriousness that Jeremiah instructed the exiles to seek Babylon's welfare — because in its welfare, you will find your own.

The exiles in Babylon did not choose Babylon. They were sent. Most of us did not choose our zip codes for missiological reasons. We went where the housing was affordable, where the schools were acceptable, where our people were. We were sent anyway. The sending is real regardless of the original intention.

Go where you are. Look at what is actually there. Begin with that.

The practical shape of this begins with something embarrassingly simple: learn the names of the people who live around your church building. Not as a program. Not as a canvassing strategy. As the basic human practice of knowing your neighbors, which the whole law and the prophets hang on (Matthew 22:39-40). Walk the blocks. Eat at the restaurants. Attend the community meetings. Read the local newspaper. Find out what the residents of the neighborhood think the neighborhood needs, and what they have already tried, and what they wish someone had offered ten years ago.

That listening — slow, patient, extending over months rather than launching in a campaign — is itself a form of witness. It says: we are here. We are not performing presence. We intend to stay. We are willing to be changed by what we learn. A congregation that has done this work for five years begins to understand its neighborhood in a way that no demographic survey can replicate, because it has developed actual relationships with actual people who have permitted the congregation into their actual lives.

The mission field is not abstract. It is the homeless man outside your building who sees the congregation arrive and depart each Sunday without eye contact. It is the apartment complex three streets over where no one from the congregation has ever been. It is the school where the neighborhood's children spend their days, where the teachers are desperate for partners. It is the small business owner who serves the neighborhood but does not know a single person in the church. It is the family that moved in eight months ago and has not spoken to a neighbor.

These are not secondary mission concerns while the real work happens elsewhere. These are the first call.

The exiles in Babylon did not choose Babylon. They were sent. Most of us did not choose our zip codes for missiological reasons. We went where the housing was affordable, where the schools were acceptable, where our people were. We were sent anyway. The sending is real regardless of the original intention.

The ends of the earth can wait. Jerusalem cannot.

There is a quiet tragedy playing out in too many pastors' homes. The congregation is growing. The ministry is bearing fruit. The pastor is present, attentive, and tender — to everyone but the person he married. He has become a wonderful shepherd to the flock and a stranger at his own table, and because the fruit at church is visible and the famine at home is private, no one intervenes until it is very late.

The lie underneath it is subtle, which is why good men believe it. The lie says the marriage is what you protect *so that* the ministry can flourish — that the home is the support structure for the real work happening at the church. Flip that and you will see the error. The marriage is not the scaffolding for the ministry. The marriage *is* a ministry — arguably the first one, the one with your name on it before any congregation existed, the one you will answer for when the platform is long gone.

Scripture is blunt here in a way we have learned to read past. When Paul lists the qualifications for an overseer, he does not start with charisma or giftedness. He starts at home — a man who manages his own household well, for "if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?" (1 Timothy 3:4–5). The home is not the offstage area. It is the proving ground and the first parish. A man failing quietly there has already failed at something the text treats as more basic than the pulpit.

I have served the lie. I have given the church the patient, present, listening version of myself and brought home the depleted remainder, and I have called the imbalance *sacrifice*, as though my wife were a line item the ministry could economize on. The hardest sentence to hear in that season was true and simple: the people at church got the husband she married, and she got the one the church was finished with. That is not a scheduling problem. It is a misplaced ministry.

---

The pattern has a history longer than any individual pastor's experience with it.

The Reformers, to their credit, pushed back against the clerical celibacy requirement and argued that marriage was a holy calling in its own right, not a concession to those who lacked the self-control for a higher vocation. Martin Luther's marriage to Katharina von Bora in 1525 was itself a theological statement: the home is not a lesser category than the monastery. [cite — confirm] But having recovered the dignity of marriage in principle, the Protestant tradition did not always honor it in practice. The pastor became a public figure whose household was a display case for the congregation's expectations, and the display case pressure created its own set of distortions. The pastor's wife became the congregation's unpaid associate, the pastor's children became exhibits in a case for family values, and the marriage itself became a platform rather than a covenant.

What was meant to be recovered as a holy thing became a performance. And performance, sustained over years, hollows out whatever it touches.

The American evangelical model deepened the problem. The rise of the celebrity pastor, the megachurch as a growth institution, the professionalization of ministry in the latter half of the twentieth century — these created a culture in which a pastor's success was measured in weekend attendance numbers and platform reach, and in which the emotional and relational labor of the pastoral calling was treated as endlessly renewable. The pastor was expected to be available, always. The congregation's needs were real, continuous, and urgent. The marriage's needs were real, continuous, and less visible. The institutional incentives rewarded one and invisibilized the other.

---

Here is what makes it so deceptive. The neglect of a marriage does not announce itself. There is no crisis on the Tuesday it begins. There is only a slow conversion of a spouse into a co-laborer, a teammate in the enterprise, a fellow manager of logistics — until the friendship that started it all has quietly become an operational partnership, efficient and loveless, and both people are too busy and too ashamed to name what has gone missing.

By the time it surfaces, years of small absences have hardened into a distance that feels like a fact rather than a choice.

The spouses of pastors know this pattern from the inside. The particular loneliness of being married to someone who is genuinely loved by many people and rarely fully present to you. The way a conversation gets interrupted by a text that is, genuinely, someone's crisis — and the way that interruption accumulates over years into a message about whose crisis matters. The way anniversaries get celebrated after the fact, vacations get cut short, evenings get surrendered to unexpected needs, and the person who absorbs all of this is expected to absorb it gracefully because ministry is a calling and sacrifice is what love does.

That is not marriage. That is an arrangement in which one party has agreed, without quite being asked, to bear the cost of the other's vocation.

---

The Ephesians 5 passage about marriage is typically read as a text about roles and submission, which is a way of reading it that keeps the hard parts at arm's length. But the actual argument Paul is making is stranger and more demanding than the role debate suggests. Husbands are called to love their wives as Christ loved the church — which is to say, sacrificially, with the kind of self-giving that is measured not by feelings but by cost. The husband who pours himself into the congregation and reserves the remainder for home has inverted the metaphor. He has given the institution the love that belongs to the covenant.

The Proverbs 31 portrait of a capable woman is often preached as a model for wives. It is also, read from the inside out, a portrait of someone whose husband "is known in the gates" (Proverbs 31:23) — someone whose public standing is partly built on what happens at home. The home is not incidental to the man's standing. It is the ground beneath it. The ancient wisdom tradition knew what the modern pastoral culture has forgotten: a man who tends his home tends something real, and a man who neglects it is building on sand regardless of what the platform looks like from the outside.

---

The steel-man objection deserves honest engagement here.

Ministry does require sacrifice. The people who need a pastor at 2 a.m. need one, and the pastor who is unavailable because he is protecting his personal time has misunderstood the calling. The seasons of a church's life are not always convenient. Church crises, pastoral emergencies, seasons of intense ministry demand — these are not invented by a congregation trying to extract labor from a professional. They are the reality of shepherding people through the most difficult moments of their lives. And there is genuine honor in the sacrifice.

This is true. And it does not resolve the problem.

The sacrifice that depletes the marriage is not the emergency response at 2 a.m. It is the pattern of fifty weeks of ordinary, low-grade unavailability — the evenings that go to administrative meetings that could be restructured, the Saturdays absorbed by ministry obligations that could be delegated, the mental and emotional bandwidth that the congregation receives first, every day, so that the person who shares the bed gets whatever is left. That is not the sacrifice of a particular emergency. That is the systematic underinvestment in a covenant relationship, and it produces the same result as any other sustained underinvestment: the thing quietly fails.

---

Tend the marriage as you tend the ministry. That means it gets your first and best hours sometimes — not only your leftovers — the unhurried attention you lavish on counselees aimed, for once, at the person you vowed it to. It means your spouse is not the unpaid associate pastor; she is the person whose flourishing is part of your actual calling, not a resource to be spent on it.

It means you guard the marriage from the church with the same vigilance you would guard the church from the world, because the threat to a pastor's marriage is rarely scandal. It is usually just the church — good, legitimate, never-ending church — crowding out the covenant that came first.

It means you have actual conversations rather than logistical check-ins. It means you know what she is carrying that has nothing to do with the ministry. It means you occasionally ask how she is doing — not how the family is managing, not how the kids are — but how she is, what she is afraid of, what she needs that she has not yet asked for because she has gotten good at not asking.

That question is a pastoral act. It is also the most ordinary act of marriage — the basic attentiveness that sustains a relationship across decades. The pastor who practices it at home and then speaks from the pulpit about the weight of covenant love is not performing a contradiction. He is testifying to something he actually knows.

---

There is grace here, not only warning.

A pastor who recovers his marriage does not lose his ministry; he gains its foundation. The congregation does not need a shepherd who sacrificed his home on its altar. It needs one whose home is a living argument that the gospel he preaches actually works — that covenant love holds, that presence is possible, that a man can be faithful in the room where it is hardest to fake.

Paul's first pastoral letter names the home as the proving ground for the public calling. The home is not the support structure for the real work. The home is where the real work is tested, and it is tested daily, in the ordinary, in the moments when nobody is watching and the sermon is finished and the man who preached it has to come back to someone who knows him completely.

That is where the ministry lives or dies.

Tend it. It had your name on it first. It will have it last.
